# SI Units & Thermodynamics SI units, gas law derivations, latent heat, specific heat capacity, and laws of thermodynamics Système International (SI) defines seven base units from which all other units are derived. In anaesthesia, the most commonly encountered derived units are the (pressure = N/m²), (energy = N·m), and (power = J/s). Temperature in gas calculations must always be in (K = °C + 273.15). 1 atmosphere = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg ≈ 1033 cmH₂O = 14.7 psi = 1.013 bar . (The cmH₂O equivalence comes from P = ρgh with ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².) Understanding these conversions is essential for interpreting arterial blood gases, ventilator settings, and gas cylinder pressures. The SI unit of pressure is the Pascal, though mmHg and cmH₂O remain in widespread clinical use. Celsius scale defines 0 °C as the freezing point and 100 °C as the boiling point of water at 1 atmosphere. The Fahrenheit scale sets water's freezing point at 32 °F and boiling at 212 °F. Conversions: °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32 °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9 . Normal body temperature (37 °C = 98.6 °F). Kelvin scale is the SI unit of temperature and is an — its zero point (0 K = −273.15 °C) represents the theoretical minimum where molecular motion ceases. The Kelvin scale has no negative values , which is why it must be used in all gas law calculations. Using Celsius in PV = nRT would give nonsensical results because a "doubling" of temperature from 10 °C to 20 °C is not a doubling of absolute temperature (283 K to 293 K is only a 3.5% increase). Why Kelvin matters for gas laws: Charles' law states V ∝ T (at constant P). If you plot volume against temperature in °C and extrapolate to zero volume, the line crosses the x-axis at −273.15 °C — this is absolute zero. A temperature-only illustration at fixed dry-gas pressure from 20 °C (293.15 K) to 37 °C (310.15 K) increases volume by approximately 5.8%; full BTPS spirometry correction additionally requires humidity and barometric-pressure adjustment. Quick Conversion Reference Celsius → Kelvin: K = °C + 273.15 (e.g., 37 °C = 310.15 K) Celsius → Fahrenheit: °F = (°C × 1.8) + 32 (e.g., 37 °C = 98.6 °F) Fahrenheit → Celsius: °C = (°F − 32) / 1.8 (e.g., 104 °F = 40 °C) Key landmarks: 0 °C = 273 K = 32 °F | 37 °C = 310 K = 98.6 °F | 100 °C = 373 K = 212 °F zeroth law of thermodynamics : the measuring device must reach thermal equilibrium with the tissue being measured. Core temperature is best reflected by the pulmonary artery catheter (gold standard), distal oesophageal probe (lower third, near the heart), and nasopharyngeal probe Peripheral sites (axillary, skin) are 0.5–1 °C lower than core. The core-peripheral gradient Thermometry Devices — Physical Principles Seebeck effect — voltage at junction of two dissimilar metals (copper–constantan). Fast, used in PA catheters Semiconductor whose resistance falls exponentially with temperature (NTC). Sensitive, used in oesophageal/rectal probes RTD (platinum): Resistance increases linearly with temperature. Very accurate laboratory standard — slower than thermistors Infrared tympanic: Detects IR radiation whose intensity is proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature (Stefan–Boltzmann law: j* = σT⁴); peak wavelength shifts with T per Wien's displacement law. Non-contact, <2 s, but accuracy affected by cerumen/positioning Liquid crystal: Cholesteric crystals change colour with T. Forehead strips — convenient but inaccurate (±1–2 °C) Perioperative temperature management: Hypothermia (<36 °C) prolongs neuromuscular blockade, reduces MAC, impairs platelet function, increases wound infection rates, and triggers shivering (↑VO₂ 200–400%). Applicable UK hypothermia guidance is NICE CG65 (2008, updated 2016); it remains active, not superseded by NG180. Induction generally waits until core temperature is ≥36.0 °C unless clinical urgency requires expedited surgery, for example bleeding or critical limb ischaemia Start active warming before surgery if temperature is below 36.0 °C, unless clinical urgency requires expedited surgery; if ≥36.0 °C, start at least 30 minutes before induction unless this delays emergency surgery. Maintain active warming intraoperatively. Measure and document temperature before induction and every 30 minutes to the end of surgery. Use forced-air warming from induction when anaesthesia lasts >30 minutes, or for shorter procedures in higher-risk patients; consider resistive warming if unsuitable. Set forced-air warming initially at maximum, then adjust to maintain ≥36.5 °C. Keep theatre ≥21 °C while the patient is exposed until active warming is established; cover adequately. Warm IV fluids of 500 mL or more and blood products to 37 °C; warm irrigation fluids in a controlled cabinet to 38–40 °C. In recovery, measure on arrival and every 15 minutes; do not arrange ward transfer until ≥36.0 °C. Use active forced-air warming if below 36.0 °C. On the ward measure on arrival and with routine 4-hourly observations; if below 36.0 °C, warm actively and measure at least every 30 minutes during warming. ideal gas equation PV = nRT (R = 8.314 J/mol/K) describes a hypothetical gas with no intermolecular forces and negligible molecular volume. All individual gas laws are special cases when certain variables are held constant: Boyle's law Charles' law (constant P, n → V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂), and Gay-Lussac's law (constant V, n → P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂). Avogadro's hypothesis states that equal volumes of all ideal gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain the same number of molecules (V ∝ n). Avogadro's constant (6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) is the number of elementary entities in one mole, and it follows that one mole of any ideal gas at STP occupies 22.4 L . Clinical example: a size E oxygen cylinder contains about 680 L of gas ≈ 30 mol (680 ÷ 22.4), so the available volume and duration at a given flow can be calculated from moles; the same logic underlies vaporiser output calculations Dalton's law (total pressure = sum of partial pressures) underpins the alveolar gas equation: PAO₂ = FiO₂(P − PH₂O) − PaCO₂/RQ. Henry's law (amount dissolved ∝ partial pressure × solubility) explains nitrogen narcosis, decompression sickness, and blood gas analysis. Real gases and the van der Waals equation molecules have negligible volume compared with the container, and (2) there are no intermolecular forces . At high pressures the molecules' own volume becomes significant, and at low temperatures (near liquefaction) attractive intermolecular (van der Waals) forces become significant. The van der Waals equation (P + a(n/V)²)(V − nb) = nRT , where the constant corrects the available volume for the finite size of the molecules. For one mole (n = 1), this reduces to (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT Critical Temperature and Pressure Critical temperature is the temperature above which a substance cannot be liquefied, no matter how much pressure is applied. Critical pressure is the pressure required to liquefy a substance at its critical temperature. Important critical temperatures are water 374 °C nitrous oxide 36.5 °C , and oxygen −118 °C liquid under pressure . Oxygen's critical temperature is far below room temperature, so oxygen is stored as a compressed gas. Its pressure falls progressively as gas is used, making the pressure gauge a useful estimate of contents in accordance with Boyle's law Specific heat capacity (c) is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K. Water has an exceptionally high c ( 4.18 kJ/kg/K ), providing thermal stability to the body (60% water) and making water an effective warming/cooling medium. Q = m × c × ΔT calculates the heat energy transferred. Latent heat is the energy required for a phase change at constant temperature. The latent heat of vaporisation of water ( 2260 kJ/kg ) is very large — evaporation is therefore extremely effective at cooling, explaining why evaporative loss is the dominant mechanism of intraoperative heat loss from exposed surgical surfaces, and why sweating is so effective. zeroth law establishes thermal equilibrium as transitive — if two systems are each in equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. This is the fundamental basis of temperature measurement. first law (conservation of energy: ΔU = Q − W) states energy cannot be created or destroyed. In an adiabatic expansion against a piston Joule–Thomson effect , is the temperature change seen when a gas undergoes expansion (throttling) through a valve or orifice with no work done and no heat exchange — the mechanism operating in cylinder pressure regulators and cryotherapy probes . The Joule-Thomson coefficient (μ is the change in temperature per unit change in pressure at constant enthalpy, and its sign determines the direction of the effect: most gases (except hydrogen and helium) have a positive μ at room temperature and cool on expansion , while hydrogen and helium have a negative μ and warm unless pre-cooled below their inversion temperature. Clinical applications and risks. carries high-pressure N₂O or CO₂ down a narrow tube to its tip, where the gas passes through a very small orifice (a throttle). The resulting rapid Joule–Thomson expansion produces intense local cooling, typically to about −70 °C , which freezes and destroys the target tissue. In a simplified first-law energy balance (ΔU = Q − W), negligible heat enters during rapid expansion and energy used in expansion is associated with a sharp temperature fall; more precisely, flow through the throttle is an process rather than piston work. This is the direct thermodynamic basis of cryotherapy . Opening a cylinder valve rapidly expands gas into the regulator, so ice can form on cylinder valves and regulators , potentially causing sticking or malfunction. The converse also matters: rapid compression of gas (for example when a cylinder valve is snapped open) generates intense heat, which can ignite oil or grease contaminants — the reason cylinder valves must be opened slowly and kept grease-free second law states heat flows spontaneously hot → cold and entropy of an isolated system always increases. This explains perioperative heat loss to the cold theatre via the four mechanisms of heat transfer: — heat transfer through direct physical contact, e.g. from the patient to a cold operating table; normally a small share (<5%). — heat carried away by the bulk movement of fluids (gases or liquids), e.g. theatre air currents (laminar flow) sweeping warmed air from the skin surface. — heat transfer via infrared electromagnetic waves, which requires no medium, e.g. an exposed patient radiating to cold theatre walls and equipment; usually the largest single mechanism. — heat lost as liquid turns to gas, drawing on the latent heat of vaporisation, from skin, the respiratory tract and open surgical wounds. radiation ≈ 40–60% convection ≈ 30% evaporation up to 20% , with conduction contributing only a small share; an older, widely-quoted breakdown from Sessler (Anesthesiology 2008) gives radiation ≈ 40%, convection ≈ 30%, evaporation ≈ 25% and conduction ≈ 5%. Under general anaesthesia these proportions change significantly as behavioural and autonomic responses are lost: radiation becomes the dominant mechanism, accounting for up to of heat loss, while convective and evaporative losses are comparatively smaller . Both data sets vary considerably with exposed surface area, ambient airflow, surgical irrigation and whether the patient is awake or anaesthetised. The third law Heat to warm 1 L of crystalloid from 20 °C to 37 °C Approximately 71 kJ. Each litre of 20 °C fluid effectively cools the patient by transferring this much heat away from them if not warmed. Temperature-only expansion — not full BTPS correction ≈4.23 L (an increase of ~5.8%), illustrating why temperatures in gas law calculations must always be converted to Kelvin. All other units are derived from these (e.g. pascal = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻², joule = kg·m²·s⁻²). State the first and second laws of thermodynamics with one anaesthetic example. First law — energy is conserved; ΔU = Q − W. Example: heat lost by patient (Q) = heat absorbed by cold IV fluids + heat lost by evaporation from open body cavity. Second law — entropy of an isolated system always increases; heat flows from hot to cold. Example: warming a patient requires an active energy input (forced-air warmer), it does not happen spontaneously. What is the triple point of water and why is it important? The triple point is the condition where solid, liquid and vapour water coexist (approximately 273.16 K and 611.657 Pa). Since 20 May 2019 the kelvin has been defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant k = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K exactly. The triple point of water is a practical calibration reference in ITS-90, not the current SI definition; the fractional triple-point definition is historical. The gas laws — all derivable from the ideal gas equation PV = nRT — have direct clinical applications from altitude physiology to anaesthetic vaporiser function. Thermodynamics governs heat transfer, phase changes, and energy conservation, with immediate relevance to perioperative temperature management, vaporiser physics, and cryotherapy.

# Mathematical Concepts Graph shapes, exponentials, logarithms, sigmoid curves and their physiological and pharmacokinetic applications First order Elimination rate is proportional to concentration, so a constant is removed per unit time. Half-life is constant. Concentration falls exponentially on an arithmetic plot and forms a straight line on a semi-log plot. Zero order The elimination pathway is saturated, so a constant is removed per unit time independently of concentration. Half-life is not constant and becomes shorter as concentration falls. The arithmetic concentration–time plot is linear; the semi-log plot is curved. Half-life, clearance and volume of distribution Volume of distribution (Vd) is the theoretical volume that would be required to contain the total amount of drug in the body at the same concentration as in plasma; a large Vd (e.g. amiodarone, digoxin) implies extensive tissue binding. Clearance (CL) is the volume of plasma irreversibly cleared of drug per unit time (e.g. mL/min), reflecting hepatic metabolism and renal excretion. The elimination rate constant links them: k = CL ÷ Vd t½ = 0.693 ÷ k , substitution gives t½ = (0.693 × Vd) ÷ CL . Half-life is therefore directly proportional to Vd and inversely proportional to clearance: a drug with a large Vd (more reservoir to empty) has a long half-life even with normal clearance, and halving clearance (renal failure) doubles the half-life at constant Vd. This is why changing half-life cannot be predicted from clearance alone sum of exponentials + B·e method of residuals (curve stripping): Plot log concentration against time and fit a straight line to the terminal linear portion (the β/elimination phase). that line back to the y-axis; its intercept is B and its slope is −β/2.303. At each early time point, subtract the extrapolated value from the measured value to give the residual. Plot the residuals on the same semi-log axes: they form a new straight line whose intercept is A and slope −α/2.303 — the distribution phase. Repeat once more if a rapid initial phase remains, as for a three-compartment model (π, α, β). log concentration extrapolated β line residual α line measured curve rate constants α and β (and hence the distribution and terminal half-lives), while the intercepts A and B allow the compartmental micro-rate constants, V₁ and clearance to be derived. This is how the classic propofol and thiopentone kinetic data — a rapid distribution phase followed by slower elimination — were originally characterised, and it explains why a single "half-life" is meaningless for such drugs : as substrate concentration rises, the reaction rate approaches a ceiling. The Michaelis-Menten equation × [C]) ÷ (K + [C]) (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of V . K is inversely related to the enzyme's for its substrate: a low K means high affinity (half-maximal rate reached at low concentration). Substrate concentration [C] Vmax (zero-order plateau) First-order: rate ∝ [C] ) the equation simplifies to Rate ≈ (V ) × [C] — rate is proportional to concentration, i.e. first-order kinetics . At high concentrations ([C] ≫ K ) it simplifies to Rate ≈ V zero-order kinetics . The graph therefore transitions smoothly from first-order to zero-order as enzymes saturate. Clinically this is the model for (small dose increments cause disproportionate rises in plasma level near saturation) and (saturated even at social doses, giving a constant elimination of roughly one unit per hour), as well as salicylates and thiopentone in overdose Categorical data are nominal (unordered groups, such as blood group) or ordinal (ordered categories, such as pain score). Numerical data are discrete counts or continuous measurements. The mean uses every value and suits approximately normal continuous data but is sensitive to outliers. The median is the middle ranked value and is preferred for skewed or ordinal data. The mode is the most frequent value and can describe categorical data. Spread and precision Variance is the mean squared deviation from the mean; SD is its square root. Population SD divides squared deviations by N, whereas sample SD divides by n − 1 to reduce bias when estimating the population. The IQR is Q3 − Q1 after ranking observations and spans the middle 50%, so it suits skewed data. SEM = sample SD/√n describes precision of the sample mean, not population variability. normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, with mean = median = mode; approximately 68% of observations lie within 1 SD, 95% within 1.96 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD of the mean. Positive skew has a long right tail and usually mean > median; negative skew has a long left tail and usually mean < median. A 95% confidence interval gives a range within which we are 95% confident that the true population parameter lies (strictly, 95% of intervals from repeated samples would contain it); its width communicates precision. For a difference between groups, a 95% CI that excludes zero corresponds to statistical significance at p < 0.05 in a two-sided test. For a ratio, the null value is 1 rather than zero t½ = τ × ln(2) = 0.693 × τ . The empirical Hill equation is fractional occupancy = [A]ⁿ/(K ⁿ + [A]ⁿ), where the Hill coefficient n is an index of cooperativity and curve steepness. When n > 1, binding is positively cooperative: one ligand increases affinity for the next (oxygen binding to haemoglobin; n ≈ 2.7). When n = 1, sites behave independently with no cooperativity (for example myoglobin or a simple drug–receptor interaction). When n < 1, binding is negatively cooperative: one ligand reduces affinity for subsequent ligand. The coefficient is not necessarily the number of binding sites ; it is an empirical summary of interaction. In pharmacology, plotting dose on a logarithmic axis converts the hyperbolic dose-response into its familiar sigmoid shape, with EC₅₀ at the midpoint. The central portion can be linearised using a probit or logit transformation Probit and logit transformations 'stretch' the y-axis of the sigmoid quantal dose-response curve, converting its central portion into a straight line. Linearisation allows simple linear regression ED₅₀ and ED₉₅ are read off accurately and the potency (position) and slope (variability of response) of different drugs compared statistically. Probit analysis assumes an underlying normal distribution of individual effective doses; the logit assumes a logistic distribution and gives almost identical results in practice Pre-oxygenation wash-in time End-tidal O₂ reaches ~95% after roughly one minute (3 time constants). The Association of Anaesthetists recommends pre-oxygenation for at least 3 minutes of tidal breathing, or until end-tidal O₂ exceeds 90% (Recommendations for standards of monitoring during anaesthesia and recovery 2021). The guideline itself is not framed in terms of time constants, but this calculation illustrates the safety margin it provides: 3 minutes extends well beyond the ~1 minute (3τ) needed for 95% wash-in, so the process is effectively complete (>5τ). Why a single time constant fails for remifentanil Equating CSHT to a first-order t½ is a fundamental pharmacokinetic error: remifentanil's offset is multi-exponential and its CSHT (~3–4 min) stays short only because rapid metabolism by non-specific esterases dominates redistribution. Use single-τ models only for genuine single-compartment processes such as nitrogen wash-out or capacitor discharge. Recognising the shape of a graph — linear, exponential, sigmoid, hyperbolic — allows you to predict how a system will behave when variables change. This topic covers the key mathematical relationships encountered in anaesthesia and intensive care, with clinical examples for each.

First order

Elimination rate is proportional to concentration, so a constant fraction is removed per unit time. Half-life is constant. Concentration falls exponentially on an arithmetic plot and forms a straight line on a semi-log plot.

Zero order

The elimination pathway is saturated, so a constant amount is removed per unit time independently of concentration. Half-life is not constant and becomes shorter as concentration falls. The arithmetic concentration–time plot is linear; the semi-log plot is curved.

Most drugs follow first-order kinetics at therapeutic concentrations; capacity-limited examples include ethanol, phenytoin at high concentrations and salicylate in overdose Half-life, clearance and volume of distribution

Volume of distribution (Vd) is the theoretical volume that would be required to contain the total amount of drug in the body at the same concentration as in plasma; a large Vd (e.g. amiodarone, digoxin) implies extensive tissue binding. # Gas Laws
Boyle's, Charles', Dalton's, Henry's laws and their clinical applications


Choose the system boundary before choosing an equation
“Expansion cools gas” is not a complete explanation. A closed mass of gas expanding against a piston, a steady stream crossing a regulator and gas left in an emptying cylinder are different systems. An adiabatic boundary means no heat exchange; it does not by itself specify constant enthalpy, constant entropy or any particular temperature change.
For a closed system doing expansion work with no heat transfer, the first law gives ΔU = −W. The familiar PVγ = constant and T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)
require the additional ideal-gas, constant-heat-capacity and reversible assumptions. A rapid real cylinder discharge is an open, transient process: mass and energy leave, heat can enter from the wall and the gas need not remain in a uniform equilibrium state. The reversible formula is a teaching comparison, not a validated prediction of cylinder surface temperature.
Why throttling conserves enthalpy rather than internal energy
For steady flow across an insulated valve, with no shaft work and negligible inlet-to-outlet kinetic and gravitational energy changes, the flow-energy balance reduces to h₁ = h₂. Enthalpy h = u + pv includes the work needed to move gas into and out of the control volume. Thus “no shaft work” does not mean that pressure-flow work has disappeared. Throttling is irreversible; constant enthalpy must not be confused with constant entropy.
For an ideal gas enthalpy depends only on temperature, so an isenthalpic pressure drop gives no temperature change. A real gas can cool or warm because enthalpy also depends on pressure through non-ideal molecular interactions. This distinguishes Joule–Thomson throttling from reversible adiabatic expansion, which can cool even an ideal gas.
The sign convention and the inversion curve
μJT = (∂T/∂P)h. In a pressure reduction, P₂ − P₁ is negative. A positive μJT therefore gives a negative temperature change; a negative coefficient gives warming. The coefficient depends on the initial state and changes along the path. The inversion condition μJT = 0 is a pressure–temperature curve, not one pressure-independent number for every use of a gas.
Calculated example, not a measured gas property:
if a hypothetical gas has an approximately constant μJT of +0.20 K/bar over a 10 bar pressure decrease, ΔT ≈ 0.20 × (−10) = −2 K. Using a quoted coefficient over a much larger pressure drop without checking its state dependence may be misleading. If condensation occurs, a single-phase linear calculation is insufficient.
Interpret cylinder and cryoprobe observations cautiously
At a regulator, assess the throttling process. In a cylinder containing liquid and vapour, withdrawal also drives evaporation and removes latent heat from the remaining contents and wall. In the remaining gas of a rapidly emptying cylinder, use an unsteady energy balance. These mechanisms can coexist, but they must not be collapsed into one “adiabatic” formula or one universal Joule–Thomson coefficient.
Frost depends on wall temperature, humidity, heat transfer and flow history; it is not a reliable quantitative contents gauge. Use the appropriate cylinder contents method. Likewise cryoprobe temperature depends on the working fluid, inlet conditions, heat exchanger, phase behaviour and tissue heat load, not merely the word “expansion.” The source establishes thermodynamic relationships, not a clinical device’s operating specification.
Learning check: does adiabatic always mean isentropic?
No. Reversible adiabatic change is isentropic. Irreversible adiabatic throttling instead conserves enthalpy under the stated steady-flow assumptions and generates entropy.

Worked clinical consequences
Decompression sickness.
At depth the ambient pressure is high, so PN₂ is high and proportionally more nitrogen dissolves in blood and tissues — fat and other lipid-rich tissues load slowly but hold most. On rapid ascent the ambient pressure and hence solubility fall faster than nitrogen can be carried to the lungs; the tissues become supersaturated and N₂ leaves solution as bubbles, causing joint and tissue damage ('the bends'), vascular occlusion, and pulmonary or neurological injury. Treatment is recompression with hyperbaric oxygen, which shrinks the bubbles (Boyle's law) and washes out nitrogen down a steep diffusion gradient.
Nitrogen narcosis.
The high inspired PN₂ at depth raises the dissolved nitrogen concentration in neuronal lipid membranes, producing a dose-dependent anaesthetic-like effect (impaired judgement and euphoria, typically from around 30 m) — the same partial-pressure logic that governs the potency of inhalational anaesthetics.
Oxygen toxicity.
At high FiO₂ or under hyperbaric conditions the raised PaO₂ increases dissolved oxygen, generating reactive oxygen species faster than antioxidant defences can handle. This causes pulmonary injury (tracheobronchitis then diffuse alveolar damage, the Lorrain Smith effect) and, at higher partial pressures, CNS toxicity with convulsions (the Paul Bert effect).
Volatile anaesthetic uptake.
The alveolar partial pressure of an agent determines the amount dissolved in blood (its blood:gas partition coefficient is a Henry's-law solubility constant) and hence the partial pressure delivered to the brain, which governs speed of onset and offset — agents with low blood solubility such as desflurane equilibrate fastest.

Adiabatic emptying of an O₂ cylinder
The reversible ideal-gas comparison gives 71.7 K (−201.5 °C), approximately 72 K (−201 °C). It does not predict a real cylinder’s final gas or surface temperature: mass outflow, irreversible processes, heat transfer and real-gas behaviour require separate consideration.
Frost line on an N₂O cylinder during heavy use
Evaporation removes latent heat from the contents and wall; regulator throttling is a separate process. Frost can indicate cooling but cannot reliably quantify remaining liquid. Assess N₂O contents by weight, not frost height or the pressure gauge while liquid remains.
Alveolar oxygen tension at altitude
PAO₂ ≈ 37 mmHg, well below the safe lower limit. Supplemental oxygen, hyperventilation, or descent are required.

> An <em>adiabatic</em> process exchanges no heat with the surroundings (Q = 0). For an ideal gas the first law gives ΔU = −W; the gas does work at the expense of its own internal energy, so its temperature falls. For a reversible adiabatic process: </p> <div className=

> When a real gas is forced through a porous plug, narrow valve or other restriction without doing external work and without heat exchange, the process is <strong>isenthalpic</strong> (H = constant). # Electricity & Magnetism Ohm's law, capacitance, inductance, transformers, and the Wheatstone bridge Changing flux, not simply the presence of current The primary winding produces magnetic flux in a shared core. A changing flux induces an electromotive force in each winding: its magnitude is N × |dΦ/dt|. Lenz’s law specifies the direction opposing the change. Because both windings link approximately the same flux, their induced voltages are proportional to their turns. This is mutual induction, not direct electrical conduction between windings. Steady DC produces no continuing change of flux and therefore no sustained secondary voltage. A brief switching transient is different from continuous transformer operation. Electronic power supplies can first switch DC into a rapidly changing waveform and then transform it. Applying steady DC directly to a winding designed for AC can cause excessive current and heating; “works with AC” describes the flux requirement, not a permission to improvise power connections. Turns ratio, current and power: an ideal model For an ideal transformer, Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ and VₚIₚ = VₛIₛ. A step-up therefore increases voltage but decreases available current for the same power; it does not create energy. A step-down does the reverse. The supply must provide the load power plus losses. Voltage ratio alone does not establish the permissible load, insulation rating or electrical safety. Calculated example: with an illustrative 10:1 primary-to-secondary turns ratio, a 230 V RMS input gives 23 V RMS ideally. A 46 W resistive load draws 2 A at the secondary and 0.2 A at the primary in the lossless model. These are calculations, not specifications of an anaesthetic machine or instructions for connecting equipment. Why real transformers heat and the loaded voltage changes Winding resistance dissipates I²R heat; this increases with load current. Changing flux also induces circulating eddy currents in the conducting core, which dissipate heat. Insulated laminations interrupt large current loops. Core magnetisation and imperfect coupling further limit the ideal model: leakage flux means not all primary flux links the secondary. Consequently efficiency is Pout/Pin, not exactly unity, and the output under load need not equal the simple turns-ratio prediction. Isolation is one layer of protection, not immunity from shock A separate-winding isolation transformer removes the intentional earth reference from its secondary circuit; an autotransformer with a shared winding does not provide this separation. In an isolated supply, a single contact to earth does not have the same return path as in an earth-referenced supply. Real equipment still has leakage paths. Contact between both secondary conductors can complete a dangerous circuit regardless of earth isolation. A first insulation fault can earth-reference the previously isolated system. A further contact or fault may then complete a current path. A line isolation monitor detects the potential for hazardous current to flow to earth; it is an alarm, not an overcurrent trip or proof that every connected device is safe. Do not ignore the alarm or disconnect life-support equipment indiscriminately: preserve patient support, identify newly connected suspect equipment and obtain trained technical assistance according to the local electrical-safety procedure. Microshock remains a separate concern: a conductive intracardiac pathway bypasses protective skin resistance. Isolation of the room supply does not replace device-specific patient isolation, suitable applied parts, protective-earth arrangements, inspection or maintenance. Theatre power-system rules vary by jurisdiction and location; the US teaching source here is not a universal UK installation standard. Learning check: can a 1:1 transformer make all shocks impossible? No. It can separate the secondary from the supply’s earth reference, but contact between both conductors, subsequent faults, leakage and intracardiac pathways remain relevant. The monitor warns of loss of isolation; it does not certify the connected equipment. UK mains supply is 230V AC at 50 Hz. The distinction between DC (constant direction, e.g., batteries) and AC (sinusoidal oscillation) is critical. Step-by-step reasoning
Recognise microshock: very small currents (>100 µA) reaching the myocardium directly via a conductive pathway can trigger VF — far below the macroshock threshold (100 mA)
The pacing wire bypasses the skin's high resistance, eliminating the safety margin of macroshock
Class CF (Cardiac Floating) equipment limits leakage to <10 µA single fault, <50 µA in fault conditions — mandatory for direct cardiac contact
Theatre supply uses an isolated (IT) system with line isolation monitor — single-fault tolerance, no large current return path
Equipotential earthing and regular electrical safety testing prevent leakage currents from summing across devices
Common traps
Class B / BF equipment is not safe for direct cardiac contact
RCDs protect against macroshock (mA range) but not microshock
Daisy-chained extension leads defeat isolated supply protection
The alarm signals a

The supply is deliberately
interrupted: power loss to bypass or ventilation would be more dangerous than the fault
Stop adding equipment; announce the alarm to the team so nobody plugs anything else in
Unplug devices in reverse order of connection — the last device that clears the alarm is the faulty one (here, most likely the newly connected warmer)
If the alarm persists with all mobile equipment unplugged, the fault is in fixed wiring: call estates, keep the patient insulated from earthed metalwork, and complete the case on the remaining safe sockets
Quarantine and label the faulty device, and report through incident and medical-device channels
Silencing the alarm and continuing — the single-fault safety margin has gone
Switching off the theatre supply reflexively during bypass
Using extension leads or multiway adaptors, which defeat isolated-supply protection

Isolation Transformer & Line Isolation Monitor (LIM)
Group 2 medical locations

isolated power system
. A 1:1 isolation transformer magnetically couples power to the theatre but removes the earth reference — both downstream conductors "float" relative to earth. Because no normal return path exists through earth, a patient or staff member touching a single live conductor cannot complete a circuit and no current flows through them.
Line Isolation Monitor (LIM)
continuously measures the impedance from each line to earth. A single insulation fault is detected and alarmed when the fault would permit a

automatically interrupted — abrupt loss of power to a ventilator or bypass pump may be more dangerous than the fault itself. Two simultaneous faults are required for a hazardous shock.

An RCD compares the live and neutral currents through a single toroidal current transformer; any imbalance > 30 mA triggers disconnection within 40 ms — fast enough to prevent ventricular fibrillation in most macroshock scenarios. RCD-protected earthed mains is the arrangement used in general clinical areas; in Group 2 locations this auto-disconnect is itself a hazard, so an isolated supply with insulation monitoring is required instead

Diathermy Hazards
Direct coupling
— the activated electrode touches, or arcs to, another conductor in the abdomen (a metal grasper, the laparoscope, a clip). Current passes through that instrument and burns whatever it is holding. Avoid activating while the tip touches other instruments or is outside the field of view.
Capacitative coupling
— an insulated active electrode passing through a metal cannula forms a capacitor (two conductors separated by a dielectric). High-frequency current is induced in the cannula even with intact insulation. If the metal cannula is anchored by a
tissue retainer the induced current has no low-resistance path to the abdominal wall, so it discharges at high current density into adjacent bowel. Use all-metal or all-plastic cannula systems, not hybrid combinations.
Insulation failure
— reusable instruments develop microscopic breaks in the shaft coating from repeated use, cleaning and sterilisation. Current escapes at the defect at high density, typically outside the visual field. Inspect shafts, use single-use or regularly integrity-tested instruments, and remember that higher voltage (coagulation/spray modes) is more likely to breach marginal insulation.
Active electrode monitoring (AEM)
— instruments with a second, earthed conductive shield surrounding the shaft continuously return any stray capacitative or insulation-failure current to the generator, which shuts down if leakage exceeds a threshold; this prevents both mechanisms.
— lowest effective power setting; short, intermittent activations; cut (low-voltage) rather than coag (high-voltage) mode where possible; never activate in open circuit or before the tip contacts the target; keep the whole active tip in view; prefer
or advanced-energy (ultrasonic, vessel-sealing) devices, which confine current between the jaws and avoid a return plate altogether
Theatre Environment — Humidity & Footwear
Why humidity matters
Theatre humidity is maintained at
50–60% relative humidity
(with temperature 20–22 °C).
At low humidity (< 40%), insulating surfaces (vinyl flooring, plastics, drapes, hair, clothing) accumulate
static charge
by triboelectric (friction-induced) charging.
Higher humidity allows a thin film of water on surfaces to act as a
conductive path
, continuously bleeding static charge to earth before it reaches a hazardous potential.
prevents spark formation
— historically critical to avoid ignition of ether/cyclopropane mixtures, but still relevant to: airway fires, alcohol-based skin prep ignition, microelectronic device damage, and patient micro-shock from static discharge to monitoring leads or intracardiac catheters.
Humidity also reduces
skin resistance
in sweating staff and patients — a trade-off that increases macroshock hazard slightly, but the dominant benefit is static dissipation.
Antistatic theatre footwear
Theatre clogs and overshoes are made of
antistatic (conductive) rubber
75 kΩ – 10 MΩ
This range is deliberately chosen as a
"Goldilocks" resistance
Low enough
continuously drain static charge
from the wearer to the conductive theatre floor (and on to earth) — preventing spark discharge.
High enough
limit current flow
if the wearer accidentally becomes part of a mains circuit — at 240 V across > 75 kΩ, current is limited to < 3 mA (well below the 15 mA let-go threshold and the 100 mA VF threshold).
Combined with a
conductive floor
(resistance 20 kΩ – 5 MΩ between two electrodes 60 cm apart), the staff member–shoe–floor system acts as a controlled, slow discharge path.
Pure rubber boots (very high resistance) would
protect against macroshock
but allow
static build-up
— and so are not used in theatre

Monophasic damped sinusoidal (MDS)
waveforms deliver current in a single direction. They require higher energies (up to 360 J for VF) and do not compensate for varying transthoracic impedance. They have been largely superseded by biphasic technology.
Biphasic waveforms

biphasic truncated exponential (BTE)
rectilinear biphasic (RLB)

impedance compensation
— the waveform automatically adjusts its duration and voltage based on measured transthoracic impedance, ensuring consistent current delivery regardless of patient characteristics.

Transcutaneous pacing
Apply anterolateral or anteroposterior multifunction pads, select demand mode and a rate around 60–80 min⁻¹, then increase current from about 50 mA until electrical and mechanical capture occurs (often 50–100 mA). Confirm a pulse for every paced complex; provide sedation and analgesia because skeletal-muscle contraction is painful. Limitations are discomfort, artefact and failure to capture.
Transvenous pacing
Insert via the internal jugular or subclavian vein and advance the electrode to the right-ventricular apex under fluoroscopy, intracavitary ECG or pressure-waveform guidance. A typical initial mode is VVI at 70 min⁻¹; set output above the measured capture threshold and sensitivity below the sensed R-wave amplitude. Complications include arrhythmia, failure to sense/capture, pneumothorax, cardiac perforation/tamponade, infection and venous thrombosis.
Transcutaneous pacing is a rapid bridge, not a substitute for prompt definitive planning when ongoing pacing is required
Pacemaker troubleshooting
Failure to capture
A pacing spike is not followed by a P wave or QRS complex. Check cables and lead position; correct ischaemia/electrolytes, increase output (mA), reposition if appropriate and arrange lead review.
Spikes occur despite intrinsic activity. Lead displacement, low-amplitude signals or an insensitive setting may be responsible. Check connections and increase sensitivity by reducing the mV value.
Failure to output
No spike appears despite a rate below the lower limit. Check power, connections and lead integrity; remove EMI causing oversensing and obtain generator support or replacement.

1. Preoperative assessment
Identify the device:
pacemaker, ICD, CRT-P/CRT-D, subcutaneous ICD, leadless pacemaker or implantable loop recorder. Use the patient's device card, chest radiograph and the last interrogation report; note manufacturer, model and implant indication.
within 12 months for a pacemaker and 6 months for an ICD/CRT-D (sooner if symptoms, recent implant <6 weeks, or generator near its elective replacement indicator)
Pacing dependence:
is there an underlying rhythm? Complete AV block, post-AV-node ablation and a persistently paced ECG mean any inhibition may cause asystole.
Programmed settings:
mode, lower rate limit, rate response, magnet response (device-specific — confirm from the manufacturer's chart), and ICD therapy zones.
Functional reserve:
underlying cardiomyopathy, ejection fraction, heart-failure symptoms, valve disease and anticoagulation all shape the anaesthetic technique far more than the device itself.
2. Deciding between magnet and reprogramming
No intervention needed
when EMI risk is low: surgery below the umbilicus with bipolar diathermy or no diathermy, and the patient is not pacing-dependent.
Magnet available and tested
is often enough for short procedures above the umbilicus: over a pacemaker it usually gives asynchronous pacing (DOO/VOO) at a fixed magnet rate; over an ICD it suspends anti-tachycardia therapy but does not change bradycardia pacing.
Formal reprogramming
is preferred when the patient is pacing-dependent and monopolar diathermy will be used above the umbilicus, when the magnet response is unknown/disabled, when the generator is inaccessible under drapes, or for procedures with prolonged EMI (TURP, transthoracic surgery, RF ablation, lithotripsy, MRI, radiotherapy fields).
Rate-response should be switched off
for procedures where ventilation, vibration, shivering or diathermy can be misread as activity (minute-ventilation and vibration sensors are the usual culprits).
3. Intraoperative conduct
External defibrillation/pacing pads applied and connected
any ICD therapy is suspended, positioned anteroposteriorly and at least 8 cm from the generator.
Continuous ECG
a mechanical monitor of perfusion — pulse oximeter plethysmograph or arterial line — because diathermy artefact makes the ECG uninterpretable at the moment risk is highest.
Bipolar diathermy first; if monopolar is unavoidable, use short bursts (<5 s) at the lowest effective power, with the return pad sited so the current vector does not cross the generator or leads.
Immediate access to atropine, adrenaline/isoprenaline, a magnet and an external pacing source; know how to convert to transcutaneous pacing quickly.
Avoid causes of spurious oversensing or arrhythmia: shivering, fasciculations from suxamethonium in a highly sensitive device, central line guidewires displacing recently implanted leads (avoid ipsilateral central access for 6 weeks after implant), and unnecessary hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia.
If the device is a CRT-D, remember that loss of biventricular pacing itself can precipitate decompensation, not merely bradycardia.
4. Recovery and postoperative care
Any suspended ICD therapy must be reactivated before the patient leaves a monitored area — this is a recognised never-event style hazard when handover is rushed. The patient stays on continuous ECG monitoring until therapies are restored.
Re-interrogate after reprogramming, after significant EMI exposure, after external defibrillation/cardioversion, and after any suspected device malfunction; document the restored settings.
Consider extended monitoring or overnight admission where interrogation cannot be completed on the day, particularly in pacing-dependent patients or those with an ICD.

What is the difference between monophasic and biphasic defibrillation?
Monophasic — current flows in one direction; 360 J for all shocks (older defibrillators). Biphasic — current reverses direction mid-shock, lowers myocardial damage and skin burns, higher first-shock success at lower energy (120–200 J device-specific). When is synchronised cardioversion indicated and why must the shock be synchronised?
For unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse (AF, atrial flutter, SVT, VT with pulse). Synchronisation delivers the shock on the R wave to avoid the vulnerable T wave period — an unsynchronised shock on the T wave can induce VF. Energy: AF 120–200 J biphasic, atrial flutter and SVT 70–120 J, VT 100 J starting.

# Pressure Measurement Transducers, manometers, and invasive monitoring principles The whole measurement chain has a dynamic response The fluid column, catheter, tubing, connections and transducer transmit a changing pressure signal. Their inertia, compliance and resistance form a system that can resonate or damp rapid changes. Static calibration alone cannot establish waveform fidelity. Natural frequency and damping must be considered together: one fixed frequency threshold or one damping coefficient does not guarantee accurate pressures at every heart rate and with every waveform. Underdamping amplifies oscillations: the upstroke may be unusually sharp, systolic pressure too high, diastolic too low and pulse pressure exaggerated. Overdamping blunts the trace, reducing systolic pressure, raising diastolic pressure and obscuring the notch. Mean pressure is often less affected than the extremes, but “less affected” does not mean always reliable. An incorrect zero or level, catheter obstruction or monitor-processing error can also distort the clinical interpretation. What the fast-flush test actually tells you A brief flush produces a square-wave perturbation; after release, inspect the return and any decaying oscillations. Ringing suggests inadequate damping; a slow return without discernible oscillations suggests excessive damping. Counting oscillations is a useful screen, not a universal pass/fail rule. The source describes evaluating both oscillation spacing and the amplitude ratio of successive waves against the system’s response characteristics. Calculated example: at a displayed sweep speed of 25 mm/s, successive peaks 5 mm apart represent a period of 0.20 s and an oscillation frequency of 5 Hz. At 1 mm separation the frequency is 25 Hz. These are calculations from a trace, not alternative “safe” thresholds. Screen rescaling, filtering and an unclear response can invalidate a simple measurement; use the monitor’s supported method. Troubleshoot methodically before changing treatment Check the patient: examine perfusion and the clinical context. Do not delay resuscitation while investigating a clearly deteriorating patient. Check reference and display: inspect level, zero, units, scale, cables and connections. Repeat assessment after a position change. Inspect the circuit: look for low flush pressure, bubbles, blood, loose/open connections and catheter or tubing kinks. Address these using the trained arterial-line procedure; do not force suspected clot into the patient. Assess the complete kit: retain approved short, non-compliant pressure tubing and avoid unnecessary stopcocks or extensions. Arbitrarily adding tubing to “fix” ringing changes both frequency and damping. repeat the trace and flush response, compare with a suitable cuff measurement and document unresolved disagreement. Consider catheter/site replacement or an approved damping device when appropriate. The source identifies these circuit and waveform checks; safe manipulation and escalation remain subject to local arterial-line procedures. Keep artefact separate from physiology A changed pulse contour may also reflect genuine changes in stroke volume, vascular tone or the arterial recording site. Peripheral amplification and radial–central differences are not necessarily equipment failures. Conversely a plausible mean number does not validate an implausibly wide pulse pressure. Describe the signal limitation in the handover rather than titrating treatment to an unverified systolic value. Learning check: can a preserved MAP validate a ringing trace? No. MAP may be less sensitive to dynamic distortion, but the systolic/diastolic values and contour can remain misleading; zero, level and the complete signal chain still require checking. >Troubleshoot methodically before changing treatment

Understanding the physics behind transducers, manometers, and invasive monitoring is essential for safe practice and FRCA examinations.

    Pressure = Force / Area. The SI unit is the Pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m². In clinical practice, pressures are commonly expressed in mmHg (arterial BP), cmH₂O (CVP, airway pressure), kPa (gas partial pressures), and bar (gas cylinders). Key conversions: 1 atm = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg = 1033 cmH₂O 1 kPa 7.5 mmHg = 10.2 cmH₂O = 0.01 bar 1 mmHg 0.133 kPa = 1.36 cmH₂O 1 cmH₂O 0.098 kPa = 0.74 mmHg 1 atm 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg = 1033 cmH₂O = 1.013 bar 1 bar 100 kPa ≈ 750 mmHg

    Pressure from a liquid column follows P = ρgh, so for a given pressure the column height needed is inversely proportional to the fluid >Worked example 1

    A ventilator shows a peak inspiratory pressure of 25 cmH₂O. What is this in mmHg?

    25 ÷ 1.36 ≈ 18 mmHg (or 25 × 0.74).

    Airway pressures are conventionally expressed in cmH₂O because the numbers are conveniently large — a legacy of the historical water manometer.

    Worked example 2

    A blood gas reports PaO₂ 12 kPa. What is this in mmHg?

    12 × 7.5 = 90 mmHg.

    Worked example 3

    CVP is reported as 8 mmHg. What is this in cmH₂O?

    8 × 1.36 ≈ 11 cmH₂O.

    These conversions are routinely tested in Primary FRCA MCQ/SBA and OSCE equipment stations. Mixing units — e.g. comparing a CVP reported in mmHg with an airway pressure in cmH₂O when estimating cerebral or abdominal perfusion pressure — is a classic error Clinical Application

    CVP was historically measured using a water manometer (cmH₂O). A 20 cmH₂O column equates to approximately 15 mmHg. Modern practice uses electronic transducers, but understanding the principle remains essential. Bourdon gauges remain ubiquitous on cylinder yokes and pipeline regulators.

    An aneroid gauge uses a sealed, evacuated flexible metal capsule or bellows. A rise in external pressure compresses it and a fall allows it to expand; springs, levers and gears amplify this displacement to move a pointer. Aneroid mechanisms are used in mechanical sphygmomanometers and barometers. A Bourdon gauge uses a C-shaped or coiled, flattened hollow metal tube of elliptical cross-section open to the pressure source. Rising internal pressure makes the cross-section more circular, forcing the tube to straighten; a lever-and-gear mechanism amplifies movement of the free end to turn a pointer over a calibrated dial. It reads gauge pressure (zero at atmospheric), spans cylinder pressures up to ~250 bar, and is used on cylinder yokes, pipeline gauges and regulators. Limitations: mechanical hysteresis and wear of the linkage, susceptibility to mechanical shock, a slow response that makes it unsuitable for dynamic waveforms, temperature-dependent tube elasticity, and the need for periodic recalibration; a ruptured tube is directed away from the operator by a blow-out disc Tiered management of raised ICP

      Interpretation and management

        Modern invasive pressure monitoring uses a Wheatstone bridge strain gauge transducer. A diaphragm deflects under pressure, changing the resistance of strain gauge elements arranged in a Wheatstone bridge circuit. The voltage change is amplified and displayed as a pressure waveform.

        The transducer must be zeroed (opened to atmosphere at the level of interest — typically the phlebostatic axis at the right atrium) and levelled. A 13 cm height error produces approximately 10 mmHg error.

        The arterial line system consists of an intra-arterial cannula, fluid-filled non-compliant tubing, a three-way tap, a flush device (300 mmHg pressure bag with heparinised saline delivering 3–4 ml/hr), and the transducer. The system must faithfully reproduce the arterial waveform.

        Waveform components and the cardiac cycle

          Abnormality Cause Large a waves Obstruction to RA emptying or reduced RV compliance — tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, RV hypertrophy Cannon (giant) a waves Atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve — complete AV dissociation/junctional rhythm, ventricular pacing Absent a waves Atrial fibrillation Large fused cv waves Tricuspid regurgitation Steep y descent (M/W trace) Constrictive pericarditis Blunted y descent Cardiac tamponade Paradoxical inspiratory rise in CVP — constrictive pericarditis

    Limitations as a measure of fluid responsiveness: CVP is a static pressure reflecting the interaction of venous return with RV function and compliance, confounded by PEEP, intra-abdominal pressure, valvular disease and vasomotor tone. Meta-analyses show no useful correlation between CVP (or ΔCVP) and fluid responsiveness, so it should not be used alone to guide fluid therapy. Dynamic indices — stroke volume variation and pulse pressure variation (requiring sinus rhythm, controlled ventilation with tidal volume ≥8 mL/kg, a closed chest and no significant arrhythmia), the passive leg raise with a flow measure, the end-expiratory occlusion test, and echocardiographic assessment are generally more informative. CVP remains useful as a marker of venous congestion (afterload on organ perfusion, e.g. renal) and as a safety limit Chamber Normal pressure RAP / CVP 2–6 mmHg RV 15–30 / 0–8 mmHg PAP 15–30 / 4–12 mmHg (mean 9–18 mmHg) PAOP (wedge) 2–15 mmHg

    PAOP approximates left atrial pressure and hence LVEDP, but this is valid only in West zone 3 lung, with no mitral valve disease and low airway/PEEP pressure; it is overestimated by mitral stenosis/regurgitation and by high airway pressure transmitted through the pulmonary vasculature.

    Derived variables: cardiac output and index (thermodilution), SVR = 80 × (MAP − CVP)/CO, PVR = 80 × (mean PAP − PAOP)/CO (normal ~50–150 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵), stroke volume, mixed venous saturation (SvO₂), and oxygen delivery/consumption.

It predicts the sensitivity of resistance to calibre and length; it does not promise an exact clinical flow ratio through every endotracheal tube, stenotic airway or rapidly infused cannula. Entrance effects, connectors, bends, pulsatility, gas compressibility and changing geometry can break the simple model. Calculated comparison: halve radius while holding pressure gradient, viscosity and length constant and the laminar-model flow falls to 1/16. If flow must instead remain constant, the required pressure gradient increases sixteenfold. These statements answer different questions. Real respiratory flow may include inertial and turbulent losses, so the result is a mechanism illustration, not a prediction of a patient’s minute ventilation. Reynolds number compares inertia with viscous effects Re = ρvd/η uses density, mean velocity, characteristic diameter and dynamic viscosity. It is dimensionless. Faster flow and greater density tend to increase inertial effects; greater viscosity tends to suppress disturbances. A number calculated for a straight laboratory tube does not locate the regime everywhere in a branching, deformable airway. Understanding laminar and turbulent flow, and the devices used to measure gas and liquid flow, is essential for anaesthetic equipment design and clinical practice.

Use the interactive diagram below to explore the differences between laminar and turbulent flow, including the velocity profiles and key equations governing each.

For laminar flow through a tube: Q = πΔPr⁴ / 8ηl, where Q = flow, ΔP = pressure gradient, r = radius, η = viscosity, l = length. Flow is proportional to the fourth power of radius — halving the radius reduces flow 16-fold.

Clinical Application

Under the equal-length laminar model, a 4.0 mm tube has 1/16 the flow of an 8.0 mm tube at the same driving pressure; this is not an exact prediction for real ETT flow. This illustrates why small tubes produce significant resistance and why even a small reduction in airway calibre (e.g., subglottic oedema) dramatically increases work of breathing.

Re = ρvd / η, where ρ = density, v = velocity, d = diameter, η = viscosity. Laminar flow occurs when Re < 2000; turbulent flow when Re > 4000. Between 2000–4000 is the transition zone. Turbulent flow has strongly density-dependent pressure losses, but viscosity remains relevant to the regime and transition. These thresholds describe idealised pipe flow, not every point in a branching airway A rotameter is a tapered glass tube with a bobbin. As flow increases, the bobbin rises. At low flows, the annular gap is narrow (tube-like) — flow is laminar and depends on viscosity. At high flows, the gap is wide (orifice-like) — flow is turbulent and depends on density.

Rotameters are calibrated for specific gases at specific temperatures and pressures, and are read at the top of the bobbin (ball floats read at centre). O₂ rotameter is placed downstream to prevent hypoxic mixtures if an upstream tube leaks.

Rotameter safety features

    Failure modes: dirt or static causing the bobbin to stick (read as a spuriously low flow), a cracked tube causing loss of gas into the room, and inaccuracy at altitude or in hyperbaric conditions (calibration is pressure- and density-dependent) For gas flowing through a constriction, raising the upstream pressure increases flow only until the gas velocity in the throat reaches the local speed of sound. Beyond this point flow is critical (choked) and cannot rise further, however much the downstream pressure is lowered This is reached when the absolute upstream pressure is roughly 1.9 times the downstream pressure for air or oxygen (approximately a 2:1 ratio) — the exact figure depends on the ratio of specific heats of the gas in question. Once flow in the throat is sonic, pressure-change information cannot propagate upstream against it, so the constriction becomes to downstream conditions and mass flow depends only on upstream pressure and temperature Clinical relevance

    Pneumotachograph: measures pressure drop across a known resistance (Fleisch — bundle of tubes; Lilly — fine mesh screen). Integrating flow over time gives volume — the basis of many ventilator spirometers.

    Pneumotachograph — principle and sources of error

    The resistive element is designed so that flow through it stays laminar; only then is the pressure drop directly proportional to flow (Hagen–Poiseuille). The Fleisch type uses many parallel fine-bore capillaries; the Lilly type uses one or more fine mesh screens, which are lighter and better suited to rapid respiratory waveforms Wright respirometer: a turbine vane flowmeter. Under-reads at low flows and over-reads at high flows. Measures expired tidal and minute volumes.

    Wright respirometer — mechanism and errors

    Gas entering tangential slots spins a lightweight flat vane; each rotation displaces a known volume, and a gear train drives a pointer over a dial calibrated in litres. It therefore measures volume by counting vane rotations, and minute volume is read over 60 seconds It measures volume by integrating flow, is unidirectional, and traditionally reads only expired volume; modern workstations have largely replaced it with heated pneumotachographs and hot-wire anemometers Hot-wire anemometer: a fine platinum wire is electrically heated and cooled by passing gas. The current needed to hold the wire at constant temperature is proportional to mass flow, giving a very fast response with no moving parts — but the wire is fragile and the reading depends on gas composition (thermal conductivity) and on water vapour deposition Ultrasonic flowmeter: paired transducers send pulses diagonally upstream and downstream. The transit-time difference is proportional to gas velocity, and multiplying by cross-sectional area gives flow. There are no moving parts, resistance is negligible, and the measurement is largely independent of gas composition, so it is used in modern ventilators and in vaporiser-free flow sensors Mass flowmeter: measures the mass rather than the volume of gas passing per unit time, so the reading is independent of temperature, pressure and (for Coriolis devices) composition. In a Coriolis meter gas passes through a vibrating tube; the mass flow generates a Coriolis force that twists the tube, and the resulting phase shift between inlet and outlet is proportional to mass flow. Thermal mass flow sensors use the heat carried away from a heated element.     Bottom line

    The Coandă effect is a favourite of FRCA Primary SAQs and Final structured orals because it links a single physics principle to several disparate clinical scenarios. Recognising the pattern — a jet, a nearby surface, asymmetric distribution — usually scores the mark.

    {/* Vignette 1 */}
    Endobronchial intubation suspicion

    A patient is ventilated with the ETT tip just above the carina. CXR shows preferential expansion of the right lung with a relatively collapsed left lung, despite the tube being above the carina. Auscultation confirms reduced breath sounds on the left.

    Why: The high-velocity inspiratory jet exiting the ETT bevel adheres to the right lateral tracheal wall (the right main bronchus is wider and more axial) and is preferentially deflected into the right main bronchus — Coandă-driven asymmetric ventilation without true endobronchial migration.

    Take-home: Asymmetric ventilation with a correctly positioned ETT may be Coandă-mediated. Reposition the bevel, consider a smaller-bore tube or change fresh gas flow to reduce jet velocity.

    {/* Vignette 2 */}
    Underestimated mitral regurgitation

    Pre-operative TTE in a patient for non-cardiac surgery shows a small, eccentric MR jet tracking along the lateral LA wall. The patient is in florid pulmonary oedema with a markedly dilated LA.

    Why: Eccentric, wall-hugging regurgitant jets entrain less surrounding blood and appear narrower on colour Doppler than free central jets of the same volume — the classic Coandă-related underestimation of severity.

    Take-home: A small wall-impinging jet can mask severe MR. Use PISA, vena contracta and indirect signs (LA size, pulmonary vein flow reversal) rather than jet area alone.

{/* Vignette 3 */}
Variable FiO₂ during high-frequency jet ventilation

During HFJV for rigid bronchoscopy, the measured FiO₂ at the carina swings unpredictably despite a constant driving pressure and entrainment fraction set on the ventilator.

Why: The jet leaving the injector hugs the tracheal wall (Coandă attachment), which alters the geometry available for room-air entrainment. Small changes in catheter position flip the jet from one wall to the other, changing the entrainment ratio and delivered FiO₂.

Take-home: Entrainment in jet ventilation is not as predictable as in a Venturi mask. Always measure delivered FiO₂ and watch SpO₂ closely.

{/* Vignette 4 */}
Bistable fluidic ventilator

An older transport ventilator with no moving parts cycles between inspiration and expiration solely from the gas supply pressure. How does it work?

Why: A jet enters a chamber with two symmetrical curved walls and attaches to one (Coandă). A small control jet at the opposite wall destabilises attachment, flipping the main jet to the other wall — a bistable fluidic switch. The oscillation drives the respiratory cycle.

Take-home: Coandă is the basis of fluidic logic — useful in MRI environments where moving / electrical parts are problematic.

{/* Vignette 5 */}
Asymmetric distribution at a Y-junction

A high-velocity infusion through a triple-lumen catheter, or rapid blood flow at an arterial bifurcation, distributes preferentially down one daughter limb even when the two limbs appear geometrically symmetric.

Why: Tiny asymmetries in the bifurcation cause the jet to attach to one wall; once attached, the low-pressure region locks it there. The branch that the jet receives a disproportionate share of flow.

Take-home: Mixing of drugs and contrast at high flow is not guaranteed to be uniform — relevant for vasoactive infusions co-running with carriers, and for selective angiographic injection.

# Temperature Measurement Thermocouples, thermistors, resistance thermometers, infrared tympanic thermometry Sensitivity, accuracy and response time are different properties Sensitivity is the change in electrical output per temperature change; accuracy describes agreement with the reference; response time describes how quickly a sensor follows a changing temperature. A high-sensitivity sensor may still be biased by placement or calibration. A fast sensor can track the wrong anatomical compartment precisely. Displaying two decimal places establishes resolution, not two-decimal-place clinical accuracy. A thermistor’s steep resistance–temperature relationship is useful across a limited range, but it requires nonlinear calibration. An RTD offers a different balance of stability, range and electrical sensitivity. Probe size, sheath, contact and surrounding fluid determine thermal response: no sensor family is invariably the “slowest” in every construction. NIST laboratory comparisons describe calibration performance, not bedside accuracy in every commercial probe. Separate electrical errors from site and lag errors Resistance sensors require an excitation current. Excess current produces I²R self-heating; lead resistance and readout calibration can add error. A thermocouple generates a voltage related to the junction-temperature difference and therefore needs a known or compensated reference junction. It is not exactly linear over every range, and a self-generating sensor does not mean the monitor requires no electrical power. The clinical measurement chain also includes the tissue–probe interface. Poor contact, incorrect insertion, nearby warming or cooling and insufficient equilibration can outweigh the sensor’s calibration uncertainty. During rapid cooling or rewarming, a delayed site can disagree with central temperature without either sensor being electronically defective. Record the site and method with the value. Choose a clinically suitable method, not an anatomical slogan NICE recommends either direct core measurement or a direct estimate of core temperature shown to be accurate within the stated tolerance. Site suitability depends on the device and clinical situation; local warming can affect even otherwise useful peripheral estimates. Do not assume an infrared ear-canal device directly measures tympanic-membrane temperature or is validated merely because the ear is near the brain. Distal oesophageal monitoring can be useful in an intubated patient when appropriately placed. Bladder readings depend on the clinical context and may lag changing central temperature. A pulmonary artery thermistor can provide a central reference when a catheter is already clinically indicated; the need for temperature monitoring alone does not justify inserting an invasive cardiac catheter. Make an unexpected temperature actionable Assess the patient and the trend rather than accepting or dismissing a single number. Confirm the sensor, compatible monitor, selected channel, site and placement; inspect for disconnection or a probe exposed to air. Review recent position, perfusion, fluid, irrigation and warming changes that can affect the reading. Allow appropriate equilibration or check with another clinically suitable method. Do not average incompatible sites to manufacture a “true” core temperature. Document persistent disagreement, the method used for treatment decisions and the required reassessment. This is a measurement-quality framework; the warming or fever investigation plan follows the patient’s clinical pathway, not the sensor specification alone. Learning check: is a highly sensitive thermistor necessarily accurate in vivo? No. Calibration, self-heating, placement, contact and thermal lag remain relevant. Laboratory sensitivity does not establish clinical agreement with core temperature.     Introduction

    Accurate temperature measurement is essential in anaesthesia and critical care. Hypothermia and hyperthermia profoundly affect pharmacokinetics, coagulation, and neurological outcome. Understanding the physics behind different thermometry devices is a core Primary FRCA topic and has direct clinical relevance for choosing the right monitoring site and device.

    Interactive Diagrams

    Thermocouple — The Seebeck Effect

    When two dissimilar metals (e.g., copper and constantan) are joined at a junction, a small voltage (EMF) is generated proportional to the temperature difference between the measuring junction (patient end) and the reference junction. This is the Seebeck effect. Type T (copper-constantan) thermocouples produce approximately 40 μV per °C.

    Advantages: Fastest response time (milliseconds), very small probe size, self-generating (no battery), wide temperature range (−200 to +400°C). Disadvantages: Very small EMF requires amplification; needs reference junction compensation (cold junction compensation).

    Thermocouple voltage represents T1 − T2, not T1 alone. In modern monitors the reference or “cold” junction is inside the monitor; a thermistor measures that internal temperature (T2), and the electronics add the equivalent reference-junction voltage to calculate patient temperature (T1). This electronic correction replaces the historical ice-bath reference Peltier and Thomson Effects

    Peltier effect is the converse of the Seebeck effect: passing a current through a junction of two dissimilar metals causes heat to be absorbed or liberated at that junction, depending on the direction of current flow. It is used for active heating/cooling — thermoelectric coolers, cold-junction compensation, and some blood/fluid warming and targeted temperature management devices Liquid Crystal Thermometers

    Disposable forehead strips contain microencapsulated cholesteryl ester liquid crystals. Temperature alters their ordered molecular structure and therefore the wavelength—and colour—of reflected light. They measure skin rather than core temperature, are influenced by ambient conditions and perfusion, and are suitable only for rough trends rather than anaesthetic or critical-care decisions Thermistor — Semiconductor Resistance

    A thermistor is a semiconductor (metal oxide bead) with a negative temperature coefficient (NTC) — its resistance falls exponentially as temperature rises. This gives it very high sensitivity (thousands of Ω per °C) but a markedly non-linear response requiring calibration or linearisation circuitry.

    Resistance is measured using a Wheatstone bridge circuit. Four resistors — R1, R2, R3 and Rx (the thermistor or RTD) — are arranged in a diamond, with an input voltage Vin applied across one pair of opposite corners and Vout measured across the other pair. The bridge is balanced when R1/R2 = R3/Rx, so Vout is zero; a change in temperature changes Rx, unbalancing the bridge and producing a Vout proportional to the resistance change Vout− Vout+

    Wheatstone bridge: balanced (Vout = 0) when R1/R2 = R3/Rx; Rx changing with temperature unbalances the bridge and generates a proportional Vout.

    Practical points: a null-deflection version adjusts a variable resistor until Vout is zero (most accurate, no current drawn), while a deflection version reads Vout directly (used for continuous monitoring). A second, identical thermistor in an adjacent arm can compensate for ambient temperature. Long lead resistance introduces error, mitigated by a three- or four-wire RTD connection. Self-heating is a key source of error: a current must pass through the thermistor to measure its resistance, and that current dissipates power (P = I²R) as heat, warming the bead slightly above the tissue it is measuring so it over-reads. It is minimised by keeping the excitation current very small Resistance Thermometer (RTD/Pt100)

    A resistance temperature detector uses a fine platinum wire coil wound around an insulating ceramic or glass core and protected within a probe sheath. Its resistance increases linearly with temperature — a positive temperature coefficient (PTC). The standard Pt100 has a resistance of 100Ω at 0°C, rising by 0.385Ω per °C.

    The relationship is described by: Rₜ = R₀(1 + αΔT) where α = 0.00385 Ω/Ω/°C. The linear response is its main advantage over the thermistor. However, it has lower sensitivity and response time depends on probe construction, thermal mass and contact rather than a universal ranking of sensor types Infrared Tympanic Thermometry

    All objects at temperatures above absolute zero emit infrared radiation. The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the power radiated is proportional to T⁴ (P = εσAT⁴). An IR tympanic thermometer uses a thermopile (multiple thermocouples in series) to detect the IR radiation emitted by the tympanic membrane.

    Proximity of the ear to the brain does not establish reliable core-temperature measurement for an infrared ear-canal device. The device may sample canal radiation rather than directly measure the tympanic membrane. Device validation and technique are essential; critically ill adults may show poor agreement with central measurements Clinical Temperature Monitoring Sites

    Core sites: PA catheter (gold standard), distal oesophagus (lower third), nasopharynx, tympanic membrane, bladder. Peripheral sites: Axilla, skin (forehead), rectal (delayed response).

    Brain temperature

    After traumatic brain injury, brain temperature is often higher than core temperature — on average about 1 °C, and by up to 2 °C or more in some patients. The gap is associated with worse outcome and changes with cerebral perfusion pressure and blood flow (a fall in CPP narrows it). Direct intraparenchymal probes (often combined with an ICP monitor) are the gold standard. Nasopharyngeal probes, near the hypothalamus and internal carotid supply, are the usual non-invasive surrogate, but they still read below injured-brain temperature; jugular bulb temperature reflects mixed cerebral venous blood and can underestimate regional brain temperature Zero-Heat-Flux Thermometry

    Principle: a dual-sensor forehead patch (e.g. 3M Bair Hugger temperature monitoring system) contains two thermistors separated by an insulating layer, plus a servo-controlled heating element.

    Mechanism: the heater warms the skin until the two thermistors read the same temperature, i.e. there is no temperature gradient and therefore zero heat flux between deep tissue and the skin surface. With heat loss abolished, the skin surface temperature equilibrates with, and so reports, the underlying deep-tissue (core) temperature. Equilibration takes a few minutes after application Fever Monitoring in ICU

    For a new fever in a critically ill adult, use a central measurement—PA-catheter, bladder-catheter or oesophageal thermistor—when already present or when precision will change diagnosis or treatment. Do not insert an invasive device solely to measure temperature. Without these devices, oral or rectal measurement is recommended. Axillary, tympanic, temporal artery and chemical dot thermometers are less reliable and should not be used for critical decisions when a better method is available. This differs from routine intraoperative practice, where distal oesophageal or nasopharyngeal probes are convenient continuous choices Accidental Hypothermia

Wet-and-dry bulb psychrometer:
one thermometer is dry and one is wrapped in a water-soaked wick. Evaporation removes latent heat and cools the wet bulb; a larger temperature difference means drier gas, and a psychrometric chart converts the pair of readings to relative humidity.
Regnault dew-point hygrometer:
cool a polished silvered surface until condensation first appears. At that dew point the adjacent gas is saturated, allowing absolute humidity to be read from saturated water-vapour data.
Hair hygrometer:
degreased organic fibres lengthen as humidity rises and mechanically move a pointer; it is simple but slow and requires calibration.
Electrical / capacitance hygrometer:
a parallel-plate capacitor whose hygroscopic dielectric (usually a thin polymer film) absorbs water vapour. Absorbed water raises the dielectric constant, so capacitance rises with humidity; the change is measured electronically (often as a shift in the resonant frequency of an oscillator circuit) and displayed directly as relative humidity. It is small, fast-responding and needs no moving parts, which is why it is the sensor used in anaesthetic machines and ICU ventilators. Resistance-based (electrolytic) variants work on the same absorption principle but measure a fall in resistance instead.
