# Ultrasound Physics Piezoelectric effect, frequency vs resolution, Doppler effect, artefacts Read a spectrum, not just its outer envelope Spectral Doppler displays the distribution of Doppler frequencies over time. After angle assumptions are applied, the vertical scale represents velocity; brightness represents signal strength at each frequency, not a direct count of red cells. The outer envelope traces the highest detected velocities. A relatively clear spectral window can occur when the sampled velocities are tightly grouped, but window appearance also depends on the sample volume and instrument settings. Spectral broadening: real velocity spread versus instrument effects Broadening means a wider range of frequencies at a given time, often filling the region between the envelope and baseline. A larger gate can include fast central flow and slower near-wall flow; disturbed or post-stenotic flow can also increase the velocity range. But finite beam geometry, the time scatterers spend in the beam, signal processing and noise can broaden the displayed spectrum even without pathological turbulence. Increasing gain can make weak signals and noise more conspicuous. Do not equate every filled window with stenosis or a particular percentage narrowing. Assess B-mode anatomy, gate position, beam alignment, reproducibility and a validated vascular-laboratory protocol. A spectrum from an oversized gate and one from a carefully positioned small gate are not directly interchangeable. The cited engineering review explains error mechanisms; it is not a current carotid-grading guideline. Aliasing is a sampling limit, not spectral broadening With pulsed-wave sampling, a Doppler frequency beyond half the pulse repetition frequency cannot be represented unambiguously and wraps across the display. Greater sample depth limits how rapidly pulses can be sent because echoes must return before the next pulse. Increase the scale/PRF where feasible, reduce depth when anatomically possible, use a lower transmitted frequency or use continuous-wave Doppler if depth localisation is no longer required. A baseline shift reallocates the available display range between positive and negative directions; it does not increase the underlying sampling rate or recover the true velocity from an ambiguous trace. Colour aliasing can help locate a high-shift region, but the colour map, scale and direction must be checked. Red and blue are configurable display conventions, not intrinsic markers of arteries and veins. Angle correction: mathematical precision cannot rescue poor alignment The Doppler equation gives v = cΔf/(2f₀cosθ). The correction cursor must describe actual flow direction, not automatically the vessel wall. Error is magnified as the angle approaches a right angle. For cardiac spectral measurements, align the beam as parallel to flow as possible; applying a vascular angle-correction convention is not a substitute for correct echocardiographic alignment. Calculated angle-error example: if the actual angle is 60° but 65° is entered, the estimated velocity is multiplied by cos60°/cos65° ≈ 1.18: about 18% too high, assuming the measured shift is otherwise correct. This illustrates error propagation, not a diagnostic tolerance. When anatomy and the spectrum disagree, reacquire rather than treating the corrected number as certain. A practical acquisition sequence Identify the anatomical target and whether depth specificity or the highest velocity is the clinical question. Optimise the acoustic window, align with flow and place the gate deliberately. Adjust scale, baseline, gain and filtering without removing real low-frequency signals or manufacturing window fill. Repeat the trace, document mode and location, and interpret it with the examination’s anatomical findings and limitations. Broadening, aliasing and angle error can coexist. Changing only one control does not prove that the final spectrum is free of all three. Learning check: does moving the baseline cure aliasing? It can display more of a predominantly one-directional signal, but it does not increase PRF. Persistent ambiguity requires a change in acquisition or Doppler mode. # MRI Physics Nuclear spin, precession, T1/T2 relaxation, MRI safety for anaesthetists hydrogen nuclei (¹H protons) , which are abundant in water and fat. Each proton has quantum spin (½) and acts as a tiny magnet. When placed in a strong external magnetic field (B₀), protons align either (low energy, spin-up) or (high energy, spin-down) to B₀. A slight excess align parallel, creating a small but detectable net magnetisation vector (M₀) along B₀. (wobbles like a gyroscope) around the B₀ axis at a frequency given by the Larmor equation: ω₀ = γ × B₀ . For hydrogen, γ = 42.58 MHz/T, giving a Larmor frequency of 63.87 MHz at 1.5T and 127.74 MHz at 3T. An RF pulse at exactly the Larmor frequency transfers energy to the protons (resonance), tipping M₀ away from B₀ into the transverse plane where it can be detected by receiver coils. T1 (spin-lattice/longitudinal) relaxation describes the recovery of magnetisation along B₀ as protons release energy to the surrounding lattice. T1 is the time for 63% recovery. Fat has a short T1 (efficient energy transfer) while water has a long T1 T2 (spin-spin/transverse) relaxation describes the loss of transverse magnetisation as protons lose phase coherence through interactions with neighbouring spins. T2 is the time to 37% remaining signal. 1/T2* = 1/T2 + γΔB₀ . A 180° pulse in a spin-echo sequence rephases the static field component and therefore measures true T2; gradient-echo sequences omit it and retain T2* susceptibility contrast. This makes GRE fast but sensitive to metal, air-tissue interfaces and blood products; susceptibility-weighted imaging exploits the effect to demonstrate deoxyhaemoglobin and haemosiderin Image weighting is controlled by TR (repetition time) and TE (echo time). T1-weighted images (short TR, short TE) show fat as bright and water as dark — best for anatomical detail. T2-weighted images (long TR, long TE) show water as bright and fat as dark — best for detecting pathology (oedema, inflammation, CSF). gradient coils explain how signal is localised in three dimensions. Three orthogonal coils (x, y, z) superimpose small, rapidly switched linear variations (a few mT/m) on B₀, so the Larmor frequency becomes a known function of position. Their switching against B₀ generates the Lorentz forces responsible for the characteristic acoustic noise (up to ~110 dB) that mandates hearing protection. Acoustic noise in more detail: current pulses switched through the gradient coils sit inside the static field B₀, so each pulse produces a Lorentz force on the coil windings. The coils flex and vibrate like a loudspeaker, giving the knocking noise. Sound levels often exceed 110 dBA on fast sequences, so hearing protection (ear plugs and/or ear defenders) is mandatory for the patient — including the anaesthetised patient — and for any staff staying in the scan room Peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS): Faraday's law , a rapidly changing magnetic field (high dB/dt) induces electric currents in conductive tissue. Above threshold these depolarise peripheral nerves, felt as twitching, tingling or tapping — usually over the trunk, shoulders or buttocks. It is more likely with high-performance gradients and fast sequences such as echoplanar imaging (diffusion, functional MRI). Scanners limit dB/dt by regulation; if it is uncomfortable, reassure the patient and the radiographer can change the sequence Slice selection — a gradient (conventionally z for axial slices) is applied the RF pulse, so only the slab whose precessional frequency matches the pulse's narrow bandwidth resonates. Slice thickness is set by the RF bandwidth and gradient steepness. Frequency encoding — a gradient applied along one in-plane axis during signal readout makes precessional frequency a map of position along that axis. Phase encoding — a brief gradient applied along the remaining axis before readout leaves spins with a position-dependent phase shift . It is stepped through many values (one per line of data), which is why phase encoding dominates acquisition time. , the raw matrix of spatial frequencies: central lines carry contrast and signal-to-noise, peripheral lines carry edge detail and resolution. A two-dimensional Fourier transform converts k-space into the final image. Understanding this explains practical anaesthetic points — scan time is driven by phase-encoding steps and repetitions, motion during acquisition corrupts whole k-space lines (ghosting), and even brief patient movement or a laryngospasm episode can force a complete sequence to be repeated Spin echo (SE) A 90° excitation followed by a 180° rephasing pulse corrects static-field dephasing, producing true T2 contrast with fewer susceptibility artefacts, but taking longer. Gradient recalled echo (GRE) Gradient reversal forms the echo without a 180° pulse. It is fast and T2*-weighted, making haemorrhage, haemosiderin, calcification and metal conspicuous. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery is T2-weighted with CSF nulled by an inversion pulse. Periventricular oedema, demyelination and subarachnoid pathology stand out against dark CSF. DWI with ADC Diffusion weighting detects restricted Brownian water motion. Acute cytotoxic oedema is bright on DWI and dark on the ADC map, often within minutes of ischaemic stroke. Susceptibility-weighted imaging combines T2*-weighted magnitude and phase data, making it exquisitely sensitive to paramagnetic blood products. It is used for diffuse axonal injury microbleeds after traumatic brain injury, cerebral cavernomas, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and to distinguish calcification from haemorrhage. four safety zones . Zone I (public), Zone II (screening/questionnaire), Zone III (controlled access, MR-trained personnel only), and Zone IV (the magnet room itself). Specific absorption rate (SAR) is RF energy absorbed per unit body mass (W/kg). It rises approximately with B₀² and also with flip angle, RF pulse number/duty cycle and patient size. In normal operating mode, the commonly quoted whole-body limit is 2 W/kg averaged over 6 minutes ; first-level controlled operation permits up to 4 W/kg averaged over 6 minutes under supervision. The scanner estimates SAR and can lengthen TR, reduce slices or reduce flip angle to remain within limits, prolonging the study. Two distinct mechanisms then generate X-rays:
Bremsstrahlung ('braking radiation')
— the dominant contributor. As an electron is decelerated and deflected by the field of a tungsten nucleus, the lost kinetic energy is emitted as a photon. This produces a
continuous spectrum

Characteristic radiation

line peaks

Four interactions matter clinically; the first two account for almost all relevant medical physics:
Photoelectric effect

— strongly favoured at low energies and high atomic number. This is what gives the bone–soft-tissue contrast on plain films and why iodinated and barium contrast (high Z) work.
Compton scattering
— the photon is partially absorbed by an outer-shell electron and scattered with reduced energy. Dominates above ~100 keV (CT, fluoroscopy primary beam) and is essentially independent of Z. Compton scattering is the source of the
scatter dose
to staff — the patient becomes the principal scatter source inside the room.
Rayleigh (coherent) scattering
— a minor process where the photon is deflected without losing energy. Contributes a small amount to image noise.
Pair production
— a photon (>1.022 MeV) interacts with a nucleus to create an electron–positron pair. Not relevant in diagnostic imaging but matters in radiotherapy and PET.

Filtered back-projection (FBP)
— the attenuation data from each projection are 'smeared' back across the image matrix. Simple back projection alone gives a blurred image with star artefacts, so the raw data are first passed through a mathematical filter/kernel that sharpens them before back projection — soft-tissue kernels favour low noise, bone/lung kernels favour spatial resolution at the cost of more noise
Iterative reconstruction (IR)
— an initial image estimate is forward-projected to create simulated raw data, compared against the measured data, and the image is repeatedly corrected over successive iterations (e.g. ASIR, IMR, and model-based IR that also models system optics and photon statistics). Lower image noise allows diagnostic images at a significantly lower radiation dose; the trade-offs are increased computation time and an altered, sometimes 'blotchy', image texture

Pitch < 1 overlaps the data — higher dose but better image quality and less helical artefact, used for high-resolution or cardiac work. On most modern scanners, however, tube current is modulated in real time to keep image noise constant, so dose does not simply fall as pitch rises

Iterative reconstruction

Activity (becquerel, Bq)
— disintegrations per second of a radionuclide source. Not directly relevant to X-ray equipment.
Absorbed dose (gray, Gy)
— energy deposited per unit mass of tissue (J/kg). A purely physical measurement.
Equivalent dose (sievert, Sv)
— absorbed dose ×
radiation weighting factor (wR)

Inverse-square law in the IR suite
Doubling the distance cuts dose-rate to ~30 µSv/h (a 4× drop); tripling it to ~13 µSv/h (a 9× drop). Distance is the most powerful single ALARA lever. Combine with a ceiling-suspended lead screen and a 0.5 mm Pb apron and you typically push residual whole-body dose well below 1 µSv/h.
Justifying a CT pulmonary angiogram in a young patient
Justify against the clinical question (a missed PE is high-cost), but in a young woman with a normal CXR and clinically suspected PE, V/Q is often the optimised first-line test. If CTPA is required, use low-dose protocols, dose modulation and lead breast shielding where local protocols allow. Document the discussion in the consent.
Pregnant anaesthetist on the IR list
Continued IR work is usually safe with the additional under-apron dosimeter, full PPE and screen use. Risk-assess monthly; remove from the rota only if doses approach the foetal limit or if procedures place her routinely close to the primary beam (e.g. pain procedures with hand exposure).
X-rays & Radiation Safety
X-ray production, photon–tissue interactions, dose units, and ALARA practice for anaesthetists
Diagnostic X-rays are produced by bombarding a tungsten anode with electrons accelerated across a high-voltage (typically 50–150 kVp) tube — output is a bremsstrahlung continuum plus characteristic K-shell line emissions
kVp controls beam energy (penetration/quality); mAs controls beam quantity (number of photons) — together they determine dose and image contrast
Four photon interactions: photoelectric (∝ Z³/E³, dominant at diagnostic energies, gives bone–soft-tissue contrast), Compton (dominant >100 keV, source of scatter), Rayleigh (minor coherent), pair production (>1.022 MeV only)
Units: activity = becquerel (Bq); absorbed dose = gray (Gy, J/kg); equivalent dose = sievert (Sv) = Gy × wR; effective dose = Sv × tissue weighting factors
ALARA = As Low As Reasonably Achievable. Three pillars: TIME (less exposure), DISTANCE (inverse-square law — doubling distance quarters dose), SHIELDING (0.5 mm Pb apron attenuates ~95% of scatter at 70 kVp)
IRR 2017 occupational limit: 20 mSv/year (avg over 5 years, max 50 mSv/year). Public: 1 mSv/year. Declared-pregnant worker: 1 mSv to the foetus over remainder of pregnancy
Stochastic effects (cancer, hereditary): no threshold, probability rises with dose. Deterministic effects (cataract, skin erythema, marrow suppression): have thresholds — ICRP 2011 lens threshold lowered to 0.5 Gy cumulative
Approximate effective doses: CXR 0.02 mSv · head CT 2 mSv · CTPA 5–10 mSv · abdomen CT 10 mSv · UK background 2.7 mSv/year
Anaesthetist's PPE for fluoroscopy: 0.5 mm Pb wrap-around apron, 0.5 mm thyroid shield, leaded glasses (cataract prevention), and where possible a ceiling-suspended lead screen — plus collar dosimeter outside apron

Step-by-step reasoning
Recognise the pattern: sudden ETCO₂ drop = reduced delivery of CO₂ to alveoli — circulation or circuit problem
Circuit: disconnection, sampling line leak, oesophageal intubation (usually no trace at all), kinked tube — inspect connections and waveform
Circulation: cardiac arrest, massive PE (including CO₂ embolism during laparoscopy), severe hypotension

Electrical safety
Shock pathways
passes through intact skin; harmful currents are in the milliampere range.
reaches myocardium through an intracardiac conductor, so currents of only tens of microamperes may trigger VF. Keep invasive cardiac conductors isolated and use CF-rated applied parts.
Equipment classes
Class I uses protective earth; Class II uses double/reinforced insulation; Class III is supplied at safety extra-low voltage. Type B applied parts provide basic protection, BF are electrically floating, and CF have the greatest leakage-current protection for direct cardiac application.
Supply protection
Fuses and circuit breakers interrupt overcurrent. Theatre isolated-power systems use an isolation transformer so the first earth fault does not stop supply; a line-isolation monitor alarms falling impedance so the fault can be found before a second fault completes a dangerous circuit.
For monopolar surgery, place the return electrode on clean, dry, well-perfused muscle with full contact and a short current path that avoids metal implants, ECG electrodes and implanted devices. Bipolar current remains between forceps tips and avoids a remote return plate. Inspect insulation and never rely on the return plate as an electrical earth.
Thresholds (mains 50 Hz)
Macroshock: ~1 mA is felt, ~10–15 mA causes muscle spasm with inability to let go, and ~100 mA can cause VF. Microshock: currents of about
100 µA
(some sources 50 µA) applied directly to the heart can cause VF. Leakage limits in normal use are therefore 100 µA for B/BF applied parts and
10 µA
for CF parts. Symbols: B is a figure on its own, BF a figure in a square, CF a heart in a square.
Equipotential bonding
All metal equipment and fittings in a cardiac or theatre area are connected by low-resistance conductors to a common earth point, so no two surfaces a patient or staff member can touch are at different voltages. This removes the potential difference that drives microshock currents.

Why vaporisers are FRCA bread-and-butter

Vaporisers convert a liquid volatile agent into a precisely metered vapour added to the fresh-gas flow. The exam tests three things repeatedly: the underlying physics (SVP, latent heat, partial pressure vs percentage), the splitting-ratio calculation, and the engineering of the Tec 6 (the only clinically used vaporiser that is not a variable bypass). Master those and the equipment viva looks after itself.

The Tec 6 — a different beast

  • Sealed reservoir of liquid desflurane heated electrically to 39 °C and pressurised to 2 atm.
  • At 39 °C and 2 atm, vapour pressure of desflurane is ~1.5 atm — always saturated, always above ambient.
  • A microprocessor reads dial position and fresh-gas flow, then opens a flow-control valve to inject measured pure vapour proportionally into the FGF — effectively a gas/vapour blender.
  • Requires mains power and time to warm up (~5–10 min) — clear visual alarms if power fails or warm-up incomplete.
  • Unlike a variable-bypass vaporiser, dialled percentage is held constant even at altitude — but, as with every vaporiser, the partial pressure delivered still falls with Patm.

Mapleson A
(Magill / Lack). During expiration, the first gas expelled (alveolar, high CO₂) leaves through the APL valve sited near the patient. The later expired gas (dead-space, low CO₂) refills the corrugated tubing. Fresh gas entering at the machine end displaces the dead-space gas back toward the patient at the next inspiration — so the patient re-inhales
CO₂-free dead-space gas.
5 L/min
0.5–1 L/min
. Mandatory monitors:
(hypoxic mixture risk as O₂ consumption approaches FGF),
inspired and expired agent
(CO₂ absorbent exhaustion). Keep FGF ≥ 2 L/min if you suspect desiccated soda lime to mitigate Compound A and CO production.
of efficiency between Mapleson A and D when you switch between spontaneous and controlled ventilation, and the chemistry of soda lime degradation (Compound A, carbon monoxide). The interactive simulator below makes the first fact visible; the schematic and tables make the second testable.
Mapleson B
inefficient for both spontaneous and controlled ventilation
: to prevent rebreathing it needs an FGF of about
2 × minute volume

Humphrey ADE and Aintree catheter
Humphrey ADE
combines Mapleson A, D and E functions in one coaxial system. In
A mode
, its lever routes expiration to an APL valve near the patient, so it behaves like a Lack circuit and is efficient for spontaneous ventilation. In
D/E mode
, that valve is isolated, the reservoir bag lies on the expiratory limb and fresh gas reaches the patient end, making it efficient for controlled ventilation. The mode can therefore change without replacing the circuit
Lever mechanism:
a lever on the metal block at the machine end directs gas either to the reservoir bag and APL valve (lever up —
) or to the ventilator port, bypassing bag and valve (lever down —
). Moving it re-routes expiratory gas; it does not change the tubing.
A mode (spontaneous):
behaves like a Lack (coaxial Mapleson A); efficient at FGF ≈ alveolar minute ventilation (around 50–70 mL/kg/min in adults)
D mode (controlled):
with a ventilator attached it behaves like a Bain (coaxial Mapleson D), efficient for IPPV.
E mode:
with low-resistance tubing and no bag in circuit, it acts as a T-piece (Mapleson E) — useful for children and spontaneous breathing with minimal resistance.
Why it was designed:
to give Mapleson A efficiency for spontaneous breathing and Mapleson D efficiency for IPPV in one device, avoiding a circuit change mid-case. A built-in safety valve limits pressure.
Aintree Intubation Catheter
is an airway-exchange catheter, not a Mapleson class. It is passed over a flexible bronchoscope through a suitable supraglottic airway, the SAD is removed, and a tracheal tube is railroaded over the catheter. Its 15 mm connector permits oxygen insufflation or connection to a breathing system, but gas egress must remain unobstructed to avoid barotrauma.
Work of breathing
. Mapleson systems have no absorber or unidirectional valves and are relatively low resistance; circle systems add valve, tubing and absorber resistance, worsened by small-bore components, wet filters or compacted granules. Excess FGF can oppose expiration and increase expiratory work. Low-resistance E/F circuits are therefore valuable in infants and in patients with limited ventilatory reserve, balanced against their high FGF requirement.

Inspiratory unidirectional valve
Inspiratory limb (corrugated, heated/humidified by absorber)
Y-piece at patient

APL valve (manual mode) / ventilator selector switch
CO₂ absorber (soda lime or Amsorb®) → reservoir bag → back to FGF inlet
Closed-circuit anaesthesia
begin with high FGF and a high inspired agent setting to denitrogenate the circuit and patient and rapidly approach the target end-tidal concentration.
reduce FGF in steps while tissue uptake remains high, replacing oxygen consumed and agent taken up.
in a true closed circuit, total FGF approximates metabolic uptake—about
200–300 mL/min
in a resting adult—so oxygen and agent delivery must track consumption continuously.
Agent may be supplied by measured liquid injection, a vaporiser-in-circuit, or a conventional out-of-circle vaporiser with brief setting/flow adjustments. The first two permit fine low-flow control; the last responds slowly because circuit volume buffers every change. Continuous inspired oxygen, inspired/expired agent, capnography, airway pressure and inspired/expired volume monitoring are mandatory.
Benefits are maximal gas and agent economy, less theatre pollution, and excellent heat and humidity conservation. Hazards are slow concentration changes, hypoxic-mixture or overdose drift, dependence on circuit integrity and absorbent function, and accumulation of nitrogen, methane, acetone and carbon monoxide. Periodic high-flow flushing removes unwanted gases but temporarily ends closed-circuit operation
Heat and humidity conservation
dry (0 mg H₂O/L) and at room temperature
. Normally the upper airway warms and saturates inspired gas so that by the carina it is at 32–34 °C with ~30 mg/L of water, reaching
37 °C and 44 mg/L (100 % relative humidity)
at the alveoli. A tracheal tube or supraglottic airway bypasses this air-conditioning function, so the burden falls on the lower airway or on the breathing system.
Consequences of dry, cold gas:
loss of the periciliary fluid layer with
impaired mucociliary clearance
, thick secretions, mucosal ulceration, atelectasis and sputum retention (important in long cases and in the ICU); loss of
latent heat of vaporisation
as the airway humidifies gas, plus convective loss, contributing perhaps 10 % of intra-operative heat loss and aggravating hypothermia with its coagulopathy, wound-infection and shivering consequences.
How a circle system conserves both:
exhaled gas is already warm and saturated and is returned to the patient, and the
soda lime reaction is exothermic
(CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O + heat), generating both heat and water of neutralisation. Inspired gas from a circle typically reaches ~28–32 °C with 20–30 mg/L of water after 20–30 minutes. The
lower the fresh gas flow, the greater the proportion of rebreathed, conditioned gas
— so low-flow (0.5–1 L/min) and closed-circuit anaesthesia give the best heat and humidity preservation, whereas high FGF or a non-rebreathing Mapleson system delivers essentially dry, cold gas
Added devices:
heat and moisture exchanger (HME)
is a passive hygroscopic/hydrophobic element at the patient end that traps expired heat and water and returns them on inspiration, achieving ~25–30 mg/L; it is cheap and simple but adds dead space and resistance and becomes less effective when wet or contaminated.
Active heated humidifiers
(hot-water bath with a heated wire circuit) deliver 37 °C and 44 mg/L, and are preferred for prolonged ventilation, paediatric practice, and where secretions are tenacious; risks are circuit condensation, scalding, extra dead space where a chamber is used, and microbial colonisation. Practical measures alongside these — warmed intravenous fluids, forced-air warming and a low fresh gas flow — matter more for whole-body temperature than the circuit alone
Breathing-system filters and HMEs
Electrostatic filters
attract charged particles; pleated hydrophobic filters combine interception, inertial impaction and diffusion. An
additionally retains expired heat and water in hygroscopic material and returns them during inspiration. At the patient Y-piece, one device protects the circuit and humidifies gas but adds apparatus dead space; at the machine end it protects equipment with less patient dead space but does not humidify the airway or isolate the whole circuit
Anaesthesia, anaesthetic machines and patient safety
builds on the Association of Anaesthetists
Checking anaesthetic equipment
guidance updated in
, which itself replaced the AAGBI 2012 version with a more pragmatic session-based check. Quote the current 2023/2024 documents, not the 2012 guidance. Together they deliberately widen the scope: the pre-use check is only one element of keeping patients safe around anaesthetic machines. Its recommendations cover the whole life-cycle of the workstation.
Pre-use checking.
A full structured check at the start of every session, following an upstream-to-downstream sequence (power and self-test → gas supplies and back-up cylinders → flowmeters and anti-hypoxia device → vapourisers → breathing system → ventilator, suction and scavenging → monitoring and alarms → airway equipment). The breathing system itself must be checked by the anaesthetist personally before every patient using the
two-bag test
, and an abbreviated check is repeated between cases and after any change to the configuration. Every check is
recorded and signed
for each machine, each session.
Equipment standards and procurement.
Machines should comply with current standards and be purchased, maintained and decommissioned under a documented departmental equipment-management programme, with scheduled servicing and electrical-safety testing.
Human factors and standardisation.
Workstation layout, gas connections, controls and monitors should be standardised within a department so that a familiar machine in one theatre behaves identically in another — reducing error when staff move between rooms or work out of hours.
Alarms and monitoring.
Capnography and airway-pressure alarms must be verified as functioning before use; alarm limits should be set appropriately and restored after temporary silencing, never permanently disabled.
An alternative oxygen supply (full cylinder) and a tested
self-inflating bag
— a means of ventilation entirely independent of the machine — must be immediately available at every location where anaesthesia is given, including remote sites.
Training and competence.
Every anaesthetist must be trained and demonstrably competent on the specific machine model in use, including its self-test, vaporiser mounting and ventilator modes; departments must provide that training for new equipment.

Mapleson classification (A–F) is defined by the geometry of fresh-gas inlet, reservoir bag and APL valve. Geometry determines whether dead-space gas or alveolar gas is preferentially vented during expiration — and therefore efficiency.
Mapleson A (Magill / Lack) — most efficient for spontaneous ventilation: FGF ≈ MV (≈ 70 mL/kg/min). Inefficient for IPPV (needs ≈ 3 × MV).
Mapleson D / Bain (coaxial D) — most efficient for IPPV: FGF ≈ MV (≈ 70 mL/kg/min in adults; 100 mL/kg/min often quoted to maintain normocapnia). Inefficient for spontaneous ventilation.
Mapleson E (Ayre's T-piece) and F (Jackson-Rees) — valveless, low resistance, designed for paediatric use. F adds an open-tailed bag for visual ventilation feedback. FGF ≈ 2–3 × MV.
Circle system — 7 components: FGF inlet, inspiratory unidirectional valve, expiratory unidirectional valve, Y-piece, APL valve, reservoir bag, CO₂ absorber. Unidirectional valves are the safety-critical components.
Low-flow anaesthesia (FGF 0.5–1 L/min) conserves agent, heat and humidity and reduces atmospheric pollution. Requires continuous FiO₂, agent, and capnography monitoring.
Soda lime: ~80 % Ca(OH)₂, ~4 % NaOH catalyst, ~1 % KOH, ~14 % water, silica hardener. Exothermic — absorbs heat and humidity into the inspiratory limb.
Compound A (nephrotoxic in rats) — sevoflurane + desiccated absorbent. Mitigate with FGF ≥ 2 L/min, fresh absorbent, and avoiding overnight FGF.
Carbon monoxide — desflurane (and other haloether agents) + desiccated KOH-containing absorbent (Baralyme, older soda lime). Amsorb® (Ca(OH)₂-only, no strong base) eliminates both CO and Compound A.
Pethick's test verifies coaxial inner tube integrity in a Bain circuit. Occlude patient end, fill bag with O₂ flush, release — functional circuits collapse the bag via Venturi entrainment past the inner tube.
Scavenging safety: 30 mm collecting connector (distinct from 22 mm/15 mm patient connectors), ±0.5 cmH₂O safety valves to prevent barotrauma or applied negative pressure if outflow occludes or active suction over-aspirates.
Pre-use check (Association of Anaesthetists / RCoA 2024, 'Anaesthesia, anaesthetic machines and patient safety'): a full structured check at the start of every session and after any change to the system, following an upstream-to-downstream sequence — machine self-test and power, gas supplies and back-up cylinders, flowmeters and anti-hypoxia device, vapouriser fill/seating and interlock, then the breathing system checked by the anaesthetist personally: visual inspection for correct configuration and patency, a two-bag test (reservoir bag on the machine end and a second bag at the patient end, occluded: APL closed to confirm no leak and correct pressure rise, then opened and the ventilator run to confirm bag movement and valve function), unidirectional valve movement, alternative oxygen supply and a working self-inflating bag immediately available, plus capnography and airway-pressure alarms confirmed. A signed, recorded checklist for each machine each session makes the check auditable; the 2024 guideline additionally covers machine procurement standards, workstation standardisation, servicing, alarm management and training.
Anaesthetic Breathing Systems
FRCA Primary / Final — Physics (Mapleson A–F, circle systems, low-flow anaesthesia)
Composition
Ca(OH)₂ ~80 %, NaOH ~4 % (catalyst), KOH ~1 % (older formulations), water ~14 %, silica hardener. Indicator dye (ethyl violet) turns blue when exhausted.
Reaction (exothermic)
CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃; H₂CO₃ + 2 NaOH → Na₂CO₃ + 2 H₂O + heat; Na₂CO₃ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + 2 NaOH (regenerated).
Compound A
Sevoflurane + desiccated absorbent → nephrotoxic in rats. Mitigate with FGF ≥ 2 L/min, fresh absorbent, no overnight FGF.
Carbon monoxide
Strong KOH/NaOH extracts hydrogen from the CHF₂ moiety of desflurane, enflurane or isoflurane, forming an unstable vinyl-halide intermediate that breaks down to carbon monoxide. The exothermic process accelerates with dryness, heat and strong-base concentration and is greatest after prolonged dry FGF, classically the first case after a weekend. Sevoflurane lacks CHF₂ and produces much less CO.
Absorbent comparison
Traditional soda lime contains Ca(OH)₂ plus NaOH/KOH catalysts and can generate heat, Compound A and CO when dry. Modern low-alkali soda lime removes KOH and reduces NaOH. Amsorb® uses Ca(OH)₂ with CaCl₂/CaSO₄, does not degrade volatile agents to Compound A or CO, but costs more and may exhaust more abruptly.
Lithium hydroxide
LiOH-based absorbents (e.g. Litholyme®) do not require water for CO₂ binding, have high absorption capacity per gram and do not generate Compound A or CO. They are lighter and remain safe when desiccated, but are generally more expensive and local compatibility/disposal guidance must be followed.
What fresh gas flow is required to prevent rebreathing in a Mapleson D / Bain circuit?
During spontaneous ventilation, FGF must equal 1.5–2 × minute volume (~150 mL/kg/min). During controlled ventilation (the efficient mode for Mapleson D), 70–100 mL/kg/min is sufficient. The Bain is a coaxial Mapleson D — fresh gas runs through the inner tube to the patient, exhaled gas returns via the outer tube; check inner-tube integrity with the Pethick test.
How does a circle system differ from a Mapleson circuit?
A circle system uses CO₂ absorber (soda lime) to scrub exhaled CO₂, allowing very low fresh gas flows (≤1 L/min — low-flow anaesthesia). Two unidirectional valves enforce flow direction, an APL valve releases excess gas, a reservoir bag dampens flow. Conserves heat, moisture and volatile agent; key risks are exhausted soda lime (colour change, rising FiCO₂) and degradation products (compound A with sevoflurane at very low flow).
What are the signs of exhausted soda lime?
Colour change of indicator (white → violet, or pink → white depending on brand), reduced thermal heat generation (cool to touch), rising inspired CO₂ on capnography, hard granules with cracked surface. Replace when 50–70 % colour-changed, do not wait until exhausted. Modern absorbers without strong alkali (lithium hydroxide, calcium hydroxide) reduce compound A and CO production from desflurane/sevoflurane.

Non-Invasive Ventilation NIV delivers positive pressure without a tracheal tube, principally CPAP or bilevel pressure support. Strong indications include acute hypercapnic COPD exacerbation and acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. An oronasal/full-face mask gives effective acute support but risks pressure injury, claustrophobia and aspiration. A nasal mask is more comfortable and permits speech but leaks through the mouth and is less suitable in severe acute failure. A helmet reduces facial pressure injury and may improve tolerance, but has large compliant internal volume, noise, CO₂ rebreathing and slower triggering/pressurisation. Ventilator and starting settings Dedicated NIV ventilators use single-limb intentional-leak circuits and superior compensation for large variable leaks, preserving trigger and cycling. Modern ICU ventilators use dual-limb circuits with an NIV algorithm and provide closer FiO₂ and monitoring. In COPD, a typical start is IPAP 10–12 and EPAP 4–5 cmH₂O; titrate pressure support to tidal volume, comfort and CO₂ clearance. Monitor response Reassess respiratory rate, accessory-muscle use, synchrony, conscious level, oxygenation, pH and PaCO₂ within 1–2 hours. Improving distress, falling respiratory rate and rising pH indicate success; worsening acidosis, hypoxaemia, agitation, exhaustion or GCS demands prompt intubation rather than prolonged NIV. Do not use NIV with respiratory arrest, fixed upper-airway obstruction, uncontrolled vomiting/inability to protect the airway, or major facial trauma preventing a seal. GCS <8, copious secretions, severe haemodynamic instability, recent upper-GI surgery and agitation are strong relative contraindications requiring expert review and an immediate intubation plan. Technical challenge: leak Leak in NIV is large and changes breath to breath. Unrecognised leak looks to the ventilator like patient inspiratory flow, causing ; in pressure support it also prevents inspiratory flow falling to the cycle-off threshold, so inspiration is prolonged (delayed cycling) . Sudden leak can drop pressure and miss efforts ( ineffective triggering ), and inspired volume differs from delivered volume. NIV software and settings NIV algorithms estimate leak continuously and re-set the baseline flow, so trigger and cycle criteria refer to patient flow rather than total flow. ICU ventilators without an NIV mode tolerate leak poorly. Practical adjustments: a less sensitive flow trigger if auto-triggering, a higher cycle-off percentage (e.g. 40–50 % of peak flow) or a maximum inspiratory time to stop prolonged inspiration in COPD, and a faster rise time for high respiratory drive. Interface choice — first choice in acute failure; less mouth leak, more dead space, claustrophobia and nasal-bridge sores. Total face — spreads pressure, useful when sores develop; larger dead space. Nasal mask / nasal pillows — comfortable, allow speech and coughing, minimal dead space, but mouth leak limits use in acute illness. — no facial pressure, but noisy, CO₂ rebreathing and slow pressurisation. Interface fit determines comfort and leak; continually reassess gas exchange, work of breathing, synchrony and need for intubation. Advanced / Non-conventional Modes Prolonged high airway pressure maintains recruitment, with brief pressure releases for CO₂ clearance and possible spontaneous breathing. Electrical diaphragm activity (Edi) triggers and proportions assistance, potentially improving synchrony. Pressure assistance varies in proportion to measured patient effort and estimated respiratory mechanics. These modes may help selected severe ARDS or refractory dyssynchrony, but evidence for improved patient-important outcomes remains limited. Ventilator Strategies in Specific Conditions Bronchopleural fistula Goal: minimise flow across the fistula and allow healing. Lowest effective PEEP, Vt 4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight, low respiratory rate, short inspiratory time, and permissive hypercapnia; pressure-controlled modes are usually preferred because they cap peak inspiratory pressure. Avoid excessive negative intrapleural suction, ensure an effective chest drain, and encourage spontaneous breathing where possible. Refractory major leaks: independent (double-lumen) lung ventilation, endobronchial valves or occlusion, high-frequency ventilation, or extracorporeal support. Acute brain injury Goal: avoid secondary injury by controlling ICP and preserving CPP. Target normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa / 35–45 mmHg) , avoid hypoxaemia and marked hyperoxaemia, use lung-protective settings (Vt 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, Pplat <30 cmH₂O), and apply PEEP cautiously with ICP monitoring since high PEEP can impede cerebral venous drainage. Permissive hypercapnia is avoided ; brief hyperventilation is reserved for impending herniation. Maintain MAP for CPP and head-up positioning. Severe obstructive disease (asthma / COPD) Goal: avoid dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP. Prolong expiration — low respiratory rate (10–14/min), I:E 1:3 to 1:4, higher inspiratory flow, low-to-moderate Vt (6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight) — and accept permissive hypercapnia with pH ≳7.20. Detect auto-PEEP with an expiratory hold manoeuvre (measured total PEEP above set PEEP) and by failure of expiratory flow to return to zero. Applied PEEP is kept low in asthma; in COPD, modest extrinsic PEEP can counterbalance intrinsic PEEP and improve triggering. Watch for hypotension and barotrauma from hyperinflation — if suspected, disconnect and allow full exhalation. Overarching principle In each case the physiological target (leak minimisation, normocapnia, expiratory time) dictates the settings; the named mode matters far less than the pressures, volumes and timing you actually deliver. Weaning readiness and the spontaneous breathing trial Screen daily: the underlying cause is improving, adequate oxygenation (PaO₂/FiO₂ > 150–200 on PEEP ≤ 5–8 and FiO₂ ≤ 0.4–0.5), haemodynamic stability with minimal vasopressor, adequate cough and conscious level, and no immediate plan for further surgery. Choosing a mode for ARDS with low compliance Why SIMV prolongs weaning PRVC paradox — air-hungry patient Every ventilator breath is defined by four phase variables: trigger (what starts the breath — time or patient effort), limit (what the breath cannot exceed during inspiration — flow, pressure or volume), cycle (what ends inspiration — time, volume or flow decay), and baseline (PEEP). AC/CMV: every breath, whether triggered by patient or timer, receives the same fully supported breath. Pressure-controlled AC delivers a square Pinsp with decelerating flow and variable Vt; volume-controlled AC delivers a fixed Vt with a constant or decelerating flow and variable Pinsp. SIMV delivers a fixed number of mandatory breaths per minute synchronised to patient effort; extra patient breaths between mandatory breaths are either unsupported or pressure-supported. SIMV prolongs weaning compared with PSV or T-piece (Brochard 1994, Esteban 1995) and is no longer recommended as a weaning mode. PSV: every breath is patient-triggered; the machine applies a set inspiratory pressure (above PEEP) and cycles to expiration when inspiratory flow falls to ~25 % of peak (flow-cycled). CPAP is the special case where pressure support = 0. PSV requires intact respiratory drive — apnoea backup is mandatory. PRVC (also VC+, AutoFlow, VG) is pressure-controlled in waveform but volume-targeted in feedback: the ventilator measures the previous breath's Vt and adjusts the next breath's Pinsp by ~75 % of the gap, within a clinician-set ceiling. Useful in changing compliance but penalises patient effort. Mode by waveform fingerprint: square Paw + decelerating flow = pressure-controlled (PCV-AC or PRVC); square flow + ramping Paw = VCV; small triggered breaths alternating with large supported breaths = SIMV + PS; flat PEEP with triggered Paw squares = PSV/CPAP. Lung-protective ventilation (ARDSnet): Vt 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, Pplat ≤ 30 cmH₂O, driving pressure ≤ 15 cmH₂O, PEEP titrated to FiO₂. Achievable in any mode that lets you control or measure Vt and Pplat — PRVC and VC-AC are the common defaults. Mechanical power (MP) is the energy the ventilator delivers to the respiratory system per minute (J/min). It joins the separate VILI risks — tidal volume, driving pressure, PEEP, respiratory rate and flow — in one number. Simplified volume-control formula: MP = 0.098 × RR × Vt (L) × (Ppeak − ½ × ΔP), where ΔP = Pplat − PEEP. There is no validated safe threshold (values above ~17 J/min have been linked with worse outcomes in observational data), but following its trend helps show whether a combined change in settings (e.g. lower Vt but higher RR) is actually less injurious. Weaning readiness: SBT on PSV 5–7 over PEEP 5 (or T-piece) for 30–120 min. Pass criteria — RSBI < 105, RR < 35, SpO₂ ≥ 90 % on FiO₂ ≤ 0.4, no haemodynamic instability, no agitation. RSBI = RR / Vt(L). Dyssynchrony — patterns and fixes

Dyssynchrony is common, increases work of breathing and ventilator exposure, and an Asynchrony Index (asynchronous events ÷ total respiratory cycles ×100) >10% is associated with longer ventilation and mortality. NIV algorithms estimate leak continuously and re-set the baseline flow, so trigger and cycle criteria refer to patient flow rather than total flow. ICU ventilators without an NIV mode tolerate leak poorly. Practical adjustments: a less sensitive flow trigger if auto-triggering, a higher cycle-off percentage (e.g. 40–50 % of peak flow) or a maximum inspiratory time to stop prolonged inspiration in COPD, and a faster rise time for high respiratory drive. Interface fit determines comfort and leak; continually reassess gas exchange, work of breathing, synchrony and need for intubation. These modes may help selected severe ARDS or refractory dyssynchrony, but evidence for improved patient-important outcomes remains limited. Screen daily: the underlying cause is improving, adequate oxygenation (PaO₂/FiO₂ > 150–200 on PEEP ≤ 5–8 and FiO₂ ≤ 0.4–0.5), haemodynamic stability with minimal vasopressor, adequate cough and conscious level, and no immediate plan for further surgery. Then run an SBT on PSV 5–7 cmH₂O over PEEP 5 (or a T-piece) for 30–120 minutes.

Waveform capnography is a core component of safe intubation protocols in critical care. A prospective multicentre study of an intubation management bundle reduced life-threatening complications from 34% to 21% and other complications from 21% to 9% Nasogastric tube placement confirmation

Standard time capnography plots CO₂ against time. Volumetric capnography (VCap, the single-breath test for CO₂) plots CO₂ against expired volume, so the area under the curve is the volume of CO₂ eliminated per breath (VCO₂) and dead space can be quantified rather than inferred

    Introduction

    Clinical measurement of haemodynamic parameters is fundamental to anaesthetic and critical care practice. Invasive arterial monitoring provides beat-to-beat blood pressure measurement and waveform analysis, while central venous pressure monitoring offers information about right heart filling and fluid status. Cardiac output measurement ranges from highly invasive (pulmonary artery catheter) to non-invasive (echocardiography, bioimpedance). Understanding the physics of transducer systems — particularly natural frequency and damping — is essential for accurate interpretation and is a core Primary FRCA topic.

    Interactive Diagrams

    Invasive Arterial Monitoring

    The arterial transducer system converts a pressure signal into an electrical signal using a strain gauge arranged in a Wheatstone bridge configuration. Pressure changes deflect a diaphragm, altering resistance in the strain gauge elements, which produces a proportional voltage change. The system requires stiff, short, wide-bore tubing (ideally <120 cm) filled with saline and free of air bubbles to maintain an adequate frequency response.

    The transducer must be zeroed (opened to atmosphere to set the reference point) and levelled to the phlebostatic axis — the level of the right atrium, approximated by the mid-axillary line at the 4th intercostal space. If the transducer is positioned below this level, hydrostatic pressure is added and readings are falsely high; if above, readings are falsely low. Approximately 1.3 cmH₂O (1 mmHg) error per centimetre of displacement.

    The arterial waveform shows systolic amplification in distal arteries — systolic pressure increases and diastolic pressure decreases as the waveform moves peripherally, due to wave reflection and decreased arterial compliance. Crucially, MAP is preserved and is the most reliable parameter for clinical decisions. The anacrotic notch is a small inflection on the ascending limb that marks aortic valve opening (before peak systolic pressure); the dicrotic notch on the descending limb corresponds to aortic valve closure Local or proximal thrombosis can cause distal ischaemia and necrosis; thrombus or air may embolise. Other complications include haemorrhage, haematoma, local infection or bacteraemia, accidental intra-arterial drug injection, adjacent nerve injury and pseudoaneurysm. Use asepsis, secure all ports and remove the cannula when no longer required. Natural Frequency & Damping

    The CVP waveform reflects right atrial pressure changes during the cardiac cycle. It comprises three positive waves (a, c, v) and two descents (x, y). The a wave represents atrial contraction (absent in AF; giant in tricuspid stenosis and pulmonary hypertension). The c wave is caused by tricuspid valve closure bulging into the atrium. The x descent represents atrial relaxation and descent of the tricuspid annulus during ventricular systole.

    The v wave occurs during passive atrial filling against the closed tricuspid valve (giant v waves indicate tricuspid regurgitation).     Physiological basis: pulse pressure variation (PPV) and stroke volume variation (SVV) arise from heart–lung interaction during positive-pressure ventilation. Each mechanical breath raises intrathoracic pressure, reducing venous return and right ventricular preload while transiently squeezing pulmonary blood into the left ventricle; a few beats later left ventricular stroke volume falls. The size of this cyclical swing depends on where both ventricles sit on the Frank–Starling curve Prerequisites and limitations

    • Fully controlled mechanical ventilation with no spontaneous effort (triggered breaths invalidate the swing).
    • Tidal volume ≥8 mL/kg predicted body weight; low tidal volumes under-read PPV.
    • Regular sinus rhythm — atrial fibrillation or frequent ectopics produce beat-to-beat variation unrelated to preload.
    • Closed chest and normal intra-abdominal pressure; open thorax and raised IAP distort transmission.
    • Unreliable in right ventricular failure, very high PEEP, low lung compliance and with vasoactive changes in tone.
    • Alternatives when prerequisites fail: passive leg raise, end-expiratory occlusion test or a 100–250 mL mini-fluid challenge with cardiac output monitoring.

The diagram below shows the absorption characteristics of oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin at the two wavelengths used by pulse oximetry.

A = εcl, where A = absorbance, ε = extinction coefficient (wavelength-specific), c = concentration, l = path length. Absorbance is logarithmic: A = log₁₀(I₀/I). The law assumes monochromatic light, dilute solutions, and no scattering — all assumptions that are violated to some degree in biological tissue.

Pulse oximetry measures SpO₂ by comparing absorption of red (660 nm) and infrared (940 nm) light. At 660 nm, deoxyHb absorbs more than oxyHb; at 940 nm the reverse is true. The isobestic point (~805 nm) is where both species absorb equally.

The oximeter derives SpO₂ from the ratio of ratios, R = (AC/DC)₆₆₀ / (AC/DC)₉₄₀. This is calculated in stages:

  • At each wavelength (red 660 nm and infrared 940 nm), the photodetector measures the total light transmitted through the tissue.
  • Each signal comprises a large steady DC component (absorption by tissue, bone, venous blood and non-pulsatile arterial blood) and a small pulsatile AC component (~1–5% of DC) produced by the cyclical influx of arterial blood with each heartbeat.
  • The microprocessor isolates the pulsatile component and computes the normalised pulsatile absorption at the red wavelength: AC₆₆₀ / DC₆₆₀.
  • It simultaneously computes the same ratio at the infrared wavelength: AC₉₄₀ / DC₉₄₀. Dividing AC by DC at each wavelength normalises for tissue thickness, skin tone and total haemoglobin, making the measurement largely independent of probe site.
  • The ratio of ratios is then calculated: R = (AC₆₆₀ / DC₆₆₀) / (AC₉₄₀ / DC₉₄₀).
  • This R value is mapped to a displayed SpO₂ via the device >Sources of Error

PCO₂ falls because room air contains almost no CO₂, and pH rises with it. PO₂ moves towards the air value (about 21 kPa at sea level): it rises in a hypoxaemic sample but falls in a sample from a patient breathing high oxygen. So "bubbles raise PO₂" is only true when the true PO₂ is below room-air level. Liquid heparin dilutes the sample. Dissolved CO₂ is diluted directly, so PCO₂ and calculated bicarbonate fall. Heparin also binds calcium, lowering ionised calcium. Pre-filled dry (lyophilised, calcium-balanced) heparin syringes avoid most of this. Delay and "leucocyte larceny" Cells in the syringe keep metabolising: PO₂ and glucose fall, PCO₂ and lactate rise, pH falls. The effect is much larger with very high white cell or platelet counts, which can make a well-oxygenated patient look hypoxaemic. Ice and plastic syringes cooling slows metabolism, but plastic is slightly permeable to oxygen and oxygen is more soluble when cold, so an iced plastic syringe can gain O₂ from the surrounding air. Analysing promptly at room temperature is usually better than icing a plastic syringe; follow the analyser manufacturer and local laboratory guidance on time limits. This paragraph is standard laboratory teaching, not part of the quotation above. What a venous gas can and cannot tell you The analyser measures whatever blood you give it, so the physics is identical. The difference is physiological: venous blood has already given up oxygen to the tissues, so venous PO₂ says nothing reliable about lung gas exchange. pH, bicarbonate, lactate and electrolytes are close enough to arterial values to be useful for trends and for screening acid–base disorders. Where venous samples add information From a central venous catheter, ScvO₂ reflects the balance of oxygen delivery and consumption, and the venous-to-arterial PCO₂ gap reflects how well blood flow clears CO₂ from the tissues. Both need a matched arterial sample to interpret. venous PCO₂ is normally slightly higher than arterial, so a normal venous PCO₂ makes significant arterial hypercapnia unlikely, but a high venous PCO₂ does not confirm it. When oxygenation or a precise PaCO₂ matters, take an arterial sample. How it works A heated sensor on the skin warms the capillary bed, increasing local blood flow and making the skin more permeable to gases. Gas diffusing through the skin reaches a miniature electrode underneath: a Clark-type electrode for PtcO₂ and a Severinghaus-type electrode for PtcCO₂. Newer sensors use optical methods instead. Why heating is a trade-off Heat "arterialises" the capillary blood, but it also raises local metabolism and shifts the gas readings, so devices apply a correction. Because the sensor is hot, its site must be moved regularly to avoid burns, which matters most in neonates with thin skin. The temperatures quoted above show how close the working range sits to the maximum tolerable level. PtcCO₂ tracks PaCO₂ well enough for trend monitoring (for example during sedation or non-invasive ventilation), while PtcO₂ falls away from PaO₂ in adults and when skin perfusion is poor, such as in shock. Confirm with an arterial sample when decisions depend on the exact value. Ion-selective electrodes Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ and ionised Ca²⁺ are measured potentiometrically: a membrane that lets through only one ion develops a voltage that follows the Nernst equation, read against a reference electrode with no current flowing. The blood gas analyser measures directly on undiluted whole blood, so it reports ion activity in plasma water. This avoids the falsely low sodium (pseudohyponatraemia) that diluted laboratory methods can give when protein or lipid levels are very high. Lactate and glucose: enzyme electrodes These are amperometric, like a Clark electrode. An enzyme layer (lactate oxidase or glucose oxidase) converts the analyte and produces hydrogen peroxide, which is oxidised at a polarised platinum anode. The current is proportional to concentration. because these sensors depend on enzyme reactions, some substances can interfere with them, and haemolysis falsely raises potassium. A blood gas potassium that disagrees with the laboratory value, in a sample that was hard to take, should be repeated before acting on it. The mechanisms in this lesson are standard clinical measurement teaching; the quotation only confirms that analysers measure these values. Why Monitor Depth of Anaesthesia?
NAP5 (2014)
5th National Audit Project. Incidence of accidental awareness during GA in the UK: 1:19,600 overall. Higher risk with TIVA (1:8,000) and NMB use. Recommended processed EEG monitoring for all TIVA cases.
NICE Guidance (2012)
Recommends considering EEG-based depth monitoring in patients receiving TIVA, at higher risk of awareness (e.g., emergency CS, cardiac surgery, trauma), or where clinical signs are unreliable.
Association of Anaesthetists Guidelines (2017)
Association of Anaesthetists: processed EEG should be used for all TIVA, considered when NMB used, and in high-risk cases. Monitor does NOT replace clinical vigilance — it is an adjunct.
Obstetric general anaesthesia
Awareness is relatively frequent during GA caesarean delivery (approximately 1 in 250–400), so it is treated as high risk. Hormonal change, expanded plasma volume and altered drug sensitivity may change baseline EEG responses; pre-eclampsia and other CNS pathology can further alter waveforms. No algorithm is specifically validated in pregnancy, so interpret pEEG with clinical and agent monitoring. An unexplained abrupt fall may also signal reduced cerebral perfusion during major haemorrhage, amniotic-fluid embolism or cardiovascular collapse.
Use in intensive care
Processed EEG can help titrate sedation, avoid over- and under-sedation and facilitate weaning; lighter ICU targets such as BIS/SE 60–80 are often used, but must complement sedation scales. Sepsis, encephalopathy, metabolic disturbance and temperature alter EEG, while shivering, movement, electrical noise and EMG cause artefact. Raw EEG remains necessary when non-convulsive status or post-arrest neurological assessment is suspected—an index alone is not prognostication.

Limitations & Artefacts
A sudden unexplained fall in BIS or Entropy can be a surrogate warning of
global cerebral hypoperfusion
: reduced oxygen delivery suppresses cerebral metabolism during major haemorrhage, amniotic-fluid embolism or cardiac arrest, sometimes before conventional monitors clearly deteriorate. First exclude a drug bolus, hypothermia, excessive hypnotic depth, poor signal and the fall caused when neuromuscular blockade removes EMG artefact.
B-Aware (2004)
BIS-guided anaesthesia reduced awareness by 82% in high-risk patients (NNT 138). First major RCT supporting processed EEG monitoring.
BAG-RECALL (2011)
BIS vs ETAG-guided anaesthesia: no difference in awareness rates in unselected surgical patients. Suggested BIS not superior to careful ETAG monitoring for volatile anaesthesia.
UK national audit: 1:19,600 awareness incidence. 1:8,000 with TIVA. Recommended processed EEG for all TIVA. Most awareness occurred during induction/emergence.
CODA (2019)
EEG-guided anaesthesia (targeting BIS >45) in elderly patients (>60 yr) did not significantly reduce postoperative delirium vs usual care. Challenged the hypothesis that depth monitoring prevents delirium.
ENGAGES (2019)
BIS-guided care vs usual care in elderly: no reduction in postoperative delirium. However, cumulative time at low BIS (<40) was independently associated with delirium.
Alpha anteriorisation
is the characteristic EEG signature of induction with GABAergic anaesthetics such as propofol and the volatile agents. In the awake, resting, eyes-closed state alpha power (8–13 Hz) is maximal over the
cortex. As consciousness is lost, alpha power shifts
, generated by thalamocortical loops that become hyper-synchronised, while occipital alpha disappears. The appearance of this coherent frontal alpha oscillation, usually with superimposed slow-delta activity, is a reliable marker of the transition to unconsciousness — more informative than any single index number. On a
density spectral array (DSA)
it is seen as a prominent warm-coloured (red) band at roughly 10 Hz appearing across the frontal channels at induction; its loss during maintenance suggests lightening, while its replacement by widespread slow-wave activity and burst suppression suggests excessive depth. Ketamine and dexmedetomidine produce different signatures — ketamine gives beta-gamma activity without frontal alpha, and dexmedetomidine gives spindles resembling non-REM sleep.
EEG patterns, anaesthetic depth and postoperative delirium
prolonged burst suppression
(any suppression ratio > 0) and sustained deep slow-wave activity with loss of frontal alpha — patterns seen when anaesthetic dose exceeds requirement. The
elderly and frail
, and patients with pre-existing cognitive impairment, are most at risk; their EEG shows lower alpha power and more suppression at any given agent concentration, so age-blind dosing reliably produces excessive depth. The proposed mechanism is anaesthetic disruption of thalamocortical and frontoparietal networks, producing persistent deficits in attention and executive function after emergence. The evidence must be qualified: the association between low BIS/burst suppression and delirium is consistent, but EEG-guided titration has not conclusively prevented it —
found no reduction in delirium with EEG-guided anaesthesia, and
similarly showed no benefit while confirming that cumulative time at low BIS was independently associated with delirium. Avoiding unnecessary depth remains rational practice rather than proven prophylaxis.
Auditory Evoked Potentials
Mid-latency auditory evoked potentials are recorded from scalp electrodes after repeated ear clicks. The A-Line ARX Index (AAI) runs from 0–100; approximately 15–25 is used for general anaesthesia. MLAEPs are less contaminated by EMG or neuromuscular blockade and may be less distorted by ketamine, but are less extensively validated than BIS, ambient noise can interfere and prolonged acoustic stimulation carries a theoretical auditory risk.
Clinical Practice Recommendations
Awareness is relatively frequent during GA caesarean delivery (approximately 1 in 250–400), so it is treated as high risk. Pregnancy physiology and urgent, deliberately light anaesthesia can confound interpretation; no algorithm is specifically obstetric-validated, but consensus supports processed EEG alongside clinical and agent monitoring. It may also reduce excessive agent use and speed recovery.
Strong indications

BIS target 40–60
for surgical anaesthesia. Values <40 associated with delirium (ENGAGES trial — but no mortality benefit).

The frequency below which 95% of total EEG power lies. Awake: 25–30 Hz. Adequate anaesthesia: 10–15 Hz. Deep anaesthesia: <8 Hz. Progressively decreases with increasing anaesthetic depth. Less susceptible to proprietary algorithm errors — a useful cross-check.
The frequency that divides the EEG power spectrum into two equal halves. Awake: ~12 Hz. Anaesthetised: 2–5 Hz. Similar trend to SEF95 but more affected by low-frequency artefact.
Percentage of time in the analysis epoch during which EEG amplitude is <0.5 µV (isoelectric). SR 0% = no suppression. SR 100% = completely flat trace. Any SR >0% indicates burst suppression — clinical action required (reduce anaesthetic). BIS reports SR over 63 seconds. Associated with postoperative delirium (CODA trial).
Pattern of alternating high-voltage bursts and isoelectric periods. Represents profound cortical depression. Can be caused by deep anaesthesia, hypothermia, severe cerebral injury, or metabolic derangement. All monitors detect it — BIS (SR%), Entropy (low SE), Narcotrend (stages E–F).
Visual time-frequency representation of EEG power. Colour-coded: typically blue = low power, red = high power. Shows evolution of EEG frequencies over time. Experienced users can identify anaesthetic transitions, artefact, and burst suppression at a glance. Available on most modern displays.
EMG Contamination
Frontalis muscle activity (shivering, pain, light anaesthesia) generates high-frequency signals that can falsely ELEVATE BIS/Entropy values. Neuromuscular blockade removes EMG but does NOT affect consciousness — BIS may paradoxically DROP when NMB given (removal of EMG artefact, not deeper anaesthesia).
Ketamine & N₂O
Ketamine causes dissociative anaesthesia with paradoxically high BIS values (>60) despite adequate anaesthesia — EEG shows beta activation. N₂O has minimal effect on BIS. These agents render processed EEG unreliable as a sole depth indicator.
Neurological Conditions
Pre-existing EEG abnormalities (epilepsy, dementia, encephalopathy, brain injury) alter baseline values and reduce reliability. Post-ictal suppression mimics deep anaesthesia. Brain death → BIS 0 with SR 100%.
Electrical Interference
Diathermy, pacing, warming devices, and forced-air warmers can generate artefact. Results in erratic or falsely high/low values. Check SQI — if <50%, value unreliable. Ensure good electrode contact and low impedance.
Age & Drug Interactions
Neonates and infants have different baseline EEG patterns. Elderly patients have greater brain sensitivity and altered pharmacokinetics, so lower propofol effect-site concentrations commonly achieve the same BIS/Entropy target of 40–60. The Marsh TCI model does not directly incorporate age; pEEG-guided titration is therefore especially useful to avoid overdose. Opioids alone cause minimal EEG change because pEEG primarily reflects hypnotic depth.
Volatile vs TIVA
All monitors perform better with TIVA (propofol) than volatile agents. Sevoflurane can cause paradoxical EEG excitation (epileptiform activity) especially at high concentrations → BIS may fluctuate unpredictably. End-tidal agent monitoring remains important for volatile anaesthesia.
No end-tidal agent to guide dosing. Risk of awareness is 5× higher with TIVA (NAP5). BIS/Entropy is the primary depth indicator alongside clinical signs.
Emergency surgery, cardiac surgery, caesarean section under GA, haemodynamically unstable patients where anaesthetic is deliberately limited, prior history of awareness.
Avoid sustained BIS <40 especially in elderly (association with delirium). Avoid BIS >60 with NMB (awareness risk). Use SQI and EMG to validate readings.
Any suppression ratio >0% = burst suppression. Reduce anaesthetic depth. Particularly important in the elderly. Suppression time >10% of total anaesthetic associated with worse outcomes.
Cross-reference with clinical signs (HR, BP, lacrimation, movement), ETAG (volatiles), plasma concentration estimates (TCI), SEF95, and raw EEG/spectrogram. The number is a guide, not a guarantee.
Depth of Anaesthesia Monitoring — When and How
Indications, devices, and target ranges for processed EEG.
What is the target BIS range for general anaesthesia and what is its evidence base?
BIS 40–60 corresponds to surgical anaesthesia. B-Aware and B-Unaware trials showed BIS-guided anaesthesia reduces awareness in high-risk patients (TIVA, paralysed, low-MAC techniques). NICE DG6 recommends DoA monitoring for TIVA and for any case where end-tidal volatile monitoring is unreliable. BIS values are derived from EEG but are not a direct EEG; they lag by 15–30 s.
How does processed EEG differ from raw EEG?
Raw EEG — continuous voltage trace, requires expert interpretation. Processed EEG (BIS, Entropy, Narcotrend) applies algorithms (frequency-domain analysis, burst-suppression detection) to produce a single dimensionless number (0–100). Newer monitors (e.g. Sedline) show colour-density spectrograms — clinically more informative than a number, especially in the elderly.
What are the limitations of BIS monitoring?
Unreliable with ketamine and nitrous oxide (BIS may remain high despite deep anaesthesia), with cerebral ischaemia/hypothermia (artificially low), with neuromuscular blockade absent (frontalis EMG inflates the value), and with paediatric brains <2 years. EMG artefact and electrocautery interfere. BIS does not abolish awareness — it reduces incidence but does not eliminate it.
