# Statistics & Evidence-Based Medicine
Study design, p-values, odds ratios, NNT, sensitivity/specificity, and common statistical tests


Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs)
are the gold standard for evaluating interventions. Randomisation minimises confounding; blinding reduces observer and participant bias.
: neither participant nor investigator knows allocation;
Cohort studies
follow exposed and unexposed groups forward (prospective) or look back (retrospective). They measure
and incidence.
Case-control studies
start with outcome (cases) and compare exposure history with controls — they measure the
odds ratio (OR)
but cannot directly calculate RR.
Cross-sectional studies
are snapshots that measure exposure and outcome simultaneously, so their key measure is
. They are quick and inexpensive, describe disease burden for service planning, and generate hypotheses. Because temporality is unknown they show association, not causation; selection and recall bias are common, and they perform poorly for rare or rapidly fatal disease.
Case reports
describe one patient with a rare condition, novel intervention or unexpected adverse event.
Case series
describe several patients sharing a condition or treatment and can identify common features of an emerging disease. Both are valuable for signal detection and hypothesis generation, but lack a control group, cannot estimate comparative risk or establish causality, and carry high selection and reporting bias.
Ecological studies
use population-level data and are prone to the ecological fallacy.
Systematic reviews
sit at the top of the hierarchy of evidence but are only as good as the included studies.
RCT variants
concurrent groups receive different treatments.
each patient receives each treatment, separated by washout; best for stable chronic disease without carry-over.
a 2×2 or larger design tests interventions and interaction efficiently.
Cluster randomised:
whole units (theatres, wards, hospitals) are randomised rather than individuals — practical for care-pathway interventions but requires analysis adjusted for the intracluster correlation.
designed to show the new treatment is better than comparator.
designed to show the two treatments differ by no more than a pre-specified margin in either direction.
tests whether a new treatment is not unacceptably worse than control by a pre-specified clinically acceptable margin — common in anaesthesia and critical care where a new agent offers practical advantages rather than greater efficacy.
Clinical trial phases
first-in-human safety, pharmacokinetics and dose-ranging, usually in few healthy volunteers.
preliminary efficacy, safety and dose selection in affected patients.
large comparative RCTs providing the main efficacy and safety evidence for approval.
post-marketing effectiveness, long-term safety and rare adverse effects.
null hypothesis (H₀)
states there is no difference between groups. The
alternative hypothesis (H₁)
states a difference exists. A
is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as observed, assuming H₀ is true. By convention, p < 0.05 is considered "statistically significant."
Type I error (α)
: rejecting a true null — false positive. The α level is conventionally 0.05.
Type II error (β)
: failing to reject a false null — false negative.
Power (1 − β)
: probability of detecting a true effect; aim for ≥0.8 (80%).
Confidence intervals (CIs)
express the precision of a sample estimate. Strictly: if the study were repeated many times, 95% of the resulting 95% CIs would contain the true population parameter — a single interval either does or does not, so CIs are not a direct probability statement about that interval. A 95% CI that does not cross the null value (0 for differences, 1 for ratios) corresponds to p < 0.05. CIs are more informative than p-values alone — they convey both magnitude and precision.
data type
(nominal, ordinal, interval/ratio) and the
shape of the distribution
. Each measure has a paired measure of spread that should be reported alongside it.
Categorical data
unordered labels such as blood group or sex; summarise with counts, proportions and mode.
ordered categories whose gaps are not necessarily equal, such as ASA grade or pain score; rank and summarise with median and IQR.
Numerical data
equal intervals but no true zero, such as °C; differences are meaningful, ratios are not.
equal intervals and a true zero, such as height, weight or heart rate; all arithmetic operations are meaningful.
values are counts;
values can take any value within a range.
Mean (x̄)
Σx / n
Best for:
symmetric, interval/ratio data (e.g. MAP, weight).
standard deviation (SD), variance, SEM.
middle value when ranked
skewed or ordinal data (e.g. ICU LOS, pain scores, Apgar).
interquartile range (IQR, Q1–Q3), range.
most frequent value
nominal data (e.g. blood group), categorical counts.
frequency table, proportions.
Choosing between them
Symmetric, normally distributed:
mean = median = mode → report mean (SD).
mean is dragged toward the tail → report median (IQR) and consider non-parametric tests.
a single mean can be misleading; report both modes and consider whether two sub-populations are present.
Categorical / nominal:
only the mode is meaningful (e.g. most common ASA grade).
Worked clinical examples
1. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) in a healthy preoperative cohort
mean ± SD →
MAP 92 ± 8 mmHg
the data are continuous, approximately normally distributed and free of meaningful outliers, so the mean is an unbiased central estimate and the SD captures variability efficiently. Use parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA) for between-group comparisons and quote a 95% CI for the mean.
2. ICU length of stay after emergency laparotomy
median (IQR) →
LOS 4 days (IQR 2–8)
LOS is positively skewed and bounded at zero — the mean is dragged up by a handful of long-stay outliers and overstates the "typical" experience. The median resists this; the IQR conveys the spread of the middle 50%. Use non-parametric tests (Mann–Whitney U for two groups, Kruskal–Wallis for three or more), or log-transform before a parametric test.
3. Postoperative pain score (NRS 0–10) at 24 h
11-point scale. In 80 day-case patients the most frequent score is 2 (n = 26), median is 3, IQR 2–5; only a few patients report ≥8.
median (IQR) — and the mode if you want to highlight the typical experience →
NRS 3 (IQR 2–5), mode 2
ordinal categories don't have equal arithmetic spacing, so the mean (e.g. 3.4) implies a precision the scale doesn't support. The median respects rank and the mode identifies the commonest response. Compare groups with non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank for paired, Mann–Whitney U for unpaired); for proportions above a clinical threshold (e.g. NRS ≥4) use χ² or Fisher's exact.
Key learning points
= Σx / n. Uses every value, so it is the most efficient summary for symmetric interval/ratio data — but is dragged toward outliers and the long tail of skewed data. Pair with
(or SEM for an estimate of the mean).
= the middle (50th centile) value when ranked. Robust to outliers and skew because it depends on rank, not magnitude. Pair with
IQR (Q1–Q3)
; it is the preferred summary for skewed or ordinal data.
= the most frequent value (peak of the distribution). The only valid measure for nominal categorical data, and useful for spotting bimodal datasets; unstable in small samples.
In a perfectly symmetric distribution:
mean = median = mode
. As skew increases, the mean moves furthest, the median shifts modestly, and the mode stays at the peak — the gap between them is itself a clue to skew.
Choose the summary that matches the data type and shape, then choose the corresponding test family: parametric (t-test/ANOVA) for mean ± SD on normal data; non-parametric (Mann–Whitney/Wilcoxon) for median (IQR) on skewed data.
spread (dispersion)
quantify this scatter and are essential for choosing reference ranges, statistical tests and clinical thresholds.
Range = max − min
quick descriptive summary; vital signs charts ("HR 60–110 bpm overnight").
Interquartile range (IQR)
IQR = Q3 − Q1 (middle 50% of data)
skewed or ordinal data — pair with median (e.g. ICU LOS, NRS pain).
Variance (s²)
s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1)
intermediate quantity — most often reported as its square root, the SD.
Standard deviation (SD)
SD = √s² (same units as the data)
symmetric interval/ratio data — pair with mean.
Standard error of the mean (SEM)
SEM = SD / √n
sample mean
, not the spread of individuals. Shrinks as the sample grows and forms the basis of the 95% CI (≈ x̄ ± 1.96 × SEM). Reporting "mean ± SEM" makes data look tighter than it is — usually inappropriate as a descriptive statistic.
precision of an estimate; building confidence intervals.
Coefficient of variation (CV)
CV = SD / mean × 100%
comparing variability across units; lab assay quality control.
Quick reference — match the spread to the centre
Data shape
Test family
Symmetric / normal
SD (and 95% CI for the mean)
Parametric (t-test, ANOVA)
Skewed / ordinal
IQR (Q1–Q3); range
Non-parametric (Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis)
Nominal / categorical
Frequency table, proportions
χ², Fisher exact
— calculated from ranked values; robust to skew.
— calculated from deviations around the mean; assume meaningful arithmetic on the values.
describes individuals;
describes the precision of the mean (SEM = SD/√n).
Always report a measure of spread alongside the centre — a mean or median in isolation hides clinically important variability.
normal (Gaussian) distribution
is a symmetrical, bell-shaped probability density curve defined entirely by its mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ). Many biological variables — height, blood pressure, haemoglobin, sample means under the central limit theorem — approximate this shape, which is why it underpins most parametric statistics.
empirical 68–95–99.7 rule
states that ±1σ contains ~68% of values, ±2σ ~95% and ±3σ ~99.7%. The same geometry generates
confidence intervals
: a 95% CI is the mean ± 1.96 × standard error — the central band that would capture the true population mean in 95 of 100 repeated samples. Use the toggle to compare 90%, 95% and 99% intervals; wider intervals trade precision for greater confidence.
Worked example
Calculating a 95% confidence interval
42 s
in 64 patients, with a standard deviation of
8 s
. Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the mean and interpret it.
SE = SD / √n = 8 / √64 = 8 / 8 = 1.0 s
95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SE = 42 ± 1.96 × 1.0
= 42 ± 1.96 s → 40.04 s to 43.96 s
42 s (95% CI 40.0–44.0 s)
include a clinically meaningful comparator (e.g. propofol's typical 30 s), the new agent is unlikely to be non-inferior on speed of onset.
Confidence interval vs standard deviation
describes the
spread of individual values
in the sample. The
95% CI of the mean
precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean
. Crucially, the CI shrinks as the sample grows (because SE = SD/√n), whereas the SD does not — adding patients makes you more certain about the average, not less variable as individuals.
Standard error (SE) — the bridge between SD and CI
standard error of the mean
is the standard deviation of the
sampling distribution of the mean
: if you repeated the study many times, the sample means would themselves scatter around the true population mean, and that scatter has SD equal to the SE.
SE = SD / √n
measures variability between
— a property of the data, roughly stable as n grows.
measures variability of the
— a property of the estimate, shrinks with √n.
95% CI
is built directly from SE:
x̄ ± 1.96 × SE
. So SE is literally the "half-width unit" of the CI.
Quick example.
SD = 8 s, n = 64 → SE = 8/√64 =
1.0 s
; 95% CI ≈ mean ± 1.96 s. Quadruple the sample to n = 256 and SE halves to 0.5 s, halving the CI width — but the SD still describes 8 s of between-patient variability.
95% confidence interval
Question answered
How spread out are the individual values?
How precisely have we estimated the population mean?
√[Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)]
x̄ ± 1.96 × SD/√n
Effect of larger n
Stable — describes the population's natural variability.
Narrows in proportion to 1/√n.
Used for
Reference ranges, describing a sample.
Inference about the underlying population, significance testing.
Same SD, very different CI
120 mmHg
with an
SD of 15 mmHg
. Study A enrols
n = 25
; Study B enrols
n = 400
. Compare the 95% CI of the mean.
Study A (n = 25)
SE = 15 / √25 = 15 / 5 = 3.0 mmHg
95% CI = 120 ± 1.96 × 3.0
= 120 ± 5.88 → 114.1 – 125.9 mmHg
Study B (n = 400)
SE = 15 / √400 = 15 / 20 = 0.75 mmHg
95% CI = 120 ± 1.96 × 0.75
= 120 ± 1.47 → 118.5 – 121.5 mmHg
the SD is identical (15 mmHg) — both studies show the same biological variability between individuals, and the reference range (mean ± 2 SD ≈ 90–150 mmHg) is unchanged. But Study B's CI is roughly four times narrower because n is sixteen times larger (√16 = 4). Study B has therefore
estimated the population mean four times more precisely
, even though the spread of individual readings is the same.
use SD when describing how variable patients are, and CI when describing how confident you are about an average. Quoting "mean ± SD" tells the reader about the population; "mean (95% CI)" tells them about the estimate.
rather than perfectly Gaussian. Skew is named for the direction of the long tail:
positive (right) skew
has a tail extending toward high values (mean > median > mode), while
negative (left) skew
has a tail toward low values (mean < median < mode).
median and IQR
, choose
non-parametric tests
, or apply a transformation (commonly a log-transform for positively skewed variables) before running parametric analyses.
Relative Risk (RR)
= incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed. Calculable only from cohort studies or RCTs.
= (a×d) / (b×c) from a 2×2 table. In case-control studies, OR approximates RR when the outcome is rare (<10%) — the
rare disease assumption
. OR is always further from 1 than the corresponding RR.
Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR)
= control event rate − treatment event rate.
Relative Risk Reduction (RRR)
= ARR / control event rate.
Number Needed to Treat (NNT)
= 1/ARR. Similarly,
= 1/absolute risk increase.
Hazard Ratio (HR)
is used in survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier curves, Cox regression) and accounts for time-to-event data. An HR of 0.7 means a 30% reduction in event rate at any given time point.
Kaplan–Meier analysis
plots time on the x-axis and estimated survival on the y-axis as a stepped curve, falling whenever an event occurs. A censored participant—lost to follow-up or event-free when follow-up ends—contributes information until censoring and is marked with a tick. Median survival is where the curve crosses 50%; the log-rank test compares whole survival curves. The
Cox proportional hazards model
is a regression model for time-to-event data that estimates hazard ratios while adjusting for confounders, assuming the hazard ratio between groups is constant over time.
= TP / (TP + FN) — proportion of true positives correctly identified. A highly sensitive test, when negative, helps
rule out
disease (
= TN / (TN + FP) — proportion of true negatives correctly identified. A highly specific test, when positive, helps
rule in
= TP / (TP + FP) — depends heavily on disease prevalence.
= TN / (TN + FN). PPV rises with higher prevalence; NPV falls. This is why screening tests in low-prevalence populations generate many false positives.
Likelihood Ratios (LR)
combine sensitivity and specificity. LR+ = sens / (1 − spec); LR− = (1 − sens) / spec. LRs are prevalence-independent and applied to pre-test probability via Fagan's nomogram or Bayes' theorem.
ROC curves
plot sensitivity (y-axis) against 1 − specificity (x-axis). The AUC (c-statistic) measures overall discriminative ability: 0.5 = no discrimination, 1.0 = perfect; AUC >0.8 is generally considered good.
Choosing a test — step by step
What type of data?
Continuous (interval/ratio), ordinal, or nominal (categorical).
→ chi-squared (Fisher’s exact if expected counts <5); paired nominal → McNemar.
Paired or unpaired?
Same subjects before/after vs independent groups.
How many groups?
Two vs more than two.
Continuous and normally distributed?
Yes (parametric) → t-test (paired or unpaired) for 2 groups, ANOVA (repeated-measures if paired) for >2. No, or ordinal (non-parametric) → Mann–Whitney U (2 unpaired), Wilcoxon signed-rank (2 paired), Kruskal–Wallis (>2 unpaired), Friedman (>2 paired).
Relationship rather than difference?
Pearson (normal, linear) or Spearman (ordinal/non-normal); regression to predict
Parametric Tests (normal distribution assumed)
Student's t-test
— compares means of 2 groups (unpaired) or before/after (paired)
— compares means of ≥3 groups; post-hoc tests (Tukey, Bonferroni) identify which pairs differ
Pearson's r
— linear association between two continuous variables (−1 to +1)
Linear regression
— models a continuous outcome as a function of predictors
Non-Parametric Tests (no distribution assumption)
Mann-Whitney U
— unpaired comparison of 2 groups
Wilcoxon signed-rank
— paired comparison
— compares ≥3 groups
Spearman's ρ
— correlation for non-normal or ordinal data
Categorical Data Tests
Chi-squared (χ²)
— compares proportions between groups (expected frequency ≥5)
Fisher's exact
— used when expected frequencies are small (<5)
McNemar's test
— paired categorical data
Logistic regression
— binary outcome with multiple predictors, yields OR
Selection bias
: systematic differences in who is enrolled (e.g., Berkson's bias).
Information bias
: systematic measurement errors, including recall bias (case-control) and observer bias (unblinded assessors).
occurs when a third variable is associated with both exposure and outcome. Address via randomisation, restriction, matching, stratification, and multivariable regression.
Intention-to-treat (ITT)
analyses every patient in the group to which they were randomised, whatever treatment they actually received or whether they completed it. It preserves randomisation (groups stay balanced for known and unknown confounders) and reflects real-world
, but non-adherence and crossover dilute the effect towards the null — conservative for superiority trials.
Per-protocol (PP)
includes only patients who completed the allocated treatment as planned. It estimates
under ideal conditions, but excluding patients breaks randomisation and introduces selection/attrition bias. ITT is the primary analysis for superiority trials; for non-inferiority trials ITT can falsely suggest equivalence, so both should be reported and agree
Internal validity
: freedom from bias within the study.
External validity (generalisability)
: applicability to other populations. Blinding, allocation concealment, and adequate follow-up are key determinants of internal validity in RCTs.
systematic review
uses a pre-defined protocol (PRISMA) to identify, appraise and synthesise all relevant studies. A
(Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) is a reporting guideline that ensures systematic reviews are transparent and completely reported. PRISMA 2020 has a
27-item checklist
flow diagram
of study selection. The 2009 diagram had four phases —
Identification, Screening, Eligibility and Inclusion
; the 2020 version merges eligibility into screening (Identification → Screening → Included).
forest plot
: each study as a point estimate with CI, pooled estimate as a diamond.
models assume one true effect;
models allow between-study variation and produce wider CIs.
Publication bias
is assessed using
funnel plots
— asymmetry suggests bias. Egger's test provides a formal statistical assessment.
GRADE methodology
GRADE separates certainty of evidence from strength of recommendation. Certainty is rated
high, moderate, low or very low
. Risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias downgrade certainty; a large effect, dose–response gradient or plausible residual confounding that would reduce an observed effect can upgrade observational evidence. Recommendations then balance certainty with benefits, harms, values and resource use.
Bayes' theorem:
post-test odds = pre-test odds × likelihood ratio.
Pre-test probability
is the estimated probability before testing, informed by prevalence and the clinical context. Convert probability to odds with
odds = p/(1−p)
. The
likelihood ratio
states how much a result changes those odds: LR+ for a positive result and LR− for a negative result. Convert the resulting odds back with
probability = odds/(1+odds)
A patient has a 20% pre-test probability of disease: pre-test odds = 0.20/0.80 = 0.25. A positive test with LR+ 8 gives post-test odds = 0.25 × 8 = 2. Post-test probability = 2/(1+2) =
. The test has raised, but not guaranteed, the probability of disease.
NNT for a perioperative intervention
ARR 2%, RRR 33%, NNT 50 — i.e. 50 patients must receive perioperative beta-blockade to prevent one additional 30-day death.
Post-test probability with likelihood ratios
≈66%. The positive test raises the probability of PE from 30% to 66% — illustrating why pre-test probability matters as much as the test characteristics.
Statistics & Evidence-Based Medicine
Study design, hypothesis testing, p-values, confidence intervals, odds ratios, and common statistical tests
A p-value is the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the data, assuming the null hypothesis is true — NOT the probability the null is true
Type I error (α): rejecting a true null (false positive). Type II error (β): failing to reject a false null. Power = 1 − β
OR compares odds of exposure in cases vs controls; RR compares incidence — RR is only valid in cohort/RCT designs
Number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 / absolute risk reduction (ARR). Contextualises clinical significance
Parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA) assume normally distributed data; non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis) do not
Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) — rules OUT disease (SnNOut); Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) — rules IN (SpPIn)
Hierarchy of evidence: systematic reviews/meta-analyses > RCTs > cohort > case-control > case series > expert opinion

# Physiology Overview: Homeostasis, Feedback & Organ Systems Homeostasis and set points, negative and positive feedback loops, and how the organ systems divide the work, with links to every physiology topic What homeostasis means Physiology is the study of how the body keeps its internal environment steady while the outside world changes. The OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology textbook (openly licensed, CC BY) puts it like this: a set point is not a single fixed value. Body temperature, blood pressure, blood glucose and plasma sodium each sit inside a normal range, and the body defends that range rather than one exact number. For temperature the set point is about 37°C; for mean arterial pressure, roughly 90–100 mmHg in a resting adult. Why it matters in anaesthesia almost everything anaesthesia does disturbs homeostasis, and almost every monitor exists to watch it happen. Induction drops blood pressure; positive-pressure ventilation changes venous return; surgery triggers a stress response; blood loss threatens oxygen delivery. The physiological pages on this site are the detail behind each defended variable: The Cardiac Cycle Oxygen-Haemoglobin Dissociation for oxygen delivery, Renal Physiology for fluid and electrolyte balance, and Endocrine Physiology for the stress response. The value has moved outside its normal range around the set point (about 37°C). Sensors in the skin and hypothalamus detect the deviation, and effectors — shivering, vasoconstriction, increased metabolic rate — act to return it. Anaesthesia blunts these responses, which is why active warming is needed. Negative feedback: the default A negative feedback loop has three working parts, defined in the source: between them sits the control centre, which compares the sensed value with the normal range and decides how strongly to drive the effector. The baroreflex is the classic anaesthetic example: stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch (sensors) report pressure to the medulla (control centre), which adjusts heart rate and vascular tone (effectors) through the autonomic nervous system — see Autonomic Nervous System . The same sensor–centre–effector pattern controls ventilation via CO₂ ( Ventilation-Perfusion Matching ) and blood glucose via insulin ( Diabetes Management Positive feedback: change that feeds itself positive feedback is useful only when it has a built-in stop: delivery ends the labour loop, and a formed clot ends the coagulation loop. Without an end point, positive feedback is a vicious cycle — the physiology of decompensation. Falling cardiac output reduces coronary perfusion, which weakens the heart further; rising intracranial pressure reduces cerebral perfusion, which worsens the pressure. Recognising these loops, and breaking them early, is the logic behind shock management on the Haemorrhagic Shock Stretch-sensitive nerve cells in the cervix are the sensors; the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary form the control centre; the uterine muscle is the effector, contracting harder as oxytocin rises. Delivery of the baby removes the stretch stimulus and ends the loop. Eleven systems, one patient the eleven systems are a useful filing scheme, but no system works alone, and the boundaries are imprecise — the pancreas belongs to both the digestive and endocrine systems. In exams and at the bedside, the skill is tracing one variable across systems: arterial oxygen content depends on the lungs, the blood, the heart and the circulation together. Where each system is covered on this site Cardiac Electrophysiology Starling Forces & Fluid Exchange . Respiratory: Lung Mechanics . Nervous and neuromuscular: Neuromuscular Transmission . Renal, gut and liver: Gastrointestinal Physiology Hepatic Physiology . Endocrine and blood: Haematology & Immunity . Life stages: Maternal Physiology Foetal Circulation Paediatric Physiology Worked examples: Henderson–Hasselbalch (DKA and COPD) osmolar gap (methanol) Starling forces (heart failure and sepsis) a worked example of integration: a fit adult haemorrhages. Baroreflex (nervous system) raises heart rate and vasoconstricts; adrenaline and cortisol (endocrine) reinforce this; the kidney retains salt and water (renal); breathing quickens as acidosis develops (respiratory); clotting activates (haematology). Every one of those responses is a negative feedback loop defending oxygen delivery — and each has a page above. Because each defended variable crosses system boundaries. Blood pressure, for example, is sensed by the nervous system, adjusted by the heart and vessels, supported by renal salt and water handling, and modulated by hormones. Organ systems share sensors, effectors and messengers, so homeostasis is a property of the whole body, not of any one system. OpenStax monitoring OpenStax set point a patient's core temperature falls to 35.5°C during a long operation. In homeostatic terms, what has happened? OpenStax negative feedback OpenStax sensor OpenStax effector OpenStax positive feedback OpenStax positive endpoint oxytocin release during labour is positive feedback. What is the sensor, the control centre and the effector, and what ends the loop? Stretch-sensitive nerve cells in the cervix are the sensors; the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary form the control centre; the uterine muscle is the effector, contracting harder as oxytocin rises. Delivery of the baby removes the stretch stimulus and ends the loop.

Because each defended variable crosses system boundaries. Blood pressure, for example, is sensed by the nervous system, adjusted by the heart and vessels, supported by renal salt and water handling, and modulated by hormones. Organ systems share sensors, effectors and messengers, so homeostasis is a property of the whole body, not of any one system.

This page is the frame for the whole physiology section: what homeostasis is, how feedback loops defend it, and how the organ systems divide the work. # Renal System Overview: Filtration, Concentration & Hormonal Control GFR and net filtration pressure, the countercurrent multiplier, renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and ADH Glomerular filtration the kidneys filter about 180 L a day yet pass only 1–2 L of urine, so almost all of the work is reabsorption. Because the net filtration pressure is only about 10 mmHg, small changes in glomerular capillary pressure or plasma oncotic pressure change filtration a great deal (teaching summary). Hypotension under anaesthesia therefore threatens filtration quickly. Detail: Renal Physiology NFP = glomerular blood hydrostatic pressure 55 − (capsular hydrostatic pressure 15 + blood colloid osmotic pressure 30) = 10 mmHg. Reabsorption and concentrating urine the loop of Henle builds a salt and urea gradient deep in the medulla. Water can only leave the collecting duct down that gradient when water channels are present, which is where ADH acts (next lesson). Loop diuretics block the solute pumps of the thick ascending limb and so wash out the gradient (teaching summary). Countercurrent: the descending and ascending limbs lie side by side with fluid flowing in opposite directions. Multiplier: solute pumps raise the concentration of urea and Na⁺ deep in the medulla. Hormonal control: renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and ADH after blood loss or dehydration, angiotensin II and ADH act together to hold on to salt and water and support blood pressure, which is one reason urine output falls after surgery even when the kidneys are healthy (teaching summary). ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers remove part of this defence, which helps explain the low blood pressure sometimes seen at induction in patients taking them (teaching summary). See AKI & renal replacement therapy for clinical detail. It moves aquaporin water channels into the apical membrane of principal cells in the collecting duct, so water leaves the duct by osmosis. Cardiac output CO = HR × SV. Stroke volume depends on preload, contractility and afterload, so any change in cardiac output can be traced to one of four factors: heart rate, preload, contractility or afterload (teaching summary). The OpenStax figures are for each ventricle, not the two added together. Detail: The Cardiac Cycle 70 × 75 = 5250 mL/min, about 5.25 L/min. Preload, Frank–Starling and afterload a fluid bolus increases preload and, while the heart sits on the steep part of the Starling curve, stroke volume. On the flat part, more fluid adds little except congestion — the basis of testing fluid responsiveness rather than giving fluid by default (teaching summary). Aortic stenosis and high vascular resistance raise afterload. Fluid exchange in the capillaries is covered on Starling Forces Within physiological limits, the force of contraction is directly proportional to the initial length of the muscle fibre, so greater stretch increases stroke volume. Blood pressure and the baroreceptors MAP is approximately diastolic pressure plus one third of pulse pressure, and it equals cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance (teaching summary). A fall in pressure reduces stretch of the carotid sinus and aortic baroreceptors, so heart rate and vascular tone rise. Many anaesthetic drugs blunt this reflex, so blood pressure falls further and recovers more slowly under anaesthesia (teaching summary). Neural pathways: Autonomic Nervous System In the sinuses of the aorta and carotid arteries; they are stretch receptors that sense the degree of stretch caused by blood pressure. How air moves: pressures and Boyle's law in spontaneous breathing the diaphragm enlarges the chest, alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric and air flows in. Positive-pressure ventilation reverses this: pressure is pushed in from outside, which raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return (teaching summary). Compliance and resistance: Lung Mechanics The thoracic volume increases, so alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows in down the pressure gradient. Gas exchange: partial pressures raising inspired oxygen raises alveolar PO₂ (Dalton) and so the dissolved oxygen in plasma (Henry). Gas moves from higher to lower partial pressure, so oxygenation depends on how well ventilation matches blood flow in each lung unit (teaching summary). See The concentration of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to its solubility and partial pressure. Carrying oxygen and carbon dioxide in the tissues, acid and CO₂ help haemoglobin release oxygen (Bohr), and deoxygenated haemoglobin picks up more CO₂ (Haldane); in the lungs both reverse. Breathing is driven mainly by CO₂ through the central chemoreceptors, and opioids and volatile agents depress this response (teaching summary). # The Cardiac Cycle Pressure-volume loops, Wiggers diagram, cardiac output aortic ~80 mmHg) → isovolumetric relaxation (aortic closes, dicrotic notch) → rapid filling (mitral opens when LV CPP = aortic DBP − LVEDP 45 mmHg (normal >60). only in diastole O₂ supply ↓ (shorter diastole, low CPP) and demand ↑ (HR, wall tension) → subendocardial ischaemia. Cannon a waves = atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve — occurs when atrial and ventricular systole coincide (AV dissociation). cannon waves = intermittent dissociation → ventricular tachycardia (AV dissociation present in ~50% of beats; ECG shows dissociated p-waves marching through). Regular cannon waves = junctional rhythm or complete heart block (consistent dissociation every beat). ventricular tachycardia (isovolumetric contraction + ejection) and (isovolumetric relaxation + filling). At a heart rate of 70 bpm, the cycle lasts ~860 ms (systole ~300 ms, diastole ~560 ms). As heart rate rises, diastole shortens disproportionately, compromising filling and coronary perfusion. It is best heard at the apex. results from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole. Physiological splitting of S2 occurs during inspiration: negative intrathoracic pressure increases systemic venous return and RV preload, increasing RV stroke volume and prolonging RV ejection so P2 is delayed. At the same time, transient pooling in the expanded pulmonary vascular bed slightly reduces LV filling and shortens LV ejection, bringing A2 earlier. The A2–P2 interval therefore becomes audible and narrows again on expiration — early diastolic, rapid filling against a stiff or volume-loaded ventricle (HF, MR; normal in young). — late diastolic, atrial contraction into a non-compliant ventricle (LVH, AS, ischaemia); absent in AF. Wide fixed split S2 — ASD. Reversed split — LBBB, severe AS. Opening snap — mitral stenosis. Ejection click — bicuspid AV / AS. Lower pressure system — RV peak ~25 mmHg vs LV ~120 mmHg; thinner, crescentic geometry. Earlier opening, later closure — pulmonary valve opens before aortic and closes after, producing physiological splitting of S2. Continuous ejection profile — low PVR allows ejection throughout most of systole, with shorter isovolumetric phases than the LV. — small rises in PVR (hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, PE) markedly reduce RV stroke volume. Ventricular interdependence — shared septum and pericardium mean RV dilation impairs LV filling (acute PE, RV infarct, tamponade). Wave / descent Pathological correlate Atrial contraction Absent in AF; large in TS, PHT, RVH; cannon in CHB / VT / junctional rhythm TV bulging into RA in early systole Rarely visible clinically Atrial relaxation + downward AV ring movement Prominent in tamponade & constrictive pericarditis Atrial filling against closed TV Giant in TR ("cv" or systolic wave) Rapid atrial emptying when TV opens Steep in constrictive pericarditis ("M/W"); blunted in tamponade Left coronary flow occurs predominantly in diastole because intramyocardial pressure during systole exceeds aortic pressure in the subendocardium. RV perfusion occurs throughout the cycle because RV intramural pressure is low. Coronary Perfusion Pressure (CPP) ≈ Aortic Diastolic Pressure − LVEDP Tachycardia shortens diastole more than systole → reduced subendocardial perfusion (rate control in AS, IHD). Aortic regurgitation and severe hypotension lower diastolic pressure and CPP. LV hypertrophy raises LVEDP and intramural pressure, predisposing to subendocardial ischaemia. , or ejection fraction (load-dependent). dP/dt is the maximal rate of LV or arterial pressure rise and reflects contractile force, although loading and arterial waveform affect non-invasive estimates. Pulse-contour systems such as LiDCO and PiCCO provide continuous CO and derived indices/trends; interpret changes rather than treating any single value as load-independent Heart Rate & Rhythm Reading the pressure–volume loop Bottom right: mitral valve closes at LVEDV; isovolumetric contraction rises vertically at constant volume. Top right: LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure and the aortic valve opens; ejection moves left across the top. Top left: aortic valve closes at LVESV; isovolumetric relaxation falls vertically. Bottom left: LV pressure falls below LA pressure and the mitral valve opens; diastolic filling returns rightwards. Loop width is stroke volume ; enclosed area is stroke work . Increased preload shifts the right boundary right and widens the loop; increased afterload makes it taller and narrower with higher ESV; increased contractility steepens ESPVR, shifts ESV left and widens the loop. Use the sliders below to reproduce each change PV loops in valvular disease Aortic stenosis: tall, narrow loop — very high peak LV pressure with a large transvalvular gradient, concentric hypertrophy steepening the end-diastolic pressure–volume relationship, and stroke volume relatively preserved until late. Stroke work rises markedly for a given output. Aortic regurgitation: wide loop shifted right (large EDV) with loss of the true isovolumetric relaxation phase, because filling begins as soon as LV pressure falls below aortic pressure. Mitral regurgitation: loop shifted right with loss of isovolumetric contraction — ejection into the left atrium starts before the aortic valve opens, so the loop has a rounded, triangular lower-right corner and reduced effective forward stroke volume. Mitral stenosis: small, narrow loop with reduced EDV and low stroke work; output is fixed and rate-dependent. It shares the same physiology and threshold range as PPV but depends on the device algorithm; PPV needs only an arterial line, whereas SVV needs a stroke-volume estimate and is more affected by vasomotor tone and waveform damping. — maximal rate of pressure rise during isovolumetric contraction, an index of contractility. Estimated from the upstroke of the arterial trace, so it is confounded by afterload, arterial compliance and catheter damping; trend it rather than trusting absolute values. Cardiac power output = MAP × CO / 451 (watts; normal ≈ 1 W). CPO below about 0.6 W is a strong predictor of mortality in cardiogenic shock and is the single most useful haemodynamic prognostic variable. Cardiac cycle efficiency — a dimensionless pulse-wave-analysis variable describing the energetic efficiency of each beat; negative values correlate with impaired LV ejection fraction. Pulse wave analysis derives stroke volume beat-to-beat from the arterial pressure waveform (pulse-contour, pressure-recording analytical or Windkessel models), then computes CO, SVV and derived efficiency/contractility indices. Accuracy falls with arrhythmia, aortic regurgitation, intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation, extreme vasoconstriction or poor waveform quality Pressure–Volume Loop Frank–Starling Curve Grade I (impaired relaxation) — E/A < 0.8, prolonged DT. Grade II (pseudonormal) — normal E/A but elevated E/e′ (>14). Grade III (restrictive) — E/A > 2, short DT, high LA pressure. Anaesthetic implications: maintain sinus rhythm, avoid tachycardia, optimise preload, treat ischaemia, avoid abrupt afterload changes. PA catheter — RA → RV (square root, large pulse pressure) → PA (diastolic step-up, dicrotic notch) → PCWP (a, c, v waves like LA, slightly delayed). Pulse pressure variation (PPV) — reflects preload responsiveness in ventilated patients (PPV > 13% suggests fluid responsiveness). S1 = AV valve closure (start of systole); S2 = semilunar valve closure (end of systole) with dicrotic notch; S3/S4 reflect filling pathology. Isovolumetric contraction and relaxation: all valves closed; pressure changes without volume change. Passive filling contributes 70–80% of LVEDV; atrial kick adds 15–25% — critical in stiff ventricles (AS, HCM, diastolic dysfunction). SV determinants: preload, afterload, contractility; CO = HR × SV; rhythm contributes via AV synchrony.  1. Atrial Systole

Corresponds to the P wave on ECG. Atrial contraction contributes the final 15–25% of ventricular filling (the ). This becomes increasingly important at higher heart rates when passive filling time is reduced. Loss of atrial systole (e.g., atrial fibrillation) can reduce cardiac output by up to 25%.

2. Isovolumetric Contraction

Begins with mitral valve closure (S1) after the QRS complex triggers ventricular depolarisation. All valves are closed; ventricular pressure rises rapidly with no change in volume. LV pressure must exceed aortic diastolic pressure (~80 mmHg) before the aortic valve opens. This phase lasts ~50 ms.

3. Rapid Ejection

The aortic valve opens when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure. Approximately two-thirds of the stroke volume is ejected during this phase. Peak LV and aortic pressures occur here (~120 mmHg). Aortic flow velocity is maximal.

4. Reduced Ejection

Ventricular repolarisation occurs (T wave). Ejection rate decreases as the pressure gradient across the aortic valve diminishes. The remaining one-third of stroke volume is ejected. LV pressure begins to fall below aortic pressure, but momentum maintains forward flow briefly.

5. Isovolumetric Relaxation

The aortic valve closes, producing S2 and the dicrotic notch on the aortic pressure trace. All valves are again closed. LV pressure falls rapidly with no change in volume. When LV pressure falls below LA pressure, the mitral valve opens and filling begins.

6. Rapid Filling

The mitral valve opens and blood flows rapidly from LA to LV down the pressure gradient. This passive filling accounts for approximately 70–80% of ventricular filling. A third heart sound (S3) may be heard at the end of this phase in young or pathological hearts.

7. Diastasis (Reduced Filling)

LA and LV pressures equilibrate; filling slows considerably. This phase is shortened at high heart rates and is the first to be compromised with tachycardia, which is why diastolic filling time is rate-dependent and why tachycardia reduces cardiac output in patients with diastolic dysfunction.

    S1 is caused by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the onset of ventricular systole. It is best heard at the apex. S2 results from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole. Physiological splitting of S2 occurs during inspiration: negative intrathoracic pressure increases systemic venous return and RV preload, increasing RV stroke volume and prolonging RV ejection so P2 is delayed. At the same time, transient pooling in the expanded pulmonary vascular bed slightly reduces LV filling and shortens LV ejection, bringing A2 earlier. The A2–P2 interval therefore becomes audible and narrows again on expiration The right ventricle (RV) follows the same sequence of phases but operates at much lower pressures.       LVEDV — determined by venous return, atrial contraction, ventricular compliance, intrathoracic pressure and cycle length. Estimated by CVP, PCWP, IVC distensibility or dynamic indices (PPV, SVV). Static filling pressures describe current loading but poorly predict fluid response. PPV/SVV exploit cyclic heart–lung interactions during positive-pressure ventilation: a preload-responsive ventricle shows larger respiratory changes in stroke volume.       Wall stress during ejection; approximated by SVR and aortic impedance. Influenced by aortic compliance, viscosity and outflow obstruction (AS, HOCM). Laplace: σ = P·r / 2h. Total safety factor ≈ 17 mmHg: capillary pressure must rise by roughly this amount above normal before clinical oedema appears. This explains why isolated hypoalbuminaemia rarely produces oedema, and why oedema then appears abruptly once the reserve is spent — the pressure–volume relationship of the interstitium becomes very compliant beyond that point The reserve is finite and is overwhelmed in disease: sepsis and ischaemia–reperfusion shed the glycocalyx (raising Kf and lowering σ, so protein leaks and the washdown factor is lost), heart failure raises Pc while raised right atrial pressure obstructs thoracic-duct lymph drainage, and lymphatic disruption (axillary clearance, filariasis) removes the largest single factor. Aggressive fluid loading adds ANP-mediated glycocalyx damage to a rising Pc, which is why oedema in critical illness appears at capillary pressures far below the 17 mmHg predicted in health Pulmonary circulation

Pc is low (~7 mmHg), interstitial pressure is more negative (≈ −8 mmHg) and interstitial oncotic pressure is relatively high because the barrier is more protein-permeable, so the oncotic gradient is small. Protection comes from a double safety factor: low Pc plus a very high-capacity pulmonary lymphatic system. Left atrial pressure must therefore rise substantially (typically >20–25 mmHg) before alveolar flooding, but once lymphatic reserve is exceeded oedema accumulates rapidly and gas exchange deteriorates within minutes.

Cerebral circulation

The blood–brain barrier (tight junctions between endothelial cells, with astrocyte end-feet) is almost impermeable to protein and small ions, so its reflection coefficient is ≈ 1.0 for most solutes and fluid flux is negligible. Water movement is governed by total osmolality rather than oncotic pressure — hence hypo-osmolar fluids cause brain swelling and mannitol/hypertonic saline reduce it. When the barrier breaks down (trauma, tumour, inflammation) protein and fluid leak into the brain, causing vasogenic oedema.

Filtration is driven by an unusually high Pc (~55 mmHg) generated between afferent and efferent arterioles, opposed by Bowman >Hepatic sinusoids

Discontinuous, fenestrated endothelium with essentially no basement membrane gives a very high Kf and a low σ, so protein passes freely into the space of Disse and the transsinusoidal oncotic gradient is minimal. Fluid balance is therefore dominated by sinusoidal hydrostatic pressure and by hepatic lymph flow — hence the ascites of portal hypertension despite modest pressure rises.

Work of Breathing
Elastic work
Overcomes lung/chest-wall recoil. It rises in fibrosis, pulmonary oedema and ARDS and is represented by inspiratory work against the compliance curve.
Resistive work
Overcomes airway and tissue resistance. It rises in asthma, COPD and with a small ETT; the inspiratory–expiratory loop area reflects resistive loss.
Inertial work
Accelerates gas and respiratory tissues and is normally negligible.
Patients minimise total work by taking rapid shallow breaths in restrictive disease (less elastic work per breath) and slower deeper breaths in obstructive disease (lower flow-related resistive work).
Factors increasing elastic work:
ARDS, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary fibrosis, atelectasis, obesity and abdominal distension (chest-wall elastance), plus large tidal volumes and PEEP that pushes tidal breathing onto the flat upper part of the compliance curve.
Factors increasing resistive work:
asthma, COPD, bronchospasm and secretions, laryngeal or tracheal narrowing, a small or kinked tracheal tube, HME/filter obstruction, high inspiratory flow and turbulent flow (resistance ∝ 1/r⁵ for turbulent flow, 1/r⁴ for laminar flow).
How ventilators unload the patient:
pressure support or pressure-control breaths supply the elastic and resistive work; adequate applied PEEP offsets auto-PEEP so less effort is needed to trigger; flow-triggering, appropriate rise time and cycling-off criteria, and automatic tube compensation reduce trigger and tube work; correcting patient–ventilator dyssynchrony removes wasted effort.

West's Lung Zones
Zone 1 (apex) — P
> P
alveolar pressure compresses the capillary throughout the cardiac cycle, so there is no flow. This is alveolar dead space (ventilation without perfusion, high V/Q). Zone 1 does not exist in the healthy upright subject because apical arterial pressure just exceeds alveolar pressure.
Zone 2 (mid-zone) — P
intermittent flow occurring only when arterial pressure exceeds alveolar pressure. Flow depends on the arterial–alveolar difference, not the arteriovenous difference — the "vascular waterfall" or Starling-resistor behaviour, so flow rises steadily down the zone as P
Zone 3 (base) — P
continuous flow determined by the arteriovenous pressure difference. Further increases in flow down this zone reflect capillary distension and recruitment. V/Q is low here because perfusion increases down the lung more steeply than ventilation.
Zone 4 (most dependent) — interstitial compression:
at low lung volumes, increased interstitial pressure around extra-alveolar vessels raises resistance and reduces flow again. Zone 4 enlarges with pulmonary oedema and at volumes near residual volume
V/Q consequences:
both ventilation and perfusion increase towards the base, but perfusion increases more, so V/Q falls from about 3.0 at the apex to about 0.6 at the base. The apex behaves like dead space and the base like a shunt; overall this gradient accounts for part of the normal alveolar–arterial oxygen difference.
Factors that alter the zones:
positive pressure ventilation and PEEP raise alveolar pressure and so expand zone 1 and 2 conditions, increasing alveolar dead space — pronounced if hypovolaemia or haemorrhage simultaneously lowers P
. Hypotension and pulmonary embolism similarly create zone 1. Exercise raises pulmonary arterial pressure, recruiting and distending apical vessels so the whole lung behaves as zone 3 with more uniform V/Q. The supine position abolishes the vertical gradient (replacing it with an antero-posterior one), and prone positioning produces more uniform perfusion — one reason it improves oxygenation in ARDS. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and interstitial oedema modify the pattern further.
Closing Volume & Closing Capacity
closing volume (CV) is the volume above residual volume at which dependent small airways begin to close; closing capacity (CC) = CV + RV, so CC is the absolute lung volume at which closure starts. In a healthy young adult CC is well below FRC (roughly 10% of TLC above RV).
the single-breath nitrogen washout — a vital-capacity breath of 100% oxygen, then a slow full expiration with continuous nitrogen measurement. Phase I is dead-space gas (no N₂), phase II the mixed transition, phase III the alveolar plateau, and the abrupt upward inflection of
phase IV
marks airway closure in dependent lung, because the remaining gas comes from apical units with a higher nitrogen concentration. The volume expired from that inflection to RV is the closing volume.
Factors increasing CC:
age (CC equals FRC at about 44 years supine and 66 years erect), smoking and chronic airflow limitation, supine posture, obesity, pulmonary oedema and bronchospasm. FRC is reduced by supine position, general anaesthesia, neuromuscular blockade, obesity, pregnancy and abdominal surgery.
Clinical significance:
when CC exceeds FRC, dependent airways close during normal tidal breathing, producing shunt, V/Q mismatch, atelectasis and hypoxaemia. Anaesthesia lowers FRC by 15–20% within minutes of induction, commonly taking it below CC — hence pre-oxygenation desaturates faster, and PEEP, recruitment manoeuvres, head-up positioning and avoidance of high FiO₂-related absorption atelectasis are used to restore FRC above CC

Auto-PEEP & Air Trapping
Causes and consequences
High minute ventilation, a long inspiratory time, short expiratory time, and increased expiratory resistance in asthma or COPD prevent complete emptying. Dynamic hyperinflation raises alveolar pressure, impedes venous return and may cause hypotension; a spontaneously breathing patient must first overcome intrinsic PEEP, increasing trigger work and dyspnoea.
Measure and manage
Suspect persistent expiratory flow at the next inspiration. In a passive patient, an
end-expiratory hold
equilibrates alveolar and airway pressure; total PEEP minus set external PEEP estimates auto-PEEP. Reduce respiratory rate and tidal volume, shorten inspiratory time by increasing inspiratory flow, allow a longer expiratory phase, treat bronchospasm and clear obstruction. In severe hypotension, briefly disconnecting the circuit permits decompression.

PV Recruitment Curve & Hysteresis
What is hysteresis?
is the difference between the inflation and deflation limbs of the static pressure-volume curve — at any given pressure, lung volume is lower on the way up (inflation) than on the way down (deflation). More pressure is needed to
a collapsed alveolus than to
keep it open
, for three related reasons: by Laplace's law, the pressure needed to expand a sphere is inversely related to its radius, so a small, collapsed alveolus needs a disproportionately high opening pressure; individual units have different critical opening (recruitment) thresholds, so they recruit progressively rather than all at once; and surfactant needs time and a change in interfacial surface area to reorganise at the air-liquid interface and lower surface tension, so its stabilising effect is greater on deflation than on inflation. The curve therefore shows a
lower inflection point (LIP)
, below which most recruitment occurs, and an
upper inflection point (UIP)
, above which the curve flattens as units become fully distended.
deflation limb lies above inflation limb —
recruited alveoli stay open at lower pressure

FRCA Primary — Physiology
Compliance = ΔV/ΔP. Total respiratory compliance (~100 ml/cmH₂O) = lung + chest wall in series.
Static compliance uses plateau pressure; dynamic compliance uses peak pressure. Dynamic < static.

Time constant τ = R × C. 3τ required for 95% equilibration. Heterogeneous τ causes V/Q mismatch.
Normal WOB = 0.3-0.6 J/L, consuming 2-3% of VO₂. Can exceed 30% in respiratory failure.

What is the difference between static and dynamic compliance?
Static compliance = ΔV / (plateau pressure − PEEP) — measured at zero flow; reflects elastic properties of lung and chest wall. Normal 60–100 mL/cmH₂O. Dynamic compliance = ΔV / (peak − PEEP) — includes the resistive component, always lower than static. A widening gap between peak and plateau suggests increased airway resistance (bronchospasm, secretions, kinked tube).

MIGET (multiple inert gas elimination technique) : an infusion of six inert gases of widely differing blood solubility (e.g. SF₆, ethane, cyclopropane, enflurane, ether, acetone) reaches steady state, then arterial, mixed venous and expired concentrations are measured. Poorly soluble gases are excreted almost entirely from high-V/Q units, while highly soluble gases are retained in low-V/Q units, so the pattern of retention and excretion can be inverted mathematically into a continuous distribution of blood flow and ventilation against V/Q ratio, including true shunt and true dead space. # Oxygen-Haemoglobin Dissociation The ODC, Bohr effect, factors shifting the curve, oxygen delivery CaO₂ = (1.34 × Hb × SaO₂) + (0.0225 × PaO₂) (mL O₂ per dL when Hb in g/dL and PaO₂ in kPa) Bound: 1.34 × 12.0 × 0.98 = 15.76 mL/dL Dissolved: 0.0225 × 13 = 0.29 mL/dL CaO₂ ≈ 16.05 mL/dL ≈ 160.5 mL/L DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ × 10 (×10 to convert dL → L) ~800 mL/min (normal ~1000 mL/min). CO has two effects on the ODC and DO₂: Affinity ~240× greater than O₂ → reduces functional Hb able to carry O₂. Shifts the remaining curve → impaired tissue offloading. ← Left Shift (↑ Affinity) • ↓ Temperature (hypothermia) • ↓ PaCO₂ / Alkalosis (↑ pH) • ↓ 2,3-DPG (stored blood) • Fetal haemoglobin (HbF) • Carbon monoxide (COHb) • Methaemoglobin Right Shift → (↓ Affinity) • ↑ Temperature (fever, exercise) • ↑ PaCO₂ / Acidosis (↓ pH) — Bohr effect • ↑ 2,3-DPG • Sickle haemoglobin (HbS) • Anaemia / chronic hypoxia Bohr effect describes the rightward shift of the ODC caused by increased CO₂ and H⁺ concentration. In metabolically active tissues, CO₂ production lowers pH locally, promoting O₂ release exactly where it is needed. In the lungs, CO₂ excretion raises pH, shifting the curve left and promoting O₂ loading. Nociception monitors attempt to quantify these responses in anaesthetised or non-communicative patients; the Surgical Pleth Index combines changes in pulse-wave amplitude and heartbeat interval. These signals are not specific for pain and are altered by hypovolaemia, vasoactive drugs, autonomic disease and anaesthetic depth, so no autonomic index replaces clinical assessment

Baroreceptor reflex: carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X) → NTS in medulla → adjusts sympathetic/parasympathetic outflow to maintain BP. Reset in chronic hypertension; blunted by volatile anaesthetics.

Oculocardiac reflex: pressure on globe → CN V₁ afferent → CN X efferent → bradycardia. Treat with stopping stimulus, atropine/glycopyrrolate. Bezold-Jarisch reflex: LV mechanoreceptors → vagal activation → bradycardia + vasodilation. May occur during neuraxial anaesthesia or haemorrhage and explains paradoxical bradycardia with hypovolaemia.

Understanding this process is essential for anaesthetists, as it underpins the pharmacology of{ >neuromuscular blocking agents , their reversal, and neuromuscular monitoring.

1. Action Potential Arrival

A motor nerve action potential propagates along the myelinated axon to the nerve terminal. The terminal is unmyelinated and contains ~300,000 vesicles, each containing approximately 5,000–10,000 molecules of acetylcholine (ACh).

2. Calcium Influx

Depolarisation of the nerve terminal opens voltage-gated calcium channels (P/Q-type). Ca²⁺ influx is essential for vesicle fusion — blocking these channels (e.g., Lambert–Eaton syndrome, aminoglycosides) impairs neuromuscular transmission.

3. Vesicle Fusion & ACh Release

Ca²⁺ triggers the SNARE protein complex (synaptobrevin, SNAP-25, syntaxin) to fuse vesicles with the pre-synaptic membrane (exocytosis). Approximately 200–300 vesicles release their ACh content into the synaptic cleft — far more than needed (safety margin of ~70%).

4. ACh Binds Nicotinic Receptors

ACh crosses the 50 nm synaptic cleft and binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR) on the post-synaptic motor end plate. The adult nAChR has the subunit composition{ } α₂βδε. Two ACh molecules must bind (one to each α subunit) to open the channel.

5. End-Plate Potential

Channel opening allows Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ influx with K⁺ efflux—a net inward positive current producing a localised depolarisation— the end-plate potential (EPP). If the EPP exceeds threshold (~−55 mV), it triggers a propagating muscle action potential via adjacent voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, leading to excitation–contraction coupling.

6. ACh Hydrolysis

Acetylcholinesterase (AChE), concentrated in the synaptic cleft, rapidly hydrolyses ACh to choline and acetate. Choline is actively reuptaken into the nerve terminal for resynthesis of ACh by choline acetyltransferase (ChAT). This rapid termination ensures each nerve impulse produces a single, discrete muscle twitch.

There are multiple receptor types at the NMJ:

  • Post-junctional nAChR (α₂βδε) — the primary target for neuromuscular blocking agents. Non-depolarising agents compete with ACh at the α subunits.
  • Pre-junctional nAChR (predominantly α₃β₂) — facilitate positive feedback, mobilising more ACh vesicles during sustained activity (explains fade with non-depolarising block). Other nicotinic and muscarinic subtypes also contribute to modulating ACh release.
  • Fetal/extrajunctional nAChR (α₂βδγ) — contain the γ subunit instead of ε. They have a longer channel open time and lower conductance. Upregulated in denervation, burns, and immobilisation — causing hyperkalaemia with suxamethonium.
The NMJ has a large safety margin: approximately 70–80% of receptors must be blocked before clinical weakness becomes apparent, and { }90% must be blocked for complete paralysis. This is exploited in neuromuscular monitoring — train-of-four fade appears when ~75% of receptors are occupied, and single twitch depression requires ~80% blockade.

# Renal Physiology
GFR, tubular function, acid-base balance, electrolyte handling


Reclamation is not regeneration: account for net acid excretion
Filtered bicarbonate has already been present in plasma. Reabsorbing it prevents loss of buffer but does not replace bicarbonate consumed when the body buffers newly produced nonvolatile acid. In the proximal tubule, secreted hydrogen combines with filtered bicarbonate; carbonic anhydrase permits carbon dioxide to cross the cell membrane, and bicarbonate is returned to blood. The hydrogen is recycled. By contrast, excreting hydrogen with a non-bicarbonate urinary buffer or excreting ammonium adds new bicarbonate to the systemic balance.
Net acid excretion = urinary ammonium excretion + titratable acid excretion − urinary bicarbonate excretion.
All terms must be expressed as amounts per time, not simply urine concentrations. For a timed collection, multiply a concentration by the urine flow rate. Free hydrogen-ion excretion is quantitatively small even in very acidic urine: buffers allow much more acid to be removed without requiring an impossibly low urine pH. A low urine pH therefore does not prove adequate total acid excretion.
Distal secretion, phosphate buffering and the bicarbonate exit route
In α-intercalated cells, carbonic anhydrase generates hydrogen and bicarbonate. Apical H⁺-ATPase and H⁺/K⁺-ATPase secrete hydrogen; basolateral AE1 exchanges bicarbonate for chloride, returning bicarbonate to blood. Hydrogen that protonates phosphate is excreted as titratable acid. The capacity of this pathway depends on buffer delivery and tubular handling: it cannot increase as flexibly as ammonium excretion during sustained acid loading. β-intercalated cells have a different transporter arrangement and can secrete bicarbonate through apical pendrin when bicarbonate disposal is required.
Ammonium is produced by the kidney, not just filtered
Proximal glutamine metabolism can generate two ammonium ions and two bicarbonate equivalents. Ammonium enters tubular fluid, with NHE3 contributing to proximal secretion. In the thick ascending limb it can substitute for potassium on NKCC2, establishing a medullary reservoir. Collecting-duct ammonia transport and hydrogen secretion then permit ammonium excretion. Urinary excretion is essential to the net bicarbonate gain; ammonia returned to the circulation and metabolised elsewhere does not have the same acid–base effect.
“Diffusion trapping” is a useful chemical explanation of NH₃ becoming NH₄⁺ in acidic fluid, but is not the entire transport mechanism. Specific proteins, including Rh glycoproteins, contribute to epithelial ammonia transport. Persistent acidosis increases ammoniagenesis and transport capacity. Hyperkalaemia suppresses renal ammonia production and transport, while hypokalaemia promotes them; potassium disturbance can therefore sustain an acid–base disorder rather than merely accompany it.
Interpret renal acidification in the patient's whole context
Establish the systemic disorder first: blood pH, bicarbonate, carbon dioxide and the plasma anion gap distinguish the problem from its compensation.
Ask whether the kidney is losing bicarbonate, failing to excrete ammonium or failing to sustain distal hydrogen secretion; these are not interchangeable defects.
Interpret urine pH together with potassium, renal function and the clinical setting. An acidic sample can coexist with low ammonium output, notably in hyperkalaemic acidification disorders.
Remember that reduced functioning nephron mass limits whole-kidney acid disposal even when surviving nephrons adapt. A single urine pH is neither a measure of that adaptation nor a stand-alone renal tubular acidosis diagnosis.
Learning check: how much net acid was excreted?
A hypothetical timed collection contains 40 mmol ammonium, 25 mmol titratable acid and 5 mmol bicarbonate per day. Net acid excretion is 40 + 25 − 5 =
60 mmol/day
. The example illustrates accounting, not a treatment target. An equally acidic urine sample with little ammonium could remove substantially less acid.

Tubular Function Summary
: reabsorbs 65–70% of filtered Na⁺, water, glucose, amino acids, HCO₃⁻. Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase on basolateral membrane drives all transport. Glucose is reabsorbed by SGLT2 (Tm ≈ 375 mg/min).
Loop of Henle
: descending limb permeable to water, ascending limb impermeable (countercurrent multiplier). Thick ascending limb: Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2) — target of loop diuretics.
: Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter (NCC) — target of thiazides.
Collecting duct
: principal cells (ENaC — aldosterone-sensitive Na⁺ channels); intercalated cells (H⁺-ATPase, H⁺/K⁺-ATPase for acid-base). ADH acts on V2 receptors → aquaporin-2 insertion → water reabsorption.
Renal Potassium Handling
K⁺ is freely filtered. About 65–70% is reabsorbed passively/paracellularly in the proximal tubule and 20–25% through NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Final balance is set in the distal nephron
Principal cells secrete K⁺ through ROMK and flow-sensitive BK channels. Aldosterone increases ENaC and basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, making the lumen negative and promoting secretion. High plasma K⁺ directly stimulates aldosterone and ROMK.
During K⁺ depletion, α-intercalated cells reabsorb K⁺ through H⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Mineral acidosis generally reduces distal K⁺ secretion, whereas alkalosis and high distal sodium/flow increase it.
Clinical links: loop/thiazide diuretics increase distal Na⁺ delivery and K⁺ loss; ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics, renal failure and hypoaldosteronism predispose to hyperkalaemia.
Countercurrent Multiplier
(1) the loop of Henle multiplier
— active NaCl reabsorption from the water-impermeable thick ascending limb, amplified by the hairpin geometry, generates the medullary osmotic gradient;
(2) the vasa recta exchanger
— slow, hairpin medullary blood flow allows passive countercurrent exchange of solute and water and so preserves rather than washes out the gradient;
(3) the collecting duct
— under the control of ADH (V2 receptor → aquaporin-2 insertion), tubular water equilibrates with the hypertonic medulla, concentrating urine to a maximum of ~1200–1400 mOsm/kg.
Renal Tubular Acidosis
normal anion gap, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis
arising from a primary defect in renal tubular acid–base handling rather than from diarrhoeal bicarbonate loss or excess acid production. Three clinically important patterns are recognised
Type 1 (distal)
α-intercalated cells in the collecting duct fail to secrete H⁺ via the H⁺-ATPase/H⁺-K⁺-ATPase, so urine cannot be acidified — urine pH remains >5.5 even during a systemic acid load. Hypokalaemia (impaired H⁺ secretion drives compensatory K⁺ loss), nephrocalcinosis and renal stones (alkaline urine with hypercalciuria and low citrate) are typical. Causes include Sjögren's syndrome and other autoimmune disease, and amphotericin B toxicity.
Type 2 (proximal)
Impaired proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption causes bicarbonate wasting. Urine is initially alkaline while filtered bicarbonate exceeds the reduced reabsorptive threshold, but once plasma bicarbonate falls to the new (lower) threshold, the distal nephron can still acidify urine to pH <5.5. Hypokalaemia occurs (increased distal Na⁺ delivery drives K⁺ secretion). Often part of a generalised proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi syndrome — glycosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria); causes include acetazolamide and myeloma-related light-chain tubular injury.
Type 4
Aldosterone deficiency or tubular resistance to aldosterone reduces distal Na⁺ reabsorption and H⁺/K⁺ secretion, and impairs ammoniagenesis (hyperkalaemia itself further suppresses proximal ammonia production). Hyperkalaemia is the hallmark, and urine pH is often <5.5 despite the acidosis because the remaining acid-secretory capacity is intact. Common causes are diabetic nephropathy (hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism), ACE inhibitors/ARBs, spironolactone/eplerenone and trimethoprim (blocks ENaC, mimicking aldosterone resistance).

Diuretic Resistance in Critical Care
Diuretic resistance
is failure to achieve adequate natriuresis and decongestion despite escalating loop-diuretic doses. Reduced renal perfusion and tubular drug delivery in cardiorenal syndrome, acute tolerance (the “braking phenomenon”), and chronic distal convoluted-tubule hypertrophy all promote downstream sodium reclamation
Recognise and optimise
Confirm congestion, adherence, adequate perfusion and exclude urinary obstruction.
Use an adequate IV loop dose; assess early urine output and urinary sodium response.
Repeated boluses or continuous infusion can maintain tubular exposure; infusion is not universally superior, so titrate to response.
Sequential nephron blockade
Add a thiazide or thiazide-like drug such as metolazone to block compensatory distal NaCl uptake.
Consider acetazolamide to inhibit proximal bicarbonate-linked sodium reabsorption.
Monitor volume status, Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, acid–base balance and renal function closely.
This stepwise, response-guided approach is supported by the ESICM expert consensus on acute diuretic use and diuretic resistance in critically ill patients with AKI

Acid-Base Handling
Bicarbonate reabsorption
About 85% of filtered HCO₃⁻ is reclaimed indirectly in the PCT. NHE3 secretes H⁺ into the lumen, where it combines with filtered HCO₃⁻ to form H₂CO₃. Brush-border carbonic anhydrase IV converts this to CO₂ and H₂O, which enter the cell. Intracellular carbonic anhydrase II reforms H₂CO₃ and then H⁺ plus HCO₃⁻: H⁺ is recycled through NHE3, while HCO₃⁻ leaves across the basolateral membrane through the Na⁺/HCO₃⁻ cotransporter. This reclaims filtered bicarbonate but does not itself excrete net acid
proximal-tubule glutamine is metabolised through glutamate to α-ketoglutarate, generating two NH₄⁺ and two new HCO₃⁻ ions per glutamine.
Proximal secretion:
NH₄⁺ substitutes for H⁺ on NHE3 and enters the tubular lumen while newly generated bicarbonate returns to blood.
Medullary recycling:
NH₄⁺ substitutes for K⁺ on NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and accumulates in the medullary interstitium.
Ammonia trapping and transport:
NH₃ entry, including protein-mediated transport, combines with hydrogen secretion to produce urinary NH₄⁺. The simple diffusion-trapping model does not explain all epithelial transport. Chronic acidosis increases this adaptive pathway
Renal Endocrine Function
granular juxtaglomerular cells release renin when afferent-arteriolar stretch falls, macula-densa NaCl delivery falls, or renal sympathetic β₁ stimulation rises. Renin cleaves hepatic angiotensinogen → angiotensin I; ACE forms angiotensin II, which causes vasoconstriction and stimulates adrenal aldosterone release.
peritubular interstitial fibroblasts sense tissue hypoxia. Stabilised hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) activates the EPO gene, increasing marrow erythropoiesis.
Vitamin D:
proximal-tubule 1α-hydroxylase converts 25-OH vitamin D to active 1,25-(OH)₂D₃. PTH stimulates the enzyme; FGF23 and high phosphate inhibit it. Calcitriol increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption.
Local prostaglandins:
PGE₂ and PGI₂ preserve afferent-arteriolar vasodilation and renal blood flow, especially during low effective circulating volume. NSAID inhibition removes this protection and can precipitate AKI
Pressure Natriuresis & Diuresis
a rise in renal arterial pressure produces a steep increase in sodium (natriuresis) and water (diuresis) excretion; a fall in pressure produces avid sodium retention.
Because autoregulation holds RBF and GFR nearly constant between about 80 and 180 mmHg, the response is chiefly
rather than filtration-driven. Higher perfusion pressure raises renal interstitial hydrostatic pressure (helped by a rigid capsule and medullary blood flow that is less well autoregulated), which reduces proximal tubule and loop of Henle sodium reabsorption — partly through internalisation of NHE3 and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase — and increases back-leak of reabsorbed sodium. Reduced renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone, and local nitric oxide and prostaglandins, reinforce the effect.
Pressure natriuresis provides the infinite-gain feedback loop for long-term blood pressure control: sodium balance can only be restored at a pressure that matches intake. A steep curve lets the kidney clear a salt load with a minimal pressure rise, whereas RAAS activation, sympathetic drive, renal disease or nephron loss shifts the curve rightwards and flattens it, so a higher pressure is required for the same excretion — the basis of salt-sensitive hypertension. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, mineralocorticoid antagonists and diuretics reset the curve leftwards
Perioperative relevance: hypotension, raised intra-abdominal pressure and venous congestion all reduce the transrenal pressure gradient and interstitial pressure changes that drive natriuresis, contributing to oliguria and fluid accumulation in critical illness.

The high-yield values that anchor most renal viva questions.
How is glomerular filtration rate regulated?
Autoregulation maintains GFR over MAP 80–180 mmHg via two mechanisms: myogenic (afferent arteriole constricts in response to stretch) and tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa senses distal tubule Na⁺/Cl⁻ → adenosine release → afferent constriction). Below MAP 80 mmHg, autoregulation fails and GFR becomes pressure-dependent — at risk in shock, ACEi use, NSAIDs.
What is the difference between osmolar and free-water clearance?
Osmolar clearance = (U_osm × V) / P_osm — volume of plasma cleared of all solute per minute. Free-water clearance = urine volume − osmolar clearance; positive in water diuresis (dilute urine, e.g. DI), negative in water conservation (concentrated urine, e.g. SIADH). Together they describe the kidney
How do loop diuretics and thiazides differ in mechanism and side effects?
Loop (furosemide) — blocks Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter in thick ascending limb; potent diuresis up to 25 % of filtered Na⁺. Side effects: hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, ototoxicity, hypovolaemia. Thiazide (bendroflumethiazide) — blocks Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in distal convoluted tubule; modest diuresis (~5 %), but causes hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia, hypercalcaemia and hyponatraemia.

A steep curve lets the kidney clear a salt load with a minimal pressure rise, whereas RAAS activation, sympathetic drive, renal disease or nephron loss shifts the curve rightwards and flattens it, so a higher pressure is required for the same excretion — the basis of salt-sensitive hypertension. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, mineralocorticoid antagonists and diuretics reset the curve leftwards <InlineRef topicId=

Delivers blood from interlobular artery to glomerulus. Dilated by prostaglandins (PGE₂/PGI₂ — blocked by NSAIDs → ↓GFR). Myogenic autoregulation + tubuloglomerular feedback maintain constant GFR over MAP 80–180 mmHg. Constricted by sympathetic stimulation and angiotensin II (but less than efferent).
PGE₂/PGI₂ → vasodilation; sympathetic → constriction
Exits glomerulus. Preferentially constricted by angiotensin II → maintains GFR when perfusion pressure drops (↑filtration fraction). ACE inhibitors dilate efferent → ↓GFR (renoprotective in diabetic nephropathy). In cortical nephrons gives rise to peritubular capillaries; in juxtamedullary nephrons gives rise to vasa recta that descend into the medulla.
Lies in the renal cortex. GFR ≈ 125 mL/min (180 L/day). Three-layer barrier: fenestrated endothelium (70–100 nm pores), glomerular basement membrane (type IV collagen + heparan sulphate — negative charge barrier), podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms (nephrin — 25–60 nm). Filters molecules <70 kDa; negatively charged proteins repelled. Net filtration pressure ≈ 15 mmHg = (P_GC 50 − P_BC 10) − (π_GC 25 − π_BC 0). Mesangial cells contract (ANG II) to ↓Kf.
Ultrafiltration (size + charge selective)
Entirely cortical. Reabsorbs 65–70% Na⁺/H₂O (isotonic), ALL glucose (SGLT2 apical + GLUT2 basolateral, Tm 375 mg/min), ALL amino acids, 85% HCO₃⁻ (CA II/IV + NHE3 — acetazolamide target), 65% K⁺. Brush border ↑surface area ×40. Abundant mitochondria power basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Secretes organic acids (PAH — basis of RPF), drugs (penicillin, furosemide), creatinine. The straight portion (pars recta) descends into the outer medulla.
Descends from cortex through outer medulla into inner medulla. Highly permeable to water via AQP1 (constitutive — not ADH-dependent), impermeable to solutes. Water moves out by osmosis into hypertonic medullary interstitium (300→1200 mOsm/kg at papilla tip). Tubular fluid becomes progressively concentrated. Thin epithelium with few mitochondria.
Inner medullary segment (only present in juxtamedullary nephrons with long loops). Impermeable to water (no aquaporins). Passive NaCl reabsorption down concentration gradient. Tubular fluid begins to dilute. Thin flat epithelium — passive component of countercurrent multiplier.
Outer medullary segment, ascends back to cortex. NKCC2 (Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻) on apical membrane — PRIMARY TARGET OF LOOP DIURETICS. Impermeable to water →

Senses tubular [NaCl] via apical NKCC2: ↓NaCl → adenosine ↓ → afferent dilation + renin release → ↑GFR (tubuloglomerular feedback). ↑NaCl → adenosine ↑ → afferent constriction → ↓GFR.
Cortical. NCC (Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter) on apical membrane — TARGET OF THIAZIDE DIURETICS. Reabsorbs 5% filtered Na⁺. Cortical segment. PRINCIPAL cells — apical ENaC (aldosterone-sensitive → amiloride/spironolactone targets) + ROMK (K⁺ secretion). INTERCALATED cells: Type A (α) — apical H⁺-ATPase, basolateral AE1 (acid secretion); Type B (β) — apical pendrin (alkali secretion). ADH → V2R → cAMP → AQP2 insertion into apical membrane.
Descends through outer and inner medulla to papilla, draining into ducts of Bellini. Final concentration of urine. ADH-dependent water reabsorption (AQP2 apical, AQP3/4 basolateral). Hairpin capillary loops arising from efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons, running PARALLEL to the loop of Henle. Descending vasa recta (DVR): continuous endothelium with UT-B and AQP1. Ascending vasa recta (AVR): fenestrated endothelium. Functions as countercurrent EXCHANGER (not multiplier): sluggish flow allows equilibration with interstitium without washing out the medullary gradient. Medullary blood flow only 5–10% of total RBF — protective for gradient, but the outer medulla is vulnerable to ischaemic injury (ATN).
Cortical capillary network arising from efferent arterioles of cortical (superficial) nephrons. Wrap around PCT, DCT and CCD in the cortex. Low hydrostatic pressure + high oncotic pressure (post-glomerular plasma is concentrated) favour reabsorption of fluid from cortical tubules into the bloodstream.
