Tall cuboidal epithelium with dense brush border (microvilli ×40 surface area) and abundant basolateral mitochondria. Reabsorbs 65–70% of filtered Na⁺, all glucose, amino acids, and 85% HCO₃⁻. Basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the primary driving force for all secondary active transport.
Tall cuboidal cells, water-impermeable ('diluting segment'). NKCC2 on the apical membrane is the key transporter. K⁺ recycling via ROMK creates a +8 mV lumen-positive potential driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption. Reabsorbs 25% of filtered Na⁺.
NCC (Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter) on apical membrane reabsorbs ~5% filtered Na⁺. Active transcellular Ca²⁺ reabsorption via apical TRPV5 → calbindin → basolateral NCX and PMCA, stimulated by PTH and 1,25(OH)₂D₃.
Aldosterone-sensitive. ENaC (epithelial Na⁺ channel) on the apical membrane allows Na⁺ entry, creating a lumen-negative potential that drives K⁺ secretion via ROMK. ADH → V2 receptor → cAMP → AQP2 vesicle exocytosis into apical membrane → water reabsorption. Basolateral AQP3/4 are constitutive.
Collecting Duct — Acid Secretion

# Hepatic Physiology Hepatic blood supply, acinar zones, drug metabolism, synthetic function, LFTs Zonation is a gradient, not three sealed compartments The acinus describes tissue according to its access to incoming blood. Portal venous and hepatic arterial blood mix in the sinusoids and flow towards terminal hepatic venules. Hepatocytes nearer inflow encounter a different oxygen and substrate environment from those downstream. Bile flows in the opposite direction through canaliculi towards portal bile ducts. The classical lobule, centred on a central vein, and the perfusion-based acinus are complementary models of the same tissue rather than competing organs. Periportal cells favour oxidative metabolism and glucose production; pericentral cells favour glycolysis and several pathways of xenobiotic metabolism. These are preferential distributions, not statements that a function occurs exclusively in one zone. Oxygen availability interacts with Wnt/β-catenin signalling, hormones, nutrition and other regulatory signals. The review describes zonation as dynamic: the patterns can change with physiological state and disease, and experimental gradients are not fixed bedside oxygen targets. Serial ammonia clearance combines different metabolic strategies The conventional model combines upstream urea synthesis with a small pericentral population expressing glutamine synthetase that scavenges escaping ammonia. These pathways have different kinetic properties, but their distribution is not absolute: in a perfused-rat-liver experiment, urea production was more uniformly distributed at low ammonia concentrations and became periportal-predominant at higher concentrations. This is an important limit on turning a zonal diagram into a rigid rule. A plasma ammonia value alone does not determine the severity of encephalopathy. Connect location to injury without overgeneralising The downstream region has less oxygen available and is vulnerable when oxygen delivery falls. Delivery depends on blood flow and arterial oxygen content, not arterial pressure alone; congestion can also impair effective perfusion. For chemicals requiring metabolic activation, zonal enzyme distribution can determine where reactive products form. Thus the common centrilobular pattern of injury has more than one possible mechanism, and “zone 3” is not a diagnosis of a particular toxin. Do not teach that every toxin, every infection or all liver disease follows a universal three-zone sequence. Different substrates, enzyme patterns and disease mechanisms produce different distributions. Nor does the model justify choosing an anaesthetic dose from a zone label: drug handling also depends on whole-organ perfusion, intrinsic clearance, binding, shunting and extrahepatic elimination. Apply the model to a perioperative explanation Identify the insult: reduced inflow, reduced oxygen content, outflow congestion or a specific metabolic injury. Explain why the downstream cells may be disproportionately affected rather than simply saying “the liver is hypoxic”. Distinguish a marker of cell injury from a measure of organ function; zonation does not turn an aminotransferase concentration into a quantitative clearance measurement. State the model's limits: human tissue has continuous, variable distributions, and much mechanistic evidence derives from experimental systems. Learning check: does normal arterial saturation exclude hepatic hypoxia? No. Saturation is only one determinant of oxygen content, and delivery also requires adequate blood flow. Anaemia, reduced cardiac output and impaired hepatic perfusion can compromise oxygen delivery despite normal saturation; downstream cells start with less oxygen reserve. The zonation model explains vulnerability but does not provide a stand-alone treatment threshold. >Apply the model to a perioperative explanation

Phaeochromocytoma preparation
Every patient with a functional phaeochromocytoma or paraganglioma should have blockade before surgery, and preparation should include a high-sodium diet and fluid intake to prevent hypotension after the tumour is removed
. Both phenoxybenzamine (non-selective) and doxazosin (selective α₁) are used: in the PRESCRIPT trial the time spent outside blood-pressure targets during resection did not differ between them, although phenoxybenzamine prevented more haemodynamic instability
. A β-blocker is added only once α-blockade is established, to control tachycardia, and never before it
. Duration of blockade, starting doses and haemodynamic targets vary between centres; follow local endocrine protocols.
Cushing's syndrome
Excess glucocorticoid may be iatrogenic, pituitary ACTH-driven (Cushing's disease), adrenal, or from ectopic ACTH. Surgical resection of the causal lesion is generally first-line. Before surgery, cortisol-dependent comorbidities need monitoring and treatment: diabetes, hypertension, hypokalaemia, infection, osteoporosis, psychiatric disorders and poor physical fitness. The guideline suggests perioperative venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and patients left hypocortisolaemic after surgical remission need glucocorticoid replacement and education about adrenal insufficiency
Conn's syndrome
Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension, often with hypokalaemia. Unilateral disease, confirmed by adrenal venous sampling, is best treated by laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, or patients unsuitable for surgery, are treated primarily with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
. Correct potassium and control blood pressure before elective surgery, and plan postoperative potassium and blood-pressure checks with the endocrine team.
Thyroid hormones
: T₄ (prohormone) → T₃ (active, intracellular receptors). ↑ BMR, ↑ O₂ consumption, ↑ CO. 99% protein-bound (TBG). Hypothyroidism: ↑ sensitivity to anaesthetics, ↓ MAC.

Assume adrenal suppression

Watch for addisonian crisis
: unexplained hypotension unresponsive to fluid and vasopressors, tachycardia, nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, confusion or fever. Treat immediately with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, 0.9% saline and glucose — do not wait for cortisol results.
Afferent neural (nociceptive) triggers
Tissue injury activates peripheral nociceptors; signals travel via A-delta and C fibres through the dorsal horn and spinothalamic tracts to the hypothalamus and brainstem, driving both sympathetic outflow and CRH/ACTH release. Depth and site of surgery, and the completeness of neural blockade, determine the size of this afferent drive
Humoral / inflammatory triggers
Damaged tissue releases IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α from macrophages and injured cells, activates the complement cascade and generates local prostaglandins and bradykinin. These mediators act independently of the neural afferent pathway — the response persists even under dense neuraxial block, though it is attenuated — and IL-6 is the best-correlated marker of surgical severity
Hormonal response
: loses its normal diurnal pattern and rises in proportion to surgical severity, promoting gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, protein catabolism and sodium retention, and suppressing the inflammatory/immune response.
: adrenaline and noradrenaline rise acutely, driving tachycardia, hypertension, glycogenolysis and lipolysis.
growth hormone
rise and add to gluconeogenesis and lipolysis, while GH also promotes insulin resistance via IGF pathways.
: secretion is initially reduced (α-adrenergic inhibition of β-cells) and peripheral insulin resistance develops in skeletal muscle and liver, producing surgical/stress hyperglycaemia even with normal or raised insulin levels later in the response.
Thyroid axis
: peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 falls (reduced 5'-deiodinase activity) producing a transient "low T3 (sick euthyroid)" state with low-normal TSH and T4 — a physiological adaptation, not primary hypothyroidism, and does not require thyroxine replacement.
Metabolic, fluid/electrolyte and haemostatic consequences
: net whole-body catabolic state — gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis and lipolysis provide substrate, while accelerated skeletal-muscle protein breakdown produces hyperglycaemia and a negative nitrogen balance that can impair wound healing and increase susceptibility to infection, particularly after major or prolonged surgery.
Fluid and electrolytes
: ADH and aldosterone rise, driving renal sodium and water retention with oliguria, and increased potassium excretion; the retained free water relative to sodium can produce a dilutional hyponatraemia, especially if hypotonic fluids are given.
Haemostasis and immunity
: a prothrombotic state develops from platelet activation, increased fibrinogen and factor VIII, and inhibition of fibrinolysis, contributing to perioperative venous thromboembolism risk; transient cell-mediated immunosuppression increases susceptibility to postoperative infection.
The magnitude of the response is broadly proportional to the severity and duration of surgical trauma — minor day-case surgery produces a modest response, whereas major open or emergency surgery produces the largest hormonal and metabolic swings
Ebb phase
(first 24–48 h): hypovolaemia, reduced cardiac output and oxygen consumption, hypothermia and a fall in metabolic rate — a resuscitation-dependent survival phase.
Flow phase
(days to weeks): hypermetabolism with raised cardiac output and oxygen consumption, catabolism of muscle protein and fat, followed by an anabolic recovery phase once the insult resolves.
Mediators beyond cortisol
: catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline) drive glycogenolysis and lipolysis; glucagon and growth hormone add to gluconeogenesis; cytokines IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α trigger the acute-phase response; ADH and aldosterone retain sodium and water.
Metabolic consequences
: insulin resistance and stress hyperglycaemia, protein catabolism with negative nitrogen balance (urinary nitrogen loss up to 15–20 g/day after major surgery), lipolysis, sodium and water retention with a fall in urine output, and hypokalaemia.
Systemic effects
: fever, leucocytosis, thrombocytosis, hepatic acute-phase protein synthesis (CRP, fibrinogen, ferritin) with reduced albumin and transferrin, and transient immunosuppression.
: neuraxial blockade (most effective — an epidural or spinal to T4 is particularly effective for lower-body/lower-abdominal surgery as it interrupts the afferent neural limb), regional analgesia techniques more generally, effective opioid analgesia (high-dose fentanyl substantially blunts the ACTH-cortisol response to cardiac surgery), minimally invasive/laparoscopic surgery (reduces tissue trauma and cytokine release), maintaining normothermia, preoperative carbohydrate loading and the wider ERAS bundle, and good perioperative glucose control — none abolishes the response completely, and neural blockade attenuates it most effectively when applied before incision
Steroid cover

Diabetic patient

SIADH vs cerebral salt wasting
: both hyponatraemic but volume status differs (euvolaemic vs hypovolaemic) — gets the fluid plan right.

Surgical Stress Response
Describe the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis response to surgical stress.
Surgical stimulus → hypothalamic CRH → anterior pituitary ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol (peaks at 4–6 h, may reach 200–500 mg/day vs basal 30 mg/day for major surgery). Cortisol promotes gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, protein catabolism, sodium retention, immunosuppression, and permissive action on catecholamines. Regional anaesthesia and opioids attenuate this response.
What is the perioperative steroid replacement regimen for adrenal suppression?
Patients on >5 mg prednisolone/day for >3 weeks are at risk of HPA suppression. Replacement scaled to surgical stress: minor — usual dose + 25 mg hydrocortisone at induction. Moderate — 25 mg at induction + 100 mg/day for 24 h. Major — 100 mg at induction + 200 mg/day for 48–72 h, then taper. Avoid abrupt withdrawal — addisonian crisis is life-threatening.
What are the perioperative implications of thyroid disease?
Hyperthyroidism — risk of thyroid storm if untreated; defer elective surgery until euthyroid. Treat with carbimazole + β-blocker; consider Lugol

# Foetal Circulation Foetal shunts, HbF, transitional circulation, persistent pulmonary hypertension Birth changes preload as well as vascular resistance Before birth, the placenta supplies gas exchange and a low-resistance vascular bed. Pulmonary resistance is high and pulmonary blood flow is relatively low. Umbilical venous blood contributes importantly to left ventricular filling through the ductus venosus and foramen ovale. The ventricles therefore operate largely in parallel rather than in the fully serial postnatal arrangement. Cord clamping removes the placental circuit, increases systemic resistance and interrupts umbilical venous return. These are separate changes: afterload rises while a source of preload disappears. If pulmonary blood flow has not yet increased, pulmonary venous return cannot immediately replace the placental contribution to left ventricular filling. A resistance-only explanation misses this vulnerable interval. Aeration establishes a replacement source of left-heart filling Aeration and falling pulmonary resistance increase pulmonary blood flow. Pulmonary venous return then becomes the major source of left ventricular preload. This is not merely a change of oxygen source: it is a handover in the circulation supplying the left heart. Effective aeration, vascular adaptation and cardiac function must work together. Bhatt and colleagues studied preterm lambs, comparing ventilation before clamping with clamping first and delaying ventilation. Ventilating first produced more stable cardiovascular transition. This is mechanistic animal evidence, not a human trial establishing a universal cord-clamping interval or a reason to delay necessary resuscitation. It does not compare every modern cord-management strategy. Flow direction and closure are different events Flow through a patent communication follows its pressure gradient. As pulmonary and systemic resistances change, shunt direction can change before anatomical closure occurs. Increasing pulmonary venous return changes atrial pressure relationships. Functional closure, permanent remodelling and reversal of flow are distinct processes, not one simultaneous switch. High pulmonary resistance may prevent the expected transition. Conversely, a patent ductus can be essential in duct-dependent congenital disease. Neither a patent ductus nor a single saturation value alone establishes adequate circulation: underlying anatomy, flow and pressure relationships matter. Build a causal viva explanation Identify the fetal sources of oxygenation and ventricular filling, rather than listing shunt names alone. Separate the effects of clamping on afterload and venous return. Explain how increased pulmonary flow supplies the left heart after aeration. Describe how poor aeration, abnormal pulmonary resistance or congenital anatomy can disrupt this sequence. # Pharmacokinetic Principles Compartment models, volume of distribution, clearance, half-life Neonates have more body water, less fat and protein binding, immature CYP/glucuronidation pathways and low GFR. Older adults have less water and lean mass, more fat, lower hepatic blood flow and falling renal clearance: hydrophilic loading volumes fall, while lipophilic terminal half-lives lengthen. Fat expands the apparent Vd of lipophilic drugs far more than hydrophilic drugs. Total-body-weight dosing can overdose many induction drugs; use ideal, lean or adjusted body weight according to the drug and whether calculating a loading or maintenance dose. Liver failure reduces flow, enzyme capacity and albumin; renal failure reduces renal clearance and permits active metabolites to accumulate. Examples: erythromycin/clarithromycin, fluconazole and other azoles, cimetidine and grapefruit juice inhibit CYP3A4 → reduced metabolism and prolonged effect of midazolam, fentanyl and alfentanil, and statin toxicity Enzyme induction requires increased enzyme synthesis, so develops and resolves over days to weeks; rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin and chronic ethanol increase metabolism of midazolam and opioids (and raise volatile/paracetamol metabolism via CYP2E1 with ethanol). Protein-binding displacement transiently raises free drug. It matters most for highly bound, narrow-therapeutic-window drugs such as warfarin, although redistribution and increased clearance often limit the duration. Clinical Application Clearance (Cl) is the volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time: Cl = elimination rate / plasma concentration . Total clearance is additive: = Cl + Cl The organ extraction ratio is the fraction removed in one pass: ER = (C − C ) / C , and organ clearance approximates blood flow × ER. High-ER (>0.7) drugs such as propofol, lidocaine and morphine are flow-limited. Low-ER (<0.3) drugs such as warfarin, diazepam and phenytoin are capacity-limited and depend more on unbound fraction and intrinsic enzyme activity Renal clearance is the net result of three processes. Glomerular filtration handles only drug — a highly protein-bound drug such as warfarin is filtered poorly regardless of GFR, so changes in free fraction matter more than changes in total concentration. Active tubular secretion in the proximal tubule uses OAT and OCT transporters and is not limited by protein binding, so clearance can exceed GFR; penicillins, methotrexate and diuretics are secreted this way, and probenecid competitively blocks the anionic transporter (historically used to prolong penicillin levels). Passive tubular reabsorption returns lipid-soluble, un-ionised drug to the blood down the concentration gradient created by water reabsorption. Because only the un-ionised form is reabsorbed, urine pH manipulation alters excretion: urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate ionises weak acids such as salicylate and phenobarbitone, trapping them in the tubular lumen and increasing elimination; acidification would conversely trap weak bases. Because propofol is no longer used for long-term sedation in children, it analysed child and adult cases separately. Its evidence is case reports, so it describes associations and the pattern of reported cases. It cannot give incidence or prove a safe dose. Different phenotypes: lipidaemia, fever and hepatomegaly were more frequent in children. Rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia were more frequent in adults. Markers of death in adults: ECG changes, hypotension, hyperkalaemia, traumatic brain injury and a mean infusion rate above 5 mg/kg/h were independently associated with mortality. In children, fever and hepatomegaly were. Dose relationship: in adults, higher cumulative propofol dose was associated with more clinical features and more organ systems involved. This is why both rate and duration matter, not a single threshold. Brugada-like ECG changes and progression to bradyarrhythmia are described in case reports. Prevention on ICU: use the lowest effective dose, combine with other sedatives or analgesia rather than escalating propofol, and give adequate carbohydrate. Understanding their mechanisms, pharmacokinetics, and clinical profiles is a core FRCA topic. The primary agents in current practice are propofol, thiopentone, ketamine, and etomidate.

Target-controlled infusion (TCI) uses pharmacokinetic models (e.g. Marsh, Schnider, Eleveld) to achieve and maintain a target plasma or effect-site concentration. Marsh (weight-based) and Schnider (age, weight, height, LBM) were derived in specific adult populations, whereas the Eleveld model (2018) is a universal model designed for a wide range of ages and body weights Formulations & Carrier Solutions

    Considerations in Specific Populations

      Adjust bolus, infusion rate, and patient covariates to see how the Marsh and Schnider models predict plasma (Cp) and effect-site (Ce) concentration over time. Note the hysteresis between Cp and Ce — the rationale for effect-site targeting.

A rare but often fatal complication of prolonged, high-dose propofol infusion. Propofol inhibits the mitochondrial electron transport chain and fatty-acid β-oxidation, producing metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and cardiovascular collapse. Classic thresholds are > 4 mg/kg/h for > 48 h, but it can occur with shorter exposures in susceptible patients The Eleveld model (2018) is a single propofol model derived from a pooled dataset of more than 1,000 subjects ranging from neonates to the very elderly and BMI 12–52. It uses allometric scaling, a maturation function, and fat-free mass — replacing the need to choose between Schnider, Marsh and paediatric models. Compare the two side by side at population extremes.

Intra-operative movement is consistently reported more frequently with propofol TIVA than with an equivalent MAC-guided volatile technique. The difference is not because propofol is a hypnotic — it is because of where each class of agent acts to produce immobility and how reliably we can measure an adequate dose at the bedside.

  • Site of immobility. Volatile agents produce immobility largely at the spinal cord (glycine and GABA_A receptors, and inhibition of dorsal-horn transmission). Propofol for propofol. With volatiles, end-tidal monitoring lets you titrate to a known ED₅₀ (and run 1.2–1.3 MAC for surgical stimulation). With TIVA you target a modelled plasma or effect-site concentration — population PK models (Marsh, Schnider, Eleveld) carry a typical bias of 20–30%, so the actual Ce can be well below the value displayed.
  • Pharmacokinetic variability. Volume of distribution, clearance, body composition, cardiac output and drug interactions all shift the true Ce. An obese, high-cardiac-output or enzyme-induced patient may sit substantially below the target Ce — and therefore move — without any change on the pump display.
  • Hysteresis and effect-site lag. After a step-up in target, equilibration between plasma and effect site takes minutes. If surgical stimulus increases before Ce catches up (skin incision, laryngoscopy, peritoneal traction), the patient can move despite an target.
  • Loss of opioid synergy. Propofol provides little intrinsic analgesia, so adequate immobility on TIVA is highly dependent on a co-administered opioid (typically remifentanil). Under-dosing or pump occlusion of the opioid line is a classic cause of intra-operative movement on TIVA.
  • Equipment failure modes. Volatile delivery failures are visible on the vaporiser dial and end-tidal trace. TIVA failures (line disconnection, extravasation, three-way tap left off, IV cannula tissued) deliver drug into the dressings instead of the patient — the pump runs normally but Ce falls rapidly.
  • No real-time depth marker. End-tidal volatile concentration is a continuous, validated surrogate for brain partial pressure. There is no equivalent for propofol — processed-EEG monitors (BIS/Entropy) are the recommended substitute, and the Association of Anaesthetists advises their routine use whenever TIVA is combined with neuromuscular blockade Practical implication: when running TIVA, pair propofol with a remifentanil infusion (or adequate intermittent opioid), use processed-EEG monitoring (especially with NMB), inspect the IV site and giving set frequently, and anticipate stimulating moments by raising the effect-site target several minutes in advance.

Context-sensitive half-time is the time for the central-compartment plasma concentration to fall by 50% after stopping an infusion of a specified duration. Propofol combines rapid metabolic clearance with redistribution, so its CSHT remains relatively short after infusions up to about eight hours, supporting predictable TIVA recovery. Thiopentone progressively fills fat and other peripheral compartments and has capacity-limited metabolism at high exposure, so its CSHT becomes very long; it is unsuitable for maintenance by infusion. Midazolam also accumulates with duration, whereas remifentanil remains near 3–4 minutes because ester hydrolysis is rapid and context-independent Thiobarbiturate. Induction dose 3–5 mg/kg Mechanism: GABA_A agonist (opens chloride channel directly at high doses, potentiates at low doses). CNS: powerful anticonvulsant, cerebral protectant (reduces CMRO₂). Other: porphyria is an absolute contraindication. Histamine release. No analgesic properties.

Cardiovascular effects: the dominant vascular action is venodilation — dilatation of capacitance vessels causes blood to pool in the splanchnic and peripheral venous beds, so venous return and preload fall, reducing stroke volume, cardiac output and arterial pressure. A baroreceptor-mediated tachycardia follows, which raises myocardial oxygen demand and is poorly tolerated in ischaemic heart disease or fixed-output states (aortic stenosis, tamponade). Superimposed direct negative inotropy compounds the fall in output, and histamine release may add a further drop in tone. This is a different mechanism from propofol, whose hypotension is driven mainly by arterial (arteriolar) vasodilation with reduced SVR and blunting of the baroreflex, so heart rate does not rise. Practical consequence: in hypovolaemia, where preload is already reduced, thiopentone produces exaggerated hypotension — reduce the dose, give it slowly, and restore volume first Phencyclidine derivative. Unique Properties

Ketamine is the only IV induction agent that provides significant analgesia. It can be given IM (useful for uncooperative patients/children). It has anti-inflammatory properties and is increasingly used in sub-anaesthetic doses for chronic pain and treatment-resistant depression.

Imidazole derivative. Dose 0.3 mg/kg IV. Most haemodynamically stable induction agent — minimal effect on HR, BP, or cardiac output. Ideal for patients with limited cardiovascular reserve. ~75% protein-bound: less affected by albumin changes than propofol or thiopentone, but the dose should still be reduced in hypoalbuminaemia.

Mechanism: GABA_A receptor (selective for β₂/β₃ subunit). Problems: adrenocortical suppression (inhibits 11β-hydroxylase — even a single dose suppresses cortisol for up to 24 hours). Pain on injection. Myoclonus (not seizure activity). High incidence of PONV. Not recommended for infusion due to adrenal suppression.

Water-soluble imidazobenzodiazepine. The diazepine ring is open and ionised at pH 3.5 (vial), making it injectable without solvent; at physiological pH the ring closes and the molecule becomes highly lipid-soluble, accounting for its rapid CNS penetration. Doses: sedation 0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV, induction 0.2–0.3 mg/kg, premed 0.5 mg/kg PO (paeds).

Mechanism: positive allosteric modulator at the α/γ interface of GABA-A receptors — increases frequency of chloride channel opening (barbiturates increase duration). Selectivity for α₁-containing receptors mediates sedation, anterograde amnesia and anticonvulsant action; α₂/α₃ mediate anxiolysis and muscle relaxation. CVS: mild ↓ SVR, well-preserved cardiac output. RS: dose-dependent respiratory depression, synergistic with opioids.

PK: t½ 1.5–2.5 h, Vd 1.0–1.5 L/kg, 96% protein-bound. Hepatic CYP3A4 → α-hydroxy-midazolam (10% potency) → UGT-glucuronidation to α-hydroxy-midazolam-glucuronide, which is active, water-soluble, and renally excreted. In AKI/CKD the glucuronide accumulates → prolonged sedation for days after stopping an infusion. Reversal: flumazenil 200 µg + 100 µg/min titrated; t½ shorter than midazolam → resedation likely.

Highly selective α₂-adrenergic agonist (α₂ : α₁ ≈ 1620 : 1) — the dextro-isomer of medetomidine. Acts at pre-synaptic α₂A autoreceptors in the locus coeruleus, reducing noradrenaline release and disinhibiting the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO). The result is a NREM-stage-2-like sedation — patients are easily roused, follow commands, and have minimal respiratory depression.

Dosing (Dexdor): maintenance infusion 0.2–1.4 µg/kg/h titrated to RASS. Optional loading dose 1 µg/kg over 10 min produces a transient hypertensive peak (peripheral α₂B vasoconstriction) followed by hypotension and bradycardia (central α₂A) — the characteristic biphasic BP response. Slow infusion without a bolus avoids the initial hypertension.

Other uses: awake fibre-optic intubation, regional block adjunct, paediatric premedication (intranasal), opioid/alcohol withdrawal. SPICE-III (2019) showed non-inferior 90-day mortality vs standard sedation, with more ventilator-free days and less delirium. Cautions: bradycardia, hypotension, hepatic dysfunction (reduce dose), and rebound hypertension on prolonged-use cessation.

Ultra-short-acting ester-based benzodiazepine (Byfavo), granted UK marketing authorisation by the MHRA in 2021 for procedural sedation in adults Mechanism: positive allosteric modulator at the α/γ interface of GABA-A receptors — identical site to midazolam, increasing chloride-channel opening frequency. Dosing (procedural sedation): 5–7 mg IV bolus over 1 min, then 2.5 mg top-ups (≥2 min apart) to effect; onset ~1–3 min, clinical duration ~10 min after a single bolus. PK: context-sensitive half-time ≈ 7–8 min even after prolonged infusion; Vd ~0.9 L/kg; clearance ~70 L/h, independent of CYP metabolism.

CVS/RS: less hypotension than propofol and less respiratory depression than midazolam, but both occur dose-dependently and are synergistic with opioids. Splanchnic and Mesenteric Microcirculation

After haemorrhage, IV anaesthetic agents alter mesenteric microcirculatory flow in different directions. Propofol >Immunomodulation

Propofol has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (structurally related to phenolic free-radical scavengers) but also delivers a significant lipid load with prolonged infusion, which can itself influence immune function. Thiopentone produces dose-dependent immunosuppression, including reduced neutrophil and lymphocyte function at high or sustained exposure. Etomidate > None of the standard IV induction agents is directly nephrotoxic. Renal blood flow and glomerular filtration are largely pressure-dependent, so hypotension from any of these drugs (particularly propofol and thiopentone) can transiently reduce renal perfusion, but this is not a specific drug effect. The exception is propofol infusion syndrome, in which impaired mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation produces rhabdomyolysis; the resulting myoglobinuria can precipitate acute kidney injury as a secondary complication rather than through direct nephrotoxicity.

Hepatic Effects

Propofol has a high hepatic extraction ratio, so its clearance is flow-limited — a fall in hepatic blood flow (from hypotension, high intra-abdominal pressure, or low cardiac output states in critical illness) reduces clearance more than any change in enzyme activity would. A substantial fraction of propofol clearance is extrahepatic (lung and kidney contribute), which partly explains why hepatic impairment alone has a relatively modest effect on single-dose recovery. In critical illness, hypoalbuminaemia increases the free (unbound) fraction of protein-bound agents, altering both effect and apparent clearance despite an unchanged total plasma concentration. None of the standard IV agents produces clinically significant hepatic enzyme induction.

Certain steroid molecules act as positive allosteric modulators of the GABA-A receptor, at a site distinct from benzodiazepines and barbiturates, producing dose-dependent sedation and general anaesthesia. The historical clinical example was alphaxalone/alphadolone (Althesin), a steroid anaesthetic combination used in the 1970s. It was formulated in a Cremophor EL (polyoxyethylated castor oil) vehicle to achieve water solubility, and this vehicle provoked an unacceptable rate of histamine-mediated hypersensitivity reactions, leading to its withdrawal from UK clinical practice in 1984.

Pregnanolone emulsion was subsequently investigated as a lipid-emulsion-based neurosteroid anaesthetic, avoiding the Cremophor EL vehicle problem, with animal data suggesting a shorter-acting and less cumulative profile than Althesin, propofol, thiopentone or midazolam Neurosteroid anaesthesia has re-emerged more recently in the form of cyclodextrin-solubilised alphaxalone, which avoids the Cremophor EL vehicle and is now used in veterinary anaesthesia. Neuroactive steroids more broadly remain of interest in other indications (e.g. status epilepticus and postpartum depression), reflecting continued interest in this receptor site as a target distinct from the benzodiazepine and barbiturate binding sites on GABA-A.

# Volatile Anaesthetic Agents MAC, Meyer-Overton, blood-gas partition coefficient, uptake and distribution From correlation to mechanism: the experiments that moved the field The Meyer–Overton correlation is real, but a correlation with oil solubility does not identify where an anaesthetic acts. Any binding site with a hydrophobic (oil-like) pocket would produce the same relationship. The lipid theory therefore had to be tested with experiments that separate “dissolves in lipid” from “binds a protein”. A lipid-free protein reproduces the correlation. Franks and Lieb showed that firefly luciferase, a soluble protein with no membrane, was inhibited by a wide range of general anaesthetics with potencies that tracked their animal anaesthetic potencies — so the Meyer–Overton relationship can arise from competitive binding to a hydrophobic protein pocket. Optical isomers separate protein from lipid effects. The two mirror-image forms of isoflurane have identical physical properties and identical effects on lipid bilayers, yet differed in their effects on specific nerve ion channels. A purely lipid mechanism cannot distinguish mirror images; a chiral protein site can. Non-immobilisers break the prediction. Koblin and colleagues identified polyhalogenated and perfluorinated compounds whose lipid solubility predicted anaesthetic potency but which did not prevent movement to a noxious stimulus at those concentrations. Some related compounds behaved as “transitional” agents with less potency than predicted. What the modern view does — and does not — claim Current evidence favours direct interactions with a limited set of protein targets (for example GABA and glycine receptors, two-pore-domain K⁺ channels and NMDA receptors), with different agents weighting these targets differently. “Anaesthesia” is also not one end-point: immobility, amnesia and unconsciousness depend on different neuronal pathways and sites, with immobility substantially mediated in the spinal cord. Evidence limits: no single target has been shown to explain all actions of every agent; much of the binding and channel data come from isolated preparations or animal models, and relating a molecular effect to a clinical end-point remains inferential. In exams, present Meyer–Overton as a robust empirical correlation that the protein theory explains, rather than as a disproved idea. Learning check: why do the isoflurane isomer experiments argue against a lipid site? Mirror-image isomers have identical solubility and identical effects on lipid bilayers, so a lipid mechanism predicts identical actions. Different effects on ion channels imply a chiral, protein-based site. Learning check: does the luciferase study prove luciferase is the anaesthetic target? No. It shows that a hydrophobic protein pocket is sufficient to reproduce the Meyer–Overton correlation, so the correlation cannot by itself prove a lipid site. The agents in current clinical use — sevoflurane, desflurane, and isoflurane — differ in their physicochemical properties, which determine their clinical characteristics including speed of onset, recovery, and potency.

All modern volatile agents are halogenated ethers (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, enflurane) or alkanes (halothane). Halogenation with fluorine increases stability and reduces flammability; the size and shape of the molecule influence potency and partition coefficients. Sevoflurane > MAC is defined as the minimum alveolar concentration of an inhaled anaesthetic at 1 atmosphere that prevents movement in response to a standard surgical stimulus in 50% of subjects. It is the ED₅₀ for immobility and provides a measure of anaesthetic potency — a lower MAC = more potent agent.

MAC Multiples in Practice

  • • MAC-awake (0.3-0.5 MAC): concentration at which 50% of patients open eyes to command
  • • MAC-BAR (1.5-1.7 MAC): blocks adrenergic response to surgical incision
  • • MAC-intubation (~1.3 MAC): prevents coughing/movement during laryngoscopy
↓ Decrease MAC
  • • Increasing age (↓ 6% per decade after 40)
  • • Hypothermia
  • • Opioids, benzodiazepines, α₂-agonists
  • • Acute alcohol intoxication
  • • Pregnancy
  • • Hyponatraemia, hypotension, anaemia
  • • Concurrent N₂O or other volatiles (additive)
  • • Young age (MAC peaks at ~6 months)
  • • Hyperthermia
  • • Chronic alcohol use / CNS stimulants
  • • Red hair (MC1R mutation)
  • • Hypernatraemia
    • Note: MAC is NOT affected by gender, duration of anaesthesia, PaCO₂ (within normal range), or PaO₂ above 20 kPa.

    The blood:gas partition coefficient (BGPC) determines the speed of onset and offset. It represents how soluble the agent is in blood relative to the alveolar gas phase. A low BGPC = fast onset because less agent is dissolved in blood, so alveolar (and therefore brain) partial pressure rises rapidly.

    N₂O 0.47 105 1.4 Fastest Desflurane 0.42 6.0 18.7 Very fast Sevoflurane 0.65 2.0 47 Fast Isoflurane 1.46 1.15 91 Moderate Halothane 2.54 0.75 224 Slow
    The Meyer-Overton hypothesis (1899-1901) states that anaesthetic potency correlates with lipid solubility. The oil:gas partition coefficient is inversely proportional to MAC — i.e., the more lipid-soluble an agent, the more potent it is. This elegant relationship holds remarkably well across diverse agents (MAC × oil:gas ≈ constant ≈ 1.82–2.05 atm).

    Limitations of Meyer-Overton

    • • Non-immobilisers: Some highly lipid-soluble compounds (e.g., perfluoroalkanes) do not produce anaesthesia despite predicted potency
    • • Stereoisomers: Enantiomers of isoflurane have different potencies despite identical lipid solubility, implying a specific protein target
    • • Cut-off effect: Beyond a certain chain length in homologous series, potency plateaus or disappears
    • • Temperature anomaly: Does not fully account for temperature-dependent changes in potency

    The Protein Theory (Modern Consensus)

    Current evidence strongly supports that volatile agents act predominantly by binding directly to specific protein targets — particularly ligand-gated ion channels and other membrane proteins. Key molecular targets include:

    Enhanced (Inhibitory) Targets
    • • GABAA receptors: Potentiate inhibitory chloride currents; major contributor to hypnosis and amnesia
    • • Glycine receptors: Enhanced inhibitory transmission in spinal cord; contributes to immobility
    • • Two-pore K⁺ channels (TREK-1, TASK): Activation hyperpolarises neurones
  • • NMDA receptors: Inhibited by N₂O and xenon, reducing glutamatergic transmission
  • • Nicotinic ACh receptors: Inhibited at clinical concentrations
  • • HCN channels: Inhibited by halogenated agents — alters thalamocortical rhythms

    • Components of Anaesthesia

    Immobility (MAC) Spinal cord (ventral horn) Glycine, GABAA, Na⁺ channels Hypnosis Cortex, thalamus GABAA, HCN, TREK-1 Amnesia Hippocampus, amygdala GABAA, nAChR
    The rate of rise of alveolar concentration (FA) towards inspired concentration (FI) determines speed of induction. Factors increasing the rate of rise of FA/FI:

    • • Low blood:gas solubility (less taken up by blood)
    • • High inspired concentration (concentration effect)
    • • High minute ventilation (delivers more agent to alveoli)
    • • Low cardiac output (less blood to carry agent away)
    • • Second gas effect (N₂O uptake concentrates companion agent)
    Distribution to Tissues

    After uptake into blood, tissue partial pressure is determined by regional blood flow and the tissue:blood partition coefficient. The vessel-rich group (brain, heart, liver and kidneys) receives high flow and equilibrates rapidly; muscle has intermediate perfusion and capacity; fat is poorly perfused but has a high fat:blood solubility and therefore forms a large, slow reservoir; vessel-poor tissues such as bone and ligaments equilibrate least. During a long anaesthetic, fat loading is greatest with more soluble agents such as isoflurane. Its later release slows the fall in alveolar partial pressure and prolongs recovery compared with less soluble sevoflurane or desflurane Two phenomena are unique to high-volume gases like nitrous oxide. They are flip-sides of the same large-volume uptake (during induction) and washout (during emergence) across the alveolar–capillary membrane.

    A/FI rises faster than it would alone — a clinically useful accelerator at induction.

    Volatile agents are persistent greenhouse gases. Their 100-year global-warming impact is not equal: desflurane is greatest, followed by isoflurane, then sevoflurane; climate impact also rises with fresh-gas flow and agent consumption Emissions scale with fresh-gas flow × delivered concentration × duration, so low-flow anaesthesia is the single most effective mitigation once the agent has been chosen
  • Use the lowest safe fresh-gas flow, avoiding unnecessary wash-in and prolonged high-flow periods.
  • Avoid desflurane and nitrous oxide where a clinically suitable lower-impact technique exists; consider sevoflurane or TIVA.
  • Use agent capture or recycling systems where validated, while recognising that preventing consumption has the largest immediate benefit.
    • Isoflurane predominantly lowers SVR and can depress myocardium, so cardiac output is less well preserved. At equivalent MAC, sevoflurane and desflurane cause a smaller SVR reduction but a greater fall in cardiac output than isoflurane; overall cardiac output is generally better maintained with sevoflurane than isoflurane. Heart rate: isoflurane and desflurane tend to increase it (baroreflex and, with desflurane, sympathetic activation); sevoflurane is broadly HR-neutral; halothane lowers MAP mainly by depressing contractility and slows the heart. Isoflurane is the most potent coronary vasodilator (historical “coronary steal”). Rapid desflurane increases can cause transient sympathetic tachycardia and hypertension Renal and hepatic effects are largely secondary to perfusion pressure: all agents reduce renal blood flow and GFR in proportion to the fall in mean arterial pressure (with preserved autoregulation above about 80 mmHg), and volatile agents reduce portal venous flow while isoflurane, sevoflurane and desflurane better preserve hepatic arterial flow and total hepatic oxygen delivery than halothane did. Reduced hepatic blood flow also slows clearance of flow-dependent drugs such as propofol, fentanyl and lidocaine. Brief exposure to a volatile agent before an ischaemic insult (anaesthetic preconditioning) or during early reperfusion (postconditioning) reduces ischaemia–reperfusion injury. The mechanisms mirror ischaemic preconditioning: opening of mitochondrial and sarcolemmal ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels, a small burst of reactive oxygen species acting as a signal, activation of protein kinase C and the survival kinase pathways (PI3K–Akt, ERK), nitric oxide signalling, and — the final common step — inhibition of mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening, which preserves ATP synthesis and prevents necrotic and apoptotic cell deathTime course

      Clinical relevance and caveats

      • Meta-analyses of coronary surgery show lower troponin release, less inotrope requirement and shorter ICU stay with volatile-based rather than purely intravenous anaesthesiaOrgan-Protective Effects: Mechanisms and the Clinical Evidence Base

        Anaesthetic preconditioning (agent given before the ischaemic insult) and postconditioning (given at reperfusion) both reduce ischaemia–reperfusion injury through a shared final pathway: opening of mitochondrial and sarcolemmal KATP channels, activation of protein kinase C and downstream survival kinases, a small, tightly controlled burst of reactive oxygen species acting as a trigger rather than causing damage, and — as the decisive convergence point — inhibition of mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening, which prevents the collapse of the mitochondrial membrane potential, preserves ATP generation and limits both necrotic and apoptotic cell death. Reduced neutrophil adhesion and activation at the endothelial surface further limits the inflammatory component of reperfusion injury In cardiac surgery the clinical evidence is strongest: volatile-based anaesthesia is consistently associated with lower peak troponin release, better preserved cardiac index and reduced inotrope requirement compared with propofol-based TIVA in meta-analyses of coronary artery bypass surgery

        Renal and cerebral protection follow the same broad principle (KATP-channel-mediated preconditioning has been demonstrated in kidney and brain models) but human outcome data are limited and inconsistent. In the brain, any protective preconditioning effect must also be weighed against volatile agents >Volatile agents are metabolised mainly by hepatic CYP2E1: halothane ~20%, sevoflurane ~3–5%, isoflurane ~0.2%, desflurane ~0.02%. The more an agent is metabolised, the greater the exposure to reactive metabolites — so desflurane’s negligible metabolism is a safety feature. Sevoflurane produces inorganic fluoride and hexafluoroisopropanol; peak fluoride may exceed the old 50 µmol/L nephrotoxic threshold without clinically significant renal injury (little intrarenal metabolism, unlike methoxyflurane). Compound A forms in the absorbent; UK practice allows low-flow sevoflurane, while US labelling advises ≥1 L/min for exposures >1 MAC-hour. Halothane forms trifluoroacetic acid by oxidation; the mild hepatic dysfunction relates to reductive metabolism or reduced liver oxygenation, whereas the rare fulminant hepatitis is immune-mediated against TFA-altered proteins All potent halogenated agents are contraindicated in malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility Sevoflurane

        Non-pungent, suitable for inhalational induction. Low BGPC allows rapid onset. Metabolised ~5% (produces inorganic fluoride and Compound A via soda lime). Minimal cardiovascular depression. Agent of choice for paediatric inhalational induction.

        Desflurane

        Lowest BGPC of potent agents — fastest recovery. Pungent and irritant to airways, so not suitable for inhalational induction. Requires a heated pressurised vaporizer (TEC 6) due to high SVP (near atmospheric at room temperature). Sympathetic stimulation with rapid increases in concentration.

        Isoflurane

        Higher BGPC means slower onset/offset. Potent coronary vasodilator — theoretical risk of coronary steal. Minimal metabolism (~0.2%). Good muscle relaxation. Commonly used in veterinary anaesthesia and ICU sedation via AnaConDa device.

Step-by-step reasoning
Assess depth: PTC 1 indicates intense (deep) neuromuscular block — neostigmine cannot reverse this depth (requires TOF count ≥2, ideally ≥4).
Choose sugammadex: a modified γ-cyclodextrin that encapsulates rocuronium (and vecuronium) 1:1, removing it from the neuromuscular junction within ~2–3 min regardless of depth.
Dose by depth: PTC 1–2 with no TOF = 16 mg/kg for immediate reversal; TOF count 1–2 = 4 mg/kg; routine reversal at reappearance of T2 = 2 mg/kg.
Confirm reversal objectively: TOF ratio ≥0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. Clinical signs (head-lift, grip) are insufficient.
Counsel and document: sugammadex inactivates hormonal contraceptives for 7 days; rare anaphylaxis (~1:2500); avoid in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) where data are limited.
Common traps
Giving neostigmine at a deep block — ineffective and risks recurarisation.
Forgetting that re-paralysis after sugammadex needs a non-aminosteroid relaxant (e.g. cisatracurium) for 24 h or a much larger rocuronium dose.
Skipping objective TOF monitoring — clinical assessment misses residual paralysis.

Suxamethonium (Succinylcholine): Mechanism of Action, Dose & Side Effects
Phase I block
(depolarising): initial fasciculations, sustained depolarisation → desensitisation. No fade on TOF, no post-tetanic potentiation.
Phase II block
: with repeated/prolonged dosing (cumulative dose >3–5 mg/kg) characteristics resemble non-depolarising block (fade, PTP).
Mechanism of phase II (desensitisation) block
Prolonged exposure to suxamethonium keeps the post-junctional receptor occupied; the membrane gradually
yet remains unresponsive to acetylcholine because the receptor enters a desensitised, non-conducting conformation.
Additional contributions come from ion channel block of the open receptor pore, pre-junctional effects reducing acetylcholine mobilisation, and receptor down-regulation
Clinical signature:
on train-of-four (TOF ratio <0.7), post-tetanic potentiation, tachyphylaxis (escalating dose requirement) and prolonged recovery — indistinguishable at the bedside from non-depolarising block.
Occurs after repeated boluses or an infusion, typically once the cumulative dose exceeds 3–5 mg/kg, and earlier in atypical plasma cholinesterase.
Management: stop suxamethonium, sedate and ventilate, and monitor with a quantitative nerve stimulator. Anticholinesterase reversal is unreliable and may deepen block if any phase I component remains, so it is not routinely recommended.

Pre-existing sensitisation (quaternary ammonium hypothesis):
the immunogenic epitope of NMBAs is the quaternary (or tertiary) ammonium group, which is shared by many everyday products — cosmetics, shampoos, disinfectants, detergents and some drugs, notably the cough suppressant pholcodine. Exposure to these quaternary ammonium compounds can generate IgE that cross-reacts with NMBAs, which is why up to half of patients react on apparent first exposure and why women are over-represented. Population-level pholcodine use correlates with NMBA anaphylaxis rates (high in Norway, low in Sweden), and pholcodine was withdrawn in Europe in 2022 on this basis

Bowman's principle
: less potent non-depolarising NMBAs have a faster onset because a larger absolute dose is required, generating a steeper plasma-to-effect-site concentration gradient and faster nAChR occupancy. This is why rocuronium (low potency, ED₉₅ ~0.3 mg/kg) has a faster onset than vecuronium or cisatracurium (high potency, ED₉₅ ~0.05 mg/kg) at equipotent doses. Onset is further accelerated by:
↑ dose
(2–3 × ED₉₅ for intubation, 3–4 × ED₉₅ for RSI) — steeper gradient.
↑ cardiac output
and high regional muscle blood flow (diaphragm and laryngeal adductors faster than adductor pollicis).
: a sub-paralysing dose (~10% of intubating dose) 3 min before induction occupies spare receptors and shortens onset by ~30 s, at the cost of awake weakness and aspiration risk.
Timing principle
: induce at peak onset of NMBA (loss of TOF at orbicularis oculi) rather than at a fixed time interval.
: anticholinesterase — increases ACh at NMJ to compete with NDMR. Must be given with glycopyrrolate or atropine (to block muscarinic effects: bradycardia, salivation, bronchospasm). Ceiling effect — cannot reverse deep block (TOF count <2). Dose 50 µg/kg.
: modified γ-cyclodextrin. Encapsulates rocuronium (and to lesser extent vecuronium) in a 1:1 complex, rendering it inactive. Can reverse profound block. Dose: 2 mg/kg (moderate block, TOF ≥2), 4 mg/kg (deep block, PTC ≥1), 16 mg/kg (immediate reversal — "can't intubate, can't oxygenate" rescue).
Sugammadex Considerations
Train-of-four (TOF)
: 4 stimuli at 2 Hz. TOF ratio = T4/T1. Ratio <0.9 = clinically significant residual blockade.
Post-tetanic count (PTC)
: for deep block (TOF count 0).
Double burst stimulation (DBS)
: fade easier to detect manually than TOF. Quantitative monitoring (acceleromyography, kinemyography) is recommended over qualitative assessment.
Postoperative residual curarisation (PORC)
is defined as a TOF ratio <0.9 at the adductor pollicis after tracheal extubation. It occurs in up to 30–40% of patients reversed with neostigmine when only qualitative (peripheral nerve stimulator) monitoring is used, and is associated with:
Upper airway obstruction and pharyngeal dysfunction (loss of airway protective reflexes at TOF ratio 0.7–0.9).
Aspiration of pharyngeal contents — silent and clinically unrecognised.
Hypoxaemia and atelectasis in the recovery room.
Increased incidence of postoperative pulmonary complications (pneumonia, reintubation, prolonged ICU stay).
Subjective distress: blurred vision, weakness, inability to swallow or speak clearly.
: quantitative TOF monitoring throughout, reversal guided by TOF count (neostigmine only at TOF count ≥2; sugammadex preferred for deep block), and confirmation of TOF ratio ≥0.9

Rocuronium: Dose, Onset, TOF & Sugammadex Reversal | AnaesthesiaCore Rocuronium bromide is the most widely used non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking drug (NMBD) in modern anaesthesia. It is an , monoquaternary ammonium compound derived from vecuronium with deliberately reduced potency to accelerate onset. Combined with the availability of Mechanism of Action competitive antagonist at the α-subunits of the postjunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) at the motor end-plate. By blocking acetylcholine binding it prevents end-plate depolarisation and propagation of the muscle action potential, producing flaccid paralysis without fasciculations. Block is characterised by fade on TOF post-tetanic potentiation , both reversible — by neostigmine when block is shallow, or by sugammadex at any depth. Cardiovascular effects At clinical doses rocuronium is essentially cardiostable — no ganglion blockade and no significant histamine release, so blood pressure and systemic vascular resistance are maintained. Weak vagolytic (M₂ antagonist) activity at high doses (≥0.9–1.2 mg/kg) may cause a modest rise in heart rate of about 5–10 beats/min; this is far less than pancuronium. Any marked tachycardia, hypotension or cardiovascular collapse after rocuronium should be treated as anaphylaxis rather than a direct drug effect. Because rocuronium does not blunt the sympathetic response to laryngoscopy, an opioid or additional induction agent is still needed in patients where hypertension is hazardous. # Local Anaesthetic Agents Mechanism, pKa, protein binding, toxicity, lipid rescue Why the “size principle” is an incomplete explanation The textbook rule — thin fibres block first — is a useful clinical summary but not a reliable law. In single-axon recordings during lidocaine perfusion, unmyelinated C fibres were susceptible to conduction block than thinly myelinated Aδ fibres, contradicting a simple diameter ordering. In vivo rat sciatic recordings found the most sensitive fibres were small myelinated Aγ motor and Aδ sensory fibres, with C fibres and large Aα/β fibres blocked later. The clinical sequence therefore emerges from several interacting factors rather than diameter alone: internodal distance and the length of nerve exposed to drug (critical blocking length), the safety factor for conduction, firing frequency (use-dependent block of open/inactivated channels), the drug's diffusion into the nerve over time, and where fibres sit within the fascicle. Test the modality relevant to surgery and repeat after adequate time. Neuraxial levels: sympathetic block typically extends above sensory block, and motor block lies below it; haemodynamic effects can therefore exceed what the sensory level suggests. They are weak bases with a pKa above physiological pH, meaning the majority exists in the ionised (charged) form at body pH. Understanding the relationship between pKa, pH, and ionisation is central to their pharmacology.

Local anaesthetics are weak bases. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation determines the proportion of ionised (BH⁺) to unionised (B) drug at any given pH. Use the interactive diagram below to explore how changing pH affects ionisation for different agents.

The Key Principle

The unionised form (B) is lipid-soluble and crosses the nerve membrane to reach the intracellular side. The ionised form (BH⁺) then binds to the intracellular portion of the voltage-gated Na⁺ channel to block it. Both forms are needed — the unionised form for membrane penetration, the ionised form for receptor binding.

All local anaesthetics share a common structure: an aromatic ring (lipophilic) linked to an amine group (hydrophilic) via either an ester or amide bond.

Cocaine, procaine, tetracaine, chloroprocaine

Metabolised by plasma cholinesterases (pseudocholinesterase). Produce PABA metabolites — higher allergy risk.

Lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine, levobupivacaine

Metabolised by hepatic amidases (CYP450). Very rare true allergy. Remember: amides have two s in the name.

Classification by Potency and Duration

Standard ( ) bupivacaine is manufactured as a 50:50 mixture of the R(+) and S(-) forms. Adrenaline (typically 1:200,000 = 5 µg/mL)

α₁-mediated vasoconstriction slows systemic absorption, so peak plasma concentration falls, duration is prolonged (most marked for lidocaine and prilocaine, least for bupivacaine and ropivacaine, which are already highly protein-bound) and the maximum safe dose rises. It also serves as an intravascular marker (tachycardia on test dose). Avoid in digital, penile and ear blocks by tradition, and in unstable ischaemic heart disease or uncontrolled hypertension.

Sodium bicarbonate

Raising solution pH increases the proportion of unionised base available to cross the axonal membrane, speeding onset and reducing injection pain. A practical recipe is 1 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate added to 10 mL of lidocaine (use only about 0.1 mL per 10 mL for bupivacaine, which precipitates readily). Mix immediately before use.

Opioids (fentanyl, diamorphine, morphine)

Act synergistically at pre- and post-synaptic µ-receptors in the dorsal horn when given neuraxially, improving block quality without added motor block. Intrathecal fentanyl 10–25 µg improves intra-operative comfort at caesarean section; diamorphine 300–400 µg or preservative-free morphine gives 12–24 h analgesia at the cost of pruritus, nausea and a risk of delayed respiratory depression.

Clonidine and dexmedetomidine (α₂-agonists)

Prolong both sensory and motor block, probably through hyperpolarisation of C fibres and spinal α₂ effects; clonidine 1 µg/kg is a common peripheral adjunct. Dose-limiting sedation, hypotension and bradycardia.

Perineural or intravenous dexamethasone prolongs analgesia after brachial plexus block; hyaluronidase aids spread in ophthalmic blocks; sodium metabisulfite and other preservatives are relevant to neurotoxicity concerns rather than efficacy.

Obstetric practice demands high-quality block with minimal motor weakness and minimal fetal exposure. Three linked physicochemical properties — pKa, lipid solubility and protein binding — explain almost all of the clinical pharmacology of local anaesthetics, and each maps onto a distinct property of the drug in usepKa Ionisation at pH 7.4 Speed of onset (lower pKa → more unionised → faster onset) Lipid solubility Membrane penetration Potency (more lipid-soluble → more potent) Protein binding Na⁺ channel binding affinity Duration of action (higher binding → longer duration)

pKa, onset and the minimum blocking concentration (Cm)

Onset speed is governed not only by pKa but also by the concentration of drug delivered relative to the minimum blocking concentration (Cm) — the lowest concentration needed to block conduction in a given nerve fibre (analogous to MAC for volatile agents). Increasing the concentration or dose delivers more molecules above Cm faster, which speeds clinical onset independent of pKa. This explains the apparent paradox of chloroprocaine: despite a high pKa (~8.7, meaning only a small unionised fraction at pH 7.4), it is used clinically in high concentration (2-3%), providing a large absolute quantity of unionised base and a rapid onset (~5 minutes) that outperforms agents with a more favourable pKa. Alkalinisation of the solution with sodium bicarbonate raises pH towards the drug > Greater lipid solubility allows easier penetration of the lipid-rich nerve membrane (and other lipid-rich membranes generally), which increases potency — highly lipid-soluble agents such as bupivacaine and tetracaine block nerves at lower molar concentrations than lidocaine or prilocaine. The same property that confers potency also drives systemic toxicity: highly lipid-soluble agents penetrate cardiac and CNS tissue readily and bind avidly to myocardial and neuronal sodium channels, so potency and toxicity rise broadly in parallel — bupivacaine is both markedly more potent and markedly more cardiotoxic than lidocaine at equivalent plasma concentrations.

Protein binding, duration and the tissue reservoir

In plasma, local anaesthetics bind principally to alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AAG), a high-affinity, low-capacity acute-phase protein, and to a lesser extent to albumin (high-capacity, lower affinity). Only the unbound (free) fraction is pharmacologically active and available to cause systemic toxicity, so protein binding is a key determinant of both duration of action at the injection site (highly bound drug dissociates more slowly from the Na⁺ channel, prolonging block) and of the safety margin in plasma. AAG is an acute-phase reactant and is reduced in neonates and in pregnancy, so a greater free fraction circulates for a given total plasma concentration in these groups, increasing the risk of systemic and fetal/neonatal toxicity at doses that would be safe in a healthy non-pregnant adult. Highly perfused, lipid-rich tissues (fat, muscle) also act as a reservoir, taking up drug and buffering the plasma concentration, but slowly releasing it back — relevant to the pattern and duration of systemic absorption after large-volume regional blocks.

Putting it together: classification by potency and duration

Combining lipid solubility (potency) and protein binding (duration) produces the practical three-tier classification used clinically: low potency, short duration (procaine, chloroprocaine — low lipid solubility and low protein binding); moderate potency and duration (lidocaine, prilocaine, mepivacaine — intermediate on both properties); and high potency, long duration (bupivacaine, levobupivacaine, ropivacaine, tetracaine — high lipid solubility and high protein binding) Systemic toxicity occurs when plasma levels exceed the toxic threshold, typically from inadvertent intravascular injection or excessive dosing. The CNS is affected first (excitation → seizures), followed by cardiovascular collapse. Bupivacaine is particularly cardiotoxic due to slow dissociation from cardiac Na⁺ channels.

Up to 70% of patients report pain on injection of propofol into a small hand vein. The pain has both an immediate component (direct irritation of the vessel and free nerve endings by the aqueous phase of the emulsion) and a delayed component (kinin cascade activation 10–20 s after injection). Mixing 20–40 mg of lidocaine with each 200 mg of propofol — or pre-treating with lidocaine under a Bier-style venous tourniquet for 30–60 s — is the most widely used and effective prophylaxis.

Receptor subtypes, clinical pharmacology of morphine, fentanyl, remifentanil

Step-by-step reasoning
CSHT comparison.
Fentanyl CSHT after 6 h infusion ≈ 200 min; remifentanil CSHT remains ≈ 3–4 min regardless of duration.
Remifentanil is hydrolysed by non-specific tissue and plasma esterases (not pseudocholinesterase) — clearance is independent of hepatic/renal function and infusion duration.
MEP compatibility.
Opioids do not depress MEPs significantly, unlike volatiles. Remifentanil + propofol TIVA is the standard for neurosurgery requiring evoked-potential monitoring.
End-of-case planning.
Rapid offset = no residual analgesia. Give a long-acting opioid (e.g. morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV) 20–30 min before stopping the remifentanil, plus paracetamol/NSAID and wound infiltration.
OIH risk.
High-dose remifentanil (> 0.2 µg/kg/min) for hours can precipitate hyperalgesia — consider ketamine 0.1–0.2 mg/kg/h infusion as cover.
Common traps
Stopping remifentanil without transition analgesia → severe pain within minutes.
Confusing CSHT with elimination half-life — t½β of fentanyl (~3 h) is misleading after long infusions because of tissue accumulation.
Forgetting that remifentanil causes profound bradycardia — have glycopyrrolate ready.
Morphine metabolism.
Hepatic glucuronidation produces M3G (~70 %, neuroexcitatory, no analgesia) and
M6G (~10 %, potent µ-agonist)
Renal excretion.
Both metabolites are renally cleared. In severe renal impairment, M6G accumulates over 24–48 h causing delayed sedation and respiratory depression.
Manage the toxicity.
Stop morphine. Naloxone 100 µg titrated IV (be aware of short duration — re-narcotisation likely → infusion 4–10 µg/kg/h).
Switch agent.
Use opioids without active renal metabolites:
, or
(caution — partly renally cleared but no active metabolite).
Reduce dose
, lengthen interval, prefer PRN over regular dosing, and add multimodal analgesia (paracetamol, regional block) to minimise opioid load.
Giving codeine or tramadol as a "safer" alternative — codeine relies on CYP2D6 conversion to morphine (same metabolite problem) and tramadol's M1 metabolite is also renally cleared.
One bolus of naloxone in a chronic build-up of M6G — recurrence within 30–60 min is the rule, infusion is required.
Forgetting non-opioid contributors: gabapentinoids and benzodiazepines also accumulate in renal failure.
Pattern recognition.
Tolerance → pain in original distribution, responds to dose escalation. OIH → diffuse / new pain distribution,
with dose escalation, improves with dose reduction.
Mechanism of OIH.
Central sensitisation via NMDA upregulation, descending facilitation from RVM, spinal dynorphin release and TLR4-mediated neuroinflammation.
Reduce the opioid dose (or rotate to a structurally different agent). Add an NMDA antagonist — ketamine 0.1–0.25 mg/kg bolus then 0.1–0.2 mg/kg/h. Layer multimodal analgesia: paracetamol, NSAID, regional block, α₂-agonist (clonidine/dexmedetomidine), gabapentinoid, magnesium.
Confirm by response.
Both can coexist — a trial of dose reduction with NMDA cover is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
Escalating PCA limits when escalation is the cause — OIH gets worse.
Rotating within the same chemical class (e.g. oxycodone → morphine) — incomplete cross-tolerance helps, but methadone (NMDA antagonism) or buprenorphine (partial agonism) are often more effective.
Missing co-existing causes: surgical complication, undiagnosed neuropathic pain, withdrawal.

Modern concepts: biased agonism & allosteric modulation
Biased agonism (functional selectivity):
MOP activation recruits two principal pathways — the

low-dose ketamine infusion restores opioid responsiveness
— often with a lower total opioid requirement afterwards — is widely described as “re-setting” or “re-sensitising” the opioid receptor. The phrase is a useful shorthand, but it is important to be precise about what it does and does not mean.
What “re-set” really means.
Ketamine does not bind the µ-opioid receptor (MOR) in any clinically meaningful way at analgesic doses, and there is no human evidence that it restores receptor
. What it does is interrupt the
NMDA-receptor-dependent adaptive plasticity
that maintains tolerance and opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH), allowing the pre-existing MOR population to signal effectively again. Functionally the patient behaves as if the receptor has been re-set; mechanistically the change is in the downstream and network-level adaptations, not in the receptor protein itself.
Why tolerance and OIH share a mechanism
Receptor-level (homologous) desensitisation
: GRK-mediated phosphorylation of the MOR C-terminus, β-arrestin-2 recruitment, uncoupling from Gi/Go and receptor internalisation, with agonist-specific differences (morphine internalises the receptor poorly and therefore desensitises without efficient resensitisation — one explanation for its relatively rapid tolerance).
Network-level (heterologous) sensitisation
: increased excitatory drive in the dorsal horn that opposes whatever analgesia remains. The second process is
, and it is the target of ketamine.
Molecular mechanisms — how ketamine reverses the adaptation
Open-channel NMDA blockade (PCP site).
Chronic opioid exposure removes the Mg²⁺ block and increases NMDA-receptor conductance. Ketamine binds within the open pore, use-dependently silencing the sensitised receptors that carry most of the wind-up current while sparing normal low-frequency transmission — the pharmacological basis for a low-dose, sub-anaesthetic infusion being sufficient.
Interrupting the PKC → MOR phosphorylation loop.
NMDA-mediated Ca²⁺ entry activates protein kinase C, which phosphorylates the MOR and uncouples it from its G-protein (heterologous desensitisation)
further relieves the Mg²⁺ block on NMDA receptors — a self-reinforcing positive-feedback loop. Blocking NMDA breaks the loop; PKC activity falls and MOR–G-protein coupling recovers. This is the closest mechanistic correlate of “re-setting”.
Reduced Ca²⁺/CaMKII and nNOS–NO–cGMP signalling.
CaMKII autophosphorylation and nitric oxide generation in dorsal-horn neurones maintain long-term potentiation of nociceptive synapses; both are downstream of NMDA Ca²⁺ flux and both fall with ketamine.
Attenuated descending facilitation and spinal dynorphin.
Chronic opioids increase on-cell activity in the rostral ventromedial medulla and upregulate spinal dynorphin, which drives pro-nociceptive CGRP/substance-P release. NMDA blockade dampens this pain-facilitating arm.
Glial and neuroinflammatory modulation.
Opioids activate microglia via TLR4/P2X7 → IL-1β, TNF-α and BDNF release; BDNF–TrkB signalling downregulates the KCC2 chloride transporter and converts GABA-ergic inhibition towards excitation. Ketamine has direct anti-inflammatory and microglia-inhibiting actions in addition to its NMDA effect.
Reduced β-arrestin-2-biased signalling.
Because ketamine allows the same analgesia at a lower opioid dose, agonist occupancy and therefore GRK/β-arrestin-2 recruitment, receptor internalisation and adenylyl-cyclase superactivation all fall — an indirect but real contribution to restored receptor responsiveness.
Secondary targets.
HCN1 channel inhibition, adenosine A₁-receptor recruitment, monoaminergic reuptake inhibition, and — for the metabolite (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine — AMPA-receptor and mTORC1-dependent synaptic plasticity that may explain benefits outlasting the infusion.
Study evidence
Key finding
Trujillo & Akil,
Rodent, MK-801 + morphine
NMDA antagonism prevented development of morphine tolerance and dependence without blocking acute analgesia — the founding proof of concept.
Joly et al.,
RCT, major abdominal surgery, high-dose remifentanil
Small-dose ketamine (0.5 mg/kg then 5 µg/kg/min) abolished remifentanil-induced peri-incisional hyperalgesia and reduced morphine use — evidence that OIH is NMDA-mediated and preventable.
Loftus et al.,
RCT, 102 opioid-dependent patients, spinal surgery
Intra-operative ketamine (0.5 mg/kg bolus + 10 µg/kg/min) cut 48-h morphine equivalents by ~37 % and lowered pain scores at 6 weeks — the key trial in the tolerant population.
Laskowski et al.,
Can J Anaesth
Systematic review, 70 trials
IV ketamine reduced opioid consumption and pain scores in ~half of trials; greatest benefit in painful surgery and opioid-tolerant patients; no increase in psychotomimetic effects at low dose.
Nielsen et al.,
RCT, 147 opioid-dependent spinal-fusion patients
Ketamine reduced 0–24 h morphine consumption (median 79 vs 121 mg) with fewer patients requiring rescue — replication of Loftus in a larger cohort.
Brinck et al., Cochrane 2018
Meta-analysis, 130 studies, 8341 participants
Perioperative IV ketamine reduces opioid consumption and postoperative nausea/vomiting; benefit is modest overall but consistent, with low adverse-event rates.
ASRA/AAPM/ASA consensus 2018
Opioid tolerance/dependence is an explicitly supported indication; suggested bolus ≤ 0.35 mg/kg and infusion ≤ 1 mg/kg/h in a monitored setting.

Set expectations:
the goal is functional analgesia and a reduced opioid requirement, not zero pain, and the effect on tolerance is partial and may not persist for months.

Paediatric Considerations
neonates and small infants have a relatively non-compliant, poorly compliant ventricle with limited contractile reserve and a near-fixed stroke volume, so cardiac output is rate-dependent and bradycardia is poorly tolerated. Immature sympathetic innervation, lower catecholamine stores and higher β-receptor sensitivity change the dose–response relationship, and the transitional circulation means high PVR states may need pulmonary vasodilators rather than more systemic vasoconstriction.
Recognition of shock:
hypotension is a late sign; tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cool or flushed peripheries, reduced urine output and altered conscious level come first. Use age-related MAP targets rather than adult thresholds.
Septic shock:
current paediatric sepsis guidance recommends adrenaline or noradrenaline in preference to dopamine as first-line vasoactive support, starting them early (including via peripheral or intraosseous access at low concentration) if perfusion remains poor after 40–60 mL/kg of fluid. Adrenaline is conventionally chosen for “cold” low-output shock with high SVR, and noradrenaline for “warm” vasodilated shock
Second-line and adjuncts:
add dobutamine or milrinone for low cardiac output with adequate perfusion pressure, vasopressin for catecholamine-refractory vasoplegia, and consider levosimendan in myocardial dysfunction; titrate to perfusion, lactate clearance and echocardiographic function rather than blood pressure alone
Typical infusion ranges:
adrenaline and noradrenaline 0.05–1 µg/kg/min; dobutamine 5–20 µg/kg/min; milrinone 0.25–0.75 µg/kg/min (accumulates in renal impairment); dopamine 5–20 µg/kg/min — still used more often in neonates than adults, particularly for hypotension of prematurity; vasopressin 0.0003–0.002 units/kg/min as an adjunct.
Steroids and adjuncts:
consider hydrocortisone in fluid- and catecholamine-refractory shock, and remember that hypocalcaemia and hypoglycaemia commonly contribute to poor contractility in infants.
Practical safety:
weight-based, standardised concentrations and double-checked pump calculations, dedicated lines, and vigilance for extravasation (small vessels, high risk of tissue injury). Escalate to advice from a paediatric intensive care retrieval service early.
See also the paediatric infusion and dosing tools in the Intensive Care section for weight-based rate calculations.
Tachyphylaxis and Catecholamine Resistance
agonist-occupied β- and α₁-adrenoceptors are phosphorylated by G-protein-coupled receptor kinases and bind β-arrestin, which uncouples them from Gs/Gq (desensitisation) and drives internalisation; sustained stimulation then reduces receptor gene transcription (downregulation). Depletion of noradrenaline from sympathetic nerve terminals contributes to tachyphylaxis with indirectly acting agents such as ephedrine and metaraminol.
Contributors in critical illness:
acidosis (impairs receptor coupling), hypoxia, hypocalcaemia, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, relative adrenal insufficiency, excessive nitric oxide and prostacyclin production, and ATP-sensitive potassium channel activation in vascular smooth muscle.
Clinical clues:
the same drug and dose produce progressively less effect; a bolus produces a transient response only; and the total noradrenaline requirement rises without a change in filling or cardiac output.

    The classification is a simplification — many drugs act on multiple channels (e.g. amiodarone, sotalol, propafenone). The Sicilian Gambit (1991) proposed a more detailed framework linking arrhythmia mechanism (re-entry, triggered activity, abnormal automaticity) to the vulnerable parameter and the appropriate drug target. While more comprehensive, the Vaughan-Williams system remains the standard for exam purposes.

    All antiarrhythmics can paradoxically cause arrhythmias:

      Abnormal substrate magnifies proarrhythmia, so drug choice must accompany specialist rhythm and sudden-death risk assessment Do not use electrical cardioversion unless immediately life-saving because it may precipitate ventricular fibrillation; avoid routine calcium in acute digoxin poisoning Electrical storm is defined as three or more distinct episodes of sustained VT, VF or appropriate ICD therapies within 24 hours. It is a state of life-threatening electrical instability with high short-term mortality, and treatment must simultaneously suppress the arrhythmia, remove triggers and address the underlying substrateImmediate goals

      • Terminate and suppress recurrent arrhythmia.
      • Find and correct reversible triggers: ischaemia, electrolyte disturbance, decompensated heart failure, hypoxia, sepsis, drug toxicity or a pro-arrhythmic drug, and inappropriate ICD programming.
      • Support haemodynamics and reduce sympathetic drive.
      Initial management

      • Optimise electrolytes: K⁺ >4.5 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ >1.2 mmol/L.
      • Intravenous β-blockade first line — esmolol infusion (titratable) or propranolol; sympathetic blockade is more effective than escalating antiarrhythmics alone.
      • Amiodarone loading 300 mg IV then 900 mg/24 h; lidocaine as an alternative in ischaemic VT.
      • Adequate sedation and analgesia — pain and anxiety from repeated shocks drive further catecholamine release.
      • Reprogramme the ICD (raise VT detection rate, enable anti-tachycardia pacing) to reduce shock burden.

      Escalation for refractory storm: deep sedation with general anaesthesia and neuromuscular blockade, percutaneous stellate ganglion block or thoracic epidural for sympathetic modulation, urgent catheter ablation, overdrive pacing for pause-dependent torsades, and mechanical circulatory support (IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO) as a bridge to ablation or transplantation.
