Understanding their mechanisms, pharmacokinetics, monitoring, and reversal is essential for safe perioperative and critical care management. This topic covers unfractionated heparin (UFH), low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWH), warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), and adjunctive agents.

Anticoagulants act at different points in the coagulation cascade. The intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge at Factor Xa, which activates thrombin (Factor IIa) to convert fibrinogen to fibrin.

Heparins bind antithrombin III (AT-III), accelerating its inhibition of serine proteases (thrombin, Xa, IXa, XIa, XIIa) by ~1,000-fold. UFH requires a minimum chain length of 18 saccharides to form the ternary heparin–AT-III–thrombin complex. LMWH chains are shorter, so they predominantly inhibit Factor Xa with less anti-IIa activity.

# Antimicrobials Antibiotics, antifungals, and antivirals — mechanisms, spectrum, resistance, and ICU considerations Selective toxicity: why aciclovir spares host cells Aciclovir is a prodrug. Herpes simplex virus-encoded thymidine kinase phosphorylates it far more efficiently than host enzymes do, so the monophosphate forms mainly in infected cells. Cellular kinases then convert it to aciclovir triphosphate, which inhibits the viral DNA polymerase more strongly than host polymerases. The two steps — activation by a viral enzyme and preference for the viral polymerase — explain its wide therapeutic margin. Clinical corollaries: thymidine-kinase-deficient or polymerase-mutant herpesviruses can be resistant, and cytomegalovirus lacks this thymidine kinase, which is why ganciclovir (activated by a different viral kinase) is used for CMV. Toxicity in ICU is driven mainly by exposure — high doses, falling renal function and dehydration — so dose to renal function and indication. Reading the trial evidence correctly an individual-patient meta-analysis of outpatient trials found a modest reduction in time to symptom relief, fewer lower-respiratory complications needing antibiotics and fewer admissions, at the cost of more nausea and vomiting. These trials enrolled outpatients; treatment of hospitalised and critically ill patients rests largely on observational data and guideline recommendation, not equivalent randomised evidence. in ACTT-1, hospitalised adults with COVID-19 recovered faster than with placebo (median about 10 vs 15 days). The benefit was clearest in patients on low-flow oxygen; the trial was not powered to show a mortality benefit, and patients already on mechanical ventilation or ECMO showed no clear benefit. in EPIC-HR, unvaccinated high-risk outpatients treated early had a large relative reduction in hospitalisation or death. This does not establish benefit for patients already critically ill. The anaesthetic and ICU hazard: ritonavir boosting Ritonavir is included to inhibit CYP3A4 and raise nirmatrelvir exposure, so it also raises concentrations of many co-administered CYP3A substrates. Before starting, or when a patient on a boosted regimen comes to theatre or ICU, check every drug with an interaction checker or pharmacist — including calcineurin inhibitors, some antiarrhythmics, anticoagulants, sedatives and opioids — and do not assume interactions end the moment the course stops. Evidence limits: trial populations, viral variants and vaccination status change over time; follow current national guidance and local infection-specialist advice for indications and doses. Learning check: why is aciclovir ineffective against CMV? CMV does not encode the thymidine kinase that efficiently activates aciclovir. Ganciclovir is phosphorylated by the CMV UL97 kinase instead. Learning check: does ACTT-1 show remdesivir reduces mortality in ventilated patients? No. Its primary benefit was shorter time to recovery, clearest in patients on low-flow oxygen; no clear benefit was shown in those already ventilated or on ECMO. Antiseptics are applied to living tissue; disinfectants to surfaces. Chlorhexidine disrupts microbial cell membranes and binds to the skin, giving a persistent (residual) effect. A thorough understanding of antimicrobial pharmacology is essential for anaesthetists and intensivists. Surgical prophylaxis, treatment of sepsis, and management of hospital-acquired infections all require knowledge of mechanisms of action, spectrum, pharmacokinetics, and adverse effects. Therapeutic Drug Monitoring in the ICU

Critical illness distorts antimicrobial pharmacokinetics: capillary leak and fluid loading expand the volume of distribution of hydrophilic drugs, hypoalbuminaemia raises the free fraction of highly bound agents, augmented renal clearance produces sub-therapeutic exposure, while acute kidney injury, renal replacement therapy and ECMO circuits move exposure in the opposite direction. Fixed dosing therefore predicts concentration poorly, and the 2020 ESICM/ESCMID position paper recommends routine monitoring of aminoglycosides, β-lactams, linezolid, teicoplanin, vancomycin and voriconazole in critically ill patients Barriers to implementation are practical rather than conceptual: assays for β-lactams and linezolid are available in few laboratories, turnaround time often exceeds the dosing interval, sampling errors (wrong timing, drawing from the infusion limb) invalidate results, and interpretation needs an MIC and a clinician or pharmacist able to act on it.

Stewardship aims to optimise clinical outcome while minimising the unintended consequences of antimicrobial use — toxicity, Clostridioides difficile infection, selection of resistance and cost. Separating the two genomic pathways is the rationale for selective glucocorticoid receptor agonists (SEGRAs/SEGRMs), designed to maximise transrepression while minimising transactivation and therefore metabolic harm. Minor surgery needs the usual oral dose only, with no additional parenteral supplementation; if fasting is brief and only one dose is missed (e.g. a minor procedure under local or regional anaesthesia), parenteral replacement is not required. Moderate surgery: usual dose + hydrocortisone 50 mg IV at induction, then 25 mg IV 8-hourly for 24 h. Major surgery: usual dose + hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 200 mg/24 h by infusion or 50 mg IV 6-hourly for 24–48 h and until stable enough to resume oral treatment. What are the major side effects of long-term corticosteroids? Cushingoid features (truncal obesity, moon face, buffalo hump — fat redistribution driven by hyperinsulinaemia and lipolysis in the limbs). Osteoporosis (DXA + bisphosphonates if >5 mg pred for >3 months) — reduced gut calcium absorption (antagonism of vitamin D action), increased renal calcium excretion, reduced osteoblast activity. Hyperglycaemia/diabetes — increased hepatic gluconeogenesis and peripheral insulin resistance. Hypertension — mineralocorticoid-mediated sodium and water retention plus enhanced vascular catecholamine sensitivity. Peptic ulcer (especially with NSAIDs) — reduced mucosal prostaglandin protection. Proximal myopathy — increased muscle protein catabolism and wasting. Immunosuppression — reduced cytokine production (NF-κB/AP-1 transrepression) and lymphocyte redistribution/apoptosis. Skin thinning/bruising — inhibition of fibroblast activity and collagen synthesis. Also cataracts, glaucoma, mood disturbance/psychosis, growth retardation in children and adrenal suppression. Withdrawal must be gradual after >4 weeks of treatment to allow HPA recovery.     euglycaemic ketoacidosis — a ketoacidosis with a normal or only mildly raised glucose that is easily missed. Current UK guidance is to omit the drug on the day of surgery and, where the procedure is major, the patient is likely to fast for more than one meal or there is a history of ketosis, to stop it up to 3 days beforehand Mechanism

    • SGLT2 blockade in the proximal tubule produces glycosuria, so plasma glucose stays low or normal even when insulin deficiency is functionally present.
    • Glucose loss plus fasting lowers insulin and raises glucagon; the low insulin:glucagon ratio drives lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis.
    • Volume depletion from osmotic diuresis and the surgical stress response (cortisol, catecholamines) amplify ketone production.
    • Because hyperglycaemia is absent, the usual clinical trigger to test for ketones never fires — hence DKA.
    Perioperative precipitants

    • Prolonged or repeated fasting and missed carbohydrate intake.
    • Major or emergency surgery, especially bowel surgery with delayed feeding.
    • Acute illness — sepsis, pancreatitis, myocardial infarction.
    • Dehydration, bowel preparation, vomiting, and very-low-carbohydrate diets.
    • Reduced insulin dose in insulin-treated patients continuing an SGLT2 inhibitor.
    Diagnosis

    • Glucose normal or only mildly raised (often < 14 mmol/L) — do not use glucose to exclude ketoacidosis.
    • Capillary ketones ≥ 3.0 mmol/L (or significant ketonuria) with a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.3, bicarbonate < 15 mmol/L).
    • Non-specific presentation: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, tachypnoea, malaise, unexplained acidosis on a perioperative gas.
    • Test ketones in any patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor with unexplained acidosis, vomiting or malaise — regardless of glucose.
    Management

    • Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and do not restart until the patient is eating, drinking and metabolically stable.
    • Resuscitate with IV crystalloid (0.9% sodium chloride), replacing potassium as guided by levels.
    • Start a fixed-rate or variable-rate insulin infusion even when glucose is normal — insulin is what switches off ketogenesis.
    • Give a glucose substrate alongside insulin (10% dextrose) to allow adequate insulin delivery without hypoglycaemia.
    • Monitor ketones, bicarbonate/pH and the anion gap hourly initially; resolution of ketosis and acidosis — not glucose — defines recovery. Involve the diabetes team, and defer non-urgent surgery until resolved.

Cranial nerves, neck triangles, larynx, trachea, bronchial tree, skull base, orbit


Step-by-step reasoning
Extend the neck and palpate the cricothyroid membrane between the thyroid (above) and cricoid (below) cartilages

Cranial Nerves & Bony Framework
Cranial nerves of anaesthetic relevance, the skull base foramina that transmit them, and the orbit (soft-tissue and bony anatomy) for ophthalmic regional anaesthesia.

Anaesthetic Relevance
Sensory to face (V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, V3 mandibular). Motor to muscles of mastication. V2 → nasal cavity sensation. Regional blocks for dental/maxillofacial surgery.
Motor to muscles of facial expression. Monitoring during parotid/mastoid surgery. Runs through middle ear — risk in ear surgery.
Sensory to oropharynx, posterior 1/3 tongue, carotid body. Gag reflex afferent. Glossopharyngeal nerve block for awake intubation.
SLN and RLN branches — laryngeal innervation. Parasympathetic to heart (bradycardia). Oculocardiac reflex afferent (V1) → efferent (X).
Motor to SCM and trapezius. Vulnerable in posterior triangle of neck (superficial). Damage → shoulder drop.
Motor to tongue muscles. Tongue deviation towards lesion side. Risk during carotid endarterectomy.

Part B
Neck — Surface, Spaces & Vascular Access
Surface anatomy of the neck triangles, the cross-sectional fascial planes at C6, the cervical plexus, and internal jugular vein cannulation.
B1. Triangles of the Neck
Anterior Triangle
Borders: midline, SCM, mandible. Contains: carotid sheath (CCA/ICA, IJV, vagus), thyroid gland, larynx, trachea, submandibular gland. Subdivided into: carotid, muscular, submandibular, submental triangles.
Posterior Triangle
Borders: SCM, trapezius, middle 1/3 clavicle. Floor: prevertebral fascia over scalene muscles. Contains: accessory nerve (superficial — vulnerable), subclavian artery, brachial plexus trunks, external jugular vein.
B2. Cross-Section at C6 Level
B3. Cervical Plexus
Superficial (cutaneous) branches
All four emerge together at the midpoint of the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid (
Erb's point
, roughly at the level of the cricoid, C6):
lesser occipital (C2)
— scalp behind the ear;
great auricular (C2,3)
— lower pinna, angle of jaw, parotid skin (blocked for tympanomastoid and awake fibreoptic ear procedures);
transverse cervical (C2,3)
— anterior neck;
supraclavicular (C3,4)
— clavicle and skin to the second rib, explaining shoulder-tip and "cape" referral and the need to supplement an interscalene block for shoulder surgery.
Deep (muscular) branches
Phrenic nerve (C3,4,5)
— sole motor supply to the diaphragm; passes over the anterior surface of scalenus anterior.
Ansa cervicalis
(superior root C1 travelling with the hypoglossal nerve, inferior root C2,3) — supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles. Segmental branches to the prevertebral muscles, rectus capitis, longus capitis and colli, scalenes, and via C2–C4 contributions to sternocleidomastoid, trapezius and levator scapulae (proprioceptive, with motor supply from CN XI).
Superficial block:
10 mL of local anaesthetic subcutaneously along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid at its midpoint (or an ultrasound-guided injection deep to the investing fascia but superficial to the prevertebral fascia). Used for carotid endarterectomy, thyroid surgery, clavicular fracture, superficial neck lesions and tunnelled line insertion.
Intermediate/deep block:
injection at the C2–C4 transverse processes or deep to the prevertebral fascia — better surgical anaesthesia for carotid endarterectomy but a higher complication rate; largely superseded by intermediate ultrasound-guided injection.
Complications of deep block
Phrenic nerve palsy (near-universal with deep block — avoid bilateral blocks and use with caution in respiratory disease), recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with hoarseness, Horner's syndrome from cervical sympathetic spread, vertebral artery or carotid puncture and rapid local anaesthetic systemic toxicity or seizure, intrathecal or epidural injection via a dural cuff, and accessory nerve injury. Aspirate frequently, inject incrementally, and monitor for LAST.
B4. Internal Jugular Vein Cannulation
Landmark Approach
Apex of triangle formed by two heads of SCM and clavicle. Needle at 30° towards ipsilateral nipple, lateral to carotid pulse. US-guided approach now standard (NICE CG49).
Medial: CCA. Posterior: vagus nerve. Anterior: SCM. Right IJV preferred — straighter path to SVC, avoids thoracic duct (left). Risks: carotid puncture, pneumothorax, air embolism.
Part C
Upper Airway — Nose & Pharynx
The conducting passages above the larynx — relevant to nasal intubation, awake fibreoptic technique, and topical anaesthesia of the upper airway.
C1. Nasal Cavity & Pharynx
sphenopalatine artery
(terminal maxillary branch) and the
anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries
(ophthalmic branches), with contributions from greater palatine and superior labial vessels. Their anterior septal anastomosis forms
Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area)
, the commonest source of epistaxis; the posterolateral venous plexus near the inferior meatus is
Woodruff's plexus
, associated with posterior epistaxis. Veins broadly accompany the arteries and communicate with facial, pterygoid and ophthalmic veins, providing a potential route for infection to the cavernous sinus
Posterior to nasal cavity, above soft palate. Contains adenoids and pharyngeal opening of Eustachian tube. Innervation: maxillary nerve (V2).
Oropharynx & Hypopharynx
Oropharynx: soft palate to epiglottis. Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides sensory innervation. Hypopharynx (laryngopharynx): epiglottis to cricoid. Vagus (X) via internal laryngeal nerve.
Pharyngeal muscles and innervation
superior, middle and inferior constrictors
; the inner longitudinal layer comprises
stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus
, which elevate and shorten the pharynx during swallowing. Motor supply is principally through the pharyngeal plexus from vagus, except stylopharyngeus, which is supplied by glossopharyngeal nerve. Sensory supply follows the three regions: V2 to nasopharynx, IX to oropharynx and X (internal laryngeal branch) to laryngopharynx
Killian's dehiscence
, a weak area through which a Zenker diverticulum may protrude. Loss of pharyngeal dilator tone during anaesthesia or unconsciousness allows the tongue and soft tissues to narrow the compliant pharynx; jaw thrust, airway adjuncts and positive pressure restore patency.
Part D
Larynx & Front-of-Neck Access
Cartilaginous skeleton and cross-sectional anatomy, vagal innervation (SLN/RLN) and palsy patterns, and the surface landmarks for emergency cricothyroidotomy and elective tracheostomy.
D1. Larynx — Painted Atlas Plates
D2. Laryngeal Skeleton & Cross-Section
Largest cartilage. Laryngeal prominence ("Adam's apple"). Calcifies with age.
Only complete cartilaginous ring. Signet-ring shape. Landmark for cricothyroidotomy (below) and cricoid pressure.
Leaf-shaped. Attached to hyoid by hyoepiglottic ligament. Vallecula is between epiglottis and tongue base (Macintosh blade tip).
Paired pyramidal cartilages. Vocal process attaches vocal ligament. Muscular process attaches intrinsic muscles.
Small cartilages within aryepiglottic folds. Visible during laryngoscopy.
Intrinsic Laryngeal Muscles
Posterior cricoarytenoid
Only abductor; opens the rima glottidis
Lateral cricoarytenoid; transverse arytenoid
Closes the membranous and posterior glottis
Tilts thyroid cartilage forward, lengthening the cords
External SLN
Thyroarytenoid and vocalis
Shorten and fine-tune vocal-fold tension
Inlet sphincter
Oblique arytenoid; aryepiglottic
Narrows the laryngeal inlet during swallowing
All intrinsic muscles receive recurrent laryngeal motor supply except cricothyroid. Bilateral posterior cricoarytenoid dysfunction therefore leaves the cords near the midline and can cause critical stridor
D3. Laryngeal Innervation
D3b. Sensory Innervation for Topical Anaesthesia
Nasal cavity — V1 and V2
Anterior septum and lateral wall: anterior ethmoidal nerve (V1, via the ophthalmic division). Posterior two-thirds of the septum, turbinates and lateral wall: nasopalatine and posterior nasal branches from the
sphenopalatine (pterygopalatine) ganglion
(V2). Technique: co-phenylcaine or lidocaine 5% with phenylephrine spray, or lidocaine gel on a nasal airway; a cotton-wool applicator soaked in local anaesthetic passed along the middle turbinate to the posterior wall blocks the sphenopalatine ganglion and vasoconstriction reduces epistaxis.
Nasopharynx — V2
Supplied by the maxillary division via the pharyngeal branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion. Blocked by the same posteriorly directed nasal spray or soaked applicator; inadequate coverage here produces discomfort as the scope turns the corner behind the soft palate.
Oropharynx, tonsils, posterior tongue — glossopharyngeal (IX)
The lingual branch of IX supplies the posterior third of the tongue, tonsillar fossae, soft palate and oropharynx and forms the afferent limb of the
gag reflex
. Techniques: lidocaine 10% metered spray or 4% nebulised/atomised solution, lidocaine lozenges, or a targeted glossopharyngeal nerve block at the base of the palatoglossal arch (2 mL lidocaine 2% just posterior to the lower pole of the tonsil) — effective but risks intra-arterial injection into the carotid and loss of airway reflexes.
Larynx above the cords — internal branch of the SLN (X)
The internal laryngeal nerve (from the superior laryngeal branch of the vagus) supplies the epiglottis, vallecula, aryepiglottic folds and larynx down to the vocal cords, and is the afferent limb of the
laryngeal closure reflex
. Techniques: spray-as-you-go through the working channel of the fibrescope, or bilateral internal laryngeal nerve block — 1–2 mL lidocaine 2% injected just inferior to the greater horn of the hyoid where the nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane, or a soaked pledget placed in the piriform fossa with Krause forceps.
Cords and trachea — recurrent laryngeal nerve (X)
Sensory supply below the cords and to the trachea. Techniques: spray-as-you-go boluses of lidocaine 1–2% delivered under direct vision at the cords and into the trachea, or a
translaryngeal (cricothyroid) injection
of 2–3 mL lidocaine 2–4% at end-expiration, which provokes a cough that distributes the drug. Translaryngeal injection abolishes the cough reflex and so is avoided where aspiration risk is high
Practical points
Keep a running total of lidocaine: mucosal absorption is rapid and the recommended airway maximum is about 9 mg/kg lean body weight — have lipid emulsion available.
Give an antisialagogue (glycopyrrolate 200 µg IV) early: local anaesthetic works poorly through secretions.
Sedation (remifentanil target-controlled infusion or low-dose dexmedetomidine) supplements but never replaces adequate topicalisation.
Allow time — most techniques need 5–10 minutes to reach full effect before instrumentation.
Warn about the resulting swallowing impairment: keep the patient nil-by-mouth until reflexes return, usually 1–2 hours.
D4. Cricothyroidotomy & Tracheostomy Anatomy
Cricothyroid membrane:
Avascular midline between thyroid and cricoid cartilages. 9 × 30 mm. Used for emergency surgical airway. Structures at risk: superior cricothyroid artery (runs transversely across upper membrane).
The stoma is placed between rings 2–3 or 3–4 — above this risks subglottic stenosis from cricoid damage, below it risks tracheo-innominate fistula and a tube too deep for the flange. Layers traversed, superficial to deep: skin → subcutaneous fat → platysma → investing (superficial) layer of deep cervical fascia → the midline "linea alba cervicalis" between the strap muscles (sternohyoid and sternothyroid) → pretracheal fascia → thyroid isthmus, which usually overlies rings 2–4 and may need retracting or dividing → pretracheal fat with the inferior thyroid vein plexus → anterior tracheal wall.
Structures at risk
Anterior jugular veins and the jugular venous arch (extend the neck and stay strictly midline), thyroid isthmus and the inferior thyroid venous plexus (haemorrhage), thyroid ima artery (present in ~10%), high-riding brachiocephalic (innominate) artery — normally crossing the trachea at the level of the sternal notch but sitting higher in children and in the kyphotic elderly, causing catastrophic tracheo-innominate fistula. The recurrent laryngeal nerves lie in the tracheo-oesophageal grooves and are spared by a midline approach; the posterior tracheal wall and oesophagus are at risk from over-deep needle or dilator passage.
Relational anatomy and practical points
Landmarks in the extended neck from above: thyroid notch → cricothyroid membrane → cricoid (C6) → rings 2–4 → sternal notch. The isthmus lies about 2–3 cm below the cricoid. Position with a shoulder roll and full extension to bring the trachea anterior and increase the working distance from the sternal notch. Pre-procedure ultrasound identifies aberrant vessels, a high brachiocephalic artery, thyroid size and tracheal depth and midline position. Percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy is guided by bronchoscopy to confirm midline puncture below ring 1 and to avoid a paratracheal or posterior-wall track. Obesity, short neck, fixed flexion, previous neck surgery, radiotherapy and coagulopathy favour a surgical approach.
D5. Fascial Layers of the Neck & Deep Neck Spaces
Superficial fascia
Subcutaneous layer containing
, cutaneous nerves of the cervical plexus, superficial veins (anterior and external jugular) and lymph nodes. Not part of the deep cervical fascia; the plane of superficial cervical plexus block.
Investing (superficial) layer of deep cervical fascia
Encircles the neck like a collar from the external occipital protuberance and mandible to the clavicles, sternum and scapular spine. Splits to enclose sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, the submandibular and parotid glands. Its unyielding nature is why a post-thyroidectomy or post-carotid haematoma compresses the airway rather than expanding outwards — a surgical emergency requiring immediate release of the sutures.
Pretracheal (visceral) fascia
Encloses thyroid, trachea and oesophagus and the strap muscles, continuing with the fibrous pericardium in the superior mediastinum. The
pretracheal space
lies anterior to this visceral compartment, deep to the infrahyoid muscles, and contains loose connective tissue, the thyroid venous plexus and variable thyroid ima vessels. Infection, blood and air can track into the anterior mediastinum.
Prevertebral fascia
Covers the prevertebral and scalene muscles and the cervical sympathetic chain, extending from the skull base to T3 and laterally as the axillary sheath around the brachial plexus. Injection deep to it produces deep cervical plexus block with a high incidence of phrenic palsy; injection superficial to it (intermediate block) is safer.
Carotid sheath
Formed by contributions from all three deep layers; contains the common/internal carotid artery (medial), internal jugular vein (lateral), vagus nerve (posterolateral, between them) and deep cervical lymph nodes. Extends from the skull base to the arch of the aorta and is the route for the spread of infection to the mediastinum.
Retropharyngeal space and the danger space
The retropharyngeal space lies between buccopharyngeal fascia and the alar layer immediately anterior to the prevertebral fascia, extending to about T4; the
"danger space"
lies between alar and prevertebral fascia and runs uninterrupted to the diaphragm — hence descending necrotising mediastinitis from dental or retropharyngeal infection. Airway assessment must anticipate trismus, limited extension and distorted, friable anatomy
Part E
Lower Airway — Trachea & Bronchial Tree
From the cricoid down to the lobar bronchi — the anatomy underpinning DLT placement, fibreoptic bronchoscopy, and the recognition of endobronchial intubation.
E1. Trachea & Bronchial Tree
C6–T4/5 (carina). 10–12 cm long, 16–20 C-shaped cartilaginous rings. Posterior membranous wall (trachealis muscle). Arterial supply: upper two-thirds from branches of the inferior thyroid artery, lower third from the bronchial arteries. Venous drainage: inferior thyroid venous plexus. Lymphatics: pre-tracheal and para-tracheal nodes — relevant to tracheostomy and tracheal surgery
Bronchial Anatomy
Right main bronchus: wider, shorter, more vertical (25°) — foreign bodies more likely to enter right side. Left main bronchus: narrower, longer, more horizontal (45°). Left-sided DLT preferred.

Complete circle in only 25% of population. Superficial system and sinuses Superficial cerebral veins drain into the superior sagittal sinus (upper border of the falx). The inferior sagittal sinus (lower free edge of the falx) joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus . The superior sagittal and straight sinuses meet at the confluence of sinuses (torcular Herophili), which drains into the paired transverse sinuses , then the S-shaped sigmoid sinuses , which leave through the jugular foramen as the internal jugular veins. Deep system The paired internal cerebral veins (draining the basal ganglia, thalamus and deep white matter) and the basal veins of Rosenthal join to form the great cerebral vein of Galen , which drains into the straight sinus. The cerebral veins and sinuses have no valves. Cavernous sinus Either side of the sella turcica. The internal carotid artery and abducens nerve (VI) run through the sinus; III, IV, V1 and V2 run in its lateral wall. It connects with facial veins through the ophthalmic veins, so infection in the "danger triangle" of the face can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis (eye swelling, ophthalmoplegia, sensory loss in V1/V2). Clinical relevance Cerebral venous thrombosis: risk factors include pregnancy and the puerperium, oral contraceptives, dehydration, thrombophilia, cancer and local infection; it presents with headache, seizures, focal signs and raised ICP. A post-dural-puncture-type headache that loses its postural pattern should prompt imaging. Head-down tilt and IJV obstruction (tight tube ties, extreme neck rotation) raise venous pressure and ICP; sinus injury in neurosurgery risks major bleeding and venous air embolism. Dura mater The tough outer meninx, formed of dense collagen and elastin fibres arranged in concentric laminae rather than the longitudinal orientation once taught — so needle-bevel orientation matters less than needle design and gauge. It is continuous with the inner (meningeal) layer of the cranial dura at the foramen magnum , where it fuses with the periosteum, and is anchored anteriorly to the posterior longitudinal ligament and laterally to the root sleeves as they exit each intervertebral foramen. Insert chest drains above the rib below to avoid the neurovascular bundle. A smaller collateral branch leaves the main intercostal nerve near the angle of the rib and runs along the superior border of the rib below . It can be missed by a single-injection intercostal block, giving incomplete analgesia, and can be injured by a drain placed hard on the upper rib border. Azygos venous system The azygos vein drains the posterior thoracic and abdominal walls, ascends on the right of the vertebral bodies and arches over the right lung root at T4/5 to enter the SVC. The inferior-left hemiazygos and superior-left accessory hemiazygos cross behind the aorta, oesophagus and thoracic duct to join it. This valveless network is a crucial collateral channel between IVC and SVC when either caval system is obstructed Parietal Pleura Lines thoracic wall, mediastinum, and diaphragm. Left pleura deviates at rib 4 (cardiac notch). Both descend to rib 8 (MCL), rib 10 (MAL), rib 12 posteriorly. Lung edge: 2 ribs above pleural reflection. Superior Mediastinum Above plane of sternal angle to T4. Contains: aortic arch and branches, SVC, brachiocephalic veins, trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct, vagus, phrenic nerves, left RLN. Inferior Mediastinum Anterior: thymus (children). Middle: heart, pericardium, phrenic nerves. Posterior: descending aorta, oesophagus, thoracic duct, azygos system, vagal trunks, sympathetic chains. Thoracic Sympathetic Chain anterior to the necks and heads of the ribs , just deep to the parietal pleura and lateral to the vertebral bodies — a few millimetres from the paravertebral space, which is why paravertebral and erector spinae blocks produce ipsilateral sympathetic block, and why an unintended pleural puncture is the corresponding hazard Structure and connections Typically one ganglion per thoracic segment (11–12, often fewer through fusion), joined by interganglionic fibres into a continuous chain that is continuous with the cervical chain above and the lumbar chain below. White rami communicantes (myelinated, pre-ganglionic, T1–L2 only) carry fibres from the spinal nerve into the chain — the anatomical reason sympathetic outflow is limited to thoracolumbar segments. Grey rami communicantes (unmyelinated, post-ganglionic) return at every level to the spinal nerves to supply vessels, sweat glands and piloerector muscle of the trunk and limbs. Fibres may synapse at their level of entry, ascend or descend within the chain, or pass through without synapsing to form the splanchnic nerves. Stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion Formed by fusion of the inferior cervical and first thoracic ganglia, present in roughly 80% of people. It lies anterior to the neck of the first rib , behind the vertebral artery and the dome of the pleura, medial to the scalene muscles and lateral to the C7/T1 vertebral bodies. It supplies sympathetic fibres to the head, neck and upper limb. Block is performed at the C6 (Chassaignac) tubercle or C7 under ultrasound for sympathetically maintained upper-limb pain, CRPS, refractory ventricular arrhythmia and vascular insufficiency. Complications follow its relations: recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (hoarseness), phrenic palsy, pneumothorax, vertebral artery injection with immediate seizure, and epidural or intrathecal spread. Splanchnic nerves Pre-ganglionic fibres that pass through the chain without synapsing and pierce the diaphragmatic crura to reach the abdominal prevertebral plexuses: greater (T5–T9) to the coeliac ganglia, lesser (T10–T11) to the aorticorenal ganglion, and least (T12) to the renal plexus. They carry the visceral afferents that make upper abdominal pain refer to the epigastrium and back, and are the target of coeliac plexus and splanchnic nerve neurolysis in pancreatic cancer pain. Clinical relevance Horner's syndrome — ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis (with enophthalmos and facial flushing) from interruption of the cervical/upper thoracic chain: an expected finding after stellate or high paravertebral block, and a warning sign after interscalene block, neck trauma, apical (Pancoast) tumour or carotid dissection. Thoracic epidural and paravertebral blockade cause segmental sympathetic block — vasodilatation, reduced venous return and hypotension, but also reduced myocardial oxygen demand and improved coronary flow in coronary disease. : endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy at T2–T4 for palmar hyperhidrosis and T2 for facial flushing; chemical or surgical sympathectomy for ischaemic pain. Compensatory sweating and Horner's syndrome are recognised complications. Cardiac sympathetic supply arises from T1–T4 — the basis of left cardiac sympathetic denervation and stellate block for refractory ventricular arrhythmias, and of referred cardiac pain to the left arm and jaw. Lung Anatomy Right Lung 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower). 2 fissures (oblique, horizontal). 10 bronchopulmonary segments. Eparterial bronchus (upper lobe bronchus arises above right PA — important for DLT placement). Left Lung 2 lobes (upper with lingula, lower). 1 oblique fissure. 8–10 segments. Cardiac notch and lingula (homologue of right middle lobe). Left main bronchus longer — left DLT preferred for OLV. Attachments (origin → insertion) Sternal part: two slips from the posterior xiphoid process. Costal part: inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages and ribs, interdigitating with transversus abdominis. Lumbar part: right crus (L1–L3 bodies, larger, encircles the oesophageal hiatus and contributes to the lower oesophageal sphincter mechanism), left crus (L1–L2), plus the medial arcuate ligament (over psoas) and lateral arcuate ligament (over quadratus lumborum). All fibres insert into the central tendon Innervation & levels Motor supply is entirely phrenic (C3,4,5) — "C3,4,5 keeps the diaphragm alive". Sensory: phrenic centrally (referred shoulder-tip pain), lower intercostal and subcostal nerves peripherally. High cervical cord injury above C3 abolishes spontaneous ventilation; interscalene block causes hemidiaphragmatic paresis. At end-expiration the right dome reaches the 5th rib and the left the 5th intercostal space (liver pushes the right higher). T8 vena caval foramen (in the central tendon): IVC + right phrenic nerve. T10 oesophageal hiatus (in the right crus): oesophagus, vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels. T12 aortic hiatus (behind the median arcuate ligament, so strictly not a diaphragmatic perforation): aorta, thoracic duct, azygos/hemiazygos veins. Mnemonic: "I ate ten eggs at twelve" (IVC 8, oesophagus 10, aorta 12). Anaesthetic relevance General anaesthesia and neuromuscular blockade cause cephalad displacement of the dependent diaphragm → atelectasis and reduced FRC. Diaphragmatic function is a major determinant of weaning from ventilation (ventilator-induced diaphragmatic dysfunction). Ultrasound of diaphragm excursion (< 10 mm) and thickening fraction (< 20%) predicts extubation failure. Hiatus hernia at the T10 hiatus increases aspiration risk. Blood supply and drainage Superior surfaces receive pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic branches of the internal thoracic arteries; the inferior surface is supplied mainly by paired inferior phrenic arteries from the abdominal aorta. Venous return follows superior and inferior phrenic veins into the internal thoracic/brachiocephalic system and IVC respectively Bronchopulmonary Segments bronchopulmonary segment is the anatomical and functional unit of the lung supplied by a single segmental (tertiary) bronchus with its own segmental branch of the pulmonary artery. Each segment is pyramidal, with its apex at the hilum and base at the pleural surface, and is separated from its neighbours by connective-tissue septa. Crucially, the pulmonary veins and lymphatics run intersegmentally in these septa, whereas the bronchus and artery run centrally — this is what makes a segment surgically resectable. The segments Right (10): upper — apical, posterior, anterior; middle — lateral, medial; lower — superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal. Why it matters clinically Allows anatomical segmentectomy with preservation of surrounding lung. Explains predictable distribution of aspiration (supine → right lower lobe superior segment; upright → posterior basal segments) and of lobar pneumonia and abscess. Provides the map for fibreoptic bronchoscopy, targeted physiotherapy and postural drainage, bronchial blocker placement, and for interpreting the segmental pattern of collapse on CXR/CT. Thoracic Duct Begins as the cisterna chyli at L1–L2, anterior to the vertebral bodies and right of the aorta. Enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus (T12) , ascends in the posterior mediastinum between the aorta (left) and azygos vein (right), behind the oesophagus.     Stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion

    Formed by fusion of the inferior cervical and first thoracic ganglia, present in roughly 80% of people. It lies anterior to the neck of the first rib, behind the vertebral artery and the dome of the pleura, medial to the scalene muscles and lateral to the C7/T1 vertebral bodies. It supplies sympathetic fibres to the head, neck and upper limb. Block is performed at the C6 (Chassaignac) tubercle or C7 under ultrasound for sympathetically maintained upper-limb pain, CRPS, refractory ventricular arrhythmia and vascular insufficiency. Complications follow its relations: recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (hoarseness), phrenic palsy, pneumothorax, vertebral artery injection with immediate seizure, and epidural or intrathecal spread.

The original evidence — Lidwell 1982 about 1.5% of operations in conventional theatres versus 0.6% with ultraclean air , with a further reduction when body-exhaust suits were worn. This remains the historical basis for HTM 03-01's ultraclean provision for prosthetic implant work. The counter-evidence — Brandt 2008 and WHO 2016 99,230 operations from a German national surveillance system (KISS) and found that laminar airflow showed no protective effect on surgical site infection in orthopaedic and abdominal surgery; for hip prosthesis surgery the infection rate was actually higher in laminar-flow rooms (adjusted OR ≈1.6). conditional recommendation that laminar airflow ventilation should not be used to reduce the risk of SSI in patients undergoing total arthroplasty (moderate quality evidence). Why the disagreement: Lidwell randomised the , but modern observational data reflect real-world theatres where laminar flow is often breached — door openings, personnel movement, ceiling-mounted equipment — and where ventilation is only one element of an SSI bundle (antibiotic prophylaxis, normothermia, skin antisepsis, surgical technique). Reconciling the guidance: UK practice (HTM 03-01) continues to provide ultraclean theatres for implant orthopaedics, while WHO and much of the international evidence base caution that the benefit is unproven or absent in contemporary practice. A good viva answer states both positions and explains the differences (trial design, adherence to airflow discipline, co-interventions). What it means for your practice: engineering cannot compensate for behaviour. Keeping the theatre door closed, minimising traffic, positioning the surgical field within the canopy, and wearing exhaust suits correctly matter as much as the air-change rate. A conditional recommendation against using laminar airflow systems to reduce SSI risk in total arthroplasty, based on moderate-quality evidence showing no protective effect (Brandt 2008). The PUMA criteria are a trace that rises with exhalation and falls during inspiration, is consistent or increasing in amplitude over at least seven breaths, has a peak more than 1 kPa above baseline, and is clinically appropriate. When in doubt, take it out.

Subglottic & tracheal obstruction
Extrathoracic vs intrathoracic compression
behave like opposite physiological mirrors, driven by the difference between intraluminal airway pressure and the surrounding pressure (atmospheric in the neck, pleural in the chest):
Extrathoracic (cervical trachea, subglottis):
during spontaneous

inspiratory stridor

Intrathoracic (lower trachea, carina, mediastinal mass):

expiratory stridor or wheeze

Fixed lesion

The failed-intubation drill
Plan A:
two attempts maximum, optimising with head position, external laryngeal manipulation, videolaryngoscopy, bougie and reduced or released cricoid pressure.
Plan B:
declare failed intubation, insert a second-generation SAD (up to two attempts), maintain oxygenation.
Plan C:
face-mask ventilation with two-person technique and airway adjuncts; then the explicit
decision using the guideline's table — maternal condition, fetal condition, surgical urgency, obesity, aspiration risk, anaesthetist's experience and the feasibility of regional anaesthesia.
Plan D:
CICO — scalpel cricothyroidotomy without delay; deliver the baby to improve maternal physiology if arrest occurs (perimortem caesarean within 5 min).
Continue cricoid pressure only while it does not impede oxygenation; keep the patient head-up and suction ready as aspiration risk persists into recovery.
extubate awake, sitting up, with full reversal confirmed; document the airway findings, complete an airway alert letter to the woman and her GP, debrief the team, and arrange anaesthetic review before any future pregnancy. The strongest preventive measure remains avoiding general anaesthesia — early effective epidural analgesia in labour and antenatal anaesthetic review of high-risk women.
Anatomical & physiological differences
A large occiput flexes the neck when supine; use a shoulder roll and neutral or slight extension in neonates, reserving the sniffing position for older children.
The tongue is relatively large, the epiglottis long and omega-shaped, and the larynx more cephalad and anterior. The infant airway is classically funnel-shaped, with the subglottis/cricoid its narrowest fixed region.
The trachea is short, so small movements can cause endobronchial intubation or extubation. Recheck tube depth after positioning.
Oxygen consumption is high (about 6–8 ml/kg/min), while FRC is low and the compliant chest wall promotes airway closure. Apnoea therefore causes rapid desaturation, followed by hypoxic bradycardia.
Equipment, tube size & depth
A straight Miller blade directly lifts the floppy epiglottis in neonates and infants; an age-sized Macintosh blade is often suitable in older children. The 2024 guideline recommends an age-adapted videolaryngoscope as first choice in neonates and infants.
Modern microcuff tubes are appropriate when correctly sized: cuffed internal diameter = age/4 + 3.5 mm; uncuffed = age/4 + 4 mm. Keep cuff pressure ≤20 cmH₂O and ensure an acceptable leak.
Approximate oral depth = age/2 + 12 cm in children; in neonates use weight + 6 cm as an initial estimate. Confirm depth clinically and with sustained waveform capnography.
Have adjacent tube sizes, age-sized masks, oral airways, second-generation SADs, suction, videolaryngoscope and rescue equipment immediately available.
Induction and rapid-sequence doses
Calculate every dose from a measured or reliably estimated weight, reduce induction doses in neonates or cardiovascular instability, and follow the local paediatric formulary.
Typical IV induction ranges: propofol 2–3 mg/kg, ketamine 1–2 mg/kg, or thiopental 3–5 mg/kg, titrated to physiology.
For rapid paralysis: rocuronium 1–1.2 mg/kg IV or suxamethonium 2 mg/kg IV in neonates/infants (1–2 mg/kg in older children). Use gentle mask ventilation when needed to prevent hypoxaemia rather than accepting prolonged apnoea.
Prepare atropine 20 micrograms/kg and emergency rescue drugs before induction; adequate anaesthetic depth and neuromuscular blockade improve intubating conditions.
Difficult-airway strategy
Predictors include craniofacial syndromes, micrognathia, mid-face hypoplasia, limited mouth opening or neck movement, airway mass, previous difficulty and severe obstructive sleep apnoea.
Prioritise oxygenation, call expert help early, use the most experienced available operator and stop repeated attempts before trauma, oedema and bleeding worsen the airway.

— the workhorse block for sub-umbilical surgery (circumcision, hypospadias, orchidopexy, inguinal hernia, lower limb). Lateral position, 22–23 G short-bevelled or cannula needle at 45° through the sacrococcygeal ligament, then flatten and advance a few millimetres only; confirm with ultrasound or the "whoosh"/swirl test and aspirate. improves block success and reduces the volume needed, and it is now standard for truncal and neuraxial blocks in infants; the Cochrane review found better success rates but no clear effect on rare severe complications. Stop Before You Block
Wrong-side block is an NHS Never Event. Immediately before needle insertion, the anaesthetist and assistant re-check the surgical-site mark and side, even if the WHO sign-in has been done — particularly after any delay or change of position
Peripheral nerve injury
Transient postoperative sensory symptoms are common in the first days, but long-term injury attributable to the block is rare (registry estimates in the order of 2–4 per 10,000). Mechanisms are needle trauma, intrafascicular injection, local anaesthetic neurotoxicity and ischaemia; surgical, tourniquet and positioning causes are often more likely. Avoid injecting against high pressure or with pain/paraesthesia, document the technique, and refer persistent or progressive deficits early for neurological assessment and nerve conduction studies
Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)
Signs range from perioral tingling, tinnitus and agitation to seizures, arrhythmia and cardiovascular collapse — sometimes cardiac signs occur first, especially under sedation or GA. Stop injecting, call for help, manage airway and seizures (benzodiazepine), and give
20% lipid emulsion 1.5 ml/kg over 1 min then 15 ml/kg/h
, repeating the bolus up to twice and doubling the infusion if unstable (maximum 12 ml/kg). Prevention: dose by lean body weight, incremental aspiration-guided injection, ultrasound, and an adrenaline-containing marker where appropriate
Other block-specific complications
Interscalene: hemidiaphragmatic paresis, Horner's syndrome, hoarseness, and rarely intrathecal/epidural or vertebral artery injection. Supraclavicular and infraclavicular: pneumothorax, phrenic palsy. Lower limb: falls from quadriceps weakness after femoral or fascia iliaca blocks. All catheters: infection, migration and secondary failure — review daily.

Advantages of TIVA
Recovery quality:
less PONV (propofol is directly anti-emetic — a number needed to treat of about 5 in high-risk patients), less emergence agitation and delirium in children, and a clear-headed, comfortable emergence.
Airway and respiratory:
obtunded airway reflexes with propofol/remifentanil, so useful in asthma and reactive airways, tubeless and shared-airway surgery, rigid bronchoscopy, laser airway surgery, jet ventilation and awake fibreoptic intubation.
Specific indications:
known or suspected malignant hyperthermia susceptibility and other myopathies, severe PONV history, prolonged transfer or remote-site anaesthesia (no scavenging), intra-operative neurophysiological monitoring (MEPs/SSEPs), awake craniotomy, and neurosurgery where a slack brain and preserved autoregulation matter.
Occupational and environmental:
no theatre pollution or occupational volatile exposure, and a much lower greenhouse-gas footprint than desflurane or nitrous oxide.
effect-site targeting with predictable decrement times allows deliberate deep anaesthesia with rapid emergence, and the same infusion can be continued seamlessly into ICU sedation or transfer.
Less PONV in detail:
volatile agents and nitrous oxide are the main anaesthetic causes of early vomiting; replacing them with propofol removes that trigger as well as adding propofol's own anti-emetic effect.
Smoother emergence:
compared with balanced volatile anaesthesia, TIVA causes significantly less coughing and a smaller blood-pressure and heart-rate response on emergence, which matters in asthma, reactive airways and surgery where straining is harmful
propofol reduces cerebral metabolic rate and blood flow and keeps autoregulation intact, whereas volatile agents dilate cerebral vessels in a dose-dependent way and can raise intracranial pressure.
Heart protection — still debated:
volatile agents have preconditioning effects, and some cardiac surgery trials favour them over propofol; others show no difference. This is not a reason to choose TIVA
Cancer surgery — evidence emerging:
propofol may preserve immune function better than volatile agents, but whether this changes cancer recurrence is unproven
Brain health after surgery:
in older patients with hip fracture, inhalational general anaesthesia was linked with a higher later dementia rate than TIVA; this is observational data and does not prove cause
TIVA is now used in about 25% of UK general anaesthetics; meta-analysis shows TIVA and inhalational anaesthesia are comparably safe, with TIVA reducing PONV and agitation while inhalational anaesthesia offers slightly faster recovery and lower cost
Disadvantages & Risks of TIVA
National guidance sets the minimum safe standards for the technique: a dedicated, visible, anti-reflux-protected line, processed EEG monitoring whenever a neuromuscular blocking drug is used, and a documented plan for the emergency drug and pump failure
No end-tidal confirmation of delivery:
unlike a volatile agent there is no measured expired concentration, so a disconnected, tissued or leaking line, an occluded valve or an empty syringe can produce awareness with no alarm. This is the single most important structural disadvantage.
NAP5 reported accidental awareness in roughly 1:8,000 TIVA cases versus about 1:135,000 with volatile maintenance, and TIVA with neuromuscular blockade was over-represented among reports.
Model inaccuracy:
pharmacokinetic models carry a median performance error of the order of 20–30% and were derived in healthy adult volunteers, so they are least reliable in the obese, the elderly, the shocked, the pregnant, the very young and in cardiac output extremes — exactly the patients who most need accuracy.
Equipment and human factors:
dedicated pumps and giving sets, correct model and covariate entry, and a visible anti-reflux-protected line are all required; wrong-model, wrong-weight and wrong-units errors are recognised critical incidents.
Venous access dependence:
difficult or single peripheral access, extravasation or a fully drawn-up but disconnected line all threaten the whole technique; propofol also causes injection pain.
propofol infusion syndrome with prolonged high-dose infusions, lipid load and hypertriglyceridaemia, hypotension and bradycardia (worse with remifentanil), remifentanil-induced acute tolerance and opioid-induced hyperalgesia, and no bronchodilator or MAC-sparing volatile effect.
Cost and workload:
more expensive than low-flow sevoflurane, greater preparation time and drug wastage, and a higher training and familiarity requirement.
Higher awareness risk (NAP5: 1:8,000 vs 1:135,000 with volatile). No end-tidal agent to confirm delivery. Requires processed EEG monitoring (BIS/Entropy). IV line disconnection = awareness. Propofol infusion syndrome with prolonged high-dose use (>4 mg/kg/hr for >48h).
anaesthetic-induced conditioning
— opening of mitochondrial K
channels, reduced reactive-oxygen-species-mediated injury and inhibition of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore — reducing troponin release in animal and small human cardiac-surgery studies. However, the MYRIAD trial (2019) randomised 5400 patients undergoing CABG to volatile or TIVA and found no difference in 1-year mortality, and propofol also has antioxidant properties. Practical position: use volatile or TIVA according to the haemodynamic needs of the case; ensure adequate depth, coronary perfusion pressure and avoidance of tachycardia, which matter far more than agent choice.
Neurocognitive outcome
. Randomised data (including depth-of-anaesthesia trials) have not confirmed causality. Delirium prevention remains driven by avoiding excessive depth and burst suppression, treating pain, and non-pharmacological measures.
Cancer recurrence
the perioperative period produces a transient, neuroendocrine- and cytokine-driven depression of cell-mediated immunity, and the maintenance agent appears to modulate it. Volatile agents up-regulate hypoxia-inducible factor 1α and insulin-like growth factor signalling, reduce natural-killer-cell number and cytotoxicity, shift the T-helper 1 to T-helper 2 balance, and promote tumour-cell migration and angiogenesis in vitro. Propofol instead inhibits cyclo-oxygenase-2 and prostaglandin E₂ production, preserves natural-killer-cell and cytotoxic T-cell function, attenuates the pro-inflammatory interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor α response and has antioxidant activity
; opioids (particularly morphine at high dose) are separately immunosuppressive and pro-angiogenic, which is a further argument for regional analgesia and opioid sparing. Retrospective cohorts have suggested a survival advantage with TIVA, but the first large randomised trial in breast-cancer surgery (Cochrane/GA-CARE-type evidence) has not shown a difference in recurrence-free survival. Current guidance is that oncological outcome should
drive the choice of anaesthetic technique; minimising opioid, providing regional analgesia, avoiding hypothermia, transfusion and hyperglycaemia are more defensible interventions.

Metabolic (pharmacokinetic) variants:

butyrylcholinesterase variants prolong suxamethonium and mivacurium block; CYP2D6 poor or ultra-rapid metabolism alters codeine and tramadol response; RYR1/CACNA1S variants define malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility, one of the strongest indications for TIVA.
Clinical bottom line:
effect sizes remain modest relative to age, weight, cardiac output and co-administered opioid, and no genotype-guided TCI model is in routine use. Pharmacogenomics therefore explains part of the observed variability and reinforces the need to

mathematical simulation of the patient
running in real time. Population pharmacokinetic analysis (usually non-linear mixed-effects modelling, NONMEM) fits measured plasma concentrations from volunteers to a compartmental structure, producing typical parameter values and explaining part of the between-patient variability with
such as weight, age, height and sex. The pump then integrates that model's differential equations and asks, every 10 seconds, “what infusion rate will bring the predicted concentration to the target?”
From data to a pump algorithm — the five steps
arterial or venous concentrations measured over hours after known doses in a defined population.
Structural model:
how many exponential phases best describe the decay — nearly always three for propofol and remifentanil, giving a three-compartment model.
Covariate model:
which patient characteristics reduce unexplained variability (weight in Marsh; age, height, weight and lean body mass in Schnider; allometric weight, age and sex in Eleveld).
PK–PD link:
an effect compartment with rate constant ke0 is added and fitted against a measured effect (processed EEG for propofol, spectral edge frequency for remifentanil), collapsing the hysteresis between concentration and effect
Control algorithm:
for plasma targeting the pump gives bolus = Ct × V1 then an infusion matching distribution plus clearance; for effect-site targeting it deliberately overshoots Cp by the smallest amount that reaches Ce = target at t-peak without exceeding it
Scaling: linear, lean-body-mass and allometric
Linear (Marsh, Paedfusor):
every volume and clearance is a fixed multiple of total body weight, e.g. V1 = 0.228 L·kg⁻¹. Simple, but it assumes a 140 kg patient has twice the clearance of a 70 kg patient, which is false.
Lean body mass (Schnider, Minto):
clearance is driven by metabolically active mass, estimated with the James equation. The James formula is non-monotonic — above a BMI of roughly 35–42 it starts to
with increasing weight and can become negative, so pumps cap the permitted input.
Allometric (Eleveld):
clearance ∝ weight⁰·⁷⁵, volumes ∝ weight¹, following the theoretical ¾-power relationship between metabolic rate and body size. Combined with a sigmoid maturation function of post-menstrual age, this lets one parameter set span neonates to the elderly
Fat-free mass:
Eleveld replaces James LBM with the Al-Sallami fat-free-mass equation, which behaves sensibly at extremes of BMI — the main reason Eleveld is preferred in obesity.
How model accuracy is actually measured
(median performance error — bias, negative = the model over-predicts),
(median absolute performance error — inaccuracy),
(intra-individual variability over time) and
(systematic drift, %·h⁻¹). A model is generally accepted as clinically usable if MDPE is within ±10–20% and MDAPE below about 20–30%. Every propofol model in routine use sits in that band, which is why no model can be trusted to better than roughly a quarter of its displayed concentration — and why processed EEG and clinical titration remain mandatory.

Selecting a TCI model for a 78-year-old, 60 kg patient
Use Schnider Ce-targeted propofol at Ce 2.5–3 µg/ml + Minto Ce 2–3 ng/ml remifentanil, titrated to BIS 40–60 — Schnider accounts for age and avoids the V1 over-dosing seen with Marsh in the elderly.
Predicting wake-up after a long propofol infusion
Wake within ~15–25 min, rate-limited by propofol decrement (CSHT ~40 min at 8 h). Always give a transitional analgesic before stopping remifentanil.

Total Intravenous Anaesthesia (TIVA)
FRCA Primary & Final / FFICM — Clinical Anaesthesia
TCI pumps use 3-compartment models to predict Cp and Ce — V1 determines bolus size, clearance determines maintenance rate
Marsh: weight-only, V1 scales with TBW, ke0 0.26 min⁻¹ — risk of overdose in obese, slower Ce equilibration
Schnider: age/sex/LBM covariates, fixed V1 (4.27 L), ke0 0.456 min⁻¹ — UK preferred for Ce targeting, safer in elderly
Eleveld: universal model (neonates to elderly), allometric scaling, accounts for opioid interaction — most modern
Minto: standard remifentanil model. CSHT ~3–4 min regardless of duration. Ce targets: analgesia 2–4, surgery 4–8 ng/mL
Effect-site targeting: pump overshoots Cp to fill effect site faster. Lower ke0 (Marsh) → larger overshoot → more haemodynamic instability
BIS/Entropy monitoring mandatory for TIVA (NAP5). Awareness risk 5× higher with TIVA vs volatile (1:8,000)
PRIS: propofol >4 mg/kg/hr for >48h → mitochondrial failure, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis. Stop propofol immediately
Principles of TIVA & TCI
TIVA vs Volatile — Cardioprotection, Neurocognition & Oncology
Pharmacokinetic Compartment Models
Represents the blood/plasma volume and highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidneys, liver). Drug is injected here. Size of V1 determines the initial bolus size — larger V1 → larger bolus to achieve target Cp. Marsh: V1 scales with TBW. Schnider: V1 is fixed at 4.27 L.
Well-perfused tissues (muscle, viscera). Drug distributes here quickly (t½ redistribution ~2–4 min for propofol). Responsible for the rapid decline in plasma concentration after a bolus. Larger V2 → more redistribution → faster Cp decline.
Poorly perfused tissues (fat, bone, connective tissue). Drug accumulates slowly during prolonged infusions. Responsible for context-sensitive half-time — prolonged infusions saturate V3, delaying elimination and recovery.
k10: metabolic elimination from V1 (hepatic/organ clearance). k12/k21: transfer between V1 and V2. k13/k31: transfer between V1 and V3. The pump continuously solves differential equations using these rate constants to predict Cp at any time.
Rate constant for drug transfer from plasma to the effect site (brain/biophase). Higher ke0 → faster equilibration → smaller initial overshoot in effect-site targeting. Marsh ke0 = 0.26 min⁻¹ (slow). Schnider ke0 = 0.456 min⁻¹ (faster). ke0 determines the time-to-peak effect (tpeak) after a bolus.
The Mathematics Behind TCI — Compartment Modelling from First Principles
Derivation & Evidence Base of Each TCI Model
Marsh (1991) — propofol
Derived by Marsh, White, Morton and Kenny from paediatric and adult data using weight-proportional scaling, and implemented as the Diprifusor, the first commercial TCI system. Structure: V1 0.228 L·kg⁻¹, V2 0.463 L·kg⁻¹, V3 2.893 L·kg⁻¹, fixed micro-constants (k10 0.119 min⁻¹). Evidence: decades of clinical use and adequate performance (MDAPE typically 20–30%) in average-sized adults; it was never designed for effect-site targeting — the ke0 of 0.26 min⁻¹ was added retrospectively and gives an implausibly late t-peak of about 4 min. Fails in obesity (V1 and hence induction dose scale without limit) and in the elderly (no age term at all).
Modified Marsh — propofol
Not a new pharmacokinetic dataset: identical Marsh volumes and clearances with ke0 raised to 1.2 min⁻¹, chosen so that the model reproduces the empirically observed t-peak of about 1.6 min after a propofol bolus. This is the version used for effect-site targeting on several UK pumps. The lesson for the exam is that ke0 and volumes are not independent — a ke0 is only valid within the parameter set against which it was fitted, and 'Marsh Ce mode' therefore behaves very differently between pumps depending on which ke0 the manufacturer implemented.
Schnider (1998) — propofol
Twenty-four volunteers aged 25–81 studied with both bolus and infusion administration, with simultaneous EEG-derived effect measurement, so the PK and the PK–PD link were derived together. V1 is fixed at 4.27 L, V3 fixed at 238 L, V2 varies with age, and metabolic clearance varies with weight, height, lean body mass and age. ke0 0.456 min⁻¹ with t-peak ≈ 1.6 min. Strengths: internally consistent PK–PD, age-sensitive clearance, small and therefore safe induction bolus, and validation in the elderly. Weaknesses: the fixed small V1 makes maintenance infusion rates the dominant determinant of concentration, and the James lean-body-mass term breaks down at high BMI.
Minto (1997) — remifentanil
Sixty-five volunteers aged 20–85 given remifentanil infusions with spectral-edge EEG as the effect measure; age and lean body mass proved to be the significant covariates for volumes, clearances and ke0 itself (ke0 falls with age, so the elderly equilibrate more slowly as well as needing less drug). Because remifentanil is hydrolysed by non-specific tissue and plasma esterases, clearance is high and largely independent of hepatic and renal function, giving a context-sensitive half-time of 3–4 min at any infusion duration. Minto remains the reference remifentanil model and is very well externally validated; an Eleveld remifentanil model now extends the same approach to a broader population.
Eleveld (2018) — propofol
A pooled analysis of 30 previously published datasets — 1,033 individuals, 10,927 concentration and 3,487 BIS observations, from neonates to patients over 80 and including the obese. # Anaesthesia Basics: EEG, Awareness & TIVA Processed and raw EEG, accidental awareness (NAP5), BIS trials, NICE depth-of-anaesthesia guidance and why TIVA changes the risk What a depth-of-anaesthesia monitor actually measures Processed EEG monitors such as the Bispectral Index (BIS), E-Entropy and Narcotrend reduce the EEG to a single number. The widely used indices assume that the same value means the same level of unconsciousness whatever drug is given. Purdon and colleagues argue that this assumption is wrong: different anaesthetics act on different receptors and neural circuits and produce distinct brain states that can be seen directly in the raw EEG. Reading the raw EEG: drug signatures Propofol sedation: alpha and beta oscillations. Propofol unconsciousness: slow-delta and alpha oscillations together; slow oscillations alone are common at induction. Burst suppression: a state of profound drug-induced brain inactivation, commonly seen in elderly patients, in anaesthetic-induced coma and in profound hypothermia. It means the brain is more deeply anaesthetised than unconsciousness requires. produces a high-frequency beta oscillation, because it blocks inhibitory interneurons. A processed index built on the propofol and volatile pattern can therefore read misleadingly "light" in a patient who is unconscious on ketamine. What NICE recommends NICE recommends EEG-based depth-of-anaesthesia monitors as an option during any general anaesthetic in patients at higher risk of adverse outcomes. That includes patients at higher risk of awareness and those at higher risk of excessively deep anaesthesia. NICE also recommends them as an option in all patients receiving TIVA . BIS, E-Entropy and Narcotrend-Compact M are treated as broadly equivalent. NICE adds that users need training and must understand the monitors' limitations. It lists high opiate or alcohol use, airway problems and previous awareness as higher-risk groups for awareness. How common is accidental awareness? NAP5 The 5th National Audit Project (NAP5) collected every reported case of accidental awareness during general anaesthesia in the UK and Ireland and matched it to a national activity survey. With neuromuscular block the incidence was about 1 in 8,200; without it, about 1 in 135,900. The reported cases were overwhelmingly cases of awareness during neuromuscular block. During Caesarean section it was about 1 in 670. Two-thirds of experiences arose at induction or emergence , not during maintenance. At induction, contributing factors were thiopental, rapid sequence induction, obesity, difficult airway management, neuromuscular block and interruptions in anaesthetic delivery while moving from the anaesthetic room to theatre. At emergence, patients often perceived residual paralysis as awareness because full return of motor power had not been confirmed. Who is at risk NAP5 found higher risk with female sex, younger adults (but not children), obesity, junior trainees, previous awareness, out-of-hours operating, emergencies, obstetric, cardiac and thoracic surgery, and neuromuscular block. ASA grade, race and the use or omission of nitrous oxide were risk factors. Does a BIS monitor prevent it? The trials disagree B-Aware (2004): 2,463 at-risk adults given relaxant anaesthesia. Awareness occurred in 2 patients in the BIS group and 11 with routine care, an 82% risk reduction. B-Unaware (2008): high-risk patients randomised to BIS-guided (target 40–60) or end-tidal gas-guided anaesthesia (0.7–1.3 MAC). There were 2 definite cases in each group, and awareness happened even with both values in range. The authors concluded their findings did not support routine BIS monitoring. BAG-RECALL (2011): 6,041 high-risk patients. Definite awareness occurred in 7 of 2,861 in the BIS group and 2 of 2,852 in the end-tidal group, so BIS was not shown to be superior. The difference is the comparator. B-Aware compared BIS with routine care, while the US trials compared BIS with a structured end-tidal gas protocol. With a volatile agent, a measured end-tidal concentration with alarms performs at least as well as BIS. That reasoning is drawn from the trial designs, not stated by any single source. Why every anaesthetist needs TIVA Volatile maintenance remains the commonest technique in the UK and Ireland. But an inhalational technique is sometimes not possible, and sometimes contraindicated, so the joint Association of Anaesthetists and Society for Intravenous Anaesthesia guideline says all anaesthetists should be able to deliver TIVA competently and safely . The guideline deliberately sets out safe practice rather than arguing that TIVA is better than volatile anaesthesia where both are possible. Why TIVA changes the awareness picture With a volatile agent you can measure the end-tidal concentration. With TIVA there is no equivalent measured drug concentration, and the infusion depends on an intact line and pump. (That is teaching reasoning, not a quoted source.) NICE recommends an EEG-based depth-of-anaesthesia monitor as an option in patients receiving TIVA. NAP5 also identified interruptions in anaesthetic delivery, such as the move from the anaesthetic room to theatre, as a contributor to awareness at induction. For pump models, target-controlled infusion and practical line set-up, see the full TIVA page. Volatile agents: MAC falls with age Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) is the end-expired concentration used to compare the potency of inhaled agents. Nickalls and Mapleson turned Mapleson's 1996 meta-analysis of MAC data into age-related iso-MAC charts for isoflurane, sevoflurane and desflurane. To give a total of 1.2 MAC with isoflurane and 67% nitrous oxide, a 95-year-old needs an end-expired isoflurane of only 0.25%, compared with 1% in a 5-year-old. The charts let a consistent total MAC be kept when the nitrous oxide concentration changes, reducing the chance of inadvertent awareness, particularly at the extremes of age. The practical point: one fixed "1 MAC" dial setting overdoses the very old and can underdose the young. That is teaching reasoning drawn from the charts, not a separate source. Nitrous oxide: ENIGMA-II ENIGMA-II randomised 7,112 patients aged 45 or over with known or suspected coronary artery disease, having major non-cardiac surgery, to anaesthesia with or without nitrous oxide. Death and cardiovascular complications at 30 days occurred in 8% of each group (relative risk 0.96). Surgical site infection was also no different (9% each). Severe nausea and vomiting was higher with nitrous oxide: 15% versus 11%. The authors concluded the findings support its safety in major non-cardiac surgery, that its emetogenic effect can be controlled with antiemetic prophylaxis, and that it reduced volatile use. Propofol versus volatile: the PONV trade-off (IMPACT) The IMPACT factorial trial randomised high-risk patients across six interventions. Propofol reduced the risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting by 19%, and avoiding nitrous oxide (nitrogen) by 12%. Together, that is TIVA, the reduction was similar to any one antiemetic (ondansetron, dexamethasone and droperidol each about 26%). All interventions acted independently, so combined relative risks can be multiplied. Absolute benefit depends on the patient's baseline risk. Hypnotic plus opioid: synergy, not addition Bouillon and colleagues gave 20 volunteers propofol and remifentanil by target-controlled infusion, alone and together. Remifentanil alone had no appreciable effect on response to shaking and shouting, or to laryngoscopy. Propofol could ablate both. Yet modest remifentanil concentrations dramatically reduced the propofol needed. The authors describe this as potent synergy. The same study found BIS was more sensitive to propofol than to remifentanil . The BIS value at which 95% of subjects did not respond depended on the drug mix, with higher propofol giving lower BIS. So an opioid-heavy technique can produce an unresponsive patient with a higher index than you might expect. That last inference is teaching reasoning, linking back to the EEG lesson. Volatile plus nitrous oxide: MAC fractions add up The iso-MAC charts let the contribution of nitrous oxide be counted towards total MAC. If nitrous oxide is turned down or off, the volatile must go up to keep the same total, or awareness risk rises, particularly at the extremes of age. Gabapentinoids plus opioids: respiratory depression In 8,567 patients having major laparoscopic surgery, Cavalcante and colleagues found gabapentin was associated with respiratory depression in recovery (odds ratio 1.47) , confirmed in a propensity-matched subset. Older patients and those given more intraoperative opioid were at higher risk, and respiratory depression lengthened recovery and increased admission to a higher level of care. The authors advise that when gabapentinoids are used, intraoperative opioids must be reduced , with increased vigilance, especially in the elderly. This was a retrospective single-centre study, so it shows an association, not proof of cause. The UK minimum standard The Association of Anaesthetists' 2021 standards set the minimum monitoring for any patient having anaesthesia or sedation under an anaesthetist in the UK and Ireland. The 2021 edition added sections on capnography, sedation and regional anaesthesia, and updated the indications for processed EEG and neuromuscular monitoring. The full guideline was not available to quote, so read it directly for the specific indications. Alternative 1: end-tidal anaesthetic concentration With a volatile agent, a measured end-tidal concentration is the main alternative to a processed EEG. In BAG-RECALL, a protocol of end-tidal concentration with alarms was compared with BIS in 6,041 high-risk patients. Definite awareness occurred in 2 of 2,852 with the end-tidal protocol and 7 of 2,861 with BIS, so BIS was not shown to be superior. Interpreting the number needs age-adjusted MAC, because the concentration needed falls steeply in the elderly. This alternative does not exist for TIVA, where NICE recommends a depth monitor as an option in every patient. Alternative 2: the isolated forearm technique The isolated forearm technique inflates a tourniquet on one arm before neuromuscular block, so that hand can still move, then asks the patient to squeeze on command. It tests consciousness of the outside world, called connected consciousness. In a six-centre study of 260 adults, 4.6% (12 of 260) responded to command after intubation, and 5 of the 12 signalled pain . Responders were younger, and their depth-monitor values were higher, but the values overlapped widely. No participant had explicit recall afterwards. In patients not on TIVA, volatile exposure before intubation reduced the odds of responding. So connected consciousness without later recall is far commoner than the 1 in 8,200 reported awareness in NAP5. The two measure different things: response during anaesthesia versus reported memory afterwards. That comparison is teaching reasoning, not stated in either source. # Pain Medicine Acute and chronic pain, neuropathic pain, multimodal analgesia, interventions Do Perioperative Gabapentinoids Work? The Verret 2020 Meta-analysis Gabapentin and pregabalin have been widely added to multimodal regimens. The Canadian PACT group pooled 281 randomised trials (24,682 adults having surgery) to test whether they improve postoperative pain. Pain scores: on a 0–100 scale, pain was lower by 10 points at 6 h, 9 at 12 h, 7 at 24 h and 3 at 48 h. Each difference fell below the minimally important difference of 10 points, so the authors judged the effect not clinically significant. results were similar for gabapentin and pregabalin. Practice point: statistically lower pain scores are not the same as meaningful benefit. Routine gabapentinoid use for acute postoperative pain is not supported, and their sedative and dizziness side effects must be weighed, especially in older patients or with opioids. What it does not cover: established neuropathic pain, where gabapentinoids remain a NICE first-line option, is a different question. Learning check: what was the largest pain reduction, and why was it judged unimportant? About 10 points on a 100-point scale at 6 h. Cardiac or kidney disease may require smaller volumes. Term neonates have a separate 10–20 mL/kg recommendation. Reassess circulation and signs of overload after each bolus; seek expert advice if 40–60 mL/kg or more is needed during initial resuscitation. Do not wait for that cumulative volume before calling for help in a deteriorating child. Haemorrhage needs haemorrhage control and appropriate blood replacement, not repeated crystalloid solely because a generic bolus calculation exists. Maintenance: daily formula versus the hourly shortcut NICE uses Holliday–Segar: 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 mL/kg/day for the next 10 kg and 20 mL/kg/day above 20 kg. The familiar hourly 4–2–1 rule is an approximation, not an exact division of those daily values by 24. Term neonates use age-dependent volumes; do not apply the older-child shortcut automatically. Worked example, 25 kg: 1,000 + 500 + 100 = 1,600 mL/day, or approximately 66.7 mL/hour. The 4–2–1 shortcut gives 40 + 20 + 5 = 65 mL/hour. NICE recommends isotonic fluid with 5–10% glucose for maintenance in term neonates aged eight days or more; in the first seven days it explicitly requires professional judgement because sodium may be unnecessary or too high and that glucose content may be insufficient. Preterm neonatal care needs its specialist pathway. Deficits and ongoing losses Assess the type of loss: vomiting or gastric drainage, diarrhoea, urine, drains and bleeding have different compositions. Adjust the prescription in addition to maintenance, using the child’s fluid status, balance and laboratory results. Avoid adding an assumed fasting deficit or unmeasured “third-space” allowance automatically; account for oral intake and reassess the clinical need. Review the prescription and whether oral fluids can resume.       A practical paediatric variant in which remifentanil is reconstituted and added directly into the propofol syringe so both drugs are delivered through one pump and one cannula. Widely used in UK paediatric centres (Bristol, GOSH, Alder Hey) for short-to-medium cases — particularly MRI, dental, ophthalmic and shared-airway lists where a second pump and second line are awkward. The mixture is named for the remifentanil concentration in micrograms per millilitre of 1% propofol: Remi 5 = 5 µg remifentanil per ml of 10 mg/ml propofol. Practical preparation: reconstitute a 1 mg remifentanil vial in 10 ml water (→ 100 µg/ml), draw up 2.5 ml (250 µg) and add it to 47.5 ml of 1% propofol → 250 µg remi in a final 50 ml = exactly 5 µg/ml remi (propofol diluted to ~9.5 mg/ml). For Remi 10 add 5 ml (500 µg) to 45 ml propofol; for Remi 2 add 1 ml (100 µg) to 49 ml propofol. Adding the remifentanil to a full 50 ml of propofol gives a slightly lower concentration (e.g. 250 µg in 52.5 ml ≈ 4.8 µg/ml).     • Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS)

    Risk rises sharply with infusions >4 mg/kg/hr for >48 hr, especially in critically ill or septic children receiving steroids/catecholamines. Presents with metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, lipaemia, cardiac failure. Avoid prolonged propofol sedation in PICU; use dexmedetomidine or midazolam-based regimens.
