    ; export function StaffRadiationTeaching() { return ( { return ( AAGBI guidelines for anaesthesia outside the operating theatre mandate the same standards of monitoring, equipment, and assistance.

    Essential Preparations
    • Self-inflating bag, oxygen supply, suction, and full airway equipment including difficult-airway trolley
    • Standard monitoring: ECG, SpO₂, NIBP, capnography (mandatory for sedation), temperature
    • Invasive monitoring (arterial line, CVC) for major procedures — TIPSS, embolisation, stent-grafting
    • Dedicated anaesthetic assistant; agreed plan for emergency transfer to theatre/ICU
    • MRI-conditional equipment if required (some hybrid suites)
    four zones with progressively restricted access, from Zone 1 (public) through Zone 4 (the scanner room itself), and only appropriately screened and trained staff should enter Zone 3/4.

    Static Field Hazards
      Projectile effect — ferromagnetic objects (oxygen cylinders, laryngoscopes, drug trolleys) can be violently attracted into the bore
    • Torque and heating of ferromagnetic implants (aneurysm clips, some prostheses)
    • Device malfunction in pacemakers, ICDs and neurostimulators — reprogramming, inappropriate pacing/shock, or inhibition
    • Any implanted device must be checked as MR-conditional and scanned within its approved conditions before entry
    RF and Gradient Hazards
    • Radiofrequency energy causes tissue and lead heating — risk of skin and internal burns, particularly from looped cables, ECG leads or monitoring wires forming conductive loops
    • Gradient coil switching produces loud acoustic noise — ear protection is mandatory for patient and staff
    Equipment Requirements
    • MR-conditional anaesthetic machine, monitors and syringe pumps sited within the approved field strength
    • Long breathing circuits and extended infusion/monitoring lines running from Zone 3 equipment through a waveguide
    • Non-ferrous laryngoscopes and aluminium/non-ferromagnetic gas cylinders only
    Monitoring Challenges
    • ECG shows spike and T-wave artefact from gradient switching and the magnetohydrodynamic effect on flowing blood
    • Pulse oximetry is prone to interference and burn risk — use fibre-optic probes routed without loops
    • Capnography has a lag due to long sampling lines
    • Limited patient access and direct visualisation once inside the bore
    Emergency Planning
      Quench (rapid loss of superconductivity, releasing helium gas) risks room asphyxia, cryogenic burns and a rapid pressure rise — know the location of the emergency quench button and door release
    Iodinated Contrast Reactions
      Severe — anaphylaxis, cardiovascular collapse, laryngeal oedema (full ABCDE, IM/IV adrenaline)
    • Most reactions are anaphylactoid (non-IgE-mediated) — direct histamine release and complement activation
    • Risk factors: previous contrast reaction (5× risk), asthma, atopy, renal impairment
    Contrast-Induced AKI (CI-AKI)
    • CA-AKI means AKI after contrast; CI-AKI means causation. Use KDIGO staging; ESUR post-contrast creatinine surveillance is 48–72 hours. Timing alone is not proof.
    • Assess AKI, CKD, route and fluid tolerance. ESUR thresholds: eGFR <45 for first-pass arterial exposure/ICU; <30 for IV/second-pass exposure.
    • Prevention: IV hydration for high-risk patients (NaCl 0.9% 1 ml/kg/h for 3–4 h before and 4–6 h after), iso-/low-osmolar contrast, minimise volume
    • No N-acetylcysteine or prophylactic dialysis. Avoid fluid overload; do not delay essential emergency imaging. ALARA principle (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) guides practice, underpinned in the UK by Stochastic vs Deterministic Effects
        Deterministic effects — require a threshold dose to be exceeded, then severity increases with dose — erythema and skin burns, epilation, cataract, tissue necrosis
    Sources of Exposure
      Scatter — the dominant source of staff exposure, arising from the patient; greatest on the X-ray tube side of the table (versus the image-intensifier side)
    Staff Dose Reduction
      Monitoring — personal dosimeter badges; annual dose limit 20 mSv/year for classified workers; pregnancy must be declared promptly with a reduced fetal dose limit applied
    Patient Dose Reduction
    • Pulsed rather than continuous fluoroscopy; low-dose modes and last-image-hold
    • Tight collimation of the beam; avoid unnecessary magnification (magnification markedly increases dose)
    • Keep the image intensifier as close to the patient as possible; minimise total screening time
    • Record dose-area product (DAP) and compare against diagnostic reference levels (DRLs)
    Units
      Dose-area product — gray·centimetres² (Gy·cm²), reflecting both dose and exposed area

# Transfer of the Critically Ill Patient Pre-departure stabilisation, packaging, ventilation/sedation in transit, neuroprotection, in-transit emergencies, ECMO retrieval, aeromedical physiology How Often Transfers Go Wrong, and What Reduces the Risk The checklists and staffing rules on this page come from studies of how often, and how, things go wrong during transfers. This lesson sets out the numbers and how strong the evidence behind each preventive measure is. How common are adverse events? (Parmentier-Decrucq 2013) A prospective study followed 262 transfers within the hospital of 184 ventilated patients from a 38-bed university ICU. of transfers had an adverse event: 26% of all transfers involved an event affecting the patient, and 16.8% an event judged serious. Independent risk factors were PEEP above 6 cmH₂O, sedation before transport, fluid loading, and changing treatment just before departure. The adverse events did not significantly increase ventilator-associated pneumonia, ventilator days or ICU stay. Learning check: why should PEEP above 6 cmH₂O make you more cautious about a CT trip? A patient needing higher PEEP has little respiratory reserve. Disconnection, switching to a transport ventilator or moving the patient can cause loss of lung recruitment and desaturation. Plan a closed-circuit transfer with clamped tubes, a transport ventilator matched to ICU settings, a check of gases after switching, and an experienced escort, or ask whether the scan is worth the risk. Why checklists? (Fanara 2010) Fanara and colleagues reviewed the literature on transfers within the hospital from 1998 to 2009 and proposed a quick-execution checklist. They were clear about the limits of the evidence. In their words, "basic training, good clinical sense and a risk-benefit analysis are currently the only deciding factors". They warned that "a critically ill patient, prepared and accompanied by an inexperienced team, is a risky combination", and said the protective effect of checklists still needed evaluation. Team training for transfers between hospitals (Droogh 2012) When the Netherlands made a mobile ICU mandatory for transfers between ICUs, the Groningen retrieval service built simulator-based crew resource management training. The four-hour scenario training covers preparation, teamwork, equipment, mobility and safety. It is run in a mock ICU and then in the mobile ICU itself. This is a description of a programme, not a trial of outcomes: it shows how training can be built, not that it reduces harm. # Anaesthesia for Emergency Surgery Emergency laparotomy, appendicectomy, ruptured ectopic, NCEPOD classification, NELA standards Urgency is a clinical decision, not just a diagnosis NCEPOD immediate intervention is life-, limb- or organ-saving, normally within minutes, with simultaneous resuscitation. Urgent intervention is normally within hours for acute or deteriorating potentially life-threatening conditions. Expedited intervention is normally within days when early treatment is needed but there is no immediate threat; elective intervention is planned. The same disease can move between categories as perfusion, bleeding, infection or organ compromise changes. Record the decision time, category and agreed theatre priority rather than assigning a rigid category solely from a procedure name. In septic shock from perforation or ischaemic bowel, antibiotics and circulatory support cannot replace source control. SSC recommends intervention as soon as medically and logistically practical after identifying an amenable source. Its discussion of benefit within 6–12 hours is based on limited studies, not a licence to wait until that deadline. Establish the least invasive effective intervention with the surgeon and radiologist, and resuscitate in parallel rather than repeatedly postponing treatment for normal laboratory values. The pre-induction briefing should expose the competing risks. Discuss aspiration, difficult airway, shock, blood availability, antibiotic administration, anticipated operation and the postoperative destination. Decompression and resuscitation can reduce risk without eliminating it. A patient who cannot survive a long optimisation period needs a coordinated operation/resuscitation plan; a stable patient may benefit from correcting a reversible problem before anaesthesia. Document what has been addressed, what remains and why proceeding is justified. Learning check: must lactate normalise before source control in septic shock? No. Ongoing infection may prevent normalisation. Resuscitate and arrange effective source control together, with senior surgical, anaesthetic and critical-care agreement. A suggested observational time window is not a reason to delay an immediately necessary intervention. Emergency intubation: distinguish oxygenation, first-pass success and survival Induction removes sympathetic compensation and spontaneous breathing; positive-pressure ventilation can reduce venous return. Plan induction dose, haemodynamic support, oxygenation and rescue together. Ketamine is an option, not a guarantee of cardiovascular stability in catecholamine-depleted shock. KETASED compared ketamine with etomidate: its primary maximum SOFA outcome did not differ significantly, and it did not establish a mortality advantage. Etomidate's adrenal suppression should not be converted into a claim that this trial proved increased septic-shock mortality. PreVent addressed hypoxaemia during ICU intubation. Among 401 critically ill adults, severe hypoxaemia occurred in 10.9% with bag-mask ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy versus 22.8% without it. This supports a considered oxygenation strategy in patients with poor reserve. Low aspiration event counts do not prove that ventilation is risk-free in bowel obstruction or active vomiting; assess aspiration risk, technique, airway pressure and the ability to ventilate. DEVICE addressed the first intubation attempt. In 1,417 critically ill adults, first-attempt success was 85.1% with video versus 70.8% with direct laryngoscopy. Severe complications were similar, 21.4% versus 20.9%. A better view and first-pass success do not remove the need for circulatory preparation or prove a survival benefit. Use a device the operator understands, with a suitable stylet/bougie, suction and a rehearsed failed-airway plan. IRIS did not settle cricoid-pressure efficacy. Aspiration occurred in 0.6% with cricoid and 0.5% with sham, but the trial failed to demonstrate non-inferiority of sham. Similar percentages are not proof of equivalence and do not establish that cricoid is either effective or unnecessary. Follow the applicable airway guidance; release pressure promptly if it impairs laryngoscopy, ventilation or supraglottic rescue. Cricoid pressure is not a replacement for suction, preoxygenation and a plan to maintain oxygenation. Learning check: did DEVICE show that video laryngoscopy prevents severe peri-intubation complications? No. It improved first-attempt success, while severe complication rates were similar. Prepare for cardiovascular collapse and hypoxaemia even when videolaryngoscopy is chosen. A short in-hospital delay in stable uncomplicated disease can be reasonable; this is not a requirement for immediate overnight surgery in every patient. Peritonitis, sepsis or deterioration changes the urgency. Abscess or phlegmon may require a different surgical/interventional strategy: do not extrapolate the uncomplicated timing rule to uncontrolled infection. Before anaesthesia, reassess hydration, vomiting, pain, pregnancy possibility and evidence of perforation. Aspiration strategy depends on the clinical risk rather than fasting time alone. During laparoscopy, consider the haemodynamic and ventilatory effects of pneumoperitoneum in a depleted patient. Agree analgesia and antiemetic treatment while accounting for renal function, infection and the planned postoperative pathway. WSES recommends a single preoperative broad-spectrum antibiotic dose, within 0–60 minutes before incision, and no postoperative antibiotics for uncomplicated appendicitis. Complicated disease, especially incomplete source control, needs a treatment course tailored to findings and the local antimicrobial pathway. Record whether disease was complicated and whether source control was adequate; do not automatically continue antibiotics merely because surgery was an emergency. Learning check: does an uncomplicated appendicectomy require postoperative antibiotics? Not routinely under WSES guidance. Give the recommended preoperative prophylaxis and distinguish uncomplicated disease from perforation, abscess or incomplete source control when planning postoperative treatment. In the absence of peritonitis, strangulation or bowel ischaemia, nonoperative management is usually appropriate: fasting, gastric decompression, fluid/electrolyte replacement and repeated review. Urgency is a clinical decision, not just a diagnosis

NCEPOD immediate intervention is life-, limb- or organ-saving, normally within minutes, with simultaneous resuscitation. Urgent intervention is normally within hours for acute or deteriorating potentially life-threatening conditions. Expedited intervention is normally within days when early treatment is needed but there is no immediate threat; elective intervention is planned.     Introduction

    Emergency surgery accounts for a significant proportion of anaesthetic workload and carries substantially higher morbidity and mortality than elective procedures. The NCEPOD classification (immediate, urgent, expedited, elective) guides timing. Key challenges include incomplete assessment, full stomach, physiological derangement, and limited time for optimisation.

      Management of Anticoagulation

      Patients on anticoagulants presenting for emergency surgery require rapid assessment of drug, timing of last dose, renal function, and bleeding severity. RSI & Cricoid Pressure — The Evidence

      Classical RSI (pre-oxygenation, predetermined dose of induction agent + suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg, no bag-mask ventilation, cricoid pressure 10 N awake → 30 N asleep) was described by Sellick in 1961 from cadaveric and small case-series data. More than six decades later almost every component has been challenged by higher-quality evidence, and contemporary RSI is now standard UK/European practice.

      Aspiration — the risk being mitigated

    Physiological goals

    • Permissive hypotension (SBP 80–90 mmHg) until surgical haemorrhage control — avoid in traumatic brain injury, where adequate cerebral perfusion pressure takes priority.
    • Minimise crystalloid; favour early 1:1:1 blood component (or whole-blood) resuscitation to limit dilutional coagulopathy.
    • Tranexamic acid within 3 h of injury/onset of bleeding.
    • Calcium replacement (ionised calcium falls rapidly with citrated blood products), active warming, and correction of acidosis.

    Haemostatic resuscitation

    Resuscitation is targeted at restoring haemostasis rather than simply volume, guided by viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) to direct component and fibrinogen replacement rather than fixed empirical ratios alone once results are available.

    Induction and maintenance

    • Ketamine or markedly reduced-dose induction agents to avoid vasodilation and cardiovascular collapse.
    • Consider TIVA with careful target reduction; high-dose opioid to blunt surgical stimulus while minimising further myocardial depression.
    • Awareness risk is increased by deliberately reduced anaesthetic dosing in shock — document rationale and consider processed EEG monitoring.

    Monitoring

    • Invasive arterial and central venous access; serial arterial blood gas, lactate and ionised calcium.
    • Continuous temperature monitoring with active warming; thromboelastography to guide component therapy.
    • Cell salvage and rapid infuser devices for high-volume blood loss.

    Postoperative management and complications

    Most deaths after emergency surgery happen after theatre, so planning critical care and spotting complications early are part of the anaesthetic job Safe transfer to critical care for ongoing resuscitation and correction of the lethal triad (temperature, coagulopathy, acidosis) before a planned return to theatre for definitive repair at 24–48 h.

    Emergency Appendicectomy

    Appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency. Typically affects young, otherwise healthy patients, but elderly patients may present late with perforation and sepsis.

      Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy

      A life-threatening obstetric emergency. Patients may present with catastrophic haemoperitoneum and haemodynamic collapse. The priority is rapid surgical haemorrhage control.

    • Do NOT delay surgery for investigations or optimisation — haemorrhage control is the resuscitation
    • Prepare for cardiovascular collapse at induction (loss of sympathetic drive)
    • Surgeon scrubbed and ready before induction — knife-to-skin within seconds
    • Cell salvage may be available but should not delay surgery
    • Anti-D: follow NICE NG126 (2026) by gestation — not offered up to 11+6 weeks; offered to RhD-negative patients at 12+0 to 12+6 weeks having surgery (see lesson below)
    • Emotional support — this is a pregnancy loss; debrief team and patient
    Intestinal Obstruction

    Patients with bowel obstruction present unique anaesthetic challenges including massive fluid shifts, electrolyte derangement, high aspiration risk, and abdominal compartment syndrome.

      Risk Scoring in Emergency Surgery
      Damage Control Resuscitation

      Damage control resuscitation (DCR) is the strategy of accepting an abbreviated operation and physiologically minimalist resuscitation in order to interrupt the self-reinforcing cycle of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy — the lethal triad — before it becomes irretrievable. It originated in military trauma but is now applied to any exsanguinating emergency laparotomy, ruptured aneurysm or obstetric catastrophe The anaesthetic contribution is to run the resuscitation in parallel with surgery: two people at the head end, a rapid infuser and fluid warmer, arterial and central access sited without delaying haemostasis, a ketamine-based cardiostable induction, minimal anaesthetic depth with a vasopressor infusion running, and repeated blood gases with calcium and viscoelastic testing every 30 minutes. Anticipate abdominal compartment syndrome, ongoing coagulopathy and the need for prolonged ICU support after transfer.

Recognition and immediate actions
Call for help, declare "major haemorrhage" and activate the hospital protocol via switchboard — this mobilises the laboratory, porters and a consultant haematologist as a single call.
Apply direct pressure, tourniquet or packing; make the definitive plan for haemostasis (surgery, endoscopy, interventional radiology) immediately — resuscitation buys time, it does not stop bleeding.
Establish large-bore access (two 14–16 G peripheral cannulae or a rapid-infusion catheter), send a full set of bloods including group and save/crossmatch, FBC, coagulation screen, fibrinogen, U&E, calcium and a blood gas with lactate.
Use group O emergency blood (O RhD-negative for women of childbearing potential) until group-specific units are available; switch as soon as possible to conserve O-negative stock.
Warm everything: fluid warmer, forced-air blanket, raise theatre temperature. Hypothermia below 35 °C independently worsens coagulopathy and platelet function.
Transfusion strategy
Empirical fixed-ratio packs (approximately 1:1 red cells to FFP) while bleeding is uncontrolled and no laboratory results are available, then switch to goal-directed therapy guided by viscoelastic testing or laboratory values as soon as they are obtainable
Targets: haemoglobin 70–90 g/L during active bleeding, platelets above 50 × 10⁹/L (above 100 × 10⁹/L with brain or eye injury or diffuse bleeding), fibrinogen above 1.5–2 g/L (FIBTEM/FIBTEM A5 below 10 mm), PT/APTT ratio below 1.5 and ionised calcium above 1.0 mmol/L.
Fibrinogen falls first in dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy — replace early with fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate rather than relying on FFP alone.
Give tranexamic acid early in traumatic and obstetric haemorrhage; the time-critical benefit lies with the first 1 g given within 3 hours.
Avoid large-volume crystalloid — it dilutes clotting factors, worsens acidosis and increases bleeding. Restrict clear fluid to a bridging role only.

Hypocalcaemia from citrate chelation — check ionised calcium every 30 minutes and replace with calcium chloride or gluconate.
Hyperkalaemia and acidosis from stored blood, compounded by hypoperfusion; correct acidosis by restoring perfusion rather than with bicarbonate.
Hypothermia, dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy — the self-reinforcing lethal triad.
TACO and TRALI, transfusion-associated hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest (particularly in children and with rapid central infusion of older units), and air embolism from pressurised infusion devices.

Decision to stop

2. Immediately after death is declared
Preserve the scene
: leave all lines, tubes, drains, drug ampoules and infusion syringes in situ — do not discard. Photograph the drug tray. The Coroner / Medical Examiner may require this.
Document contemporaneously
: anaesthetic chart, drugs given (with batch numbers), times, vital signs trend, interventions, who attended and when, decision-making.

if anaphylaxis is possible — mast-cell tryptase at 0, 1–2 h and 24 h.

3. Communication

Duty of Candour

Hospital chain

Coroner / Procurator Fiscal

5. Non-technical skills during the arrest
non-technical skills
as by technical resuscitation knowledge
Leadership and explicit role allocation
: one clinician declares themselves CPR leader and stands back from hands-on tasks to direct; nominate a
to log times/drugs/rhythm and a
for equipment and blood products. Ambiguous or absent leadership is a recurring theme in incident reports.
Situational awareness
: the leader should continuously scan the surgical field (ongoing blood loss, surgical manipulation), physiological trends on the monitor (not just the current number), and the state of the team (fatigue, task fixation, rising stress).
Closed-loop communication
: instructions are directed at a named individual, acknowledged back, and confirmed once complete (e.g. "give 1 mg adrenaline" → "giving 1 mg adrenaline now" → "1 mg adrenaline given"). This reduces omitted or duplicated interventions.
Structured hot debrief
immediately after the event, using a simple framework such as
(Summarise, Things that went well, Opportunities to improve, Points to action, Set a follow-up date) or a
diamond debrief
(facts → feelings → future actions, widening from the individual to the team). Keep it brief, blame-free, and focused on systems.
Human factors framework (applies to every critical incident).
Non-technical skills are the cognitive, social and personal-resource skills that complement technical knowledge and contribute to safe, efficient performance. The
(Anaesthetists' Non-Technical Skills) taxonomy groups them into four categories, and a large share of contributory factors in incident reports map onto them
Task management
: planning and preparing (drugs drawn up, difficult-airway trolley checked), prioritising (oxygenation before diagnosis), and identifying and using resources — e.g. delegating dantrolene mixing to two helpers.
Team working
: calling for help early, coordinating activities, exchanging information, and supporting others — e.g. declaring "this is anaphylaxis, I am leading, please start the QRH".
Situation awareness
: gathering information, recognising and understanding it, and anticipating — e.g. noticing a steadily rising EtCO₂ before tachycardia appears in MH.
Decision making
: identifying options, balancing risks, selecting and re-evaluating — e.g. deciding to wake the patient versus proceeding to front-of-neck access, and reviewing that decision as SpO₂ changes.

for every instruction and

such as the Association of Anaesthetists Quick Reference Handbook and local crisis checklists should be read aloud by a nominated "reader" rather than recalled from memory. Finally, incidents rarely stem from a single
active error

Recognise the

in detail — the involved clinician(s) themselves become a casualty of the event, with acute stress reactions, sleep disturbance, intrusive recollection, guilt, loss of confidence, and risk of subsequent defensive practice or burnout. This can affect anaesthetists, ODPs, scrub staff, and surgeons alike, and may be underestimated by colleagues.

# Anaesthesia in Resource-Poor Settings WHO–WFSA standards, draw-over vaporisers, ketamine, spinal-first practice, Lifebox, SAFE courses, global surgery Spinal or General Anaesthesia for Caesarean Delivery in Africa: What ASOS Shows Caesarean delivery was the commonest operation in the African Surgical Outcomes Study. A 2024 secondary analysis looked at 3,709 caesarean deliveries in 22 African countries. Spinal anaesthesia was used in 2,968 (80%) and general anaesthesia in 741 (20%). Who received general anaesthesia? General anaesthesia was independently associated with ASA III (adjusted OR 11.84) and ASA IV (11.48), eclampsia (3.92), placental abruption (6.23), ruptured uterus (3.61) and increasing gestational age (1.093 per unit).     How big is the workforce gap? The WFSA survey

    The WFSA Global Anesthesia Workforce Survey (2015–16) collected data from 153 of 197 countries, covering 97.5% of the world >Non-physician providers make up a large share of the workforce, especially where resources are limited.     The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery (2015) set a target of at least 20 specialist surgical, anaesthetic and obstetric (SAO) physicians per 100,000 population by 2030.What happens to patients? The African Surgical Outcomes Study (ASOS)

    ASOS was a 7-day prospective cohort of 11,422 adult inpatients from 247 hospitals in 25 African countries (2016). Hospitals had a median of 0.7 specialist surgeons, obstetricians and anaesthetists combined per 100,000 population served. The patients were young (mean age 38.5 years) and low-risk (median ASA 1).     In eight hospitals across high-, middle- and low-income settings (including Ifakara, Tanzania and New Delhi, India), outcomes were compared in 3,733 patients before and 3,955 patients after the checklist was introduced. # Mechanical Ventilation Ventilator modes, ARDS protocols, lung-protective strategies, weaning Weaning, liberation and extubation are different decisions Weaning is reducing ventilatory support; liberation is ending invasive mechanical ventilation when it is no longer required. Extubation is removal of the endotracheal tube. An adult may breathe without ventilatory assistance yet still need an artificial airway because of poor airway protection or secretion clearance. A spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) assesses breathing with minimal or no positive-pressure assistance, usually for 30–120 minutes . Readiness is a clinical screen, not an RSBI gate The AARC 2024 guideline supports a simple readiness screen: some reversal of the cause of respiratory failure, adequate oxygenation, haemodynamic stability and the ability to initiate an inspiratory effort. # ICU Ventilation Protocols Standardised admission settings (ARDSNet), monitoring of plateau and driving pressure, paired sedation and weaning protocols, protocolised and automated weaning evidence Teaching reasoning (not a quoted guideline): Why admission settings are standardised The ARDS Network trial compared tidal volumes of 6 and 12 ml/kg predicted body weight in acute lung injury and ARDS, with plateau pressure limits in the low-volume arm. The trial was stopped after the enrollment of 861 patients because mortality was lower in the group treated with lower tidal volumes than in the group treated with traditional tidal volumes (31.0 percent vs. 39.8 percent, P=0.007), and the number of days without ventilator use during the first 28 days after randomization was greater in this group (mean [+/-SD], 12+/-11 vs. 10+/-11; P=0.007). The mean tidal volumes on days 1 to 3 were 6.2+/-0.8 and 11.8+/-0.8 ml per kilogram of predicted body weight (P<0.001), respectively, and the mean plateau pressures were 25+/-6 and 33+/-8 cm of water (P<0.001), respectively. a written admission protocol makes the low-volume start automatic rather than dependent on who is on call. A typical unit checklist: measure height, calculate predicted body weight, set the initial tidal volume from it, set PEEP and FiO₂ from the unit table, document target SpO₂ and pH, and check plateau pressure once the patient is settled. Driving pressure (ΔP) is plateau pressure minus PEEP, which equals tidal volume divided by respiratory system compliance. # Bronchospastic Respiratory Failure Life-threatening asthma, IECOPD, pharmacology, NIV, ventilation strategies, inhaled volatiles via Sedaconda What "intrinsic PEEP" means Intrinsic PEEP (PEEPi, also called auto-PEEP) is the pressure left in the alveoli at the end of expiration, over and above the PEEP set on the ventilator. It happens when the next breath arrives before the previous one has been fully exhaled: the unexhaled gas is trapped, and the lung fails to return to its relaxed volume (functional residual capacity). That failure is called dynamic hyperinflation. Intrinsic PEEP, auto-PEEP and dynamic hyperinflation are often used interchangeably, but strictly intrinsic PEEP is the pressure and dynamic hyperinflation is the extra volume. The term separates two parts of the end-expiratory pressure. Set PEEP (external or applied PEEP) is what you dial in. Total PEEP is the actual end-expiratory alveolar pressure. Intrinsic PEEP is the difference: total PEEP minus set PEEP. The ventilator's normal pressure display cannot show it, because during expiration the gauge reads circuit pressure, not alveolar pressure, while gas is still flowing out. Why it builds up in bronchospasm: time constants Passive expiration empties the lung exponentially. The rate is set by the expiratory time constant (τ), the product of resistance and compliance. After one τ about 37% of the tidal volume remains, after two τ 14%, and after three τ 5%. A patient therefore needs an expiratory time longer than about three time constants to exhale the breath before the next one starts. Bronchospasm greatly raises resistance, lengthens τ and makes the available expiratory time too short at normal rates. Each breath then leaves a little more gas behind, until a new, higher steady state is reached. Because τ calculated at the bedside uses resistance measured during inspiration, it may underestimate the true expiratory time constant when airway resistance is higher in expiration, as it is in asthma. How to detect and measure it Flow–time waveform: if expiratory flow has not returned to zero when the next inspiration starts, gas is trapped. This is the quickest bedside sign. End-expiratory hold: occluding the expiratory port at end-expiration lets proximal airway pressure equilibrate with alveolar pressure, so the plateau reached is total PEEP, and the amount above set PEEP is intrinsic PEEP. The patient must be relaxed, because active expiratory muscle contraction raises the reading without adding hyperinflation. Only lung units still connected to the airway equilibrate, so when airways close during expiration the hold can intrinsic PEEP. Treat a low value with suspicion if the plateau pressure is rising without another explanation. Trapped volume (VEI): the volume exhaled during 20–60 seconds of apnoea in a paralysed patient is the volume above functional residual capacity at end-inspiration. In Tuxen and Lane's work, a VEI above 20 ml/kg predicted hypotension and barotrauma in ventilated severe asthma. Why it matters raised intrathoracic pressure impedes venous return; severe hyperinflation causes hypotension and can progress to cardiac arrest (see the cardiovascular box below). rising end-inspiratory volume and plateau pressure increase the risk of pneumothorax. Smaller breaths in pressure control: the trapped pressure reduces the gradient for inflow, so each breath delivers less volume. Ineffective triggering: a spontaneously breathing patient must first lower alveolar pressure by the whole intrinsic PEEP before reaching the trigger threshold below set PEEP. Efforts that fail to trigger increase work of breathing and cause distress and agitation. This applies to flow triggering too. Reducing it Once bronchodilator and other medical treatment is under way, reducing minute ventilation is by far the most effective way to reduce gas trapping : lower the rate and tidal volume and accept hypercapnia. Lengthening expiratory time (shorter inspiratory time, no inspiratory pause) helps too, but the gain becomes modest once minute ventilation is 10 L/min or less. Adding set PEEP is a different question in controlled and spontaneous breathing. In a patient who is triggering, raising set PEEP to just below total PEEP reduces the pressure that has to be overcome to trigger a breath. In controlled ventilation, external PEEP in severe asthma is controversial: it can raise total PEEP and worsen trapping. In Caramez's study of eight patients with obstruction under controlled ventilation, responses to stepwise external PEEP were not predictable: some patients showed no change until a threshold, others overinflated progressively, and a few deflated paradoxically. Any change therefore needs measuring (plateau pressure, total PEEP, blood pressure) rather than assuming. Learning check: set PEEP 5, end-expiratory hold reads 14 cmH₂O. What is the intrinsic PEEP, and could it be higher? Intrinsic PEEP is 14 − 5 = 9 cmH₂O (total PEEP 14). It could be higher: if some airways close during expiration, the hold only measures the units still communicating with the airway, so it can underestimate the trapped pressure. Learning check: a ventilated asthmatic's τ is 1 s and expiratory time is 2 s. What happens? Expiration lasts only two time constants, so about 14% of the tidal volume is still in the lung when the next breath starts. Gas trapping and intrinsic PEEP build up. Expiratory time should exceed about three time constants, mainly by lowering the rate and minute ventilation. # Circulatory Failure, Shock & Mechanical Circulatory Support Hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive and obstructive shock; vasopressor rationale; IABP, Impella, LVAD, VV/VA-ECMO Teaching calculator: MAP, shock index and cardiac power output Heart rate Systolic (mm Hg) Diastolic (mm Hg) Cardiac output (L/min, optional) MAP about Shock index Cardiac power output Enter heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure (diastolic not above systolic). Arithmetic only. A calculated MAP is not a measured arterial line MAP and does not tell you the cause of shock or what to give. Latest Guidelines and Bedside Management of Shock Shock is inadequate tissue oxygen delivery for demand. At the bedside the first job is not to name the type but to restore perfusion while you find out. A quick look at the heart with ultrasound, the jugular veins, the skin and the lactate usually sorts the four types — hypovolaemic, distributive, cardiogenic and obstructive — within minutes. Mixed shock is common: a septic patient can also be dry and have septic cardiomyopathy. What the recent trials changed Bedside meaning What MAP? SSC 2021: initial MAP 65 mm Hg over higher targets. 65 trial (age ≥65): permissive MAP 60–65 gave 41.0% vs 43.8% 90-day mortality, not significant. Start at 65; in older vasodilated patients, chasing higher numbers adds vasopressor without proven benefit. Individualise for chronic hypertension or raised intracranial pressure. Which vasopressor first? SOAP II: no mortality difference, but arrhythmias 24.1% with dopamine vs 12.4% with noradrenaline. Noradrenaline is the default first agent; dopamine has fallen out of use. What resuscitation endpoint? ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: capillary refill-targeted 34.9% vs lactate-targeted 43.4% 28-day mortality (P = .06), less organ dysfunction at 72 h. Capillary refill time is a valid, fast, repeatable target; lactate falls slowly and is not only a perfusion marker. Routine VA-ECMO in infarct shock? ECLS-SHOCK: 47.8% vs 49.0% 30-day mortality; more bleeding and vascular complications. Do not use VA-ECMO routinely; reserve it for selected patients in experienced centres. Microaxial pump (Impella CP)? DanGer Shock (STEMI shock, selected, no coma): 45.8% vs 58.5% mortality at 180 days , but safety events 24.0% vs 6.2%. The first device trial to show a survival benefit, in a narrow group; limb ischaemia, bleeding and renal replacement were more common. Bedside checklist: the first hour Call for help. Airway, breathing, two large-bore cannulas, bloods with lactate and a blood gas. Look: mottling, capillary refill (press 10 s on the finger pad; normal ≤3 s), conscious level, urine output. Point-of-care ultrasound: big or small heart, poor or good function, pericardial fluid, right heart strain, free abdominal fluid, lung B-lines. Treat the type you find: fluid or blood for hypovolaemia; antibiotics and source control for sepsis; reperfusion and inotropes for cardiogenic; decompress for tension pneumothorax or tamponade; thrombolysis for massive pulmonary embolism. Start noradrenaline early if MAP stays below 65 — peripherally through a good cannula while central access is arranged. Insert an arterial line; non-invasive cuffs are unreliable in shock. Reassess every 15–30 minutes. Stop fluids when the patient no longer responds or develops lung water. In cardiogenic shock from a heart attack, call cardiology for the catheter lab early and discuss mechanical support only in a shock centre. Worked case (fictional) A 71-year-old woman is cold and confused 6 hours after an anterior heart attack. HR 115, BP 82/58, lactate 5.2, capillary refill 6 s. Calculated MAP is about 66 and the shock index 1.4. Ultrasound shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle and B-lines, so this is cardiogenic, not hypovolaemic: the team gives no fluid bolus. Noradrenaline holds the MAP at 65, an arterial line goes in and she goes straight to the catheter lab. Cardiac output by thermodilution is 2.8 L/min, giving a cardiac power output of about 0.41 W. The shock team discusses a microaxial pump, weighing the DanGer Shock survival benefit against the limb and bleeding risks. Learning check: what did ECLS-SHOCK show about routine VA-ECMO? No survival benefit (47.8% vs 49.0% at 30 days) and more bleeding and vascular complications. It should not be used routinely in infarct-related cardiogenic shock. These are teaching notes, not a shock protocol. # Cardiac Output Monitoring
PA catheter, PiCCO, oesophageal Doppler, echocardiography


1. Introduction & Curriculum Scope
Curriculum mapping
FRCA Final (RCoA):
principles of CO measurement; Fick principle; indicator dilution and thermodilution; pulse contour analysis; oesophageal Doppler; echocardiography for haemodynamic assessment; advantages and limitations of available monitors.
FFICM (FICM):
haemodynamic monitoring in shock; fluid responsiveness assessment; SvO₂/ScvO₂ interpretation; appropriate selection and interpretation of CO monitoring; evidence base (PAC-Man, FACTT, OPTIMISE) and limitations of each modality.
Common SBA / structured oral themes:
Stewart-Hamilton equation, dynamic vs static preload markers, sources of error, choosing a monitor for a clinical scenario.
2. Why Measure Cardiac Output?
Define the type of shock
using a haemodynamic profile (CO, SVR, preload, oxygenation indices).
Predict fluid responsiveness
before committing to volume that may worsen lung water.
Titrate vasoactive drugs
(inotropes vs vasopressors) to a physiological endpoint.
Calculate oxygen delivery
(DO₂ in mL/min = CO in L/min × CaO₂ in mL/dL × 10, or CO × CaO₂ when content is mL/L) — the link between haemodynamics and tissue oxygenation.
Detect and trend deterioration
earlier than BP, lactate, or urine output.
3. Physiological Foundations
Fick principle (the reference standard)
Oxygen content:
CxO₂ (mL/dL) = (Hb (g/dL) × 1.34 × SxO₂ (fraction)) + (PxO₂ (kPa) × 0.0225); use 0.003 if PO₂ is in mmHg. CaO₂ uses arterial values; CvO₂ uses a true mixed venous sample from the pulmonary artery.
measured by indirect calorimetry (metabolic cart) from inspired–expired O₂ differences and minute ventilation; normally about 250 mL/min (≈ 120–140 mL/min/m²).
Error sources:
requires a steady metabolic state; VO₂ measurement is inaccurate at high FiO₂ and with circuit leaks in ventilated patients; needs simultaneous arterial and PAC samples; intrapulmonary O₂ consumption in inflamed lungs is not counted. Hence a research or validation tool rather than a bedside monitor.
Indicator dilution & the Stewart-Hamilton equation
CO = (V
× (T
− T
) × K) / ∫ ΔT · dt
= volume injected, T
= blood/injectate temperature, K = computation constant, and ∫ΔT·dt = area under the temperature-time curve at the thermistor. A small AUC reflects rapid wash-out and high CO; a large AUC reflects slow wash-out and low CO.
Doppler principle
v cos θ) / c. Multiplying the velocity-time integral (VTI, "stroke distance") by the cross-sectional area of the vessel gives stroke volume. Underpins both the oesophageal Doppler (descending aorta) and echocardiographic SV (LVOT VTI × LVOT area).
Pulse contour analysis
Bioimpedance & bioreactance
a low-amplitude, high-frequency current is applied across the thorax through skin electrodes. Thoracic bioimpedance measures the beat-to-beat fall in electrical impedance as blood volume in the aorta rises during systole, and converts the rate of change into stroke volume through a population-derived equation. Bioreactance (NICOM) instead measures the
phase shift
(time delay) between the applied and received signal, which tracks aortic flow and is less corrupted by static tissue, fluid and motion artefact.
four thoracic pads give continuous, entirely non-invasive cardiac output and stroke-volume-variation trending with no vascular access — attractive in theatre recovery, the emergency department, obstetrics, and for passive-leg-raise testing in patients who do not warrant an arterial line.
a systematic review and meta-analysis of completely non-invasive devices (37 studies, 1543 patients) found a pooled bias of −0.13 L/min but limits of agreement of −2.38 to +2.12 L/min and a
percentage error of 47%
, far outside the 30% limit of acceptance — so these devices are
interchangeable with bolus thermodilution for absolute values and should be used for trends only
. Accuracy degrades further with pulmonary oedema, large pleural effusions, arrhythmia, patient movement, diathermy and poor electrode contact.
4. Reference Standard & Validation Hierarchy
Understanding percentage error
in response to an intervention (fluid, inotrope), assessed formally with concordance analysis (four-quadrant plots) or polar plots rather than single absolute readings.
Gold standard (research)
Direct Fick
Validation only — too cumbersome clinically
Clinical reference
PAC bolus thermodilution (mean of 3)
Reference for new device studies
Calibrated continuous
PiCCO / LiDCO / continuous-CO PAC
Bedside, beat-to-beat, periodic recalibration
Uncalibrated continuous
FloTrac, oesophageal Doppler
Trending, intra-operative GDT
NICOM, ClearSight (volume-clamp), TTE
Screening, ambulatory, perioperative
5. Thermodilution Methods
Right-heart thermodilution (PAC)
10 mL iced saline injected via the RA port; thermistor at the PA tip detects the temperature change. Short transit time. Provides intermittent (or continuous via a heated filament) CO, plus PAOP, CVP, PAP, SvO₂, and derived PVR/SVR.
PA rupture is rare (well under 0.2% of insertions) but carries a mortality of about 50%; avoid over-wedging and deflate the balloon after each wedge reading.
Transpulmonary thermodilution (TPTD, PiCCO/EV1000)
15–20 mL iced saline via CVC; thermistor at the femoral artery. The longer transit through both ventricles and the pulmonary circulation allows mathematical derivation of GEDV (preload) and EVLW (lung water) from the mean transit time and exponential down-slope of the curve.
From the curve:
mean transit time (MTt) × CO = intrathoracic thermal volume (ITTV); exponential downslope time (DSt) × CO = pulmonary thermal volume (PTV). GEDV = ITTV − PTV.
ITBV ≈ 1.25 × GEDV; EVLW = ITTV − ITBV; PVPI = EVLW / PBV (PBV ≈ 0.25 × GEDV).
Typical normal values:
GEDI 680–800 mL/m² (preload); EVLWI 3–7 mL/kg, > 10 mL/kg indicates pulmonary oedema; PVPI 1–3.
high EVLWI with PVPI < 3 suggests hydrostatic (cardiogenic or overload) oedema; high EVLWI with PVPI > 3 suggests permeability oedema (ARDS).
Why volumes:
unlike CVP and PAOP, these volumetric markers are not directly distorted by intrathoracic and PEEP-related pressures, which matters in ventilated ARDS patients.
Sources of error:
respiratory variation (inject at end-expiration), tricuspid regurgitation (recirculation distorts the curve), intracardiac shunts (loss of indicator), warm/incorrect injectate volume, thermistor drift, and rapid changes in patient temperature (CRRT, ECMO).
6. Pulse Contour & Uncalibrated Devices
Standard arterial line + dedicated transducer. Compliance estimated from age, sex, height, weight, and the waveform itself; updated every 20 s. Convenient (no calibration) but accuracy degrades in vasoplegia, rapid SVR change, severe arrhythmia, and aortic regurgitation. It is characteristically inaccurate in hyperdynamic, low-resistance states — the classic example being cirrhosis/end-stage liver disease undergoing liver surgery, where percentage error against thermodilution has been reported at ~54%, well beyond the 30% limit of acceptance, with bias increasing as peripheral resistance falls (
). In such states absolute CO values are unreliable and only trends should be used. Latest software (4th-generation) has improved but not eliminated this limitation.
6a. The Edwards Acumen IQ Sensor & Hypotension Prediction Index (HPI)
Acumen IQ
is a next-generation arterial-line pressure transducer from Edwards Lifesciences that plugs into the
platform. It uses the fourth-generation FloTrac pulse-contour algorithm, so it is
minimally invasive and uncalibrated
— a peripheral (typically radial) arterial cannula is the only vascular access required. What sets it apart from a standard FloTrac is that it also outputs advanced haemodynamic variables and the machine-learned
Hypotension Prediction Index (HPI)
, a scalar (0–100) that forecasts an impending hypotensive episode (MAP < 65 mmHg for ≥ 1 min) approximately 15 minutes in advance.
How it works
Signal acquisition
A high-fidelity pressure transducer samples the arterial waveform at 100 Hz. No thermodilution or lithium calibration is required; patient demographics (age, sex, height, weight) initialise the vascular-compliance estimate.
FloTrac 4th-gen — CO/SV
SV =
, where σ
is the standard deviation of the arterial pressure over a 20 s window and χ is a compliance/impedance factor updated every 20 s from waveform morphology (skewness, kurtosis, heart rate). CO = SV × HR.
Advanced parameters
(preload responsiveness);
(maximal upstroke slope — a surrogate of LV contractility);
(dynamic arterial elastance = PPV/SVV — predicts MAP response to fluid).
HPI — the ML layer
A logistic-regression model trained on more than 20 features extracted from each pressure beat (upstroke slope, dicrotic notch position and height, systolic area, complexity, beat-to-beat variability). Output is a 0–100 probability score updated every 20 s; an alarm at HPI ≥ 85 flags likely hypotension within ~15 min, prompting a "hypotension bundle" (fluid, vasopressor, or inotrope guided by SVV, SVR and dP/dt).
Evidence base
Hatib et al., Anesthesiology 2018
Algorithm derivation & validation on 1334 arterial waveforms
HPI predicted hypotension 15 min ahead: sensitivity 88%, specificity 87%, AUROC 0.95. 10 min: 89/90%. 5 min: 92/92%.
Wijnberge et al.,
, JAMA 2020
Single-centre RCT, 68 adults, elective non-cardiac surgery
HPI-guided care reduced median time-weighted average of hypotension from 0.44 to 0.10 mmHg (a 74% reduction). No change in AKI or 30-day outcomes in this small trial.
Maheshwari et al., Intensive Care Med 2020
Multicentre RCT, 214 ICU patients
No significant reduction in time-weighted MAP < 65 mmHg vs standard care — a reminder that pre-warning alone is not enough; the accompanying treatment protocol matters.
Schneck et al., BJA 2020; Davies et al., A&A 2020
External validations
Reproduced 15-min prediction performance, but noted that HPI is strongly correlated with the current MAP itself — some of the "prediction" reflects a MAP already trending down. Interpret HPI in the context of the arterial trace, not in isolation.
EU-HYPROTECT registry, 2023
Prospective observational, 749 major non-cardiac surgical patients
HPI-guided haemodynamic management associated with a low burden of intra-operative hypotension, supporting real-world feasibility.
Limitations & controversy:
HPI shares all the pulse-contour caveats (aortic regurgitation, IABP, severe arrhythmia, rapid SVR change, damped or under-damped arterial trace). Independent analyses (Enevoldsen & Vistisen, 2022) have argued that a simple "MAP < 72 mmHg now" rule performs almost as well, so HPI's incremental value over vigilant MAP monitoring plus a good treatment protocol remains debated. Currently endorsed as a decision-support tool rather than a standalone target.
7. Echocardiography for Haemodynamic Assessment
of haemodynamic derangement, not just the haemodynamic profile. SV is calculated as LVOT VTI × LVOT cross-sectional area (π × (LVOT diameter / 2)²); CO = SV × HR.
TTE — focused protocols
FATE, FUSIC HD, FOCUS, RUSH. Rapid binary assessment of LV function, RV strain, pericardial fluid, IVC collapsibility, and gross valve disease. Accreditation routes via BSE Level 1 / FUSIC.
TOE — when to use
Better windows in the ventilated, obese, or post-cardiac-surgery patient; intra-operative cardiac surgery; suspected endocarditis or aortic dissection; persistent unexplained shock when TTE windows are inadequate. Risks: oesophageal injury (~0.02%), bleeding, displacement of ETT.
8. Assessing Fluid Responsiveness
Requirements / pitfalls
SVV / PPV
Sinus rhythm, mandatory ventilation, V
≥ 8 mL/kg, closed chest, no significant RV failure or raised intra-abdominal pressure
Passive leg raise (PLR)
↑ SV ≥10%
Reversible "auto-bolus" of ~300 mL — works in spontaneous breathing and arrhythmia. Needs continuous SV monitoring (Doppler, PiCCO, echo VTI)
End-expiratory occlusion
↑ CO ≥5%
15 s expiratory hold ↑ preload; useful when SVV/PPV unreliable
IVC distensibility (TTE)
ΔIVC >18% (vent) / >50% collapse (SB)
Subcostal view; affected by raised intra-abdominal pressure and RV failure
Mini-fluid challenge
↑ SV ≥6% after 100 mL over 1 min
Avoids overload if non-responsive
FTc (oesophageal Doppler)
<330 ms
Static surrogate of preload — historically used to drive intra-op GDT
Tidal volume challenge
ΔPPV >3.5% (or ΔSVV >2.5%)
Transiently increase V
from 6 to 8 mL/kg PBW for 1 min; requires sinus rhythm, fully passive (controlled) ventilation and no severe RV failure
Tidal volume challenge:
in ARDS patients ventilated at low V
(6 mL/kg), baseline PPV and SVV are unreliable predictors of fluid responsiveness because the tidal swing in intrathoracic pressure is too small to load-unload the ventricles adequately. Transiently increasing V
to 8 mL/kg predicted body weight for one minute amplifies this swing; an absolute increase in PPV >3.5 percentage points (or SVV >2.5 points) reliably predicts fluid responsiveness. Return V
to 6 mL/kg once the manoeuvre is complete
8a. Haemodynamic Monitoring on ECMO
Pulse contour analysis (uncalibrated or calibrated — FloTrac, PiCCO, LiDCO)
is unreliable because VA-ECMO flow is largely non-pulsatile; the arterial waveform morphology reflects the combination of native and extracorporeal flow, not native stroke volume alone.
Thermodilution (PAC or transpulmonary)
is inaccurate on ECMO because injected indicator is lost into the extracorporeal circuit and the membrane oxygenator's heat exchanger confounds the thermal signal.
Native cardiac function must instead be assessed with echocardiography (TTE/TOE)
— LVOT VTI, aortic valve opening (a marker of adequate LV ejection and a warning sign for LV distension if fixed closed), global and regional ventricular function, cannula position, and exclusion of tamponade — together with the pulse pressure on the arterial trace as a bedside surrogate of native ejection.
Monitor the circuit itself
: pump (blood) flow, pre- and post-membrane pressures, sweep gas flow/FiO₂, pre- and post-oxygenator blood gases, and circuit/mixed venous oxygen saturation.
Perfusion surrogates
: lactate trend and regional/differential oxygenation (right radial vs lower limb saturation — the "Harlequin" or North-South syndrome seen with peripheral VA-ECMO and a recovering native heart ejecting poorly oxygenated blood into the aortic root).
9. Oxygen Delivery, SvO₂ & ScvO₂
DO₂ (mL/min) = CO (L/min) × CaO₂ (mL/dL) × 10; CaO₂ = 1.34 × Hb (g/dL) × SaO₂ (fraction) + 0.0225 × PaO₂ (kPa)
. Use 0.003 for PaO₂ in mmHg. With CaO₂ already in mL/L, omit ×10. Resting DO₂ is approximately 1000 mL/min in a 70 kg adult. Tissue extraction (VO₂ ≈ 250 mL/min) gives a normal mixed venous saturation of 65–75%.
SvO₂ (PA sample)
True mixed venous, sampled from the PA via a PAC. Normal 65–75%. Falls when DO₂ falls (low CO, anaemia, hypoxaemia) or VO₂ rises (fever, shivering, agitation). Continuous fibre-optic measurement is possible.
ScvO₂ (CVC sample)
Sampled from a CVC tip in the SVC — surrogate for SvO₂, usually ~5% higher. Easier to obtain. Used in early goal-directed sepsis bundles (target >70%); subsequent trials (ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe) showed no mortality benefit from protocolised ScvO₂-guided care, but it remains a useful marker of global DO₂/VO₂ balance.
Veno-arterial CO₂ gap (Pv-aCO₂):
the difference between central venous and arterial PCO₂ (normal
2–6 mmHg, 0.3–0.8 kPa
Physiological basis:
tissues continuously produce CO₂, and its removal depends on venous blood flow to wash it out. When flow is low, CO₂ accumulates in the tissues and in the effluent venous blood (an effect amplified by the Haldane effect in desaturated blood), so the gap widens even though total CO₂ production may be unchanged or reduced.
a gap >6 mmHg indicates that cardiac output is inadequate to clear the CO₂ being produced — a marker of global hypoperfusion — and it stays informative when ScvO₂ is misleadingly normal or high (sepsis with microcirculatory shunting, cyanide toxicity, AV shunts).
Clinical utility:
in septic shock, a persistently wide gap after initial fluid resuscitation argues for improving flow (inotrope, or reassessing fluid responsiveness dynamically) rather than reflexively giving more fluid, since further expansion may cost ventilator-free days and worsen pulmonary oedema and RV failure
Ratio analysis:
the Pv-aCO₂ / Ca-vO₂ ratio (normal <1.4 mmHg per mL/dL) rises when metabolism becomes anaerobic and is a useful adjunct to lactate when interpreting persistent shock.

Stroke volume from LVOT VTI (echo)
SV ≈ 57 mL, CO ≈ 5.1 L/min, CI ≈ 2.8 L/min/m² — within normal limits. A small error in LVOT diameter is squared, so this is the dominant source of error in echo-derived CO.
Stewart-Hamilton & oxygen delivery from a PAC
DO₂ is preserved by a high CO, but the low SvO₂ and widened extraction ratio show that VO₂ has outstripped delivery — typical 'high-output but inadequate' septic profile. Treat the cause; do not be reassured by a normal CO.
Fluid responsiveness — when SVV is invalid
Do not act on the low SVV. Perform PLR (or mini-fluid challenge) and, given the ARDS context, also check EVLWI on PiCCO before further volume — high EVLWI argues for vasopressor and inotrope rather than fluid.
Choosing a monitor — RV failure on the unit
Insert a PAC. Trend PAP, PVR and SvO₂ as therapy is escalated. Avoid fluid loading guided by CVP alone — RV is preload-sensitive both ways.
CO = SV × HR; CI 2.5–4.0 L/min/m². BP can be preserved despite a falling CO via compensatory vasoconstriction — measure flow, don't assume it.
Direct Fick is the research gold standard; bolus PAC thermodilution is the clinical reference against which other devices are validated (Bland-Altman, percentage error ≤30% = interchangeable).
Stewart-Hamilton: CO is inversely proportional to the area under the indicator concentration-time curve.

Definition & Classification Haemodynamic Definition (2022 ESC/ERS) Pulmonary hypertension: resting mPAP ≥20 mmHg measured by right heart catheterisation (lowered from the previous ≥25 mmHg threshold) Pre-capillary PH: mPAP ≥20, PAWP ≤15 mmHg, PVR >2 Wood units (e.g. PAH, chronic thromboembolic, lung disease) Isolated post-capillary PH: mPAP ≥20, PAWP >15 mmHg, PVR ≤2 (left heart disease) Combined pre- and post-capillary PH: mPAP ≥20, PAWP >15, PVR >2 (advanced left heart disease with reactive pulmonary remodelling) Exercise PH: mPAP/CO slope >3 mmHg/L/min between rest and exercise — recognised in 2022 update WHO Clinical Groups Group 1 — PAH: idiopathic, heritable (BMPR2), drug-induced (anorexigens, methamphetamine), connective tissue disease (scleroderma), HIV, portopulmonary, congenital L→R shunts Group 2 — Left heart disease: HFrEF, HFpEF, valvular disease (commonest cause of PH overall) Group 3 — Lung disease/hypoxia: COPD, ILD, OSA, high altitude Group 4 — Chronic thromboembolic PH (CTEPH): potentially curable by pulmonary endarterectomy Group 5 — Multifactorial/unclear: sarcoidosis, haematological disorders (sickle cell), metabolic disorders Severity Markers WHO functional class III/IV, syncope, signs of right heart failure (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral oedema) 6-minute walk test <165 m, NT-proBNP >1100 ng/L, RA area >26 cm², pericardial effusion Cardiac index <2.0 L/min/m², RA pressure >14 mmHg, mixed venous saturation <60% These translate to a 1-year mortality >20% in the ESC/ERS risk stratification table Pathophysiology — From Endothelial Injury to RV Failure The thin-walled RV is designed for a low-impedance circulation; it tolerates volume but not pressure overload Acute rises in PVR cause RV dilatation → tricuspid regurgitation → further RV dilatation (a vicious cycle) RV dilatation shifts the interventricular septum leftwards (reverse Bernheim effect) → reduced LV preload, reduced cardiac output, systemic hypotension Unlike the LV, the RV is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle; once RV pressure approaches aortic pressure, RV perfusion becomes systolic-only and ischaemia develops The result is a "spiral of death": ↑PVR → RV failure → ↓LV filling → ↓MAP → ↓RV coronary perfusion → worsening RV failure Targeted Pulmonary Vasodilator Therapy Three Pathways of PAH Therapy Nitric oxide / cGMP pathway: phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil); soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator (riociguat — used in CTEPH) Endothelin pathway: endothelin receptor antagonists — bosentan (dual ETA/ETB), ambrisentan and macitentan (selective ETA). Hepatotoxicity with bosentan; teratogenic Prostacyclin pathway: inhaled iloprost, IV epoprostenol (very short half-life, 3–5 min — abrupt cessation is fatal), subcutaneous/IV treprostinil, oral selexipag (IP receptor agonist) Group 1 PAH is treated with combination therapy from diagnosis (AMBITION trial — ambrisentan + tadalafil) These agents are indicated for groups 2 or 3 — they may worsen pulmonary oedema by increasing pulmonary blood flow Inhaled Selective Pulmonary Vasodilators Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO): 10–40 ppm — selective for ventilated alveoli, no systemic vasodilatation (rapidly inactivated by haemoglobin). Rebound PH on cessation; wean over hours. Emergency surgery Major thoracic or intra-abdominal surgery Laparoscopic surgery with pneumoperitoneum (raised intra-abdominal pressure increases PVR and reduces venous return) Prolonged surgery (>3 # Arrhythmias & ECG Interpretation
Systematic ECG approach, brady- and tachyarrhythmias, heart block, bundle branch block, peri-arrest algorithms, electrolyte disturbances, ICU pacing & defibrillation


ICU red-flag patterns
Wide-complex tachycardia
— assume VT until proven otherwise (especially with structural heart disease).
New LBBB + chest pain or ROSC
— treat as STEMI equivalent; consider PPCI.
QTc > 500 ms
— stop QT-prolonging drugs, replete K⁺ > 4.5 and Mg²⁺ > 1.0 mmol/L.
Peaked T waves + wide QRS
— hyperkalaemia, give 10 mL 10 % calcium gluconate
U waves + flat T + long QU
— hypokalaemia → torsades risk.
Reciprocal change is your friend
Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) often shows ST depression in I/aVL. Posterior STEMI shows tall R + ST depression in V1–V3 — confirm with V7–V9.
Right-sided leads
Inferior STEMI: always do V4R. ST elevation = RV infarct → preload-dependent → cautious nitrates, fluid load, avoid β-blockers.
at the time of the ECG, the
ST segment is isoelectric
, and the
troponin is often normal
— yet without angiography they are at very high risk of an extensive anterior MI within days. Pattern A (biphasic T, ~25%) and pattern B (deep symmetric T inversion, ~75%) in V2–V3.
de Zwaan diagnostic criteria
· Recent angina, now resolved
· Biphasic or deeply inverted T in V2–V3 (± V1, V4)
· Isoelectric or minimally elevated ST (< 1 mm)
· Preserved precordial R waves, no Q waves
· Normal or only minimally elevated troponin
Pseudonormalisation pitfall
active re-occlusion
of the LAD, not improvement.
(β-blockers, digoxin, dexmedetomidine, opioids, amiodarone),
(inferior MI affects the SA/AV nodal supply via RCA),
(hyperkalaemia, hypothermia),
raised ICP
(Cushing's reflex), and
use a weighted score:
Concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm
In any lead, same direction as QRS — 5 points.
Concordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm
In V1–V3 — 3 points.
Excessive discordant ST elevation
≥ 5 mm, in leads with a negative QRS — 2 points.
Smith-modified (Sgarbossa) criteria
replace the fixed 5 mm discordant ST-elevation threshold with a
proportional ratio of ST-elevation to S-wave depth ≥ 0.25 (25 %)
ventricular-paced rhythms
, which produce an analogous discordant pattern. In practice: new LBBB (or a new pacing pattern) with ongoing ischaemic symptoms, haemodynamic instability, or in the post-ROSC patient should still prompt urgent PPCI discussion regardless of the calculated score.
narrow vs wide
, then
regular vs irregular
. New-onset AF affects up to a third of ventilated septic patients and is often the first sign of evolving shock, fluid overload, or electrolyte derangement — treat the cause before reaching for amiodarone.
accessory atrioventricular pathway (bundle of Kent)
with symptomatic tachyarrhythmia. The pathway is a strand of working myocardium bridging the atrioventricular annulus, so it conducts fast but — unlike the AV node — has
no decremental conduction
and often a very short refractory period. Antegrade conduction down the pathway pre-excites the ventricle, and the pathway also provides the return limb for a re-entrant circuit
Resting ECG in sinus rhythm
Short PR interval < 120 ms
— the AV node is bypassed.
Delta wave
— slurred, slow upstroke of the QRS as the pre-excited myocardium depolarises cell-to-cell.
Broad QRS (> 110 ms) with secondary ST/T discordance that can mimic ischaemia or bundle branch block.
Pre-excitation may be intermittent or concealed (retrograde-only pathway) — a normal ECG does not exclude it.
Associated tachyarrhythmias
Orthodromic AVRT
(commonest): antegrade down the AV node, retrograde up the pathway → regular
-complex tachycardia with no delta wave during the run.
Antidromic AVRT
: antegrade down the pathway, retrograde up the node → regular
-complex tachycardia, indistinguishable from VT at the bedside — treat as VT unless the diagnosis is certain.
Pre-excited atrial fibrillation
: irregularly irregular, broad, bizarre and varying QRS complexes at very high rates. This is the lethal presentation — the pathway can conduct at > 300/min and degenerate into VF.
Why AV nodal blockers are contraindicated in pre-excited AF
Adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, β-blockers and digoxin must be avoided.
Blocking the AV node removes the only decremental route out of the atrium, so the entire atrial rate is diverted down the accessory pathway. Ventricular rate accelerates and the rhythm can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation
. Digoxin and verapamil may also shorten accessory-pathway refractoriness directly.
if unstable (or if there is any doubt) —
synchronised DC cardioversion
under sedation/anaesthesia. If stable and expert help is available, a pathway-blocking antiarrhythmic such as
, ibutilide or amiodarone with caution may be used, followed by early electrophysiology referral for pathway ablation, which is definitive
. Orthodromic (narrow-complex) AVRT may be terminated with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine, but have the defibrillator attached in case AF is unmasked.
. Treat the precipitant first — rhythm often settles once the trigger is corrected.
Rate vs rhythm control
Rate control is first-line unless the patient is haemodynamically unstable or new-onset AF is itself driving the shock state, in which case synchronised DCCV is indicated
Electrolyte replacement
Replace K⁺ to > 4.0 mmol/L and Mg²⁺ to > 1.0 mmol/L before/alongside rate-control drugs — correction alone can restore sinus rhythm.
Rate-control drug choice
Esmolol / metoprolol
— first choice in most; caution in shock or reduced LVEF (negative inotropy).
— effective but avoid in LV dysfunction/heart failure.
— 300 mg IV over 20–60 min then 900 mg/24 h infusion; preferred agent in heart failure or when β-blockers/calcium-channel blockers are contraindicated.
— 500 µg IV loading (repeat to max ~1 mg/24 h); useful in heart failure or hypotension where other agents are relatively contraindicated, but slow onset and unreliable rate control in high sympathetic tone (sepsis, catecholamines).
Rhythm control and anticoagulation
Rhythm control with amiodarone or synchronised DCCV if rate control fails or instability persists. Thromboprophylaxis is guided by CHA₂DS₂-VASc, balanced against ICU-specific bleeding risk (indwelling lines, recent procedures, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia); timing of anticoagulation should be individualised. New-onset AF in critical illness frequently recurs after ICU discharge and warrants outpatient cardiology follow-up.

synchronised DCCV ×3

Bradycardia algorithm
(shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, heart failure) →
atropine 500 mcg IV
, repeated every 3–5 min to a maximum total of 3 mg (the 2021 RCUK adult bradycardia algorithm uses a 500 mcg first dose, not 1 mg)

Expect nausea and vomiting (protect the airway), hyperglycaemia and hypokalaemia; supplies are often limited, so escalate early to high-dose insulin–euglycaemia therapy, calcium, and pacing or mechanical support as required.

as a bridge — sedate; capture is mechanical (palpate pulse), not just electrical.

transvenous pacing wire
± permanent device.
Cardiac arrest — shockable rhythms (VF / pulseless VT)
• Defibrillate immediately — biphasic 120–150 J first shock (manufacturer-specific), then 150–200 J.
• 2 min CPR (30:2 if no advanced airway; continuous if intubated). Minimise hands-off time.
• Adrenaline 1 mg IV after the 3rd shock, then every 3–5 min. Amiodarone 300 mg after the 3rd shock; further 150 mg after the 5th.
• Search for the
4 Hs and 4 Ts
: Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hyper/hypokalaemia & metabolic, Hypothermia · Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis.
eFAST + arterial line + ETCO₂
during CPR: ETCO₂ < 10 mmHg suggests poor compressions or futility; sudden ↑ ETCO₂ heralds ROSC.
Temporary transvenous pacing — set-up and troubleshooting
symptomatic bradycardia refractory to atropine/isoprenaline, high-risk AV block (Mobitz II, complete heart block), overdrive pacing for recurrent torsades.
right internal jugular (most direct route to the RV) or left subclavian, femoral if needed; via a sheath, ideally under fluoroscopy or echo. With a balloon-tipped wire inflate in the SVC/RA, float through the tricuspid valve, deflate before advancing. Contact with the RV endocardium gives ST elevation on the intracardiac electrogram and a LBBB-pattern paced QRS.
Initial settings:
VVI (or DDD with an atrial wire), rate 60–80/min, output initially 5–10 mA, sensitivity about 2 mV.
Capture threshold:
reduce output until capture is lost (ideally < 1 mA), then set at 2–3× threshold; confirm mechanical capture with a pulse or arterial trace, not only pacing spikes.
Sensing threshold:
with an intrinsic rhythm, raise the mV value (less sensitive) until sensing is lost, then set to about half that value. Check thresholds daily.
failure to capture — displacement, perforation, rising threshold (reposition, increase output, check connections); undersensing — lower the mV value; oversensing (inhibition by T waves or interference) — raise the mV value; pacing-wire perforation can cause tamponade.
and what their underlying rhythm is
Magnet response
Pacemaker: switches to fixed-rate asynchronous pacing (typically 70–100 bpm, manufacturer-specific) — useful to unmask the underlying rhythm or terminate pacemaker-mediated tachycardia, but removes sensing, risking R-on-T/VF if a paced beat lands on a native T wave in a pacing-dependent patient. ICD: a magnet suspends tachytherapies (antitachycardia pacing and shocks) but does not change the pacing mode/rate.
AF with a CIED
Watch for rapid ventricular pacing or inappropriate atrial tracking (dual-chamber devices tracking fibrillatory activity); mode-switch algorithms should engage automatically. In CRT devices, loss of biventricular capture from AF/frequent ectopy reduces resynchronisation benefit and can precipitate decompensation.
VT in a patient with an ICD
Distinguish appropriate shocks (true VT/VF) from inappropriate shocks (SVT with rapid conduction, lead fracture, oversensing). VT storm: β-blockade, IV amiodarone, sedation, and treat ischaemia/electrolytes; consider transiently deactivating tachytherapies (with external pacing/defibrillation pads applied and continuous monitoring) if shocks are frequent and non-terminating.
External defibrillation with a CIED
If ICD therapies fail or the device is deactivated, defibrillate externally with pads placed ≥ 8 cm from the generator (anterior–posterior preferred) to reduce the risk of device damage
Peri-procedural management
• Pre-op device interrogation; disable tachytherapies (ICD) or apply a magnet for the duration of surgery involving diathermy.
• Use bipolar diathermy where possible; if monopolar is required, keep the current path away from the device and use short bursts.
• Continuous ECG monitoring with external pacing/defibrillation pads applied and a plan for asynchronous pacing if inhibition occurs in a pacing-dependent patient.
• Post-op re-interrogation and reprogramming to restore tachytherapies and normal pacing mode before the patient leaves a monitored area.
Interpreting the monitor
Continuous-flow LVAD and full-flow VA-ECMO produce a narrow or non-pulsatile arterial trace, so pulse oximetry and non-invasive BP are unreliable — use the invasive arterial line, ECMO/LVAD flow and power readings, ScvO₂, lactate and echocardiography. IABP counterpulsation triggers off the ECG or arterial waveform and will fail to time correctly in AF, frequent ectopy or tachycardia > ~130 bpm; switch trigger mode or accept reduced augmentation. Pacing spikes, device electrical noise and chest compressions all corrupt automated rhythm analysis.
Why arrhythmia still matters
Loss of the atrial or right-ventricular contribution reduces LVAD and ECMO preload, causing suction events and low-flow alarms; on VA-ECMO, a fibrillating and non-ejecting left ventricle plus a closed aortic valve risks LV distension, pulmonary oedema and intracardiac thrombus. Sustained VT/VF also causes ongoing myocardial injury and delays recovery.
Management priorities
• Correct the reversible drivers first: potassium 4.0–4.5 mmol/L, magnesium > 1.0 mmol/L, hypovolaemia, cannula or LVAD inflow malposition, ischaemia, and irritation from a pulmonary artery catheter or guidewire.
• Antiarrhythmics as usual (amiodarone, β-blockade, lidocaine), accepting negative inotropy is well tolerated on full support.
• Cardiovert or defibrillate when indicated — this is safe on ECMO and with an LVAD in place, keeping pads away from the generator and driveline; consider overdrive or atrial pacing for recurrent VT.
• On VA-ECMO, add or maintain LV decompression (raise flow, add an Impella or IABP, or perform septostomy) and keep some pulsatility to avoid aortic-root stasis.
• Chest compressions are usually avoided on established ECMO or LVAD support (risk of cannula/anastomotic disruption) unless flow is lost — follow the local device pathway and call the ECMO or ventricular-assist-device team early.
Anticoagulation and rhythm control
New AF on an LVAD raises thromboembolic and pump-thrombosis risk — maintain target INR/anti-Xa and treat rate aggressively. Discuss ICD programming with the device team, since supported patients often tolerate VT and repeated inappropriate shocks are harmful.
Immediate post-ROSC
12-lead within 10 min. STEMI / new LBBB → urgent PPCI. Aim SpO₂ 94–98 %, normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa), MAP ≥ 65 mmHg.
Targeted temperature management
Routine therapeutic hypothermia is
no longer recommended
: TTM2 (2021) found no mortality or functional benefit from targeting 33 °C compared with strict normothermia. Current RCUK / ERC–ESICM 2025 practice is continuous core-temperature monitoring with
active fever prevention targeting ≤ 37.5 °C for at least 72 h
in patients who remain comatose after ROSC, using surface or intravascular devices with feedback control if simple measures fail
Recurrent arrhythmia prevention
Replace K⁺ to 4.5 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ > 1.0 mmol/L. Continue / start β-blocker. Amiodarone infusion for refractory VT/VF.
ICD considerations
Survivors of VF/VT arrest without reversible cause meet secondary-prevention ICD criteria. Liaise with cardiology before discharge from ICU.
Wide-complex tachycardia in a septic ventilated patient
Synchronised DCCV is the immediate priority because adverse features are present. Electrolyte correction and reversible-cause search run alongside but do not delay shock.
Hyperkalaemia with peaked T waves
Calcium first (cardio-protection within 1–3 min), then insulin–dextrose ± salbutamol to shift K⁺, then RRT for definitive removal. Re-check K⁺ at 30 min and 1 h.

Hyperkalaemia: treat the rhythm with calcium first, the number afterwards

How is new-onset AF in critical illness managed?
Treat underlying sepsis/electrolytes; rate control with β-blocker (esmolol/metoprolol) or amiodarone if heart failure; DC cardioversion if haemodynamically unstable; anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc balanced against bleeding risk.
What is the initial management of polymorphic VT (torsades)?
IV magnesium 2 g, correct K⁺ and Ca²⁺, stop QT-prolonging drugs, overdrive pacing or isoprenaline if bradycardia-dependent; DC shock if unstable.
How are wide-complex tachycardias approached when the diagnosis is uncertain?
Assume VT until proven otherwise — particularly with structural heart disease; treat with synchronised DC if unstable, amiodarone 300 mg IV if stable, avoid verapamil which can collapse VT into VF.

A 64-year-old man, day 3 of ventilator-associated pneumonia, develops a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 165 bpm. BP 78/42, MAP 54, lactate rising. K⁺ 3.2, Mg²⁺ 0.6. Recent amiodarone load.
Adverse features present (shock, ischaemia risk). Per RCUK 2021: assume VT in wide-complex tachycardia with structural/critical illness. Plan: synchronised DCCV ×3 under sedation/GA; if fails → amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–20 min then re-shock. In parallel: replete K⁺ to >4.5 and Mg²⁺ to >1.0 (give 2 g IV Mg²⁺ now), exclude reversible 4Hs/4Ts (hypoxia, ischaemia, tension PTX from VAP, electrolytes).
Anuric AKI patient, K⁺ 7.4, ECG shows peaked symmetric T waves and broadening QRS. HR 48, BP 92/50.
Treat the rhythm, not the number. Step 1 — membrane stabilisation: 10 mL 10% calcium gluconate IV over 2–5 min (or CaCl₂ 10 mL centrally), repeat in 5 min if ECG unchanged. Step 2 — intracellular shift: 10 units actrapid in 50 mL 50% dextrose IV over 15 min; salbutamol 10–20 mg neb. Step 3 — removal: urgent RRT given anuria. Avoid sodium bicarbonate unless severely acidotic.

# Cardiac Arrest & Post-Resuscitation Care Post-ROSC bundle, targeted temperature management (TTM2), multimodal neuroprognostication (clinical, NSE, EEG, SSEP, MRI), ECMO-CPR (eCPR), withdrawal & donation Oxygen Targets After Cardiac Arrest: the BOX Trial BOX used a 2-by-2 factorial design in comatose adults after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Patients were randomised to a restrictive PaO₂ target of 9–10 kPa or a liberal target of 13–14 kPa, and separately to one of two blood-pressure targets (reported separately). In 789 patients, death or severe disability/coma within 90 days occurred in 32.0% vs 33.9% (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.75–1.21; P = 0.69). 90-day mortality was 28.7% vs 31.1%, and median neuron-specific enolase at 48 h was similar (17 vs 18 µg/L). What it means: within the range of 9–14 kPa, the exact target did not change outcome. Normoxaemia, rather than a specific number within that range, is a reasonable aim. What it does not test: neither arm allowed hypoxaemia or marked hyperoxaemia. The trial therefore does not show that very high PaO₂ is safe, or that tolerating values below 9 kPa is. Practice point: after ROSC, titrate FiO₂ down from 1.0 once arterial gases or reliable SpO₂ are available, avoiding both extremes. Learning check: what PaO₂ ranges did BOX compare? 9–10 kPa (restrictive) versus 13–14 kPa (liberal). The primary outcome did not differ. >Practice point: after ROSC, titrate FiO₂ down from 1.0 once arterial gases or reliable SpO₂ are available, avoiding both extremes.
60 µg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h, highly malignant EEG after 24 h, status myoclonus ≤ 72 h, diffuse anoxic injury on CT or MRI. eCPR: ARREST and Prague OHCA show benefit only in highly selected witnessed shockable arrests with rapid cannulation (< 60 min); INCEPTION emphasises system speed. VA-ECMO: anticipate limb ischaemia (distal perfusion cannula), Harlequin syndrome (right radial sat monitoring → consider VAV), LV distension (vent with IABP/Impella). Avoid the self-fulfilling prophecy — do not withdraw before multimodal assessment is complete. Refer DCD candidates to SNOD before WLST is raised with the family — preserves donation potential without altering care.
