Confirm arrest, call for help and start chest compressions at 100–120 min⁻¹, depth 5–6 cm, with full recoil and minimal interruptions. Attach defibrillator pads as soon as available and assess rhythm every 2 minutes. For VF/pVT: deliver a shock (biphasic 120–200 J per manufacturer, then equal or escalating), resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes, give adrenaline 1 mg IV after the third shock and every 3–5 minutes thereafter, and amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock with a further 150 mg after the fifth. For non-shockable rhythms (asystole / PEA): give adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as access is obtained and every 3–5 minutes, continue CPR, and actively look for reversible causes. Secure the airway (supraglottic device or tracheal tube) and switch to continuous compressions with asynchronous ventilations once an advanced airway is in place. Use waveform capnography throughout. What are the 4 Hs and 4 Ts and how do I treat each at the bedside? The reversible causes are Hypoxia (high-flow O₂, secure airway, check ETT position and ventilation), Hypovolaemia (rapid IV/IO crystalloid, control haemorrhage, consider blood/MTP), Hyper/hypokalaemia and other metabolic disorders (10 mL 10% calcium chloride, 10 U insulin + 50 mL 50% dextrose, salbutamol, sodium bicarbonate; correct hypoglycaemia and acidosis), and Hypothermia (active rewarming, extended resuscitation and consider eCPR — ); Tension pneumothorax (needle decompression / finger thoracostomy then chest drain), Tamponade (pericardiocentesis or resuscitative thoracotomy in trauma), Toxins (antidotes — naloxone, flumazenil, digibind, intralipid 20% for local-anaesthetic toxicity, sodium bicarbonate for TCAs), and Thrombosis (thrombolysis with alteplase 50 mg for suspected pulmonary embolism, then continue CPR for 60–90 minutes; primary PCI for coronary cause). When should defibrillation energy be escalated and what Use the manufacturer-recommended first biphasic energy (typically 120–200 J). If the manufacturer dose is unknown, default to the maximum available. Subsequent shocks should be of equal or higher energy. The DOSE-VF trial (Cheskes, NEJM 2022) randomised refractory VF after 3 standard shocks to (a) continued standard defibrillation, (b) vector-change (pad reposition anterior-posterior), or (c) double sequential external defibrillation (DSED, two defibrillators delivered ~1 second apart): DSED improved survival to hospital discharge (30.4% vs 13.3%) and survival with good neurological outcome. Vector-change was also superior to standard. That is trial evidence, not the UK recommendation: DOSE-VF was a single-system Canadian trial stopped early by COVID-19. RCUK 2025 advises considering a vector change (antero-posterior pads) after three failed shocks once correct antero-lateral positioning is ensured, and does not recommend routine dual (double) sequential defibrillation. Does adrenaline actually improve outcome — what did PARAMEDIC2 show? PARAMEDIC2 (Perkins, NEJM 2018, n = 8 014 OHCA) compared 1 mg IV adrenaline every 3–5 minutes with placebo. Adrenaline increased survival to 30 days (3.2% vs 2.4%, OR 1.39) but the absolute increase in survivors with favourable neurological outcome (modified Rankin 0–3) was small (2.2% vs 1.9%) and no different statistically, with a higher proportion of survivors having severe neurological impairment (31% vs 18%). Interpretation: adrenaline improves ROSC and short-term survival but the marginal neurological benefit is debated. UK/ERC guidance retains 1 mg IV after the third shock in shockable rhythms and as soon as access is obtained in non-shockable rhythms, recognising the trade-off and the absence of a superior alternative. Should I cool post-arrest patients to 33 °C or aim for active normothermia? What changed after TTM2? HACA (NEJM 2002) and Bernard (NEJM 2002) first showed benefit of 32–34 °C for 12–24 h after witnessed VF OHCA. TTM (Nielsen, NEJM 2013, n = 950) found no significant difference between 33 °C and 36 °C (no superiority shown; this is not proof of equivalence) — both were and both prevented fever. TTM2 (Dankiewicz, NEJM 2021, n = 1 850) compared 33 °C with normothermia targeting ≤ 37.5 °C, with device cooling triggered at ≥ 37.8 °C and found no difference in 6-month mortality (50% vs 48%) or neurological outcome. Current UK advice (RCUK / ERC–ESICM 2025) is to actively prevent fever by targeting ≤ 37.5 °C in patients who remain comatose after ROSC; the RCUK narrative gives 36–72 h, and its March 2026 algorithm states at least 72 h, which this page follows. The superseded 2022 update used > 37.7 °C. If a hypothermic target is used, rewarm slowly (TTM2 used about 0.33 °C/h). Who is an appropriate candidate for eCPR and what does ARREST, Prague OHCA and INCEPTION tell us? ARREST (Yannopoulos, Lancet 2020, n = 30, single-centre Minnesota) randomised refractory shockable OHCA and was stopped early for benefit — 43% vs 7% survival to discharge with eCPR. Prague OHCA (Belohlavek, JAMA 2022, n = 256) compared invasive (eCPR + cath lab) with standard advanced ALS and showed a non-significant trend to better 180-day favourable neurological outcome (31.5% vs 22.0%); subgroup analysis favoured the invasive strategy with longer arrest durations. INCEPTION (Suverein, NEJM 2023, n = 134) was a multicentre Dutch trial and was neutral — reflecting the impact of system speed and operator volume. Suitable candidates have: witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, initial shockable rhythm, age < 65–75, no major comorbidity, ETCO₂ > 10 mmHg sustained, and a realistic prospect of cannulation within 60 minutes of collapse. Outside high-volume eCPR centres with rapid pathways, benefit is unlikely. What is multimodal neuroprognostication and when do I perform it? Neuroprognostication is performed in the comatose post-cardiac-arrest patient at ≥ 72 hours after ROSC, only once confounders (sedation, NMBA, hypothermia, severe metabolic derangement, hypoglycaemia, hypotension, ongoing seizure activity) are excluded. The entry criterion is GCS motor ≤ 3 (abnormal flexion, extension, or no motor response) at ≥ 72 h. ERC/ESICM 2021 consider poor outcome likely when two or more of these are present: (1) bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at ≥ 72 h (quantitative pupillometry may be used); (2) bilaterally absent N20 SSEP waves at ≥ 24 h; (3) highly malignant EEG (suppressed background or burst-suppression) at > 24 h; (4) NSE > 60 µg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h; (5) status myoclonus ≤ 72 h; (6) diffuse and extensive anoxic injury on CT or MRI. No single marker is sufficient on its own. Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy in the first 72 hours risks self-fulfilling prophecy. How should I manage the airway and ventilator in the first 6 hours post-ROSC? Intubate if not already (or replace a supraglottic with a tracheal tube once stable). Set tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, PEEP 5–10 cmH₂O, FiO₂ titrated to SpO₂ 94–98% (avoid hyperoxia — observational data link PaO₂ > 40 kPa to higher mortality; but the EXACT RCT found lower survival when pre-hospital SpO₂ was targeted at 90–94%, so avoid aiming below 94%). Avoid prolonged NMBA except briefly for shivering not controlled by sedation and counter-warming. Global myocardial stunning affects most patients after prolonged arrest: cardiac index falls within hours, is typically lowest at 8–24 h and usually recovers by 48–72 h. It is reversible ischaemia–reperfusion injury (calcium overload, oxidative stress, cytokine release), distinct from infarct-related pump failure — although the two coexist every 2 minutes. The first pharmacological dose of adrenaline (1 mg IV) follows the third shock in VF/pVT, and is given as soon as access is obtained in non-shockable rhythms.

Why prognostication matters withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (WLST) for predicted poor neurological outcome. Premature or wrong prognostication therefore bad outcomes — making a structured, multimodal, evidence-based approach an ethical imperative, not a procedural one. Short-latency somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) Bilateral absence of the N20 cortical response ≥ 24 h after ROSC (and after rewarming) predicts poor outcome with a false-positive rate close to 0 % when recorded and interpreted by an experienced neurophysiologist. Among the most robust single criteria — but still must be paired with a second concordant modality. Technical pitfalls that invalidate an "absent N20" Noisy recording: ICU electrical interference (pumps, CRRT, warming devices, mains 50 Hz artefact) and muscle activity raise the noise floor. Absence can only be declared when background noise is low (peak-to-peak amplitude < 0.25 µV) — otherwise the result is "uninterpretable", not "absent". No proof the stimulus arrived: the peripheral (Erb's point, N9) and cervical (N13) responses must be present bilaterally to confirm intact conduction; peripheral nerve injury, critical-illness neuropathy, oedematous wrists, cervical cord or brachial plexus pathology otherwise produce a false "absent N20". Physiological and drug confounders: temperature below about 33 °C (and especially < 32 °C), high-dose sedation — notably barbiturate coma or high-dose propofol/anticonvulsant loading, which can attenuate cortical responses, hypotension, and severe metabolic derangement — record after rewarming and with confounders minimised. Timing and repetition: record at ≥ 24 h after ROSC, ideally repeat, and require reproducible bilateral absence in two independent averaged trials read by an experienced neurophysiologist. Interpretation asymmetry: N20 has poor specificity for good outcome — it does not predict recovery, and unilateral absence is not a poor-outcome criterion 4. Biomarkers Neuron-specific enolase (NSE) remains the only biomarker formally embedded in the ERC/ESICM algorithm. Released from injured neurons; concentrations peak 48–72 h after ROSC. Threshold for poor outcome: NSE > 60 µg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h ; a trend strengthens the prediction. Reject haemolysed samples — NSE is abundant in erythrocytes and even mild haemolysis falsely elevates results. Other sources of false elevation: neuroendocrine tumours, small-cell lung cancer, ECMO-related haemolysis. Emerging biomarkers (not yet part of the formal ERC/ESICM criteria, but increasingly reported in exam-level and clinical literature): GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) — released from injured astrocytes; peaks slightly later than NSE, at around 48–72 h post-ROSC. Meta-analytic data show good discriminatory accuracy for poor outcome (AUC ≈ 0.88 at 72 h), but it remains pending standardised assay cut-offs and external validation before routine clinical use Neurofilament light chain (NfL) — a marker of axonal injury with a later and more prolonged peak than NSE or GFAP; may add prognostic value for assessment (> 7 days post-ROSC) in patients with an initially indeterminate multimodal result, but is not part of the 72 h algorithm. — released from astrocytes and adipocytes (less neurospecific than NSE or GFAP); still not incorporated into the ERC/ESICM algorithm. 5. Useful when MRI not feasible. MRI brain (2–7 days) Diffuse restricted diffusion on DWI involving cortex and deep grey nuclei. ADC values < 650 × 10⁻⁶ mm²/s in > 10 % of brain tissue predict poor outcome. Best obtained 2–5 days post-ROSC. Putting it together — multimodal algorithm At ≥ 72 h, confirm entry criteria (comatose, M ≤ 3, confounders excluded). Examine pupillary and corneal reflexes — if both absent, this is criterion 1. Document any status myoclonus within the first 72 h — criterion 2 if present. Send NSE at 48 h and 72 h (non-haemolysed) — criterion 3 if > 60 µg/L and/or rising. Record SSEPs after rewarming — bilateral absent N20 = criterion 4. EEG (continuous or routine ≥ 24 h post-ROSC) — highly malignant pattern = criterion 5. Imaging — diffuse anoxic injury on CT or MRI = criterion 6. Poor outcome is "likely" when ≥ 2 criteria are concordant . Neuroprognostication with posterior fossa injury — why it demands caution diffuse hypoxic–ischaemic cortical injury . Posterior fossa pathology — cerebellar infarction or haemorrhage, brainstem stroke (e.g. basilar artery occlusion), or a mass lesion causing direct brainstem compression — breaks several of those assumptions at once, and applying the standard algorithm uncritically can produce both falsely pessimistic and falsely confident predictions Clinical examination can be misleadingly terrible. A brainstem lesion can abolish pupillary, corneal, cough and gag reflexes by direct structural injury , while the cerebral hemispheres remain relatively preserved. Absent brainstem reflexes in this setting reflect focal anatomy, not necessarily diffuse bihemispheric death of cortex — the pattern the post-arrest criteria were validated against. A patient with a small midbrain/pontine lesion can meet "poor outcome" clinical criteria yet retain intact cortical function, or vice versa. SSEPs and biomarkers can be falsely reassuring or falsely alarming. The N20 requires an intact lemniscal pathway through the brainstem; brainstem injury can attenuate or abolish the cortical response via the focal lesion rather than cortical necrosis, mimicking the "bilaterally absent N20" poor-outcome criterion. Conversely, NSE and neuron-specific markers reflect the volume of neuronal injury, and a small but strategically placed brainstem lesion produces little biomarker release despite devastating functional impact. Coma may be a problem of arousal, not awareness. Pontine lesions can produce locked-in syndrome or severe motor impairment with retained consciousness; EEG background may be preserved and even reactive. Behaviourally unresponsive patients here overlap with the cognitive-motor dissociation population, and prognosis hinges on tests of covert cognition, not reflexes. The lesion is dynamic, not static. Cerebellar swelling peaks at 3–5 days and can cause progressive brainstem compression, hydrocephalus and secondary deterioration; equally, timely surgical decompression (suboccipital craniectomy, EVD) or thrombectomy for basilar occlusion can transform the outlook. Early prognostication — before swelling resolves or before a potentially reversible lesion is treated — embeds a self-fulfilling prophecy. The evidence base does not apply. The ERC/ESICM 2021 poor-outcome criteria were derived in post-anoxic coma cohorts and were not validated in focal brainstem or cerebellar pathology . Prognostic scores and reflex-based rules carry unquantified false-positive rates here, and outcome after decompressive surgery for cerebellar infarction is frequently better than the early clinical picture suggests, especially in younger patients. Practical approach: treat posterior fossa injury as a hard exclusion from the standard post-arrest algorithm. Establish the exact lesion and its reversibility with CT/MRI (including vascular imaging for basilar occlusion), exclude hydrocephalus and evolving swelling, defer any prognostic statement until the lesion has been treated and allowed to declare itself — often well beyond 72 h — and make decisions only after MDT review with neurology and neurosurgery. Where reflexes are absent but cortex is potentially spared, prioritise EEG background/reactivity and MRI over brainstem reflexes and SSEPs, and actively consider testing for covert consciousness before any discussion of treatment withdrawal. Cognitive-motor dissociation (covert consciousness) Cognitive-motor dissociation (CMD) describes a state in which a patient shows no behavioural or motor response to command (motor score M1–M3) despite demonstrable, preserved higher-order cortical processing detectable only on neurophysiological or functional imaging testing a proportion of behaviourally unresponsive patients (M1–M3) who appear to lack awareness on bedside examination retain some degree of covert consciousness — a critical caveat for prognostication and WLST decision-making. EEG motor-imagery paradigms — asking the patient to imagine repetitive movement (e.g. "keep imagining opening and closing your right hand") and looking for a reproducible, task-appropriate EEG response over sensorimotor cortex; equivalent paradigms using functional MRI (imagined motor or spatial-navigation tasks) can show appropriate cortical activation despite absent overt behaviour. CMD is a key argument for assessment and against decisions based on clinical examination or a single test alone. Extreme caution is warranted before WLST in patients with an indeterminate multimodal result, particularly where the EEG background is benign/reactive with sleep–wake cycles, as this combination raises the possibility of covert awareness or later recovery. Why prognostication matters

Hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury (HIBI) is the leading cause of death after cardiac arrest admission. Two-thirds of in-hospital deaths in comatose post-arrest patients are preceded by withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (WLST) for predicted poor neurological outcome. Premature or wrong prognostication therefore causes bad outcomes — making a structured, multimodal, evidence-based approach an ethical imperative, not a procedural one.

Poor neurological outcome — CPC 3–5 or modified Rankin 4–6 (severe disability, vegetative state, or death) at 3–6 months. Good outcome — CPC 1–2 (no/moderate disability, independent living).

{/* Entry criteria & timing */}

ERC/ESICM 2021 — entry criteria & timing

Formal prognostication begins only when all of the following are true. Premature assessment is the single commonest source of false-positive predictions.

  • ≥ 72 h have elapsed since ROSC (not since rewarming).
  • Patient remains comatose with motor score M ≤ 3.
  • Sedation and analgesia have been stopped long enough for clearance (≥ 5 half-lives — longer in obesity, hepatic / renal failure, prolonged infusions).
  • Neuromuscular blockade has been excluded (train-of-four).
  • Normothermia (≥ 36 °C) for at least 24 h.
  • No major metabolic or electrolyte derangement, severe shock, or hepatic/renal failure causing drug accumulation.

If any criterion is unmet, defer prognostication. Continue active care and re-evaluate every 24–72 h. Late awakening (≥ 7 days post-ROSC) is not rare, particularly after TTM.

Two configurations
— gas exchange only. Blood drained from and returned to the venous system. Use for refractory respiratory failure with preserved cardiac output.
— cardiac and respiratory support. Venous drainage, arterial return. Use for refractory cardiogenic shock or cardiac arrest (ECPR).
Modern circuits are shorter, heparin-coated and centrifugal-pump based, allowing longer support with fewer complications.
Typical cannulae
Femoral V → Femoral V (VV)
Drainage 23–25 Fr femoral V (tip at hepatic IVC), return 19–21 Fr contralateral femoral V (tip at RA)
Fastest peripheral access; suitable for percutaneous insertion in ED/ICU
Highest recirculation (10–30%); patient bed-bound; femoral access compromises mobilisation
Femoral V → Internal Jugular V (VV)
Drainage 25 Fr femoral V, return 21 Fr right IJ (tip at SVC/RA junction)
Lower recirculation; permits limb mobilisation
Two access sites; IJ cannulation in coagulopathy

27–31 Fr right IJ dual-lumen — drainage ports in SVC and IVC, return port directed at tricuspid valve

Drainage 23–25 Fr femoral V (tip at RA), return 15–19 Fr femoral A + 6–8 Fr distal perfusion cannula

Central VA (post-cardiotomy)

Sizing rule of thumb:
target circuit blood flow of 60–80 mL/kg/min (full VV support) or 50–70 mL/kg/min (VA support). For a 70 kg adult, this is 4–5 L/min — achievable with a 23–25 Fr drainage and a 19–21 Fr return cannula. The most common cause of inadequate flow is undersized drainage.

Changing configuration: VV → VA and hybrid (VAV)
Triggers to convert
Progressive biventricular or RV failure with low native cardiac output despite full VV support; refractory arrhythmia or cardiac arrest on VV-ECMO; sepsis-related cardiomyopathy; massive PE; escalating inotropes with rising lactate and falling mixed venous saturation despite adequate ECMO flow. Confirm with echocardiography before committing.
How it is done
Ultrasound-guided arterial access (femoral, with an obligatory distal perfusion cannula, or axillary/central in selected cases), heparin bolus, then either (a) reuse the existing venous drainage and move the return limb to the artery (VA), or (b) split the return with a Y-connector between the internal jugular vein and the artery to create a
circuit when gas exchange still needs support — flow to each limb is balanced with a clamp or flow probe.
Immediate risks after conversion
LV distension and pulmonary oedema from retrograde afterload (consider IABP, Impella or septostomy), Harlequin syndrome, limb ischaemia, bleeding at the new site, and differential flow with recirculation in VAV. Re-echo, re-check right radial SpO₂ and arterial blood gases from the right arm, and reassess anticoagulation.
Accidental hypothermia and ECLS
Extracorporeal rewarming is
for hypothermic cardiac arrest and for a hypothermic patient with cardiac instability that does not respond to medical management: core temperature < 28 °C with instability, < 32 °C with a refractory arrhythmia or shock, or hypothermic cardiac arrest. Confirm potential reversibility (serum potassium generally < 12 mmol/L, no lethal injury, use the HOPE score where available), continue CPR during transfer to an ECLS centre, rewarm at about 3–4 °C per hour, and remember "not dead until warm and dead"

Limitations of all three scores:
they were derived in selected cohorts before modern practice (and before COVID-19), they discriminate only moderately (c-statistic ≈ 0.7), they do not include frailty, functional baseline or patient wishes, and they must never be used alone to refuse or withdraw ECMO in an individual patient.
bridge to nowhere
. Agreeing the exit strategy at cannulation and reviewing it daily prevents protracted, non-beneficial support.
Pre-cannulation conversation:
document the bridge (e.g. "bridge to recovery within 14 days"), the criteria for withdrawal, and what will not be offered (e.g. transplant in a contraindicated patient).
Daily review:
trajectory, organ recovery, neurology, eligibility for transplant or VAD. If none of the exits remains achievable, escalate to MDT discussion.
Family communication:
ECMO support is highly visible and patients may look "well". Explicit communication about prognosis and the meaning of the device prevents false hope.
Withdrawal of ECMO:
usually achieved by reducing sweep gas (VV) or flow (VA) to zero, with continued sedation and symptom management. Decannulation post-mortem may be required for organ donation pathways.
Donation after circulatory death on ECMO:
emerging pathway — engage the donation team early.

Refractory VF arrest — is ECPR indicated?
VV-ECMO provides respiratory support only (gas exchange); VA-ECMO provides combined respiratory and haemodynamic support but generates LV afterload and risks Harlequin syndrome in peripheral configurations.
EOLIA criteria for VV-ECMO referral in severe ARDS: PaO₂/FiO₂ < 50 mmHg for > 3 h, or < 80 mmHg for > 6 h, or pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥ 60 mmHg for > 6 h, despite optimal lung-protective ventilation and proning.
CESAR (2009) showed referral to an ECMO centre improved 6-month disability-free survival in severe respiratory failure; EOLIA (2018) was stopped early for futility but a Bayesian re-analysis suggested a mortality benefit. Modern ELSO criteria reflect both.
Harlequin (North–South) syndrome in peripheral VA-ECMO: monitor the right radial pulse oximeter — it reflects upper-body / coronary / cerebral oxygenation. Manage by optimising native lung function, increasing ECMO flow, or converting to VAV.
LV distension on VA-ECMO is driven by increased afterload from retrograde aortic flow plus persistent venous return. Recognised by rising PAOP, pulmonary oedema, absent aortic valve opening. Manage by inotropy, IABP, atrial septostomy or trans-aortic vent (Impella).
Recirculation in VV-ECMO: oxygenated blood from the return cannula is re-aspirated by the drainage cannula, falsely raising pre-membrane SvO₂ and limiting effective oxygen delivery. Reduce flow, reposition cannulae, or change configuration.
Anticoagulation: unfractionated heparin to APTT 1.5–2× normal or ACT 180–220 s. Bivalirudin is the agent of choice if HIT is confirmed. Balance bleeding (commonest complication) against circuit thrombosis.
Sweep gas (gas flow through the oxygenator) controls CO₂ clearance; FdO₂ and blood flow control oxygenation. Increasing sweep without changing FdO₂ removes more CO₂ but does not improve PaO₂.
ECPR (ELSO criteria): witnessed arrest with bystander CPR < 5 min, shockable initial rhythm, low-flow < 60 min, age < 70, no major comorbidity, end-tidal CO₂ > 1.3 kPa during CPR. ARREST and Prague-OHCA support; INCEPTION negative — outcomes depend on system performance.
Weaning: VV-ECMO is weaned by reducing sweep gas to zero while maintaining blood flow (the sweep-down trial) and assessing native gas exchange. VA-ECMO is weaned by stepwise flow reduction with echo assessment of LV / RV function — never clamp the circuit while flow continues.
Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO)
FFICM / EDIC — Intensive Care (ELSO / EOLIA / CESAR-based practice)
Drainage cannula size and tip position are the main determinants of achievable flow (resistance falls steeply with radius and rises with length). Large-bore (21–29 Fr), multi-fenestrated. Femoral vein → IVC/RA most common. Pre-pump pressure should be negative but > –100 mmHg to avoid haemolysis and cavitation.
Magnetically levitated impeller (e.g. CentriMag, Rotaflow). Preload- and afterload-sensitive — flow drops if venous return is poor or systemic resistance rises. Watch for line chatter (hypovolaemia). Afterload-sensitive: flow falls with hypertension or a kinked return line, so flow must be measured, not inferred from RPM. Replaced roller pumps, which are occlusive, displace a fixed volume and generate dangerous pressures if a line is obstructed.
Polymethylpentene hollow-fibre. Blood flows on one side, sweep gas the other. FdO₂ controls oxygenation; sweep flow controls CO₂ removal. Monitor pre- and post-oxygenator pressures: a rising trans-membrane gradient, falling post-membrane PaO₂, visible clot, and falling platelets/fibrinogen with rising D-dimer signal failure and the need for change-out.
Usually integrated with the oxygenator; water circulating around the blood path maintains normothermia (or a target temperature) — large extracorporeal flows otherwise cool the patient quickly and can mask fever.
VV: internal jugular → SVC/RA, or contralateral femoral vein. VA: femoral artery (peripheral) or aorta (central). Distal perfusion cannula essential for femoral arterial return.
Bleeding
Commonest complication. Cannulation sites, ICH, GI, surgical sites. Driven by heparin, acquired vWF deficiency (high shear), thrombocytopaenia. Targ

# ICU Discharge Planning and Longer-Term Recovery Rehabilitation risk assessment during the stay, timing and handover of ward transfer, ward step-down, home discharge information and 2–3 month review Discharge planning starts during the ICU stay rehabilitation needs are found by assessing the patient, not by waiting until discharge. Table 1 includes non-physical risks such as recurrent nightmares. One named coordinator keeps the plan going across ICU, ward and community. Now, during the critical care stay — NICE CG83 lists inability to self-ventilate on 35% oxygen or less and inability to get out of bed as examples of risk. Transfer to the ward: timing and handover the patient moves to a ward with far fewer nurses per patient. The ICU and ward teams share responsibility, so the written plan must be something the ward can actually deliver. Outreach follow-up after transfer is a common local safety net (teaching synthesis). Both teams share responsibility, supported by a formal structured handover (medical and nursing) and a written plan. Ward step-down and going home going home is not the end of critical care recovery. Patients and families need written information on physical recovery, driving, work and support services. Stress symptoms after traumatic memories are managed using the NICE PTSD guideline. At least 6 weeks, based on clinical judgement and the patient's needs. Longer-term recovery and review the 2–3 month review checks recovery against the goals set during the stay and refers the patient on if they are recovering slowly. Physical, cognitive and mental-health problems after critical illness (PICS), follow-up clinics and support for families are covered on PICS & follow-up . The full patient journey is on The ICU Inpatient Journey At 2 to 3 months, face to face, by an appropriately skilled professional familiar with their critical care course. Survival, length of stay and readmission rates after ICU are covered on ICU Outcomes NICE CG83 early assessment NICE CG83 table 1 NICE CG83 start early A ventilated patient on 40% oxygen cannot get out of bed. entries.topic_title: ICU Outcomes: Survival, Length of Stay and Readmission
entries.text:
# ICU Outcomes: Survival, Length of Stay and Readmission
Short- and long-term survival after critical illness, ICU length of stay and functional recovery, readmission rates, predictors and associated mortality


Survival: leaving hospital is not the end point
ICU mortality, hospital mortality and long-term mortality are different numbers and must not be mixed. Some deaths happen on the ward after ICU discharge, and survivors who needed mechanical ventilation keep an excess risk for months afterwards. Wunsch studied elderly US Medicare patients, so the absolute figures do not transfer directly to younger or UK populations (teaching summary). UK national figures are in the ICNARC lesson below.
UK survival after hospital discharge
Lone used Scottish linked national registries: adult general ICU admissions in 2005 who survived hospital discharge, compared with matched hospital controls. Five-year mortality was 32.3% versus 22.7%; equivalently, survival was 67.7% versus 77.3% (arithmetic complements, not a new estimate). The clock starts at hospital discharge, so these percentages exclude deaths during the index admission. This is useful long-term UK evidence, but it is a historical cohort, not the 2024–25 ICNARC population or a prediction for a present-day patient. Comorbidity, pre-illness function, age and diagnosis matter; association with ICU admission does not establish that ICU care caused the excess deaths.
In the first 6 months after hospital discharge.
UK national audit: ICNARC Case Mix Programme
Where these data come from:
every figure above is quoted word for word from the public summary of the ICNARC Case Mix Programme (CMP) Public Report 2024-25, the national clinical audit of admissions to adult critical care in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, covering April 2024 to March 2025 across 286 participating units. The CMP is observational audit data, not a trial: the 11.5% critical care mortality and 15% acute hospital mortality are raw, unadjusted figures for a very mixed case mix, and they describe populations, not individual risk. Individual units are compared using risk-adjusted (not raw) mortality through the ICNARC model (teaching summary).
Latest public annual report located, checked 15 October 2026:
the 2024–25 report was released in 2026. It includes 209,047 patients but 222,377 admissions: a patient can have more than one admission. Scotland is not included in this CMP summary. Do not apply the national averages to sepsis, ARDS, elective postoperative care or another specific diagnosis without examining the relevant case mix.
Public rounding versus the clinical summary
The clinical summary reports hospital survival as 84.6%, rounded to 85% in the public version; critical care survival is 88.5% in both. Its mean stays are 5.9 days in critical care and 20.4 days in acute hospital (public version: 6 and 20). Means are not medians: a minority of long stays can raise the average. Hospital length of stay includes the hospital episode, not simply time on the ward after ICU. The public chart gives 7 critical care days and 16 hospital days for critical care non-survivors; its survivor/non-survivor grouping is by critical care outcome.
Denominator caution:
ICU survival, hospital survival, unique patients and admissions are different measures. The reports' rounded headline percentages do not establish a ward-only death rate: outcome follow-up, transfers, repeat admissions and eligible denominators must be checked first. The percentage-point difference is not the percentage of ICU survivors who died on a ward. ICNARC is an audit of acute outcomes; it does not supply a national return-to-work or PTSD rate in this summary.
11.5% died in critical care; 15% died in acute hospital (85% survived to hospital discharge).
Length of stay and functional recovery
a long ICU stay is a marker of severe illness and a cause of muscle wasting, weakness and lost weight. Length of stay is not a quality measure on its own: it reflects case mix, ward capacity and delayed discharge as well as care (teaching summary). Long stays are one of the NICE CG83 rehabilitation risk factors, covered on
ICU Discharge Planning
; physical, mental and cognitive consequences are on
PICS & follow-up
Five years on
the lungs largely recover, but physical function does not return to normal even at five years, and the burden extends to family caregivers. Both Herridge cohorts were small Canadian ARDS groups of relatively young patients, so they show the pattern of recovery rather than the figures for every ICU survivor (teaching summary).
Disability is broader than lung function
In this five-centre Australian cohort of hospital survivors ventilated for more than 24 hours, 65 of 262 followed-up survivors (25%) reported moderate or severe disability at six months using the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0. This is not a UK all-admission rate or simply a measurement of muscle strength. Function includes mobility, self-care, cognition, relationships, usual activities and participation. Compare with the patient's pre-illness baseline: discharge home, normal spirometry and independence in daily life are not interchangeable endpoints.
Extrapulmonary problems, most prominently muscle wasting and weakness — lung volumes and spirometry were normal by 6 months, though gas transfer stayed low.
436 m, 76% of predicted; neither younger nor older patients returned to normal predicted physical function.
Severity scoring and fair comparison
raw mortality cannot be compared between units because case mix differs. Severity scores predict the expected death rate for a population; dividing observed by expected deaths gives a standardised mortality ratio, and this is how the ICNARC audit compares units (teaching summary). A score describes groups: it should not be used alone to decide whether an individual patient is admitted or treatment is withdrawn (teaching summary). Note the authors' own condition — the score works best
combined with an accurate description of disease
Initial values of 12 routine physiological measurements, age and previous health status; range 0 to 71.
Because units admit different case mixes; adjustment compares observed deaths with those expected for that severity of illness.
Readmission to ICU
Current UK audit versus historical all-readmission estimates:
ICNARC 2024–25 reports 1.1% unplanned readmissions within 48 hours. Rosenberg's approximately 7% concerns broader readmission definitions in older studies. Different time windows and planned/unplanned classifications explain why these figures cannot be used as competing estimates of the same outcome. An early return may reflect deterioration, premature transfer or unavoidable disease progression; a low rate may also reflect limits on readmission. Interpret alongside case mix and mortality, not as an isolated quality score.
readmitted patients do much worse, but the review warns that readmission rates are not yet proven to measure quality of care. Unstable vital signs at discharge are the most consistent warning sign, and night-time discharge was an independent predictor of death in one Australian cohort — consistent with NICE advice to avoid it. These are associations from observational studies, not proof that changing discharge timing alone saves lives (teaching summary).
About 7% (range 4–14%); unstable vital signs at the time of ICU discharge.
Cognitive recovery: attention, memory and executive function
BRAIN-ICU enrolled 821 US adults with respiratory failure or shock. Among patients assessed at 12 months, 34% had global cognition scores comparable to those seen after moderate traumatic brain injury and 24% comparable to mild Alzheimer's disease. These are comparisons of test performance,
not diagnoses of either disorder
; the more severely impaired group overlaps the broader group, so do not add the percentages. These are follow-up participants, not 34% and 24% of all original admissions.
Difficulty remembering instructions, managing medicines, planning a task or sustaining concentration can persist despite good physical recovery, including in younger survivors. Longer delirium duration was independently associated with worse later cognition, but observational association does not prove that a particular delirium intervention prevents this disability. Pre-existing impairment, deaths and loss to follow-up affect estimates. A review should distinguish new problems from baseline impairment and arrange assessment when daily function is affected; see
PICS follow-up
No. They describe the severity of cognitive test scores, not a new neurological diagnosis; the two percentages overlap and apply to assessed survivors.
Return to work is a participation outcome
Kamdar's review included 52 studies and 10,015 survivors who were employed before critical illness. Pooled return to work was 36% at 1–3 months (95% CI 23–49%), 60% at 12 months (50–69%) and 68% at 42–60 months (51–85%). These are study-specific follow-up groups pooled at each interval, not a single cohort's recovery curve. They do not describe retired people, all ICU admissions or the probability that an employed patient will survive and return to work.
Returning to any job is not returning to the same duties, hours or sustained employment. The reported ranges for subsequent job loss, occupation change and worse employment come from individual studies, not pooled risks to add together. Physical fatigue, cognitive difficulty and psychological symptoms may all limit work; job demands, employer flexibility and the welfare system also matter. The evidence search ended in February 2018 and between-study heterogeneity was high (I² 87%), so this 2020 review is a useful benchmark, not a current UK national statistic.
Ask about previous work, caring responsibilities, driving, finances and the tasks the person now finds difficult. A supported graded return and occupational-health input may be appropriate, but an ICU discharge date or a normal lung test alone cannot certify readiness for a safety-critical job. Practical rehabilitation and information about work and benefits are covered in
Previously employed survivors in the included follow-up studies, not all ICU admissions; return to work does not guarantee the same hours or lasting employment.
Post-traumatic stress: the threshold changes the rate
Parker's general-ICU meta-analysis found clinically important PTSD symptoms in 25% at 1–6 months using an Impact of Event Scale threshold ≥35, versus 44% with the less restrictive ≥20 threshold. At 7–12 months the respective estimates were 17% and 34%. Thus “the PTSD rate” needs a time point, instrument and threshold. These are symptom-screen estimates, not the proportion with a diagnosis confirmed by a clinical interview. Do not confuse the original IES thresholds with IES-Revised thresholds used elsewhere.
Depression and anxiety can persist as well
With Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale subscale thresholds ≥8, pooled depressive symptoms were 29%, 34% and 29% at 2–3, 6 and 12–14 months; anxiety symptoms were 32%, 40% and 34% at the same intervals. These older systematic reviews are reference estimates rather than a present-day UK audit. PTSD, depression and anxiety overlap: adding them gives an invalid overall morbidity rate. A positive screen warrants clinical assessment; it does not establish a psychiatric diagnosis or show that ICU alone caused the symptoms.
Explore intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance, hyperarousal, low mood, loss of interest, anxiety and sleep problems alongside physical and cognitive recovery. Pre-existing mental ill health and frightening or delusional ICU memories can influence later symptoms. Persistent distress or impaired daily function should prompt appropriate psychological assessment; urgent concerns about self-harm need immediate clinical help, not a routine follow-up appointment. The
PICS Follow-Up Plan
covers the assessment pathway and conflicting diary trials.
Different screening thresholds identify different groups. Neither symptom percentage is automatically a clinician-confirmed PTSD diagnosis.
2026 evidence: common morbidity, but no single universal PICS rate
This review was published online in January 2026 and searched studies through October 2024. Its pooled prevalence of PICS was 60.3% and incidence 52.4%, but it accepted each primary study's definition and assessment method. PICS means new or worsening physical, cognitive or psychological problems after critical illness; a person need not have all three. Prevalence (problems present at assessment) and incidence (new cases under the study definition) are different measures and are not two stages of the same trajectory.
The very high heterogeneity (I² 98.67% for prevalence) means the pooled estimate is a broad signal of burden, not “six in ten of every UK ICU population”. Timing, baseline function, screening cutoffs, diagnosis, geography and who survives or attends follow-up change the result. Report the outcome domain and its definition alongside any percentage. Family members can also experience psychological and practical consequences; patient percentages should not be repurposed as family prevalence.
Latest psychological-intervention review
Cesari's review, published online in June 2026, included 39 studies of ICU or post-ICU interventions. Evidence remained heterogeneous: 14 studies found improvement in at least one psychological outcome, 23 found no benefit and two evaluative interventions were associated with worse outcomes. Counting positive studies does not establish a pooled treatment effect; narrative and multimodal approaches had signals of benefit but methodological limitations. Screening and referral are important, but neither follow-up attendance nor an ICU diary guarantees prevention of PTSD, depression or anxiety.
At the recommended 2–3 month review for patients with rehabilitation needs, document survival status, mobility and self-care, cognition, psychological symptoms, work/usual activities and progress against the person's goals. Use baseline-aware reassessment rather than a percentage to decide the next step. This page summarises source-checked evidence as of 15 October 2026, not individual prognostication or consultant certification.
No. Definitions, follow-up times and populations vary markedly; it describes a heterogeneous body of evidence, not an individual prognosis or a UK national audit rate.
What an ICU day costs
Dasta analysed 51,009 adult ICU patients in 253 US hospitals in late 2002, converting billed charges to costs with hospital cost-to-charge ratios. Costs are front-loaded: day 1 is the most expensive, so shortening a stay by a day saves less than the mean daily cost suggests, because the day removed is usually a cheaper late day (teaching summary). These are 2002 US dollars in a US billing system; they are not NHS costs or current prices (NHS figures follow below). The ventilated group was also sicker and stayed longer, so the unadjusted difference is not all due to the ventilator; the adjusted increment is $1,522 per day.
NHS costs: what an English critical care bed day costs

On the NHS figures, a critical care day costs about 5.5 times a standard bed day (£1,881 ÷ £345; arithmetic, not a published ratio) — though the ward figure excludes treatment, so the true gap is smaller. The US and NHS columns cannot be compared by an exchange rate: they come from different decades, costing methods (US charges reflect billing, NHS unit costs reflect trust-reported expenditure), case mix and age groups, and the £1,881 average includes neonatal and paediatric care. A 2002 dollar figure would also need inflation adjustment. The most defensible UK statement is the NHS figure itself: an average critical care day in England in 2020/21 cost £1,881, and 2020/21 was a COVID-affected year (teaching summary).
Adult-only NHS costs by organs supported
For an adult-only comparison, NHS England's National Schedule of NHS Costs lists adult critical care separately, as cost per bed day by the number of organ systems supported (HRGs XC01Z–XC07Z). Combining every adult unit type in the 2019/20 schedule, weighted by bed days (our arithmetic, rounded to the nearest pound):
Organs supported that day

The adult-only average of £1,620 per bed day (2019/20, the last full pre-COVID year) is the closer match to Dasta's adult population than the £1,881 all-ages figure, but the decades and costing methods still differ, so no exchange-rate conversion is valid. A day with six or more organs supported cost about twice a one-organ day. These are trust-reported costs, not the prices commissioners pay, and they vary between trusts. Costs by unit type and a worked example are on
ICU Costs
(teaching summary).
The 2021/22 column fills the gap after the COVID-affected 2020/21 year: it is the latest adult-only schedule we could download and check (later years are dashboard-only). Its national averages come from the Total HRGs worksheet, which already combines every adult unit type; the all-adult £2,144 is our bed-day-weighted arithmetic. Costs rose about a third from 2019/20, and in 2021/22 a day with no organs supported (£1,640) cost slightly more than a one-organ day (£1,587) — that is how the figures were published, probably reflecting few, unusual zero-organ days, so do not read it as a clinical effect. Bed-day columns differ slightly between years. These are cash figures, not inflation-adjusted (teaching summary).
How NHS critical care costs have risen over a decade
Using the same adult critical care currencies (HRGs XC01Z–XC07Z) in each year's national schedule, the average cost per adult bed day can be tracked from 2013/14 to 2021/22. The year averages are bed-day-weighted arithmetic from the published rows (ours), in cash terms, not adjusted for inflation:

In cash terms the adult average rose from £1,190 to £2,144 per bed day, about 80% over eight years (our arithmetic), with the steepest rise after 2019/20. Several things limit what this shows: the figures are not inflation-adjusted; the collection changed from Reference Costs to the National Cost Collection, with different costing methods, so part of any step change may be method rather than spending; 2021/22 still carried COVID-era pressures; and these are trust-reported costs, not prices paid. The trend says costs per day rose — not why, and not whether care became better or worse value. We could not download later years, which are published only as an interactive dashboard (teaching summary).
Cost per condition

NHS England does not openly publish critical care cost by diagnosis — its schedule costs bed days by organs supported, so the cost of a condition depends mainly on how many days and how many organs it needs. The studies above are the condition-specific UK figures we could verify. They use different years, costing methods and cost scopes (ICU stay, hospital stay or patient-related ICU costs only), so they show relative scale, not a league table. Sepsis acquired later in the stay cost more mainly because those patients stayed longer. We found no verifiable current UK per-admission costs for pneumonia acquired in the community, trauma or cardiac surgery, so those are omitted (teaching summary).
Costs continue after discharge
In Scottish linked data, hospital survivors of ICU used more hospital care over five years than matched hospital controls, even after adjustment. The economic burden of critical illness therefore extends well beyond the index admission, which supports rehabilitation and follow-up planning (see
). The costs are reported in US dollars by the authors and describe a 2005 cohort; they measure hospital resource use only, not social care, lost earnings or carer time, which the work and caregiver evidence on this page shows are also substantial (teaching summary).
Day 1 (US$10,794 ventilated; $6,667 not ventilated); costs fell on day 2 and became stable after day 3.
£1,881 per day, averaged across adults, children and neonates (standard ward bed £345 excluding treatment). The adult-only average in the 2019/20 National Schedule was £1,620 per bed day.
A mean of £26,857 per initial ICU stay, at £1,738 per ICU day (Marti 2016, 795 UK patients).

The National Schedule costs adult critical care per bed day by number of organs supported, not by diagnosis; condition costs come from individual studies with different years and methods.
It rose from about £1,240 (1 organ) to £2,330 (6 or more organs) — roughly double; the adult-only average across all support levels was £1,620.

Diagnosis shapes expected stay
APACHE IV predicts ICU stay from day-1 data with admission diagnosis among its inputs, and it matched observed group means for 93% of 116 diagnoses. It explained 62% of the variation between ICUs but only 21.5% between individual patients: diagnosis-based benchmarks are useful for judging unit throughput, not for telling one family how long their relative will stay. The 3.86-day US mean is lower than ICNARC's UK mean of about 6 days; case mix, admission thresholds, bed numbers and discharge delays differ, so neither figure is "correct" for the other system (teaching summary).

Standard deviations larger than the mean (Dasta) show a right-skewed distribution: most patients stay briefly and a few stay very long, so medians are usually lower than means. Patients who die early shorten average stay, so a unit with a shorter mean stay is not necessarily providing better care (teaching summary). NHS figures by organ support and more conditions are on
ICU Length of St

# Anaphylaxis in Critical Care Recognition and mimics, IM adrenaline doses and repeats, refractory anaphylaxis and adrenaline infusion, fluids, antihistamine and steroid roles, tryptase and biphasic reactions Recognise it, then give IM adrenaline anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis: sudden airway, breathing or circulation problems, usually with skin or mucosal changes, after a likely trigger. In the ICU the commonest triggers are drugs (antibiotics, neuromuscular blockers, chlorhexidine) and contrast. Skin signs can be absent. Stop the suspected trigger first. Perioperative reactions are covered on Critical Incidents Stop the infusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL). Repeat after 5 minutes if airway, breathing or circulation problems persist. Refractory anaphylaxis: the critical care phase after two IM doses the problem becomes an infusion problem: a low-dose IV adrenaline infusion with a rapid fluid bolus, given by people experienced in IV adrenaline. Bolus IV adrenaline outside specialist settings risks arrhythmias. Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems. Infusion doses and second-line vasopressors follow local and RCUK protocols; receptor pharmacology is on Vasoactive Agents No. This is refractory anaphylaxis: start a low-dose IV adrenaline infusion with a fluid bolus and get critical care help. Steroids may be considered only after initial resuscitation and never in place of adrenaline. Tryptase, biphasic reactions and follow-up a fixed 6–12-hour observation can miss many biphasic reactions, so how long to observe depends on how severe the reaction was and how much adrenaline it needed. Record the suspected trigger and refer the patient to an allergy clinic (teaching synthesis; check the RCUK guideline for timed tryptase sampling). No. RCUK 2021 notes that this strategy may miss over 50% of biphasic reactions. # The General Adult ICU: Staffing and Costs GPICS V3 baseline staffing standards for every ICU, and NHS 2019/20 general adult critical care bed-day costs Cost figures are adult bed-day averages from NHS England's National Schedule of NHS Costs 2019/20, weighted across organ-support levels (our arithmetic from the published rows). The schedule describes the type of patient a unit mainly treats, not each patient's diagnosis, and small specialist groups rest on few trust submissions — treat them as descriptive, not as the cost of treating a condition. The full table is on ICU Costs Staffing: the GPICS V3 baseline The general adult ICU is the baseline every specialist chapter builds on. These minimum standards come from the GPICS V3 staffing chapters and apply to every ICU, whatever its case mix. Role-by-role detail, including bank/agency limits, nursing associates and allied health professionals, is on ICU Staffing Ratios ; what other unit types add is on ICU Staffing by Unit Type 1:1 for level 3 patients and 1:2 for level 2 patients, plus a clinical shift leader with no patient allocation. Cost: general adult critical care General units carry most of England's adult critical care activity, so their average sits close to the all-unit average of £1,620. Within CCU01, cost still rises with organs supported — from £1,096.41 with none to £2,066.08 with six or more (published row values). About £1,689, across 838,376 bed days. Staffing: GPICS V3 cardiothoracic intensive care The general ratios still apply; the chapter adds a cardiothoracic surgeon alongside the on-site ICU doctor or ACCP, a CALS-trained rota able to reopen the chest 24/7, readily available perfusion and theatre staff, and a job-planned cardiothoracic consultant directing care. Consultants covering out of hours must work daytime cardiothoracic sessions. Cardiac Surgery Advanced Life Support (CALS), with the capability to reopen the chest 24/7. Cost: cardiac surgical critical care Cardiac surgical is the largest specialist group in the schedule and its average (£1,660) sits just below the general figure — consistent with short, planned post-operative stays at low organ-support levels, though the schedule does not break this down by diagnosis. Slightly lower: about £1,660 per bed day versus £1,689 for general adult critical care. Staffing: GPICS V3 neurocritical care Neurocritical care keeps the general ratios. Its additions are consultant-specific: out-of-hours consultants must have daytime neurocritical care sessions, care must be directed by a job-planned consultant trained in neuro intensive care, and the unit must have access to a defined list of neuroscience specialties — access, not co-location. Neurosurgery, spinal surgery, neurology, stroke, diagnostic and interventional neuroradiology, neurophysiology and neurorehabilitation. Cost: neurosciences critical care The neurosciences average (£1,616) is close to the all-unit average of £1,620. The schedule gives no diagnosis-level split, so this cannot be read as the cost of, for example, subarachnoid haemorrhage or traumatic brain injury. About £1,616, across 69,779 adult bed days. Staffing: no dedicated GPICS V3 chapter GPICS V3 has specialist chapters for cardiothoracic, neurocritical care, burns, smaller remote and rural units and enhanced care — but none for liver intensive care. Liver units therefore work to the general staffing chapters, quoted below. This absence is our reading of the V3 contents, not a GPICS statement; specialist liver service specifications may add requirements locally. None — liver units follow the general staffing chapters; there is no liver-specific chapter in V3. Cost: liver critical care Liver is a small group — 8,376 bed days from a handful of specialist centres — so one hospital's accounting can move the average. At £1,760 it sits above the general figure, consistent with high organ-support intensity, but the schedule does not separate transplant from non-transplant patients. It rests on few trust submissions (8,376 bed days), so individual hospitals' accounting can shift it; it is descriptive, not a per-condition cost. GPICS V3 has no obstetric critical care chapter, so the general staffing standards below apply. Obstetric patients are usually cared for in general ICUs or enhanced care areas with obstetric team input; local maternity and critical care networks set additional requirements. This is our reading of the V3 contents, not a GPICS statement. For the obstetric emergencies themselves, see Severe Pre-eclampsia and Eclampsia No — there is no obstetric chapter; the general staffing chapters apply. Cost: obstetric and gynaecology critical care This is the highest unit-function average in the schedule and the smallest group (8,008 bed days), so it is the most sensitive to individual trusts' accounting. It should not be read as the cost of caring for a critically ill pregnant patient. Obstetric and gynaecology, at about £2,303 — from the smallest bed-day group. # ICU Staffing: Roles, Specialist Units and International Standards GPICS V3 staffing by role and shift, specialist-unit and enhanced-care requirements, and Australian/New Zealand, European and US comparisons Four standards side by side The table is our summary of the quoted standards below. The documents differ in status: GPICS V3 and CICM IC-1 are professional minimum standards, ESICM 2011 is a set of recommendations for Europe that it says may need adapting for each country, and Leapfrog is a US purchaser-led safety standard covering doctors only. UK — GPICS V3 (2026) Australia & NZ — CICM IC-1 (reviewed 2016) Europe — ESICM (2011) US — Leapfrog (2026) On nursing for the sickest patients, the UK, Australian/New Zealand and European standards agree closely: one nurse per patient. They differ most on doctors: the UK fixes a consultant ratio and a 30-minute attendance time, Australia and New Zealand require a specialist rostered to the unit at all times, and the US standard measures intensivist presence and response times rather than a ratio. Comparing them does not show which is safer; they reflect different health systems and training models. Nursing for the sickest patients: one nurse per patient (1:1). UK: GPICS V3 baseline Full role-by-role detail is on ICU Staffing Ratios , and specialist unit additions on ICU Staffing by Unit Type . GPICS covers adult units; it does not set children's ICU ratios. Within 30 minutes, and continually contactable 24/7. Australia and New Zealand: CICM IC-1 The College of Intensive Care Medicine's minimum standards cover Level I, II and III and paediatric units. The nurse ratios are quoted from the Australian College of Critical Care Nurses guidelines. IC-1 was last reviewed in 2016, ten years before GPICS V3, so check the CICM website for any newer version. Unlike GPICS, it organises specialists by pods of 8–15 beds rather than a patient ratio, and it says "should" for the team leader and ward rounds where GPICS says "must". More than one specialist should be rostered: one per pod of 8–15 beds. Europe: ESICM recommendations ESICM's 2011 recommendations define three levels of care (III highest) and link nurse ratios and nursing posts per bed to each. ESICM is the only one of the four to give nursing whole-time posts per bed (6 per level III bed), which makes planning a rota explicit. It is also the oldest (2011) and is a recommendation for many health systems, not a binding standard. Individual European countries set their own rules, which we have not covered here. Six, matching a 1:1 nurse/patient ratio. United States: Leapfrog ICU physician staffing There is no single national US ICU staffing standard. Leapfrog, a group of employers and purchasers, scores hospitals against its ICU Physician Staffing standard. It covers doctors only. Leapfrog sets presence and response times rather than ratios, and allows a remote intensivist (telemedicine) if there is also on-site intensivist cover. We did not include US nurse ratios: there is no national ICU nurse ratio standard, and we have not checked individual state laws. More than 95% of the time. # ICU Costs: NHS Trends, Conditions and International Comparisons Organised NHS adult bed-day costs, historical timeline, costs by condition, PICU, international comparisons, post-discharge costs and teaching calculator Five health systems side by side The table summarises the quoted sources below. The figures differ in currency, year, costing method and what is included, so they are not directly comparable — read the caveats in each country lesson before quoting any number. Source and year of data What it covers No row here can be converted into another by exchange rate alone: the years span 2002 to 2021, the methods range from trust-reported expenditure to charge-derived costs, and the case mix differs. The European studies show that even within one study using one method, costs vary widely between countries and between units. The data are from 2013/14, use a different costing method (operational expenditure excluding capital and overheads), and cover a different case mix — exchange rate conversion ignores all three. United Kingdom: NHS reference costs Full detail is on ICU Costs : the 2019/20 adult average is about £1,620 per bed day (our arithmetic from published rows), rising from about £1,240 with one organ supported to about £2,330 with six or more. These are reported hospital costs, not tariffs or prices. Healthcare Resource Groups XC01Z–XC07Z, based on the number of organs supported each day. Australia: ANZICS registry costing Hicks and colleagues surveyed Australian ICUs through the ANZICS Centre for Outcome and Resource Evaluation registry. Larger units and higher occupancy were each significantly associated with lower cost per bed-day, suggesting economies of scale. An older single-unit study gives a lower figure from an earlier era: Rechner and Lipman costed one tertiary referral ICU in 2002/03; staff were about 69% of costs. The two studies used different methods and their data are about a decade apart (2002/03 versus 2013/14), which is why their figures differ so much. Higher ICU bed number and higher occupancy. New Zealand: a single-board figure This figure comes from Auckland District Health Board's response to an Official Information Act request about COVID-19 costs. It is not a national costing study: it covers one board, one financial year during the pandemic, and a respiratory case mix, and it bundles in laboratory, radiology, pharmacy and theatre costs that other studies count separately. We could not find a published national New Zealand ICU bed-day costing study, so treat this as an indicative local figure only. It is one district health board, in the COVID-era 2020/21 year, for adult patients with a respiratory complaint, and it includes laboratory, radiology, pharmacy and theatre costs. Europe: standardised cross-country studies Tan's team applied one standardised costing method to seven ICUs in Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and the UK, so the remaining differences reflect real variation in practice and input prices rather than method. An earlier study used purchasing power parities to compare four countries: Both studies are old, and both show wide variation even with a common method. Labour was the largest cost component everywhere Tan looked — the same pattern as the Australian and NHS data. Labour, at every department. United States: charge-derived costs Dasta's 2002 figures are derived from charges in a large US database, a different method from the trust-reported costs in the NHS schedule or the microcosting in the European studies. US figures also reflect a payer system with different input prices. The comparison lesson on explains why these cannot be converted into NHS costs by exchange rate. entries.text:
# ICU Length of Stay by Condition and Organ Support ICNARC and NHS Hospital Episode Statistics critical care length of stay, support days by organ, condition-specific stays, deprivation and interpretation Costs for individual conditions, UK beside US, are on ICU Cost by Condition The headline NHS figure £1,881 is the average cost of one critical care bed day in England in 2020/21, averaged across adult, paediatric and neonatal critical care. A critical care day therefore cost about 5.5 times a standard bed day (£1,881 ÷ £345 — arithmetic, not a published ratio), but the £345 excludes treatment, so the real gap is smaller. 2020/21 was a COVID-affected year. Adult-only costs from the National Schedule NHS England's National Schedule of NHS Costs lists adult critical care separately from paediatric and neonatal care, as cost per bed day for each Healthcare Resource Group (HRG). The 2019/20 schedule supplies the detailed unit-function breakdown and calculator below; the timeline also includes a verified 2021/22 spreadsheet. Years from 2022/23 onwards are not quoted because we could not independently verify their dashboard figures here. Adding up every adult critical care row in 2019/20 gives 1,326,594 bed days costing about £2.15 billion, an average of £1,620 per adult bed day (our arithmetic from the published rows). That is the last full year before COVID-19 and is in 2019/20 prices. It averages adult, paediatric and neonatal critical care (2020/21 cost collection data). NHS costs rise with organs supported Adult critical care is paid and costed by the number of organ systems supported on each day (HRGs XC01Z–XC07Z, from the Critical Care Minimum Dataset). The table combines every adult unit type, weighting each row by its bed days (our arithmetic from the 2019/20 schedule, rounded to the nearest pound). A day with six or more organs supported cost about twice a one-organ day. Most adult bed days (about 64%) involved one or two organs. Costs flatten above four organs because nursing at 1:1 is already the main cost; more organ support adds drugs and equipment rather than staff (teaching interpretation). These are reported costs, not the price commissioners pay, and they vary between trusts. Worked example (fictional) A fictional patient spends 2 days on 3 organs, 3 days on 2 organs and 2 days on 1 organ: 2 × £1,947 + 3 × £1,704 + 2 × £1,240 = £11,486 at 2019/20 average costs. This is arithmetic for teaching, not a real bill or tariff. About £1,240 versus £2,330 — roughly half. Cost by type of unit The schedule also splits costs by unit function — the closest open NHS breakdown to cost "by condition". It describes the type of patient a unit mainly treats, not each patient's diagnosis. Averages below combine all organ-support levels, weighted by bed days (our arithmetic from the 2019/20 rows). Differences between unit types partly reflect case mix and partly how few trusts submitted data: small specialist groups (obstetric, burns, spinal, renal) come from a handful of trusts, so one hospital's accounting can move the average a lot. Treat them as descriptive, not as the cost of treating a condition. Diagnosis-level NHS costs are not published openly. Unit function describes the predominant patient type of a unit, not each patient's diagnosis, and small groups rest on few trust submissions. US costs and why they don't convert US 2002 costs were derived from hospital charges; NHS figures are trust-reported expenditure. Different decades, costing methods and case mix mean you cannot compare them by exchange rate. Both show the same pattern: the first day and organ support (especially ventilation) drive cost. Costs after discharge Hospital costs continue for years after ICU and exclude social care, lost earnings and carer time. See ICU Outcomes for recovery and work, and ICU Length of Stay for how many days are bought. US$1,522 per day. UK national averages In ICNARC's 2024–25 audit, the average critical care stay was 6 days and the acute hospital stay 20 days. Non-survivors stayed slightly longer in critical care (7 days) but shorter in hospital (16), because many died in the unit. NHS England hospital statistics Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) count each critical care record. Weekend admissions stayed longer, which NHS Digital suggests may be because more are emergencies. The day-of-discharge pattern (longest for Monday discharges, shortest for Saturday) suggests that weekend discharge practice affects stay, not just illness (teaching interpretation). 6 days in critical care; 20 days in acute hospital. NHS England: days by type of organ support Average support days per critical care period, from NHS Digital's 2018-19 column (the most recent column clearly labelled in the table; men and women shown separately). These are days of each support, not total stay. Gastrointestinal support (mainly feeding) lasts longest because it continues through most of a long stay; advanced cardiovascular support is short because it is either weaned or the patient dies (teaching interpretation). Patients often receive several types at once. Gastrointestinal support (8.5 days in men, 7.6 in women). Length of stay by condition NHS England does not openly publish ICU stay for each diagnosis. The figures below come from published studies; they differ in country, year and whether they report means or medians, so compare with care. Predicting stay from diagnosis Diagnosis-based prediction works for groups and units, not individuals. The UK pancreatitis median (3.8 days) is shorter than many expect because early deaths and quick recoveries pull the median down; survivors and non-survivors had similar stays. 3.8 days, similar for survivors and non-survivors. Deprivation and stay In 2019-20, patients from the most deprived tenth of areas averaged 4.19 days per critical care record against 3.82 in the least deprived. HES records are per unit episode, so they are shorter than ICNARC's per-admission average, and these figures are not adjusted for illness severity. Reading length-of-stay figures Stays are right-skewed: a few very long stays raise the mean above the median. Early deaths shorten averages, so a short mean stay is not automatically good care. Delayed discharge for lack of ward beds also adds days that are not illness — see ICU Discharge Planning . Costs per stay follow from days and organ support: see ICU Costs HES counts each critical care record (unit episode); ICNARC reports per admission and covers different units and years. entries.topic_title: Severe Pre-eclampsia and Eclampsia in Critical Care
entries.text:
# Severe Pre-eclampsia and Eclampsia in Critical Care Magnesium sulfate (Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen, Magpie), severe hypertension control, fluid restriction and critical care Recognise it, then give IM adrenaline anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis: sudden airway, breathing or circulation problems, usually with skin or mucosal changes, after a likely trigger. In the ICU the commonest triggers are drugs (antibiotics, neuromuscular blockers, chlorhexidine) and contrast. Skin signs can be absent. Stop the suspected trigger first. Perioperative reactions are covered on Critical Incidents Stop the infusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL). Repeat after 5 minutes if airway, breathing or circulation problems persist. Refractory anaphylaxis: the critical care phase after two IM doses the problem becomes an infusion problem: a low-dose IV adrenaline infusion with a rapid fluid bolus, given by people experienced in IV adrenaline. Bolus IV adrenaline outside specialist settings risks arrhythmias. Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems. Infusion doses and second-line vasopressors follow local and RCUK protocols; receptor pharmacology is on Vasoactive Agents No. This is refractory anaphylaxis: start a low-dose IV adrenaline infusion with a fluid bolus and get critical care help. Steroids may be considered only after initial resuscitation and never in place of adrenaline. Tryptase, biphasic reactions and follow-up a fixed 6–12-hour observation can miss many biphasic reactions, so how long to observe depends on how severe the reaction was and how much adrenaline it needed. Record the suspected trigger and refer the patient to an allergy clinic (teaching synthesis; check the RCUK guideline for timed tryptase sampling). No. RCUK 2021 notes that this strategy may miss over 50% of biphasic reactions. Magnesium sulfate: prevention and treatment of fits magnesium is the anticonvulsant of choice; benzodiazepines and phenytoin are not substitutes. Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output during the infusion, because magnesium is renally excreted and toxicity causes loss of reflexes, then respiratory depression (teaching synthesis — follow local monitoring and antidote protocols). Obstetric anaesthetic issues are on Obstetric Anaesthesia A further 2–4 g IV over 5–15 minutes, and continue the infusion for 24 hours after the last fit. Do not switch to diazepam or phenytoin. Severe hypertension severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia is treated immediately because it can cause stroke in the mother. Choose one of the three listed drugs and follow local doses and blood-pressure targets. Hydralazine can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure, which is why NICE pairs it with a small fluid preload (next lesson). Labetalol (oral or IV), oral nifedipine, or IV hydralazine. Fluid restriction pre-eclampsia causes leaky capillaries and low oncotic pressure, so these women are prone to pulmonary oedema. Fluid is restricted unless there are ongoing losses such as haemorrhage. This is the opposite of the reflex fluid bolus in septic shock . Delivery is the definitive treatment, and the risk of fits continues after birth. 80 mL/hour (NICE NG133 1.8.12). entries.topic_title: ICU Resuscitation: The First Hour of Septic Shock
entries.text:
# ICU Resuscitation: The First Hour of Septic Shock Recognition, lactate, immediate antimicrobials, 30 mL/kg crystalloid with reassessment, MAP 65 and noradrenaline, and lung-protective ventilation if intubated Step 1 — Recognise shock and measure perfusion do not wait for every Sepsis-3 criterion before acting: hypotension or hypoperfusion with suspected infection starts resuscitation now, and the label is confirmed later. Screening uses a broad tool; qSOFA alone is not enough. Lactate and capillary refill give a baseline you can re-measure after each intervention. Full criteria and screening are on Sepsis & Septic Shock No. Hypotension with suspected infection is enough to start resuscitation; lactate guides and tracks it but should not delay it. Step 2 — Antimicrobials immediately possible septic shock is the highest-urgency group — "immediately, ideally within 1 h". Seymour's observational data link faster antibiotics, not a faster first fluid bolus, with lower adjusted mortality; association is not proof of cause. Send cultures when it does not meaningfully delay the first dose, and look for a source that needs control. Teaching synthesis, not a prescription — follow local antimicrobial guidance. Rapid antibiotics (and the 3-hour bundle); rapid completion of the initial fluid bolus was not associated with lower mortality. Step 3 — Fluids, then vasopressors to MAP 65 30 mL/kg within 3 hours is a weak suggestion, not a fixed bolus. Give fluid in steps and reassess perfusion and fluid tolerance after each one. Do not leave a patient hypotensive while waiting to finish fluid before starting noradrenaline. Arterial line, MAP targets, vasopressin and steroids are covered on Septic Shock: Vasopressors, MAP & Steroids ; fluid choice on Fluid Balance and Tonicity Stop routine boluses (fluid intolerance) and start or escalate noradrenaline to a MAP of 65 mm Hg, reassessing perfusion. Step 4 — Airway and lung-protective ventilation if intubated intubating a patient in septic shock is high-risk: induction drugs and positive pressure can make hypotension worse. Teaching synthesis: resuscitate first where possible, have a vasopressor running or ready, and reduce induction doses. Drug choice is discussed on Mechanical Ventilation sepsis is a leading cause of ARDS. Set tidal volume by predicted body weight (not actual weight) and watch plateau pressure. ARDSNet studied patients with ARDS/acute lung injury, so using it for all ventilated septic patients is an extrapolation. PEEP and mode choice: PEEP Management No — predicted body weight. ARDSNet's low-tidal-volume arm used about 6 mL/kg predicted body weight. SSC 2021 ESICM Shock 2014 SSC 2021 MAP target SSC 2021 norepinephrine SSC 2021 vasopressin After 1.5 L crystalloid, MAP is 60 mm Hg and crackles are developing. Next step? In practice the steps happen in parallel. Quotations reuse verified records; the order and explanation are teaching synthesis, not a protocol or prescription.

# Septic Shock: Vasopressors, MAP & Steroids Sepsis-3 shock criteria, lactate and capillary refill, MAP 65, noradrenaline and vasopressin, the 65 trial, corticosteroids and ADRENAL Defining septic shock and measuring perfusion both criteria are required — vasopressor need for MAP ≥65 mm Hg AND lactate >2 mmol/L after adequate fluid. Lactate and capillary refill then guide resuscitation. Initial fluid volume and timing are covered on Sepsis & Septic Shock No — the lactate criterion is not met. It is sepsis with hypotension needing vasopressors, which still requires the same urgent management. MAP target and vasopressor choice vasopressin adds a non-adrenergic vasoconstrictor (V1 receptors), so it can spare catecholamine dose. The guideline's own remark that it is usually started at noradrenaline 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min is a practice note, not a separate recommendation. Is 65 too high for older patients? the 65 trial (UK, age ≥65) targeted MAP 60–65 mm Hg and reduced vasopressor exposure without a significant mortality difference; the confidence interval does not exclude benefit. See Vasoactive Agents for receptor pharmacology. Add vasopressin rather than continuing to escalate noradrenaline. Corticosteroids as a septic-shock adjunct ADRENAL found no 90-day mortality benefit but faster shock reversal; the recommendation is "suggest" (weak). This is a haemodynamic adjunct, not replacement of a missing hormone — patients with known adrenal insufficiency need full replacement doses (see Adrenal Crisis ADRENAL did not show this; steroids are suggested for ongoing vasopressor need, mainly to speed shock reversal.       Source Control

      Identify and control the source of infection as rapidly as possible. Drainage of abscesses, debridement of infected tissue, removal of infected devices. Delay in source control is independently associated with increased mortality. Consider CT imaging early if source unclear.

Unlike conventional antigens, they bypass normal antigen processing by binding directly outside the peptide-binding groove, cross-linking MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells with the T-cell receptor Vβ region.
