Uncomplicated versus complicated UTI — and why it matters
uncomplicated UTI
complicated UTI (cUTI)
is any UTI occurring in the presence of a factor that raises the risk of treatment failure: obstruction or stasis (calculi, tumour, BPH, stricture, neurogenic bladder), an indwelling catheter or stent, recent instrumentation, incomplete bladder emptying, renal impairment or transplantation, diabetes, immunosuppression, pregnancy, or male sex
. Essentially every urosepsis presentation on the ICU is a cUTI.
most infection is ascending — perineal and faecal flora colonise the periurethral area, ascend the urethra, and adhere to urothelium via fimbriae/adhesins. In the uncomplicated tract, urine flow, low pH and osmolality, urothelial shedding and Tamm–Horsfall glycoprotein clear this efficiently. Obstruction or stasis abolishes that washout, raises intraluminal pressure, and allows bacteria to reach the renal pelvis and multiply in a poorly perfused, high-pressure system. Rising pressure drives
pyelovenous and pyelolymphatic backflow
, so organisms and endotoxin enter the circulation directly — which is why an obstructed infected system produces fulminant septic shock and why antibiotics alone do not work.
Consequences for management:
a cUTI mandates imaging (CT-KUB or ultrasound) to exclude obstruction, broader empiric cover for resistant Gram-negatives (previous cultures guide choice), longer treatment courses, and
emergency decompression
— retrograde stent or percutaneous nephrostomy — for any obstructed infected system. Catheters and stents are biofilm reservoirs: exchange or remove them as part of source control. Distinguish asymptomatic bacteriuria (do not treat, except in pregnancy or before urological instrumentation) from infection.

# Antimicrobials in ICU Empiric therapy, antimicrobial resistance, stewardship, PK/PD dosing The Trial Evidence on Antibiotic Duration and Carbapenem-Sparing Two questions come up on every ICU ward round: how long to treat, and whether a carbapenem is really needed. This lesson sets out the randomised evidence behind the duration and drug-choice advice on this page, including the groups the trials excluded. Ventilator-associated pneumonia: 8 versus 15 days (Chastre 2003) In 51 French ICUs, 401 patients with VAP proven by quantitative bronchoscopic culture, who had already received appropriate empirical therapy, were randomised to 8 or 15 days of antibiotics. At 28 days, 8 days was not worse for mortality (18.8% vs 17.2%) or recurrence (28.9% vs 26.0%), and patients had more antibiotic-free days (13.1 vs 8.7). The key caveat: VAP caused by non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa , recurred more often with 8 days (40.6% vs 25.4%), although outcomes were not worse. Learning check: who was the 8-day result tested in? Patients whose VAP was proven microbiologically and whose first empirical antibiotics were already appropriate. The result should not be applied blindly to undiagnosed "possible VAP" or to a failing empirical regimen. With non-fermenters, expect more recurrence and watch for it. Bloodstream infection: 7 versus 14 days (BALANCE 2025) BALANCE randomised 3,608 hospitalised patients with bloodstream infection (55% in ICU) across 74 hospitals in seven countries. By 90 days, 14.5% had died in the 7-day group and 16.1% in the 14-day group (difference −1.6 percentage points), so 7 days was shown to be non-inferior. Infections came mostly from the urinary tract, abdomen and lung. Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia, severe immunosuppression, infection sites needing prolonged treatment, and single positive cultures that could be contaminants. Of note, 23.1% of the 7-day group were treated for longer than assigned. Learning check: does BALANCE support 7 days for S. aureus was excluded, as were infections needing prolonged treatment (for example endocarditis or undrained collections). The 7-day result applies to the Gram-negative-dominated, controlled-source population that was actually studied. ESBL bacteraemia: piperacillin–tazobactam versus meropenem (MERINO 2018) MERINO tested whether piperacillin–tazobactam could be used to spare carbapenems as definitive treatment for bloodstream infection with ceftriaxone-non-susceptible E. coli that tested susceptible to piperacillin–tazobactam. 30-day mortality was 12.3% (23/187) with piperacillin–tazobactam versus 3.7% (7/191) with meropenem, so non-inferiority was not shown. The practical result is that meropenem remains the definitive treatment for serious ESBL bloodstream infection , even when the lab reports susceptibility to piperacillin–tazobactam. Learning check: why does MERINO matter for stewardship? It shows that carbapenem-sparing has to be backed by outcome evidence, not just lab susceptibility. Stewardship here means using a carbapenem for proven serious ESBL bacteraemia, while shortening courses (Chastre, BALANCE) and de-escalating promptly elsewhere. # Acid-Base Disorders Stewart approach, strong ion difference, anion gap, base excess item.label === label); if (!ref?.excerpt) return null; return Park and Sidebotham's Metabolic alkalosis and mixed acid–base disturbance in anaesthesia and critical care (BJA Education, 2023;23:128–135) is available in full through its freely readable archived copy . The short quotations below are the authors' wording; the accompanying explanations are teaching synthesis. Recognise the process, not just the pH Metabolic alkalosis is the non-respiratory alkalinising process. Read pH, bicarbonate and PaCO₂ together: a raised bicarbonate may instead be compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis. Mixed disorders can leave the measured pH normal or low; compare previous gases and assess the anion gap, albumin and clinical history rather than excluding alkalosis from pH alone. Separate generation from maintenance Vomiting or gastric drainage removes acid and chloride; diuretics promote renal electrolyte losses; bicarbonate or metabolised precursors can add alkali. Ask separately why the kidney has not removed it: volume/chloride depletion, potassium deficiency and impaired renal function can maintain the disturbance after the original cause stops. Volume depletion activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), favouring sodium retention and hydrogen/potassium loss. Check the clinical setting before choosing treatment Review gastric losses, diuretic and alkali exposure, volume status, blood pressure, chloride, potassium, magnesium and kidney function. Urine chloride can help classify the mechanism, but active diuretics and the examination matter; it is not an automatic instruction to give fluid. For a genuinely volume-depleted patient able to receive fluid, chloride-rich replacement can restore renal bicarbonate excretion. Potassium chloride addresses concomitant hypokalaemia; replacement needs local protocols, renal assessment and repeat measurements. A fluid-overloaded or mineralocorticoid-driven patient needs a different, cause-led strategy—not indiscriminate saline. Post-hypercapnic alkalosis and treatment limits When ventilation rapidly lowers chronically elevated PaCO₂, renal adaptation can persist, revealing metabolic alkalosis. Review previous gases, ventilation goals and chloride/potassium deficits; this is not a reason to deliberately hypoventilate. Acetazolamide may lower bicarbonate, but biochemical improvement is not evidence of faster weaning: Alkalaemia can lower ionised calcium through increased albumin binding. Symptomatic or worsening disturbance requires senior assessment of the patient, ECG, electrolytes, gas trend and fluid balance; this is clinical safety synthesis, not an automatic pH-based treatment rule. The generating event has ended, but renal maintenance persists. Assess volume status, kidney function and electrolyte deficits, stop ongoing contributors and replace losses appropriately. A normal pH would not exclude a concurrent alkalosis if another acidifying process were present. # Critical Care Overview: Structure, Team & Communication ICS 2021 levels of care, GPICS admission/discharge standards, medical and nursing ratios, intensivist staffing evidence, daily goals, structured handover and family communication Teaching reasoning (not a quoted guideline): What GPICS is The Guidelines for the Provision of Intensive Care Services (GPICS) are the joint FICM/Intensive Care Society standards for how UK intensive care is organised and staffed: GPICS V3 (2026) is the definitive reference source for the planning, commissioning and delivery of adult intensive care services in the UK. This latest version is broken down into five sections covering intensive care structure, workforce, clinical care, service development and preparedness. Standards versus recommendations GPICS grades its advice. In V3 the two tiers were renamed to make the distinction clearer: For V3, the previously named ‘standards’ have been renamed ‘minimum standards’ and are defined as something we expect all ICUs in the UK to be able to meet. ‘Recommendations’ are now ‘recommendations for a quality service’ and are intended to act as markers for a high quality intensive care service. when you read a GPICS statement, check which tier it is. A minimum standard is a commissioning floor every unit should meet; a quality recommendation marks out a high-quality service. The time standards and staffing ratios quoted in the other lessons on this page have been re-checked word for word against GPICS V3 (2026). Where V3 changed a V2.1 standard, the lesson says so. Editions and who uses it The first version of GPICS was published in 2015. In 2016, GPICS Edition 1 was subject to a review. Edition 2 began in Summer 2017 and was published Summer 2019. Edition 2.1 was published in Summer 2022. GPICS is not just an internal document — regulators and auditors use it to judge units: Groups that check hospital quality, such as the Care Quality Commission (CQC) in England, also use GPICS. In Scotland, Scottish Intensive Care Society Audit Group (SICSAG) uses GPICS to help check how well intensive care units are working. this is why GPICS gaps matter beyond the unit: they can surface in CQC inspections and national audit comparisons, and they are the evidence base when a unit bids for more staff, beds or equipment. It would still fall short: minimum standards are “something we expect all ICUs in the UK to be able to meet”, so a missed minimum standard is a gap in the floor of provision, however many quality recommendations are met. Quality recommendations mark a high-quality service built on top of the minimum standards. Levels of care describe the patient, not the bed UK critical care is organised around the Intensive Care Society levels of care. The 2021 second edition is explicit about what the levels mean: Levels of Adult Critical Care Second Edition, as in the original guidance, describes the care a patient requires, not where they are receiving it, nor does it measure the actual care being delivered. a level 3 patient waiting in recovery or the emergency department is still a level 3 patient. The level tells you what nursing, monitoring and senior input they need now, wherever they physically are. What changed in 2021 It merges the pre-existing level 0 and level 1 into ward care. This frees up ‘level 1’ of critical care to represent the emerging Enhanced Care, with Level 2 and 3 remaining. So the current scheme is: ward care; level 1 (enhanced care, for example single-organ basic support or step-down patients); level 2; and level 3. Two of the level 2 descriptors are worth learning word for word: Patients needing one organ systems monitored and supported at an advanced level (other than advanced respiratory support). Level 3 starts with the ventilated patient: Patients needing advanced respiratory monitoring and support alone. Patients requiring monitoring and support for two or more organ systems at an advanced level. Delirium was added as a reason to step up a level, because an agitated patient needs more nursing to stay safe: Patients who experience delirium and agitation in addition to requiring level 2 care. Getting in and getting out: UK time standards The Guidelines for the Provision of Intensive Care Services (GPICS V3, 2026) set time standards around admission and discharge: Unplanned admissions to the ICU must occur within four hours of making the decision to admit and the completion of the essential resuscitation and imaging. Patients must be reviewed, in person, by a consultant responsible for the ICU as urgently as the clinical state dictates, and always within 14 hours of admission to intensive care. Discharge from intensive care to a general ward must occur only between 0700hrs and 2159hrs, except for reasons of surge. Discharge from intensive care to a general ward should occur within four hours of the decision. What changed from V2.1: the consultant review limit moved from 12 to 14 hours and now refers to “a consultant responsible for the ICU”; the four-hour admission clock now starts once essential resuscitation and imaging are complete; and four-hour discharge dropped from a minimum standard to a recommendation for a quality service, while the 07:00–21:59 window stays a minimum standard (with a surge exception). the 14-hour standard is a maximum, not a target. A deteriorating patient needs consultant review as soon as their condition demands. Night-time discharges are avoided because ward staffing and senior cover are thinner then, so problems are less likely to be picked up. For pre-operative decisions about who needs level 2 or 3 care after surgery, see Critical Care of the High-Risk Surgical Patient . For moving patients between units, see Transfer Medicine Level 3: “advanced respiratory monitoring and support alone” is enough on its own. Contrast a patient on a single vasopressor without ventilation: advanced support for one organ other than the lungs is a level 2 descriptor. Doctors: consultant-led care GPICS V3 sets ratios for medical staff: The daytime consultant in ICM to patient ratio must not normally exceed a range between 1:8 and 1:12. The staff to patient ratio must not normally exceed 1:8 24/7. the 1:8 ratio for the on-site resident rota (doctors and ACCPs) was a daytime “should”; V3 makes it a 24/7 minimum standard. The consultant range of 1:8 to 1:12 is unchanged. The reason for intensivist-led care comes mainly from observational data. A systematic review compared “high-intensity” staffing (mandatory intensivist input or a closed unit) with “low-intensity” staffing: High-intensity staffing was associated with lower hospital mortality in 16 of 17 studies (94%) and with a pooled estimate of the relative risk for hospital mortality of 0.71 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.62-0.82). More is not always better. When one US academic unit randomised days to having an in-house intensivist overnight, on top of daytime intensivist care and resident cover: In an academic medical ICU in the United States, nighttime in-hospital intensivist staffing did not improve patient outcomes. the observational studies compared having intensivists with not having them, and could not fully adjust for differences between hospitals. The randomised trial added overnight presence to a unit already run by intensivists. The lesson is that intensivists direct care. It is not that every extra consultant hour saves lives. Nurses: the core of the unit Level 3 patients must have a minimum registered nurse:patient ratio of 1:1 to deliver direct care. Level 2 patients must have a minimum registered nurse:patient ratio of 1:2 to deliver direct care. There must be a clinical shift leader, who is not allocated a patient, on duty 24/7 in all ICUs. the 1:1 and 1:2 ratios are unchanged from V2.1; V3 renames the supernumerary coordinator the clinical shift leader. The shift leader has no patients of their own so that they can cover breaks, run emergencies, manage beds and spot problems across the unit. If they have to take a patient, that whole safety layer is lost. The wider team on the ward round V3 keeps twice-daily consultant rounds but now specifies that one must be in person: A consultant in ICM must undertake ward rounds twice a day, one of which will be face-to-face, 7 days a week. V3 sets separate staffing chapters for pharmacists, physiotherapists, dietitians, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and psychologists. Each role covers a different risk. Pharmacists catch drug doses and interactions, especially in kidney failure. Physiotherapists help clear secretions and start rehabilitation early. Dietitians plan feeding. Speech and language therapists assess swallowing after a breathing tube or tracheostomy. Psychologists support recovery from distressing ICU experiences. Advanced critical care practitioners increasingly fill resident-grade roles. Recovery after discharge is covered in PICS Follow-up 11 (1:1 for level 3) + 2 (1:2 for three level 2 patients, rounded up) = 13 bedside nurses, plus a clinical shift leader, who must not take a patient. The unit also has more than ten beds, and GPICS V3 requires at least one additional enhanced critical care nurse who is not allocated a patient. (Arithmetic from the standards; actual rostering also depends on how sick each patient is.) Every GPICS V3 staffing role, with day and night requirements and worked examples, is on ICU Staffing Ratios Shared daily goals A busy ward round can end with everyone leaving with a different idea of the plan. In one surgical ICU, a written daily goals form showed how large that gap was: At baseline, less than 10% of residents and nurses understood the goals of care for the day. After implementing the daily goals form, greater than 95% of nurses and residents understood the goals of care for the day. this was a before-and-after study in a single unit, so it shows that teams understood the plan better. It does not prove patients did better. In practice, finish each patient’s review by stating the goals out loud: what must happen today, what would trigger a call, and who is doing each task. Structured handover The best multicentre evidence for structured handover comes from I-PASS, a programme for resident doctors in children’s hospitals. It used a memory aid, training, observation of handovers and a standard written document: In 10,740 patient admissions, the medical-error rate decreased by 23% from the preintervention period to the postintervention period (24.5 vs. 18.8 per 100 admissions, P<0.001), and the rate of preventable adverse events decreased by 30% (4.7 vs. 3.3 events per 100 admissions, P<0.001). Discharge from ICU is a handover between teams too, and GPICS requires both spoken and written handover: The receiving (ward) team responsible for ongoing care need to be directly involved in this process and there should be a verbal as well as written handover. I-PASS was a package tested in children’s wards, not adult ICUs, and it was not randomised. Its message is that a memory aid only works alongside training and a standard document. SBAR, call-outs and check-back for urgent escalation are taught on the Non-technical Skills Communicating with families Families are part of ICU communication too. In a French trial of relatives of patients dying in ICU, a planned end-of-life meeting plus a bereavement leaflet reduced psychological harm: On day 90, the 56 participants in the intervention group who responded to the telephone interview had a significantly lower median IES score than the 52 participants in the control group (27 vs. 39, P=0.02) and a lower prevalence of PTSD-related symptoms (45% vs. 69%, P=0.01). in the trial, relatives in the intervention group talked for more of the meeting. Listening is part of the treatment. Detailed family-meeting technique is covered in End-of-Life Care & Communication (24.5 − 18.8) ÷ 24.5 ≈ 0.23, a relative reduction of 23%. The absolute reduction is 5.7 errors per 100 admissions. Because the study compared periods before and after the programme rather than randomising, other changes over the same period could explain some of the difference. It was also done in children’s hospitals rather than adult ICUs. GPICS V3 definitive GPICS V3 sections GPICS V3 minimum standards GPICS V3 quality recommendations GPICS editions GPICS CQC SICSAG a unit meets every GPICS quality recommendation but misses one minimum standard. How would GPICS describe this? ICS Levels 2021 purpose ICS Levels 2021 enhanced care ICS Levels 2021 level 2 ICS Levels 2021 level 3 ICS Levels 2021 delirium GPICS V3 admission timing GPICS V3 consultant review GPICS V3 discharge GPICS V3 discharge four hours a patient is intubated for pneumonia but needs no other organ support. What level of care is this? GPICS V3 consultant ratio GPICS V3 resident ratio Pronovost 2002 staffing Kerlin 2013 night staffing GPICS V3 nurse ratios GPICS V3 coordinator GPICS V3 ward round a 14-bed unit has eleven level 3 and three level 2 patients. What is the minimum number of registered nurses needed for direct care? Pronovost 2003 daily goals Starmer 2014 I-PASS GPICS V3 discharge handover Lautrette 2007 family the I-PASS programme reduced the medical-error rate from 24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions. # The ICU Inpatient Journey: Admission to Discharge Referral and ICS 2021 triage, GPICS V3 admission and review standards, daily rounds and goals, handover, discharge timing and follow-up, linking to each treatment page item.label === label); if (!ref?.excerpt) return null; return This page follows one adult through critical care, from ward deterioration to follow-up. Quotations are the sources' own wording; the surrounding sequence is teaching synthesis, not a local admission policy. Each stage links to the page that teaches it in depth. Recognition and referral Most unplanned admissions begin with a deteriorating ward patient: rising early-warning scores, new organ dysfunction or a clinician's concern. Referral should state the problem, the physiological trajectory, treatment already given and the patient's known wishes or treatment limits. Suspected infection with organ dysfunction should prompt the pathway in parallel with referral, not after it. NICE CG50 predates NEWS2, so its score bands are local; the principles — an immediate response to a high score and a consultant-to-consultant admission decision — still hold. Triage: what level of care does the patient need? Levels describe the support a patient needs, not the bed they occupy. Ward care now absorbs the old levels 0 and 1; level 1 represents enhanced care. Triage also weighs whether critical care can achieve an outcome the patient would value. Where it cannot, a ward-based plan with clear ceilings of treatment is an active decision, discussed on Prognostication & Ethics End-of-Life Communication Level 3. The ICS 2021 definition places advanced respiratory monitoring and support alone at level 3, even with no other organ failing. Time standards after the decision to admit Delay between decision and arrival is time spent at the wrong level of care; resuscitation continues wherever the patient is. If the patient must move between hospitals or departments, follow Transfer Medicine The first hours A typical sequence (teaching synthesis): structured ABCDE reassessment; secure the airway and start mechanical ventilation if needed; establish monitoring and vascular access; resuscitate the circulation ( Circulatory Failure Fluid Balance ); send gases and cultures ( ABG Analyser ); start source control and ; document the admission plan, escalation limits and next-of-kin contact. Staffing at the bedside GPICS V3 requires unplanned admission within four hours of the decision (once essential resuscitation and imaging are complete); 5.5 hours breaches it unless those were still under way. The consultant must still review in person within 14 hours of admission. The daily cycle: ward rounds and goals Each round should review the cause of admission, each organ system and every line, tube and drug, then state explicit goals for the next 24 hours. The Pronovost study measured staff understanding of goals, not patient mortality. Organ support and prevention bundles Treatment pages for the commonest problems: PEEP management AKI & RRT Neurointensive care Transfusion & coagulation . Daily care also covers sedation and delirium , thromboprophylaxis, glucose control, pressure-area care and early mobilisation. This checklist is teaching synthesis. Shift handover and family communication I-PASS was studied in paediatric residents, and Lautrette in relatives of patients dying in ICU; applying them elsewhere is extrapolation. Liberation from support As the patient improves, the plan moves to weaning: readiness screening, spontaneous breathing trials and extubation are taught on ICU Ventilation Protocols The ABC trial paired daily sedation interruption with a breathing trial and found more ventilator-free days, shorter ICU and hospital stays and lower one-year mortality, with more self-extubations but similar reintubation. It was a single trial; "suggest" is the authors' own wording. Rehabilitation planning therefore starts during the ICU stay, not at discharge. During the critical care stay, as early as clinically possible (NICE CG83 1.2), not at ward transfer. No. It showed that staff understanding of the day's goals rose from under 10% to over 95%; it did not measure mortality. Timing of discharge to the ward Night-time and delayed discharges matter because the patient leaves a 1:1 or 1:2 nursing environment for a ward with far fewer staff per patient. A discharge decision should state why the patient no longer needs critical care and what would prompt readmission. Handover to the ward team A good discharge summary covers diagnoses, procedures, ongoing drugs and antimicrobial plan, lines to remove, nutrition and swallow status, mobility, delirium, treatment limits and the follow-up plan (teaching synthesis). Outreach review after discharge helps catch early deterioration. Discharge planning and longer-term recovery have their own page: ICU Discharge Planning and Longer-Term Recovery Life after critical care Survivors often have physical, cognitive and psychological problems after discharge. Rehabilitation, follow-up clinics and support for families are taught on PICS & follow-up . When the outcome is death or organ donation, see Organ Donation Discharge to a general ward must occur only between 07:00 and 21:59, except for reasons of surge. A 23:30 move breaches the standard; the patient should stay until morning unless there is a safer alternative. NICE CG50 adds that a transfer between 22:00 and 07:00 should be documented as an adverse incident. At 2 to 3 months, face to face, by a professional familiar with their critical care course (NICE CG83 1.23–1.24). What level of care is this? GPICS V3 admission timing GPICS V3 consultant review GPICS V3 nurse ratios the decision to admit is made at 22:00 and the patient arrives at 03:30. # Haemorrhagic Shock & Resuscitation Shock index and lactate, cuff vs arterial blood pressure in shock, permissive hypotension, PROPPR, PAMPer, RePHILL, CRASH-2 timing, calcium and ITACTIC Teaching reasoning (not a quoted guideline): Why the textbook shock classes mislead The ATLS table links estimated blood loss to heart rate, blood pressure and conscious level in four neat classes. Registry data show that real patients rarely fit those boxes: A retrospective analysis of data derived from the TraumaRegister DGU(®) indicated that only 9.3% of all trauma patients could be allocated into one of the ATLS(®) shock classes when a combination of the three vital signs heart rate, systolic blood pressure and Glasgow Coma Scale was assessed. compensation hides blood loss. Sympathetic vasoconstriction and tachycardia hold systolic pressure up until late, so a "normal" blood pressure does not exclude major bleeding. Older patients, beta-blocked patients and athletes may not become tachycardic. Treat the trend and the mechanism, not a single number. Shock index: a bedside ratio Shock index (SI) is heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure. The German trauma registry study grouped 21,853 patients as follows: group I, SI <0.6; group II, SI ≥0.6 to <1.0; group III, SI ≥1.0 to <1.4; and group IV, SI ≥1.4 Worsening of SI was associated with increasing injury severity scores from 19.3 (± 12) in group I to 37.3 (± 16.8) in group IV, while mortality increased from 10.9% to 39.8%. Of patients, 31% in group III and 57% in group IV required ≥10 blood units until ICU admission. Lactate and base deficit We recommend blood lactate as a sensitive test to estimate and monitor the extent of bleeding and tissue hypoperfusion; in the absence of lactate measurements, base deficit may represent a suitable alternative (Grade 1B). The lethal triad Damage control resuscitation is not one technique, but, rather, a group of strategies which address the lethal triad of coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia. each part worsens the others. Hypoperfusion produces lactic acidosis; acidosis and cold slow the clotting enzymes; ongoing bleeding deepens the shock. Warming, early blood products and early bleeding control break the cycle together. The trauma page covers the lethal triad in more detail 120 ÷ 100 = 1.2, which is group III (SI ≥1.0 to <1.4). In the registry, 31% of group III patients needed 10 or more blood units before ICU admission, even though the systolic pressure is still 100 mmHg. (Arithmetic; teaching reasoning, not a patient-specific prediction.) Cuffs over-read in shock Automated cuffs work out pressure from oscillations in the cuff. In low-flow, vasoconstricted states those oscillations are small and the reading becomes unreliable. A study comparing cuff and arterial line readings in 30 hypotensive emergency patients found: Oscillometric MAP was markedly higher than invasive MAP with a mean of the differences of 13 ± 15 mmHg (oscillometric-invasive), 95% limits of agreement - 16 to 41 mmHg, percentage error was 76%. In 64% of readings, values obtained by the upper arm cuff were not able to detect hypotension. Oscillometric blood pressure measurement is not able to reliably detect hypotension in emergency patients. Therefore, direct measurement of blood pressure should be established as soon as possible in patients suffering from shock. the study was small (75 paired readings) and done in the emergency department, so the size of the error should not be applied to every patient. The direction matters most: a cuff can look reassuring while the true pressure is dangerously low. An arterial line also gives beat-to-beat readings during induction and blood sampling, but placing one must not delay bleeding control. Which number to target In the initial phase following trauma, we recommend the use of a restricted volume replacement strategy with a target systolic blood pressure of 80–90 mmHg (mean arterial pressure 50–60 mmHg) until major bleeding has been stopped without clinical evidence of brain injury (Grade 1B). In patients with severe TBI (GCS ≤ 8), we recommend that a mean arterial pressure ≥ 80 mmHg be maintained (Grade 1C) If a restricted volume replacement strategy does not achieve the target blood pressure, we recommend the administration of noradrenaline in addition to fluids to maintain target arterial pressure (Grade 1C). UK guidance gives no number in hospital. NICE NG39 asks for a restrictive approach while bleeding continues: For patients with active bleeding use a restrictive approach to volume resuscitation until definitive early control of bleeding has been achieved. if haemorrhagic shock is the dominant condition, continue restrictive volume resuscitation or if traumatic brain injury is the dominant condition, use a less restrictive volume resuscitation approach to maintain cerebral perfusion. MAP is the pressure that drives flow to organs and is what an arterial line measures most accurately, while systolic pressure is easier to estimate by palpation in the field. Permissive hypotension buys time to reach theatre or interventional radiology; it is not a treatment in itself. For pulse and bolus details, see the trauma lesson on fluid boluses and blood pressure targets In the Meidert study, cuff MAP was on average 13 mmHg higher than the arterial line, and 64% of cuff readings missed hypotension. A cuff MAP of 68 could hide a true MAP near 55. (Arithmetic from the mean difference; teaching reasoning, not a correction factor for an individual.) Ratios in hospital PROPPR compared 1:1:1 with 1:1:2 plasma, platelets and red cells. The trauma page explains the NICE 1:1 recommendation in its transfusion ratios lesson ; the key numbers are: No significant differences were detected in mortality at 24 hours (12.7% in 1:1:1 group vs 17.0% in 1:1:2 group; difference, -4.2% [95% CI, -9.6% to 1.1%]; P = .12) or at 30 days (22.4% vs 26.1%, respectively; difference, -3.7% [95% CI, -10.2% to 2.7%]; P = .26). In the initial management of patients with expected massive haemorrhage, we recommend one of the two following strategies: Fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate and pRBC (Grade 1C) FFP or pathogen-inactivated FFP in a FFP/pRBC ratio of at least 1:2 as needed (Grade 1C) In addition, we suggest a high platelet/pRBC ratio (Grade 2B). If erythrocyte transfusion is necessary, we recommend a target haemoglobin of 70–90 g/L (Grade 1C). Blood before hospital: two trials, two answers Mortality at 30 days was significantly lower in the plasma group than in the standard-care group (23.2% vs. 33.0%; difference, -9.8 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -18.6 to -1.0%; P=0.03). The composite primary outcome occurred in 128 (64%) of 199 participants randomly assigned to PRBC-LyoPlas and 136 (65%) of 210 randomly assigned to 0·9% sodium chloride (adjusted risk difference -0·025% [95% CI -9·0 to 9·0], p=0·996). PAMPer (US air ambulance, thawed plasma) found a mortality benefit; RePHILL (UK, red cells plus freeze-dried plasma vs saline) found no benefit on its composite outcome of death or poor lactate clearance. The trials differed in setting, transport time, product and outcome, so neither settles the question alone. UK exams expect you to know both. Tranexamic acid: timing is everything Early treatment (≤1 h from injury) significantly reduced the risk of death due to bleeding (198/3747 [5.3%] events in tranexamic acid group vs 286/3704 [7.7%] in placebo group; relative risk [RR] 0.68, 95% CI 0.57-0.82; p<0.0001). Treatment given after 3 h seemed to increase the risk of death due to bleeding (144/3272 [4.4%] vs 103/3362 [3.1%]; RR 1.44, 1.12-1.84; p=0.004). Calcium and test-guided therapy We recommend that ionised calcium levels be monitored and maintained within the normal range following major trauma and especially during massive transfusion (Grade 1C). We recommend the administration of calcium chloride to correct hypocalcaemia (Grade 1C). At 24 h, there was no difference in the proportion of patients who were alive and free of massive transfusion (VHA: 67%, CCT: 64%, OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.76-1.73). 28-day mortality was not different overall (VHA: 25%, CCT: 28%, OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.54-1.31) citrate in stored blood binds calcium, so ionised calcium falls during rapid transfusion and weakens clotting and heart contraction. ITACTIC found that adding viscoelastic tests (ROTEM/TEG) to a ratio-based protocol did not change overall outcomes, so these tests guide product choice rather than replace an early fixed-ratio start. After 3 hours, death due to bleeding was 4.4% with tranexamic acid vs 3.1% with placebo (RR 1.44): it seemed to increase risk. Before 1 hour, risk fell from 7.7% to 5.3%. Give it as early as possible; late first doses may harm. 7.7% − 5.3% = 2.4 per 100, so about 1 for every 42 treated. (Arithmetic from the quoted figures; not a quoted number needed to treat.) Shock index: a bedside ratio

Shock index (SI) is heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure. The German trauma registry study grouped 21,853 patients as follows:

group I, SI <0.6; group II, SI ≥0.6 to <1.0; group III, SI ≥1.0 to <1.4; and group IV, SI ≥1.4

120 ÷ 100 = 1.2, which is group III (SI ≥1.0 to <1.4). In the registry, 31% of group III patients needed 10 or more blood units before ICU admission, even though the systolic pressure is still 100 mmHg. (Arithmetic; teaching reasoning, not a patient-specific prediction.)

After 3 hours, death due to bleeding was 4.4% with tranexamic acid vs 3.1% with placebo (RR 1.44): it seemed to increase risk. Before 1 hour, risk fell from 7.7% to 5.3%. Give it as early as possible; late first doses may harm.

# Peritonitis & Intra-abdominal Sepsis Primary, secondary and tertiary peritonitis, WSES 2017, SIS–IDSA, source control, emergency laparotomy preparation and STOP-IT antibiotic duration Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum. In ICU it is almost always : a hole or dead bowel lets gut contents into the abdomen (perforated ulcer or diverticulum, appendicitis, ischaemic bowel, anastomotic leak). (spontaneous bacterial) peritonitis occurs in ascites without a hole and is treated with antibiotics alone. peritonitis persists or returns after apparently adequate source control, often with resistant organisms or fungi, and carries a high mortality. The cornerstones of effective treatment of IAIs are early recognition, adequate source control, and appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Prompt resuscitation of patients with ongoing sepsis is of utmost important. Recognition is harder in ICU A sedated, ventilated patient cannot report pain or guard. Clues are a rising lactate or vasopressor need without another cause, new feed intolerance, ileus, distension, rising intra-abdominal pressure, abnormal drain fluid, and a raised CRP after the expected post-operative peak (often day 3–5 for an anastomotic leak). CT with contrast is the usual test; in an unstable patient, bedside ultrasound or a decision to go straight to theatre may be needed. Source control comes first

Antibiotics cannot sterilise a leaking bowel. Source control means draining pus, closing or removing the leaking bowel and washing out contamination — by surgery or, for a contained abscess, by radiological drainage. The sooner it happens in septic shock, the better; most guidance aims for within hours of diagnosis once the patient is resuscitated enough to go. In very frail patients, the honest discussion may be about whether surgery is in their interests at all.

How long should antibiotics run? STOP-IT

STOP-IT randomised 518 patients with complicated intra-abdominal infection and adequate source control to a fixed course of about 4 days or to treatment until 2 days after fever, white count and ileus had resolved.

Surgical-site infection, recurrent intraabdominal infection, or death occurred in 56 of 257 patients in the experimental group (21.8%), as compared with 58 of 260 patients in the control group (22.3%) The median duration of antibiotic therapy was 4.0 days (interquartile range, 4.0 to 5.0) in the experimental group, as compared with 8.0 days (interquartile range, 5.0 to 10.0) in the control group

Half the antibiotics gave the same outcome. The result only applies once the source is controlled; most patients were not in septic shock, so ICU teams still review each patient rather than stopping automatically.

Teaching tool: STOP-IT course end date

After theatre in ICU

  • Wean vasopressors as perfusion improves; avoid a large positive fluid balance, which worsens bowel oedema and intra-abdominal pressure. See Abdominal Compartment Syndrome.
  • Start enteral feeding early when the bowel is in continuity and the patient is stable.
  • If the patient fails to improve by 48–72 hours, look again for a persisting source: CT, drain fluid, return to theatre.
  • Send peritoneal fluid for culture and narrow antibiotics to the results.

Worked case (fictional)

A 68-year-old woman, day 4 after anterior resection, becomes confused with HR 120, MAP 58 and lactate 4.1. CT shows free gas and fluid around the anastomosis. Cultures are taken and piperacillin–tazobactam given within the hour. Two 500 mL boluses improve capillary refill only briefly, so noradrenaline starts. After a rapid-sequence induction the surgeons take down the anastomosis and form a stoma. Source control is on 30 October; a 4-day course would end around 3 November, and her antibiotics are stopped then after review because she has improved.

These are teaching notes, not an antibiotic or surgical protocol.

# Fluid Balance and Tonicity Isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic fluids, NICE resuscitation and maintenance, hospital-acquired hyponatraemia and 3% saline Teaching reasoning (not a quoted guideline): Osmolarity in the bag versus tonicity in the patient Osmolarity counts every dissolved particle. Tonicity counts only the particles that cannot freely cross cell membranes, so it decides whether water moves into or out of cells. Sodium and chloride stay mainly outside cells and are "effective" osmoles. Glucose behaves the same way only until it enters cells and is metabolised; urea crosses membranes and adds osmolality without adding tonicity. a fluid is best classified by what it does to plasma sodium and cell volume after infusion, not only by the osmolarity printed on the bag. Glucose 5% is close to plasma osmolarity in the bag, but once the glucose is taken up it delivers free water and behaves as a hypotonic fluid. This is why glucose-containing maintenance fluids can lower plasma sodium. Three working groups Classification by effective tonicity (teaching synthesis) Where the water goes Main use 0.9% sodium chloride; balanced crystalloids Stays outside cells, distributing across plasma and interstitium Resuscitation and replacement Glucose 5%; 0.18% sodium chloride in 4% glucose Free water moves into cells as well Water replacement and some adult maintenance regimens 3% sodium chloride Draws water out of cells, including brain cells Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia; osmotic therapy under specialist protocols Arithmetic, not a quotation: 0.9% sodium chloride is 9 g/L. Dividing by the molar mass of sodium chloride (58.44 g/mol) gives about 154 mmol/L each of sodium and chloride, which is why saline carries more chloride than plasma and can cause the hyperchloraemic acidosis discussed in the saline vs balanced fluids lesson Because glucose is metabolised after infusion, leaving free water that spreads into cells. Its effect on plasma sodium is that of water, even though its bag osmolarity is near plasma. Resuscitation uses sodium-rich crystalloid NICE recommends that adult resuscitation fluid falls in a narrow sodium band and is given as a defined, reassessed bolus: "If patients need IV fluid resuscitation, use crystalloids that contain sodium in the range 130 to 154 mmol/l, with a bolus of 500 ml over less than 15 minutes." For children and young people, NICE gives a weight-based bolus and requires glucose-free fluid: "use glucose‑free crystalloids that contain sodium in the range 131–154 mmol/litre, with a bolus of 10 ml/kg over less than 10 minutes." Saline or balanced crystalloid? Both sit inside the NICE sodium band. The difference is chloride. In SMART (15,802 adults), a major adverse kidney event within 30 days occurred in 14.3% with balanced fluid and 15.4% with saline; in the blinded multicentre PLUS trial (5,037 patients), 90-day death was 21.8% v 22.0%. The full trial discussion lives in the Saline, Balanced Fluids and Outcome lesson on Acid-Base Disorders isotonic fluid is not "free" fluid. Each bolus should answer a clinical question (is perfusion improving?), and continued boluses without response add oedema rather than benefit. The NICE "500 ml over less than 15 minutes" wording sets a unit for reassessment, not a total volume. 10 ml/kg × 20 kg = 200 ml of glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 131–154 mmol/litre, over less than 10 minutes, then reassess. Adult maintenance: small amounts of sodium, some glucose NICE sets the starting adult maintenance requirement as: "25 to 30 ml/kg/day of water and approximately 1 mmol/kg/day of potassium, sodium and chloride and approximately 50 to 100 g/day of glucose to limit starvation ketosis." That sodium content is low relative to the water, so a typical adult maintenance regimen is hypotonic. NICE names one such regimen and attaches a hyponatraemia warning to it: "consider using 25 to 30 ml/kg/day sodium chloride 0.18% in 4% glucose with 27 mmol/l potassium on day 1 (there are other regimens to achieve this). Prescribing more than 2.5 litres per day increases the risk of hyponatraemia." Children: isotonic maintenance The paediatric guideline takes a different starting position: "If children and young people need IV fluids for routine maintenance, initially use isotonic crystalloids that contain sodium in the range 131 to 154 mmol/litre." hospitalised patients often have non-osmotic antidiuretic hormone release (pain, nausea, surgery, stress), so they cannot excrete the free water in hypotonic fluid. Children have less brain space for swelling, which is why NICE uses isotonic maintenance for them. In adults, hypotonic regimens remain acceptable within limits, but plasma sodium must be monitored. 25–30 ml/kg/day × 70 kg = 1,750–2,100 ml/day , with roughly 70 mmol each of sodium, potassium and chloride. This stays below the 2.5 litres per day that NICE links to higher hyponatraemia risk. 3% saline for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia Hypertonic saline raises plasma tonicity, drawing water out of swollen brain cells. The European guideline gives a bolus-based protocol with explicit limits on the rate of rise: "We recommend prompt i.v. infusion of 150 ml 3% hypertonic saline over 20 min. We suggest checking the serum sodium concentration after 20 min while repeating an infusion of 150 ml 3% hypertonic saline. We suggest aiming for a 5 mmol/l per 24-h increase in serum sodium concentration. We suggest limiting the increase in serum sodium concentration to 10 mmol/l during the first 24 h and 8 mmol/l during every 24 h thereafter." Bolus versus continuous infusion SALSA randomised 178 patients with symptomatic hyponatraemia to rapid intermittent boluses or slow continuous infusion of hypertonic saline: "Overcorrection occurred in 15 of 87 (17.2%) and 22 of 91 (24.2%) patients in the RIB and SCI groups, respectively (absolute risk difference, -6.9% [95% CI, -18.8% to 4.9%]; P = .26)." Overcorrection was not significantly different, but fewer bolus-group patients needed treatment to lower sodium again (41.4% v 57.1%). the danger of hypertonic saline is speed, not the fluid itself. Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination, so sodium is rechecked frequently and the 24-hour limit is treated as a ceiling. Hypertonic saline is given under a local protocol with senior and usually critical care involvement; this page does not set patient-specific orders. 8 mmol/L already. The guideline limit is 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h, so only about 2 mmol/L remain for the next 12 hours; active hypertonic treatment would normally stop and sodium be monitored closely. # Acute Kidney Injury & RRT KDIGO staging, CRRT, IHD, indications for renal replacement therapy Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) is the older term for contrast-induced acute kidney injury (CI-AKI). Modern teaching must distinguish contrast-associated AKI (CA-AKI) — AKI after contrast, whatever its cause — from , the subset actually caused by contrast. A creatinine rise after a scan does not prove nephrotoxicity. In ICU, sepsis, shock, venous congestion, surgery, other drugs and obstruction commonly coexist. This distinction prevents an essential diagnostic scan being withheld for an exaggerated risk RCR–RCEM joint advisory: emergency contrast CT must not be delayed Royal College of Radiologists and Royal College of Emergency Medicine joint advisory statement (5 June 2023) addresses emergency CT with intravenous iodinated contrast . An emergency means potential risk to life or limb, or delay to immediate definitive treatment with potentially adverse consequences. The requesting clinician decides whether the scan is an emergency; emergency departments should involve senior clinical decision makers and use iRefer to select appropriate imaging Proceed without waiting for renal-function blood results: measurement of renal function is not a prerequisite for an emergency scan. Do not delay because of pre-existing renal disease, diabetes or metformin use. These can inform ongoing care, but are not reasons to hold up emergency diagnostic imaging Age alone must not delay scanning: the statement says age is not an independent risk factor for CI-AKI. Do not wait for prehydration: IV fluid administration is not a prerequisite. The statement describes weak evidence for routine precontrast fluids in emergencies and highlights potential harm from prehydration, particularly in older patients and those with heart failure How to apply this in ICU: obtain time-critical diagnostic imaging while resuscitation, medication review and renal monitoring proceed as clinically indicated. “Do not delay” does not mean “no renal risk”, that fluids are never needed, or that metformin must always be continued during AKI or shock. This emergency IV-CT advisory does not replace elective-imaging or first-pass arterial protocols; retain the named guideline distinctions and post-scan management below. Definition, recognition and causality Use the KDIGO criteria already described above to diagnose and stage AKI: creatinine rise ≥26.5 µmol/L within 48 hours, ≥1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. ESUR uses a post-contrast surveillance window of 48–72 hours for its creatinine-based CA-AKI definition. These windows serve different purposes; neither demonstrates that contrast was the cause. Compare with a reliable pre-illness baseline and examine the entire trajectory, including deterioration before imaging Creatinine is a delayed functional marker, affected by muscle mass, fluid dilution and changing production. Calculated eGFR assumes steady-state creatinine and can be misleading during evolving AKI: a displayed eGFR above a threshold is not reassuring if creatinine is rapidly rising. Oliguria may appear earlier. No routinely available biomarker, urinary cast or fractional-excretion result uniquely identifies CI-AKI. The usual described creatinine course begins within 24 hours, peaks within about 4 days and often returns towards baseline in 7–10 days; severe or persistent AKI requires reassessment rather than an assumption of inevitable recovery Pathophysiology: plausible mechanisms, not proof in an individual patient Medullary oxygen supply–demand mismatch. The outer medulla has relatively limited oxygen availability despite energy-intensive tubular sodium transport. Proposed contrast-related vasoconstriction, disturbed endothelial signalling and impaired microcirculation can reduce oxygen delivery; hypovolaemia, low cardiac output and shock compound this vulnerability. Direct tubular injury. Experimental work describes oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and epithelial cell injury from chemotoxic effects. Reactive oxygen species can impair nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilation, coupling cellular injury to hypoxia. Much mechanistic evidence is experimental; it cannot establish the attributable incidence with modern intravenous agents. Physical properties and tubular exposure. Osmotic effects and increased viscosity during tubular concentration may alter flow and prolong epithelial exposure, especially with reduced filtration and low tubular flow. Osmolality and viscosity are different properties: iso-osmolar does not automatically mean least nephrotoxic. ACR states that the exact pathophysiology remains incompletely understood. These mechanisms explain biological plausibility, not why every post-scan creatinine rise should be labelled CIN. Cholesterol embolisation after arterial instrumentation is a separate vascular injury, not direct contrast toxicity How large is the risk with contemporary contrast? Historical uncontrolled angiography series mixed contrast exposure with haemodynamic instability, arterial instrumentation and background AKI. Controlled CT studies and propensity matching suggest that the causal risk of modern intravenous iodinated contrast is much smaller than these series implied. ACR–NKF estimates CI-AKI risk at approximately 0% with stable eGFR ≥45, 0–2% at 30–44, and 0–17% below 30 mL/min/1.73 m². The wide lowest-eGFR range reflects uncertain observational evidence, not a validated ICU bedside prediction. CA-AKI is more common because it includes unrelated injuries Selection bias remains important: clinicians may avoid contrast in the sickest patients, and matching cannot remove unmeasured confounding. A 2022 meta-analysis of 21 propensity-matched CT cohorts found no evidence of increased AKI, dialysis or mortality with eGFR ≥45, while urging caution in eGFR ≤30 and hypertension. Neither this result nor stable elective-patient trials proves absence of harm in septic shock, active AKI or advanced CKD Newer ICU evidence (2025): Ferguson and DuSablon’s retrospective propensity-matched cohort of critically ill patients with severe AKI found similar renal recovery over 120 hours, progressive AKI and later RRT use with low-osmolar IV contrast versus unenhanced CT. This is reassurance from observational data, not randomized proof of safety; an eGFR calculated during AKI is not interchangeable with stable stage-4 CKD Important counterweight (2026): Nyman and colleagues’ critical review of propensity-adjusted studies, searching through December 2024, found an association with increased AKI and dialysis in emergency/inpatient CKD cohorts, particularly GFR <30. The weighted absolute increases were 4.0 percentage points for AKI and 1.8 for dialysis in that stratum. These are review-level observational associations, not causal patient-specific probabilities. Selection bias and recovery of acute renal dysfunction can mask risk. The defensible conclusion is neither “contrast always causes AKI” nor “contrast never harms kidneys” Evidence status, checked 21 October 2026: the ACR manual is the 2026 edition, ESUR the 2025 edition and NICE NG148 was updated in October 2024 (some hydration recommendations remain from 2019). Sympathetic activation, stress hormones (cortisol, catecholamines, glucagon). Insulin resistance with high endogenous glucose production. Trophic feeds only — overfeeding is harmful.

Flow / Catabolic (48 h – weeks)

Hypermetabolism, muscle wasting (up to 1 kg/day in the first week). Negative nitrogen balance. Gradual increase to target calories. Recovery phase: anabolism, rehabilitation.

Why the ebb/flow distinction changes feeding: in the ebb phase, endogenous glucose production of 500–1400 kcal/day cannot be suppressed by exogenous feed, so early full-calorie delivery simply adds to total energy load and produces hyperglycaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, CO₂ retention and suppression of autophagy — the cellular clearance mechanism thought to protect mitochondrial function during acute illness. This is the mechanistic explanation for the harm of early aggressive feeding in EPaNIC, and for hypocaloric (≤ 70% of measured requirement) early nutrition with protein escalated gradually. In the flow phase the problem reverses: anabolic resistance means muscle protein synthesis responds poorly to amino acid delivery while inflammation, immobility and insulin resistance persist, so protein alone cannot prevent wasting — it must be paired with early mobilisation, and much of the recovery of muscle mass and function happens only in the post-ICU rehabilitation phase, when appetite is often poor and intake must be actively supported.     Essential co-factor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase; deficiency blocks aerobic entry of pyruvate into the Krebs cycle, forcing anaerobic metabolism and causing a lactic acidosis. # Endocrine Emergencies in ICU
DKA, HHS, thyroid storm, adrenal (Addisonian) crisis, myxoedema coma, phaeochromocytoma crisis, pituitary apoplexy


DKA: treat insulin deficiency, not just the glucose
Insulin stops lipolysis and hepatic ketone production. A falling glucose does not prove that ketoacidosis has resolved: continue insulin with glucose supplementation when needed, and continue the usual long-acting basal insulin. Use blood β-hydroxybutyrate rather than urine ketones to follow recovery; urine ketones can remain positive during conversion of β-hydroxybutyrate to acetoacetate. Confirm the diagnosis and look for infection, insulin omission, infarction, pregnancy or a drug precipitant while treatment proceeds.
Potassium is a separate safety decision.
Osmotic diuresis depletes total-body potassium even when the admission result is high. Insulin moves potassium intracellularly. The JBDS replacement table specifies no potassium above 5.5 mmol/L, 40 mmol/L of replacement fluid at 3.5–5.5 mmol/L, and senior review with additional replacement below 3.5 mmol/L. The treatment target is 4.0–5.5 mmol/L: a replacement threshold is not the same as the desired range. Severe hypokalaemia requires urgent monitored correction and a senior insulin plan, not automatic use of a standard bag or an unsupervised concentrated infusion. Renal failure and oliguria also change replacement safety.
An inadequate biochemical response is a troubleshooting problem.
Track hourly glucose and blood ketones; a ketone fall of 0.5 mmol/L/h, bicarbonate rise of 3 mmol/L/h or glucose fall of 3 mmol/L/h are JBDS response targets. Before increasing insulin, inspect the prescription, concentration, pump, cannula and connections; reassess perfusion and the precipitant. Add 10% glucose when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L; consider reducing insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h under the JBDS pathway to reduce hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia while maintaining ketone clearance.
Resolution is ketones <0.6 mmol/L and venous pH >7.3.
Do not require bicarbonate normalisation at this stage: chloride-rich fluid can leave a non-ketotic acidosis. Conversely, normal glucose with persistent ketones is not recovery. Once resolved and able to eat, arrange subcutaneous insulin with the prescribed overlap before stopping IV insulin; if not eating, a variable-rate regimen may be needed. The diabetes team should address the cause, injection technique, sick-day rules and access to insulin before discharge.
HHS: follow osmolality and perfusion together
Use measured sodium in calculated osmolality: 2 × sodium + glucose + urea, with all concentrations in mmol/L. As glucose falls, water moves back into cells and measured sodium may rise.
That rise alone is not a reason to switch to hypotonic fluid.
Assess the osmolality trajectory, fluid balance and clinical perfusion. JBDS aims for an osmolality fall of 3–8 mOsm/kg/h, glucose fall no faster than 5 mmol/L/h and sodium fall no faster than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours. Consider 0.45% sodium chloride only if osmolality is not declining despite adequate replacement with 0.9% sodium chloride and positive fluid balance.
In HHS without significant ketosis, start with isotonic fluid and reassessment, adapting the rate for heart failure, renal disease and frailty. Start insulin at 0.05 units/kg/h once osmolality stops falling with fluid replacement alone; earlier insulin can worsen circulatory collapse and osmotic shifts. Significant ketonaemia changes the pathway: insulin then starts alongside IV fluids, and mixed DKA/HHS with acidosis needs the DKA insulin regimen rather than a blanket delayed-insulin rule. Start 5% or 10% glucose once blood glucose is below 14 mmol/L, alongside the insulin infusion. Use prophylactic anticoagulation unless contraindicated, not therapeutic anticoagulation merely because the HHS is severe.
HHS recovery is holistic: osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg, correction of hypovolaemia with urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/h, glucose below 15 mmol/L and cognition back to the premorbid state. Persistent confusion requires reassessment for stroke, infection, medication effects or another diagnosis, rather than assuming that normalising glucose has completed treatment.
Learning check: sodium rises while glucose falls in HHS. Must the fluid change?
No. Review calculated osmolality, volume replacement and perfusion. A rising sodium is expected as hyperglycaemia corrects. The indication for 0.45% saline is failure of osmolality to decline despite adequate isotonic replacement, not sodium alone. Do not accelerate correction simply to normalise a single number.
Thyroid storm: a clinical syndrome, not a hormone cutoff
Storm is systemic decompensation in a thyrotoxic patient: fever, arrhythmia or heart failure, central nervous system disturbance and gastrointestinal/hepatic dysfunction. Thyroid hormone concentrations alone do not distinguish storm from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis. Sepsis can both precipitate storm and mimic it, so investigate and treat both when appropriate. A Burch–Wartofsky score supports, but does not replace, judgement: ATA recommends aggressive treatment at a score of at least 45; scores of 25–44 require clinical assessment rather than automatic reassurance or diagnosis.
Treat several mechanisms in parallel.
Thionamides block synthesis, iodide blocks release, corticosteroids reduce peripheral conversion and cover adrenal insufficiency, and cooling, respiratory support and treatment of the trigger address organ failure. Under the ATA regimen, iodide follows the thionamide by at least one hour. Do not wait for a β-blocker to work before beginning the other treatments. PTU also reduces conversion of T4 to T3; methimazole is an alternative, and liver injury, route availability and specialist advice affect the choice.
Tachycardia is not always safe to suppress immediately.
Assess perfusion and cardiac function. In low-output failure or shock, an abrupt reduction in sympathetic support can cause collapse. If β-blockade is appropriate, titrate with close monitoring; a short-acting agent permits reassessment but is not harmless. Propranolol at high doses reduces T4-to-T3 conversion; esmolol should not be credited with the same conversion effect. Persistent organ failure despite treatment warrants joint endocrine/ICU review for rescue measures, rather than simply escalating a long-acting β-blocker.
Myxoedema coma: support breathing and replace cortisol first
Profound hypothyroidism impairs ventilatory drive, cardiac output and water excretion; coma is not required for the diagnosis. Hypothermia can conceal infection. Protect ventilation, assess glucose and sodium, seek the precipitant and give empiric IV glucocorticoid coverage before thyroid hormone. A low or normal TSH does not exclude central hypothyroidism.
ATA recommends IV levothyroxine initially: a loading dose of 200–400 micrograms, reduced for smaller or older patients and those with coronary disease or arrhythmia. Subsequent replacement is weight based, with the IV dose reduced to 75% of the equivalent oral dose. IV liothyronine may be added selectively, but high doses should be avoided; this is not an interchangeable fixed-dose T3-or-T4 recipe. Follow mental state, cardiac and pulmonary function as well as thyroid tests. The recommendations are strong but supported by low-quality evidence because this emergency is rare.
Learning check: why not reflexively give propranolol to a shocked patient with storm?
The tachycardia may be sustaining output in severe cardiac dysfunction. Assess haemodynamics and cardiac function, obtain senior input and titrate only when appropriate. Begin the other storm treatments and organ support without waiting for rate control.
Adrenal crisis: distinguish cortisol from aldosterone loss
Cortisol deficiency impairs vascular responsiveness and glucose production and increases vasopressin-mediated water retention. Both primary and secondary insufficiency can cause shock, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia. Primary adrenal failure additionally loses aldosterone and can produce salt wasting and hyperkalaemia. In glucocorticoid-induced or pituitary insufficiency, aldosterone is usually preserved: absence of hyperkalaemia does not exclude crisis, and its presence needs assessment for renal failure or another cause.
If feasible, take cortisol and ACTH before treatment, but do not wait for results or a stimulation test. Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately, followed by 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg every six hours, alongside isotonic fluid resuscitation and correction of hypoglycaemia. Reassess for fluid overload in older patients or renal impairment. Treat infection, missed replacement or another trigger; ongoing hypotension also requires evaluation for bleeding, cardiogenic shock and other causes.
High-dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity during crisis. Introduce fludrocortisone when hydrocortisone falls below 50 mg/day
only in primary adrenal insufficiency
; it is not routinely needed in steroid-induced or pituitary disease. Reduce stress replacement with clinical recovery under endocrine advice, rather than applying a universal daily-halving rule. Before discharge, arrange sick-day advice, a steroid emergency card, an emergency injection kit where indicated and a plan for vomiting or inability to take oral treatment.
Pituitary apoplexy: endocrine resuscitation and visual assessment
Sudden severe headache with visual impairment, ophthalmoplegia or altered consciousness should raise suspicion of haemorrhage or infarction in a pituitary tumour, even without a previous diagnosis. Exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage and meningitis where appropriate. MRI is the investigation of choice; a reassuring routine CT does not rule out apoplexy. Assess visual acuity and fields, haemodynamics and electrolytes while contacting endocrine and neurosurgical teams.
The emergency guidance identifies haemodynamic instability, altered consciousness, reduced visual acuity or severe visual field defects as indications for empiric steroids. Take endocrine samples if doing so does not delay resuscitation. Urgent referral is not the same as automatic surgery: severe or persistent visual deficits and deteriorating consciousness support decompression after medical stabilisation, while selected stable patients can be managed conservatively with close specialist review. Replace deficient cortisol before thyroxine, and monitor urine output and sodium for evolving water-balance disorders.
Learning check: does a normal potassium exclude steroid-induced adrenal crisis?
No. Aldosterone is usually preserved in secondary insufficiency. Cortisol deficiency alone can produce life-threatening shock, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia. Treat promptly when suspected; fludrocortisone is not routinely required for this form of insufficiency.
SGLT2 inhibitors: glucose can conceal ketoacidosis
Glycosuria lowers glucose while fasting, illness and relative insulin deficiency promote ketogenesis. An unwell patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor needs blood ketones and a blood gas even with near-normal glucose. Do not attribute a high-anion-gap acidosis to fasting without evaluating DKA, lactate, renal failure and other causes. Treat confirmed ketoacidosis with insulin plus appropriate glucose, electrolyte replacement and resuscitation; a normal glucose is not a reason to stop ketone-clearing insulin.
MHRA's March 2020 advice is to interrupt SGLT2 treatment during hospitalisation for major surgery or acute serious illness, monitor blood rather than urine ketones, and restart only when ketones are normal and the patient's condition is stable.
That notice does not specify a three-day elective cessation interval.
Use the current local perioperative pathway for elective timing; do not delay life-saving surgery merely to complete a drug-free interval. Following an episode of DKA, restarting needs diabetes-specialist review of the cause and recurrence risk.
A safe handover identifies the last SGLT2 dose, usual basal insulin and steroid replacement, ketone/pH/potassium trends, fluid balance and the next scheduled tests. Hormone replacement and insulin are time-critical medicines: an omitted dose during a move to theatre or ICU can undo initial treatment. Clinical deterioration should trigger reassessment of both the endocrine diagnosis and coexisting infection, bleeding or cardiac disease.
Learning check: glucose is 8.5 mmol/L, ketones 4.2 and pH 7.18 on empagliflozin. Is DKA excluded?
No. This is compatible with euglycaemic DKA. Stop the drug, begin the DKA pathway with glucose support as required, assess potassium and volume status, and seek diabetes/critical-care input. Track ketones and pH rather than glucose alone.

Giving Hypertonic Saline: Bolus or Infusion? (SALSA)
SALSA randomised 178 adults with symptomatic hyponatraemia (mean sodium 118.2 mmol/L, mean age 73) to rapid intermittent boluses or a slow continuous infusion of hypertonic saline.
Overcorrection (primary outcome):
17.2% with boluses vs 24.2% with infusion. The difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.26).
Re-lowering treatment
was needed less often with boluses (41.4% vs 57.1%; number needed to treat 6.3), and more bolus patients reached the target rise within 1 hour (32.2% vs 17.6%).
Symptoms and overall sodium rise
did not differ between groups.
Practice point:
both methods worked, and about one patient in five overcorrected either way. Frequent sodium checks and a plan to re-lower are essential whichever method is chosen.
Learning check: did SALSA show that boluses cause less overcorrection?
No. Overcorrection was 17.2% vs 24.2%, which was not significant. Boluses did reduce the need for re-lowering treatment.
Preparing for Phaeochromocytoma Surgery: Guideline and PRESCRIPT
initial testing should be plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines; CT is suggested for first imaging.
every patient with a functional tumour should have preoperative blockade, with a high-sodium diet and fluid intake to prevent hypotension after removal.
minimally invasive adrenalectomy for most phaeochromocytomas; open resection for most paragangliomas.
Which α-blocker? PRESCRIPT:
134 patients in 9 Dutch centres were randomised to phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin for 2–3 weeks before surgery. Time outside blood pressure targets (SBP >160 or MAP <60 mmHg) did not differ: 11.1% vs 12.2% (P = .75).
Secondary results:
phenoxybenzamine gave a lower haemodynamic instability score (38.0 vs 50.0, P = .02). 30-day cardiovascular complications were 8.8% vs 6.9% (P = .68), with no deaths. Whether the steadier course improves outcome could not be established.
Anaesthetic point:
expect surges on induction and tumour handling, and hypotension after the veins are tied. Both α-blockers are reasonable; the trial was open-label and too small to compare complications.
Learning check: in PRESCRIPT, did phenoxybenzamine reduce time outside blood pressure targets compared with doxazosin?
No — 11.1% vs 12.2% (P = .75). It did lower the instability score, a secondary measure.
Phaeochromocytoma Crisis: Not Only Hypertension
Evidence base:
crisis is an endocrine emergency with significant mortality, and there is little published guidance; this clinical practice update draws on published cases and proposes a classification.
it is strongly associated with surviving a crisis.
for sustained hypotension, mechanical circulatory support such as an intra-aortic balloon pump or ECMO is strongly recommended. Do not assume the crisis will look like hypertension.
Timing of surgery:
defer it until the patient is medically stable; emergency adrenalectomy in a crisis is not the default.
this is a review of case reports and series, not trials, so the associations may reflect who was well enough to be treated.
Learning check: a patient in phaeochromocytoma crisis has sustained hypotension despite treatment. What does the review strongly recommend?
Mechanical circulatory support (e.g. intra-aortic balloon pump or ECMO), with surgery deferred until medical stabilisation.
Which Fluid in DKA? Balanced Crystalloid vs Saline
Saline can cause hyperchloraemic acidosis, which can slow the fall in acidosis that defines DKA recovery. This analysis took the 172 adults with DKA from two Nashville cluster-randomised trials (SALT-ED and SMART): 94 received balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's-type or Plasma-Lyte) and 78 saline.
median time to DKA resolution was 13.0 h with balanced crystalloid vs 16.9 h with saline (adjusted HR 1.68, 95% CI 1.18–2.38).
the insulin infusion was stopped sooner — median 9.8 h vs 13.4 h (adjusted HR 1.45).
a secondary subgroup analysis from one US centre, young patients (median age 29), using US resolution criteria; it was not designed to show differences in harm or death.
UK practice point:
the JBDS pathway above remains the local standard. This evidence explains why bicarbonate may lag behind ketone clearance with saline, and why resolution is judged on ketones and pH.
Learning check: what was the median time to DKA resolution with balanced crystalloid vs saline?
13.0 h vs 16.9 h, in a secondary analysis of two cluster-randomised trials.
Pituitary Apoplexy: What the UK Guideline Can and Cannot Say
classical apoplexy is a medical emergency, and rapid hydrocortisone replacement may be life-saving.
sudden headache, vomiting, visual impairment and reduced consciousness from haemorrhage or infarction of the gland, with or without palsies of cranial nerves II, III, IV and VI.
refer to a multidisciplinary team including a neurosurgeon and an endocrinologist.
Surgery or not:
surgery is indicated when neurological symptoms are worsening. For most other patients it is unclear whether conservative or surgical management gives the better outcome, and the guideline calls for trials.
ICU point:
give steroids first and watch vision and consciousness closely; a change in either moves the patient into the surgical group.
Learning check: which apoplexy patients does the UK guideline clearly say need surgery?
Those with worsening neurological symptoms. For most others the best approach is uncertain.
