Recognise cortisol failure before the full biochemical pattern appears
Adrenal insufficiency means inadequate cortisol availability for the stress of illness. Primary adrenal failure also impairs aldosterone secretion; pituitary disease or suppression from exogenous glucocorticoids usually preserves aldosterone. Therefore hyperkalaemia supports primary disease but is not required for crisis. Consider the diagnosis in a patient with known adrenal disease, pituitary disease, omitted replacement or prolonged steroid exposure who develops vomiting, volume depletion, hypotension, confusion or hypoglycaemia. Infection can trigger a crisis and coexist with it.
First decisions: sample if feasible, replace immediately, resuscitate in parallel
Take paired cortisol and ACTH before hydrocortisone if this can be done immediately. Record the time of sampling and steroid administration for later interpretation. An unstable patient must not wait for a cortisol result or a Synacthen test; endocrine confirmation can follow recovery. Obtain electrolytes, renal function and glucose while assessing haemodynamics and the precipitant.
Teaching reasoning (not a quoted guideline):
the first-hour saline recommendation is not permission to give an unreviewed daily fluid total. Reassess perfusion, lung findings, urine output and fluid balance after resuscitation, especially with renal or cardiac disease. Treat hypoglycaemia using the local emergency protocol. Persistent shock needs parallel reassessment for sepsis, bleeding and cardiac dysfunction; a response to hydrocortisone alone cannot prove the cause.
Recovery is more than a normal blood pressure
Arrange endocrine review, taper stress hydrocortisone after clinical recovery and establish the underlying diagnosis. In primary insufficiency, fludrocortisone is introduced when daily hydrocortisone falls below 50 mg; it is not routinely required for secondary insufficiency. Explain sick-day replacement, provide a steroid emergency card and teach emergency injection use. Prolonged vomiting needs parenteral replacement rather than repeated oral doses that may not be absorbed.
Learning check: can normal potassium rule out adrenal crisis after missed prednisolone?
No. Secondary insufficiency generally preserves aldosterone. If crisis is suspected, give emergency hydrocortisone without delaying for diagnostic confirmation. In the quoted infusion regimen, 200 mg over 24 hours equals about 8.3 mg/hour; that is arithmetic, not a pump prescription or concentration instruction.
Three steroid decisions that must not be confused
distinguish replacing missing cortisol in suspected adrenal crisis, maintaining replacement during severe infection in someone with established insufficiency, and giving adjunctive corticosteroids in septic shock. These are different indications. Sepsis is not synonymous with adrenal failure, and vasopressor use does not itself establish Addison's disease. Infection may precipitate both DKA and adrenal crisis, so address the endocrine emergency and infection together.
What the sepsis guidelines actually recommend
SSC 2021 makes a weak recommendation with moderate-quality evidence for IV corticosteroids in adult septic shock with an ongoing vasopressor requirement. Its suggested vasopressor dose/timing is an implementation remark, not an adrenal diagnostic test. Do not wait for that remark's threshold when adrenal crisis is suspected.
The SCCM 2024 update is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. These recommendations concern septic shock, not routine steroid treatment for every patient with infection. They do not replace antimicrobial therapy, source control, haemodynamic reassessment or appropriate organ support. Broader management remains on the
Sepsis page
Benefits, harms and what not to infer
SSC's synthesis favoured faster shock resolution and more vasopressor-free days, but did not establish a clear mortality benefit. That is not the same as proof of no benefit in any patient, and the 2024 panel graded its updated recommendation separately. Do not present these guideline conclusions as a guarantee of survival or as proof that the patient had cortisol deficiency.
document the indication and review plan, avoid duplicate steroid prescriptions, and follow glucose, electrolytes, fluid balance, infection progress and weakness. If a patient has DKA as well as a genuine steroid indication, anticipate changing insulin requirements rather than omitting needed cortisol replacement. The emergency adrenal-crisis bolus and the warning against high-dose septic-shock pulse courses describe different clinical decisions.
Learning check: does sepsis without shock automatically need hydrocortisone?
No. The cited sepsis recommendations concern septic shock. Established replacement needs or suspected adrenal crisis are separate indications. Do not use a random cortisol result or a single noradrenaline dose as an automatic diagnosis.
Recognise DKA even when glucose is not high
The 2024 international adult consensus was endorsed by ADA, EASD, JBDS, AACE and DTS. It complements the UK JBDS 2023 pathway already described above; it does not justify mixing isolated thresholds from different protocols. Assess diabetes history or hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis together. Glucose alone cannot establish recovery or exclude DKA.
Reduced intake, pregnancy and SGLT2 inhibitors can accompany euglycaemic presentations. Check blood ketones and a venous gas in an unwell at-risk patient. Treat the precipitant alongside the metabolic emergency: suspected infection needs clinical assessment, not an assumption that every DKA episode is sepsis.
Potassium is the insulin safety gate
Serum potassium may initially look normal or high despite depletion. Insulin and correction of acidosis can uncover a dangerous deficit. The international consensus explicitly delays insulin below 3.5 mmol/L until potassium is above 3.5. The JBDS table instead directs urgent senior review and additional replacement below 3.5; use the locally adopted monitored pathway rather than converting this lesson into a concentrated-potassium prescription. Renal impairment and urine output change replacement safety.
Falling glucose means add substrate, not abandon ketone clearance
The international threshold is 13.9 mmol/L, conventionally rounded to 14 in the UK pathway. Dextrose permits insulin to continue while ketoacidosis resolves. Keep glucose, ketones, venous acid–base status and potassium trends visible together. For the UK monitoring schedule use the JBDS section above; the international report uses a different sampling schedule, so do not silently substitute it.
Resolution and safe transition
The consensus requires ketone clearance plus either the pH or bicarbonate criterion. The UK JBDS pathway uses ketones below 0.6 mmol/L AND venous pH above 7.3, and advises against using bicarbonate at this stage. These are explicitly different definitions, not a new combined rule. Urinary ketones and the anion gap can mislead during recovery; saline-related hyperchloraemia can persist after ketosis clears.
before stopping IV insulin, document that the chosen protocol's resolution criteria are met, the subcutaneous-insulin/overlap plan, oral intake and the next glucose check. Identify why DKA occurred and address medicine access, injection problems and sick-day planning. A normal bedside glucose is not a discharge criterion.
Learning check: glucose 10, ketones 2.4, pH 7.25 — may insulin stop?
No. These fictional observations show persisting ketoacidosis. Continue the adopted DKA pathway with glucose support and potassium review. For a fictional 70 kg adult, 0.1 units/kg/hour is 7 units/hour and 0.05 units/kg/hour is 3.5 units/hour: arithmetic illustrating the guideline rates, not an individual prescription.

# Thyroid Storm Clinical diagnosis and Burch–Wartofsky score, thionamides and iodide timing, beta-1 blockade, steroids, cooling, plasmapheresis and perioperative prevention This page adopts the 2016 Japan Thyroid Association / Japan Endocrine Society (JTA/JES) thyroid storm guideline as its main framework, because it is openly readable and gives graded recommendations; the 2016 American Thyroid Association (ATA) guideline is quoted where the two differ. Quotations are the sources' own wording; the surrounding explanation is teaching synthesis. Why it matters A clinical diagnosis Thyroid storm is decompensated thyrotoxicosis with organ dysfunction: fever, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, heart failure, gastrointestinal or liver dysfunction and agitation, delirium or coma, usually after a trigger (infection, surgery, stopping antithyroid drugs, iodine load, trauma, childbirth). Thyroid hormone levels confirm thyrotoxicosis but do not distinguish storm from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis, so treatment should not wait for them. The Burch–Wartofsky Point Scale (1993) scores temperature, heart rate, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, gut–liver dysfunction, central nervous system disturbance and a precipitating event. As reproduced in the JTA/JES guideline, a total of 45 or more is highly suggestive of storm, 25–44 suggests impending storm and under 25 makes it unlikely. The score is empirical: it supports, rather than replaces, clinical judgement. in theatre or recovery, storm can mimic malignant hyperthermia, sepsis, phaeochromocytoma crisis, neuroleptic malignant syndrome or a drug reaction. A rising end-tidal CO₂ with rigidity points to malignant hyperthermia; known or suspected hyperthyroidism, goitre or eye signs point to storm. No. Hormone levels in storm overlap with uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by a scoring system, and treatment starts as soon as storm is suspected. Step 1 — stop new hormone synthesis Antithyroid drugs (thionamides) block new hormone synthesis. Propylthiouracil (PTU) also reduces peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, which is why it is traditionally preferred in storm; carbimazole/methimazole is longer acting and avoids PTU's risk of severe liver injury. Both can be given via a nasogastric tube in an unconscious patient. Drug choice and doses should follow local endocrine advice; the drug properties here are standard pharmacology teaching rather than quotations. Step 2 — stop release of stored hormone with iodide, and the timing difference Iodide blocks release of stored hormone quickly. The two guidelines differ on timing: the ATA advises giving the antithyroid drug at least an hour first, so the gland cannot use the iodide to make more hormone; JTA/JES advises giving both together. In exams, state the ATA "thionamide first" sequence and acknowledge the JTA/JES position. Without a thionamide on board, the thyroid can use the iodide load as substrate to make more hormone (organification). Blocking synthesis first prevents that. JTA/JES favours short-acting beta-1-selective drugs (landiolol, esmolol, or oral bisoprolol). Propranolol is the traditional choice in many UK and US texts because it also modestly reduces T4-to-T3 conversion, but JTA/JES does not recommend it for tachycardia in storm. in a patient with thyrotoxic heart failure, beta-blockade can precipitate cardiovascular collapse, so a titratable infusion with close monitoring is safer than a large bolus. Steroids treat relative adrenal insufficiency in the hypermetabolic state and reduce T4-to-T3 conversion. JTA/JES uses 300 mg hydrocortisone a day outright; the ATA regimen totals more on day 1 because of its 300 mg loading dose, settling to an equivalent 300 mg/day maintenance rate (100 mg every 8 hours) thereafter. Cooling and the choice of antipyretic JTA/JES also advises against aspirin and some other anti-inflammatory antipyretics because they may increase free thyroid hormone by displacing it from binding proteins (paraphrased from the guideline). Look for and treat infection as a trigger. When standard treatment fails Endocrine Emergencies for the overview and the related myxoedema coma lesson. Paracetamol (acetaminophen), with mechanical cooling. Aspirin may raise free thyroid hormone by displacing it from binding proteins. Anaesthesia and the thyrotoxic patient the main anaesthetic lesson is prevention. Elective surgery in an uncontrolled thyrotoxic patient should be postponed until they are clinically euthyroid. For urgent surgery, prepare with an antithyroid drug, beta-blockade, steroids and (after the antithyroid drug) iodide, with endocrine input. Avoid drugs that worsen tachycardia where alternatives exist, and treat intraoperative storm with the same multimodal sequence plus active cooling and critical care. # Pituitary Apoplexy Recognition versus SAH, MRI, empirical steroid indications and doses, early surgery evidence and follow-up This page adopts the Society for Endocrinology 2016 emergency guidance (Baldeweg et al.) and the 2011 UK pituitary apoplexy guideline (Rajasekaran et al.). Quotations are the sources' own wording; surrounding explanation is teaching synthesis. What it is Pituitary apoplexy is sudden bleeding into, or infarction of, the pituitary gland, usually within an existing (often undiagnosed) adenoma. The swelling compresses the optic chiasm and cavernous sinuses, and destroys hormone-producing tissue. When to suspect it The guidance lists three groups: patients in whom subarachnoid haemorrhage and meningitis have been excluded, patients with neuro-ophthalmic signs, and patients with a known pituitary tumour (list paraphrased). Typical features are sudden severe headache, often with vomiting; reduced visual acuity or a bitemporal field defect; and ocular palsies, most often a third nerve palsy. Reduced consciousness, fever and neck stiffness can make it look like subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis. Both cause a sudden severe headache, and blood in the subarachnoid space from apoplexy can cause neck stiffness, photophobia and reduced consciousness. MRI of the pituitary distinguishes them. Steroids first in unstable or visually threatened patients Acute ACTH deficiency is common and is the immediate threat to life. Take blood for cortisol and other pituitary hormones if it causes no delay, then give hydrocortisone. Check sodium and fluid balance closely: hyponatraemia may come from cortisol deficiency, and diabetes insipidus is uncommon at presentation but can follow surgery. these doses are higher in the infusion arm than the adrenal crisis regimen on the Adrenal Crisis page. Use the regimen the guidance gives for the condition in front of you, and agree it with the endocrine team. Haemodynamic instability, altered consciousness, reduced visual acuity and severe visual field defects. Surgery or watchful management The evidence is observational: patients with severe or worsening visual or neurological signs go for early transsphenoidal decompression after medical stabilisation, and others are often managed conservatively with close visual monitoring. Management should be decided by a joint neurosurgical and endocrine team. SIADH is euvolaemic, CSW is hypovolaemic. Getting it wrong is dangerous: fluid restriction in CSW worsens cerebral perfusion and precipitates vasospasm-related infarction in SAH.

Diagnostic flowchart

Sequential bedside approach: serum Na⁺ → plasma/urine osmolality → urine Na⁺ → urine output → volume status.

Step 1 — Serum Na⁺

Na⁺ < 135 → hyponatraemia pathway (Step 2)
Na⁺ > 145 + polyuria → suspect DI (Step 5)
Step 2 — Plasma & urine osmolality

>275 → pseudo-/hypertonic (glucose, mannitol). Stop.
<275 + urine osm <100 → primary polydipsia / low solute. Stop.
>100 → ADH-driven → Step 3.
Step 3 — Urine Na⁺

<20 → extra-renal loss / hypovolaemia (D&V, third-spacing). Not SIADH/CSW.
>40 → renal Na⁺ wasting → SIADH vs CSW (Step 4).
Step 4 — Urine output & volume status (the decider)

Euvolaemic + normal/low UO

Normal CVP, no postural drop, neutral/positive balance, low urate, normal Hct/urea.

→ SIADH

Rx: fluid restrict 0.8–1 L/day (avoid in SAH); hypertonic saline if symptomatic; tolvaptan if persistent.

Hypovolaemic + polyuria (>3 L/day)

↓CVP, postural drop, negative balance, ↑Hct/urea, weight loss.

→ Cerebral salt wasting

Rx: 0.9% or hypertonic saline + fludrocortisone 0.1–0.4 mg/day. Never fluid restrict.

Step 5 — Hypernatraemia + polyuria (DI pathway)

UO >3 mL/kg/h, urine osm <300, plasma osm >295, urine SG <1.005.

DDAVP trial: urine osm rises >50%

→ Cranial DI

Rx: DDAVP 1–2 µg IV/SC or 10–20 µg intranasal; replace UO with 0.45% saline / 5% dextrose.

DDAVP trial: no response

→ Nephrogenic DI

Rx: treat cause (lithium, hyperCa²⁺, hypoK⁺); thiazide + low-salt diet; amiloride if lithium-induced.

Lab interpretation guide

What a high urine osmolality and high urine Na⁺ actually mean in each condition — the physiology behind the numbers.

Urine osmolality (normal 50–1200 mOsm/kg)

Reflects ADH activity at the collecting duct. High = ADH is acting (water reabsorbed → concentrated urine). Low = no ADH effect (dilute urine).

    SIADH: urine osm CSW: urine osm also <300 (complete DI <200) despite plasma osm >295. Kidneys cannot concentrate — either no ADH (cranial) or tubules unresponsive (nephrogenic). Patient pours out dilute urine and becomes hypernatraemic.
Urine Na⁺ (spot sample)

Reflects renal Na⁺ handling. <20 mmol/L = avid Na⁺ retention (true volume depletion or oedematous states). >40 mmol/L = renal Na⁺ wasting OR euvolaemic excretion matching intake.

    SIADH: urine Na⁺ DI: urine Na⁺ is variable and unhelpful — usually low if dehydrated (intact RAAS conserving Na⁺). Diagnosis rests on osmolality and DDAVP response, not urine Na⁺.

# ICU Sedation & Delirium RASS, CAM-ICU, dexmedetomidine, sedation protocols, ABCDEF bundle Sedation Assessment (RASS) . Daily sedation holds (SAT) paired with spontaneous breathing trials (SBT) reduced ventilator days and 1-year mortality in the ABC trial . Early deep sedation is associated with longer ventilation and higher mortality, so each day of deep sedation must be justified against one of the following indications: Severe ARDS — to secure ventilator synchrony, permit low tidal volume / prone positioning and prevent patient self-inflicted lung injury (P-SILI); mandatory when neuromuscular blockade is used. Refractory intracranial hypertension — reduces CMRO₂ and cerebral blood volume, blunts coughing and ventilator dyssynchrony that spike ICP. Status epilepticus — anaesthetic infusions titrated to seizure suppression or EEG burst suppression. Targeted temperature management / therapeutic hypothermia — to abolish shivering, which raises CMRO₂, CO₂ production and metabolic demand. Unmanageable agitation posing immediate danger to the patient (line/tube removal) or staff, after non-pharmacological measures and analgesia have failed. ECMO cannulation , transport of the unstable patient, and open-abdomen/proning procedures. approach — treat pain before deepening sedation. Violent, immediate danger to staff +1 to +3 Anxious, aggressive, pulling at lines Alert & calm Spontaneously attentive −1 to −2 Light sedation Drowsy, eye opening to voice (> 10 s) −3 to −4 Moderate / deep Movement or eye opening to voice or physical stimulation No response to voice or physical stimulation Sedative Agents titrating sedation depth detecting cerebral abnormalities such as non-convulsive seizures Sedation titration in patients receiving neuromuscular blockade, and recommends against it as the primary sedation measure in non-comatose, non-paralysed patients . Indices correlate imperfectly with RASS: electromyographic artefact, frontal dominance of the montage and agent-specific EEG signatures (dexmedetomidine slow-delta spindles vs propofol alpha) all degrade accuracy. Seizure & abnormality detection .     Processed EEG Monitoring in ICU

    Processed EEG (pEEG — e.g. BIS, SedLine/PSI, Narcotrend) condenses raw frontal EEG into a dimensionless index (roughly 0–100) using spectral and burst-suppression features. In ICU it has two distinct roles: detecting cerebral abnormalities such as non-convulsive seizures.

    Sedation titration

    Clinical scales (RASS, SAS) remain first-line. The SCCM PAD guideline suggests objective brain-function monitoring as an{ } adjunct in patients receiving neuromuscular blockade, and recommends against it as the primary sedation measure in non-comatose, non-paralysed patients . Indices correlate imperfectly with RASS: electromyographic artefact, frontal dominance of the montage and agent-specific EEG signatures (dexmedetomidine slow-delta spindles vs propofol alpha) all degrade accuracy.

    Seizure & abnormality detection

    Most ICU seizures are non-convulsive and invisible clinically. Continuous EEG detects electrographic seizures in ~19% of monitored critically ill patients, 92% entirely non-convulsive . The CERTA randomised trial found continuous EEG detected more seizures and led to more antiseizure treatment changes than repeated routine EEG, with no difference in 6-month mortality . Raw-EEG review (or quantitative displays such as density spectral array) is needed — a pEEG index alone cannot exclude seizures.

    • Indications for continuous EEG (ACNS consensus): persistent altered consciousness after convulsive status, acute brain injury (TBI, SAH, cardiac arrest), suspected non-convulsive status, and paralysed patients at seizure risk .
    • Practical use for sedation: track the trend, not a single number; a falling index with rising burst-suppression ratio signals excessive depth and prompts dose reduction — useful during deep sedation for ICP crises, status asthmaticus or ECMO.
    • Limitations: no validated outcome benefit for routine pEEG-guided sedation; indices do not distinguish sedative agents, miss focal/posterior seizures on frontal montages, and are confounded by hypothermia, metabolic encephalopathy and EMG artefact.

Reading the WSACS Statements The 2013 WSACS update graded its statements using GRADE. Strong are made when benefits clearly outweigh harms. Weaker are made when the balance is less certain. Where evidence was insufficient, it made no recommendation . The authors concluded that the overall quality of evidence was generally low and that intervention trials are urgently needed. In a viva, separating these tiers shows you understand what the guideline does and does not establish. Statements (WSACS 2013) Measure IAP when risk factors are present; avoid sustained IAH; use protocolised IAP monitoring and management; perform decompressive laparotomy for overt ACS; in the open abdomen, use negative-pressure wound therapy and aim for fascial closure during the same hospital stay. Medical therapies (sedation/analgesia, neuromuscular blockade, nasogastric/rectal decompression); percutaneous catheter drainage of intraperitoneal fluid; consider body position; avoid a positive fluid balance after initial resuscitation; enhanced plasma:red-cell ratios in trauma; prophylactic open-abdomen strategies in selected patients; avoid routine early biological mesh. Targeting abdominal perfusion pressure, diuretics, renal replacement therapy, albumin and acute component-parts separation. Applying it at the bedside Screen, don't wait: the strongest statements concern detection — measure IAP in at-risk patients and act on sustained elevation before organ failure develops. Escalate in steps: the medical options are suggestions, so use them as a time-limited trial while reassessing. Overt ACS with new organ dysfunction is the recommended indication for decompression. Fluid is a modifiable cause: after initial resuscitation, aim to avoid an ongoing positive balance. Removing fluid with diuretics or RRT may be reasonable in an individual patient, but WSACS made no recommendation for them. The open abdomen is a treatment with its own risks: plan early fascial closure from the outset. Learning check: is targeting abdominal perfusion pressure (MAP − IAP) a WSACS recommendation?     Practice point: IAH matters in medical patients, not only after trauma or surgery. Because the pressure that develops during the stay is what matters, measure serially in at-risk patients rather than once on admission. Measure via the bladder: supine, end-expiration, maximum 25 mL sterile saline, transducer zeroed at the mid-axillary line, no abdominal muscle contraction. Primary ACS = intra-abdominal/pelvic pathology (trauma, ruptured AAA, pancreatitis, peritonitis). Secondary ACS = extra-abdominal cause, typically massive resuscitation (burns, sepsis). Recurrent ACS = re-develops after decompression. # Critical Care of the High-Risk Surgical Patient Risk stratification (P-POSSUM/SORT/CPET/CFS), level-2/3 indications, structured handover, goal-directed therapy, MINS surveillance, NELA/CPOC standards The Trial Evidence Behind High-Risk Postoperative Care Three interventions are often presented as standard for the high-risk surgical patient: cardiac output-guided fluids, routine critical-care admission and prophylactic CPAP. The large trials are more cautious than that, and this lesson sets out what they actually found. Cardiac output-guided haemodynamic therapy: OPTIMISE and OPTIMISE II OPTIMISE randomised 734 high-risk patients aged 50 or over having major gastrointestinal surgery in 17 UK hospitals. They received either cardiac output-guided fluid with dopexamine during surgery and for 6 hours afterwards, or usual care. Complications or death at 30 days occurred in 36.6% vs 43.4% (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.71–1.01; P=0.07). That is a possible benefit, but the trial did not show it conclusively. OPTIMISE II was designed to settle the question. It randomised 2,498 patients aged 65 or over at 55 hospitals worldwide, using cardiac output-guided fluid with low-dose inotrope during surgery and for 4 hours afterwards. Postoperative infection was not reduced (23.2% vs 22.7%; adjusted OR 1.03). Acute cardiac events within 24 hours were more common in the intervention group (3.0% vs 1.7%), mainly arrhythmias. Learning check: does goal-directed therapy reduce complications after major surgery? The best current evidence says no, at least for older patients having elective GI surgery within modern enhanced-recovery care. The positive trend in OPTIMISE was not confirmed by the larger OPTIMISE II, which also found more early arrhythmias with inotrope. Cardiac output monitoring still has a place in unstable patients, but a protocol with routine inotrope should not be presented as proven. Does routine critical-care admission improve survival? (Kahan 2017, ISOS) This planned analysis of the International Surgical Outcomes Study included 44,814 elective surgical patients from 474 hospitals in 27 countries. Patients admitted straight to critical care after surgery died more often (2% vs 0.3%; adjusted OR 3.01). This probably reflects their higher risk at baseline. At hospital level, mortality was not associated with direct critical-care admission, with admission to treat complications, or with how many critical-care beds a hospital had. The result was the same when only high-risk patients were analysed. This is observational data, so it cannot show that critical care makes no difference to individual patients. Its message is that routinely admitting patients to critical care is not, on its own, a proven way to save lives. Recognising deterioration on the ward and escalating care quickly when complications develop (failure to rescue) may matter as much as where a patient goes first. Learning check: how would you reconcile ISOS with UK advice to admit patients with predicted mortality ≥5%? UK advice (NCEPOD, NELA) is based on the observed harm of under-provision and of late escalation for patients who are clearly high-risk. ISOS shows that blanket admission after elective surgery has not been proven to improve survival. Both point the same way: target admission to risk, and make sure the ward can spot and rescue complications. Prophylactic CPAP after major abdominal surgery (PRISM 2021) PRISM randomised 4,806 patients aged 50 or over having elective major open abdominal surgery at 70 hospitals in six countries. Patients received either CPAP within 4 hours of the end of surgery or usual care. Pneumonia, re-intubation or death within 30 days occurred in 8.1% vs 8.2% (adjusted OR 1.01). Adverse events occurred in 8.9% of patients who received CPAP, most often claustrophobia. Learning check: should every patient get CPAP after open abdominal surgery? No. PRISM found no reduction in pneumonia, re-intubation or death with routine prophylactic CPAP. CPAP remains a treatment for established hypoxaemia or atelectasis, and for patients who already use it for obstructive sleep apnoea. It is not a routine preventive measure. # Paediatric Intensive Care & Emergencies Age-specific physiology, paediatric sepsis, congenital heart disease, neurocritical care, sedation, and resuscitation The FEAST Trial: When Fluid Boluses Harmed Children FEAST randomised children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion in Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania to 20–40 mL/kg boluses of 5% albumin or 0.9% saline, or no bolus. All children received antimicrobials, maintenance fluids and supportive care; those with malnutrition or gastroenteritis were excluded. Recruitment stopped early after 3,141 children. 48-hour mortality was 10.6% with albumin, 10.5% with saline and 7.3% with no bolus (any bolus vs control RR 1.45, 95% CI 1.13–1.86). The excess persisted at 4 weeks (12.2%, 12.0%, 8.7%). Albumin vs saline: no difference (RR 1.01), so the harm was linked to bolus volume, not fluid type. Applying it: about 57% of the children had malaria, and intensive care and ventilation were not available. The trial therefore cannot be transferred directly to settings with PICU support. It is one reason current guidance favours smaller 10 mL/kg boluses with reassessment and earlier vasoactive drugs, rather than large fixed volumes. Learning check: did albumin perform better than saline in FEAST? No. 48-hour mortality was almost identical (10.6% vs 10.5%). Both bolus arms did worse than the no-bolus group. Learning check: why should you be careful applying FEAST to UK PICU practice? The children were treated where ventilation and intensive care were unavailable, and many had malaria. Children with malnutrition or gastroenteritis were excluded. # Burns Intensive Care Major-burn pathophysiology, airway/inhalation injury, fluid resuscitation (Parkland/modified Brooke), escharotomy, sepsis, nutrition, AKI, and ICU referral criteria The Evidence Behind Major-Burn Resuscitation and ICU Care This lesson sets out the trial and guideline evidence that sits behind the resuscitation, hypermetabolism and surgical timing advice on this page — and, just as importantly, where the evidence is weak or absent. Fluid resuscitation: from Parkland to 2 mL/kg/%TBSA The 2024 American Burn Association clinical practice guideline on burn shock resuscitation systematically reviewed 5,978 titles and found only 24 studies that met its criteria — a striking illustration of how thin the evidence base is for the most common decision in burns ICU. Its central recommendation is to start resuscitation at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA rather than the traditional Parkland 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, in order to reduce total resuscitation fluid volumes, and to consider human albumin (especially in larger burns) to lower crystalloid requirements and improve urine output. It recommends selective monitoring of intra-abdominal and intra-ocular pressure during resuscitation, makes only a weak recommendation for computer decision-support software, and explicitly does recommend transpulmonary thermodilution-derived variables to guide resuscitation. Notably, the guideline could make no recommendation at all on high-dose vitamin C (66 mg/kg/h), fresh frozen plasma, early continuous renal replacement therapy, or vasopressors as resuscitation adjuncts, because the studies were too few or too small. Mortality was deliberately excluded as a formal outcome because no study of sufficient size and quality exists to support a recommendation on survival. For the exam, this is the key message: the "obvious" adjuncts (vitamin C, FFP, early RRT) are unproven rather than proven ineffective, and the only interventions with guideline support are a lower starting rate and albumin. The rationale for starting lower is fluid creep — the well-documented phenomenon that modern burn patients receive far more fluid than the Parkland formula predicts, with the excess appearing largely after the first 8 hours as progressive oedema in unburned tissue. Saffle's review linked this to abdominal compartment syndrome and other serious complications, and proposed three practical strategies: avoid early over-resuscitation, use colloid as a routine component or for "rescue" when crystalloid alone is failing, and adhere to a written protocol rather than ad hoc titration. Learning check: why does the ABA now recommend starting at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA rather than 4? Because modern practice consistently over-delivers fluid relative to the Parkland formula ("fluid creep"), and the excess is associated with abdominal compartment syndrome, ARDS and peripheral oedema. Starting at a lower rate and escalating only if urine output is inadequate reduces total volume without evidence of harm. The formula is a starting point; the patient is the monitor. Hypermetabolism and β-blockade: the propranolol trials The catecholamine-driven hypermetabolic response roughly doubles resting energy expenditure and drives severe muscle-protein catabolism for weeks after a major burn. Propranolol is the best-studied countermeasure. In a landmark randomised trial, Herndon and colleagues studied 25 children with burns of more than 40% TBSA and titrated oral propranolol to reduce resting heart rate by 20% from baseline; over two weeks, propranolol decreased resting energy expenditure and skeletal-muscle protein catabolism compared with untreated controls — a genuinely mechanistic, randomised demonstration that β-blockade can reverse the catabolic state rather than merely treat its consequences. A later large prospective randomised controlled trial (406 children with burns >30% TBSA) established the dose–response: propranolol 1 mg/kg/day reduced heart rate by 15% versus controls, with higher doses producing progressively greater reductions in cardiac work. This is why the "1–4 mg/kg/day titrated to a 15–20% fall in resting heart rate" dosing on this page is the evidence-based approach — the endpoint is a physiological target, not a fixed milligram dose. Learning check: what physiological endpoint guides propranolol dosing in major burns, and why? A 15–20% reduction in resting heart rate. The catabolic response is driven by catecholamines, and the trials titrated to this HR endpoint rather than a fixed dose — 1 mg/kg/day achieved 15% in the dose–response trial, with higher doses needed in some patients to reach the target. Caution: β-blockade can mask the tachycardic response to sepsis and hypovolaemia, so it requires close monitoring in a critical-care setting. Early excision: strong historical data, more nuanced modern synthesis The case for early excision rests largely on a 1989 randomised trial by Herndon and colleagues in 85 adults with burns greater than 30% TBSA. In patients aged 17–30 inhalation injury, early excision and grafting reduced mortality from 45% to 9% — a dramatic result. Crucially, the trial found no mortality difference in patients older than 30 or in those with concomitant inhalation injury, and it did not establish benefit in the elderly. These caveats are frequently lost when "early excision saves lives" is stated as a universal rule. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled ten comparative studies (5,070 patients, including two RCTs) and found that early excision was not associated with lower mortality (risk difference −0.01, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.03), but associated with a significantly shorter duration of hospitalisation (standardised mean difference −0.64), with no difference in hospital cost or graft success rate. The modern reading is therefore that early excision remains standard practice — it shortens stay, reduces wound sepsis burden and enables earlier rehabilitation — but the mortality benefit seen in the 1989 trial has not been reproduced consistently in contemporary practice, where resuscitation, critical care and infection control have all improved. Learning check: an examiner asks "does early excision reduce mortality?" What is the best answer? It depends on the population and the era. The classic 1989 RCT showed a large mortality reduction (45% → 9%) in young adults without inhalation injury, but no benefit in older patients or with inhalation injury. A 2026 meta-analysis of 5,070 patients found no overall mortality difference, though hospital stay was shorter. The defensible modern answer: early excision is standard of care for wound control, length of stay and rehabilitation, but its mortality benefit is not universal and depends on patient factors. Physiological Management of the Donor
15 mg/kg (max 1 g) single IV dose — attenuates the systemic inflammatory response and improves lung function/oxygenation, increasing lungs suitable for retrieval.
Infusion 0.5–4 units/h (NHSBT bundle) — dual role treating vasoplegia and diabetes insipidus; spares catecholamines and reduces noradrenaline requirement.
Controversial evidence but commonly used with cardiovascular instability, e.g. thyroxine (T4) 20 mcg bolus then 10 mcg/h infusion.
Infusion targeting glucose 4–10 mmol/L — counters steroid- and stress-induced hyperglycaemia and improves pancreas/whole-organ viability.
Why the Donation Team Requests Specific Drugs
The physiology has changed
After coning, the catecholamine storm is followed by loss of medullary vasomotor tone and pituitary failure. The resulting shock is vasoplegic and endocrine, not a failure of adrenergic drive — the donor is already maximally catecholamine-exposed and adrenoceptors are downregulated and desensitised.
Vasopressin exploits a different receptor
V1 receptor agonism restores vascular tone independently of α₁ adrenoceptors, so it works where escalating noradrenaline does not, and it restores the low endogenous vasopressin level caused by posterior pituitary infarction. NHSBT bundle range 0.5–4 units/h.
It is catecholamine-sparing
High-dose noradrenaline causes myocardial injury (calcium overload, contraction-band necrosis, β-receptor downregulation), splanchnic and renal vasoconstriction, and pulmonary venoconstriction with extravascular lung water. Retrieval teams grade hearts partly by the vasopressor dose the donor needed; getting noradrenaline down improves the chance a heart, liver and kidneys are accepted.
One drug treats two problems
Around two-thirds of DBD donors develop cranial diabetes insipidus. Vasopressin also provides V2 antidiuretic activity, so it simultaneously controls polyuria, protects intravascular volume and limits the rise in serum sodium that damages liver grafts (NHSBT target Na⁺ < 150 mmol/L).
What it is not
It is not a rescue for hypovolaemia — restore preload first (CVP 4–12 mmHg, MAP 60–80 mmHg). Watch for excessive vasoconstriction with reduced cardiac output and splanchnic ischaemia, so titrate to the lowest effective rate and use echocardiography or cardiac-output monitoring if the heart is being considered.
Selective V2 agonist for diabetes insipidus when polyuria persists despite vasopressin, or when vasopressin is not needed haemodynamically. Chosen over more vasopressin when you want antidiuresis without additional vasoconstriction — protects circulating volume, sodium and kidney grafts.
Brainstem death releases a systemic inflammatory cascade that injures grafts before retrieval, and cortisol production falls. Steroid attenuates this inflammation, reduces extravascular lung water and improves oxygenation, so it measurably increases the number of lungs suitable for transplant. Given early, once donation is a possibility and authorisation is in place.
Pituitary failure lowers circulating thyroid hormone, and low T3 states are associated with impaired myocardial energetics. Used mainly for cardiovascular instability that persists despite volume, vasopressin and modest noradrenaline. The evidence is genuinely contested, so present it as a rescue component of the hormonal bundle rather than routine.
Steroids, catecholamines, dextrose-containing fluids and loss of insulin sensitivity all drive hyperglycaemia, which causes osmotic diuresis, worsens the sodium load and is associated with poorer pancreas and kidney graft function. Insulin also has direct anti-inflammatory and anabolic effects on grafts.
Requested before or during the hypertensive catecholamine surge to protect the heart and lungs from afterload injury and neurogenic pulmonary oedema. Short-acting agents are chosen deliberately so that the profound vasodilatation that follows can be managed without a lingering drug effect.
Aimed at achieving PaO₂/FiO₂ > 300 with lung-protective settings. Salbutamol enhances alveolar fluid clearance, bronchoscopy clears secretions and confirms graft suitability, and careful diuresis reduces extravascular lung water; over-diuresis is avoided because it compromises kidneys.
Requested to treat known or suspected donor infection and to reduce the risk of transmitting infection to an immunosuppressed recipient. Cultures taken before starting them guide recipient prophylaxis, so the microbiology results matter as much as the treatment itself.
Prevents microvascular thrombosis so that cold preservation fluid perfuses the whole graft. In DBD it is given by the retrieval team just before aortic cross-clamp. In DCD its timing is a legal and ethical matter: any pre-mortem administration is a 'pre-mortem intervention' that requires specific authorisation and must not harm the patient, so in UK practice it is not routine and is agreed case-by-case with the SN-OD and the treating team, not prescribed unilaterally.
Some pathways use prostacyclin or alteplase in the perfusate to improve microcirculatory flush, particularly for livers and lungs. These are retrieval-team drugs given after death is confirmed and are outside the ICU prescription.
Prescribed solely for symptom control at withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, titrated to distress in the usual way. They are never escalated to shorten life or to shorten the functional warm ischaemic time — that boundary is what keeps the DCD pathway lawful and must be stated explicitly in the viva.
Neuroprotective measures (osmotherapy targeted at ICP, tight temperature control for the brain), enteral feed and drugs with no organ benefit are discontinued after confirmation of death. Continued neuromuscular blockade may still be requested to prevent spinal reflexes during retrieval, which reassures staff and prevents movement that could be misinterpreted.
Step-by-Step Donation Algorithm — Pre- and Post-Mortem
Catastrophic brain injury with treatment no longer in the patient's best interests. Mandatory referral of every potential donor to the SN-OD — referral is not consent, it is a trigger for a co-ordinated pathway.
No drug is started or stopped yet for the recipient's benefit. Maintain neuroprotective care for DBD candidates (CPP, normocapnia, temperature) and comfort care where relevant.
SN-OD-led approach, checking the NHS Organ Donor Register. Under deemed consent in England/Wales/Scotland the family conversation still happens; no retrieval proceeds against sustained family objection.
Blood tests (virology, tissue typing, crossmatch), donor characterisation and organ offers begin now, in parallel with the testing or withdrawal plan below.
Two sets of tests by two doctors; time of death = completion of the second set. From this moment the therapeutic goal switches from brain protection to organ protection.
If the hypertensive surge is ongoing: short-acting agents only (GTN, esmolol, sodium nitroprusside) so the vasoplegia that follows is not compounded by a lingering drug.
Methylprednisolone 15 mg/kg IV (max 1 g) single dose; insulin infusion to glucose 4–10 mmol/L; T4 20 µg bolus then 10 µg/h is added for persisting cardiovascular instability rather than routinely.
As the storm resolves into vasoplegic, endocrine shock: start vasopressin 0.5–4 units/h and titrate noradrenaline down. Rationale — V1 agonism bypasses downregulated adrenoceptors, the V2 effect treats the diabetes insipidus (~65% of donors), and catecholamine-sparing protects the heart, liver and kidneys. Done within hours of confirmation, aiming for the lowest catecholamine dose before the heart is assessed.
Desmopressin 1–4 µg IV titrated to effect when urine output remains high despite vasopressin, or when antidiuresis is wanted without further vasoconstriction. Corrects Na⁺ toward <150 mmol/L to protect liver grafts.
NHSBT bundle targets: MAP 60–80 mmHg, CVP 4–10 mmHg, cardiac index >2.1 L/min/m², ScvO₂ >60%, VT 4–8 mL/kg with PEEP 5–10, PaO₂ ≥10 kPa, temperature 36–37.5 °C, urine output 0.5–2 mL/kg/h. (Hb thresholds are not set by the bundle — follow local SN-OD advice.) Broad-spectrum antibiotics for donor infection; bronchoscopy and lung recruitment as requested.
Retrieval team gives heparin (typically 25,000–30,000 units) immediately before aortic cross-clamp, then cold perfusion. Continued neuromuscular blockade prevents spinal reflexes. Organ-directed ICU drugs are stopped once cross-clamp occurs — the graft is now managed ex situ.
Catastrophic injury with treatment futile, but the brainstem is not dead — so death must be confirmed by circulatory criteria. The patient is alive until then; comfort, not organ protection, governs the prescription.

# Prognostication, Ethics & Outcomes Prognostic scoring, treatment escalation plans, medical ethics, withdrawal of treatment, PICS, long-term outcomes What PICS means The Society of Critical Care Medicine stakeholders' conference agreed post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) as the term for new or worsening problems in physical, cognitive or mental health that arise after a critical illness and persist beyond the acute hospital stay . The term can apply to the survivor or to a family member (often called PICS-F). It is a description of problems across three domains, not a single diagnosis with fixed criteria. Physical: the legacy can last years Herridge's cohort followed 109 survivors of ARDS for five years. At 5 years the median 6-minute walk distance was 436 m, 76% of predicted . Younger patients recovered faster, but neither younger nor older patients returned to normal predicted physical function , even though lung function was normal or near-normal. Other physical and psychological problems persisted in patients and family caregivers for up to five years. The limitation is therefore mainly outside the lung: muscle weakness, poor exercise tolerance and reduced physical quality of life. Cognitive: comparable to brain injury or early dementia BRAIN-ICU enrolled 821 adults with respiratory failure or shock; only 6% had cognitive impairment at baseline, and 74% developed delirium in hospital. At 3 months, 40% had global cognition scores similar to moderate traumatic brain injury and 26% similar to mild Alzheimer's disease. Deficits affected younger as well as older patients and persisted to 12 months. Longer delirium was independently associated with worse cognition and executive function at 3 and 12 months. Sedative and analgesic use was consistently associated with long-term cognitive impairment. The modifiable target the trial points to is delirium duration, not one drug class. That is an association, not proof that shortening delirium prevents impairment. Psychological: common, overlapping and linked to mortality A UK-wide cohort of 21,633 ICU admissions sent questionnaires to 13,155 survivors; 38% replied. Of the respondents, 55% passed the threshold for anxiety, depression or PTSD at 3 or 12 months : anxiety 46%, depression 40% and PTSD 22%. Patients with depression symptoms were 47% more likely to die in the first 2 years after ICU discharge (HR 1.47). With only 38% responding, the true prevalence in all survivors may be lower or higher; non-responders are a known source of bias in postal surveys. Prevention in the ICU: the ABCDEF bundle The bundle is: ssess, prevent and manage pain; oth spontaneous awakening and breathing trials; hoice of analgesia and sedation; elirium assessment and management; arly mobility and exercise; amily engagement. In the ICU Liberation Collaborative (over 15,000 adults), complete bundle performance was associated with lower delirium (AOR 0.60), coma (AOR 0.35), next-day ventilation (AOR 0.28), physical restraint (AOR 0.37), ICU readmission (AOR 0.54) and discharge somewhere other than home (AOR 0.64). This was an observational quality-improvement study, so it shows association, not that the bundle prevents PICS itself. After the ICU: what NICE asks for For the full step-by-step plan, see the PICS Follow-Up Plan During the ICU stay: a short clinical assessment as early as possible to find patients at risk of physical and non-physical morbidity, followed by a comprehensive assessment of rehabilitation needs for those at risk. 2–3 months after critical care discharge: review patients with rehabilitation needs, with a face-to-face functional reassessment of health and social care needs. Do follow-up clinics and diaries work? ICU diaries: in a randomised trial of 352 patients with ICU stays over 72 hours, receiving a diary of their stay 1 month after discharge reduced new PTSD at 3 months from 13% to 5%. Nurse-led follow-up clinics: the UK PRaCTICaL trial (286 patients, three hospitals) found no evidence that a nurse-led follow-up programme improved quality of life at 12 months, and it cost more. The authors suggested future work should focus on early physical rehabilitation, delirium, cognitive dysfunction and relatives. So "follow-up clinics reduce PTSD" is not supported as a general statement; the evidence is specific to the intervention. # PICS Follow-Up Plan
Step-by-step NICE CG83 pathway after critical illness: early risk check, rehabilitation goals, ward and home discharge, the 2–3 month review, and the evidence on ICU diaries and follow-up clinics


Why a plan is needed
Post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) describes new or worsening physical, cognitive or mental health problems that arise after critical illness and persist beyond the hospital stay, in the survivor or a family member.
In a UK cohort, 55% of survivors who replied had anxiety, depression or PTSD symptoms, and depression was linked to 47% higher death risk over 2 years; only 38% replied, so true rates are uncertain.
Step 1: short risk check, as early as possible in ICU
NICE asks for a
short clinical assessment during the critical care stay, as early as clinically possible
, to find patients at risk of physical and non-physical morbidity. Patients at risk then get a
comprehensive assessment
of current rehabilitation needs, and short- and medium-term rehabilitation goals are agreed.
NICE's examples of risk markers:
unable to get out of bed independently; anticipated long stay; obvious significant physical or neurological injury; not cognitively able to continue exercise independently; unable to self-ventilate on 35% oxygen or less; premorbid respiratory or mobility problems; unable to mobilise independently over short distances.
recurrent nightmares, particularly if the patient tries to stay awake to avoid them; intrusive memories; new or recurrent anxiety or panic attacks; wanting not to talk about the illness.
NICE notes this list is not exhaustive.
Step 2: start rehabilitation and inform the family
One competent professional should coordinate the rehabilitation pathway for continuity. For patients at risk,
rehabilitation starts as early as clinically possible
, based on the assessment and goals. Information about the illness and treatment goes to the patient and also to family or carer unless the patient disagrees.
Step 3: before leaving critical care
Patients earlier judged
low risk get a repeat short assessment before discharge
from critical care, because risk can change.
Step 4: on the ward
Patients at risk are offered an individualised, structured rehabilitation programme. NICE says to
consider a structured, supported self-directed rehabilitation manual for at least 6 weeks
after critical care discharge. Patients with stress symptoms from traumatic incidents or memories should be referred along the NICE PTSD pathway with preventive strategies started.
Step 5: before going home
Give the patient, and family or carer if the patient agrees, information on physical recovery against the ward goals, diet and continuing treatment, daily living, and where relevant
driving, returning to work, housing and benefits
, plus local support services such as support groups.
Step 6: the 2–3 month rehabilitation review
Review patients with rehabilitation needs 2 to 3 months after critical care discharge.
The functional reassessment should be
face to face
, in the community or in hospital, by a suitably skilled professional who knows the patient's critical care problems and pathway. Refer on to rehabilitation or specialist services if recovery is slower than the goals predicted, or if new physical or non-physical problems appear.
ICU diaries: two trials, two answers
Jones 2010:
352 patients with ICU stays over 72 hours received a diary 1 month after discharge.
New PTSD at 3 months fell from 13% to 5%.
Garrouste-Orgeas 2019 (JAMA, 35 French ICUs):
657 ventilated patients randomised, diary written by clinicians and family. Significant PTSD symptoms at 3 months were
29.9% with a diary versus 34.3% without, not a significant difference
. The authors concluded the findings do not support diaries for preventing PTSD symptoms.
The trials differ in when the diary was given, who wrote it and how PTSD was measured, and only about half of patients completed the French trial. A fair summary is that diaries may help some patients but are not proven to prevent PTSD. That synthesis is teaching reasoning, not a quoted source.
Follow-up clinics
The UK PRaCTICaL trial found a
nurse-led ICU follow-up programme showed no evidence of being effective or cost-effective
for quality of life in the year after discharge. The authors suggested future work focus on early physical rehabilitation, delirium, cognitive dysfunction and relatives.
This does not remove the NICE 2–3 month review; it means the content of follow-up matters, not just holding a clinic.

# End-of-Life Care & Communication Breaking bad news, family meetings, withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, symptom control at end of life, conflict resolution, cultural and spiritual care What the Trials Show About Supporting ICU Families Communication in end-of-life care is often taught as a matter of instinct, but it has been tested in randomised trials. The results show that some well-meant interventions help, some make no difference to distress, and one may cause harm. A proactive family conference plus a bereavement leaflet (Lautrette 2007) Relatives of 126 patients dying in 22 French ICUs were randomised to a proactive end-of-life conference (structured around VALUE) with a bereavement leaflet, or to the usual conference. Intervention conferences were longer (median 30 vs 20 minutes) and families did more of the talking (median 14 vs 5 minutes). At 90 days, relatives in the intervention group had fewer PTSD-related symptoms (45% vs 69%), less anxiety (45% vs 67%) and less depression (29% vs 56%). Learning check: what was the active ingredient? Most likely letting families speak: clinicians listened more and talked proportionally less. The leaflet and the longer meeting were part of the package, so the trial cannot separate their effects. It is still the main evidence base for the VALUE approach. A multicomponent family-support programme (PARTNER, White 2018) In a stepped-wedge cluster trial of 1,420 high-risk patients in five ICUs, a family-support intervention delivered by the ICU team did reduce surrogates' anxiety and depression at 6 months (HADS 11.7 vs 12.0) or PTSD symptoms. It did improve how families rated the quality of communication (69.1 vs 62.7) and patient- and family-centredness, and ICU stay was shorter (6.7 vs 7.4 days). Learning check: if better communication does not reduce distress, is it worth doing? Yes. Families rated communication as better and the care as more centred on the patient, and stays were shorter. But a viva answer should not claim that structured support prevents psychological harm in surrogates: PARTNER did not show that. A handwritten condolence letter (Kentish-Barnes 2017) 242 bereaved relatives in 22 ICUs were randomised to receive, or not receive, a handwritten condolence letter from the doctor and nurse caring for the patient. The letter did not reduce distress at 1 month. At 6 months, the letter group had HADS scores, more depression symptoms (36.6% vs 24.7%) and more PTSD-related symptoms (52.4% vs 37.1%). The authors concluded that the letter failed to ease grief and may have made depression and PTSD-related symptoms worse. Learning check: what is the general lesson? Kind gestures are not automatically harmless. Bereavement follow-up should be planned, offered and tested, not assumed to help. A one-way letter without any chance to talk may revive distress without offering support. The Evidence Behind Non-Technical Skills Tools
ANTS: how a behavioural marker system was validated
ANTS was built from human-factors research. It has four skill categories — task management, team working, situation awareness and decision making — divided into 15 elements, each with example good and poor behaviours. In its evaluation, 50 consultant anaesthetists were trained to use it and rated an anaesthetist in eight simulated scenario videos. The system appeared complete, the skills were observable, and ratings showed acceptable agreement and accuracy.
What it proves:
trained raters can reliably observe and score these behaviours in a simulated setting.
What it does not prove:
the evaluation was experimental and depended on rater training. It did not show that higher scores improve patient outcomes. The authors called for testing in real training environments.
Using it well:
ANTS is best used for structured, specific feedback after simulation or observed practice ("you verbalised the plan but didn't confirm who was calling for help"). It should not be used as a pass/fail score without calibrated raters.
The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
In eight hospitals across high- and low-income settings, introducing a 19-item checklist designed to improve team communication was associated with a fall in deaths from 1.5% to 0.8% and in inpatient complications from 11.0% to 7.0%, in patients aged 16 or over having non-cardiac surgery.
this was a before-and-after study, so the reductions are associations. Changes in awareness, practice and data collection over the same period may contribute.
the checklist works mainly through what it prompts — team introductions, shared anticipation of critical events, and confirmation of antibiotics and equipment. Ticking boxes without the conversation loses much of its purpose.
ICU translation:
the same principles underpin checklists for bedside tracheostomy, intubation and proning. Pre-brief roles, verbalise the plan and failure options, and debrief afterwards.
Learning check: does the Haynes 2009 study prove the checklist halves surgical mortality?
No. It showed an association in a before-and-after design across eight hospitals. Causation is plausible but not established by that design alone.
An operational debrief is an after-action conversation about how the team worked: what happened, what helped, what obstructed care and what should change next time. It is not a retrospective test of the most junior clinician, a substitute for incident investigation, or a treatment for traumatic stress. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS describes accurate event reconstruction, analysis, reinforcement of effective behaviours and a method for incorporating lessons into the next plan.
Start with readiness, not a rigid clock
AHRQ describes debriefs that can be very short, including about three minutes or less; this is an example, not a minimum duration or an instruction to interrupt care. In clinical application, first ensure continuing care, safe handover and cover for other patients. Offer a quiet, appropriate setting rather than discussing identifiable events in a public coffee room. A short early review and a later multidisciplinary review can serve different purposes; neither “within 24 hours” nor “one to two weeks” is a universal TeamSTEPPS requirement.
A practical learning sequence
Teaching synthesis from the AHRQ debrief checklist:
adapt these prompts to the event and local incident-response arrangements; they are not a separately validated named debrief model.
Set the purpose.
Explain that the aim is to understand team performance, not allocate blame. Invite contributions across roles, including people who observed rather than performed the main procedure. Ask whether anyone has an immediate safety concern.
Reconstruct the shared facts.
Recap the intended plan, key changes and actions. Separate observations from assumptions: “the request was not acknowledged” is more useful than “nobody cared”. Where recollections differ, record the uncertainty rather than forcing agreement.
Explore work as it actually happened.
Ask what information each person had at the time, whether roles were clear, whether requests were heard and what equipment or workload constraints shaped decisions. Avoid judging earlier choices solely using facts learned afterwards.
Preserve strengths as well as identify gaps.
Name a behaviour worth repeating, then explore a specific improvement. “The runner repeated the destination and confirmed the call” is actionable; “communication was good” is not sufficiently specific.
Close the improvement loop.
Agree what changes, who owns it and when progress will be checked. Escalate unresolved hazards through the local safety system. A conversation without follow-through does not establish that a risk has been controlled.
These prompts apply AHRQ’s performance-improvement approach. Any formal record, information sharing or incident response must follow local governance; do not promise absolute confidentiality or use a quick debrief to decide culpability.
Facilitating the conversation
Teaching synthesis:
the person leading the debrief sets the tone. Open with the purpose and ground rules, keep contributions balanced across roles and seniority, and summarise aloud what has been agreed. A facilitator who was the team leader during the event should state their own uncertainties early — this makes it safer for others to speak. Where the event involved harm or is likely to be formally investigated, agree beforehand what the debrief is for and how its outputs will be recorded; do not improvise that boundary in the room.
Advocacy with inquiry:
pair an observation with a genuine question — “I noticed the second syringe was drawn up before the first was checked; what was happening for you at that point?” This surfaces the reasoning behind an action instead of assuming it.
a quick structure that asks what went well (plus) and what should change next time (delta). It is a prompt for brevity, not a substitute for exploring why something happened.
Silence is data:
if a group that worked together has nothing to say, the barrier is usually psychological safety, not an absence of learning points. Ask each role in turn rather than accepting a general nod.
Where the debrief sits in the wider system
A team debrief is one layer of learning, not the whole response. In the NHS, the Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (PSIRF) replaced the old serious-incident framework with a system-focused approach: a rapid debrief can feed into, but does not replace, the proportionate learning response the framework describes.
Underpinning this is a just culture: staff are treated fairly, honest mistakes are distinguished from reckless behaviour, and people are not punished for raising concerns — the conditions that make a debrief honest rather than defensive.
Practical boundary:
if the debrief surfaces a possible individual performance or conduct issue, that is a separate process with its own fairness requirements — it should not be adjudicated in a group learning conversation.
Operational learning is not psychological debriefing
NICE’s recommendation concerns psychologically-focused debriefing intended to prevent or treat PTSD, not every conversation after an incident. It is not limited to compulsory sessions. Do not require staff to recount distressing emotions or relive the event as a purported preventive treatment. Equally, the recommendation does not prohibit compassionate listening, practical support or access to appropriate mental-health assessment. An operational debrief should not be advertised as proven PTSD prevention.
Worked application
Fictional teaching example:
after an emergency airway event, the team identifies that a request for additional help was made but nobody was named to make the call. The useful output is not “the nurse failed”: it is an agreed named caller, check-back of the request, confirmation that help is on the way, and an owner to rehearse that process at the next simulation. A staff member who is distressed is offered individual support without being made to disclose feelings in the group. This is educational reasoning, not a patient record or an outcome prediction.
Learning check: should everyone describe their worst feelings to prevent PTSD?
No. NICE advises against psychologically-focused debriefing for PTSD prevention or treatment. Keep the operational review focused on facts, team performance and agreed improvements; offer support separately without compelling emotional disclosure. A short debrief does not replace incident reporting or specialist assessment.
Speaking up in a crisis means making a safety concern audible, understandable and actionable, then checking that it has been addressed. Merely thinking that the leader must have noticed is not communication. TeamSTEPPS places advocacy and assertion within mutual support: the person raising a concern and the person receiving it both have responsibilities. The purpose is safer shared decision making, not winning an argument.
CUS: make the safety signal explicit
AHRQ’s canonical tool is
CUS: Concerned, Uncomfortable, Safety issue.
State the observation, explain why it worries you and ask for a specific response. If the concern remains unresolved, explicitly identify the safety issue. Local PACE or CUSS versions may add a “Stop” step; that adaptation is not the expansion of AHRQ’s three-letter CUS tool.
Fictional teaching dialogue, not an AHRQ quotation:
“Alex, I am concerned that this syringe label does not match the prescription.” If unresolved: “I am uncomfortable giving it until we confirm the drug and concentration.” If the hazard persists: “This is a safety issue. Please pause this administration while we check it.” The specificity matters: an unexplained “Are you sure?” can be heard as routine uncertainty rather than a warning.
The two-challenge rule is an escalation aid, not a waiting rule
If the initial assertion is ignored, repeat the concern assertively so that it is heard. If the response remains unacceptable, take stronger action through the supervisor or chain of command. AHRQ frames this for potential high-risk harm; it is not a requirement to repeat every minor disagreement twice. Repeating the same vague question without securing acknowledgement does not resolve the hazard.
Clinical application:
imminent danger is not a reason to work slowly through a script. Give an unambiguous warning, seek immediate help and use the applicable emergency pathway; do not wait to complete two polite challenges before protecting a patient. The communication tool does not replace clinical algorithms or confer authority to perform an intervention beyond one’s competence.
Receiving a challenge is a leadership skill
Acknowledge the concern, establish what the colleague has observed and explicitly resolve the discrepancy before proceeding where feasible. If the concern reflects different information rather than an error, explain that information and check agreement on the next step. A silent nod is not a shared plan. Invite challenge before an emergency and thank the person who raises it; do not frame safety as a junior clinician’s duty to overcome a hostile senior alone.
DESC: address conflict without distracting from resuscitation
DESC structures a discussion around
Describe, Express, Suggest and Consequences
: describe the specific situation, express the concern, suggest an alternative, and explain its consequences for team goals. AHRQ describes its particular usefulness for interpersonal conflict and recommends thoughtful timing, a private location and “I” statements. It is not a reason to postpone a time-critical safety warning for a private meeting.
Teaching application after stabilisation:
“When my concern was dismissed before I could explain the label mismatch, I worried we would miss an error. Can we agree that a stated safety concern receives a read-back and check? That lets us clarify quickly and work together.” Persistent intimidation or an unresolved safety hazard also needs the appropriate local reporting or speaking-up process; practising scripts does not repair an unsafe organisational culture on its own.
Graded assertiveness: match the strength of the signal to the risk
UK anaesthesia teaching often frames escalation as a graded ladder — probe with a question, alert with a statement of concern, then challenge with an explicit safety statement, and finally act in an emergency. One widely taught version is
: Probe, Alert, Challenge, Emergency. This is a local teaching adaptation, not an AHRQ tool, and its steps overlap with CUS rather than replacing them. The principle both share is that the language becomes more explicit as the unresolved risk rises — while imminent danger still justifies skipping straight to the strongest signal.
“Can we talk through the plan for the blood pressure before induction?” — invites the leader to share their reasoning.
“I’m concerned the systolic has been under 90 for ten minutes.” — states the observation and the concern.
“This is a safety issue — please treat the hypotension before we proceed.” — explicit, directed, actionable.
act within your competence and call for immediate help when delay itself is the danger.
Why hierarchy makes this hard: the Bromiley case
Elaine Bromiley died in 2005 after a “can’t intubate, can’t ventilate” emergency during routine ENT surgery. Two experienced consultants persisted with repeated intubation attempts while the oxygen saturation fell; nurses who recognised the severity — one fetched a tracheostomy kit, another phoned the ICU — did not feel able to state their concerns directly to the consultants, and their actions were not picked up. The case is widely taught as an illustration of how steep authority gradients suppress exactly the information a team most needs.
The lesson for both sides:
the junior team members had the right information and even acted on it, but the message never reached the decision-makers in a form they registered. Speaking up is necessary but not sufficient — the leader must actively invite, hear and visibly respond to challenge, especially when absorbed in a difficult task.
Evidence limits:
these AHRQ pages define communication and escalation tools, not a guaranteed reduction in mortality from using an individual phrase. Rehearse with the whole team, including how leaders respond, rather than treating a mnemonic as an independently proven treatment.
Learning check: must you complete two challenges before stopping an immediately unsafe action?
No. The two-challenge rule supports escalation when an initial concern is ignored; it is not a mandatory delay in imminent danger. State the hazard and requested action clearly, seek immediate help and follow the applicable emergency pathway. The receiver should acknowledge and address the concern, not just demand more assertiveness.
means Team Strategies and Tools to Enhance Performance and Patient Safety. The AHRQ framework organises teachable teamwork behaviours around communication, team leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support, with team structure at the centre. Unlike ANTS, which is a behavioural marker system for anaesthetists, TeamSTEPPS supplies a multidisciplinary toolkit for coordinating work. The frameworks overlap, but their category names are not interchangeable.
Brief, huddle and debrief: three different jobs
Brief — establish the plan:
identify the team and roles, current situation, intended actions, contingencies and resource needs. In a teaching application to an ICU procedure, name the lead, operator, monitor and caller for help; agree what would trigger a change of plan.
Huddle — update an existing plan:
reconvene when the patient’s condition, team membership or workload changes, or the plan is not working. AHRQ explicitly allows any team member observing a need for adjustment to convene one. It is not a meeting reserved for the consultant.
Debrief — learn after the event:
reconstruct key events, reinforce effective actions and agree improvements for the next case. A debrief is not the right label for a mid-crisis reassessment that changes current care.
a huddle need not stop ongoing life-saving treatment. The leader can request a short verbal update while essential tasks continue, summarise what has changed, redistribute work and confirm the new plan. The purpose is an updated shared mental model, not a ceremonial pause of fixed duration.
SBAR: finish with an actionable request
Situation states the current problem; Background gives relevant context; Assessment states what you think is happening and the uncertainty; Recommendation or Request identifies what you need next. Distinguish observed data from interpretation, and avoid a long history that buries the urgent concern. The receiver must still clarify urgency, responsibility and the response; a structured monologue alone does not close the loop.
“I am the ICU nurse in bed four. The patient has deteriorated during transfer preparation. They are ventilated and receiving vasopressor support. I am concerned the current plan is no longer safe. Please attend now and confirm who will review the airway and circulation.” This illustrates communication structure, not a clinical diagnosis or a prescribed treatment response.
Call-out versus check-back: broadcast is not confirmation
A call-out makes important information available to the team; a named task request identifies who should respond. A check-back verifies exchanged information: the sender states the message, the receiver repeats it, and the sender confirms or corrects the repeat. “Someone call for help” does not establish ownership; hearing “OK” does not establish that the correct message was received.
Fictional teaching dialogue:
“Sam, call the ICU consultant to bed four now.” “I will call the ICU consultant to bed four now.” “Correct.” Sam then confirms the call was made and communicates any response. Read-back checks understanding; completion reporting separately checks execution. Neither guarantees that help has arrived. These are teaching examples, not quotations from the source.
How the curriculum is organised
The four modules correspond to the four skill domains — communication, team leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support — built around team structure. The tools in this lesson map onto those domains: SBAR, call-out and check-back are communication tools; briefs, huddles and debriefs are leadership tools; and CUS, the two-challenge rule and DESC sit within mutual support. Knowing which domain a tool belongs to helps you diagnose what is failing: a team that never updates its plan has a leadership gap, however polished its SBAR handovers are.
Implementation: training alone does not change behaviour
organisations that get value from TeamSTEPPS treat it as a change programme, not a one-off course. Common practical steps include identifying a specific local problem first (for example, poor handover or repeated never-event near misses), training a mixed group that includes senior clinicians, agreeing the exact shared wording the unit will use, and then coaching the behaviours in real work and simulation. A course certificate without rehearsal, leadership modelling and feedback tends to fade within months.
Start narrow:
introduce one or two tools against a named problem rather than the whole toolkit at once.
Leaders go first:
staff judge whether speaking up is safe from how the most senior person responds to the first challenge they receive after training.
Measure behaviours, not attendance:
observe whether briefs actually happen, whether check-backs close the loop and whether concerns get escalated — completion of e-learning proves neither.
Make the toolkit observable
start with a locally relevant failure mode, agree shared wording, practise in simulation and observe whether the loop closes in real work. Useful process questions include whether roles were named, whether the changed plan reached everyone and whether an unresolved concern was escalated. Include patients and family caregivers when appropriate to the setting and their wishes; urgent care, privacy and capacity still govern what is feasible.
tool descriptions support how these techniques are used; they do not establish a particular mortality benefit or make a ticked checklist proof of effective teamwork. Evaluate actual behaviours and unintended burdens, not merely whether staff can recite the acronyms.
Learning check: the plan changes mid-crisis and a request is met with “OK”. What is missing?
Use a huddle to communicate the revised plan and ownership while essential treatment continues. Obtain a specific check-back, confirm or correct it, then ask for completion reporting. Acknowledgement alone is not verified understanding or task completion; the after-action debrief comes later.
