>Call-out versus check-back: broadcast is not confirmation</h3> <p>A call-out makes important information available to the team; a named task request identifies who should respond. A check-back verifies exchanged information: the sender states the message, the receiver repeats it, and the sender confirms or corrects the repeat. “Someone call for help” does not establish ownership; hearing “OK” does not establish that the correct message was received.<R label=
>Fictional teaching dialogue:</strong> “Sam, call the ICU consultant to bed four now.” “I will call the ICU consultant to bed four now.” “Correct.” Sam then confirms the call was made and communicates any response. Read-back checks understanding; completion reporting separately checks execution. Neither guarantees that help has arrived. These are teaching examples, not quotations from the source.</p> <h3 className=
>How the curriculum is organised</h3> <SourceQuote label=
>Teaching synthesis:</strong> organisations that get value from TeamSTEPPS treat it as a change programme, not a one-off course. Common practical steps include identifying a specific local problem first (for example, poor handover or repeated never-event near misses), training a mixed group that includes senior clinicians, agreeing the exact shared wording the unit will use, and then coaching the behaviours in real work and simulation. A course certificate without rehearsal, leadership modelling and feedback tends to fade within months.</p> <ul className=
>Measure behaviours, not attendance:</strong> observe whether briefs actually happen, whether check-backs close the loop and whether concerns get escalated — completion of e-learning proves neither.</li> </ul> <h3 className=
>Teaching synthesis:</strong> start with a locally relevant failure mode, agree shared wording, practise in simulation and observe whether the loop closes in real work. Useful process questions include whether roles were named, whether the changed plan reached everyone and whether an unresolved concern was escalated. Include patients and family caregivers when appropriate to the setting and their wishes; urgent care, privacy and capacity still govern what is feasible.<R label=
>Evidence limits:</strong> tool descriptions support how these techniques are used; they do not establish a particular mortality benefit or make a ticked checklist proof of effective teamwork. Evaluate actual behaviours and unintended burdens, not merely whether staff can recite the acronyms.</p> <details className=
Step-by-step reasoning
Situation awareness: declare 'CICO' aloud, recognise SpO₂ trend, time-stamp events
Decision-making: commit to DAS Plan D (FONA) rather than persistent intubation attempts — avoid task fixation
Team-working: assign explicit roles (airway lead, surgical airway, drugs, runner, scribe), use closed-loop communication, call for senior help early
Task management: prepare FONA kit, ensure adequate paralysis, monitor SpO₂/ETCO₂, plan post-event debrief
Cognitive aids: use the DAS CICO cognitive aid on the wall; rehearse with simulation
Common traps
Hierarchy preventing junior team members from speaking up — graded assertiveness (CUS, PACE)
Plan continuation bias — repeated DL attempts after failure
Failing to debrief after the event — second-victim impact and learning loss
framework, the
model of human factors, and Crisis Resource Management (CRM) principles are core to FFICM, EDIC and CCT-level practice. This topic frames the four ANTS categories, the cognitive traps that lead to error, and the team and organisational tools used to mitigate them.
ANTS — Anaesthetists' Non-Technical Skills
ICU example
Situation awareness
Gathering information · recognising & understanding · anticipating
Spotting a rising lactate trend before haemodynamic collapse; mental model of where the patient is on their illness trajectory.
Decision making
Identifying options · balancing risks & selecting · re-evaluating
Choosing between further volume, vasopressor escalation, or RRT; setting time-limited trial endpoints.
Task management
Planning & preparing · prioritising · resource ID & utilisation · standards
WHO checklist before bedside tracheostomy; pre-briefing for prone positioning; cognitive aids for crisis algorithms.
Team working
Coordinating · exchanging information · using authority & assertiveness · supporting others
Closed-loop communication during peri-arrest; nominating roles in MET call; calling for help early.
Cognitive Errors & Bias
Dual process theory
underpins all of this.
System 1
thinking is fast, automatic, intuitive, pattern-based and emotionally coloured — efficient for the routine work that fills most of a clinical day, but the seat of heuristics and bias.
System 2
thinking is slow, deliberate, logical and effortful — needed for novel, complex or ambiguous problems. Most critical incidents arise when System 1 is relied on inappropriately in a non-routine situation that demanded System 2, particularly under fatigue, time pressure or task saturation
Fixation error / plan continuation bias
— sticking with an action plan when the situation has changed (the laryngoscopy example).
Confirmation bias
— interpreting new data as confirming the working diagnosis.
— over-weighting the first piece of information (the handover diagnosis).
Premature closure
— accepting a diagnosis before fully verifying it.
Availability heuristic
— recent or memorable cases bias the differential.
Authority gradient
— junior team members fail to challenge the senior.
Cognitive overload
— task saturation in a crisis impairs decision-making (Yerkes-Dodson curve).
Debiasing strategies (cognitive forcing strategies)
— thinking about your own thinking: "am I falling into a trap here? What am I assuming?"
Consider alternatives
— deliberately generate at least two other differentials: "what else could this be?"
Consider the opposite
— "why might this
be the case?" — and actively seek disconfirming evidence rather than confirmation.
Slow down
— when the situation allows, force the switch from System 1 to System 2; a deliberate 10-second pause ("10-for-10") buys analytic capacity.
— imagine the patient has come to harm and work backwards to identify how, before committing to the plan.
Group strategies
— invite challenge explicitly, verbalise the working diagnosis aloud, use structured handover and checklists so others can cross-check your reasoning.
Crisis Resource Management — Key Principles
Team behaviours
Call for help early
Establish clear leadership; leader hands-off when possible
Nominate role allocation aloud (airway / circulation / drugs / scribe / runner)
Closed-loop communication ("adrenaline 1 mg IV given — confirmed")
Use names not pronouns; use SBAR for handover
Graded assertiveness — scripted language that escalates a concern firmly but respectfully:
: Probe → Alert → Challenge → Emergency
: "I am
oncerned" → "I am
ncomfortable" → "this is a
afety issue" → "
top, let's resolve this"
Cognitive behaviours
Use cognitive aids (don't rely on memory under stress)
Anticipate and plan ahead ("if this fails we will…")
Distribute workload — leader not task-saturated
Re-evaluate frequently ("10-second-for-10-minutes")
Mobilise all available resources (people, equipment, expertise)
Know your environment — equipment locations, switchboard codes
Psychological safety
(Edmondson) is the shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — that a member can ask a question, admit uncertainty or error, or challenge a senior decision without fear of humiliation, blame or punishment. It is the foundational requirement for every tool above: PACE and CUSS scripts, incident reporting and honest debriefing all fail in a team that is not psychologically safe
It flattens the authority gradient, so concerns surface early rather than after harm.
It increases error and near-miss reporting, and so the raw material for learning and a just culture.
It is actively created by leaders — introducing the team by name, framing the case as a shared learning problem, inviting challenge explicitly ("tell me if you see something I've missed"), modelling curiosity, and acknowledging their own fallibility.
It is destroyed quickly by public criticism, dismissing a concern, or punishing the messenger — one such episode silences a team for months.
Human Factors — SHEEP Model
ystems — protocols, equipment design, IT, staffing levels
uman interaction — communication, hierarchy, team dynamics
nvironment — noise, lighting, interruptions, ergonomics
quipment — usability, alarm fatigue, default settings
ersonal — fatigue, stress, hunger, illness, cognitive bias (the "IM SAFE" check: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Eating)
Swiss Cheese Model
: incidents occur when latent system holes line up with active human error. Effective interventions usually target the system layers, not the individual.
Briefing, Debriefing & Handover
Pre-procedure brief
WHO checklist (ICU adaptation), patient ID, planned procedure, anticipated difficulties, role allocation, equipment check, escalation plan.
Operational debriefs review events, team performance and improvements after care is safely handed over. Timing and duration depend on circumstances; do not confuse learning with psychologically-focused debriefing for PTSD prevention.
Handover tools
SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation); ISBAR (adds Identification); ICU board rounds with daily goals (FAST-HUG-BID, ABCDEF bundle).
Patient Safety & Incident Response
Just culture
(Reason; Marx 2001) — distinguish three categories of behaviour and respond proportionately. Neither blame-free nor punitive:
Human error
— an unintentional slip or lapse.
the individual and fix the system that allowed the error.
At-risk behaviour
— a choice where the risk is not recognised or is mistakenly believed justified (e.g. a workaround).
the individual; remove incentives for the workaround.
Reckless behaviour
— conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk.
(NHS England Patient Safety Incident Response Framework, 2022) — replaces SI framework; emphasises learning, proportionate response, family/staff involvement.
Duty of candour
— statutory (England, since 2014); be open and honest when something goes wrong.
Datix / equivalent
— incident reporting; NRLS, learn from incidents.
Speaking up
— Freedom to Speak Up Guardians; PACE/CUSS scripts.
Second victim
— clinicians involved in adverse events need active support; structured peer support programmes (e.g. RISE).

The trainee believes a videolaryngoscope or front-of-neck access is now indicated but says nothing. Which non-technical skill failure is most prominently demonstrated?

During an ICU crisis the existing plan is no longer working. Which TeamSTEPPS tool updates the current care plan?

Applying ANTS in a 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' scenario
Use ANTS categories (situation awareness, decision-making, teamwork, task management) alongside DAS algorithms and cognitive aids to maintain coordinated CICO management and debrief afterwards.
Non-Technical Skills & Human Factors
FFICM / EDIC — Intensive Care
ANTS taxonomy: Situation awareness · Decision making · Task management · Team working — memorise for SOEs.
Up to 70% of critical care adverse events are non-technical; competence is examinable and assessable.
Fixation error and plan continuation bias are the most cited cognitive failures in airway disasters (Bromiley case).
AHRQ CUS means Concerned, Uncomfortable, Safety issue; repeat ignored concerns and escalate unresolved safety risks.
Closed-loop communication and named role allocation are CRM cornerstones in any crisis.
Cognitive aids reduce error in low-frequency / high-stakes events — use them, don't rely on memory.
A just culture distinguishes error and at-risk behaviour (system response) from reckless behaviour (accountability).
Operational debriefs review team performance and improvements; do not offer psychologically-focused debriefing to prevent or treat PTSD.
The Swiss Cheese Model frames adverse events as system holes aligning — fix the system, not just the person.
Statutory duty of candour applies in England since 2014 — be open promptly when harm occurs.
Debriefing: operational learning and staff support
Speaking up in a crisis: CUS and escalation
TeamSTEPPS: briefs, huddles and closed-loop communication
What are the four domains of ANTS (Anaesthetists
Task management, team working, situation awareness and decision making — each with behavioural markers used for structured debrief and assessment (Fletcher et al., BJA 2003).
Situation awareness is individual perception of cues, comprehension and projection (Endsley); shared mental model is the team-wide common understanding of the problem and plan — built by closed-loop communication and structured handover (e.g. SBAR).
How does cognitive aid use improve crisis management?
Cognitive aids (e.g. AAGBI Quick Reference Handbook, ASA Critical Events) reduce omission errors in low-frequency emergencies — RCTs show measurable improvement when a dedicated reader is appointed within the team.
Define the four ANTS categories (situation awareness, decision making, task management, team working) and their elements.
Recognise common cognitive biases and fixation errors that contribute to ICU adverse events.
Apply Crisis Resource Management principles in simulated and real ICU emergencies.
Use structured tools (SBAR, CUS, two-challenge rule, PACE/CUSS, WHO checklist) to support safe communication and handover.
Distinguish operational debriefing from psychologically-focused PTSD interventions, and apply TeamSTEPPS briefs, huddles and check-backs.
Explain just culture, duty of candour and the NHS PSIRF approach to incident response.
Loss of situation awareness by the consultant alone
Failure of graded assertiveness / speaking up by the trainee

A just culture (Reason; Marx) distinguishes inadvertent error and at-risk behaviour — addressed by system redesign, coaching and support — from reckless behaviour (conscious disregard of substantial risk), which warrants accountability. It is neither a

entries.text:
# Operations Library: Surgical Steps for Anaesthetists
Searchable step-by-step summaries of 82 operations across 14 specialties, with anaesthetic notes for each step and diagrams

## Orchidopexy (undescended testis) (Paediatric)
Day-case operation in infants and young children to bring an undescended testis into the scrotum, usually through a groin and a scrotal incision. A palpable testis is usually corrected by open inguinal orchidopexy; an impalpable testis may need laparoscopy and staged surgery, which this entry does not illustrate.
Position: Supine; small child on a warmed mattress with the groin and scrotum prepared.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Confirm side, examine under anaesthesia, and plan open or laparoscopic approach. Anaesthetic note: Paediatric pre-assessment: recent upper respiratory infection, fasting, parental presence at induction. Inhalational or intravenous induction with a supraglottic airway is common for a short day case.
2. Make a groin incision and open the inguinal canal to find the testis. Anaesthetic note: Skin incision and canal opening are stimulating; give caudal or ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric block before incision, or deepen anaesthesia. Laryngospasm can follow light anaesthesia.
3. Mobilise the testis and spermatic cord, separating the patent processus vaginalis. Anaesthetic note: Traction on the cord can cause a vagal bradycardia and laryngospasm; alert the surgeon, deepen anaesthesia and treat bradycardia promptly.
4. Create a scrotal pouch through a second incision and fix the testis in it without tension. Anaesthetic note: A caudal covers both incisions; an ilioinguinal block alone may not cover the scrotum. Supplement with local infiltration by the surgeon.
5. Close the wounds and recover the child for same-day discharge. Anaesthetic note: Plan regular paracetamol and NSAID if suitable. Warn parents about leg weakness after a caudal and post-operative nausea; confirm voiding policy per local guidance.
Laryngospasm at light anaesthesia
Spermatic cord traction and bradycardia
Block coverage of the scrotal incision
Day-case discharge criteria
Caudal block and ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric block are both used; the scrotal incision needs sacral dermatomes or local infiltration.
Laparoscopic orchidopexy for an impalpable testis adds pneumoperitoneum and possible staged surgery.
Associated conditions (e.g. prematurity, some syndromes) change the airway and day-case plan.
Sources: GOSH Undescended Testis; OpenAnesthesia Infant Spinal

## Hypospadias repair (Paediatric)
Reconstruction in which the abnormally placed urinary opening is moved to the tip of the penis, the penis straightened and excess foreskin removed. Distal repairs are often one stage; proximal hypospadias may need staged surgery with grafts. The diagram shows a one-stage tubularised repair.
Position: Supine, sometimes with frog-legged hips; long microsurgical procedure for proximal forms.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Examine under anaesthesia, assess curvature with an artificial erection test and mark incisions. Anaesthetic note: Plan for a 1–3 hour case in a young child: warming, eye care and pressure care. Caudal block is common; some surgeons prefer penile block, depending on local practice and concern about outcomes.
2. Deglove the penile skin and correct curvature. Anaesthetic note: Surgical stimulation is high; confirm the block works before incision. A tourniquet at the base of the penis may be used; record its time.
3. Create the new urethra from the urethral plate and tubularise it over a catheter. Anaesthetic note: Requires a still field during fine suturing; avoid coughing and movement. Adrenaline-containing infiltration may be used by the surgeon: watch for arrhythmia.
4. Cover the repair with a vascularised tissue layer and reconstruct the glans and skin. Anaesthetic note: Total local anaesthetic dose must include caudal and surgical infiltration. Prepare for emergence without coughing or straining.
5. Leave a urethral catheter or stent and apply the dressing. Anaesthetic note: Plan analgesia for catheter discomfort and bladder spasm; arrange antibiotics per surgical plan. Parents need clear advice about dressing and catheter problems at home.
Block confirmation before degloving
Total local anaesthetic dose
Prolonged case in a small child: heat loss and pressure care
Smooth emergence protecting the repair
Caudal block is widely used; the association between caudal block and urethral fistula is debated, so follow the surgical team's evidence-informed preference.
Proximal or redo hypospadias is longer and may be staged, with grafts and more bleeding.
Postoperative bladder spasm may need specific treatment such as oxybutynin according to local protocol.
Sources: GOSH Hypospadias Repair; OpenAnesthesia Infant Spinal

## Ureteroscopy and laser lithotripsy (Urology)
Endoscopic treatment of ureteric or kidney stones: a telescope passes through the urethra and bladder into the ureter or kidney, and a laser breaks the stone; fragments are removed or left to pass. A temporary JJ stent is sometimes left in place.
Position: Lithotomy; sometimes modified with the opposite leg lowered.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Confirm side, imaging and urine culture; insert a cystoscope and pass a safety guidewire up the ureter under X-ray. Anaesthetic note: General or spinal anaesthesia; the BAUS leaflet notes that both are discussed. Untreated infection behind an obstructing stone can cause sepsis: treat infection before elective stone surgery.
2. Pass a rigid or flexible ureteroscope, sometimes through an access sheath, to the stone. Anaesthetic note: Coughing or movement risks ureteric injury: maintain adequate depth and consider muscle relaxation or apnoea briefly at critical moments. Lithotomy positioning risks apply.
3. Fragment the stone with the laser; irrigation keeps the view clear. Anaesthetic note: Irrigation under pressure can raise pressure inside the kidney and cause bacteria to enter the bloodstream; watch for fever, rigors and hypotension after the case. Laser safety: eye protection for staff.
4. Remove fragments with a basket or leave dust to pass; inspect the ureter for injury. Anaesthetic note: Respiratory movement can move the kidney; brief ventilation pauses may help the surgeon. Report any perforation, which changes the plan.
5. Place a JJ stent if needed, drain the bladder and recover as a day case where possible. Anaesthetic note: Stent discomfort and bladder spasm are common; plan analgesia. Fever after ureteroscopy needs urgent sepsis assessment.
Sepsis from infected obstructed system
Patient movement during ureteric access
Raised intrarenal pressure from irrigation
Lithotomy positioning harm
Most cases are short day cases with a supraglottic airway, but brief muscle relaxation or apnoea may be requested.
Pregnancy, anticoagulation and solitary kidney change the plan and need specialist discussion.
Post-operative fever is a sepsis warning sign, not a routine finding.
Sources: BAUS Ureteroscopy; Warner lithotomy 2000

## Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) (Urology)
Removal of large kidney stones through a tract made from the skin of the back into the kidney. A ureteric catheter is placed first; the kidney is punctured under X-ray or ultrasound, the tract dilated, and the stone broken and removed. A nephrostomy or stent may be left.
Position: Lithotomy for ureteric catheter, then prone (or supine/Galdakao-modified Valdivia position per surgeon).
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Under general anaesthesia, place a ureteric catheter from the bladder up to the kidney using a cystoscope. Anaesthetic note: General anaesthesia with a secure tracheal tube for prone positioning. Check urine culture and give antibiotics per policy: large infection stones are a major sepsis risk.
2. Turn the patient prone (or position supine) and inject contrast to outline the kidney. Anaesthetic note: Prone turn: secure tube and lines, protect eyes, face, breasts and genitals, free abdomen, and check ventilation. Prone positioning risks apply.
3. Puncture the kidney through the back and dilate a tract; insert a sheath. Anaesthetic note: An upper-pole puncture above the 12th rib risks pleural injury: watch for falling saturation, rising airway pressure or hypotension suggesting pneumothorax or fluid in the chest. Bleeding can be sudden.
4. Break the stone with ultrasound, laser or pneumatic devices and remove fragments. Anaesthetic note: Large irrigation volumes can be absorbed, causing hypothermia, fluid overload and electrolyte change; use warmed fluids and track input–output. Watch for sepsis (fever, hypotension) intraoperatively.
5. Place a nephrostomy tube or stent, turn supine and recover with a chest and bleeding check. Anaesthetic note: Assess for haemothorax/pneumothorax and haematuria; check haemoglobin if bleeding was significant. Plan analgesia for the nephrostomy site (paravertebral or erector spinae blocks are options).
Prone turn and airway security
Supracostal puncture: pneumothorax/hydrothorax
Tract bleeding
Intraoperative urosepsis
Irrigation absorption and hypothermia
Supine PCNL avoids the prone turn and may suit patients with poor respiratory reserve or obesity.
Bleeding needing transfusion is uncommon but tract or arterial bleeding may need embolisation.
Combine the regional, positioning and sepsis risk sections of Anaesthetic Risk when consenting.
Sources: BAUS PCNL; Edgcombe prone 2008

## Transvaginal cervical cerclage (Obstetric)
A supporting suture is placed around the cervix during pregnancy in selected patients at risk of preterm birth. History-, ultrasound- and examination-indicated procedures differ: rescue cerclage with exposed membranes is not equivalent to an elective stitch. This entry illustrates a transvaginal McDonald-type stitch; Shirodkar and transabdominal techniques differ.
Position: Lithotomy with supported legs; avoid sustained aortocaval compression as gestation advances and coordinate any head-down tilt with the obstetric team.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Confirm gestation, indication, cervical findings and suitability, including assessment for labour, infection, bleeding and ruptured membranes. Anaesthetic note: Agree maternal assessment, fasting/aspiration strategy and appropriate fetal assessment. Rescue cases may be urgent and have a greater risk of membrane rupture and pregnancy loss; anaesthesia cannot make an unsuitable cerclage safe.
2. Establish regional or general anaesthesia, position and expose the cervix with vaginal instruments. Anaesthetic note: Check neuraxial contraindications and adequate block before instrumentation. Treat maternal hypotension promptly; general anaesthesia requires a pregnancy-appropriate airway plan. Cervical traction can provoke a vagal response.
3. Identify the cervix and, if necessary, carefully reduce exposed membranes; pass a circumferential cervical suture. Anaesthetic note: Maintain immobility and communicate any bleeding or suspected membrane rupture. Reduction of membranes and needle placement are surgical decisions; the drawing is not a guide to needle depth.
4. Tie the suture to support the cervix without occluding its canal; inspect the operative field and trim the ends. Anaesthetic note: Reassess blood loss and comfort. Unexpected pain, bleeding or cardiorespiratory change warrants reassessment rather than assuming a short procedure is risk-free.
5. Remove instruments, complete maternal and appropriate fetal checks, and document follow-up and stitch-removal plans. Anaesthetic note: Confirm block recovery, analgesia and discharge suitability. Give a clear handover for contractions, bleeding, fluid loss or fever. Labour with a stitch in situ requires urgent obstetric review to prevent cervical injury.
Suitability for rescue cerclage
Maternal hypotension and positioning
Membrane rupture during cervical instrumentation
Labour with the stitch in situ
Regional or general anaesthesia may be appropriate; the choice depends on urgency, gestation, patient preference, contraindications and local expertise.
A cervical stitch reduces risk in selected patients but does not guarantee a term birth. Antibiotics, tocolysis and fetal monitoring follow the indication and local obstetric plan, not a universal anaesthetic prescription.
Transabdominal cerclage is a separate abdominal operation and has different future delivery/removal implications.
Sources: RCOG Cervical Stitch; NICE NG25 Cerclage

## Peripartum hysterectomy (including placenta accreta spectrum) (Obstetric)
Removal of the uterus at or after delivery for uncontrollable haemorrhage or planned treatment of placenta accreta spectrum (PAS). Planned PAS surgery with a specialist multidisciplinary team differs from emergency hysterectomy for refractory postpartum bleeding. A total or subtotal procedure may be chosen according to pathology, bleeding and anatomy; the diagram illustrates total hysterectomy after caesarean delivery.
Position: Usually supine with uterine displacement before delivery; possible lithotomy for vaginal access. Maintain access to the airway, vascular lines and blood-product delivery.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Agree specialist surgical, anaesthetic, neonatal and blood-bank plans, or activate the emergency haemorrhage pathway. Anaesthetic note: Prepare reliable large-bore access, monitoring, warming, rapid transfusion and a critical-care destination. In planned PAS, review imaging, anticipated bladder involvement and conversion to general anaesthesia if starting neuraxially; in an emergency, resuscitation and source control run together.
2. Expose the uterus and deliver the baby if still pregnant, with the uterine incision selected to avoid the placenta where possible. Anaesthetic note: Coordinate delivery with the neonatal team and reassess haemodynamics immediately. For planned caesarean hysterectomy in PAS, leave the placenta in situ rather than attempting separation, which may trigger massive bleeding.
3. Develop distorted pelvic planes, identify ureters and bladder, and control vascular pedicles. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding may be sudden and extreme, especially with invasion near the bladder. Follow physiological response, measured losses, haemoglobin/coagulation and local major-haemorrhage guidance; correct hypothermia and monitor ionised calcium during transfusion.
4. Remove the uterus using the selected total or subtotal technique and repair associated injury if required. Anaesthetic note: Communicate ongoing bleeding, acidosis and vasoactive requirements. Pelvic vascular-control adjuncts are selected specialist measures, not guaranteed prevention of haemorrhage; their risks and monitoring needs should be discussed before use.
5. Secure haemostasis, close the vault or cervical stump as appropriate and transfer with an explicit organ-support plan. Anaesthetic note: Reassess coagulation, temperature, fluid balance and ventilation before extubation. Ongoing shock, large transfusion or organ injury may require critical care. Arrange thromboprophylaxis when safe, pain relief and sensitive follow-up after fertility loss and difficult birth.
Emergency induction in haemorrhagic shock
Placental separation in suspected PAS
Pelvic/bladder dissection and major haemorrhage
Transfusion-related hypocalcaemia and coagulopathy
Postoperative organ support
The recommendation to leave the placenta in situ concerns the caesarean-hysterectomy approach to PAS; it is not a instruction to leave every retained placenta untreated. Conservative PAS approaches are separate selected specialist pathways.
Neuraxial, general or combined strategies depend on anticipated bleeding, urgency and patient factors. No technique guarantees haemodynamic stability.
Total and subtotal hysterectomy have different distal anatomy. Quantified blood loss and repeated physiological assessment matter more than the qualitative High badge.
Sources: ACOG PAS Consensus; Reale Farber PAS 2022

## Laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy (Gynaecology)
Laparoscopic removal of an ovarian cyst while aiming to preserve viable ovarian tissue. Management depends on symptoms, imaging, fertility wishes and malignancy risk; not every cyst needs surgery. The operation may change to oophorectomy, laparotomy or an oncology pathway if anatomy or findings require it. An emergency torsion pathway is not identical to elective cyst removal.
Position: Supine or modified lithotomy with Trendelenburg as needed; secure the patient, protect pressure points and move both legs together.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Confirm imaging, pregnancy assessment where appropriate, malignancy-risk assessment and consent for possible change of approach or ovarian removal. Anaesthetic note: Review anaemia, pain, comorbidity and urgency. Vomiting or an acute abdomen changes aspiration risk; choose monitoring and blood availability from the patient and expected dissection rather than a routine day-case label.
2. Establish laparoscopic ports and pneumoperitoneum, position and inspect the pelvis. Anaesthetic note: Recheck tube, lines and ventilation after tilt. Insufflation may cause bradycardia, raised airway pressures or hypercapnia; severe instability also requires assessment for entry-related vascular injury.
3. Open the ovarian surface and develop the plane between the cyst wall and healthy ovarian tissue. Anaesthetic note: Maintain appropriate relaxation and perfusion while tracking bleeding. Adhesions and endometriosis may extend dissection close to bowel, ureter or vessels. Avoid assuming cyst rupture is benign: contents and malignancy risk matter.
4. Separate the cyst, retrieve it in a suitable bag, manage spillage if present and secure ovarian haemostasis. Anaesthetic note: Communicate blood loss and operative extension. Irrigation and specimen retrieval can prolong surgery; haemostasis must balance bleeding control with preservation of ovarian tissue. Conversion or oophorectomy is a surgical decision.
5. Reinspect the pelvis, remove ports and close; agree recovery and follow-up for histology. Anaesthetic note: Use multimodal analgesia and PONV prevention and assess bleeding and recovery before discharge. Worsening abdominal pain, fever, dizziness or instability warrants assessment for haemorrhage, visceral injury or other complications.
Laparoscopic entry injury
Pneumoperitoneum and head-down positioning
Cyst dissection and ovarian bleeding
Spillage or unexpected malignant features
The diagram shows local coronal anatomy and one preserved ovary; it is not a guarantee of ovarian preservation or a prediction of fertility.
Dermoid spillage can provoke chemical peritonitis; suspected malignancy requires appropriate specialist planning, not indiscriminate drainage.
Apply procedure-appropriate multimodal analgesia, nausea prevention and risk-based VTE prophylaxis. Emergency torsion or haemorrhage can invalidate an elective recovery pathway.
Sources: Royal Berkshire Ovarian Cystectomy 2025; Henny Pneumoperitoneum 2005

## Vaginal hysterectomy (Gynaecology)
Removal of the uterus through the vagina for suitable benign disease, often alongside prolapse repair. The cervix is removed in a total vaginal hysterectomy; ovary/tube removal and pelvic-floor reconstruction are separate decisions. Vaginal access avoids abdominal ports but does not eliminate bleeding, visceral injury or postoperative urinary problems.
Position: Lithotomy with carefully supported legs and access for vaginal surgery; protect pressure points and avoid excessive hip flexion/abduction.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Confirm the indication, uterine size, prolapse and intended adnexal or pelvic-floor procedures; catheterise and expose the cervix. Anaesthetic note: Review anaemia, frailty, cardiopulmonary reserve and anticoagulants. Agree general versus regional anaesthesia, expected duration, blood availability and postoperative bladder-care needs.
2. Incise around the cervix, mobilise the bladder and enter the appropriate peritoneal planes. Anaesthetic note: Ensure adequate block/anaesthetic depth before traction; a vagal response is possible. Scarring from previous surgery can make bladder dissection difficult and increase injury risk.
3. Sequentially divide and secure supporting ligaments and uterine vascular pedicles. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding from deep pedicles can be concealed from direct anaesthetic view. Communicate suction/swab loss and haemodynamics; the ureters lie close to the operative field and require surgical protection.
4. Deliver and remove the uterus vaginally, completing any separately agreed adnexal procedure or prolapse repair. Anaesthetic note: Unexpected uterine size, adhesions or bleeding can prolong surgery or require another approach. Reassess position and block duration rather than assuming the original anaesthetic will remain adequate.
5. Check haemostasis, provide appropriate apical support and close the vaginal vault; confirm packs and postoperative drainage plans. Anaesthetic note: Record any vaginal pack and its removal plan. Provide multimodal analgesia, antiemesis and risk-based thromboprophylaxis; postoperative bleeding or urinary retention needs assessment before discharge.
Lithotomy-related pressure/nerve injury
Bladder mobilisation
Uterine pedicle bleeding and ureteric injury
Pack accounting and urinary recovery
Vaginal hysterectomy is not the same as vaginal prolapse repair alone, and the ovaries are not routinely removed solely because the uterus is removed.
Regional anaesthesia is an option when suitable, not a requirement. A more extensive repair or change of approach alters duration and recovery.
Support early mobilisation and oral intake as appropriate; escalating pain, bleeding, fever or oliguria warrants evaluation for complications.
Sources: Manchester Vaginal Hysterectomy 2024; ERAS Gynaecology 2019; Gill 2019 well-leg

## Skin lesion excision and local reconstruction (Dermatology)
Excision of a skin lesion for diagnosis or treatment, with closure selected for the defect: primary suture, local flap or graft. Margin and depth depend on diagnosis, site and oncological guidance; an ellipse in the diagram is not a universal cancer margin. Most small procedures use local anaesthesia; larger, sensitive-site or complex reconstructions may require additional anaesthetic support.
Position: Determined by lesion and reconstruction site; supine, lateral or prone. Plan airway access and pressure protection before draping.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Confirm lesion, site, consent and the intended excision/reconstruction, including histology and anticoagulant plans. Anaesthetic note: Assess comorbidity, anxiety, ability to remain still and whether sedation is really needed. Review bleeding and thrombosis risks individually; do not automatically stop prescribed antithrombotic treatment.
2. Mark the lesion and planned margins, prepare the field and infiltrate local anaesthetic or establish another agreed technique. Anaesthetic note: Reconcile local-anaesthetic type and cumulative dose from every operator/site. Inject incrementally with appropriate precautions and be ready to recognise systemic toxicity; sedation does not replace effective local analgesia.
3. Excise the lesion to the selected plane, orient the specimen and send it for histology. Anaesthetic note: Facial/scalp fields may bleed more than the Low badge suggests. Maintain verbal contact if awake and protect airway access when face drapes restrict visibility. The excision plane must follow pathology, not the schematic.
4. Achieve haemostasis and assess defect size, tension and the choice of primary closure, local flap or skin graft. Anaesthetic note: Electrosurgery requires fire precautions, especially with oxygen near the face. Larger reconstruction may need more infiltration, time or a change of anaesthetic plan; record every additional dose.
5. Complete reconstruction and dress the wound; provide bleeding, wound-care and pathology follow-up plans. Anaesthetic note: Confirm recovery after any sedation and appropriate escort/discharge arrangements. Give instructions for persistent bleeding, expanding haematoma, infection or compromised flap/graft; histology may require further treatment.
Correct-site marking and pathology-dependent margins
Cumulative local-anaesthetic exposure
Facial oxygen/electrosurgery fire risk
Postoperative bleeding and reconstruction viability
The illustration shows primary closure of one small defect; it does not prescribe a melanoma margin or cover every flap/graft technique.
Small skin surgery usually does not need general anaesthesia. Sedation requires monitoring and rescue capability appropriate to its depth, particularly when airway access is limited.
Larger oncological resections and complex reconstruction can have materially greater bleeding and physiological risk than a minor lesion excision.
Sources: UHD Skin Excision Reconstruction; BSDS Antithrombotics 2023

## Mohs micrographic surgery (Dermatology)
Staged skin-cancer excision with mapped microscopic assessment of peripheral and deep margins, aiming to conserve uninvolved tissue. Further tissue is removed from mapped positive areas until clearance, then reconstruction is planned. Used for selected cancers and sites; it is not interchangeable with a routine excision or an automatic indication for every skin cancer.
Position: Usually awake with local anaesthesia, positioned for the lesion site and repeated access. Allow comfort and pressure protection during waiting periods.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Confirm the diagnosis, lesion/site and appropriateness for Mohs; explain repeated stages, waiting periods and reconstruction options. Anaesthetic note: Review ability to tolerate a potentially lengthy awake procedure, anxiety and comorbidity. Make an individual antithrombotic plan; medically necessary treatment is not routinely stopped simply because skin surgery is planned.
2. Infiltrate local anaesthetic, debulk as appropriate and remove the first thin layer with orientation and mapping. Anaesthetic note: Account for all local-anaesthetic doses, including any later reconstruction. Assess analgesia before cutting; communicate vasoconstrictor use and watch for toxicity rather than relying on a single injection being small.
3. Process and examine mapped peripheral/deep margins microscopically while protecting the wound. Anaesthetic note: Maintain comfort, hydration appropriate to the planned anaesthetic and clear communication during waiting. If sedation is used, monitoring continues during processing; its risks do not disappear when surgery pauses.
4. Excise further tissue only from mapped positive regions and repeat microscopy until margins are clear. Anaesthetic note: Duration and final defect size are unpredictable. Reconcile additional infiltration, bleeding and patient tolerance at each pass; a new anaesthetic plan may be required for extended or complex reconstruction.
5. After clearance, reconstruct by the selected closure/flap/graft or arrange delayed repair; dress and plan follow-up. Anaesthetic note: Agree whether reconstruction stays under local anaesthesia or needs theatre support. With facial surgery, manage oxygen/electrosurgery fire risk and airway access. Give bleeding and wound-care advice and reassess discharge after sedation.
Mapped specimen orientation and margin assessment
Repeated infiltration and cumulative local-anaesthetic dose
Unpredictable duration/defect size
Facial reconstruction and airway/fire precautions
Five teaching stages do not mean five excision passes. The fourth stage may repeat; the positive sector shown in the diagram is illustrative, not a patient result.
Microscopic margin control conserves tissue but does not promise freedom from recurrence. Diagnosis, histology, site and patient factors determine the treatment pathway.
Most Mohs procedures use local anaesthesia without an anaesthetist; anaesthetic input is particularly relevant to sedation, difficult positioning, severe comorbidity or substantial reconstruction.
Sources: BAD Mohs Surgery 2025; BSDS Antithrombotics 2023

## Abdominoperineal resection (AP resection) (General & GI)
Removal of the rectum, anal canal and sphincter complex with an end colostomy, usually for low rectal cancer when sphincter preservation is unsuitable. Unlike anterior resection, there is no colorectal anastomosis and the colostomy is permanent. Open, laparoscopic and robotic abdominal approaches and conventional or extralevator perineal excision vary by tumour and team.
Position: Abdominal phase supine or Lloyd-Davies/lithotomy; perineal phase in lithotomy or prone jackknife. Two-team simultaneous surgery or repositioning may be used.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Confirm operative extent, marked colostomy site and perineal positioning; establish abdominal access and explore. Anaesthetic note: Assess anaemia, nutrition, frailty and effects of neoadjuvant treatment. Agree blood availability, analgesia, monitoring and postoperative destination. Secure the airway and lines before head-down tilt or a later prone turn.
2. Mobilise the sigmoid/left colon and divide selected mesenteric vessels, protecting the ureters and autonomic nerves. Anaesthetic note: Pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg affect ventilation and venous return. Titrate fluids and vasoactive support to perfusion, avoiding both overload and hypovolaemia; watch for vascular or splenic injury during mobilisation.
3. Dissect the rectum and mesorectum through the pelvis to meet the planned perineal plane. Anaesthetic note: Deep pelvic and presacral venous bleeding can be abrupt. Communicate suction loss and haemodynamics; prolonged lithotomy requires careful leg support, pressure protection and vigilance for well-leg compartment syndrome.
4. Perform perineal excision of anus and sphincters, with levator excision where indicated; remove the specimen. Anaesthetic note: If turning prone, coordinate the turn, recheck tube, ventilation, eyes and lines, and keep the abdomen free of compression. Perineal dissection adds bleeding and pain; flap reconstruction, if needed, extends the operation.
5. Close or reconstruct the perineal defect, mature the end colostomy and close the abdomen. Anaesthetic note: Provide analgesia for both abdominal and perineal wounds. Reassess temperature, haemostasis and airway oedema before extubation; arrange stoma support, VTE prevention and an appropriate recovery/critical-care plan.
Presacral or pelvic haemorrhage
Lithotomy-related nerve injury and well-leg compartment syndrome
Airway/line security during prone repositioning
Two operative wounds and possible flap reconstruction
Elective enhanced recovery includes nutritional/anaemia optimisation, multimodal analgesia, individualised fluids and early mobilisation; emergency obstruction or sepsis changes this plan.
APR permanently separates stool passage from the perineum: there is no colorectal join to leak, but pelvic collections, wound breakdown, urinary dysfunction and stoma complications remain possible.
Neuraxial analgesia depends on surgical approach, coagulation, anticoagulants and local expertise; it is not mandatory for every APR.
Sources: APR StatPearls 2024; ASCRS SAGES Operative ERAS 2023; Gill 2019 well-leg

## Right hemicolectomy (General & GI)
Resection of the caecum, ascending colon and a variable portion of transverse colon with terminal ileum, commonly for cancer. Continuity is usually restored with an ileocolic anastomosis. Extended resections remove more transverse colon; emergency ischaemia, obstruction or perforation may require a stoma or staged reconstruction instead.
Position: Usually supine, with tilt adjusted for laparoscopic/robotic exposure; open surgery uses a suitable abdominal incision.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Explore the abdomen and establish open or minimally invasive access. Anaesthetic note: Assess anaemia, bowel preparation-related dehydration and obstruction. Decide aspiration precautions from the clinical state; pneumoperitoneum can cause bradycardia, raised airway pressures and hypercapnia.
2. Mobilise the right colon and hepatic flexure, protecting the duodenum, right ureter and retroperitoneal structures. Anaesthetic note: Maintain relaxation and reassess ventilation after tilt. Mobilisation can injure adjacent structures; unexpected blood loss or instability needs immediate discussion rather than assuming an insufflation effect.
3. Divide the ileocolic pedicle and other vessels required by the planned resection; complete mesenteric division. Anaesthetic note: Dissection is close to major mesenteric veins, so bleeding may be sudden. Monitor perfusion and temperature and communicate significant haemodynamic changes during vessel division.
4. Divide terminal ileum and colon, remove the specimen and form an ileocolic anastomosis when appropriate. Anaesthetic note: Assess blood loss and perfusion before reconstruction; avoid both excessive fluids and undue restriction. A stapled or sutured, intracorporeal or extracorporeal join may be used; unstable emergency patients may need a different strategy.
5. Inspect haemostasis and bowel viability, close incisions and agree postoperative care. Anaesthetic note: Use approach-appropriate multimodal analgesia and PONV prevention. Plan early feeding/mobilisation as tolerated; escalating pain, tachycardia, fever or organ dysfunction warrants assessment for leak, bleeding or sepsis.
Aspiration risk in obstructed patients
Mesenteric vascular bleeding
Pneumoperitoneum and tilt
Physiological suitability for anastomosis
Right hemicolectomy usually joins ileum to colon, not colon to rectum. Resection extent and vessel ligation depend on pathology and anatomy.
Elective ERAS principles include optimisation, opioid-sparing analgesia, individualised balanced fluids and early recovery; invasive monitoring and critical care depend on risk rather than the operation name.
Open surgery may benefit from thoracic epidural where appropriate; routine epidural use is not recommended for laparoscopic colorectal surgery.
Sources: Hemicolectomy StatPearls 2023; ASCRS SAGES Operative ERAS 2023

## Left hemicolectomy (General & GI)
Removal of the descending colon with variable distal transverse/sigmoid colon, commonly for cancer. Reconstruction may be colocolic or colorectal depending on the remaining bowel; the diagram shows one colorectal reconstruction. This is not synonymous with low anterior resection, and it does not necessarily involve total mesorectal excision.
Position: Supine or modified lithotomy, with tilt adjusted for minimally invasive exposure and access needed for reconstruction.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Explore and establish open, laparoscopic or robotic access; assess disease and planned resection. Anaesthetic note: Assess hydration, anaemia and cardiorespiratory reserve. Use aspiration precautions where obstruction is present; secure the patient and airway before tilt.
2. Mobilise descending colon and, where needed, splenic flexure, protecting the left ureter and spleen. Anaesthetic note: Splenic capsular injury can produce unexpected bleeding. Adjust ventilation for pneumoperitoneum/tilt and protect pressure points; track lithotomy duration when legs are elevated.
3. Divide the required vascular pedicles and mesentery, preserving adequate supply to the retained bowel. Anaesthetic note: Vessel division may cause significant blood loss. Support systemic perfusion without fluid overload; surgical assessment of bowel viability remains essential and cannot be inferred from normal blood pressure alone.
4. Divide and remove affected colon; construct a tension-free colocolic or colorectal join if clinically suitable. Anaesthetic note: Communicate hypothermia, acidosis, vasopressor needs and bleeding before reconstruction. Anastomotic assessment and any protective stoma are surgical decisions based on local and systemic risk.
5. Assess haemostasis and anastomosis as appropriate, close and implement the postoperative plan. Anaesthetic note: Tailor analgesia to incision and approach, minimise opioid-related ileus, and monitor recovery for bleeding, ileus, anastomotic leak and sepsis. Critical-care admission depends on physiology and risk.
Splenic injury during flexure mobilisation
Mesenteric bleeding
Positioning injury during prolonged surgery
Anastomotic perfusion and tension
The retained bowel determines whether the join is colocolic or colorectal; the illustrated configuration is not universal.
Apply elective colorectal enhanced recovery where appropriate, including early feeding and mobilisation, VTE prevention and tailored fluids; emergency contamination or shock changes priorities.
Distinguish left hemicolectomy from Hartmann's procedure: Hartmann leaves a closed distal stump and end colostomy rather than a primary join.
Sources: Hemicolectomy StatPearls 2023; ASCRS SAGES Operative ERAS 2023; Gill 2019 well-leg

## Hartmann's procedure (General & GI)
Resection of diseased sigmoid/rectosigmoid colon, closure of the distal rectal stump and formation of an end colostomy without a primary anastomosis. Often used for perforated diverticulitis or other high-risk emergency colorectal disease, but not the default for every perforation. Restoration of continuity is a separate later operation and is not guaranteed.
Position: Supine or modified lithotomy; often open abdominal access in unstable patients, with minimally invasive approaches in selected cases.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Resuscitate and prepare for source control; explore the abdomen and identify perforation, contamination or obstruction. Anaesthetic note: Give indicated antibiotics promptly and manage hypovolaemia/sepsis alongside urgent surgery. Plan induction for aspiration risk and possible cardiovascular collapse, including appropriate monitoring and vasoactive support.
2. Mobilise affected sigmoid/rectosigmoid bowel and identify/protect ureters within inflamed tissue. Anaesthetic note: Inflammation distorts tissue planes and may increase blood loss. Track haemodynamics, temperature, urine output and acid-base trends, interpreting them together rather than using one target alone.
3. Control mesenteric vessels and resect the diseased bowel to suitable margins. Anaesthetic note: Communicate escalating vasopressor needs, coagulopathy, acidosis and hypothermia. In extreme instability, abbreviated damage-control surgery may supersede completing the planned procedure.
4. Close the distal rectal stump and bring viable proximal colon to an end-colostomy site; do not form a primary join. Anaesthetic note: Maintain perfusion and reassess losses. A closed rectal stump can still leak and cause pelvic sepsis; absence of an anastomosis does not eliminate postoperative intra-abdominal complications.
5. Complete source control, mature the colostomy, close when appropriate and transfer with a clear postoperative plan. Anaesthetic note: Reassess ventilation, perfusion and organ support before deciding on extubation. High-risk septic patients may require ongoing critical care; hand over antibiotics, fluid balance, vasoactive drugs and concerns about source-control adequacy.
Induction in shock or bowel obstruction
Dissection through inflamed planes and bleeding
Adequacy of source control
Postoperative organ support and rectal-stump leak
WSES 2020 recommends Hartmann for diffuse diverticular peritonitis in critically ill patients and selected patients with multiple comorbidities; the recommendation is strong but based on low-quality evidence. Selected stable patients may instead undergo primary anastomosis with or without diversion.
A later reversal requires reassessment of fitness and pelvic anatomy; many patients retain a permanent stoma. Do not promise reversal.
Balance rapid source control with resuscitation, multimodal analgesia, VTE prevention and stoma care. Elective fasting/carbohydrate pathways are not automatically appropriate for obstructed or septic emergency patients.
Sources: WSES Hartmann 2020; Hartmann Reversal Audit 2018; ERAS Emergency Laparotomy 2023

## Operative hysteroscopy (polypectomy or submucosal fibroid resection) (Gynaecology)
A hysteroscope passes through the cervix into a fluid-distended uterine cavity. Polyps or selected submucosal fibroids are removed using mechanical or electrosurgical instruments. Larger/deeper fibroids may need staged treatment; a diagnostic outpatient hysteroscopy is a different procedure.
Position: Lithotomy, with both legs moved together; protect pressure points and allow continuous access to fluid-balance monitoring.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Assess the lesion, bleeding/anaemia, pregnancy exclusion, comorbidities and intended distension medium; agree fluid-deficit stop limits. Anaesthetic note: Distinguish saline used with bipolar/mechanical systems from electrolyte-free media used with some monopolar systems. Tailor limits to cardiac/renal reserve; the surgeon and anaesthetist must agree them before starting.
2. Establish the agreed anaesthesia, position in lithotomy, dilate the cervix if required and introduce the hysteroscope. Anaesthetic note: General, regional or selected local techniques depend on procedure and patient. Cervical manipulation can cause vagal bradycardia; perforation can occur during dilation or insertion.
3. Distend and inspect the uterine cavity, identifying the lesion and tubal ostia. Anaesthetic note: Track inflow minus recovered outflow continuously, including spillage. A measured deficit is not identical to intravascular absorption. Use the lowest distension pressure compatible with visibility.
4. Resect the polyp or fibroid under direct vision and retrieve tissue for histology. Anaesthetic note: Opened venous channels allow intravasation. Saline overload can cause pulmonary oedema; hypotonic media can also cause hyponatraemia. Suspect perforation or vascular gas embolism with sudden hypotension, hypoxaemia or an abrupt capnography change.
5. Check haemostasis and final fluid deficit, withdraw instruments and plan recovery or escalation. Anaesthetic note: Communicate the medium, deficit and any suspected injury. New breathlessness, confusion, hypoxaemia or instability requires assessment for overload, electrolyte disturbance, haemorrhage or perforation rather than routine discharge.
Cervical entry — perforation or vagal response
Intravasation through opened uterine vessels
Abrupt cardiorespiratory deterioration — gas embolism or bleeding
Final fluid reconciliation and recovery assessment
Fluid-deficit limits are stop/escalation safeguards, not quantities known to be safe for an individual patient. Avoid treating every recorded deficit as absorbed fluid.
This entry covers transcervical intrauterine surgery, not laparoscopic hysterectomy. Confirm equipment, electrosurgical mode, medium and local emergency pathway at the brief.
Sources: BSGE ESGE Hysteroscopy Fluid 2016; Operative Hysteroscopy Anaesthesia 2021

## Transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) (Urology)
A resectoscope enters through the urethra and removes visible bladder tumour with tissue for pathological staging, often including detrusor muscle where appropriate. Lateral-wall electrosurgery can stimulate the obturator nerve and cause an abrupt adductor contraction. Tumour burden and repeat/re-staging procedures vary.
Position: Lithotomy with protected legs and pressure points; urinary drainage and irrigation remain accessible.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Review tumour site/size, haematuria, anaemia, anticoagulants, infection and the resection plan. Anaesthetic note: Identify a lateral-wall tumour before choosing anaesthesia. Agree how to prevent obturator-mediated leg movement; neuraxial anaesthesia alone does not reliably block this reflex.
2. Establish anaesthesia, position and insert the resectoscope through the urethra. Anaesthetic note: General anaesthesia with adequate neuromuscular block or regional anaesthesia with selected obturator nerve block may be used according to the plan. Avoid assuming immobility because the patient is unconscious.
3. Survey the bladder under irrigation, locating tumour, ureteric orifices and the intended resection margins. Anaesthetic note: Avoid overdistension and track irrigation losses. Bipolar saline avoids the classic hypotonic-medium mechanism but does not eliminate fluid overload or extravasation.
4. Resect tumour and obtain appropriate base/deep tissue for staging, then coagulate bleeding points. Anaesthetic note: An obturator jerk can drive the loop through the bladder wall. Stop and reassess sudden leg movement, abdominal distension, pain in an awake patient, or unexplained instability; perforation may be intraperitoneal or extraperitoneal.
5. Confirm haemostasis, retrieve specimens and establish drainage; decide whether immediate intravesical treatment is appropriate. Anaesthetic note: Suspected perforation or bleeding requiring irrigation changes the postoperative plan and can contraindicate immediate intravesical chemotherapy. Handover haematuria, catheter/irrigation requirements and any suspected injury.
Lateral-wall resection — obturator jerk
Bladder perforation and irrigation extravasation
Haemostasis and postoperative clot retention
Low blood-loss risk is a qualitative badge: large, vascular or extensive tumours can bleed substantially. Differentiate TURBT from prostate resection rather than copying a TURP plan.
Coordinate analgesia, nausea prevention and monitoring with the intended day-case or inpatient pathway; persistent bleeding, pain or physiological change needs reassessment.
Sources: TURBT Technique Review 2020; Obturator Jerk Review 2018; EAU TURBT Instillation 2025

## Burn excision and split-thickness skin grafting (Breast & Plastics)
Non-viable burned tissue is excised to a suitable wound bed and covered with a thin autologous skin graft, often meshed. The donor retains part of its dermis so it can heal. Large burns commonly need staged operations; temporary coverage may be used when definitive autograft is not yet feasible.
Position: Depends on burn and donor sites; supine, lateral or prone. Plan turning, pressure protection and secure airway/vascular access before draping.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Review burn extent/depth, time since injury, inhalation injury, resuscitation, organ function, infection and donor sites. Anaesthetic note: The early shock phase and later hypermetabolic phase differ. Assess airway oedema or contracture, available access, haemoglobin and blood availability; small grafts do not share the risk of extensive excision.
2. Establish anaesthesia, position and warm the patient; prepare recipient and donor sites. Anaesthetic note: Large exposed surfaces create substantial heat loss. Warm fluids and theatre measures must remain compatible with skin injury and fire safety. Altered drug responses and repeated anaesthetics require individual assessment.
3. Excise eschar tangentially or to the selected deeper plane; achieve haemostasis. Anaesthetic note: Diffuse wound bleeding can be rapid and underestimated in soaked swabs/drapes. Reconcile losses, perfusion, haemoglobin and coagulation with the team; local adrenaline or tourniquet measures do not replace monitoring.
4. Harvest partial-thickness donor skin, mesh if selected, and apply/fix the graft to the prepared bed. Anaesthetic note: The donor site adds pain and bleeding. Maintain perfusion and temperature without indiscriminate fluid loading; consider appropriate regional/local analgesia as part of a multimodal plan.
5. Dress graft and donor sites, protect immobilisation and transfer with a recovery/critical-care plan. Anaesthetic note: Handover blood products, fluid balance, temperature, analgesia and graft positioning. Major burns, inhalation injury or ongoing instability may require continued ventilation and critical care rather than immediate extubation.
Airway control with inhalation injury or contracture
Excision — deceptively rapid blood loss
Extensive exposure — hypothermia
Transfer and dressing-related positioning requirements
Burn resuscitation formulae are starting guides, not automatic intraoperative replacement prescriptions; use measured physiological endpoints and the burns-team plan.
Suxamethonium can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia after burn-related receptor upregulation; avoid its use outside the immediate acute window and follow specialist guidance. Resistance to non-depolarising relaxants may develop; use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring.
Graft and donor-site pain are distinct from background burn pain. Agree dressing-change analgesia, nutrition and rehabilitation with the specialist team.
Sources: Bittner Burn Perioperative 2015; Burn Debridement Grafting 2023

## Bimaxillary orthognathic surgery (Le Fort I and mandibular sagittal split) (Oral & Maxillofacial)
Planned osteotomies reposition the maxilla and mandible to correct skeletal jaw relationships. A Le Fort I mobilises the maxilla; bilateral sagittal splits mobilise the tooth-bearing mandible. Splints/temporary fixation establish occlusion before plates secure the new position. Jaw order, movements and additions vary.
Position: Supine with supported head and agreed head-up tilt; protect eyes, teeth and nerves. The surgeon shares the airway and needs dental occlusion.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Review airway, jaw anatomy, OSA, nasal patency, imaging, orthodontic plan and anticipated blood loss. Anaesthetic note: Agree nasal versus alternative airway access and postoperative fixation/rescue plans. Restricted oral opening or abnormal craniofacial anatomy may alter airway strategy; elective nasal intubation is not automatically safe in every patient.
2. Secure the agreed airway, protect pressure points and expose intraoral tissues. Anaesthetic note: Fix the tube away from the operative field and recheck it after movement. A throat pack is not routine; if selected, record insertion/removal. Local vasoconstrictors require dose communication and haemodynamic observation.
3. Perform Le Fort I maxillary mobilisation and bilateral sagittal mandibular splits in the planned order. Anaesthetic note: Maxillary/pterygoid bleeding can be brisk. Monitor blood loss and be ready for trigeminocardiac bradycardia during manipulation. A field-quality strategy must not compromise cerebral or systemic perfusion.
4. Reposition the jaw segments using the occlusal splint; apply temporary intermaxillary fixation and secure plates/screws. Anaesthetic note: Dental fixation removes oral airway access. Know how fixation will be released in an emergency; coordinate tube position and any release before extubation.
5. Check haemostasis and occlusion, remove any pack, suction under direct vision and implement the agreed extubation plan. Anaesthetic note: Blood, facial swelling, nasal obstruction and residual sedation can compromise breathing. Selected high-risk patients need delayed extubation. Ensure fixation-release equipment, antiemesis and trained postoperative staff.
Shared-airway access and tube protection
Maxillary mobilisation — bleeding or trigeminocardiac reflex
Intermaxillary fixation — loss of oral access
Extubation with swelling and altered jaw anatomy
The diagram is a local lateral teaching view, not a blueprint for osteotomy angles or a complete vascular map. Genioplasty and other adjuncts alter the sequence.
Use multimodal analgesia and nausea prevention, especially if elastics/fixation remain. Postoperative airway strategy must account for OSA and the direction of jaw movement, not just procedure duration.
Sources: Haq Orthognathic Anaesthesia 2024; RCoA Dental GPAS

## Total laryngectomy (ENT & Head and Neck)
Removal of the entire larynx, usually for cancer, permanently separates the trachea from the pharynx. The trachea is sutured to the neck skin as an end stoma; the pharynx is closed for swallowing. Neck dissection or flap reconstruction may be added. Partial laryngectomy preserves different anatomy and is not covered by this sequence.
Position: Supine, head supported with agreed neck extension; protect irradiated or restricted cervical tissues and maintain access to the airway and lines.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Review endoscopy/imaging, tumour obstruction, prior radiotherapy, nutrition and the resection/reconstruction plan; agree primary and rescue airway strategies. Anaesthetic note: Stridor, a friable tumour or restricted neck/mouth opening can make induction hazardous. An awake approach or awake surgical airway may be appropriate after specialist assessment; avoid assuming a standard asleep oral intubation will be safe.
2. Establish anaesthesia and the agreed airway; expose the neck and perform neck dissection if indicated. Anaesthetic note: Secure the tube away from the field and keep rescue access available. Assess access/arterial monitoring and blood availability by anticipated extent; previous radiotherapy increases technical difficulty.
3. Mobilise the larynx, divide the trachea and transfer ventilation to a sterile cuffed tube through the distal trachea. Anaesthetic note: Explicitly coordinate the airway handover. Protect the cuff from cutting instruments; use airway-fire precautions around an open oxygenated trachea. Confirm sustained waveform capnography, depth and fixation before abandoning the previous airway.
4. Remove the larynx, close or reconstruct the pharyngeal defect, and mature the permanent tracheal end stoma; a voice prosthesis may be placed. Anaesthetic note: After separation, mouth/nose oxygen and oral intubation cannot reach the lungs. Check stomal-tube depth to avoid endobronchial placement; flap reconstruction adds prolonged surgery, perfusion and donor-site considerations.
5. Complete haemostasis, drains and airway checks; transfer with a laryngectomy-specific handover and bedhead sign. Anaesthetic note: Oxygenation, suction and any ventilation are through the stoma. Ensure humidification, suitable emergency equipment and trained staff. Monitor bleeding, plugging and swelling; do not remove a TEP voice prosthesis during routine airway troubleshooting.
Induction with a potentially obstructed tumour airway
Tracheal division and transfer of ventilation
Permanent loss of mouth-to-lung connection
Postoperative stoma obstruction or bleeding
A total laryngectomy is not a tracheostomy: the upper airway no longer connects to the lungs. If anatomy is uncertain in an emergency, oxygenate face and stoma until clarified.
Plan multimodal analgesia, nutrition, communication support and postoperative care with the head-and-neck team. Pharyngocutaneous fistula and wound problems are later surgical concerns.
These are typical high-level stages, not a dissection guide; combined neck dissection/flap work changes duration and blood-loss risk. Emergency recommendations follow NTSP.
Sources: Stephens Elective Laryngectomy 2017; NTSP Operative Laryngectomy Safety; ERAS Head & Neck 2017

## Glossectomy (partial, hemi- or total tongue resection) (ENT & Head and Neck)
Resection of part or all of the tongue for cancer. A small accessible defect may be closed directly; larger defects can need regional or free-flap reconstruction, sometimes with neck dissection. The extent and location of resection determine airway, swallowing and speech consequences; total tongue resection is not equivalent to a small partial glossectomy.
Position: Supine with head supported; oral access and tube route agreed before draping. A flap donor site may need simultaneous access and careful limb positioning.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Review tumour site/extent, mouth opening, endoscopy/imaging, bleeding, swallowing, aspiration risk, nutrition and prior radiotherapy. Anaesthetic note: Agree the primary airway and rescue plan with the surgeon. Large tongue/base-of-tongue lesions can obstruct ventilation and be damaged by instrumentation; consider awake airway management in an at-risk patient.
2. Secure the airway using the agreed route and expose the oral cavity; elective tracheostomy may be performed for extensive surgery. Anaesthetic note: Nasal intubation can improve oral access when appropriate, but is not mandatory or suitable for every case. Plan postoperative airway protection before resection, not after swelling appears.
3. Resect the involved tongue with oncological margins; control lingual vessels and perform neck dissection if indicated. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding can be brisk and enter the shared airway. Track suction losses and haemoglobin by clinical need; recheck the tube after retractors or head movements. Margins and resection extent are surgical decisions.
4. Close the defect or reconstruct with a flap; free-flap vessels are joined to recipient neck vessels and perfusion assessed. Anaesthetic note: Maintain temperature, oxygenation and adequate perfusion without indiscriminate fluid loading. Goal-directed fluids and judicious vasopressors may be appropriate; protect donor-site pressure points and communicate perfusion concerns.
5. Check haemostasis and the reconstructed airway; recover with planned tracheostomy care, delayed extubation or selected immediate extubation. Anaesthetic note: Tongue/floor-of-mouth oedema, flap bulk and haematoma can obstruct the airway and make reintubation difficult. Extubation requires an assessed rescue plan and appropriate monitoring; no single strategy suits all resections.
Initial airway control with a friable or obstructing tumour
Lingual vessel bleeding in a shared airway
Flap reperfusion and prolonged reconstruction
Postoperative obstruction from oedema, flap bulk or haematoma
Tracheostomy is not routine for every small partial glossectomy, but may be essential for extensive or high-risk resections; evidence from selected reconstruction cohorts cannot override individual assessment.
Plan opioid-sparing analgesia, aspiration precautions, enteral nutrition and speech/swallow rehabilitation with the multidisciplinary team.
Blood loss and care requirements rise with neck dissection, extensive resection and free-flap reconstruction; the moderate-risk badge is qualitative, not a predicted volume.
Sources: Ma Oral Reconstruction 2024; Madgar Reconstruction Airway 2022; ERAS Head & Neck 2017; McCauley Free Flap Anaesthesia 2022

## Microlaryngoscopy (biopsy or endoscopic laryngeal surgery) (ENT & Head and Neck)
A rigid suspension laryngoscope exposes the larynx for magnified inspection, biopsy or treatment of vocal-fold lesions. Cold instruments or a laser may be used. The surgeon and anaesthetist share the same narrow airway; stenosis or an obstructing lesion can make a short procedure high risk.
Position: Supine in an individually suitable laryngoscopy position; protect teeth, lips, eyes and cervical spine. Suspension limits airway access.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Review airway symptoms, endoscopy, lesion/stenosis, respiratory reserve and cervical/dental issues; agree surgical and ventilation plans. Anaesthetic note: Stridor and severe obstruction demand specialist planning, including rescue access and whether spontaneous breathing should initially be preserved. Select a small tube or a specialist tubeless technique according to lesion, access and team expertise.
2. Induce anaesthesia using the agreed approach and establish ventilation; protect teeth and insert the suspension laryngoscope. Anaesthetic note: Insertion is strongly stimulating. TIVA is often useful for open-airway techniques; muscle relaxation depends on the strategy. Reassess ventilation and tube/catheter position after suspension rather than assuming the airway is unchanged.
3. Inspect the larynx under magnification and perform biopsy or the planned lesion treatment. Anaesthetic note: A small tracheal tube may restrict surgical access and increase resistance. Tubeless approaches need explicit oxygenation, ventilation and rescue plans; oxygen insufflation alone does not guarantee carbon-dioxide clearance.
4. If jet ventilation or laser treatment is selected, apply its dedicated safety plan throughout treatment. Anaesthetic note: Jet ventilation requires unobstructed expiration: impaired egress can cause gas trapping and barotrauma. Monitor oxygenation and CO2 by methods appropriate to the technique. For laser use, choose wavelength-appropriate laser-resistant equipment when a tube is used, minimise oxidiser enrichment as safely feasible, avoid nitrous oxide and coordinate ignition/oxygen delivery. Tubeless oxygen also carries fire risk.
5. Secure haemostasis, remove instruments and reassess the airway before emergence and recovery. Anaesthetic note: Look for bleeding, oedema or residual obstruction; suction appropriately and agree extubation or continued airway support. Watch for laryngospasm, stridor, hypoventilation and barotrauma; recovery/discharge depends on airway status, not just procedure length.
Induction with laryngeal obstruction
Suspension — restricted access or displaced tube
Jet ventilation — inadequate expiration and barotrauma
Laser activation — airway fire
Emergence — laryngospasm or oedema
Small-tube ventilation, intermittent apnoea, spontaneous ventilation and jet ventilation are alternatives with different limitations; none is a default for all lesions.
Jet pressures, frequencies and apnoea intervals require specialist equipment and patient-specific protocols, not values inferred from this summary.
For suspected airway fire, stop surgery and oxidiser delivery, remove burning airway material and extinguish with saline/water, then re-establish ventilation and assess injury according to the local emergency protocol.
Sources: Pearson Laryngotracheal Anaesthesia 2017; Dow Jet Ventilation 2023; Rogers Tracheostomy Fire 2001

## Paediatric dental extractions under general anaesthesia (Paediatric)
Removal of diseased teeth, sometimes alongside restorations, during one general anaesthetic. The dental team and anaesthetist share the airway; the extent of treatment is agreed before starting.
Position: Supine with head supported; dental access, tube route and table rotation agreed with the team.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Review the dental plan, consent, medical history, fasting and airway; agree recovery and discharge arrangements. Anaesthetic note: Assess age, respiratory illness, obstructive sleep apnoea and comorbidities. Complex or high-risk children need an appropriate paediatric service, not simply a longer routine day-case slot.
2. Induce anaesthesia and secure an airway compatible with the dental work; nasal tracheal intubation is common when suitable. Anaesthetic note: The airway is shared and may become inaccessible. Confirm tube position, fixation and the rescue plan; nasal instrumentation can itself cause bleeding.
3. Examine the teeth; extract the planned teeth, with local anaesthetic and restorative treatment where indicated. Anaesthetic note: Record all local anaesthetic administered by both teams to avoid cumulative toxicity. Suction blood and debris; communicate before moving the head or applying instruments near the tube.
4. Achieve socket haemostasis and clear the mouth; confirm removal of any throat pack used. Anaesthetic note: A throat pack is not automatically required. If used, its insertion and removal must be explicitly recorded and checked; do not rely on a pack to replace airway protection or suction.
5. Recover the airway and observe until appropriate for discharge. Anaesthetic note: Anticipate laryngospasm, obstruction, pain, nausea and bleeding. Choose the extubation strategy by aspiration and airway risk; give carers clear bleeding, hydration and analgesia advice.
Airway instrumentation and restricted access
Blood/debris during extraction
Pack-removal check if used
Emergence — laryngospasm or obstruction
Blood loss is usually small but must be judged against the child's size and extent of surgery.
Coordinate multimodal analgesia and antiemetics without duplicating drugs given by the dental team.
Service guidance supports the care setting; it does not prescribe the extraction technique.
Sources: RCoA Dental GPAS; NHS Child Dental GA

## Paediatric circumcision (Paediatric)
Removal of the foreskin for an agreed indication. This entry concerns hospital surgery in children, not neonatal bedside device circumcision; technique and anaesthesia depend on age and clinical circumstances.
Position: Supine, with warming and modesty maintained; local access without excessive leg abduction.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Confirm indication, consent and operative plan, including anatomical abnormalities and bleeding history. Anaesthetic note: Assess age, prematurity, respiratory illness and day-case suitability; postoperative respiratory observation is individualised.
2. Provide anaesthesia and analgesia: commonly general anaesthesia with a penile/ring block or another agreed regional technique. Anaesthetic note: Selected infants may have spinal anaesthesia in experienced services. Track total local anaesthetic across all injections; a block does not remove the need for respiratory monitoring.
3. Prepare the field, release adhesions as required and excise the foreskin using the planned technique. Anaesthetic note: Check that analgesia is adequate before incision. Surgical methods vary; this is not a cutting or block-placement guide.
