4. Control bleeding, suture skin edges and apply the planned dressing. Anaesthetic note: Persistent bleeding warrants surgical reassessment, even when the expected blood loss is low. Avoid assuming a distressed child only has pain.
5. Recover and provide wound, pain and urinary advice. Anaesthetic note: Plan opioid-sparing analgesia; review bleeding and ability to pass urine according to the service's discharge pathway. Former preterm infants may need extended observation.
Regional/local injection — cumulative dose
Incision before block onset
Bleeding and postoperative urinary problems
General, local and neuraxial approaches are not interchangeable in every child.
Use age- and risk-appropriate recovery arrangements; no universal discharge time is set here.
Sources: NHS Child Circumcision; OpenAnesthesia Infant Spinal

## Paediatric inguinal hernia repair (Paediatric)
Closure of a patent processus vaginalis causing an indirect hernia. Open herniotomy or laparoscopic closure may be used; routine childhood repair usually does not require the mesh reinforcement used in adults.
Position: Supine; open groin exposure or laparoscopic abdominal ports.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Confirm side, reducibility, urgency and evidence of incarceration or compromised bowel. Anaesthetic note: An incarcerated hernia can bring dehydration, obstruction and aspiration risk; it is not equivalent to a well elective infant. Assess prematurity and respiratory risk.
2. Induce anaesthesia or establish an agreed regional technique in a selected infant. Anaesthetic note: An awake spinal approach can reduce some early respiratory events but does not abolish postoperative apnoea risk; sedation and conversion plans matter.
3. Open approach: expose and separate the sac from cord structures. Laparoscopic approach: inspect the internal ring and hernia contents. Anaesthetic note: Maintain warmth. Laparoscopic insufflation affects ventilation and venous return; communicate pressure and positioning concerns rather than applying adult assumptions.
4. Reduce contents and close the sac neck/internal ring while protecting adjacent structures. Anaesthetic note: If bowel is compromised, the operation and postoperative needs may expand. Contralateral inspection or repair is an individual surgical decision, not automatic.
5. Close and recover with a risk-based respiratory and analgesia plan. Anaesthetic note: Former preterm and young infants may need monitored admission. Observe for apnoea irrespective of apparently uncomplicated surgery or the anaesthetic technique.
Incarceration — possible obstruction
Infant induction or regional conversion
Pneumoperitoneum if laparoscopic
Postoperative apnoea risk
Adult hernia guidance and routine mesh repair should not be transferred to infants.
Regional analgesia and local infiltration can reduce opioid requirements; discharge depends on infant risk and local policy.
Sources: AAP Inguinal Hernias 2023; OpenAnesthesia Infant Spinal

## Mitral valve repair or replacement (Cardiothoracic)
Repair of native valve leaflets/chordae and often the annulus, or replacement with a prosthesis. Sternotomy and minimally invasive approaches differ; this entry does not cover transcatheter edge-to-edge repair.
Position: Supine for sternotomy; modified supine for right mini-thoracotomy, with peripheral cannulation access if planned.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Review lesion, ventricular and right-heart function, pulmonary pressures and the operative approach; establish monitoring and anaesthesia. Anaesthetic note: Mitral stenosis and regurgitation have different haemodynamic priorities. Avoid generic valve targets; assess rhythm, filling and cardiac output using the actual lesion and physiology.
2. Expose the heart, anticoagulate and cannulate for cardiopulmonary bypass; clamp the aorta and give cardioplegia. Anaesthetic note: Confirm anticoagulation and bypass readiness. Peripheral cannulation adds limb/vascular risks; minimally invasive work may require lung isolation and makes airway access harder.
3. Open the left atrium and repair or replace the valve. Anaesthetic note: Coordinate perfusion, temperature and blood conservation. Repair may use a ring and leaflet/chordal techniques; the chosen repair is not represented by one universal sequence.
4. Close, de-air, release the clamp and separate from bypass with transoesophageal echocardiographic assessment. Anaesthetic note: Assess residual regurgitation/gradient, ventricular function and complications such as systolic anterior motion after repair. Troubleshoot low output with the surgeon and perfusionist rather than treating every cause alike.
5. Reverse anticoagulation when agreed, achieve haemostasis and transfer to cardiac critical care. Anaesthetic note: Plan bleeding surveillance, rhythm/pacing and ventilatory support. Postoperative antithrombotic treatment depends on repair versus prosthesis, rhythm and the cardiology/surgical plan.
Induction in severe valve disease
Cannulation and anticoagulation
De-airing and separation from bypass
Residual valve dysfunction or low output
High bleeding risk reflects bypass and major cardiac surgery, not a predicted transfusion requirement.
TOE use requires expertise and assessment of contraindications; minimally invasive and sternotomy pathways differ.
Sources: Minimally Invasive Mitral Review; EACTS CPB 2024

## Pneumonectomy (Cardiothoracic)
Removal of an entire lung, usually for malignancy. This is more physiologically demanding than lobectomy; postoperative reserve, right-heart load and protection of the remaining lung dominate planning.
Position: Lateral decubitus with the operative side uppermost; approach may be open or minimally invasive.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Confirm resection extent and cardiopulmonary fitness, including predicted postoperative lung function and exercise assessment when indicated. Anaesthetic note: Review right ventricular function, pulmonary hypertension and previous treatment; a completion pneumonectomy can be especially complex. Agree analgesia and postoperative care before induction.
2. Induce anaesthesia, establish lung isolation and position laterally. Anaesthetic note: Confirm device position bronchoscopically and recheck after positioning. Protect dependent pressure points and ensure access to the airway and vascular lines.
3. Enter the chest and dissect the hilum, dividing pulmonary vessels and the main bronchus in the surgeon's chosen sequence. Anaesthetic note: Anticipate major vascular bleeding and hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation. Communicate before vessel occlusion; protect the ventilated lung and investigate sudden haemodynamic change.
4. Remove the lung and check bronchial stump closure, haemostasis and the surgical drainage plan. Anaesthetic note: Stump tests require coordinated ventilation. Drain management after pneumonectomy is procedure-specific; do not automatically apply lobectomy suction practices.
5. Close, restore two-airway communication as appropriate and recover for close respiratory/cardiac surveillance. Anaesthetic note: Use careful, individualised fluid management to avoid both hypoperfusion and remaining-lung oedema. Watch for respiratory deterioration, arrhythmias and right-heart dysfunction.
One-lung ventilation — hypoxaemia
Hilar vessel division — major bleeding
Bronchial stump and drainage plan
Remaining-lung injury and postoperative arrhythmia
Avoid fluid overload; a rigid fluid volume is not prescribed by this summary.
Analgesia must allow effective breathing and coughing without excessive sedation. Planned recovery location reflects physiological risk, not operation name alone.
Sources: Pneumonectomy Anaesthesia Review; ERAS Thoracic 2019

## Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (General & GI)
A small gastric pouch is joined to a Roux limb of jejunum; a second bowel join reunites it with the biliopancreatic limb. The excluded stomach usually remains in situ. This differs from sleeve gastrectomy and one-anastomosis bypass.
Position: Supine, usually head-up during laparoscopy; secure against sliding and protect pressure points.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Review bariatric assessment, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiometabolic disease, airway and thromboprophylaxis plans. Anaesthetic note: Plan preoxygenation, airway equipment and postoperative respiratory support; obesity does not itself justify treating all patients as having identical aspiration or airway risk.
2. Induce anaesthesia, position and establish laparoscopic ports/pneumoperitoneum. Anaesthetic note: Rapid desaturation and difficult mask ventilation may occur. Reassess tube position, ventilation and haemodynamics after insufflation and head-up positioning.
3. Create the small gastric pouch and divide the jejunum to form the Roux and biliopancreatic limbs. Anaesthetic note: Stapling/dissection can cause bleeding. Coordinate any gastric tube positioning or withdrawal before stapling; prevent accidental incorporation of the tube.
4. Construct the gastrojejunostomy and jejunojejunostomy, in the surgeon's chosen order; close relevant mesenteric defects. Anaesthetic note: Maintain stable perfusion and ventilation through a potentially prolonged operation; technique and limb lengths vary and are not prescribed here.
5. Check the joins as planned, remove instruments and recover through the bariatric pathway. Anaesthetic note: Use multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, PONV prevention and risk-based respiratory support. Unexplained tachycardia, pain or deterioration may indicate bleeding or leak and warrants urgent review.
Induction — limited oxygen reserve
Insufflation and head-up
Stapling near gastric tube
Postoperative bleeding, leak or respiratory compromise
VTE prevention, early mobilisation and safe nutrition follow the bariatric programme.
Sleep-apnoea support is individualised; do not replace the patient's established plan with a blanket rule.
Sources: NHS Roux-en-Y; Bariatric Anaesthesia Review; ERAS Bariatric 2022

## Pars plana vitrectomy and retinal repair (Ophthalmic)
Removal of vitreous through small scleral ports, followed by treatment of retinal pathology. Laser, membrane peeling and gas or silicone-oil tamponade may be used; external scleral buckling is a different or additional technique.
Position: Supine with head still under ophthalmic drapes; postoperative posture depends on the repair.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Confirm eye, indication, previous ocular gas and choice of local/regional anaesthesia with monitored care or general anaesthesia. Anaesthetic note: Assess ability to lie still and tolerate duration/drapes. Check block risks and cardiopulmonary disease; general anaesthesia may be appropriate when cooperation or airway safety is uncertain.
2. Prepare the eye and insert pars plana ports with an infusion system. Anaesthetic note: Prevent coughing, movement and straining during intraocular work. Sedation must not compromise ventilation under restricted-access drapes.
3. Remove vitreous and perform the indicated retinal repair, such as membrane peeling or laser. Anaesthetic note: Ocular manipulation, particularly accompanying scleral buckle work, can trigger bradycardia. Alert the surgeon, stop the stimulus and assess oxygenation/ventilation before further treatment.
4. Use gas or oil tamponade if needed; close the ports. Anaesthetic note: Do not use nitrous oxide when intraocular gas is present: bubble expansion can raise intraocular pressure and cause permanent visual loss. This also applies to later anaesthetics and nitrous-oxide analgesia while gas remains.
5. Recover with antiemetic/analgesic treatment and explicit gas/posture instructions. Anaesthetic note: Record the gas and ophthalmic restrictions. Air travel, altitude and future anaesthesia advice lasts until ophthalmology confirms gas resolution, not a universal number of days.
Ocular block and immobility
Oculocardiac reflex
Gas tamponade — nitrous oxide exclusion
Postoperative posture and future anaesthesia advice
A Low blood-loss category does not mean low consequence from ocular haemorrhage.
Gas and silicone oil are not interchangeable; nitrous oxide restrictions specifically concern gas.
Sources: AAO Vitreoretinal Anaesthesia; RCOphth Intraocular Gas Safety 2018

## Lumbar microdiscectomy (Orthopaedic & Spine)
Removal of a herniated lumbar disc fragment compressing a nerve root, through open microscopic or minimally invasive access. It is not a spinal fusion; exposure and extent of disc removal vary.
Position: Usually prone on supports that avoid abdominal compression, with eyes and pressure points protected.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Confirm symptoms, baseline neurology, level, imaging and consent; identify urgent deficits or cauda equina features. Anaesthetic note: Record neurological deficits before anaesthesia. Agree any neuromonitoring, positioning limitations and postoperative neurological review.
2. Provide anaesthesia and turn prone with a secured airway and coordinated team. Anaesthetic note: Recheck tube, ventilation, lines, eyes and pressure areas after turning. The abdomen should not be compressed; prone positioning reduces access for airway rescue.
3. Confirm the level with imaging, expose the operative area and perform limited bony/ligamentous access as required. Anaesthetic note: Wrong-level prevention is a team check. Monitor haemodynamics and blood loss; an apparently small operation can still cause a vascular or dural injury.
4. Identify/protect the nerve root and remove the compressing fragment under magnification. Anaesthetic note: Communicate unexpected bleeding or physiological change. A dural tear may change the surgical closure and postoperative mobilisation plan.
5. Check decompression/haemostasis, close, turn supine and recover. Anaesthetic note: Check limb movement and symptoms against baseline once assessable. New weakness, worsening pain or bladder dysfunction needs urgent surgical assessment rather than attribution to residual anaesthesia.
Turning prone — airway/eye/line protection
Level confirmation
Disc removal — neural or dural injury
New postoperative neurological deficit
Multimodal analgesia and early mobilisation are individualised to the procedure and any complication.
Fusion-specific blood-loss estimates and protocols do not automatically apply to microdiscectomy.
Sources: UCLH Microdiscectomy; ASA Visual Loss 2019

## Manual removal of retained placenta (Obstetric)
Manual separation and removal of a retained placenta after vaginal birth under appropriate anaesthesia. Bleeding and haemodynamic state determine urgency; suspected placenta accreta spectrum requires senior obstetric planning, not forced separation.
Position: Lithotomy in theatre, with safe supports and access for haemorrhage resuscitation.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Assess retention, blood loss, uterine tone and haemodynamic state; escalate and prepare theatre. Anaesthetic note: Visible bleeding may underestimate total loss. Activate the obstetric haemorrhage pathway when indicated, obtain access and prepare blood products according to the clinical situation.
2. Establish regional or general anaesthesia appropriate to urgency, circulating volume and any existing epidural. Anaesthetic note: Neuraxial extension is not automatically safe in major hypovolaemia. General anaesthesia needs an obstetric airway and aspiration-risk plan; communicate the resuscitation priorities.
3. Support the uterus externally and pass a hand through the cervix to locate the placental separation plane. Anaesthetic note: Ensure adequate anaesthesia and monitor continuing blood loss; uterine manipulation is painful and may provoke rapid physiological change.
4. Separate and remove the placenta if a safe plane exists; assess completeness and uterine cavity. Anaesthetic note: If no plane can be found, stop and seek senior help for possible accreta. Do not force detachment; haemorrhage may escalate and require a different operative strategy.
5. Treat uterine atony/haemorrhage, give prophylactic antibiotics per the adopted protocol and arrange recovery. Anaesthetic note: Reassess haemostasis, perfusion, coagulation and analgesia. Uterotonic choice and drug doses follow the local obstetric pathway; continue surveillance for bleeding and infection.
Haemorrhage and anaesthetic choice
Painful uterine exploration
No separation plane — possible accreta
Persistent atony or bleeding after removal
High risk describes the potential for major postpartum haemorrhage, not a prediction that every patient will bleed heavily.
This summary deliberately does not set a universal time-to-removal or drug regimen.
Sources: NHS Scotland Retained Placenta; MSF Manual Placenta Removal

## Carotid artery stenting (Vascular)
Endovascular treatment of selected carotid stenoses with a stent. This is not carotid endarterectomy: plaque remains in place, and patient selection, embolic protection and antiplatelet planning are central.
Position: Supine on a radiolucent table; access may be femoral, radial or a selected direct carotid approach.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Confirm the planned access, antiplatelet preparation and baseline neurological examination; obtain arterial access, commonly under local anaesthesia. Anaesthetic note: Preserve communication for neurological assessment where feasible. Sedation must not obscure a new deficit or compromise ventilation; establish access to the patient despite the imaging equipment.
2. Navigate catheters and perform angiography to define the lesion. Anaesthetic note: Review renal function, contrast exposure and allergy history. Access injury may cause groin or concealed retroperitoneal bleeding despite an apparently low-blood-loss procedure.
3. Administer procedural heparin before crossing the lesion and establish the chosen embolic protection strategy. Anaesthetic note: Document heparin and anticoagulation monitoring with the operator. Distal filters and proximal flow reversal are different techniques; protection choice is not universal.
4. Selective predilatation, self-expanding stent deployment and selective postdilatation. Anaesthetic note: Carotid sinus stimulation can cause bradycardia, hypotension or asystole. Agree anticholinergic preparation and haemodynamic support before balloon inflation; report neurological change immediately.
5. Completion angiography, removal of protection devices and access closure. Anaesthetic note: Reassess neurology, blood pressure and the access site. Persistent haemodynamic depression or new headache, seizure or deficit needs urgent assessment; plan observation and the prescribed antiplatelet course.
Lesion crossing — cerebral embolisation
Balloon inflation — bradycardia and hypotension
New neurological deficit
Access bleeding and postprocedural blood-pressure disturbance
CIRSE 2024 provides technical standards of practice, not a substitute for individual treatment selection or local emergency pathways.
GALA studied endarterectomy, not stenting: do not transfer its general-versus-local trial result to this procedure.
A qualitative Low blood-loss category does not exclude catastrophic vascular injury. Assess antithrombotic and access-related bleeding risk individually.
Sources: CIRSE Carotid Stenting 2024; ESVS 2023 carotid

## Common femoral endarterectomy (Vascular)
Open removal of obstructing plaque at the common femoral artery, sometimes extending into its branches. A patch may widen the repair; additional angioplasty or stenting makes this a hybrid procedure rather than a bypass.
Position: Supine with the operative groin exposed; hybrid cases need imaging access and preparation for additional arterial access.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Confirm the revascularisation plan and expose the femoral artery through a groin incision. Anaesthetic note: General or spinal anaesthesia is selected by the patient and team. Review cardiovascular, renal and diabetic comorbidity and the antithrombotic plan before choosing a neuraxial technique.
2. Obtain vascular control and open the narrowed artery. Anaesthetic note: Agree and document the procedural anticoagulation plan; prepare for bleeding during arterial exposure. This is local arterial control, not an aortic cross-clamp.
3. Remove plaque from the common femoral artery and any involved branch origins. Anaesthetic note: Maintain stable physiology, warming and adequate analgesia during the period of interrupted limb flow; the extent and duration depend on the disease.
4. Close the arteriotomy, using a patch where appropriate; restore and check limb flow. Anaesthetic note: Communicate before restoration of flow and document the postoperative limb assessment. A cold, painful limb or new deficit requires prompt vascular review.
5. If planned, treat other stenoses with angioplasty or stenting; then close the groin wound. Anaesthetic note: Hybrid work adds procedure time, imaging and contrast exposure. Monitor the access site and arrange analgesia and observation appropriate to the patient's vascular risk.
Arterial exposure and anticoagulation — bleeding
Restoration of flow and limb assessment
Hybrid angioplasty — additional access and contrast
The NHS leaflet supports the broad sequence and anaesthetic options; GVG supplies the limb-revascularisation context, not fixed anaesthetic drug or pressure targets.
The choice of open, endovascular or hybrid treatment depends on disease distribution and patient risk. BASIL-2 is not a trial of anaesthesia for femoral endarterectomy.
Sources: Gloucestershire Femoral Endarterectomy; GVG CLTI 2019

## Kidney transplantation (recipient) (Urology)
Placement of a donor kidney in the recipient's lower abdomen, joining its artery, vein and ureter to the recipient. This entry covers implantation, not donor nephrectomy; native kidneys usually remain in place.
Position: Supine; lower abdominal incision into the chosen iliac fossa, with access to the bladder.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Confirm the graft and recipient plan; induce anaesthesia and prepare the lower abdomen. Anaesthetic note: Check recent dialysis, potassium, acid-base balance, fluid status and cardiovascular disease. Preserve dialysis access; review aspiration risk and renal handling of drugs.
2. Expose recipient vessels and prepare the graft in the iliac fossa. Anaesthetic note: Maintain temperature, perfusion and access for resuscitation. Agree timing of locally prescribed immunosuppression and antimicrobial prophylaxis; infusions may have specific haemodynamic risks.
3. Join the graft vein and artery to recipient vessels under vascular control; the precise sequence varies. Anaesthetic note: Know when reperfusion is approaching. Use clinical assessment and, where appropriate, haemodynamic monitoring to guide volume rather than loading every patient to a fixed central venous pressure.
4. Release vascular control and assess graft perfusion. Anaesthetic note: Anticipate blood-pressure change and reassess potassium, acid-base status and volume. Maintain perfusion without fluid overload; titrated vasopressors may be needed despite adequate filling.
5. Join the donor ureter to the bladder, commonly with a temporary ureteric stent; achieve haemostasis and close. Anaesthetic note: Monitor urine output and postoperative renal biochemistry. Immediate urine production is not guaranteed and its absence alone does not establish graft failure; delayed graft function needs transplant-team assessment.
Induction in a dialysis patient with cardiovascular or electrolyte disturbance
Graft reperfusion
Balancing perfusion against pulmonary fluid overload
Postoperative oliguria or electrolyte disturbance
Renal clearance alters the duration of several drugs. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and an appropriate reversal plan are important.
The 2024 anaesthesia review supports balanced crystalloids and assessment of fluid responsiveness; no single fluid volume or pressure target is appropriate for every recipient.
Postoperative analgesia and medication choices must account for changing graft function; follow the transplant service's monitoring and immunosuppression pathway.
Sources: NHSBT Kidney Transplant Surgery; Kim & Jung Renal Transplant 2024

## Inguinal hernia repair (open or laparoscopic) (General & GI)
Reduction of a groin hernia and reinforcement of the defect, commonly with mesh. Open anterior repair, totally extraperitoneal (TEP) and transabdominal preperitoneal (TAPP) repairs are distinct approaches; tissue repair is an alternative in selected circumstances.
Position: Supine; laparoscopic repair may use head-down tilt. Agree unilateral or bilateral repair and the planned approach.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Open: groin incision with local, general or selected regional anaesthesia. Laparoscopic: ports and creation of the operative space, usually under general anaesthesia. Anaesthetic note: HerniaSurge recommends local anaesthesia for reducible open repair when the team is experienced. This recommendation is not for laparoscopic surgery or strangulated bowel.
2. Identify the sac and reduce its contents; assess bowel viability if incarcerated or strangulated. Anaesthetic note: An emergency obstruction is not an uncomplicated day-case hernia: assess aspiration, dehydration and sepsis risks and agree whether bowel resection may be necessary.
3. Reinforce the defect, usually with mesh in the tissue plane appropriate to the chosen approach. Anaesthetic note: During laparoscopy, monitor the effect of insufflation on airway pressures, oxygenation and carbon dioxide, and adjust ventilation. During awake open repair, respond to pain with supplementation rather than excessive sedation.
4. Complete haemostasis; release insufflation if used and close the wounds. Anaesthetic note: Use multimodal analgesia and nausea prevention to support mobilisation. Recovery and discharge depend on pain, physiology, social circumstances and any complications, not just the small incision.
Pain or movement during awake open repair
Laparoscopic insufflation
Unexpected ischaemic bowel in an emergency repair
HerniaSurge 2023 suggests general or local rather than regional anaesthesia for older patients, reflecting medical-complication risk; anaesthetic choice remains individualised.
These stages describe a broad repair pathway, not identical mesh placement for TEP, TAPP and open surgery.
The NHS patient information supports the operative overview; HerniaSurge provides the technique-specific anaesthetic recommendations.
Sources: NHS Inguinal Hernia Repair; HerniaSurge Update 2023; Jo & Kwak Laparoscopy 2017

## Laparoscopic appendicectomy (General & GI)
Laparoscopic removal of the appendix for appendicitis. Perforation, abscess or peritonitis changes the source-control and postoperative plan; this entry describes surgery once that treatment has been selected.
Position: Supine, with table tilt adjusted for exposure and pressure areas protected.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Induce general anaesthesia; establish laparoscopic access and CO₂ insufflation. Anaesthetic note: Assess aspiration risk, fasting, vomiting, ileus and physiological disturbance individually. Monitor respiratory mechanics and haemodynamics after insufflation.
2. Inspect the abdomen, identify the appendix and assess perforation or contamination. Anaesthetic note: Confirm antimicrobial prophylaxis and communicate any sepsis or hypovolaemia. The operative findings determine whether postoperative antibiotics and higher-acuity observation are needed.
3. Separate and control the mesoappendix, including its vessels. Anaesthetic note: Maintain stillness and adequate anaesthesia. Bleeding is usually limited but monitor both surgical bleeding and physiological deterioration.
4. Secure the appendiceal base, divide the appendix and retrieve it, usually in a bag. Anaesthetic note: Closure may use ligatures, clips or a stapler according to tissue condition and surgeon judgement; there is no universal device for every appendix.
5. Complete source control and haemostasis, desufflate and close. Anaesthetic note: Plan analgesia, nausea prevention and postoperative destination. Routine lavage or drains should not be assumed; the adopted guideline and intraoperative findings guide management.
Induction when aspiration or sepsis risk is present
Pneumoperitoneum — altered ventilation
Perforation or peritonitis — source control and postoperative planning
WSES 2020 is cited for surgical technique, stump closure and antibiotic principles; it is explicitly a 2020 guideline, not a claim that all local pathways are unchanged.
Do not equate appendicectomy with emergency laparotomy: many uncomplicated cases recover rapidly, whereas complicated disease may need prolonged treatment.
The laparoscopy review supports assessment and adjustment of ventilation, not a universal ventilator setting.
Sources: HSE Appendicitis Treatment; WSES Appendicitis 2020; Jo & Kwak Laparoscopy 2017

## Endoscopic transsphenoidal pituitary surgery (Neurosurgery)
Endoscopic access through the nasal passage and sphenoid sinus to remove a pituitary tumour. Hormone excess or deficiency, proximity to the optic apparatus and carotid arteries, and skull-base reconstruction shape the anaesthetic plan.
Position: Supine, head positioned for endoscopic nasal access, commonly elevated; secure the oral tube away from the surgical field.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Assess endocrine status, vision and airway; induce anaesthesia and secure an oral tracheal tube. Anaesthetic note: Acromegaly, obesity and sleep apnoea may complicate airway management. Agree cortisol replacement with endocrinology; the review notes variable practice, so no universal steroid regimen is implied.
2. Clear the nasal corridor and pass the endoscope through the sphenoid sinus towards the sella. Anaesthetic note: Access to the airway is restricted. If a throat pack is used, record insertion and removal explicitly; monitor cardiovascular responses to stimulation and any locally used vasoactive agents.
3. Access the pituitary region and resect the tumour under endoscopic vision. Anaesthetic note: Provide stable neuroanaesthesia and absolute stillness. Carotid injury is uncommon but potentially catastrophic; agree a haemorrhage and interventional neuroradiology rescue pathway.
4. Achieve haemostasis and reconstruct the skull base if needed, repairing a CSF leak with the chosen graft or material. Anaesthetic note: A thigh or abdominal donor site may need preparation and analgesia. Avoid emergence that disrupts reconstruction; CSF leak management is part of the surgical plan.
5. Remove any pack, clear blood and secretions and undertake a planned smooth extubation. Anaesthetic note: Balance avoidance of coughing against an awake, protected airway in higher-risk patients. Check vision and neurology early; monitor sodium, urine output and endocrine function after surgery.
Difficult airway in hormone-excess syndromes
Carotid injury or major bleeding
CSF leak and reconstruction
Extubation and postoperative water/sodium disturbance
The BJA Education review supports a multidisciplinary endocrine plan, smooth emergence and postoperative neurological assessment; local steroid practices should not be presented as universal guidance.
New polyuria or sodium disturbance needs assessment for arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) and other causes. Delayed hyponatraemia may occur after discharge; follow the endocrine monitoring pathway.
Plan postoperative breathing support jointly when sleep apnoea coexists with skull-base reconstruction, rather than assuming nasal positive-pressure treatment is automatically safe.
Sources: Raveendran Pituitary Surgery 2024; Dunn Nemergut Pituitary 2013

## Carotid endarterectomy (Vascular)
Removal of atheromatous plaque from the carotid bifurcation to reduce stroke risk in symptomatic (or selected asymptomatic) carotid stenosis.
Position: Supine, head turned away from the operative side, neck slightly extended; arm on the operative side tucked.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Incision along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid; dissection through platysma and division of the common facial vein. Anaesthetic note: Under regional anaesthesia the patient is awake: keep them comfortable and communicative; supplement local anaesthetic if the surgeon reaches the carotid sheath and the patient feels pain.
2. Exposure of the common, internal and external carotid arteries, protecting the vagus and hypoglossal nerves. Anaesthetic note: Manipulation near the carotid sinus can cause sudden bradycardia and hypotension — alert the surgeon (they will usually pause) and treat promptly; have atropine or glycopyrronium ready. Routine prophylactic carotid-sinus blockade is not recommended.
3. Systemic heparin before clamping. Anaesthetic note: Give and document heparin as requested; it must have circulated before the clamps go on.
4. Cross-clamping of the internal, common and external carotid arteries. Anaesthetic note: The critical moment for the brain. Maintain blood pressure at or above the patient's baseline to support collateral flow. In an awake patient, test speech, contralateral hand grip and consciousness immediately and repeatedly; under general anaesthesia, cerebral monitoring (e.g. stump pressure, near-infrared spectroscopy or transcranial Doppler) guides shunt use.
5. Arteriotomy and, if needed, insertion of a temporary shunt from the common to the internal carotid artery. Anaesthetic note: New neurological deficit during clamping in an awake patient is the usual trigger for a shunt; tell the surgeon immediately. Shunt insertion can embolise.
6. Plaque removal (endarterectomy), then closure of the arteriotomy, often with a patch. Anaesthetic note: Keep the patient still; coughing or movement is dangerous with an open artery.
7. Back-bleeding and flushing, then release of clamps (external carotid first, then internal). Anaesthetic note: Reperfusion can cause hypertension, hypotension or bradycardia. Watch for new neurology after unclamping.
8. Haemostasis, sometimes protamine; drain and closure. Anaesthetic note: Aim for a smooth emergence without coughing or hypertension, which increase the risk of neck haematoma.
Carotid sinus manipulation — bradycardia and hypotension
Cross-clamping — cerebral ischaemia; keep pressure up and assess neurology
Unclamping — haemodynamic swings and hyperperfusion
Emergence and the first hours — neck haematoma can compress the airway; open the wound early if the airway is threatened
GALA found no significant difference in the composite of stroke, myocardial infarction or death by 30 days (4.8% general vs 4.5% local); this does not prove equivalence. Choose by patient, surgeon and anaesthetist preference.
Regional technique: superficial (± intermediate) cervical plexus block with surgical local anaesthetic supplementation; deep cervical plexus block carries more risk (phrenic block, intravascular injection).
Arterial line before induction or block; measure blood pressure in both arms preoperatively and use the higher-reading arm.
Postoperative blood pressure control matters: hypertension raises the risk of hyperperfusion syndrome (headache, seizures, intracerebral haemorrhage) and haematoma.
Cranial nerve injury (hypoglossal, recurrent laryngeal, marginal mandibular) may affect swallowing or the airway after surgery.
Sources: GALA 2008; ESVS 2023 carotid

## Open infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm repair (Vascular)
Replacement of the aneurysmal infrarenal aorta with a synthetic tube or bifurcated graft through a laparotomy or retroperitoneal approach.
Position: Supine with arms out; long midline or transverse laparotomy (or left flank for retroperitoneal approach).
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Laparotomy, packing the bowel aside and opening the retroperitoneum over the aorta. Anaesthetic note: Large evaporative heat and fluid losses: active warming, warmed fluids and cell salvage should be running. Bowel handling can cause mesenteric traction syndrome (flushing, hypotension).
2. Dissection of the aneurysm neck below the renal arteries and of both iliac arteries. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding can be brisk, especially from the left renal vein and iliac veins; keep blood products available.
3. Systemic heparin, then clamping of the iliac arteries and the aorta below the renal arteries. Anaesthetic note: Cross-clamp raises afterload suddenly: hypertension and possible myocardial ischaemia or LV failure. Anticipate with deeper anaesthesia or vasodilators (e.g. GTN) just before clamping; the higher the clamp, the bigger the effect and the greater the kidney and gut ischaemia.
4. Opening of the aneurysm sac, removal of thrombus and oversewing of back-bleeding lumbar arteries. Anaesthetic note: Back-bleeding from lumbar and inferior mesenteric arteries can be significant; return salvaged blood.
5. Proximal then distal anastomosis of a tube or bifurcated graft. Anaesthetic note: Before declamping, assess volume status and cardiac function, correct hypovolaemia, acidosis, calcium and haemoglobin, and prepare titrated vasopressors — rather than giving a routine fluid load.
6. Sequential release of the clamps, one limb at a time. Anaesthetic note: Declamping causes hypotension: sudden fall in afterload, reactive hyperaemia and washout of acid, potassium and vasodilators from the ischaemic legs. Agree slow, staged release with the surgeon; give fluid and vasopressors; reclamp if pressure collapses.
7. Closure of the sac over the graft, retroperitoneum and abdomen; check leg and bowel perfusion. Anaesthetic note: Watch for colonic ischaemia, lower limb ischaemia (trash foot) and abdominal compartment syndrome after closure.
Aortic cross-clamp — acute rise in afterload
Declamping — hypotension and metabolic washout
Major haemorrhage at any stage
Closure — rising airway pressures or falling urine output may signal intra-abdominal hypertension
Arterial line, central venous access, large-bore cannulae, cell salvage, warming and invasive monitoring; thoracic epidural is commonly used for analgesia if not contraindicated.
Plan critical care admission after surgery.
Renal protection: the main strategies are maintaining perfusion pressure and normovolaemia and minimising clamp time; no drug has proven renal protective benefit.
Coronary disease is common in this group; perioperative myocardial injury is a leading cause of death.
NICE NG156 recommends offering open repair (rather than EVAR) for unruptured infrarenal aneurysms unless there are anaesthetic or medical contraindications or a hostile abdomen — EVAR has lower early mortality but more long-term reintervention.
Sources: NICE NG156; ESVS 2024 AAA; EVAR-1 2004

## Endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) (Vascular)
A covered stent graft is passed from the femoral arteries and deployed inside the aneurysm to exclude it from the circulation.
Position: Supine on a radiolucent table with arms out of the X-ray field; often in an interventional suite or hybrid theatre.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Femoral artery access — open cut-down or percutaneous puncture with closure devices. Anaesthetic note: Can be done under general, regional or local anaesthesia with sedation; the patient must lie flat and still for a long time.
2. Heparin, then guidewires and sheaths passed into the aorta; angiography to mark the renal arteries. Anaesthetic note: Iodinated contrast: protect the kidneys with adequate hydration and avoid nephrotoxins. Breath-holding on request improves imaging.
3. Deployment of the main body of the stent graft just below the renal arteries. Anaesthetic note: Some teams request brief hypotension or apnoea during precise deployment; agree this in advance.
4. Cannulation of the contralateral gate and deployment of the iliac limb(s). Anaesthetic note: Long periods with little stimulation then sudden balloon inflation; keep the patient still and comfortable.
5. Balloon moulding of the seal zones, then completion angiography looking for endoleak. Anaesthetic note: Balloon inflation in the aorta briefly occludes flow — a short afterload spike.
6. Sheath removal and femoral closure. Anaesthetic note: Check distal leg perfusion; groin haematoma or access-vessel injury can cause concealed bleeding.
Precise graft deployment — stillness, sometimes breath-hold or controlled hypotension
Rupture or access-vessel injury — sudden conversion to open repair is possible; be prepared for major haemorrhage
Post-implantation syndrome (fever, raised inflammatory markers) in the first days
EVAR-1 showed lower 30-day mortality with EVAR than open repair (1.7% vs 4.7%), but this early advantage did not translate into long-term survival benefit and EVAR needs lifelong surveillance.
Radiation protection for staff; limited access to the patient once draped and under the C-arm.
Spinal cord ischaemia is rare with infrarenal EVAR but a recognised risk with more extensive (thoracic or complex) stent grafts.
Hypothermia is less of a problem than with open repair but procedures can be long.
Sources: EVAR-1 2004; NICE NG156; ESVS 2024 AAA

## Ruptured AAA repair (open or endovascular) (Vascular)
Emergency control of haemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm, by open repair or emergency EVAR when anatomy allows.
Position: Supine; patient fully prepped and draped before induction.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Rapid CT (if stable enough) to decide open versus endovascular repair; activation of major haemorrhage protocol. Anaesthetic note: Restricted resuscitation (permissive hypotension) before aortic control: ESVS suggests a systolic pressure of around 70–90 mmHg while the patient stays conscious; individualise (e.g. myocardial ischaemia) and avoid aggressive fluid that worsens bleeding.
2. Patient prepped and draped awake; surgeon scrubbed and ready before induction. Anaesthetic note: Induction can cause cardiovascular collapse by losing sympathetic tone and the tamponading effect of abdominal muscle tone. Use cautious doses and have vasopressors and blood running. For EVAR, use local anaesthesia where tolerated and feasible, with a clear plan for conversion to general anaesthesia.
3. Open: immediate laparotomy and supracoeliac or infrarenal aortic clamp. EVAR: aortic occlusion balloon if needed, then stent graft deployment. Anaesthetic note: Clamp or occlusion balloon restores proximal pressure; resuscitate with blood products in balanced ratios and correct coagulopathy, calcium and temperature.
4. Graft insertion as for elective repair; declamping. Anaesthetic note: Declamping after prolonged shock causes profound hypotension and acidosis.
5. Closure — sometimes left open or with a temporary closure. Anaesthetic note: High risk of abdominal compartment syndrome, especially after EVAR with a large retroperitoneal haematoma.
Induction — collapse is common; induce only when the surgeon is ready
Aortic control
Massive transfusion and coagulopathy
Abdominal compartment syndrome after surgery
IMPROVE found no significant difference in 30-day mortality between an endovascular-first strategy and open repair (35.4% vs 37.4%); local anaesthesia for EVAR was associated with lower mortality in observational analyses within the trial.
Follow the major haemorrhage protocol: point-of-care coagulation testing, cell salvage and warming; tranexamic acid is used in many protocols, though rAAA-specific evidence of benefit is limited.
Plan critical care with renal replacement available.
Sources: IMPROVE 2014; ESVS 2024 AAA

## Femoro-popliteal bypass (Vascular)
Bypass around an occluded superficial femoral artery from the common femoral to the popliteal artery, using vein (usually great saphenous) or a prosthetic graft.
Position: Supine, leg externally rotated and knee flexed on a support.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Groin incision to expose the common femoral artery and its branches. Anaesthetic note: Neuraxial or general anaesthesia are both used; check anticoagulant and antiplatelet timing before any neuraxial technique.
2. Exposure of the popliteal artery above or below the knee. Anaesthetic note: Long procedure: pressure-area care, warming.
3. Harvest of the great saphenous vein (or preparation of the vein in situ), or tunnelling of a prosthetic graft. Anaesthetic note: Vein harvest adds a long incision and time.
4. Heparin, clamping, then proximal and distal anastomoses. Anaesthetic note: Limb clamping has little systemic effect, unlike aortic clamping.
5. Release of clamps, completion imaging or Doppler, closure. Anaesthetic note: Graft patency depends on good flow — avoid hypotension and hypothermia after surgery.
Neuraxial timing against antiplatelet and anticoagulant use
Maintaining perfusion pressure after reperfusion for graft patency
Heparin before arterial clamping
Patients usually have widespread arterial disease, diabetes, renal impairment and often frailty.
BASIL-2 found that, for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia needing infrapopliteal revascularisation, a best-endovascular-first strategy gave better amputation-free survival than vein bypass first, mainly through fewer deaths. It should not be extrapolated directly to isolated femoro-popliteal disease; treatment is chosen by anatomy, vein availability, patient risk and MDT review.
Graft failure in the first hours may need urgent return to theatre.
Sources: GVG CLTI 2019; BASIL-2 2023

## Aorto-bifemoral bypass (Vascular)
A bifurcated graft from the infrarenal aorta to both femoral arteries for extensive aorto-iliac occlusive disease.
Position: Supine with both groins and abdomen prepped.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Bilateral groin incisions to expose the femoral arteries. Anaesthetic note: Major open aortic surgery: invasive monitoring, warming, cell salvage, epidural if appropriate.
2. Laparotomy (or retroperitoneal approach) and exposure of the infrarenal aorta. Anaesthetic note: As for open AAA: bowel handling, heat and fluid losses.
3. Tunnelling of the graft limbs from abdomen to groins behind the inguinal ligament. Anaesthetic note: Tunnelling can injure veins and cause bleeding.
4. Heparin, aortic cross-clamp and proximal anastomosis, then femoral anastomoses. Anaesthetic note: Clamp effects are often smaller than in aneurysm repair because collateral vessels have developed around chronic occlusion — but still anticipate them.
5. Staged declamping of each limb; closure. Anaesthetic note: Declamping hypotension and reperfusion of two limbs; communicate with the surgeon.
Aortic cross-clamp
Staged declamping
Bleeding from tunnelling or anastomoses
Similar planning to open AAA repair including critical care admission.
Endovascular aorto-iliac stenting is now often preferred where anatomy allows.
Sources: GVG CLTI 2019; ESVS 2024 PAD

## Major lower limb amputation (Vascular)
Amputation below or above the knee for unsalvageable ischaemia, infection or necrosis.
Position: Supine; tourniquet sometimes used for below-knee amputation.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Skin flaps marked and incised (e.g. long posterior flap for below-knee). Anaesthetic note: Patients are often frail, septic or diabetic with poor reserve; consider neuraxial or regional anaesthesia, timed against anticoagulants.
2. Muscle division and ligation of the major vessels. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding is usually controlled but can be significant in above-knee amputation.
3. Nerve division — nerves are pulled down and cut cleanly so they retract. Anaesthetic note: A perineural catheter placed by the surgeon on the sciatic or tibial nerve at this step can provide prolonged analgesia.
4. Bone section with a saw and bevelling of the bone end. Anaesthetic note: Highly stimulating; deepen anaesthesia or supplement the block.
5. Myoplasty or myodesis, flap closure and dressing. Anaesthetic note: Plan multimodal analgesia; pain before surgery and poorly controlled acute pain are associated with phantom and stump pain.
Bone section — strong stimulus
Sepsis-related haemodynamic instability
Postoperative delirium and pain in frail patients
Perineural catheters, nerve blocks and neuraxial techniques are all used; no technique reliably prevents phantom limb pain.
High perioperative mortality reflects the underlying disease: treat it as high-risk surgery.
Sources: GVG CLTI 2019; NCEPOD 2014 amputation

## Arteriovenous fistula formation (Vascular)
Surgical joining of an artery to a vein in the arm to create haemodialysis access.
Position: Supine with the arm on an arm board.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Incision at the wrist (radiocephalic) or elbow (brachiocephalic). Anaesthetic note: Commonly done under brachial plexus block; regional anaesthesia causes venous dilatation, which may help the surgeon.
2. Mobilisation of the vein and artery. Anaesthetic note: Avoid cannulas, cuffs and blood tests on the operative arm — and preserve veins in the other arm for future access.
3. Heparin, clamping, arteriotomy and venotomy, and anastomosis. Anaesthetic note: Short procedure; the patient must keep the arm still.
4. Release, check for a thrill and for distal hand perfusion, closure. Anaesthetic note: Hypotension after surgery risks early thrombosis of the fistula. New hand pain, pallor, coldness or numbness suggests access-related ischaemia (steal) and needs urgent surgical review.
Avoiding hypotension for fistula patency
Block or induction with high potassium or fluid overload
Checking hand perfusion (steal) after the anastomosis
Patients have end-stage kidney disease: check potassium, timing of last dialysis, fluid status and drug dosing.
Avoid suxamethonium if potassium is raised; drugs cleared by the kidney accumulate.
In a randomised trial, brachial plexus block improved 3-month fistula patency compared with local infiltration.
Sources: ESVS 2018 vascular access; Aitken Regional AVF 2016

## Coronary artery bypass grafting (on-pump) (Cardiothoracic)
Grafting of arterial (internal mammary) and venous conduits to the coronary arteries beyond blockages, usually on cardiopulmonary bypass with an arrested heart.
Position: Supine, arms tucked; median sternotomy; leg prepped for vein harvest.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Median sternotomy while the saphenous vein or radial artery is harvested. Anaesthetic note: Sternotomy is very stimulating; deflate the lungs during the saw cut to avoid lung injury. Antifibrinolytic is usually started.
2. Harvest of the left internal mammary artery from the chest wall. Anaesthetic note: Retractor on one side of the chest can impair ventilation and cause arrhythmias.
3. Full heparinisation, then aortic and right atrial cannulation. Anaesthetic note: Confirm adequate anticoagulation (activated clotting time) before cannulation; keep systolic pressure low during aortic cannulation to reduce dissection risk.
4. Cardiopulmonary bypass started, aorta cross-clamped and cardioplegia given to arrest the heart. Anaesthetic note: Stop ventilation and volatile delivery via the ventilator once on full bypass (anaesthesia continues via the bypass circuit or intravenously); monitor depth of anaesthesia.
5. Distal anastomoses to the coronary arteries, then proximal vein graft anastomoses to the aorta. Anaesthetic note: Management of temperature, blood gases and glucose is shared with the perfusionist.
6. Rewarming, de-airing, cross-clamp removal, and weaning from bypass. Anaesthetic note: Restart ventilation; pacing, inotropes or vasopressors may be needed; use transoesophageal echo to assess function.
7. Protamine to reverse heparin, decannulation, haemostasis, drains, sternal wires and closure. Anaesthetic note: Protamine can cause hypotension, pulmonary hypertension or anaphylaxis — give slowly. Correct coagulopathy guided by point-of-care tests.
Sternotomy
Cannulation
Going on and coming off bypass
Protamine reversal
Post-bypass bleeding
Arterial line before induction, central venous access, and transoesophageal echocardiography.
Careful induction: maintain coronary perfusion pressure and avoid tachycardia.
ERAS Cardiac Society guidance supports multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, glycaemic control and early extubation pathways.
Awareness risk during bypass; use depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring when using total intravenous anaesthesia.
Sources: ERAS Cardiac 2019; EACTS CPB 2024

## Aortic valve replacement (surgical) (Cardiothoracic)
Excision of a diseased aortic valve and implantation of a mechanical or biological prosthesis on cardiopulmonary bypass.
Position: Supine, sternotomy (full or mini).
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Sternotomy, heparin, cannulation and bypass as for CABG. Anaesthetic note: In aortic stenosis, induction is high risk: maintain sinus rhythm, a normal-to-slow heart rate, preload and systemic vascular resistance. Have a vasopressor (e.g. metaraminol or phenylephrine) drawn up.
2. Cross-clamp, cardioplegia, aortotomy. Anaesthetic note: Cardioplegia may be given directly into the coronary ostia because the valve is incompetent or about to be removed.
3. Excision of the valve and removal of calcium from the annulus. Anaesthetic note: Calcium debris can embolise.
4. Sizing and sewing in the prosthesis, closure of the aorta, de-airing. Anaesthetic note: Transoesophageal echo checks valve function, leak and residual air.
5. Weaning from bypass, protamine, closure. Anaesthetic note: After replacement for aortic stenosis, the hypertrophied left ventricle is stiff and preload-dependent; after surgery for regurgitation, the ventricle may instead be dilated with reduced systolic function. Tailor management to the original lesion and post-bypass TOE. Conduction block may need pacing.
Induction in severe aortic stenosis
Weaning from bypass
Heart block after surgery
Hypotension in severe aortic stenosis reduces coronary perfusion and can spiral into arrest; treat promptly with vasopressor rather than waiting.
Transcatheter (TAVI) is an alternative for many patients, often under sedation.
Sources: ERAS Cardiac 2019; EACTS CPB 2024

## VATS lobectomy (Cardiothoracic)
Removal of a lung lobe (usually for cancer) through small ports with a camera.
Position: Lateral decubitus, operative side up, table flexed to open the rib spaces.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Port insertion and deflation of the operative lung. Anaesthetic note: Requires one-lung ventilation via a double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker; confirm position with a fibreoptic scope after turning.
2. Division of the pulmonary vein, artery branches and bronchus with staplers. Anaesthetic note: Hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation: check tube position, increase FiO₂, recruit and add PEEP to the ventilated lung, CPAP to the operative lung if the surgeon allows. Injury to a pulmonary artery branch can cause sudden major bleeding and conversion to thoracotomy.
3. Fissure completion and lymph node sampling. Anaesthetic note: Lung-protective ventilation of the dependent lung.
4. Specimen removed in a bag; leak test with the lung re-inflated under saline. Anaesthetic note: Re-inflate the lung gently on request, manually or with a set pressure.
5. Chest drain and port closure. Anaesthetic note: Paravertebral or erector spinae block (or surgically placed catheters) for analgesia; aim for early extubation and mobilisation.
Lung isolation and hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation
Pulmonary vessel injury
Air leak test
ERAS thoracic guidance supports regional analgesia (paravertebral preferred to epidural for minimally invasive surgery), avoiding fluid overload and early mobilisation.
Preoperative lung function and predicted postoperative values guide risk.
Sources: ERAS Thoracic 2019; Grichnik OLV 2005

## Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (General & GI)
Removal of the gallbladder through laparoscopic ports.
Position: Supine, reverse Trendelenburg and tilted left side down.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Umbilical port and creation of pneumoperitoneum with CO₂. Anaesthetic note: Insufflation can cause vagal bradycardia (even asystole) and reduced venous return; rising end-tidal CO₂ from absorption needs increased ventilation.
2. Further ports; head-up tilt to expose the gallbladder. Anaesthetic note: Head-up reduces venous return and blood pressure.
3. Dissection of Calot's triangle to identify the cystic duct and artery (critical view of safety). Anaesthetic note: Good muscle relaxation helps the surgeon at low insufflation pressures.
4. Clipping and division of cystic duct and artery; dissection of the gallbladder from the liver bed. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding from the liver bed is usually minor.
5. Removal of the gallbladder through a port; desufflation and closure. Anaesthetic note: Shoulder-tip pain from residual CO₂; PONV prophylaxis and multimodal analgesia; usually day case.
Insufflation — bradycardia, hypotension, CO₂ rise
Rare: CO₂ embolism (sudden fall in end-tidal CO₂ and collapse)
Head-up tilt — reduced venous return
Moderate to high PONV risk — give at least two antiemetics where risk factors are present.
Local anaesthetic port infiltration reduces opioid need.
Sources: PROSPECT Lap Chole 2024; Henny Pneumoperitoneum 2005

## Laparoscopic anterior resection (General & GI)
Removal of the rectum and its mesorectum (often for cancer) with a colorectal anastomosis, sometimes protected by a loop ileostomy.
Position: Lithotomy (Lloyd-Davies) with steep Trendelenburg, arms tucked.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Ports, pneumoperitoneum and steep head-down tilt. Anaesthetic note: Steep Trendelenburg plus pneumoperitoneum raises airway pressures and reduces FRC; secure the patient against sliding, protect eyes and pressure areas, and check tube position after tilting.
2. Ligation of the inferior mesenteric vessels; mobilisation of the left colon and splenic flexure. Anaesthetic note: Long procedure in lithotomy — calf pressure risks compartment syndrome; minimise continuous leg elevation and calf compression, record lithotomy time and plan leg-lowering breaks in long cases. Severe leg pain or new neurology after surgery needs urgent assessment for compartment syndrome.
3. Total mesorectal excision down into the pelvis. Anaesthetic note: Presacral venous bleeding can be sudden and severe.
4. Division of the rectum with a stapler and extraction of the specimen through a small incision. Anaesthetic note: Extraction site incision increases pain.
5. Stapled colorectal anastomosis; leak test; often a defunctioning loop ileostomy. Anaesthetic note: Maintain perfusion and avoid fluid overload or hypovolaemia; anastomotic perfusion depends on cardiac output.
Steep head-down positioning
Pelvic bleeding
Lower limb compartment syndrome after long lithotomy
ERAS colorectal guidance: avoid prolonged fasting, carbohydrate loading, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia (spinal opioid or abdominal wall blocks for laparoscopy), goal-directed fluid where appropriate, early feeding and mobilisation.
Facial and airway oedema after prolonged head-down tilt — check for a cuff leak if concerned before extubation.
Sources: ERAS Colorectal 2018; Gill 2019 well-leg

## Emergency laparotomy (General & GI)
Open abdominal exploration for perforation, obstruction, ischaemia or bleeding, with source control.
Position: Supine, midline incision.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Rapid sequence induction (risk of aspiration with obstruction or ileus). Anaesthetic note: Decompress the stomach with a nasogastric tube before induction where possible; expect hypotension in sepsis or hypovolaemia.
2. Midline laparotomy and full exploration. Anaesthetic note: Release of a tense abdomen can cause sudden hypotension.
3. Source control — resection of perforated or ischaemic bowel, adhesiolysis, washout. Anaesthetic note: Sepsis management: antibiotics given, vasopressors, lactate-guided resuscitation. Bowel handling and endotoxin release may cause instability.
4. Anastomosis, stoma, or damage-control surgery with a planned return to theatre. Anaesthetic note: Physiological derangement (acidosis, hypothermia, coagulopathy) may make damage control the safer choice — share this information with the surgeon.
5. Closure (or temporary abdominal closure). Anaesthetic note: Decide postoperative destination by assessed risk; high-risk patients should go to critical care.
Induction — aspiration and cardiovascular collapse
Opening a distended abdomen
Ongoing sepsis
Formal risk assessment (e.g. NELA or P-POSSUM) before surgery, consultant anaesthetist and surgeon present for high-risk cases.
ERAS emergency laparotomy guidance covers timely source control, goal-directed haemodynamics and early critical care for high-risk patients.
Sources: ERAS Emergency Laparotomy 2021; ERAS Emergency Laparotomy 2023

## Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) (General & GI)
Removal of the pancreatic head, duodenum, gallbladder and bile duct (and sometimes part of the stomach) with three reconstructions: pancreatic, biliary and gastric/duodenal.
Position: Supine, arms out; upper midline or rooftop incision.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Laparotomy and assessment of resectability (looking for metastases and vascular involvement). Anaesthetic note: Long operation (often many hours): warming, pressure areas, arterial line, central access as required.
2. Kocher manoeuvre, cholecystectomy and division of the bile duct. Anaesthetic note: Obstructive jaundice affects coagulation (vitamin K) and kidney function.
3. Division of the stomach or duodenum and jejunum; dissection of the pancreatic head off the portal and superior mesenteric veins. Anaesthetic note: The highest-risk point for major venous bleeding.
4. Pancreatic neck transection and removal of the specimen. Anaesthetic note: Monitor glucose.
5. Reconstruction: pancreaticojejunostomy (or pancreaticogastrostomy), hepaticojejunostomy and gastro/duodenojejunostomy. Anaesthetic note: Avoid excessive fluids, which may contribute to anastomotic oedema; maintain perfusion.
Dissection off the portal and superior mesenteric veins — bleeding
Prolonged surgery and heat loss
Fluid balance — avoiding both overload and hypovolaemia
ERAS pancreatoduodenectomy guidance covers nutrition, avoidance of fluid overload, and epidural or alternative analgesia.
Pancreatic leak (fistula) is the major surgical complication.
Sources: ERAS Pancreatoduodenectomy 2020; Kelliher Pancreatic Anaesthesia 2022

## Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy (General & GI)
Two-stage removal of the lower oesophagus: abdominal mobilisation of the stomach, then right thoracotomy (or thoracoscopy) for oesophageal resection and an intrathoracic anastomosis.
Position: Supine for the abdominal stage, then left lateral (right side up) for the chest stage.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Abdominal stage (open or laparoscopic): mobilisation of the stomach on the right gastroepiploic artery, conduit preparation and lymphadenectomy; pyloric intervention and feeding access (e.g. jejunostomy) according to the operative plan. Anaesthetic note: Double-lumen tube placed at the start for the later chest stage; thoracic epidural or alternative regional analgesia.
2. Turn to the lateral position. Anaesthetic note: Recheck double-lumen tube position and all lines after the turn.
3. Right thoracotomy and one-lung ventilation; mobilisation of the oesophagus and division of the azygos vein. Anaesthetic note: One-lung ventilation for a long period; lung-protective strategy. Compression of the heart and great vessels causes hypotension and arrhythmia.
4. Gastric conduit pulled into the chest; oesophagogastric anastomosis. Anaesthetic note: Conduit perfusion depends on systemic blood pressure and cardiac output; avoid prolonged hypotension and excessive vasoconstriction — balance fluids and vasopressors with the surgeon.
5. Chest drains and closure. Anaesthetic note: Aim for extubation at the end if possible; avoid aspiration (the conduit has no sphincter) — keep head up after surgery.
Repositioning and tube displacement
Prolonged one-lung ventilation
Conduit perfusion
Respiratory complications after surgery
ERAS oesophagectomy guidance covers prehabilitation, nutrition, epidural analgesia, goal-directed fluids, and early extubation and mobilisation.
Pneumonia and anastomotic leak are the leading complications; new atrial fibrillation may be an early warning sign of leak.
Sources: ERAS Oesophagectomy 2019; Carney Oesophagectomy Anaesthesia 2015

## Hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture (Orthopaedic & Spine)
Replacement of the femoral head (but not the acetabulum) for a displaced intracapsular hip fracture, usually with a cemented stem.
Position: Lateral, fractured side up (or supine for some approaches).
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Lateral or posterior approach to the hip capsule. Anaesthetic note: Spinal or general anaesthesia; a femoral nerve or fascia iliaca block helps positioning and analgesia.
2. Capsulotomy and removal of the femoral head; neck cut. Anaesthetic note: Move the patient carefully — frail skin and bones.
3. Preparation of the femoral canal (reaming/broaching), and washing and drying it. Anaesthetic note: The surgeon should announce when cement is about to be inserted.
4. Cement inserted retrograde with a gun, then the stem. Anaesthetic note: Bone cement implantation syndrome (hypoxia, hypotension, arrhythmia, arrest) can occur during canal preparation, cement and stem insertion, and joint reduction. The surgeon announces cementing; keep systolic pressure within 20% of pre-induction values, use an arterial line in higher-risk patients, and have vasopressors drawn up. A sudden fall in end-tidal CO₂ under general anaesthesia may signal right heart failure.
5. Head attached, joint reduced, closure. Anaesthetic note: Postoperative delirium prevention: avoid excess sedation and anticholinergics; treat pain.
Femoral canal preparation, cement and stem insertion, and reduction — bone cement implantation syndrome
Positioning a frail patient with a fracture — analgesia first
Early postoperative delirium and hypotension
The hip fracture guideline recommends surgery on the day of or day after admission, with a block for analgesia and spinal or general anaesthesia chosen by individual factors.
The safety guideline on cemented hemiarthroplasty describes team roles: identify high-risk patients, surgeon announces cementing, anaesthetist watches for early signs.
Sources: AoA Hip Fracture 2020; AAGBI BCIS 2015

## Total hip replacement (Orthopaedic & Spine)
Replacement of the acetabulum and femoral head for arthritis, with cemented or uncemented components.
Position: Lateral (posterior or lateral approach) or supine (anterior approach).
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Approach, capsulotomy, dislocation and resection of the femoral head. Anaesthetic note: Spinal anaesthesia (± sedation) is common; tranexamic acid reduces blood loss unless contraindicated.
2. Reaming of the acetabulum and insertion of the acetabular cup. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding mainly from bone.
3. Preparation of the femoral canal and insertion of the femoral stem (cemented or press-fit). Anaesthetic note: Femoral instrumentation and stem insertion — especially cemented — can cause embolic cardiovascular compromise (bone cement implantation syndrome): watch for hypoxia, hypotension and right heart failure.
4. Trial reduction, final components, closure. Anaesthetic note: Early mobilisation pathways rely on good analgesia without dense motor block.
Femoral stem cementing (if cemented)
Neuraxial or general anaesthesia and positioning
Hip reduction and blood loss
Local infiltration analgesia and multimodal analgesia support same-day or next-day mobilisation.
NICE NG157 advises intravenous tranexamic acid for primary elective hip replacement.
Sources: AAGBI BCIS 2015; NICE NG157

## Total knee replacement (Orthopaedic & Spine)
Resurfacing of the femur, tibia (± patella) with metal and polyethylene components; a tourniquet is often but not always used.
Position: Supine, leg on a foot rest; thigh tourniquet if used.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Tourniquet inflation (if used) and medial parapatellar approach. Anaesthetic note: Document tourniquet pressure and time; visible blood loss is low under a tourniquet but hidden and postoperative loss can be substantial; tourniquet pain can break through a spinal over time.
2. Bone cuts with jigs, ligament balancing. Anaesthetic note: Stimulating but well covered by neuraxial anaesthesia.
3. Trial components then cemented implants. Anaesthetic note: Cement reactions are less common than in hip surgery while the tourniquet is up.
4. Local infiltration, closure, tourniquet deflation. Anaesthetic note: Deflation can cause transient hypotension and a rise in end-tidal CO₂ and potassium from washout.
Tourniquet deflation
Tourniquet inflation time
Postoperative pain while preserving quadriceps strength
PROSPECT recommends paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor (unless contraindicated), IV dexamethasone, a single-shot adductor canal block plus periarticular local infiltration, with opioids reserved for rescue; this preserves quadriceps strength for early mobilisation.
NICE NG157 recommends tranexamic acid for knee replacement unless contraindicated.
Sources: PROSPECT TKA 2022; NICE NG157

## Posterior lumbar spinal fusion (Orthopaedic & Spine)
Decompression and fixation of lumbar vertebrae with pedicle screws and rods, often with bone graft or interbody cages.
Position: Prone on a frame or Jackson table, head in a padded headrest.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Turning the patient prone onto the frame. Anaesthetic note: Plan the turn with the team: secure tube and lines, keep the abdomen free (reduces venous bleeding), keep the head neutral, avoid any pressure on the eyes.
2. Midline incision and subperiosteal muscle stripping to expose the posterior elements. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding from muscle and bone; tranexamic acid and cell salvage for multilevel surgery.
3. Pedicle screw insertion under imaging or navigation. Anaesthetic note: Neuromonitoring (if used) needs a compatible anaesthetic, usually total intravenous anaesthesia without ongoing muscle relaxant.
4. Decompression (laminectomy) and interbody cage placement if planned. Anaesthetic note: Dural tear or nerve root injury may occur.
5. Rod placement, bone graft, closure. Anaesthetic note: Turn supine; assess vision and neurology early.
Prone positioning
Blood loss in multilevel surgery
Neuromonitoring alerts
The ASA practice advisory on perioperative visual loss identifies prolonged prone surgery with large blood loss as higher risk; keep the head at or above heart level, avoid direct pressure on the eyes, and consider staging very long procedures.
Multimodal analgesia; ketamine, intrathecal morphine or erector spinae blocks are used in some centres.
Sources: ASA Visual Loss 2019; ERAS Lumbar Fusion 2021

## Craniotomy for supratentorial tumour (Neurosurgery)
Opening of the skull to resect a brain tumour, often with neuronavigation, then replacement of the bone flap.
Position: Supine (or lateral/prone depending on site), head fixed in pins, head slightly up.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Application of the head pins. Anaesthetic note: Pin insertion is intensely stimulating — give a bolus of opioid or anaesthetic, or local anaesthetic at pin sites, to avoid a hypertensive surge.
2. Scalp incision, burr holes and raising of the bone flap. Anaesthetic note: Scalp block reduces stimulation; venous air embolism is possible, particularly with head-up positions.
3. Opening of the dura. Anaesthetic note: A tight brain needs brain relaxation: head up, normocapnia or mild hypocapnia briefly, avoid hypotonic fluids, osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline) on request.
4. Tumour resection with microscope and navigation. Anaesthetic note: Keep the patient completely still; maintain cerebral perfusion pressure.
5. Haemostasis, dural closure, bone flap replacement and scalp closure. Anaesthetic note: Smooth emergence without coughing or hypertension to allow early neurological assessment.
Head pinning
Dural opening — brain swelling
Emergence
Awake craniotomy is used for tumours near speech or motor areas — needs a cooperative patient and a defined plan for the awake phase.
Continue existing antiseizure medication. SNO/EANO guidance advises against routine primary anticonvulsant prophylaxis in seizure-naïve patients with newly diagnosed brain tumours; steroids are individualised for tumour-related oedema.
PROSPECT craniotomy guidance supports paracetamol, NSAIDs where safe, and scalp block or wound infiltration, with opioids for rescue.
Sources: PROSPECT Craniotomy 2023; SNO/EANO 2021

## Transurethral resection of the prostate (Urology)
Endoscopic resection of obstructing prostate tissue through a resectoscope, with continuous irrigation.
Position: Lithotomy.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Cystoscopy and insertion of the resectoscope. Anaesthetic note: Spinal anaesthesia is common and lets you detect early TURP syndrome (confusion, restlessness, nausea) in an awake patient.
2. Resection of the prostate in chips with a diathermy loop, with continuous irrigation. Anaesthetic note: With monopolar resection, hypotonic glycine irrigation can be absorbed through opened venous sinuses — risk of fluid overload, hyponatraemia and glycine toxicity (visual disturbance). Bipolar resection uses saline, which avoids hyponatraemia but can still cause fluid overload. Track resection time and irrigation balance.
3. Haemostasis with diathermy. Anaesthetic note: Blood loss is hard to estimate because it mixes with irrigation fluid.
4. Removal of chips and insertion of a three-way catheter for irrigation. Anaesthetic note: Bladder perforation can cause abdominal or shoulder pain in the awake patient.
Absorption of irrigation fluid (TURP syndrome)
Bladder perforation
Hidden blood loss
Check sodium if the resection is long, absorption is suspected, or the patient becomes confused, bradycardic or hypertensive.
Spinal anaesthesia lets early confusion from fluid absorption be noticed; bipolar resection with saline lowers but does not abolish absorption risk.
Sources: O'Donnell & Foo 2009; Ortner Irrigation Absorption 2022

## Robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy (Urology)
Removal of the prostate and seminal vesicles for cancer using a robotic platform, with vesico-urethral anastomosis.
Position: Lithotomy with steep Trendelenburg; robot docked between the legs.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Ports, pneumoperitoneum, steep head-down and docking of the robot. Anaesthetic note: Once docked, the table and patient must not move — ensure full neuromuscular block and no coughing. Access to the patient is very limited.
2. Bladder dropped, dissection of the prostate, ligation of the dorsal venous complex. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding is usually controlled by pneumoperitoneum pressure but can increase on desufflation.
3. Removal of prostate and seminal vesicles (± lymph node dissection). Anaesthetic note: Avoid fluid overload during prolonged head-down (to limit facial and airway oedema) while keeping the patient euvolaemic with adequate organ perfusion.
4. Vesico-urethral anastomosis, undocking and specimen removal. Anaesthetic note: In an emergency, undocking takes time — rehearse the steps.
Steep head-down positioning
Patient movement while docked
Emergency undocking
Steep head-down plus pneumoperitoneum raises airway, intracranial and intraocular pressure; secure the patient against slipping and protect the eyes.
Once docked, the patient cannot be moved quickly — plan arrest and undocking drills.
Before extubation, return to flat, check for facial and airway oedema (e.g. cuff-leak) and confirm full neuromuscular recovery.
Sources: Irvine & Patil 2009; Hernandez-Meza RALP 2023

## Thyroidectomy (ENT & Head and Neck)
Removal of all or part of the thyroid gland through a transverse neck incision, preserving the recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroid glands.
Position: Supine, neck extended with a shoulder roll, head ring.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Collar incision and raising of subplatysmal flaps; separation of the strap muscles. Anaesthetic note: Check the airway: a large or retrosternal goitre may compress or deviate the trachea — review imaging and plan intubation accordingly.
2. Ligation of the superior thyroid pole vessels, protecting the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Anaesthetic note: Nerve monitoring tubes (with surface electrodes) need correct depth and minimal or no muscle relaxant after intubation.
3. Identification of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroid glands; division of the inferior vessels. Anaesthetic note: Keep the patient still; the surgeon may stimulate the nerve.
4. Removal of the lobe(s), haemostasis (often with a Valsalva test), closure. Anaesthetic note: A Valsalva manoeuvre on request shows hidden bleeding points.
Airway management with a large goitre
Emergence and extubation
Post-operative haematoma — airway compression
DAS extubation guidance classes this as at-risk extubation; plan for a smooth wake-up and consider checking vocal cord movement.
Neck haematoma with airway compromise: call for help, give oxygen and decompress immediately at the bedside using SCOOP (Skin exposure, Cut sutures, Open skin, Open muscles, Pack wound), then follow the emergency airway plan.
Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes stridor after extubation; hypocalcaemia from parathyroid injury appears later.
Sources: DAS Extubation 2012; DAS/BAETS haematoma 2022

## Tonsillectomy (ENT & Head and Neck)
Removal of the palatine tonsils, commonly in children for recurrent tonsillitis or obstructive sleep-disordered breathing.
Position: Supine with shoulder roll; mouth gag (e.g. Boyle-Davis) placed by the surgeon.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Insertion of the mouth gag. Anaesthetic note: The gag can kink, compress or dislodge the tube or laryngeal mask; check ventilation after it is opened and suspended.
2. Dissection of the tonsils (cold steel, diathermy or coblation). Anaesthetic note: Shared airway: blood can track to the larynx; keep the tube cuff sealed or the LMA well positioned.
3. Haemostasis and suction of the pharynx. Anaesthetic note: Check the airway and stomach for blood before waking.
4. Removal of the gag. Anaesthetic note: Suction under direct vision and confirm haemostasis first. Choose deep or awake extubation by aspiration, obstruction and airway-rescue risk — favour awake extubation when these risks are higher (e.g. severe OSA, difficult airway, bleeding).
Gag insertion — tube obstruction or displacement
Extubation with blood in the airway
Post-tonsillectomy bleeding
Children with obstructive sleep apnoea are more sensitive to opioids: use opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, avoid codeine, and plan postoperative monitoring or admission by OSA severity, age and comorbidity.
Return to theatre for bleeding: treat as a full stomach (swallowed blood), the patient may be hypovolaemic, and visualisation may be difficult.
Sources: Zalan 2020; AAO-HNS Tonsillectomy 2019

## Caesarean section (Obstetric)
Delivery of the baby through a lower segment uterine incision via a Pfannenstiel (transverse) abdominal incision.
Position: Supine with left lateral tilt or uterine displacement to relieve aortocaval compression.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Pfannenstiel skin incision, division of rectus sheath and separation of rectus muscles.
