Anaesthetic note: Under spinal or epidural anaesthesia, confirm and document bilateral loss of light touch to T5 or higher with satisfactory motor block before incision (cold alone is unreliable). Confirm prophylactic antibiotics have been given before skin incision.
2. Opening of the peritoneum, bladder reflected, lower segment uterine incision. Anaesthetic note: Spinal hypotension: NICE recommends starting prophylactic phenylephrine immediately after the spinal, with crystalloid co-loading, aiming for systolic pressure at least 90% of baseline and avoiding below 80%.
3. Delivery of the baby (fundal pressure may be needed). Anaesthetic note: Fundal pressure and uterine exteriorisation are the most uncomfortable moments for the mother — take any reported pain seriously: ask the surgeon to pause when safe, assess and treat promptly, and offer conversion to general anaesthesia when appropriate. Reassurance or sedation is not a substitute for adequate anaesthesia.
4. Delivery of the placenta and uterotonic given. Anaesthetic note: For routine haemorrhage prophylaxis follow current NICE NG192, which now links to its carbetocin recommendation (slow IV injection); oxytocin remains widely used for treatment. Rapid uterotonic boluses cause hypotension and tachycardia. Watch blood loss and uterine tone.
5. Uterine repair (NICE advises against routine exteriorisation or routine peritoneal closure), then sheath and skin closure. Anaesthetic note: Postpartum haemorrhage may need further uterotonics, tranexamic acid and blood products.
Spinal hypotension
Delivery
Uterotonic administration
Postpartum haemorrhage
NICE NG192 recommends regional anaesthesia for caesarean birth where possible.
Classify urgency (categories 1–4) to guide the time available and anaesthetic choice.
General anaesthesia risks: difficult airway and aspiration — follow obstetric difficult airway guidance.
Sources: NICE NG192; Plaat 2022 intraoperative pain

## Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) (Vascular)
Stent-graft repair of descending thoracic aortic disease (aneurysm, dissection, traumatic transection or penetrating ulcer) delivered from the femoral artery under fluoroscopy.
Position: Supine with arms out or tucked to allow C-arm access; left arm access may be needed for left subclavian work.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Femoral access (percutaneous or cut-down); large-bore sheath; systemic heparin. Anaesthetic note: General or local anaesthesia with sedation; arterial line (right radial is usual because the left subclavian origin may be covered). Large-bore IV access and cross-matched blood for access-vessel injury.
2. Angiography and measurement; the planned landing zone may mean covering the left subclavian artery (with or without prior bypass). Anaesthetic note: Covering the left subclavian reduces vertebral and spinal collateral flow: higher risk of stroke and spinal cord ischaemia.
3. Stent-graft advanced and deployed; blood pressure may be lowered briefly during deployment to prevent graft migration. Anaesthetic note: Agree the target pressure and the drug (e.g. short-acting vasodilator, or rapid ventricular pacing in some units) before deployment; restore pressure promptly afterwards.
4. Ballooning of seal zones and completion angiography for endoleak. Anaesthetic note: Ballooning briefly occludes the aorta, causing a pressure spike proximally.
5. Sheath removal and access closure. Anaesthetic note: Reverse heparin if asked; check distal limb perfusion.
Deployment — controlled hypotension on request
Left subclavian coverage — stroke and spinal cord ischaemia risk
After repair — keep spinal cord perfusion pressure up; check leg power repeatedly
ESVS guidance recommends measures to protect the spinal cord when extensive thoracic aortic coverage is planned, including cerebrospinal fluid drainage in selected high-risk patients and maintaining an adequate mean arterial pressure.
A lumbar CSF drain needs coagulation and anticoagulation planning; drain complications include headache, bleeding and infection.
Spinal cord ischaemia can be delayed: serial neurological checks after surgery; new weakness needs immediate pressure augmentation and CSF drainage if a drain is in place.
A 2023 meta-analysis found no clear reduction in spinal cord ischaemia with prophylactic drainage in TEVAR and a small risk of serious drain complications, so drainage is selective rather than routine.
Sources: ESVS 2017 thoracic aorta; Chen CSF Drainage TEVAR 2023

## Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (General & GI)
Laparoscopic removal of most of the greater curve of the stomach, leaving a narrow tube, for severe obesity.
Position: Supine, reverse Trendelenburg (head-up), often with legs apart; secure strapping and padding for a heavy patient.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Pneumoperitoneum and port placement; liver retractor inserted. Anaesthetic note: Ramped preoxygenation and head-up positioning; expect rapid desaturation at induction. Dose drugs by an appropriate weight scalar (lean or adjusted weight for most).
2. Greater curve mobilised from the omentum, dividing short gastric vessels. Anaesthetic note: Keep good muscle relaxation for workspace; recruitment and PEEP help oxygenation with pneumoperitoneum.
3. Bougie passed orally into the stomach along the lesser curve to size the sleeve. Anaesthetic note: The anaesthetist usually passes the bougie: remove any nasogastric or temperature probe first, and pass gently — oesophageal perforation is a recognised complication. Communicate clearly with the surgeon.
4. Stomach divided with sequential staple firings alongside the bougie; staple-line leak test (air or dye) may be done. Anaesthetic note: Withdraw the bougie before the final staple fire unless the surgeon asks otherwise, so it is not stapled in.
5. Specimen removed and ports closed. Anaesthetic note: Multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia and PONV prophylaxis; extubate awake, head-up, fully reversed.
Induction and intubation — rapid desaturation
Bougie passage
Stapling — confirm all oesophageal devices are out
Extubation — obstructive sleep apnoea risk
ERAS bariatric guidance supports multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia, PONV prophylaxis and thromboprophylaxis.
Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea (e.g. STOP-BANG); patients using CPAP should bring and use it after surgery.
Monitor neuromuscular block quantitatively and ensure full reversal before extubation.
Sources: ERAS Bariatric 2022; Bariatric Anaesthesia Review

## Liver resection (hepatectomy) (General & GI)
Open or laparoscopic removal of part of the liver, usually for colorectal metastases or primary liver cancer.
Position: Supine; arms out. Open surgery often uses a subcostal (rooftop or J-shaped) incision.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Laparotomy or laparoscopy; liver mobilised and intraoperative ultrasound to map lesions and vessels. Anaesthetic note: Arterial line; central venous access is common. Epidural, wound catheters or intrathecal morphine for analgesia, depending on coagulation and local practice.
2. Inflow control: hepatic artery and portal vein to the resected part divided; intermittent Pringle manoeuvre (clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament) may be used. Anaesthetic note: Pringle reduces bleeding; it causes a small rise in afterload and a fall in venous return. Record clamp times.
3. Parenchymal transection. Anaesthetic note: The main bleeding phase. A low central venous pressure strategy (restricting fluid, head-down, vasodilators) is often used to reduce back-bleeding from hepatic veins — balance against hypotension and air embolism risk.
4. Haemostasis and bile-leak check; once transection is complete, restore normovolaemia. Anaesthetic note: Give fluid back after transection; check lactate, glucose and coagulation.
5. Closure, with or without drain. Anaesthetic note: Post-hepatectomy liver failure and coagulopathy can develop over days; adjust drug choice (e.g. paracetamol dose, avoid NSAIDs if renal risk).
Pringle manoeuvre
Transection — haemorrhage, venous air embolism
Restoring volume after transection
ERAS liver surgery guidance recommends a low central venous pressure approach during transection and multimodal analgesia.
Major resections may cause postoperative coagulopathy — this affects the timing of epidural catheter removal.
Have cell salvage available where appropriate (oncological use depends on local policy).
Sources: ERAS Liver 2022; Hughes Low CVP Meta-analysis 2015

## Radical cystectomy with ileal conduit (Urology)
Removal of the bladder (with prostate in men, or uterus and anterior vaginal wall in women) and pelvic lymph nodes for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, with urine diverted through an ileal conduit or neobladder. Open or robotic.
Position: Supine, or lithotomy with steep head-down for robotic surgery.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Access (laparotomy or robotic ports with pneumoperitoneum) and pelvic lymph node dissection. Anaesthetic note: Long case: careful pressure-point care, warming, arterial line. Steep head-down for robotic cases raises airway pressure and causes facial/airway swelling.
2. Bladder pedicles divided and bladder (with prostate or uterus) removed. Anaesthetic note: Major pelvic venous bleeding can be sudden; urine output cannot be measured once the ureters are divided.
3. Isolation of a segment of ileum; bowel continuity restored. Anaesthetic note: Goal-directed fluid therapy guides fluids when urine output is unavailable.
4. Ureters joined to the ileal conduit, which is brought out as a stoma (or a neobladder is made). Anaesthetic note: Urine appears again from the stoma or catheter once joined.
Pelvic dissection — sudden bleeding
Ureteric division — loss of urine output monitoring
Long head-down duration (robotic)
ERAS cystectomy guidance supports avoiding prolonged fasting, multimodal analgesia, thromboprophylaxis and early feeding.
Patients are often older smokers with cardiovascular and renal disease; check renal function before and after.
Sources: ERAS Cystectomy 2013; Patel Urological Anaesthesia 2022

## Head and neck cancer resection with free flap reconstruction (ENT & Head and Neck)
Resection of a head and neck cancer, often with neck dissection and tracheostomy, reconstructed with tissue (e.g. radial forearm or anterolateral thigh flap) whose vessels are joined microsurgically to neck vessels.
Position: Supine, head extended and turned; two teams may work at once (head and donor site).
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Airway secured — sometimes awake intubation or awake tracheostomy for obstructing tumours. Anaesthetic note: Plan the airway jointly with the surgeon; a shared, distorted airway is common. Avoid the flap donor arm for cannulas and blood pressure cuffs.
2. Tumour resection and neck dissection; tracheostomy if planned. Anaesthetic note: Carotid sinus handling can cause bradycardia. Swap to the tracheostomy tube with the surgeon in a planned, step-by-step way.
3. Flap raised at the donor site. Anaesthetic note: Long operation: warming, pressure care, urinary catheter, thromboprophylaxis.
4. Microvascular anastomosis of flap artery and vein to neck vessels; flap inset. Anaesthetic note: Flap perfusion depends on cardiac output and blood pressure: aim for normovolaemia, normothermia and an adequate mean pressure; avoid both under-filling and over-filling (oedema).
5. Closure; postoperative flap monitoring. Anaesthetic note: Smooth emergence; tracheostomy care. Avoid neck ties that compress the flap vessels.
Airway at induction
Tracheostomy formation
Flap anastomosis and reperfusion
Early postoperative flap failure (needs urgent return to theatre)
ERAS head and neck free flap guidance supports goal-directed fluids, avoidance of fluid excess, multimodal analgesia and thromboprophylaxis.
Many patients are smokers or heavy drinkers: screen for alcohol withdrawal, malnutrition and cardiorespiratory disease.
Sources: ERAS Head & Neck 2017; McCauley Free Flap Anaesthesia 2022

## Total laparoscopic hysterectomy (Gynaecology)
Laparoscopic removal of the uterus (and often tubes and ovaries) for benign disease or early cancer.
Position: Lithotomy with steep Trendelenburg (head-down); arms tucked; anti-slip mattress.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Uterine manipulator inserted vaginally; pneumoperitoneum and ports. Anaesthetic note: Check position and padding before head-down; watch airway pressures and end-tidal CO2 after insufflation and tilting.
2. Division of round ligaments, uterine vessels and ligaments. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding from uterine vessels can be brisk; ureteric injury is a surgical risk near this step.
3. Colpotomy (cutting the vagina around the cervix) and removal of the uterus vaginally. Anaesthetic note: Loss of pneumoperitoneum is common at this point.
4. Closure of the vaginal vault and port sites. Anaesthetic note: High PONV risk: multimodal prophylaxis. Check for facial and airway oedema after long head-down.
Steep head-down with pneumoperitoneum
Uterine vessel division
Emergence — PONV
ERAS gynaecological/oncology guidance supports minimal fasting, carbohydrate loading, PONV prophylaxis, opioid-sparing analgesia and thromboprophylaxis.
Lithotomy carries risk of common peroneal nerve injury and compartment syndrome in long cases.
Sources: ERAS Gynaecology 2019; Laskov Steep Trendelenburg 2021

## Mastectomy with immediate breast reconstruction (Breast & Plastics)
Removal of breast tissue (with sentinel node biopsy or axillary clearance) and same-operation reconstruction with an implant or the patient's own tissue, such as a free DIEP flap from the abdomen.
Position: Supine with arms out on boards; sat up during surgery to check symmetry.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Mastectomy and axillary surgery; blue dye or isotope may be used for sentinel node. Anaesthetic note: Blue dye can cause falsely low pulse oximetry readings and, rarely, anaphylaxis.
2. Implant reconstruction: pocket formed and implant placed. Flap reconstruction: abdominal flap raised on deep inferior epigastric vessels. Anaesthetic note: Regional options include paravertebral or chest wall fascial plane blocks; for flaps, abdominal wall (e.g. TAP or rectus sheath) catheters help.
3. Free flap: microvascular anastomosis to the internal mammary vessels. Anaesthetic note: As for any free flap: warm, well filled but not overloaded, adequate blood pressure; avoid prolonged vasoconstriction.
4. Patient sat up to check shape; closure with drains. Anaesthetic note: Secure the airway and lines before sitting up; check blood pressure after position change.
Blue dye injection
Flap anastomosis
Sitting the patient up
ERAS breast reconstruction consensus supports PONV prophylaxis, multimodal analgesia, normothermia and avoiding fluid excess.
Chronic post-mastectomy pain is common; good acute analgesia may help.
Sources: ERAS Breast Reconstruction 2017; PROSPECT Breast 2020

## Cataract surgery (phacoemulsification) (Ophthalmic)
Day-case removal of the clouded lens by ultrasound and insertion of an intraocular lens, usually under local anaesthesia.
Position: Supine and flat, head still, face draped; the patient must be able to lie flat for the procedure.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Local anaesthesia: topical with intracameral, sub-Tenon's, or less often peribulbar/retrobulbar block. Anaesthetic note: Needle blocks carry risks of globe perforation, retrobulbar haemorrhage and brainstem anaesthesia; sub-Tenon's and topical reduce needle risk. Monitoring, IV access and resuscitation equipment must be available.
2. Small corneal incisions; capsulorhexis (opening the lens capsule). Anaesthetic note: The patient must stay still and avoid coughing; check they can lie flat and communicate. Minimal or no sedation is preferred.
3. Phacoemulsification of the lens and aspiration. Anaesthetic note: Ocular manipulation can trigger the oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia), though less often than in squint surgery.
4. Intraocular lens inserted; incisions self-seal. Anaesthetic note: Patient goes home the same day.
Needle block placement
Patient movement during intraocular steps
Over-sedation under drapes with no airway access
Joint RCoA/RCOphth guidance: routine fasting is not required for topical or sub-Tenon's LA without sedation, and routine blood tests are not needed; check anticoagulation but usually continue it (block choice may change).
General anaesthesia is reserved for patients who cannot cooperate or lie still.
Sources: RCoA/RCOphth LA 2012; Pucchio Ophthalmic Anaesthesia 2023

## Pyloromyotomy (open or laparoscopic) (Paediatric)
Division of the hypertrophied pyloric muscle down to the mucosa in an infant with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. A medical, not surgical, emergency: fluid and electrolyte correction comes first.
Position: Supine infant on a warmed table; open right upper quadrant/umbilical incision or laparoscopic ports.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Preoperative resuscitation and correction of the hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Anaesthetic note: Do not list the infant until electrolytes and acid-base status are corrected per local paediatric criteria; alkalosis is associated with delayed emergence and postoperative apnoea.
2. Gastric emptying before induction via nasogastric or orogastric tube (gastric ultrasound may be used to assess the antrum). Anaesthetic note: Aspiration risk is high. Ensure adequate depth and complete neuromuscular block before laryngoscopy; agree the induction technique (rapid sequence or modified) with the team.
3. Access to the pylorus (open or laparoscopic) and delivery of the pyloric 'olive'. Anaesthetic note: Laparoscopic insufflation in an infant reduces compliance and can raise end-tidal CO₂; keep the infant warm.
4. Longitudinal seromuscular incision and splitting of the muscle until the mucosa bulges; mucosal integrity may be tested with air via the gastric tube. Anaesthetic note: The surgeon may ask for air to be injected down the gastric tube to check for a leak — be ready.
5. Closure and local anaesthetic infiltration or block. Anaesthetic note: Analgesia options include rectus sheath block, TAP block or wound infiltration; minimise opioids and extubate fully awake. Monitor for apnoea postoperatively.
Induction — regurgitation and aspiration
Mucosal perforation check
Emergence and early postoperative period — apnoea
Surgery is never an emergency before metabolic correction.
Regional or local techniques reduce opioid need in this apnoea-prone age group.
Exact laboratory targets and induction technique are local-pathway decisions; this summary does not set them.
Sources: Craig & Deeley Pyloromyotomy 2018; Rich Dolgin Pyloric Stenosis 2021

## Burr-hole drainage of chronic subdural haematoma (Neurosurgery)
One or two burr holes are made over a chronic subdural collection, the membrane is opened, the liquefied haematoma is irrigated out and a drain is usually left. Patients are often elderly and anticoagulated.
Position: Supine with the head turned and supported on a head ring; head-up tilt per surgeon.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Preoperative review: neurology, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use and reversal plan, comorbidities. Anaesthetic note: Agree reversal with the neurosurgical and haematology teams. Older patients with frailty and cardiac disease are common.
2. Anaesthesia: general anaesthesia or local anaesthesia with or without sedation, depending on patient and surgeon. Anaesthetic note: General anaesthesia allows ventilatory control; local techniques avoid airway instrumentation but require a cooperative, still patient. Avoid hypercapnia and hypotension.
3. Scalp incision and burr hole(s); dura and outer membrane opened. Anaesthetic note: Scalp infiltration helps analgesia; the release of a large collection may cause transient haemodynamic change.
4. Irrigation of the cavity with warm saline; drain placement (subdural or subperiosteal). Anaesthetic note: Surgeons may request a Valsalva manoeuvre to help expel fluid and air — coordinate with ventilation.
5. Closure; postoperative drain management and neurological observation. Anaesthetic note: Plan a smooth emergence with prompt neurological assessment; prevent PONV and screen for delirium.
Anticoagulation reversal before incision
Membrane opening and decompression
Emergence — neurological reassessment
Choice of anaesthesia depends on neurological status, haematoma size and location and surgical approach.
Recurrence is common; reoperation patients need the same review.
Local-versus-general comparisons are largely observational; do not treat them as proof of superiority.
Sources: Rosenblatt CSDH Anaesthesia 2021; Ebel Burr Hole 2020

## Arthroscopic shoulder surgery (e.g. rotator cuff repair, subacromial decompression) (Orthopaedic & Spine)
Arthroscopic repair or decompression in the shoulder through several small portals with fluid distension of the joint. Pain can be severe; position carries haemodynamic and cerebral risks.
Position: Beach chair (sitting) or lateral decubitus with arm traction.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Regional anaesthesia: interscalene brachial plexus block or a phrenic-sparing alternative (e.g. suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks). Anaesthetic note: Interscalene block causes ipsilateral phrenic nerve palsy in most patients — caution in respiratory disease. Consider alternatives; check for Horner's, hoarseness and local anaesthetic toxicity.
2. Positioning in beach chair or lateral; head secured in neutral. Anaesthetic note: In beach chair, cerebral perfusion pressure is lower than arm BP suggests; correct BP measurement for height difference and avoid hypotension. Protect eyes, neck and pressure points.
3. Portal placement and joint distension with irrigation fluid; surgeon may request controlled hypotension for visibility. Anaesthetic note: Agree acceptable BP limits — deliberate hypotension in the sitting position risks cerebral ischaemia. Fluid can extravasate into neck tissues; check airway at the end.
4. Repair (anchors, sutures) or decompression; closure of portals. Anaesthetic note: Awake or sedated surgery under block is possible; otherwise GA with a secured airway accessible despite drapes.
Block placement — phrenic, vascular and neuraxial complications
Sitting up — hypotension and cerebral hypoperfusion
Rebound pain when the block wears off
Integrate preoperative education, regional anaesthesia and multimodal postoperative analgesia.
Plan for rebound pain on block regression with regular oral analgesia.
Sources: Hewson Shoulder RA 2019; Salazar Beach Chair 2019

## Open reduction and internal fixation of mandibular fracture (Oral & Maxillofacial)
Fracture fragments are reduced, the teeth placed in correct occlusion, and the bone fixed with miniplates through intraoral (or sometimes external) incisions. The surgeon needs the teeth to meet, which shapes airway choice.
Position: Supine, head ring, shared airway with the surgeon; table often turned 90–180°.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Airway assessment: mouth opening (trismus from pain versus mechanical block), bleeding, associated head, cervical spine and midface injuries. Anaesthetic note: Plan the airway jointly. Options include videolaryngoscopy, awake tracheal intubation, nasal intubation, submental intubation or tracheostomy, depending on injuries and occlusion needs.
2. Intubation — commonly nasotracheal, so the teeth can be brought together. Anaesthetic note: Nasal intubation is avoided or approached cautiously if there are midface or skull-base fractures. Secure the tube well; throat pack per local safety checks.
3. Intermaxillary fixation (temporary or arch bars) to restore occlusion. Anaesthetic note: Once jaws are fixed, there is no oral access to the airway. Know how and who removes the fixation.
4. Fracture reduction and miniplate fixation through intraoral incisions; fixation released if not required postoperatively. Anaesthetic note: Ensure haemostasis and remove the throat pack before emergence; suction the pharynx.
5. Extubation fully awake, with postoperative airway plan. Anaesthetic note: If the jaws stay wired, wire cutters must accompany the patient and staff must know how to use them. Give antiemetics to reduce vomiting with fixed jaws.
Induction and intubation
Intermaxillary fixation — loss of oral airway access
Throat pack removal and extubation
Facial trauma may coexist with brain and cervical spine injury.
Senior anaesthetic input and teamwork are required; direct laryngoscopy may not be the safest option.
Sources: Harper Maxillofacial Trauma 2023; Morosan OMFS Emergencies 2012

## Cleft lip and palate repair (Paediatric)
Staged reconstruction of the lip (typically in infancy) and palate (later in infancy) by a cleft team. The airway is shared with the surgeon, can be difficult, and is at risk of obstruction after palate repair.
Position: Supine with head ring and shoulder roll (neck extended); table turned; patient fully draped.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Preoperative assessment for associated syndromes and congenital anomalies, feeding, weight and recent respiratory infection. Anaesthetic note: Cleft anomalies are associated with numerous congenital abnormalities; look specifically for features predicting difficult laryngoscopy and for cardiac disease.
2. Induction and oral intubation with a preformed south-facing RAE tube secured in the midline below the lower lip. Anaesthetic note: Laryngoscopy may be difficult (blade can fall into the cleft); confirm tube tip position visually and by auscultation, since the preformed curve may not fit the child.
3. Positioning with neck extension; throat pack; for palate surgery, insertion of the Dingman mouth gag. Anaesthetic note: Recheck the tube after every move. The gag can kink or displace the tube or raise airway pressures, and throat pack insertion/removal can cause accidental extubation.
4. Infiltration with local anaesthetic and adrenaline; lip or palate repair. Anaesthetic note: Infiltration reduces bleeding and adds analgesia. Use multimodal analgesia and titrate opioids carefully because of the risk of respiratory events.
5. Throat pack removal, suction under direct vision and awake extubation; postoperative airway monitoring. Anaesthetic note: Oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal swelling in nasal-breathing infants can obstruct the airway; a nasopharyngeal airway or tongue suture may be placed. Monitor for obstruction throughout recovery.
Laryngoscopy and intubation
Mouth gag insertion and head movement — tube kinking or displacement
Extubation and recovery — airway obstruction
Effective communication with the surgeon about the shared airway is essential.
Timing of lip and palate surgery and analgesic doses follow the local cleft team protocol; this summary does not set them.
Sources: Denning Cleft Anaesthesia 2021; Desalu Cleft Airway 2010

## Surgical (open) tracheostomy (ENT & Head and Neck)
An opening is made in the anterior trachea (usually around the second to fourth rings) and a tracheostomy tube inserted, for prolonged ventilation, airway obstruction or head and neck surgery. The most dangerous moment is the handover from the tracheal tube to the tracheostomy tube.
Position: Supine with shoulder roll and neck extended (if the cervical spine allows); head ring.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Planning: indication, airway plan if the tracheostomy fails, anticoagulation, and equipment (tube sizes, capnography). Anaesthetic note: Agree in advance who withdraws the tracheal tube and when; have a plan for re-intubation from above.
2. Neck incision, division of strap muscles and division or retraction of the thyroid isthmus. Anaesthetic note: Bleeding from the isthmus or anterior jugular veins is possible. Keep the patient deeply anaesthetised and paralysed.
3. Opening of the trachea (window or flap). Anaesthetic note: Reduce inspired oxygen as far as is safe and stop diathermy before the trachea is opened — airway fire risk. The cuff may be punctured if the tube is not withdrawn appropriately.
4. Withdrawal of the tracheal tube under direct vision until its tip is just above the stoma, then insertion of the tracheostomy tube. Anaesthetic note: Do not remove the tracheal tube fully until correct tracheostomy placement is confirmed by sustained capnography; then remove it.
5. Securing the tube (ties/sutures), chest auscultation and handover with bedhead signs. Anaesthetic note: Displacement in the early days is dangerous because the tract is not formed; follow National Tracheostomy Safety Project emergency algorithms.
Tracheal opening — airway fire and cuff damage
Tube exchange — loss of the airway
Early displacement after surgery
Confirm placement with waveform capnography every time.
Ensure the ward knows whether the upper airway is patent (tracheostomy) or not (laryngectomy).
Sources: McGrath NTSP Guidelines 2012; Rogers Tracheostomy Fire 2001

## Radical nephrectomy (open or laparoscopic), including IVC tumour thrombus (Urology)
Removal of the kidney with its fat and fascia, usually for renal cell carcinoma. Most cases are laparoscopic or robotic; tumour extending into the renal vein or inferior vena cava (IVC) turns it into a major open vascular operation.
Position: Lateral (flank) with the table broken, or supine for open transperitoneal and IVC cases.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Moderate
1. Preoperative staging including the level of any venous tumour thrombus; assessment of renal function and the remaining kidney. Anaesthetic note: Thrombus level dictates the plan: higher levels may need large-bore access, cell salvage discussion, transoesophageal echo and, rarely, cardiopulmonary bypass. Plan for reduced renal reserve afterwards.
2. Positioning in the lateral flank position with kidney rest and table break. Anaesthetic note: Lateral flexion can reduce venous return and cause hypotension; protect the dependent arm, eyes and brachial plexus, and check ventilation of the dependent lung.
3. Mobilisation of the kidney; control and division of the renal artery, then the renal vein. Anaesthetic note: Sudden bleeding from the renal vessels or IVC is the main intraoperative danger. Pneumothorax can follow pleural breach in flank approaches.
4. For IVC thrombus: clamping of the IVC above and below the thrombus, cavotomy and thrombus removal. Anaesthetic note: Caval clamping can sharply reduce venous return and cardiac output; the thrombus can embolise to the lungs — echo helps track it. Coordinate clamping with the surgeon.
5. Haemostasis and closure; postoperative analgesia and renal monitoring. Anaesthetic note: Epidural, wound catheters or multimodal analgesia depending on approach; avoid nephrotoxins and dose renally cleared drugs for the new renal function.
Renal hilum and IVC dissection — massive bleeding
Caval clamping — loss of venous return
Thrombus manipulation — tumour embolism
Most uncomplicated nephrectomies are low-to-moderate blood loss; IVC extension changes this fundamentally.
High-level thrombus cases belong in high-volume multidisciplinary centres.
Sources: Novacescu RCC Tumour Thrombus 2026; Fukazawa IVC Thrombus Anaesthesia 2014

## Awake craniotomy (tumour resection with brain mapping) (Neurosurgery)
Craniotomy during which the patient is awake for part of the operation, so speech or movement can be tested while the surgeon maps and removes tumour near eloquent cortex. Communication, comfort and airway access are central.
Position: Supine or semi-lateral, head in pins; drapes arranged so the patient's face can be seen and the airway reached.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Patient selection and preparation: ability to cooperate, anxiety, airway, obesity and sleep apnoea; rehearsal of intraoperative tests. Anaesthetic note: Poor cooperation and difficult airway are relative contraindications; agree the technique (sedation/monitored care or asleep-awake-asleep) with the team.
2. Scalp block and pin-site infiltration; head fixation. Anaesthetic note: Effective local anaesthesia is essential whatever technique is used; respect maximum local anaesthetic doses.
3. Bone flap and dural opening under sedation or general anaesthesia (supraglottic airway in asleep-awake-asleep). Anaesthetic note: Avoid hypercapnia and airway obstruction with sedation; dural opening is painful unless infiltrated.
4. Awake phase: cortical stimulation mapping and tumour resection while the patient talks or moves. Anaesthetic note: Patient must be awake but comfortable. Seizures can be provoked by stimulation — have cold saline for the cortex and anticonvulsant drugs ready. Watch for nausea, pain and agitation.
5. Closure, often with sedation or general anaesthesia resumed; early neurological assessment. Anaesthetic note: Plan smooth emergence or deepening; continue PONV prophylaxis and pain control.
Airway obstruction or apnoea during sedation
Intraoperative seizure during stimulation
Loss of cooperation in the awake phase
No single technique is optimal; choose for the patient and surgeon.
A supraglottic airway, or conversion to general anaesthesia, must be immediately available.
Sources: Lunardi Dinsmore Awake Craniotomy 2025; Kulikov Awake Craniotomy 2018

## Posterior spinal fusion for scoliosis (Orthopaedic & Spine)
Pedicle screws and rods are used to straighten and fuse a curved spine, usually in adolescents. Neuromuscular scoliosis (cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophies) carries much higher respiratory, cardiac and bleeding risk than idiopathic scoliosis.
Position: Prone on a spinal frame with abdomen free; head in a pressure-relieving headrest.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Preoperative assessment: lung function, cardiac function (especially muscular dystrophies), nutrition, seizures and secretions; postoperative critical care bed. Anaesthetic note: Neuromuscular patients have a higher risk of perioperative complications; plan for postoperative ventilation or non-invasive support where reserve is poor. Avoid suxamethonium in muscular dystrophies.
2. Induction, large-bore access, arterial line; prone positioning. Anaesthetic note: Protect eyes, face, breasts/genitals and limbs; keep the abdomen free to lower venous pressure and bleeding.
3. Exposure and pedicle screw insertion across many levels. Anaesthetic note: Blood loss can be large: tranexamic acid and cell salvage are commonly used. Total intravenous anaesthesia suits motor evoked potential monitoring; avoid neuromuscular block after baseline.
4. Rod insertion and curve correction. Anaesthetic note: Highest risk of spinal cord injury. If neuromonitoring signals fall, raise blood pressure, correct anaemia and temperature, and agree with the surgeon whether to release correction or do a wake-up test.
5. Bone graft, closure and postoperative care. Anaesthetic note: Multimodal analgesia (often intrathecal morphine or PCA); monitor for respiratory depression, ileus and ongoing bleeding.
Prone positioning
Correction manoeuvre — spinal cord ischaemia
Major blood loss during long instrumentation
Blood pressure, haemoglobin and anaesthetic depth all affect neuromonitoring — keep them stable.
Exact transfusion and tranexamic acid regimens follow local protocols; this summary does not set them.
Sources: Hudec Neuromuscular Scoliosis 2023; SRS Neuromonitoring 2020

## Orthotopic liver transplantation (General & GI)
The diseased liver is removed and a donor liver implanted, with vascular anastomoses (caval, portal, arterial) and biliary reconstruction. Three phases — dissection, anhepatic and neohepatic — each bring distinct anaesthetic problems, peaking at graft reperfusion.
Position: Supine with arms out; access for large-bore lines, cell salvage and possible venovenous bypass.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): High
1. Assessment of end-stage liver disease: coagulopathy, portopulmonary hypertension, hepatopulmonary syndrome, hepatorenal syndrome, cardiomyopathy and sarcopenia. Anaesthetic note: Portopulmonary hypertension and cardiac disease can make transplant unsafe; check echocardiography and right heart assessment per the transplant unit protocol.
2. Dissection (pre-anhepatic) phase: mobilisation of the native liver despite portal hypertension and collaterals. Anaesthetic note: Major bleeding is common: large-bore access, rapid infuser, cell salvage and point-of-care viscoelastic testing guide replacement. Monitor for hypocalcaemia from citrate.
3. Anhepatic phase: vascular clamping (caval or piggyback technique) and removal of the native liver. Anaesthetic note: Venous return falls with full caval clamping; no liver means no citrate or lactate clearance and worsening acidosis. Watch potassium.
4. Graft implantation and reperfusion through the portal vein. Anaesthetic note: Post-reperfusion syndrome: sudden hypotension, bradycardia, hyperkalaemia and pulmonary hypertension; intracardiac thrombus can occur. Prepare vasopressors, calcium and treatment for hyperkalaemia; transoesophageal echo helps.
5. Neohepatic phase: arterial and biliary anastomoses, haemostasis; transfer to critical care. Anaesthetic note: Graft function shows as falling lactate, improving coagulation and acid-base. Avoid fluid overload that congests the graft.
Dissection — massive haemorrhage
Caval clamping — loss of venous return
Reperfusion — post-reperfusion syndrome and hyperkalaemia
Specialist transplant anaesthesia team; protocols for transfusion and coagulation management are centre-specific.
Intracardiac thrombus and right heart failure may need advanced support including mechanical circulatory support.
Sources: Ramanujan Liver Transplant 2026; Siniscalchi Post-reperfusion 2016

## Laparoscopic adrenalectomy for phaeochromocytoma (General & GI)
Removal of a catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumour, usually laparoscopically. Tumour handling can cause severe hypertension and arrhythmias; after the adrenal vein is tied, blood pressure and glucose can fall sharply.
Position: Lateral decubitus (transperitoneal) or prone (retroperitoneoscopic).
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Preoperative preparation with an endocrinologist: biochemical confirmation, cardiac assessment and medical preparation (commonly α-blockade, then β-blockade if needed). Anaesthetic note: Practice varies: a 21-centre review found many patients had surgery without α-blockade with low complication rates, so follow the local multidisciplinary pathway.
2. Induction and arterial line before induction; vasodilators and short-acting β-blocker ready. Anaesthetic note: Avoid triggers of catecholamine release: light anaesthesia, hypoxia, hypercapnia, histamine-releasing drugs and metoclopramide.
3. Pneumoperitoneum and tumour mobilisation. Anaesthetic note: Insufflation and handling cause hypertensive surges and tachyarrhythmias; treat promptly (e.g. magnesium, phentolamine, nitroprusside or GTN, esmolol per local practice) and tell the surgeon.
4. Ligation of the adrenal vein. Anaesthetic note: Catecholamine levels fall: expect hypotension needing fluid and vasopressors. Stop vasodilators in advance.
5. Tumour removal, closure and postoperative monitoring in HDU. Anaesthetic note: Monitor for persistent hypotension and rebound hypoglycaemia; give steroid cover after bilateral adrenalectomy.
Tumour handling — hypertensive crisis
Adrenal vein ligation — sudden hypotension
Early postoperative — hypoglycaemia
Close surgeon–anaesthetist communication during handling is essential.
There are no randomised trials comparing preparation strategies.
Sources: Groeben Catecholamine Tumours 2020; Araujo-Castro Phaeo Protocol 2021

## Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) (ENT & Head and Neck)
Endoscopic clearance of diseased sinus tissue and polyps to restore drainage. Small amounts of bleeding ruin the endoscopic view, so the anaesthetic aim is a still patient and a dry surgical field. The orbit and skull base lie close by.
Position: Supine, reverse Trendelenburg (head-up), head slightly turned towards the surgeon; table often turned.
Blood loss risk (qualitative): Low
1. Preoperative assessment: asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, anticoagulants and obstructive sleep apnoea. Anaesthetic note: Nasal polyps often coexist with asthma and NSAID sensitivity — check before giving NSAIDs.
2. Topical vasoconstrictor to the nose; induction and airway (reinforced tracheal tube or reinforced supraglottic airway with throat pack). Anaesthetic note: Topical vasoconstrictors (e.g. cocaine or adrenaline preparations) can cause hypertension and arrhythmias.
3. Optimising the field: head-up tilt, controlled heart rate and blood pressure. Anaesthetic note: Evidence favours TIVA over volatile anaesthesia for a better surgical field with less blood loss; tranexamic acid is also used. Agree acceptable blood pressure limits.
4. Endoscopic uncinectomy, ethmoidectomy and opening of sinus ostia. Anaesthetic note: Orbital or skull-base injury can occur: watch for sudden eye swelling or CSF leak and tell the surgeon.
5. Haemostasis, packing, throat pack removal and smooth emergence. Anaesthetic note: Suction the pharynx under direct vision; avoid coughing and straining. Patients with nasal packs breathe through the mouth.
Topical vasoconstrictor — hypertension and arrhythmia
Bleeding obscuring the field
Orbital or skull-base injury
Very low blood pressure targets risk organ hypoperfusion; balance field quality with patient safety.
Throat pack removal must be part of the sign-out check.
Sources: De Sousa Machado ESS Anaesthesia 2023; Lu TIVA ESS Meta-analysis 2020

After the patient is prepped and draped with the surgeon ready
Induction can cause collapse; the surgeon must be ready to gain control immediately.
The surgeon should announce cementing so the anaesthetist can watch for hypoxia and hypotension.
TURP syndrome — fluid absorption and hyponatraemia
Check sodium, stop irrigation and finish surgery quickly.
During Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy, the gastric conduit
Systemic blood pressure and cardiac output
The conduit relies on one gastroepiploic artery; avoid prolonged hypotension.

. Reconstruction principles:
Cleft palate repair and velopharyngeal dysfunction (2014)
Assessment
Assess feeding, growth, respiratory infection, syndromic features and cardiac disease. Review previous airway problems and agree a difficult-airway plan.
Secure the airway
Induce anaesthesia and secure an oral south-facing RAE tube in the midline below the lower lip. Check depth, ventilation and capnography; the preformed curve may not fit every child.
Position and expose
Position the head and insert the Dingman mouth gag. Recheck tube patency and position after head movement or gag adjustment. A throat pack is optional, not a required step.
Reconstruct the palate
After local infiltration, mobilise the tissues and repair the nasal lining, reconstruct the levator sling and close the oral layer. Flap design and the precise sequence vary with the cleft and chosen technique.
Emergence and recovery
Release the gag, confirm removal of any pack, check haemostasis and suction under direct vision. Plan awake extubation when appropriate and monitor the airway throughout recovery; higher-risk children need an individual plan.

# Anaesthetic Risk & Informed Consent
Adverse-event frequencies and national audits, individual risk prediction, absolute-risk communication, material risks, capacity and shared decisions


Neuraxial techniques: landmark versus ultrasound-assisted
Spinals and epidurals are usually placed by palpated landmarks; a nerve stimulator has no routine role. Pre-procedure ultrasound of the spine helps find the midline and interspace. In a meta-analysis of 14 trials (1,334 patients), it reduced failed procedures (risk ratio 0.21) and traumatic procedures (risk ratio 0.27), as well as attempts and needle redirections.
These trials were too small to show any effect on rare harms such as permanent nerve injury, haematoma or abscess, so NAP3 figures still apply. The practical benefit is mostly in patients whose landmarks are hard to feel, such as obesity, scoliosis or previous spinal surgery. Risks that depend on the type of neuraxial technique:
Single-shot spinal:
a fine pencil-point needle; the main issues are hypotension, high block and a lower headache risk than an accidental puncture with a large epidural needle.
Epidural (catheter):
accidental dural puncture with a large needle (high headache risk), catheter migration into a vein (LAST) or the intrathecal space (high or total spinal), and a catheter that must be removed safely in relation to anticoagulant timing.
Combined spinal–epidural:
combines both sets of risks; an untested epidural catheter makes later top-ups less predictable.
Peripheral blocks: landmark, nerve stimulator and ultrasound
A Cochrane review of 32 randomised trials (2,844 adults) compared ultrasound with nerve stimulation, landmark or transarterial techniques. Ultrasound gave more blocks adequate for surgery (odds ratio 2.94) and fewer needing supplementation or conversion to general anaesthesia (odds ratio 0.28). It also reduced paraesthesia during the procedure and vascular puncture, but those results came from fewer studies and were rated as imprecise.
In the Australian and New Zealand registry, ultrasound was also associated with less LAST.
Permanent nerve injury is not proven to be lower with ultrasound.
The ASRA advisory on neurological complications finds that no method — ultrasound, nerve stimulation, or the two combined — has been shown to reduce the rate of nerve injury. The RCoA figure of 2–5 per 10,000 should therefore be quoted whichever method is used.
Nerve stimulator:
a motor response at a very low current suggests the needle tip is close to or inside the nerve, but a response may be absent even when the tip is inside the nerve, so it is not a reliable safeguard. Avoid forceful or painful injection; injection-pressure monitoring is an extra precaution.
Ultrasound plus stimulator:
stimulation can confirm a target that is hard to see; the combination has not been shown to reduce serious harm compared with ultrasound alone.
Landmark-only techniques:
rely on anatomy and loss-of-resistance or paraesthesia. Historically they carried higher vascular puncture and failure rates and, near the pleura, a greater risk of pneumothorax.

Risks of regional anaesthetic techniques
Regional anaesthesia changes the risk profile rather than removing risk. Discuss neuraxial and peripheral techniques on their own terms: the figures below come from different populations and cannot be merged into one “regional risk” number. NAP3 covers central neuraxial blocks; the RCoA peripheral-block leaflet and the Australian and New Zealand registry cover peripheral nerve blocks; none of them predicts an individual patient.
Neuraxial block: permanent harm, and the more common problems
NAP3 (2009) estimated permanent harm after central neuraxial block at 4.2 per 100,000 pessimistically and 2.0 per 100,000 optimistically — approximately 1 in 23,500 to 1 in 50,500, across 707,455 blocks, with “permanent” meaning symptoms beyond six months. These are alternative case classifications,
not confidence limits
. Risk was not uniform: obstetric neuraxial blocks carried substantially lower risk than perioperative and chronic-pain settings, so do not quote the pooled figure unchanged to a labouring patient or an elderly patient having emergency hip surgery.
Post-dural-puncture headache:
the RCoA patient leaflet gives a combined risk of 1 in 100 to 1 in 500 procedures after an epidural or spinal. Accidental dural puncture with a large epidural needle and headache after a fine spinal needle are different events; young patients and obstetric patients are more susceptible. Describe the postural, severe nature of the headache and that treatment, including epidural blood patch, exists.
Common, usually temporary effects:
hypotension from sympathetic block, urinary retention, itch from neuraxial opioids, shivering and incomplete or failed block with possible conversion to general anaesthesia. These are far more likely than permanent injury and belong in every consent discussion.
High or total spinal:
excessive cephalad spread can cause respiratory compromise and cardiovascular collapse; it is a recognised emergency of neuraxial and some peripheral techniques, not a reason to quote a fatality figure we do not have.
Vertebral canal haematoma and abscess:
rare but time-critical. New severe back pain, progressive leg weakness or bladder/bowel dysfunction after neuraxial block is a red flag needing urgent assessment and imaging, because delayed decompression worsens outcome. Antithrombotic drugs, spinal pathology and sepsis modify risk; follow drug-specific timing guidance rather than memory.
Peripheral nerve blocks: nerve injury and local anaesthetic systemic toxicity
The RCoA 2024 leaflet reports that fewer than 10 in 100 patients notice temporary nerve symptoms after a peripheral block, about 1 in 100 still has symptoms a year later, and 2–5 in 10,000 have permanent nerve damage. Most temporary injuries recover within weeks to about three months. These are communication estimates across block types; a specific block in a specific patient may differ, and surgery, positioning and tourniquets also injure nerves — not every post-block deficit is needle- or drug-caused.
Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) is uncommon but life-threatening. In the Australian and New Zealand registry (25,336 peripheral blocks, 2007–2012), LAST occurred in 0.87 per 1,000 blocks (95% CI 0.54–1.3), and ultrasound guidance was associated with a lower incidence. Presentation can be delayed and may begin with neurological symptoms — perioral tingling, metallic taste, agitation, seizure — before cardiovascular collapse. Management follows the ASRA 2020 checklist: call for help, give 20% lipid emulsion early, treat seizures with a benzodiazepine, use smaller-than-normal adrenaline doses (start <1 microgram/kg), avoid vasopressin, calcium-channel blockers and beta-blockers, and observe after stabilisation. LAST resuscitation differs from standard ALS.
Wrong-site block:
a never event. The Stop Before You Block campaign requires a site check immediately before needle insertion with the team; voluntary registries do not reliably capture it, so no trustworthy incidence figure is quoted here.
Block-specific harms:
pneumothorax with blocks near the pleura, phrenic nerve involvement and dyspnoea with interscalene approaches, Horner syndrome, vascular puncture and haematoma. Name the harms of the actual block planned rather than reciting a generic list.
Block failure:
partial or failed blocks are common enough that every plan needs an agreed fallback — supplementation, repeat block or conversion to general anaesthesia — discussed in advance.
Consent for regional techniques
Apply the same material-risk standard as for general anaesthesia: explain benefits, common temporary effects, serious rare harms, the possibility of failure and conversion, and reasonable alternatives including no regional technique. An awake patient’s experience — hearing, pressure sensations, the possibility of sedation — should be described honestly. A capable patient may refuse a block even when the team believes it is the safer option; respect that refusal and agree an alternative.
Learning check: can you quote NAP3’s 1 in 23,500–50,500 as the nerve-injury risk of a popliteal sciatic block?
No. NAP3 studied central neuraxial blocks. For peripheral blocks, the RCoA leaflet’s 2–5 permanent injuries per 10,000 is the closer communication estimate, and even that spans block types. Use the source that matches the technique.
Learning check: a patient develops agitation and a seizure minutes after a peripheral block. What is the treatment framework?
Treat as LAST: call for help, stop injection, manage airway and seizure (benzodiazepine), start 20% lipid emulsion early, and use reduced adrenaline doses if resuscitation is needed — per the ASRA 2020 checklist, not standard ALS dosing.
Learning check: does ultrasound guidance let you quote a lower permanent nerve-injury risk for a peripheral block?
No. Ultrasound improves block success and reduces vascular puncture and LAST, but no method of guidance has been shown to reduce permanent nerve injury.

Risks of patient positioning during surgery
An anaesthetised patient cannot report pain from pressure or stretch, and anaesthesia blunts the circulatory reflexes that normally protect against posture changes. Positioning harm is therefore shared by the whole team, and the risks are position-specific. Most published figures come from single centres or closed-claims registries: they show which harms occur and which factors are associated with them, not a personal probability for a given patient.
All positions: peripheral nerve injury and pressure injury
The ASA practice advisory recommends limiting arm abduction to about 90° in supine patients, positioning the forearm to reduce pressure on the ulnar groove, padding pressure points, avoiding prolonged hip flexion and stretch, and assessing nerve function after surgery so that new deficits are recognised early. Ulnar neuropathy is the classic upper-limb injury and can occur despite correct padding; brachial plexus injury follows abduction, head rotation and shoulder braces.
Skin and soft-tissue pressure injury rises with long procedures, low perfusion and immobility.
Prone position
Postoperative visual loss:
rare but devastating, most often ischaemic optic neuropathy after long spinal fusion. In the ASA Postoperative Visual Loss Study Group case-control study (80 cases, 315 controls), independent risk factors were male sex (OR 2.53), obesity (OR 2.83), Wilson frame use (OR 4.30), anaesthesia duration (OR 1.39 per hour) and estimated blood loss (OR 1.34 per litre), while a higher colloid share of non-blood fluid was protective (OR 0.67 per 5%). These odds ratios describe associations, not a personal risk. Direct globe pressure causes a different injury — central retinal artery occlusion — so the eyes must be free of pressure and checked regularly. For high-risk patients, discussing visual loss during consent and considering staged procedures are reasonable.
Airway and lines:
the tube, lines and monitoring can be dislodged during turning or hidden under drapes; access is poor if the airway is lost. Plan the turn, secure the tube, and have a plan for supine return and resuscitation, including a prone CPR approach.
Circulation and ventilation:
abdominal compression raises intra-abdominal pressure, reducing venous return and increasing epidural venous bleeding; supports should leave the abdomen free. Oxygenation is usually preserved, but compression of chest or abdomen raises airway pressures.
Pressure points:
face, chin, breasts, genitalia, iliac crests and knees; facial oedema, tongue swelling and cervical injury from excessive neck rotation or extension.
In a prospective Mayo series of 991 adults under general anaesthesia in lithotomy, 15 (1.5%; 95% CI 0.8–2.5%) developed lower-limb neuropathy — obturator, lateral femoral cutaneous, sciatic and common peroneal nerves. All were sensory, began within four hours, and 14 of 15 resolved within six months; time in lithotomy beyond 2 hours was a major risk factor.
Prolonged lithotomy, especially with head-down tilt and calf support, is also linked to well-leg compartment syndrome — the same complication discussed for long pelvic surgery in the Operations Library. Limit duration, use symmetrical, gradual leg movement, and lower the legs periodically in long cases.
Sitting and beach-chair positions
Upright positioning under anaesthesia lowers the blood pressure at the head relative to the arm cuff by roughly the hydrostatic column between them; uncorrected, a “normal” arm pressure can hide cerebral hypoperfusion. A medicolegal case series reported four cases of ischaemic brain and spinal cord injury in middle-aged patients after beach-chair shoulder surgery. Reference blood pressure to the external auditory meatus or correct for the height difference.
The sitting craniotomy adds venous air embolism, because surgical veins sit above the heart, and paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale.
Lateral and steep head-down positions
dependent brachial plexus and axillary vessel compression (hence the chest roll below the axilla), dependent ear and eye pressure, peroneal nerve compression at the fibular head, and ventilation–perfusion mismatch between lungs.
Steep Trendelenburg (for example robotic prostatectomy):
raised intracranial and intraocular pressure, facial and airway oedema that can cause post-extubation stridor, endobronchial tube migration, and sliding with brachial plexus stretch from shoulder braces. Check cuff leak or airway swelling before extubation in long cases.
Consent and documentation
Positioning risks are often material: a spinal fusion patient may want to know about visual loss, and a musician about ulnar nerve symptoms. Discuss position-specific risks when they are relevant to that patient, document the position, padding and checks performed, and record any new deficit promptly. Even well-performed positioning does not eliminate injury, so a deficit is not proof of negligence.
Learning check: does an arm blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg guarantee cerebral perfusion in the beach-chair position?
No. The brain sits above the cuff, so its perfusion pressure is lower by the hydrostatic gradient. Reference pressure to head level or correct for the height difference.
Learning check: which modifiable factors were associated with ischaemic optic neuropathy after prone spinal fusion?
Wilson frame use, longer anaesthesia, greater blood loss and a lower colloid share of non-blood replacement. Male sex and obesity were non-modifiable associations. These are odds ratios from a case-control study, not individual risk predictions.

Cognitive effects: postoperative cognitive dysfunction and lasting decline
Patients often ask whether “the anaesthetic” will affect their memory. The honest answer separates three things: cognitive change after surgery is common, especially in older people; it is hard to show that general anaesthesia itself, rather than surgery, illness and age, is the cause; and good evidence that a single anaesthetic causes permanent decline or dementia is lacking.
The 2018 international nomenclature uses “perioperative neurocognitive disorders” as the umbrella term: postoperative delirium (an acute event), delayed neurocognitive recovery (decline found up to 30 days), and postoperative neurocognitive disorder (up to 12 months). Older studies used “POCD”, defined by test-score change rather than clinical diagnosis, so their rates are not directly comparable.
How common is postoperative cognitive dysfunction?
In ISPOCD1 (older patients after major non-cardiac surgery), POCD was present in 25.8% at 1 week and 9.9% at 3 months, compared with 3.4% and 2.8% of matched controls tested at the same intervals. Age, duration of anaesthesia, less education, a second operation, infection and respiratory complications were early risk factors; only age predicted late POCD. Low oxygen levels and low blood pressure were not risk factors.
These figures describe test-score decline in a study population, not a personal prediction, and most early change resolves.
Is general anaesthesia the cause?
The best test is to randomise patients to general or regional anaesthesia. In a trial of 438 older patients, POCD at 7 days was 19.7% after general versus 12.5% after regional anaesthesia (P = 0.06, not significant), and at 3 months 14.3% versus 13.9% (P = 0.93). The authors concluded that there was no significant difference at 3 months, so general anaesthesia was not shown to cause lasting POCD.
The persistence of POCD in both groups points to surgery, inflammation, illness and the patient’s baseline brain health as major contributors.
Permanent decline and dementia
Observational studies linking anaesthesia to later dementia are confounded: people who need surgery are often older and sicker, and early, undiagnosed cognitive impairment raises both the need for surgery and the chance of later diagnosis. Such associations cannot prove causation.
Postoperative delirium is the clearest warning sign. It is associated with later cognitive decline and is partly preventable; prevention and screening are covered under delirium in the age and risk-reduction sections.
ASA 2025 guidance for older adults is not evidence that any particular anaesthetic technique prevents dementia; avoid promising that one choice protects long-term brain health.
Animal studies raised concern about anaesthetic effects on the developing brain, and the US FDA issued a 2016 safety warning about repeated or lengthy (over 3 hours) anaesthetic exposure in children under 3 and in pregnancy.
Human evidence for short single exposures is reassuring. In the GAS randomised trial, under 1 hour of general anaesthesia in infancy (median 54 minutes) did not change IQ at 5 years compared with awake-regional anaesthesia.
In the PANDA sibling study, a single anaesthetic before 36 months was not associated with a difference in later IQ; the authors called for more study of repeated, prolonged exposure and vulnerable groups.
Necessary surgery should not be delayed because of these concerns.
How to discuss it
For older patients: temporary memory or concentration problems after major surgery are common and usually improve; delirium is a real risk that the team works to prevent; and the evidence does not show that a general anaesthetic causes permanent decline or dementia. Patients with existing cognitive impairment, or for whom cognition is especially important, should have this discussed as a material risk.
Learning check: does choosing regional anaesthesia prevent long-term cognitive dysfunction?
Not on current evidence. In the randomised trial of 438 older patients, POCD at 3 months was 14.3% after general and 13.9% after regional anaesthesia, with no significant difference.

Pre-existing conditions and anaesthetic risk
Most serious perioperative harm comes from the interaction of the patient’s illnesses with the stress of surgery, not from the anaesthetic drugs themselves. Conditions change the type of risk as well as the size, so state which outcome a figure describes. ASA physical status is a useful shared language, but it is subjective and is not a numerical prediction tool.
Cardiac disease:
the 2022 ESC guideline combines patient factors with the risk category of the operation (low <1%, intermediate 1–5%, high >5% 30-day cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction) and supports the RCRI as a simple bedside index. Ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes and creatinine above 177 µmol/L are the RCRI patient factors; the sixth factor is high-risk surgery.
Respiratory disease:
lung complications depend on both patient and operation. ARISCAT combines age, oxygen saturation, recent chest infection, anaemia, upper-abdominal or chest incision, long surgery and emergency surgery.
Obstructive sleep apnoea:
often undiagnosed, and linked to difficult airways and breathing problems after surgery, particularly with opioids. In the STOP development study, 27.5% of 2,467 surgical patients screened as high risk; STOP-Bang adds BMI, age, neck size and sex to improve sensitivity. It is a screening tool, not a diagnosis.
CPOC guidance asks for HbA1c in the referral pathway and optimisation before elective surgery, because poor control is associated with infection, longer stay and other complications. An HbA1c threshold is a trigger for review, not a fixed risk number.
Frailty and cognitive impairment:
frailty predicts complications, longer stay and loss of independence better than age alone. Cognitive impairment raises delirium risk and affects consent.
Other conditions
— anaemia, kidney disease, liver disease, neuromuscular disease and previous airway difficulty — enter the scoring tools below or need specific planning rather than a separate generic number.
Age-related risks: older adults and children
Older adults
In US Veterans Affairs hospitals, 30-day mortality after major non-cardiac surgery was 8% for patients aged 80 and over versus 3% for younger patients, but under 2% for many common operations such as hernia repair, knee replacement and carotid endarterectomy. One in five patients aged 80 and over had a complication, and those with complications had 26% mortality compared with 4%.
The lesson for consent is that age raises risk mostly by reducing the ability to survive a complication. Frailty, function and the type of operation matter more than the number of years.
common after major and emergency surgery in older people, and linked to longer stay and later cognitive decline. ESAIC 2024 recommends screening risk, avoiding unnecessary deep anaesthesia and drugs such as benzodiazepines, and using non-drug prevention.
Brain health:
ASA 2025 guidance covers perioperative care of older adults having inpatient surgery. It does not show that any particular anaesthetic technique prevents dementia, so avoid promising that one choice protects long-term brain health.
Loss of function:
for many older patients, being able to live at home matters more than survival figures. Ask about it and discuss it.
APRICOT studied 31,127 anaesthetics in children across 261 European hospitals. Severe critical events occurred in 5.2% (95% CI 5.0–5.5), mostly respiratory (3.1%, such as laryngospasm and bronchospasm), with cardiovascular instability in 1.9%; 30-day in-hospital mortality was 10 per 10,000 and did not depend on the type of anaesthesia. Younger age and poorer health were the main risk factors, and greater experience of the most senior anaesthetist was protective.
For parents, explain that breathing problems during the anaesthetic are the most common serious event and that a recent cold increases them.
Risk prediction for specific types of surgery
General tools such as SORT and NSQIP work across many operations, but specialist scores are built on data from one type of surgery and are usually better calibrated for it. Each score predicts a defined outcome in the population it was built on; check that the patient and the outcome match before quoting it.
What it predicts and key evidence
Emergency laparotomy
NELA risk calculator

A score supports, not replaces, clinical judgement: in an international study of 22,631 patients, a model combining SORT with doctors’ estimates was developed, and all methods tested overpredicted risk.
Exercise testing can add information for major surgery but has its own limitations.
Learning check: can you use the NELA calculator to counsel a patient before elective bowel surgery?
No. It was built from emergency laparotomies and predicts emergency 30-day mortality; use a tool developed or validated for elective surgery instead.

General risk prediction tools: choose the right endpoint
Risk is the combination of the patient, operation, anaesthetic technique and care pathway. Frailty, functional capacity, organ disease, urgency, sepsis, blood loss, duration and available postoperative support matter. A healthy person having a short elective procedure and a critically ill person having emergency laparotomy cannot be assigned the same anaesthetic risk. A score complements assessment; it does not decide whether surgery should proceed.
Postoperative mortality is not anaesthesia-attributable mortality.
SORT, NELA and NSQIP estimate outcomes after surgery, reflecting illness, surgery and the whole perioperative course. They cannot tell you the probability of death caused solely by an anaesthetic. Discuss survival, complications, function, loss of independence, prolonged recovery and the consequences of not operating as separate outcomes.

A practical preoperative sequence
Clarify the indication, urgency, alternatives and likely natural history without surgery with the surgical team.
Establish baseline function, frailty, cardiopulmonary reserve, renal disease, previous anaesthetic problems, allergies, airway, dentition, PONV and patient priorities.
Select an applicable tool and document its version, endpoint, time horizon and assumptions. Missing values should be obtained or explicitly acknowledged, not silently entered as normal.
Check whether the estimate is plausible for this patient and whether its calibration is appropriate. Good discrimination (ranking patients) is not good calibration (matching observed probabilities).

Informed consent for anaesthesia: current UK guidance
Consent for anaesthesia 2026
from the Association of Anaesthetists and the GMC’s
Decision making and consent
, updated in August 2026. The Association’s 2026 revision updates timing, mode, conduct and content of discussions and adds perioperative medicine. Its public summary is cited here; the detailed principles below are grounded in the accessible GMC guidance and judgments, not presented as quotations from an unavailable full guideline.
Material risk is patient-centred, not a numerical cutoff
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board
[2015] UKSC 11 requires reasonable care to make patients aware of material risks and reasonable alternative or variant treatments. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient’s position would attach significance to it, or the clinician knows or should reasonably know this particular patient would. A rare vocal injury can be highly material to a singer; persistent hand weakness may dominate a pianist’s decision. There is no universal “below 1% need not be discussed” rule.
McCulloch v Forth Valley Health Board
[2023] UKSC 26 addresses whether an alternative is reasonable using the professional-practice test. It does not replace the patient-centred material-risk disclosure standard. Offer clinically reasonable options; a patient may refuse, but is not entitled to demand an unsafe or inappropriate anaesthetic technique.
The discussion: options, benefits, harms and values
Establish what matters:
previous distress, pain, nausea, being awake, cognitive recovery, occupation, independence, beliefs, blood products and postoperative ventilation. Ask rather than assume.
Describe reasonable options:
general anaesthesia, neuraxial or peripheral regional techniques, local anaesthesia, sedation or combinations where appropriate. Explain expected sensations, practical limits and possible conversion to general anaesthesia. Regional or sedation techniques are not inherently risk-free.
Individualise harms:
common temporary effects, serious uncommon harms, technique-specific risks and risks unusually important to this patient. Include block failure, nerve injury, headache or urinary retention when relevant; include airway/dental injury and awareness when relevant to general anaesthesia.
Discuss benefits and uncertainty:
analgesia, conditions for surgery and recovery, what prevention can and cannot achieve, likely postoperative care, and uncertainties in personalised estimates.
Include no action:
explain the consequences of declining anaesthesia or surgery with the treating team, without coercion. Risk of not treating may be high, but does not extinguish choice.
Support understanding:
qualified interpreter where needed, accessible information, time for questions and teach-back. Supply information before the day of elective surgery where practicable; confirm the agreed plan when circumstances change.
Capacity, voluntariness and refusal
Presume adult capacity. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific; disability, communication difficulty, an unwise choice or disagreement is not proof of incapacity. Support decision-making and address reversible problems. In England and Wales, the Mental Capacity Act framework asks whether an impairment or disturbance of mind/brain makes the person unable to understand, retain, use or weigh relevant information, or communicate the decision. Apply the correct law for the jurisdiction: Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland do not have identical statutory arrangements.
A capable adult can refuse a proposed technique or life-saving treatment. Explore reasons, understanding and alternatives without coercion, and document the limits and implications. Sedation, severe pain or shock may affect capacity but do not automatically remove it. Avoid seeking a first meaningful elective consent discussion after premedication or during induction.
When capacity is lacking, identify valid applicable advance decisions and legally authorised decision-makers, and use the appropriate best-interests/overall-benefit framework. In England and Wales, “next of kin” has no automatic power to consent for an adult. Family and carers can provide important evidence of wishes; a health-and-welfare attorney or court deputy may have relevant authority within their powers. Complex disagreement needs senior and legal advice; do not label assent from a relative as patient consent.
Emergency anaesthesia and treatment limits
An emergency still requires seeking consent from a conscious capable patient. If capacity is lacking and wishes cannot be established, GMC guidance permits immediately necessary treatment to save life or prevent serious deterioration, using the least restrictive appropriate option. Known valid applicable refusals and treatment limits must be considered; urgency is not a general waiver of consent. Explain what was done and why once the person can participate.
Agree the implications of advance care plans, blood-product refusal and ceilings of postoperative organ support before anaesthesia where possible. A DNACPR decision is not automatically suspended for surgery; clarify its perioperative application, reversible causes and acceptable interventions with the patient and team. Follow current local policy and specialist/legal advice for uncertainty.
Documentation is the record, not the consent itself
Record the discussion, options, material risks, patient priorities, questions, estimates and their sources, limitations or refusals, support/capacity issues, and the agreed plan. Document who participated and whether further discussion is needed. A signed form does not prove understanding and is not a substitute for tailored dialogue. Consent is ongoing: revisit material changes in technique, health or operative plan.
Learning check: a patient refuses a block after hearing about rare nerve injury. Can you proceed because it is safer overall?
Not with that block against a capable refusal. Check understanding and explore clinically reasonable alternatives, but respect the decision. A clinician’s preferred benefit–risk balance does not replace the patient’s values.
Communicating probabilities without false reassurance
Give an absolute frequency and a percentage, using a consistent denominator and time horizon. Say what the event actually means, how severe or lasting it can be, which population was studied and whether the estimate is historical, contemporary or individualised. “Rare” alone is ambiguous; “99% safe” omits which harm is being counted. Pair positive and negative framing and check understanding.
Relative effects can exaggerate perceived benefit: a fictional reduction from 2% to 1% is a 50% relative reduction but only a 1-percentage-point absolute reduction (100 fewer events per 10,000; NNT 100 over the specified period). An odds ratio is not a risk ratio, and either needs a baseline risk before translating into a patient-facing absolute estimate. Confidence intervals and calibration uncertainty should temper precision.
Why published numbers disagree
Spontaneous reporting detects fewer awareness experiences than repeated structured interviews. A change in ascertainment is not automatically a change in underlying safety.
“Any sore throat” is not the same as persistent voice injury; temporary tingling is not permanent motor deficit; perioperative arrest is not death caused by anaesthesia.
A denominator of all anaesthetics differs from general anaesthetics with muscle relaxation, central neuraxial blocks or elderly patients after major inpatient surgery.
Older trials without prophylaxis describe baseline risk, not risk after current prevention. Audit year, case-mix, reporting completeness and confidence intervals matter.
Do not add complication percentages: outcomes overlap, are not independent, and may use different denominators. Do not subtract unrelated cohorts to claim benefit from a technique.
The arithmetic above is educational, not a validated anaesthetic-risk calculator. Accurate arithmetic does not validate an input probability or make a treatment recommendation.
Learning check: can a one-in-100,000 figure be irrelevant simply because it is very small?
No. Severity, alternatives and the patient’s own circumstances may make a rare harm material. Explain uncertainty without burying a risk the patient would reasonably find important.

Adverse events and side effects: frequencies with context
Evidence reviewed October 2026. The latest source available is not necessarily a newly collected dataset: NAP4 and NAP5 remain important historical national audits; NAP7 provides more recent arrest data. RCoA patient leaflets are communication estimates, often for routine surgery, and are not patient-specific predictions. Their denominators below describe natural frequencies, not necessarily underlying study sample sizes.
No single “overall anaesthetic risk” percentage exists.
