# Psychiatric Disease & Substance Misuse Antidepressants, antipsychotics, lithium, ECT, serotonin syndrome, alcohol, opioid and stimulant use disorders, capacity and withdrawal Step-by-step reasoning phenylephrine at reduced starting dose , titrated carefully. pethidine and tramadol Common traps Giving pethidine or tramadol for "safer" opioid analgesia — both are classic serotonin syndrome precipitants with MAOIs. Using ephedrine as first-line vasopressor — indirect action risks hypertensive crisis. Assuming the MAOI must be stopped preoperatively — not feasible or advisable for emergency surgery given the 2-week washout. ketamine infusion as an opioid-sparing, anti-hyperalgesic adjunct given the tolerance and hyperalgesia risk. Withholding maintenance methadone perioperatively "to be safe" — precipitates withdrawal and increases pain and agitation. Under-dosing opioids because of a stigmatising assumption of "drug-seeking" — tolerance genuinely raises requirements. Full-dose naloxone reversal — causes acute withdrawal and severe pain; titrate in small increments. = [ ["Should buprenorphine be stopped before surgery?", "Current multisociety guidance recommends continuing buprenorphine perioperatively in most cases rather than routine discontinuation, using multimodal analgesia and titrated full-agonist opioids alongside it; stopping risks relapse and does not reliably improve analgesia."], ["How do you distinguish serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome?", "Serotonin syndrome has a rapid onset (usually Psychotropic Drugs & Anaesthesia SSRIs / SNRIs Inhibit platelet serotonin uptake → mildly impaired platelet aggregation and a small increase in surgical bleeding risk, notably with concurrent NSAIDs or anticoagulants. SIADH-mediated hyponatraemia, especially in the elderly — check sodium preoperatively if symptomatic or long-standing therapy. Serotonergic interaction risk with tramadol, pethidine, linezolid, methylene blue and MAOIs — continue the SSRI/SNRI but avoid these combinations Tricyclic Antidepressants Anticholinergic effects: dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, reduced gastric motility. Quinidine-like membrane effect → QT prolongation and arrhythmia risk, particularly in overdose or with other QT-prolonging drugs. Chronic use depletes presynaptic catecholamine stores, causing an exaggerated pressor response to indirect-acting sympathomimetics (e.g. ephedrine) and an unpredictable response to direct agonists — titrate vasopressors cautiously. Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid): monoamine oxidase activity takes ~2 weeks to recover after cessation, so continuing perioperatively with modified technique is usually preferred to a risky washout before urgent/emergency surgery. (moclobemide): shorter half-life, lower interaction risk, but the same precautions are prudent. Tyramine-containing foods precipitate hypertensive crisis via accumulated noradrenaline release — same mechanism explains exaggerated response to indirect sympathomimetics. Avoid pethidine, tramadol and indirect-acting vasopressors (ephedrine, metaraminol) — risk of serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis. Use a direct-acting agent (phenylephrine) at reduced starting dose , titrated with invasive monitoring Narrow therapeutic range 0.4–1.0 mmol/L (higher end, up to 1.2, for acute mania); toxicity above ~1.5 mmol/L. Precipitants of toxicity: dehydration, sodium depletion, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, diuretics (especially thiazides), and perioperative fluid shifts — check levels and renal function preoperatively for major surgery. Prolongs both depolarising and non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade — use peripheral nerve stimulation to guide dosing and reversal. Monitoring: routine 12-hour post-dose trough levels every 3–6 months normally, more frequently perioperatively if levels are borderline or renal function changes. QT prolongation (particularly haloperidol IV, quetiapine, and some atypicals) — check ECG and electrolytes if other QT-prolonging drugs are used. α1-blockade causes hypotension and an exaggerated response to vasodilating anaesthetic agents. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare but life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction — see comparison table below. Serotonin Syndrome Malignant Hyperthermia Dopamine antagonist (or dopaminergic withdrawal) Serotonergic drug combination Volatile agent / suxamethonium Hours (<24 h) "Lead-pipe" rigidity, hyporeflexia Hyperreflexia, clonus, myoclonus Rigidity (masseter spasm) Very high Mildly raised or normal Very high, rapid rise Stop drug, dantrolene, bromocriptine, cooling Stop drug, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine, cooling Stop trigger, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg, cooling Benzodiazepines & Clozapine Long-term benzodiazepine users have cross-tolerance to anaesthetic agents; abrupt discontinuation risks withdrawal seizures — continue usual dose perioperatively. Clozapine: risk of (mandatory FBC monitoring) and myocarditis; continue where possible as abrupt cessation risks rebound psychosis and cholinergic rebound, but liaise closely with psychiatry perioperatively Hunter Criteria & Triggers Requires a serotonergic agent plus one of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus + agitation or diaphoresis; ocular clonus + agitation or diaphoresis; tremor + hyperreflexia; hypertonia + temperature > 38°C + ocular or inducible clonus Common perioperative triggers in combination: SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs with pethidine, tramadol, methylene blue, linezolid, ondansetron (weak), or each other. Stop all serotonergic agents immediately. Supportive care: active cooling for hyperthermia, IV fluids, benzodiazepines for agitation and to reduce autonomic instability and hyperthermia (avoid physical restraint, which worsens hyperthermia via isometric muscle activity). For moderate–severe/refractory cases: cyproheptadine 12 mg orally/NG loading dose, then 2 mg every 2 hours until improvement (maximum ~32 mg/24 h) — a 5-HT2A antagonist. Severe cases (temperature > 41°C, rigidity): sedation, paralysis and intubation may be needed — do not rely on antipyretics, which are ineffective (hyperthermia is due to muscular activity, not hypothalamic reset). Distinguish from NMS (slower onset, rigidity with hyporeflexia, dopamine antagonist trigger) — see comparison table above. Anaesthesia for ECT Physiology of the Seizure parasympathetic discharge immediately after the stimulus — bradycardia, hypotension, occasionally brief asystole. Followed by a sympathetic surge during the tonic-clonic seizure — tachycardia, hypertension, ↑ intracranial and intraocular pressure, ↑ myocardial oxygen demand Postictal phase: transient confusion, headache, and occasionally further bradycardia. Agent Choice & Seizure Threshold Propofol 0.75–1 mg/kg is the most common induction agent; it raises seizure threshold and shortens seizure duration, which can be a disadvantage if seizure quality is poor. is the classic "gold standard" agent — minimal effect on seizure threshold/duration but limited availability in the UK. lengthen seizure duration and are useful when seizures are difficult to elicit or inadequate on propofol; ketamine may also benefit refractory depression. Suxamethonium 0.5 mg/kg (lower than intubation dose) provides adequate muscle relaxation to attenuate the motor component and reduce injury risk while preserving a visible/EEG-monitored seizure. Technique & Precautions Preoxygenate, bag-mask ventilate, insert a bite block before stimulus (dental/tongue injury prevention); no routine airway instrumentation is required if ventilation is adequate. to mild hypocapnia before the stimulus lowers the seizure threshold and improves seizure quality. Anticholinergic pre-treatment (glycopyrrolate) may be used in patients with a history of significant bradycardia or on beta-blockers. Contraindications/high-risk conditions: recent MI (<3 months), unstable angina, recent stroke, raised intracranial pressure, aortic aneurysm, retinal detachment, phaeochromocytoma — proceed only after cardiology/senior anaesthetic input where risk factors exist. Recovery: monitor for postictal confusion, ensure return of full consciousness and orientation before discharge from recovery, and treat post-ECT headache with simple analgesia. Alcohol Use Disorder Acute Intoxication vs Chronic Tolerance Acute intoxication potentiates the sedative and cardiodepressant effects of anaesthetic agents — reduced induction doses required, aspiration risk raised. Chronic use induces hepatic enzymes (CYP2E1), producing tolerance and to volatile agents, propofol, and benzodiazepines — higher doses often needed in the non-intoxicated chronic drinker. Withdrawal & Delirium Tremens Timeline: tremor, anxiety, tachycardia from 6–12 h; seizures peak at 24–48 h; delirium tremens (confusion, hallucinations, autonomic instability) typically 48–96 h after last drink. Use a symptom-triggered, CIWA-Ar-guided reducing regimen of chlordiazepoxide (or diazepam if IV/parenteral route needed) titrated to symptom severity rather than a fixed schedule Delirium tremens: high-dose benzodiazepines, consider IV lorazepam/diazepam, correct electrolytes (magnesium, phosphate, potassium), and manage in a monitored environment given autonomic instability and seizure risk. Wernicke's Prophylaxis parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) before or with any glucose administration — glucose without thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's encephalopathy in a thiamine-deplete patient. Classic triad: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia — often incomplete; treat any suspicion empirically without waiting for the full triad Associated Organ Dysfunction Alcoholic cardiomyopathy — dilated cardiomyopathy with impaired systolic function; assess with echocardiography before major surgery. Coagulopathy from impaired hepatic synthetic function and thrombocytopenia (marrow suppression, splenic sequestration). Chronic liver disease — see the dedicated hepatic disease topic for Child-Pugh/MELD-based risk stratification and coagulation management. Opioid Dependence, Methadone & Buprenorphine General Principles Continue maintenance methadone or buprenorphine throughout the perioperative period — it treats dependence and prevents withdrawal but provides minimal acute analgesia at maintenance doses. Expect significantly higher supplementary opioid requirements from tolerance and opioid-induced hyperalgesia Prioritise regional anaesthesia/analgesia and multimodal non-opioid strategies (paracetamol, NSAIDs where appropriate, gabapentinoids, regional blocks/catheters) to reduce total opioid exposure. is a useful opioid-sparing adjunct given the anti-hyperalgesic, NMDA-antagonist mechanism relevant to tolerant patients. Buprenorphine Specifics High-affinity partial mu-agonist with a ceiling effect — historically stopped preoperatively for fear of blocking full agonists, but current guidance favours with careful titration of additional full agonists and multimodal analgesia Introducing a full agonist too soon after stopping buprenorphine, or introducing another partial agonist/antagonist while buprenorphine is active, risks precipitated withdrawal due to displacement from the mu receptor by a lower-efficacy or antagonist ligand. Naloxone & Naltrexone Timing Naloxone should only be given in small titrated increments for respiratory depression in an opioid-tolerant patient — full reversal doses precipitate acute severe withdrawal and uncontrolled pain. Oral naltrexone (used for relapse prevention) should be discontinued approximately 72 hours before elective major surgery where significant opioid analgesia is anticipated, with a plan for postoperative resumption once analgesic needs have settled. Stimulants & Other Drugs Blocks catecholamine reuptake → tachycardia, hypertension, and coronary artery vasospasm which can cause myocardial ischaemia/infarction even in young patients with normal coronaries. unopposed beta-blockade — blocking beta-2-mediated vasodilation leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, worsening coronary spasm and hypertension. First-line treatment of cocaine-associated chest pain/hypertension: (reduce central sympathetic drive) and for coronary vasodilation; phentolamine (alpha-blocker) is an alternative Defer elective surgery for at least 24 hours after last use where possible given ongoing sympathomimetic and arrhythmogenic risk. Amphetamines & MDMA Sympathomimetic toxidrome: hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypertension, and — specific to MDMA — from excess ADH release and compulsive water intake, risking cerebral oedema and seizures. Management is supportive: active cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation, cautious fluid management with sodium monitoring. Cannabis, Ketamine Misuse & Novel Psychoactive Substances Cannabis: chronic use associated with airway hyperreactivity, tachycardia, and (rarely) cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; may alter anaesthetic drug requirements. Chronic recreational ketamine use causes a characteristic ulcerative cystitis/uropathy with severe bladder pain, frequency and haematuria — relevant to differential diagnosis of pelvic pain and to renal function assessment. Novel psychoactive substances ("legal highs", synthetic cannabinoids, synthetic cathinones) have unpredictable and highly variable sympathomimetic, sedative or dissociative effects — manage symptomatically with vigilance for atypical toxidromes. Capacity, Consent & Safeguarding Mental Capacity Act 2005 Capacity is assumed unless proven otherwise, is decision-specific and time-specific , and patients are supported to make their own decision wherever possible. Two-stage test: (1) is there an impairment or disturbance in the functioning of mind or brain; (2) does that impairment mean the person cannot understand, retain, weigh, or communicate the decision-relevant information If a patient lacks capacity, treatment proceeds in their best interests , using the least restrictive option and consulting those close to the patient, an IMCA where appropriate, or any valid advance decision/Lasting Power of Attorney for health and welfare. Interaction with the Mental Health Act Detention under the Mental Health Act authorises treatment only for the mental disorder — it does not itself authorise unrelated surgical or medical treatment. A detained patient may retain capacity to consent to, or refuse, treatment for a physical health problem; capacity must be assessed separately for that decision. Where a detained patient lacks capacity for the physical health decision, proceed under the Mental Capacity Act best-interests framework, involving psychiatric and legal advice for complex or contested cases. Consider safeguarding referral where self-neglect, exploitation, or coercion is suspected in patients with severe mental illness or substance dependence. Document capacity assessments, best-interests decisions, and any restraint or restrictive practice clearly and contemporaneously. Irreversible MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) require avoidance of indirect sympathomimetics, pethidine and tramadol (risk of hypertensive crisis or serotonin syndrome); direct-acting phenylephrine can be used at reduced dose if a vasopressor is needed. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range (0.4–1.0 mmol/L) and prolongs the action of both depolarising and non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers; toxicity is precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics. Serotonin syndrome is diagnosed clinically using the Hunter Criteria and typically evolves within 24 h of a precipitant; management is supportive — stop the causative drug, cool, benzodiazepines, and cyproheptadine 12 mg then 2 mg 2-hourly for refractory cases. During ECT, an initial parasympathetic discharge (bradycardia, even asystole) is followed by a sympathetic surge (tachycardia, hypertension); propofol 0.75–1 mg/kg raises seizure threshold and shortens seizure duration, whereas ketamine and etomidate lengthen it. Alcohol withdrawal is managed with a symptom-triggered, CIWA-Ar-guided reducing regimen of chlordiazepoxide, with parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) given before glucose to prevent precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy. Patients on methadone or buprenorphine maintenance should continue their usual dose perioperatively; expect significantly higher opioid requirements from tolerance, and use multimodal and regional analgesia rather than abrupt substitution to avoid precipitated withdrawal. Capacity is decision- and time-specific under the Mental Capacity Act 2005; a patient detained under the Mental Health Act may still retain capacity to consent to or refuse treatment unrelated to their mental disorder. Emergency laparotomy in a patient taking phenelzine (irreversible MAOI) Continue the MAOI, avoid pethidine/tramadol and indirect sympathomimetics, use direct-acting phenylephrine at reduced dose with invasive monitoring, and favour fentanyl/morphine with multimodal, regional-based analgesia. Major trauma laparotomy in a patient on methadone maintenance Continue the maintenance methadone dose, expect markedly higher supplementary opioid requirements, use multimodal and regional analgesia with a ketamine adjunct, and avoid partial agonists/antagonists that would precipitate withdrawal. Psychiatric Disease & Substance Misuse Perioperative management of psychotropic medication, ECT, and alcohol/substance use disorders Describe the perioperative implications of common psychotropic drug classes — antidepressants, MAOIs, lithium, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines and clozapine. Recognise and manage serotonin syndrome, distinguishing it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome and malignant hyperthermia. Plan safe anaesthesia for electroconvulsive therapy, including drug choice, physiological response to the seizure, and precautions. Manage the perioperative patient with alcohol use disorder, including withdrawal, delirium tremens and Wernicke Plan perioperative analgesia for patients on methadone or buprenorphine maintenance therapy without precipitating withdrawal or undertreating pain. Anticipate the cardiovascular and metabolic complications of stimulant and other recreational drug use in the perioperative setting. Apply the Mental Capacity Act 2005 and Mental Health Act framework to consent and treatment decisions in patients with psychiatric illness.   1. Irreversible MAOIs cannot be stopped safely in time for emergency surgery (recovery of monoamine oxidase activity takes ~2 weeks after cessation) — proceed with the drug in situ and modify the anaesthetic instead.

How do you distinguish serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome? Serotonin syndrome has a rapid onset (usually <24 h), hyperreflexia, myoclonus and clonus, and diarrhoea; NMS develops over days, features rigidity, hyporeflexia and very high CK, and follows dopamine antagonist exposure or dopaminergic withdrawal rather than serotonergic drugs. Why does bradycardia occur immediately after the ECT stimulus? The electrical stimulus produces an initial brief parasympathetic discharge (vagal outflow) causing bradycardia or even brief asystole, followed within seconds by a sympathetic surge causing tachycardia and hypertension during the tonic-clonic seizure; anticholinergic pre-treatment (glycopyrrolate) may be used in patients at risk of significant bradyarrhythmia. # Anaesthesia for Patients with Complex Needs
Learning disability, autism, severe phobia, behaviour that challenges, capacity and restraint, plus anaesthesia for patients in prison custody


Step-by-step reasoning
Preassessment away from the day of surgery
— meet the patient with his family/paid carers, obtain the hospital passport, identify triggers (noise, touch, waiting), calming strategies, favoured distractions, and how he expresses pain.
Capacity assessment
for the specific decision. If he lacks capacity, hold a best-interests meeting under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 with family, carers, dentist, anaesthetist and (if no one appropriate to consult) an IMCA; document the decision, the least-restrictive option considered and any planned restraint.
Bundle the procedures
— arrange for bloods, ECG, examination, dental treatment and any deferred investigations (e.g. audiology, cervical screening where relevant) under one anaesthetic to avoid repeated distressing episodes.
Reasonable adjustments
— first on the list, admission direct to a quiet side room or straight to theatre, minimal staff, carers present until asleep and in recovery, lights and monitor alarms reduced, no unnecessary gowning or fasting-time drift.
Planned premedication
rather than improvised force: oral or buccal midazolam, or oral clonidine given at home/on the ward with carer support; intranasal or buccal dexmedetomidine and oral ketamine are alternatives where benzodiazepine premedication has previously failed or caused disinhibition.
— inhalational sevoflurane induction with the patient in a chair or on a trolley, carer-assisted, is often kinder than pursuing intravenous access; secure the cannula only once anaesthetised. Have a clear, rehearsed plan for clinical holding limited to the induction period if needed, with named roles and an agreed abort point.
— extubate deep or smoothly, plan for emergence agitation, return carers to the bedside immediately, use a behavioural pain tool the carers recognise, and give long-acting multimodal analgesia plus local anaesthetic infiltration to reduce postoperative distress and opioid need.
Common traps
Bringing the patient to a busy morning ward and only then discovering he will not tolerate cannulation.
Treating physical restraint as the plan rather than as a documented, proportionate last resort.
Accepting carer consent as valid — no adult can consent on behalf of another; only a valid health and welfare LPA or court deputy can, otherwise a best-interests decision is required.
Failing to bundle procedures, guaranteeing another traumatic anaesthetic in a few months.
Clinical equivalence
— care must be equivalent to that of any other patient. Prison custody is not a reason to alter analgesic, anaesthetic or critical-care decisions.
Consent and capacity
— the prisoner consents for himself exactly as any adult with capacity does; he may refuse surgery. Neither custody staff nor the prison governor can consent for him or override refusal.
— history-taking should happen out of officers' hearing wherever the risk assessment allows; share with escorts only the operational minimum (timings, likely admission, mobility, whether he will be sedated). Do not disclose diagnosis, drug history or bloodborne-virus status for convenience.
— ask for handcuffs and any escort chain to be removed for induction, surgery and recovery. Metal restraints are incompatible with safe positioning, venous access, diathermy return-plate placement, MRI and emergency airway access; if the security risk assessment requires them, document the discussion, the reason and who authorised it, and insist an officer with the key remains immediately available.
Comorbidity profile
— anticipate higher rates of smoking, opioid and alcohol dependence, bloodborne viruses, undertreated mental illness and self-harm; check the prison drug chart, since opioid substitution therapy (methadone or buprenorphine) must be continued and will markedly raise analgesic requirements.
Analgesia and diversion risk
— prescribe on clinical need with multimodal and regional techniques; where controlled drugs are needed, plan a supervised, non-divertible route and a clear handover plan with prison healthcare rather than under-treating pain.
Discharge and continuity
— write a discharge plan the prison healthcare team can deliver (dressings, VTE prophylaxis, analgesia, follow-up escorts), because access to review, mobilisation and simple analgesia is not guaranteed in custody.
Staff safety and dignity
— agree in advance who stays in theatre, avoid discussion of the offence, and ensure the patient is not identifiable as a prisoner to other patients any more than security requires.
Anaesthetising a handcuffed patient because nobody asked for the restraint to be removed.
Taking the history with officers at the bedside and breaching confidentiality by default.
Withholding opioid substitution therapy or adequate analgesia because of assumed drug-seeking.
Assuming the escorting officer can sign the consent form.
Worked case study
General Principles & Reasonable Adjustments
The legal duty
Disability is a protected characteristic and services have an anticipatory duty to make
— the adjustment must be in place before the patient arrives, not negotiated at the theatre door
Typical adjustments: double or triple appointment times, a quiet waiting area or direct-to-theatre admission, first or last on the list, familiar carers present until induction and immediately in recovery, easy-read or pictorial information, and avoidance of repeated staff handovers.
Flag the patient's needs on the theatre list and at the safety briefing so the whole team behaves consistently.
Preparation is the intervention
Early preassessment
, ideally away from the day of surgery and with the people who know the patient best; read the hospital passport or communication plan in advance.
Bundle procedures
— combine dental treatment, blood tests, imaging, examination under anaesthesia and screening into one anaesthetic to minimise lifetime exposure to distressing encounters.
Desensitisation and rehearsal
— theatre or ward familiarisation visits, photographs of the room and staff, social stories, play-specialist or clinical-psychology input, topical local anaesthetic cream applied at home.
Agree the plan in writing
: premedication, induction route, who holds what if holding is needed, agreed abort criteria, recovery plan and analgesia.
Team and service factors
Involve the hospital
learning disability liaison nurse
or acute liaison team early; they coordinate adjustments, best-interests meetings and follow-up.
Provision of anaesthesia services should include identified pathways and staff training for patients with additional needs, and staff in England are now required to receive learning disability and autism training
Document what worked so the next admission starts from an evidence base rather than from zero.
Learning Disability
Why outcomes are worse
People with a learning disability die substantially younger than the general population, and reviews repeatedly judge a large share of those deaths avoidable with better care
Diagnostic overshadowing
— new symptoms are attributed to the disability rather than investigated. A patient who becomes withdrawn, aggressive or immobile may be in pain, obstructed, hypoxic or septic.
Communication barriers delay presentation and consent; pain is frequently under-recognised and under-treated.
Associated physical comorbidity
— continue antiepileptics perioperatively, plan the fasting-period doses and a parenteral route, and avoid unnecessarily proconvulsant drug choices.
Aspiration risk
— dysphagia, gastro-oesophageal reflux, drooling, thickened-fluid diets and previous chest infections; consider modified induction and airway protection.
Airway and skeletal issues
— kyphoscoliosis, restrictive lung disease, limited neck movement, dental disease, and syndrome-specific airways (e.g. Down syndrome: atlanto-axial instability, subglottic narrowing, obstructive sleep apnoea, congenital heart disease).
Constipation, dehydration and polypharmacy
— antipsychotics and antiepileptics bring QT prolongation, sedation and drug-interaction risk.
Difficult venous access
after years of procedures; plan ultrasound-guided access and consider inhalational induction first.
Assessing pain without self-report
Use an observational tool and — crucially — the carers' knowledge of this individual's pain behaviours (vocalisation, guarding, rocking, withdrawal, appetite change, aggression).
Prescribe regular multimodal analgesia and local/regional blocks rather than relying on as-required opioids that depend on the patient asking.
Reassess after treating: improvement in behaviour after analgesia is itself diagnostic information.
Autism Spectrum Disorder
What actually causes distress
Autism is not a learning disability, and many autistic patients have full capacity and normal or high intellectual function — adjust the environment, not the level of explanation
Sensory load
: noise, alarms, bright lights, strong smells (alcohol gel, volatile agents), unexpected touch, tight blood-pressure cuffs, gowns and adhesive dressings.
: long unexplained waits, changing staff, changing plans, and being told "just a little scratch" when it is not.
Perioperative planning built around sensory and communication needs reduces distress, restraint and cancelled procedures
Practical adjustments
Ask the patient (or their supporter) what helps: headphones, sunglasses, own clothes, a weighted blanket, a specific comfort object, no eye contact, written rather than spoken instruction.
Give exact, literal information with timings; avoid euphemism and avoid promising what may not happen.
Reduce the number of people in the anaesthetic room to the minimum; one person speaks.
Consider a "straight to theatre" pathway, no premedication if not wanted, or self-administered inhalational induction with the patient controlling the mask.
Plan for emergence: unfamiliar recovery areas are a common flashpoint — quiet bay, familiar supporter present, avoid abrupt awakening and repeated questioning.
Severe Needle & Anaesthetic Phobia
Specific phobias (trypanophobia, mask phobia, fear of loss of control or of awareness, claustrophobia in scanners) cause avoidance of surgery altogether, late presentation, and vasovagal collapse at induction.
Ask directly at preassessment about previous traumatic anaesthetic or dental experiences, fainting with needles, and what the patient fears specifically — "the mask", "not waking up", "being awake and paralysed" all demand different answers.
Consider intraoperative awareness anxiety in patients with prior awareness or with a family history; depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring and an explicit plan can be therapeutic.
Management ladder
Psychological first
: explanation and control-giving (the patient decides the arm, counts down, applies the mask), graded exposure, distraction, hypnosis or CBT for elective cases with time available; clinical psychology referral where surgery is repeatedly cancelled.
Vasovagal precautions
: supine or head-down cannulation, applied tension technique, avoid the patient watching, avoid prolonged fasting-related hypovolaemia.
Topical anaesthesia
: high-concentration lidocaine/prilocaine or tetracaine cream applied early and to more than one site, plus ethyl chloride spray or a vapocoolant, and a small-gauge cannula in a well-warmed hand.
: oral or buccal benzodiazepine premedication, nitrous oxide/oxygen 50:50 self-administered for cannulation, intranasal or buccal dexmedetomidine, or a sevoflurane inhalational induction avoiding needles altogether until asleep.
Record which combination worked, so the next episode of care is not a fresh trauma.
Behaviour That Challenges & Sedation Strategies
Behaviour is communication
Behaviour that challenges usually reflects unmet need — pain, fear, hunger, thirst, constipation, needing the toilet, sensory overload or loss of routine. Exclude physical causes before escalating sedation
Non-pharmacological de-escalation, environmental modification and a proactive support plan come before medication; psychotropics must not be used as a substitute for adjustment.
Premedication and induction options
Oral or buccal midazolam
— rapid, familiar, but can cause paradoxical disinhibition; ask carers whether previous benzodiazepines helped or worsened behaviour.
Oral clonidine
— smoother, longer-onset anxiolysis with sedation and analgesic sparing; plan for bradycardia and hypotension and allow adequate onset time.
Intranasal or buccal dexmedetomidine
— useful where midazolam has failed; produces cooperative sedation with maintained airway, again with bradycardia and slower onset.
Oral ketamine
— effective in the highly resistant patient, with dissociation and greater secretion/emergence-phenomena risk; consider an antisialagogue and quiet recovery.
Inhalational induction
with sevoflurane, carer-assisted, avoids the needle entirely; secure access once anaesthetised. Intramuscular ketamine is a rescue option only within an agreed, documented plan.
Doses for all of these are set out in the premedication section of the preoperative assessment topic; give them where the patient is monitored and reversal, airway equipment and trained staff are immediately available.
Safety of premedication in this group
Obstructive sleep apnoea, obesity, hypotonia, chronic lung disease and existing psychotropic load all increase the risk of over-sedation and airway obstruction — monitor with oximetry and never leave the patient unattended.
Beware additive QT prolongation, and additive hypotension/bradycardia when clonidine or dexmedetomidine is added to existing antipsychotics or antihypertensives.
If the patient is already sedated when the list slips, keep them monitored; do not let the delay convert planned premedication into an unmonitored one.
Communication Strategies
Find out how this person communicates — before they arrive
Read the
hospital passport / communication passport
and ask carers or family how the patient expresses yes/no, pain, fear and refusal. Behaviour is communication: withdrawal, rocking, echolalia, grabbing or aggression may all mean "no" or "it hurts".
Document the patient's preferred name, pronouns, first words/signs and their tolerance for touch, eye contact and personal questions; hand this to every member of the team at the briefing.
Book professional communication support in advance: British Sign Language or deafblind interpreters, Makaton signers, speech-and-language therapy input, and learning-disability liaison nurses
Adapt the message
Easy-read and pictorial information
: simple sentences, one idea per line, photographs of the actual environment, equipment and (where possible) the staff who will be present. Anaesthesia-specific easy-read leaflets exist and should be offered as standard.
Social stories and visual timetables
for autistic patients: a step-by-step "what will happen" sequence with real timings, which can be rehearsed at home and updated if the list order changes.
Verbal style
: short concrete sentences, no idioms or euphemism ("you will feel a scratch" is dishonest — say "a sharp sting for a few seconds"), one question at a time, and allow processing time before repeating.
Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC)
: communication boards, symbol sets, picture-exchange systems, electronic voice-output devices and the patient's own tablet — ensure the device goes with the patient to theatre and recovery.
Demonstrate equipment (mask, cannula, saturation probe) on a teddy, a carer or the patient's own hand first; allow the patient to handle it.
Communication as consent support, and communication under anaesthesia
Every practicable step to help the patient understand, retain, use/weigh and communicate their decision must be taken before concluding they lack capacity — adapted communication is a legal requirement of the capacity assessment, not an optional extra
One designated communicator (often the supporter the patient trusts) reduces confusion; brief them that they support the patient's own decision, not make it for them.
For patients having awake procedures, agree signals in advance (raise a hand for a break, a buzzer for stop) and check understanding before starting.
Record what communication worked and what did not, so the next episode of care starts from a known position.
Sedation Alternatives
Non-pharmacological alternatives — always the first rung
Preparation techniques
: graded exposure and desensitisation programmes, rehearsal visits, play-specialist and clinical-psychology input, and CBT or hypnotherapy for needle and mask phobia where time allows.
Distraction and control-giving
: tablets/video, music through headphones, guided breathing, counting down with the patient, the patient applying their own mask or choosing the arm for cannulation.
Virtual and augmented reality
headsets for cannulation and regional blocks, with growing evidence for procedural anxiety in children and adults with additional needs.
Sensory modulation
: weighted blankets, dimmed lights, noise reduction, familiar objects and own clothing frequently make sedation unnecessary.
Scheduling as treatment
: first on the list, minimal fasting drift, direct-to-theatre admission and a single trusted team reduce anticipatory arousal more effectively than any drug.
Procedural alternatives to sedation or general anaesthesia
Regional anaesthesia alone
— a spinal, epidural or peripheral block with generous explanation, a screened-off field, music and a familiar supporter is often better tolerated than expected; pair with the communication strategies above and agree "stop" signals in advance.
Local anaesthesia with infiltration or topical agents
for suitable procedures, with slow injection, buffering and small-gauge needles; offer nitrous oxide/oxygen 50:50 (Entonox) self-administered as an adjunct for the needle-phobic patient with capacity.
Sedation under regional block
where full wakefulness is intolerable: low-dose propofol target-controlled infusion, or a single-agent strategy with depth monitoring — but remember sedation in a patient who cannot reliably report distress requires the same monitoring standards as anaesthesia and an agreed abort plan.
Choice of general anaesthetic technique
when GA is unavoidable: patient-controlled inhalational induction with sevoflurane, TIVA to reduce postoperative nausea and emergence phenomena, and deep extubation where appropriate to smooth emergence.
Escalating safely
Move up the ladder only when the rung below has genuinely been offered: adjustments → preparation/distraction → topical/local/regional → inhaled nitrous → oral/buccal/intranasal premedication → inhalational induction → (rarely, within a documented plan) intramuscular rescue
Each step up increases monitoring requirements and the need for trained staff, reversal agents and airway equipment immediately available — never administer sedating medication in an unmonitored corridor.
Record which rung succeeded; "sedation ladder that works for this patient" is among the most valuable entries in the hospital passport.
Capacity, Consent & Restraint
Capacity framework
Capacity is assumed, is decision- and time-specific, and must be supported — easy-read material, pictures, interpreters, communication passports and a supporter all count as support before any conclusion of incapacity
Where capacity is lacking, treatment proceeds in the patient's
best interests
using the least restrictive option, with a documented best-interests meeting, consultation of family/carers, and an IMCA where there is no one appropriate to consult.
Check for a valid
Lasting Power of Attorney for health and welfare
, court-appointed deputy or advance decision; serious or contested decisions (including sterilisation or withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment) go to the Court of Protection.
Fluctuating capacity, and capacity for one decision but not another, are both common — reassess rather than carrying forward a label.
Restraint and clinical holding
Lawful only where the patient lacks capacity, it is
necessary to prevent harm
to them, and is
in degree and duration to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm
Plan it: who holds which limb, for how long, agreed abort criteria, the minimum number of staff, and the least restrictive method — usually brief supportive holding for an inhalational induction, not prolonged force for cannulation
Document the assessment, the alternatives tried, who was consulted, what was done and for how long; debrief the team, the patient's carers and the patient afterwards.
Consider whether the arrangements amount to a
deprivation of liberty
requiring separate authorisation, particularly with prolonged inpatient stays or continuous supervision.
Consent in Practice
A staged consent pathway
Start early
— consent for this group is a process over weeks, not a signature on the day. Begin at the surgical referral, continue at a dedicated preassessment, and confirm on the day.
Provide information in the right format first
— easy-read leaflets, photographs, videos or a familiarisation visit; document what was given and how the patient engaged with it. Information the patient cannot process is not information.
Assess capacity for this specific decision
, with all communication support in place and at the patient's best time of day. Support includes quiet surroundings, the trusted supporter, and repetition across more than one visit
Check for existing legal instruments
: health-and-welfare LPA, court-appointed deputy, advance decision to refuse treatment, or a previous best-interests decision for the same procedure.
Document the discussion and the plan
: what the patient understood, what they value (e.g. "must have mum present"), agreed adjustments, premedication plan, and any holding plan if capacity is lacking.
When the patient cannot consent
Convene a
best-interests meeting
: anaesthetist, surgeon/proceduralist, carers/family, learning-disability liaison nurse and an IMCA where no one appropriate can be consulted. Record options considered, the least-restrictive choice and the reasons.
Best interests are not best medical interests alone — weigh the patient's past and present wishes, beliefs and values, and the views of those who know them
Serious, finely-balanced or contested decisions, and procedures such as sterilisation, require the
Court of Protection
; allow time for this at the start of the pathway, not the night before surgery.
Deprivation-of-liberty safeguards: prolonged admission, continuous supervision or sedation/restraint regimes may need separate authorisation — escalate to the hospital safeguarding team.
Emergencies, refusal and fluctuating capacity
In a genuine emergency, treatment immediately necessary to save life or prevent serious deterioration may proceed in best interests without a meeting — document why delay was impossible and consult retrospectively.
Respect a capacitous refusal even when it seems unwise, and even when the family disagree; a patient with a learning disability who retains and weighs the decision can decline surgery.
Fluctuating capacity (delirium, seizure activity, metabolic encephalopathy, time-of-day variation) means reassessing at the decision point — capacity gained overnight can restore the patient's right to decide for themselves.
Plan for refusal scenarios in advance where refusal is predictable: agree with the team and family what will happen if the patient says no on the day, and under what circumstances the case is stood down rather than escalated.
Anaesthesia for Patients Who Are Prisoners
Principle of equivalence
People in prison are entitled to healthcare equivalent in quality and access to that of the wider population; custody must not change the clinical decision

Managing an intra-operative myotonic crisis/contracture
Myotonia is a
sarcolemmal membrane phenomenon
, not a problem at the neuromuscular junction or in central control of tone — it is therefore
NOT abolished
by non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade, by spinal or epidural anaesthesia, or by deepening volatile anaesthesia. This distinguishes it clearly from malignant hyperthermia (which responds to dantrolene and removal of the trigger) and from ordinary post-operative shivering (which usually responds to warming and opioids).
Masseter or generalised muscle contracture can make bag-mask ventilation, laryngoscopy and surgical access impossible, even though the block appears otherwise adequate.
Direct infiltration
of the affected muscle with local anaesthetic (e.g. lidocaine) can relax a focal contracture rapidly and is often the first practical step.
Systemic membrane-stabilising drugs
: IV procainamide (where available), IV phenytoin, or quinine (historic, rarely used now) may be given for more generalised contracture. Both procainamide and phenytoin are negative inotropes and pro-arrhythmic, which is particularly hazardous in a patient who may already have underlying cardiac conduction disease.
Supportive measures: active warming and avoidance of shivering and hypothermia, minimising mechanical or electrical stimulation of muscle, and avoiding the recognised triggers — suxamethonium, neostigmine and hyperkalaemia.

Keep the patient sedated, mechanically ventilated and normothermic until neuromuscular function recovers — hypothermia and acidosis further prolong block.

Neostigmine is contraindicated in the early phase — it inhibits residual plasma cholinesterase activity and paradoxically prolongs the block; sugammadex has no affinity for suxamethonium (a depolarising, non-steroidal agent) and is ineffective.

Meticulous blood pressure control — avoid both hypertension (risk of dissection/rupture) and hypotension (risk of malperfusion in already fragile vasculature); smooth induction and emergence, blunt the pressor response to laryngoscopy.

Haem arginate
3 mg/kg/day (max ~250 mg/day) for 4 days via a large-bore central vein or a large peripheral vein — it is highly irritant and causes thrombophlebitis in small/peripheral veins. It provides negative feedback that downregulates hepatic ALA synthase, switching off overproduction of the neurotoxic precursors ALA and PBG.
High-carbohydrate load
(10% glucose, aiming ≥300 g/day, e.g. via a central line if peripheral tolerance is limited) also suppresses ALA synthase, but large volumes of dextrose risk dilutional hyponatraemia — monitor sodium closely and balance against SIADH-driven hyponatraemia from the attack itself.

Malignant Hyperthermia (RYR1 / CACNA1S)
Genetics
RYR1 (~70%), CACNA1S; autosomal dominant. Penetrance variable.
Triggers
All volatiles (sevo, iso, des), suxamethonium. NOT N₂O, propofol, opioids, NMBAs (non-dep), regional.
First sign
Unexplained ↑EtCO₂ despite ↑MV; masseter spasm after sux; tachycardia; mixed acidosis.
Dantrolene
2.5 mg/kg IV bolus, repeated every 5–10 min until control; >10 mg/kg may be required, so stock at least 36 vials. Each vial = 20 mg + 60 mL water; Ryanodex 250 mg / 5 mL.
Adjuncts
Stop trigger, 100% O₂ high-flow, charcoal filters, active cooling, treat hyperK⁺ and acidosis, forced diuresis to urine output >1 mL/kg/h.
Confirmation
EMHG IVCT (caffeine-halothane contracture test) on muscle biopsy = gold standard. Genetic testing complementary.

Marfan syndrome (FBN1)
Aorta / cardiovascular
Progressive aortic root dilatation and type-A dissection are the leading causes of death. Continue β-blockers (reduce dP/dt); target systolic BP <120 mmHg and gentle heart rate. Pre-op CT/MRI aorta if not recent. Mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation common. Place defibrillation pads if root >45 mm.
Respiratory
Pectus excavatum, kyphoscoliosis and apical bullae increase pneumothorax risk — especially with positive pressure ventilation. Use lowest airway pressures possible; high index of suspicion for spontaneous pneumothorax if desaturation or ↑airway pressures.
Ophthalmology
Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) — upward/subluxation is characteristic. Protect eyes during positioning; avoid pressure on globes. Consider avoiding anticholinergics (less relevant in modern practice).
Neuraxial
Dural ectasia (widening of the spinal canal) makes spinal block unpredictable and increases risk of post-dural-puncture headache. Dural ectasia also enlarges the dural sac itself, so if a dural puncture headache occurs and an epidural blood patch is required, a larger volume of autologous blood may be needed for it to be effective, the patch is technically more difficult to perform, and repeat patching is more often required. Epidural is preferred over subarachnoid block if neuraxial technique is chosen; expect patchy spread and higher volumes needed.
Musculoskeletal
Joint laxity, scoliosis, pectus deformity and long limbs can make positioning difficult. Hyperextensible joints risk nerve stretch — pad well, avoid extreme positions. Cervical spine instability is uncommon but reported.
Practical
Continue β-blockers on day of surgery; use arterial line for beat-to-beat BP monitoring. Treat intubation response (laryngoscopy → hypertension) with opioid ± esmolol/labetalol. Avoid Valsalva, straining and hypertensive surges perioperatively.

Hypermobile EDS (hEDS)
Generalised joint hypermobility, chronic widespread pain, easy bruising and skin laxity. Associated with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) — expect exaggerated haemodynamic swings with position change and induction. Chronic pain and long-term opioid use commonly produce opioid tolerance and hyperalgesia — anticipate higher perioperative analgesic requirements and use multimodal/regional strategies. Joint laxity demands careful positioning and padding; dislocation risk during airway manoeuvres and limb positioning.
Vascular EDS (vEDS, COL3A1)
Defective type III collagen causes fragile arteries, bowel and uterus. Spontaneous arterial dissection or rupture (including of major vessels), spontaneous rupture of hollow organs (classically the sigmoid colon, or the gravid uterus in pregnancy) and spontaneous pneumothorax are recognised catastrophic presentations. Diagnosis is often only made after a sentinel vascular or bowel event.
Ehlers-Danlos (vascular type, COL3A1)
Tissue fragility, vessel rupture, easy bruising, poor wound healing. Caution with arterial lines/CVCs, gentle laryngoscopy, avoid IM injections.
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Brittle bones — careful positioning, avoid BP cuff trauma, difficult intubation (cervical fragility, dentinogenesis imperfecta), risk of MH (low-grade association).
Loeys-Dietz
Aggressive arterial dissection at smaller diameters than Marfan — strict BP control essential.

Generally structurally normal heart, but obstructive sleep apnoea and chronic hypoxaemia may produce pulmonary hypertension and right-heart strain — screen with echo if symptomatic.

Atoms of one element with different neutron numbers are : chemically near-identical, but differing in mass and sometimes in nuclear stability. Ions: why electrolytes carry charge An atom that loses electrons becomes a positive ; one that gains electrons becomes a negative . Sodium readily loses its single valence electron to form Na⁺; chlorine gains one to form Cl⁻. Calcium and magnesium lose two (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺). This is why plasma concentrations of divalent ions are sometimes quoted in mEq/L — one mmol of Ca²⁺ carries two equivalents of charge. Isotopes you meet clinically Radioactive tracers: unstable isotopes such as technetium-99m (nuclear medicine imaging) and iodine-131 (thyroid treatment) behave chemically like their stable counterparts, so they follow the same physiological pathways while emitting detectable radiation. Stable isotopes: carbon-13 in the urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori is not radioactive; it is detected by its different mass. The mole links atoms to doses One mole is Avogadro's number (about 6.022 × 10²³) of particles. A substance's molar mass in grams contains one mole: 58.44 g of NaCl contains one mole of formula units, and dissolves to give one mole of Na⁺ and one mole of Cl⁻. So 0.9% saline (9 g/L) contains about 154 mmol/L of each ion. Molar thinking is what lets you compare drugs, electrolytes and osmolality on the same footing — see Solutions & Concentration. On Pauling's scale fluorine is the most electronegative element (3.98), followed by oxygen (3.44), nitrogen and chlorine (both about 3.0–3.2), while sodium (0.93) and potassium (0.82) hold their valence electrons weakly. Electronegativity rises across a period and falls down a group. From electronegativity difference to bond type Large difference — ionic: Na (0.93) and Cl (3.16) differ by about 2.2. The electron is effectively transferred, giving a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Intermediate difference — polar covalent: O–H (about 1.2) and C–F (about 1.4) share electrons unequally, giving partial charges (δ+ / δ−) and a bond dipole. Small difference — essentially non-polar: C–H (about 0.35) and C–C (zero). the commonly taught cut-off of about 1.7 between ionic and covalent is a rule of thumb, not a physical boundary. Bonding is a continuum: every "ionic" bond has some covalent character and vice versa. Answer exam questions with the trend and an example rather than defending a sharp threshold. Why bond polarity is not the same as molecular polarity A molecule can contain polar bonds but have no overall dipole if they cancel by symmetry. Carbon dioxide has two polar C=O bonds pointing in opposite directions, so the molecule is non-polar overall — yet it is very water-soluble because it reacts with water to form carbonic acid. Volatile agents have asymmetric C–F, C–Cl and C–O bonds, so they carry a net dipole, which contributes to their solubility in blood and tissue. The 2011 IUPAC definition is broader than the classic school version ("H bonded to F, O or N"). Those are the strongest and most clinically relevant donors, but the definition requires only that X is more electronegative than H and that there is evidence of a bond actually forming. Water: one molecule, up to four hydrogen bonds each water molecule can donate two hydrogen bonds (through its two O–H groups) and accept two (through the oxygen lone pairs). This extensive network is why water, despite its small molecular mass (18), is liquid at body temperature, has a high specific heat capacity (about 4.18 kJ/kg/K) and a high latent heat of vaporisation. Clinically, evaporation of sweat and of water from an open abdomen or airway removes large amounts of heat — one reason for heat loss during surgery. Hydrogen bonds in drug and protein structure Protein shape: hydrogen bonds stabilise α-helices and β-sheets in receptors, ion channels and enzymes. Drug–receptor binding: most drugs bind reversibly through a combination of ionic, hydrogen-bond and van der Waals interactions. Each is individually weak, so binding depends on several fitting together — which is the basis of selectivity. Contrast with covalent binding: a few drugs form covalent bonds with their target, making the effect effectively irreversible until new protein is made — for example aspirin acetylating platelet cyclo-oxygenase, and phenoxybenzamine alkylating α-adrenoceptors. That is why their effects outlast their plasma half-lives. O'Hagan explains that although the C–F bond is highly polarised, it gains stability from the electrostatic attraction between the δ+ carbon and δ− fluorine. Fluorine is also a weak coordinator: its lone pairs are held tightly and are rarely donated. Consequences for volatile anaesthetics these are the standard structure–property links taught for the Primary FRCA, derived from the bond chemistry above rather than quoted from the source. Metabolic stability: strong C–F bonds resist oxidative metabolism. Desflurane (halogenated with fluorine only) is metabolised far less than halothane, whose weaker C–Br and C–Cl bonds are attacked by hepatic enzymes — relevant to the immune-mediated hepatitis linked to halothane's trifluoroacetylated metabolite. heavy halogenation makes modern agents non-flammable, unlike diethyl ether and cyclopropane. Low boiling point and low solubility: fluorine's tightly held electrons are poorly polarisable, so van der Waals attraction between molecules is weak. Desflurane boils at about 23 °C and has the lowest blood:gas partition coefficient of the volatiles (about 0.45), giving fast onset and offset. Environmental cost: the same stability means fluorinated agents persist in the atmosphere. Desflurane has much the highest global warming potential of the volatiles in use — a chemical property with direct consequences for agent choice. The weaker the forces holding molecules in a liquid, the more escape into the vapour phase at a given temperature, and the higher the saturated vapour pressure (SVP). A liquid boils when its SVP equals the surrounding pressure. Rising temperature increases SVP; ambient pressure does not change it. Desflurane: when SVP is close to atmospheric pressure Desflurane's SVP at 20 °C is close to one atmosphere, so in a conventional variable-bypass vaporiser small temperature changes would cause large, unpredictable changes in output. The Tec 6 therefore heats and pressurises the agent and injects vapour into the fresh gas, rather than splitting gas through a vaporising chamber. Altitude: the common exam trap A conventional variable-bypass vaporiser delivers an approximately constant partial pressure at altitude: the percentage rises as barometric pressure falls, so no dial adjustment is needed. The heated desflurane vaporiser behaves differently. So at altitude the desflurane dial setting must be increased to achieve the same partial pressure — and hence the same clinical effect — as at sea level. Because the reaction is endothermic, Kw rises with temperature. Neutrality is defined as [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so neutral pH = ½ pKw. At 25 °C Kw ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, giving neutral pH 7.0. At 37 °C standard textbook tables give Kw ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴, so neutral pH is about 6.8 — these values are textbook figures, not part of the quotation. blood at pH 7.40 and 37 °C is therefore about 0.6 units alkaline to neutral. The normal range itself is quoted below; the "distance from neutrality" idea is what alpha-stat theory tries to preserve. No. [H⁺] and [OH⁻] have risen equally, so it is still neutral; only the pH value of neutrality has fallen. What happens to a blood sample as it cools in a closed sample (no gas exchange), cooling increases CO₂ and O₂ solubility, so their partial pressures fall, and the dissociation of buffer groups — chiefly histidine imidazole on proteins — shifts so pH rises. A commonly taught rule of thumb is that blood pH rises by roughly 0.015 per °C of cooling; this is a textbook approximation, not a quoted figure. blood-gas analysers warm every sample to 37 °C before measuring. Results can be reported "at 37 °C" (uncorrected) or mathematically corrected to the patient's temperature. Neither number is wrong; they answer different questions. ABG Analyser & Gas Measurement for how the electrodes are thermostatted. Higher pH and lower PaCO₂ than the 37 °C values, because cooling raises gas solubility and lowers PaCO₂ in the closed sample. Alpha-stat versus pH-stat alpha-stat manages ventilation using the uncorrected (37 °C) values, aiming for pH 7.40 and PaCO₂ about 5.3 kPa as measured. This keeps the ionisation state ("alpha") of histidine imidazole constant, so enzyme function and cerebral autoregulation are preserved. pH-stat uses temperature-corrected values and adds CO₂ to hold the corrected pH at 7.40; the extra CO₂ dilates cerebral vessels, increasing brain blood flow and cooling uniformity. the quotation describes adult deep hypothermic circulatory arrest. In adults alpha-stat is usual; pH-stat is often preferred in paediatric cardiac surgery before circulatory arrest, where more even brain cooling is the priority. That paediatric point is standard teaching, not part of the quoted review. Clinical uses: temperature control after brain injury , cardiopulmonary bypass, and accidental hypothermia. The added CO₂ causes cerebral vasodilatation and loss of autoregulation, so more blood — and any microemboli it carries — reaches the brain. Receptors are themselves chiral (built from L-amino acids), so the two enantiomers can interact with a binding site differently. The Easson–Stedman hypothesis explains why: stereoselective activity requires at least three points of simultaneous contact between drug and receptor. Only one enantiomer's three substituents can align correctly with all three complementary receptor sites at once; its mirror image can achieve at best two of the three contacts, so it binds more weakly (or not at all). The more potent, "better-fitting" enantiomer is termed the ; the less potent (or less desirable) mirror image is the . The ratio of their potencies is the eudismic ratio — a large ratio means high stereoselectivity and a strong case for using the single eutomer clinically. Bupivacaine: the eutomer S(-)-bupivacaine ( ) is the therapeutically desired isomer, with a similar local anaesthetic potency to the racemate but less affinity for cardiac Na⁺ channels. The distomer, R(+)-bupivacaine, contributes disproportionately to (fast-in/slow-out sodium channel block, refractory ventricular arrhythmias) seen with racemic bupivacaine — the rationale for preferring levobupivacaine or ropivacaine (a pure S-enantiomer from first synthesis) in high-dose regional blocks. Ketamine: S(+)-ketamine is the eutomer, roughly 3–4× more potent as an NMDA-receptor antagonist and analgesic than R(-)-ketamine, with a more favourable emergence and recovery profile; the eudismic ratio favours using S-ketamine alone where available. Dexmedetomidine is itself a single, pharmacologically active enantiomer (the dextrorotatory, S-configured enantiomer of medetomidine — "d" describes optical rotation and "S" absolute configuration, two separate naming systems that do not always coincide) selected specifically for its high α2:α1 selectivity — a further example of enantiomer selection improving the therapeutic index rather than using a racemate. Saying enantiomers have "identical" pharmacology because they share a molecular formula — physical properties (melting point, solubility) are identical, but receptor interactions and hence pharmacodynamics/toxicity often are not. Confusing eutomer/distomer with agonist/antagonist — both enantiomers usually act at the same receptor with the same general mechanism, just different affinity. Forgetting that a racemate is not simply "half as potent"; distomer effects (e.g. bupivacaine cardiotoxicity) may be disproportionately harmful rather than merely inactive. Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon-containing compounds. Almost every drug used in anaesthesia is an organic molecule. Understanding functional groups tells you about a drug t need to memorise complex synthetic pathways. What matters is recognising the key functional groups present in anaesthetic drugs and understanding how they influence clinical behaviour.

What the Donnan effect is Plasma proteins carry a net negative charge at body pH and cannot easily cross the capillary wall. Small ions can. To keep each side electrically neutral, extra cations (mainly Na⁺) are held on the protein side and some diffusible anions (such as Cl⁻) are pushed to the other side. The result is slightly more total small-ion particles on the plasma side. Why it matters for oncotic pressure Those extra ions add osmotic pressure on top of the protein molecules themselves. So the measured colloid osmotic pressure is larger than the protein concentration alone would predict. # Oxidation, Reduction & Electrochemistry Redox reactions, electrode potentials, clinical electrodes, free radicals transfer of electrons between species. They are fundamental to energy metabolism (electron transport chain), drug metabolism (cytochrome P450), clinical measurement (Clark and Severinghaus electrodes), and pathology (free radical injury). OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain. The species that loses electrons is and acts as the reducing agent ; the species that gains electrons is oxidising agent standard electrode potential (E⁰) of a half-reaction is measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂, defined as E⁰ = 0.0 V) under standard conditions (298 K, 1 atm, 1 M concentration). A positive E⁰ indicates a strong oxidising agent (high affinity for electrons); a negative E⁰ indicates a strong reducing agent (tends to donate electrons). O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O: E⁰ = +1.23 V (standard conditions); falls to ≈ +0.82 V at pH 7 because the Nernst equation is H⁺-dependent Cytochrome c (Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺): E⁰ ≈ +0.25 V NAD⁺/NADH: E⁰ = −0.32 V (strong reducing couple) Nernst equation , E = E⁰ − (RT/nF)lnQ, describes how the actual electrode potential varies with the concentration (activity) of reactants and products (Q) around the standard value, where R is the gas constant, T absolute temperature, n the number of electrons transferred, and F the Faraday constant. This concentration-dependence is the working principle of ion-selective electrodes (pH glass electrode, Na⁺/K⁺ electrodes) and explains why electrode readings shift predictably with analyte concentration rather than being fixed. oxidised from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ . MetHb cannot bind oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve of remaining HbO₂ to the left, worsening tissue hypoxia. Common precipitants: prilocaine, benzocaine, dapsone, GTN, sulphonamides, and inhaled nitric oxide methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV (acts via NADPH–methaemoglobin reductase). Methylene blue is itself an oxidiser at high doses and is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency — use ascorbic acid or exchange transfusion instead. Clark electrode (PO₂) : amperometric. A polarising voltage (~0.6 V) is applied between a platinum cathode and a silver/silver-chloride anode in KCl electrolyte. O₂ diffuses through a polypropylene membrane and is reduced at the cathode; the resulting current is proportional to PO₂. Cathode (platinum, made negative by about −0.6 V): O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ — O₂ is reduced. Anode (silver/silver chloride): Ag + Cl⁻ → AgCl + e⁻ — silver is oxidised, supplying the electrons. Polarising voltage: at about −0.6 V the current reaches a plateau where it depends only on the rate at which O₂ arrives at the cathode, so current is proportional to PO₂ and not to small voltage changes. Membrane (polypropylene or Teflon): lets O₂ through but keeps out proteins and blood cells, which would otherwise coat the cathode and slow or distort the reading. Temperature control: the electrode is kept at 37 °C, because both membrane diffusion and gas solubility change with temperature. two-point, using an O₂-free gas or solution (zero point) and a gas of known O₂ concentration (for example 12% or 21%), because the current drifts as the membrane and electrolyte age. Severinghaus electrode (PCO₂) : CO₂ diffuses across a Teflon membrane into a thin film of sodium bicarbonate solution, forming carbonic acid and lowering the pH. The pH change is measured by a glass electrode and converted to PCO₂. Galvanic (fuel) cell : a self-contained battery-like O₂ analyser used for the constant-threshold O₂ alarm on the anaesthetic machine backbar. It generates a current proportional to pO₂ without needing any external polarising voltage — the chemical reaction itself is the power source. A lead anode gold cathode sit in a potassium hydroxide (KOH) electrolyte: at the anode, Pb + 2OH⁻ → PbO + H₂O + 2e⁻; at the cathode, O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Because the lead anode is progressively consumed, cell lifespan is finite — typically 1–2 years , and cells are rated in ampere-hours (or "oxygen-hours") of remaining life. Response is relatively slow (~ 20 s ), but there is no calibration drift over the short term, making it well suited to constant-threshold alarm duty rather than breath-by-breath analysis. polarographic (Clark) electrode requires an externally applied polarising voltage (~ 600 mV ) to drive O₂ reduction at its platinum cathode. It responds faster but is prone to calibration drift and membrane fouling, requiring more frequent recalibration than the galvanic cell. Ion-selective electrodes (ISE) : an ion-specific membrane — glass for H⁺/Na⁺, valinomycin for K⁺, or an ion-exchange resin for Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ — develops a potential difference across it that is described by the , measured against a reference electrode under zero-current ( ) conditions. ISEs measure ion , not concentration, so results are affected by protein and lipid content in the sample; measuring with an ISE on a blood gas analyser avoids the seen with indirect, diluted flame-photometric methods in samples with high protein or lipid content. Glucose sensor : amperometric. Glucose oxidase oxidises glucose to gluconolactone, generating hydrogen peroxide ; the H₂O₂ is then oxidised at a polarised platinum anode (~ +0.6 V ), producing a current proportional to glucose concentration — a Clark-type cell arrangement. Readings can be affected by interfering substances such as paracetamol, ascorbate and icodextrin superoxide (O₂⁻·), hydroxyl radical (OH·) and peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻) . Endogenous antioxidants — superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione, and dietary vitamins C and E — keep ROS in check. Oxygen toxicity : hyperoxia drives excess mitochondrial and enzymatic production of superoxide (O₂⁻·) , which is dismutated to and then, via iron-catalysed Fenton and Haber-Weiss chemistry, to the highly reactive hydroxyl radical (OH·) . When generation overwhelms endogenous defences — superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase — the result is lipid peroxidation of cell membranes and DNA damage Clinical manifestations are pulmonary and CNS. Pulmonary: tracheobronchitis with substernal chest pain and cough after roughly 12–24 hours at FiO₂ 1.0, reduced vital capacity, and absorption atelectasis ; prolonged exposure progresses to diffuse alveolar damage with an ARDS-like picture. Risk is increased by chronic alcohol use, enzyme induction, malnutrition/low baseline glutathione, and staggered overdose. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) acts as a cysteine/glutathione precursor, replenishing hepatic glutathione and allowing direct conjugation of NAPQI; it also improves microcirculatory oxygen delivery. The resulting failure of ATP generation produces rhabdomyolysis, bradyarrhythmia progressing to cardiac failure, severe lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly. Accumulation of ROS from a dysfunctional electron transport chain contributes to the picture, but the primary pathology is cellular energy failure rather than oxidative injury per se. Oxidation–reduction (redox) reactions involve the transfer of electrons between species. They are fundamental to energy metabolism (electron transport chain), drug metabolism (cytochrome P450), clinical measurement (Clark and Severinghaus electrodes), and pathology (free radical injury).

Remember OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain. The species that loses electrons is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent; the species that gains electrons is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent.
